units.la: Uo capita, Viri Generosi ac Prænobiles, potissimum (sunt enim & alia) à vobis in tabulas accepti mihi relata sunt, quæ me movent & cogunt exiguam hanc opellam Generosis ac Prænobilibus Vestris nominibus inscribere. Primum mihi cum Clarissimis meis Collegis est commune, alterum ad officium meum privatum pertinet. Gratitudo primum jubet prædicare vestrum favorem erga lyceum
units.tr: Two heads, Noble and Distinguished Gentlemen, of those you have set down for me in writing (for there are others as well), especially move me and compel me to inscribe this small work to your noble and distinguished names. The first is shared with my most distinguished colleagues; the second belongs to my private duty. Gratitude first bids me proclaim your favour towards the lyceum.
DEDICATION.

units.la: ceum nostrum, labores & curas, quas etiam nuper in visitatione istius ostendistis, ut id ad splendorem erudítionis & gloriæ magis magisque adsurgeret, & Ecclesiæ, Principi, Patriæque ac Vobis vota rependeret. Officium meum jubet vobis, quibus & cura Patriæ & Academiæ à Serenissimo, Potentissimo ac Clementissimo nostro Principe mandata est, reddere rationes otii mei ac studiorum. Utriusque specimen, sed exiguum fateor, ut exhibeat hæc Juris Ecclesiastici Historia, ( quam Præfationis loco, Antonio Augustino de emendatione Gratiani,destinaveram, paucorum primum foliorum, quæ tamen ubertate materiæ in librum excrevit,) ad Vos destinata est: ut publicè referat gratias vestris curis, laboribus, & accuratissimæ visitationi & restituti nostri lycæi, deinde quoque ut aliquam saltem rationem studiorum hoc schediasmate, quod inter typographorum operas natum est, vobis
units.tr: our lyceum, and for the labours and cares which you showed lately in the visitation of it, so that it might rise ever more and more to the splendour of learning and glory, and might render back vows to the Church, the Prince, the Fatherland and to yourselves. My duty requires that I give an account of my leisure and studies to you, to whom the care of the Fatherland and of the Academy has been entrusted by our Most Serene, Most Powerful and Most Merciful Prince. This History of Ecclesiastical Law, which I had intended as a preface to Antonius Augustinus's work on the emendation of Gratian (it has grown into a book from a few first pages because of the richness of the material), shows a sample of both, though I admit it is a small one. It is dedicated to you so that it may publicly give thanks for your cares, labours and most exact visitation and restoration of our lyceum, and also so that this little essay, born among the printers' works, may give you some account of my studies.
DEDICATION.

units.la: vobis exhiberem. Deplorandum sane est, quod Studium Antiquitatis & Juris Ecclesiastici ita desertum, inculº tum & intactum jaceat, maxime quod id negligant ij, quibus post exactum legitimæ scientiæ curriculum ab Imperatore nostro Justiniano destinatur pars aliqua reipublicæ regenda, in qua sane Ecclesia ejusque incolumitas primum studium & curas flagitat. Nolo hic in laudes juris Ecclesiastici potissimum illius veri & primigenii ire; abunde eas alii suggesserunt, & suis locis quoque,quantum brevitatis studium permisit, ex historia nostra hauriri possunt: in quam quoque, suis locis judicia Doctorum Virorum, de Corpore Canonico, seu sequiori jure Ecclesiastico, inseruimus. Nolo quoque enarrare incommoda, quæ ab iis in Eeclefiam dimanant, qui cruda sua studia & quæ jura Ecclesiastica ne à limine quidem salutarunt, ad clavum reipublicæ propellunt, quia in propatulo quotidie omnium ocu-lis,
units.tr: I was about to present it to you. It is truly to be lamented that the study of antiquity and of ecclesiastical law lies so neglected, uncultivated and untouched, especially because it is neglected by those to whom, after the completed course of legitimate learning, the Emperor Justinian assigns some part of the commonwealth to govern, in which the Church and its safety rightly demand first attention and care. I do not wish here to go into praise of ecclesiastical law, especially that true and original law; others have amply supplied such praise, and it may also be drawn from our history in its own places, so far as the aim of brevity allowed. Into that history we have also inserted, in their places, the judgments of learned men concerning the Canonical Corpus, or the later ecclesiastical law. Nor do I wish to recount the evils that flow from those who, not having even tasted their crude studies or the ecclesiastical laws at the threshold, push themselves to the helm of the commonwealth, since these evils lie open daily before the eyes of all.
DEDICATION.

units.la: lis, proh dolor! patent; dum sibi Ecclesiam, Rempublicam & omnia administrant: id volo dicere; dum secundum crudum suum & incultum judicium, non scita Dei & Canones Sanctiores, item ad suum, non Ecclesiæ & Reipublicæ commodum & gloriam Dei, eam regunt. Hæc inquam hic prætereunda, quia altioris indaginis sunt, nec paucis hisce lineis includi possunt, quibus constitutum tantum Vestris Generos. & PræNob. nominibus hoc opusculum consecrare. Accipite itaque Generosi, Prænob. ac Amplissimi Viri, exile hoc munusculum, & conatus meos, favore vestro ac humanitate, vobis qua par est observantia oblatos ac consecratos: eosque ab invidorum & zoilorum morsibus potentia vestra defendite, atque hac tutela novo beneficio me mactate; qui Deo supplex ero, ut Vos Reipublicæ natos & consecratos, diu conservet, ut curæ vestræ in Ecclesiæ, Reipublicæ & Aca-
units.tr: alas, to our sorrow, they are open to view! While they manage the Church, the commonwealth and everything else for themselves; I mean this: while they govern according to their own crude and uncultivated judgment, not according to God's decrees and the holier canons, and for their own advantage, not for the good of the Church and the commonwealth and the glory of God. I say these things must be passed over here, because they require deeper investigation and cannot be contained in the few lines that I have set aside for dedicating this little work to your names, most noble and distinguished gentlemen. Accept therefore, noble sirs, distinguished and most eminent men, this slight gift, and my efforts, offered and dedicated to you with the reverence that is due, relying on your favour and kindness. Defend them with your power against the bites of envious detractors and Zoilus, and reward me with this protection as a new kindness; I shall pray to God that he may preserve you, born and dedicated to the commonwealth, for many years, so that your care may be for the Church, the commonwealth and the Acad[emy].
DEDICATION.

units.la: SI gratam Gratianus opem, nomenq; decusq; Intulit Ausoniis per sua thura sacris; Præsul & augustum tulit Augustinus honorem, Commoda contortis substituendo locis; Quid Tua, quid tantas infra sit gloria luces; Qui lucem celebri fundis Utrique manu, MYSTA SAGAX, JURIS JUBAR, HISTORIÆQUE MEDULLA, ET CONSULTA SACRI VOXQUE MANUSQUE FORI? Te referente suas Ecclesia noscere leges Incipit & tanti prodit origo Sacri. Ortus & accedens ausis Papalibus ætas; Mox grave Juris opus; denique mole ruens; Et si quid reliquum cupiat mens avida rerum, Cuncta patent nitido condecorata stylo.
units.tr: If Gratian brought welcome help, and name and glory to the Ausonian sacred rites through his incense; and if Augustine, as a prelate, bore august honour by substituting apt readings in the twisted passages; how far beneath you is the glory of those lights? You who pour light upon both with your famous hand: wise initiate, lamp of the law, marrow of history, and voice and hand of the consulting forum! Through your telling the Church begins to know its laws, and the origin of so great a sacred thing comes forth. The age rises and advances with Papal presumptions; soon a heavy body of law; at last it collapses under its own mass. And if the eager mind desires anything else of things, all lies open, adorned in a bright style.
Now Gratian exults, now Augustine flies through the world

units.la: SERVATOR noster Jesus Christus perfecto negotio redemtionis nostrae, in coelum, Ecclesiae suae supremus Rex, abiturus, Apostolos suos, quos vivus elegerat, ad colligendam Ecclesiam Christianam per universum orbem, cum potestate docendi & scribendi misit. Hi fidei nostrae principia, modumque cultus, novo foederi congruum cum fideliter tradidissent, & sanguine doctas veritates plerique obsignantes, ad Patriam coelestem οἰκίαν illam ἀχωρη- [?]
units.tr: Our Saviour Jesus Christ, having completed the work of our redemption and about to depart into heaven, the supreme King of his Church, sent out his Apostles, whom he had chosen while alive, to gather the Christian Church throughout the whole world, giving them the power to teach and to write. When they had faithfully handed down the principles of our faith and the manner of worship fitting to the new covenant, and most of them had sealed the sound truths with their blood, they went to that heavenly home [οἰκίαν] ἀχωρη- [?]

units.la: a ἀχείγο- [?] ἀχειροποίητον, ἀιώνιον ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς, ad cu-jus spem & præmium fideles erudierant, abiissent; non diu populus Christianus in dogmatibus fidei, aut disciplina morum & ritibus ecclesiasticis (quorum magnam partem liberæ cujusque Ecclesiæ determinationi, observata tantum ordinis decentia, reliquerant Apostoli) concors fuit; sed in primordiis fere vel astutia Sathanæ, summi concordiæ & veritatis ecclesiasticæ osoris; vel humani ingenii superbia, inquietudine, mutabilitate rerumque novarum studio & pruritu, in fide, moribus & ceremoniis ecclesiasticis, à prima simplicitate & veritate, ad superstitionem, (ad quam, utpote propria figmenta indoles humana propendet,) & exitialia dogmata multi deflexerunt: neque deflexisse satis erat, aut inveniisse errores, debuerunt etiam defendi, & propagari tanquam salutaria inventa.
units.tr: ...not made with hands [ἀχειροποίητον], eternal in the heavens, the hope and reward of which they had taught the faithful. Yet the Christian people did not remain long of one mind about the doctrines of the faith, the discipline of morals and the ecclesiastical rites (most of which the Apostles had left to the free determination of each Church, provided only that good order was kept). In the very beginnings, partly through the cunning of Satan, the enemy of concord and of ecclesiastical truth, and partly through human pride, restlessness, fickleness and a craving for novelties, many turned aside in faith, morals and ceremonies from the first simplicity and truth towards superstition, to which the human disposition, being inclined to its own inventions, is naturally prone, and towards deadly doctrines. Nor was it enough to have strayed and devised errors; they went on to defend them and spread them abroad as wholesome discoveries.

units.la: Quibus hominibus & dogmatibus perditis, cum ii, quibus reipublicæ Ecclesiasticæ cura mandata erat, se opponerent, necesse aliquando fuit convocare Presbyteros, seu Episcopos (ejusdem enim officii utrumque nomen primis Christianismi primordiis fuit) Doctores, aliaque ecclesiæ membra illustriora & in rebus fidei versatiora; idque vel unius aliquando urbis seu collegii, vel diversarum, aut aliquando etiam, si negotii pondus id exigeret, latiusque exitiale dogma serperet, omnium quantum possibile erat, per totum Christianum Orbem Ecclesiarum, ut illi unanimi sententia, invocato spiritus sancti auxilio, de dogmate disquirerent, probarent vel improbarent, & quid impostorum observandum esset decernerent. In his imitati Apostolos, qui primum istiusmodi conventum Hierosolymæ instituerunt, cum quidam in re Christiana nondum satis eruditi, συμβίβαζον Judaici & Christiani cultus urgerent. Hæc initia & causæ conciliorum & synodorum fuerunt, quæ primis tribus Christianismi seculis purioribus, & à superstitione magis alienis rarissima fuerunt, quarto & quinto invalescere, & sequentibus in consuetudinem abire coeperunt. Quidquid in his à Patribus decernebatur, illud canonis nomen accepit, quod regulam & normam præscriberet credendi & vivendi; mutuo sumpto nomine à scripturis sacris iisque canonicis, ideo sic dictis, quia suprema Lex credendi & vivendi in iis tradebatur; ad quas tamen etiam translata est vox primum ab artificibus mechanicis, qui ad canonem exigebant, an quid rectum esset; adposite Æschines. ὥσπερ ἐν τῇ τεχνικῇ, ὅταν εἰδέναι βαλώμεθα τὸ ὀρθὸν θὸν καὶ τὸ μὴ, κανόνα προσφέρομεν. Ab his postea omnes cæteræ significationes sumtæ, & per metaphoram vox translata est ad leges, quibus quod rectum præscriptum; item ad scientias, in quibus regulæ, seu canones inventi& traditi, ad quos rectitudo scientiarum examinanda erat, docente id eleganter Porphyrio in Harmonicis, ex Ptolemaide Cyrenaica clarissima fœmina, de scientia canonica quæ postea Harmonica dicta est, à qua ad alias scientias hæc transferri possunt; verba Ptolemaidis hæc refert Porphyrius. H' ἓν κανονικὴ πραγματεία κατὰ τίνας μᾶλλον ἐστὶ καθόλκ; κατὰ τὰς Πυθαγορικάς. Ἠν δὲ νῦν Ἁρμονικὴ λέγομεν, ἐκεῖνοι Κανονικὴ ὠνόμαζον. Ἀπὸ τινὸς κανονικὴ αὐτὴ λέγομεν; Οὐχ' ὡς ἔνιοι νομίζουσι, ἀπὸ ξ κανόνος ὀργάνου παρωνομάσθεισαν, ἀλλ' ἀπὸ τῆς ἀξιότητος, ὡς ἀφ' ταύτης τῆς πραγματείας τὸ ὀρθὸν ἐν λόγῳ εὑρόντος. Latine sic verti possunt: Canonicum vero studium, juxta quos est generalius? Juxta Pythagoricos. Quam enim nos nunc vocamus Harmonicam, illi appellabant Canonicam. Sed cur illam Canonicam vocamus? Non ut censent quidam à Canone instrumento, sed à rectitudine. Quoniam ratio invenit id, quod rectum est, quando utitur regulis seu canonibus harmonicis. Hic canonem à קנה Kaneh, deducatur, ut Stephanus notat, quod septuaseptuaginta Interpretes κάλαμον vel καλαμίσκον reddunt, unde & Canna, videtur esse, quod antiquitus ea recti esset mensura; an rectius per Metathesin ab קנה, quod canonem seu perpendiculum notat; ut ex Beckmanni originibus, hoc cum multis aliis notat Clarissimus Vossius, aliis dispiciendum relinquimus. Neque etiam nunc evagandum in disquisitionem variarum significationum hujus vocis, abunde id Viri Doctissimi fecerunt, & maxime de lingua Græca bene meritus Henr. Stephanus in Thesauro; nobis tantum tradendæ significationes ecclesiasticæ, quæ potissimum ad institutum nostrum faciunt. Harum quinque Magnus Beza Stephano suggessit, quas præpostero ordine recensebimus, quia is maxime facit ad rem præsentem. Primo κανὼν, est ἐκκλησιαστικὴ τάξις Synod. Laod. 24. id est catalogus eorum qui ecclesiis in quocunque munere serviunt, quorum alios vocabant Clericos generali nomine, ut Apost. Can. 25. 31. 85. & 1. Constant. synod. can. 6. & horum rursus alii ἐξ ἐκλησίας vocabantur, puta Episcopi, Presbyteri & Diaconi, quos Ordines postea majores vocarunt, alios vero Clericos speciali nomine, ut animadvertere licet ex Apostolico canone 17. & Laodic. units.tr: When such men and such doctrines had gone astray, and those to whom the care of the Church's government had been entrusted opposed them, it was at times necessary to call together the elders, or bishops (for in the earliest days of Christianity both names belonged to the same office), the teachers, and the other more distinguished members of the Church who were more experienced in matters of faith. This was done sometimes of one city or one assembly, sometimes of several, and sometimes, if the weight of the matter demanded it and the deadly doctrine crept more widely, from all the Churches of the whole Christian world as far as possible; so that they, with one mind and with the help of the Holy Spirit invoked, might inquire into the doctrine, approve or reject it, and decree what was to be observed. In this they imitated the Apostles, who first instituted such an assembly at Jerusalem, when certain men, not yet sufficiently taught in Christian matters, were insisting that Jewish and Christian worship be combined [συμβίβαζον]. These were the beginnings and causes of councils and synods. They were very rare in the first three centuries of Christianity, which were purer and further from superstition; but in the fourth and fifth centuries they began to grow strong, and in the following ages they became customary. Whatever was decreed by the Fathers in these assemblies received the name canon, which prescribes a rule and norm of believing and living. This name was borrowed from the holy Scriptures and the canonical books, so called because the supreme law of believing and living is delivered in them. Yet the word was first transferred from the craftsmen, who used a canon to determine whether something was straight, as Aeschines aptly says: "As in the art, when we wish to know what is right and what is not, we apply a canon" [ὥσπερ ἐν τῇ τεχνικῇ, ὅταν εἰδέναι βαλώμεθα τὸ ὀρθὸν καὶ τὸ μὴ, κανόνα προσφέρομεν]. After this, all the other meanings were taken up from this, and by metaphor the word was carried over to laws, in which what is right is prescribed; also to the sciences, in which rules or canons are found and handed down, by which the correctness of the sciences is to be tested. Porphyry in his Harmonics reports this elegantly, citing Ptolemais of Cyrene, a most distinguished woman, on the canonical science which was later called harmonic, from which these terms can be transferred to other sciences. Porphyry gives Ptolemais's words thus: "What is the canonical study, and with what is it chiefly concerned? With the things of the Pythagoreans. That which we now call Harmonic, they called Canonic. But why do we call it Canonic? Not, as some think, from the canon as an instrument, but from rectitude, since reason finds what is right when it uses harmonic rules or canons." [Ἡ ἓν κανονικὴ πραγματεία κατὰ τίνας μᾶλλον ἐστὶ καθόλκ; κατὰ τὰς Πυθαγορικάς. Ἠν δὲ νῦν Ἁρμονικὴ λέγομεν, ἐκεῖνοι Κανονικὴ ὠνόμαζον. Ἀπὸ τινὸς κανονικὴ αὐτὴ λέγομεν; Οὐχ' ὡς ἔνιοι νομίζουσι, ἀπὸ ξ κανόνος ὀργάνου παρωνομάσθεισαν, ἀλλ' ἀπὸ τῆς ἀξιότητος, ὡς ἀφ' ταύτης τῆς πραγματείας τὸ ὀρθὸν ἐν λόγῳ εὑρόντος.] Here the author's own Latin rendering would be: "What is the canonical study, and by which standards is it more general? By the Pythagoreans's standards. What we now call Harmonic, they called Canonic..." Concerning the derivation of canon from the Hebrew [קנה] kaneh, as Stephanus notes, which the Seventy render as [κάλαμον] or [καλαμίσκον], whence also the English word cane seems to come, since in antiquity a reed was the measure of what is straight; or whether it is more correctly derived by metathesis from [קנה], which denotes a plumb line or measuring rod, as Vossius, a most distinguished man, notes along with many others from the origins in Beckmann, we leave for others to examine. Nor shall we now wander into an inquiry into the various meanings of this word; learned men have done this abundantly, and Henri Estienne, who deserved well of the Greek language, did so especially in his Thesaurus. We shall only set out the ecclesiastical meanings, which bear most upon our purpose. Magnus Beza suggested five of these to Stephanus, and we shall list them in reverse order, since that order serves our present subject best. First, [κανών] means the ecclesiastical order (Synod of Laodicea, canon 24), that is, the register of those who serve the Churches in any office. Of these some were called clerics in a general sense (as in the Apostolic Canons 25, 31, 85 and the first canon of the Synod of Constantinople), and of these again some were called [ἐξ ἐκκλησίας], namely bishops, presbyters and deacons, whom later they called the major orders; others were called clerics in a special sense, as may be seen from the Apostolic Canon 17, from Laodicea, canons 24, 27, 30, and from some others.
The various meanings of the word canon.

units.la: 6. Primæ nonnullis. Cæteros autem sic à laicis distinguebant ut non essent quidem ἐν κλήρῳ κατα-γεγραμμένοι, quoniam χειροθεσίαν non habebant, ut loquitur 2. canon Chalced. synod. qui etiam dicuntur οἱ ἐν ἐκκλησιαστικῷ τάγματι ejusdem synod. can. 6. & κατάλεγμένοι can. 10. & εἰς ἐκκλησίαν πλήντες can. 20. sed illa generali appellatione dicerentur ἐν τῷ κανόνι ἐξεταζόμενοι, ut Nicen. synod. can. 14. & οἱ τῶν κανόνων Chalced. synod. can. 2. Secundo κανῶν λειτουργίας, à quibusdam Græcis Theologis & Latinis recentioribus certa benedictionis cœnæ mysticæ formulam denotat. Tertio κανὼν est positus; pro fidelium episcoporum & præsertim Martyrum catalogo, quorum in solemnibus precibus memoria celebrabatur; cujus consuetudinis aliqua vestigia in Græcæ & Latinæ liturgiæ canone adhuc retinentur. Hunc autem olim etiam morem fuisse ex quorundam veterum Theologorum scriptis liquido constat, & ex recentioribus scriptoribus Nicephorus præsertim multis explicat lib. 14. cap. 25. & 26. ubi contentionem illam narrat de Chrysostomi nomine in Mysticas tabulas referendo, inde factum arbitror, ut canonizati dicti sint, quorum memoria publico Ecclesiæ consensu celebrabatur; unde orta tandem divorum vorum invocatio. Porro κανῶν ideo pro catalogo ponitur, quod catalogus certa norma & regula esset, iis dignoscendis, qui in illo recensebantur. Quarto κανῶν pro sacrorum librorum catalogo, ut multis locis nominat Eusebius, quorum inviolabilis est auctoritas, & ad quos velut certissimam normam exigenda sunt omnis Christianæ religionis dogmata, ut in canone Apostolico 85. hanc inscriptionem habent quædam editiones, κανῶν βιβλίων κανῶν, qui hujus vocis usus invenitur in synopsi divinæ scripturæ Athanasio attributæ, ubi & κανονικὰ βιβλία vocantur libri ea comprehensi. Tandem quinto κανῶν est regula & norma disciplinæ sive politiæ Ecclesiasticæ, ut est Apostolicis primum παράδοσι, deinde synodis legitimis descripta, unde & canones vocantur constitutiones his de rebus factæ; interdum copulantur hæc duo, διατυπώσεις & κανόνες, tum alibi, tum in Græca concilii Nicæni historia. Ab hac autem κανόνος significatione jus canonicum, quod vocant, nomen invenit. Verum harum significationum prima & tertia, sunt eædem, & est tum κανῶν idem cum diptychis ecclesiasticis, de quibus late à nobis actum est in Schediasmate de Susceptoribus Infantium ex baptismo. Ubi dyptycha ecclesiastica distinximus mus in vivorum & mortuorum, vivorum dypticha sunt κανὼν eorum qui Ecclesiis ser-viebant in quocunque munere; Mortuorum vero sunt in quæ nomina, status, ordo & obitus Episcoporum referebatur. Vid. pag. 37. & seq. Ubi & de aliis dyptychis. Secunda significatio ad quintam referenda est, quia κανὼν ille λειτουργίας nil aliud est quam de-finitio per canonem ecclesiasticum formulæ, quomodo mystica cœnæ benedictio peragi debeat; quemadmodum κανὼν in jure & legibus vocatur, quod lege est definitum & determinatum; item tributum il-lud, quod certa lege est statutum & indictum, ut videri potest apud Asconium Padianum, qui inter pensitationum genera vocat canonem, oblationem, & indictionem; & qui hunc canonem exigebant canonicari, vocantur Novella 30. & 136. item apud Cassiodor. lib. 11. & 12. var. & Centies in jure nostro canon vocatur præstatio quædam quæ legibus vel pactis est definita. Cujus tractatio non est hujus loci: Sed, quod magis affine est nostræ tractationi, κεκανονισμένοι συνόδοι leguntur, in synodi Chalcedonensis canone, qui in Codice canon. Eccles. universa est 197. istius synodi 19. quas interpretatur Justellus, canonibus constitutas synodos, Dionysius Exiguus & Cod. canonum
units.tr: The first meaning, in some writers. But they distinguished the rest from the laity in this way: they were not indeed [ἐν κλήρῳ κατα-γεγραμμένοι], enrolled in the clergy, because they did not receive the laying on of hands, as the second canon of the Council of Chalcedon says. These were also called [οἱ ἐν ἐκκλησιαστικῷ τάγματι], those in the ecclesiastical order, in the sixth canon of the same council, and [κατάλεγμένοι], those listed, in canon 10, and [εἰς ἐκκλησίαν πλήντες], those entering the Church, in canon 20. But by that general name they were called [ἐν τῷ κανόνι ἐξεταζόμενοι], those examined in the canon, as in the fourteenth canon of the Council of Nicaea, and [οἱ τῶν κανόνων], those of the canons, in the second canon of Chalcedon. Second, [κανὼν λειτουργίας], the canon of the liturgy, which some Greek theologians and more recent Latin writers use to denote a fixed formula of blessing for the mystical Supper. Third, [κανών] means a list of faithful bishops, and especially of martyrs, whose memory was celebrated in the solemn prayers; some traces of this custom are still retained in the canon of the Greek and Latin liturgy. That this custom also existed long ago is clear from the writings of some ancient theologians, and among more recent writers Nicephorus explains it at length in book 14, chapters 25 and 26, where he relates that famous dispute about entering the name of Chrysostom in the mystical tablets. I think from this it came about that those whose memory was celebrated by the common consent of the Church were called canonized; and from this at last arose the invocation of the saints. Moreover, [κανών] is used for a list because a list is a certain norm and rule for recognizing those who are enrolled in it. Fourth, [κανών] means the list of the sacred books, as Eusebius names it in many places. Their authority is inviolable, and by them, as by the most certain norm, all the doctrines of the Christian religion must be tested. In the Apostolic Canon 85 some editions bear this heading, [κανῶν βιβλίων], canon of books, and this use of the word is found in the synopsis of Scripture attributed to Athanasius, where the books included in it are also called [κανονικὰ βιβλία], canonical books. Finally, fifth, [κανών] is the rule and norm of ecclesiastical discipline or polity, as first set down by the Apostles and then by lawful synods; hence the decisions made on these matters are also called canons. Sometimes the two are joined, [διατυπώσεις] and [κανόνες], both elsewhere and in the Greek history of the Council of Nicaea. From this meaning of [κανών] the so-called canon law takes its name. But the first and third of these meanings are the same, and the canon is then the same as the ecclesiastical diptychs, about which we have treated at length in our dissertation On the Sponsors of Infants at Baptism. There we distinguished the ecclesiastical diptychs into those of the living and those of the dead: the diptychs of the living are the canon of those who served the Churches in any office; those of the dead are the lists in which the names, status, order and death of bishops were recorded. See page 37 and following, where also other diptychs are discussed. The second meaning should be referred to the fifth, because that canon of the liturgy is nothing other than the definition, by ecclesiastical canon, of the form in which the mystical blessing of the Supper ought to be performed. In the same way, in law and in the statutes, a canon is that which is defined and determined by law; likewise that tax which is fixed and imposed by a certain law, as may be seen in Asconius Pedianus, who among the kinds of payments names the canon, the offering and the indiction; and those who exacted this canon were called canonicari, as in Novels 30 and 136; also in Cassiodorus, books 11 and 12 of the Variae; and a hundred times in our law a canon is a certain payment defined by statute or agreement. Its treatment does not belong to this place. But what is more closely related to our treatment is that [κεκανονισμένοι συνόδοι], synods set in order by canons, are read in the canon of the Council of Chalcedon, which in the Code of the Church canons is number 197 and of that council number 19. Justellus interprets these as synods constituted by canons, and Dionysius Exiguus and the Code of the canons of the Roman Church as councils established by decree; this canon means provincial councils which by ecclesiastical canons were decreed and ordered to be convened twice a year. The fourth meaning, however, is primary and truly ecclesiastical, by which the sacred books, because they provide the perpetual rule of life and morals,

units.la: Eccles. Rom. statuta concilia; intelligit autem canon iste, Provincialia ista concilia, quæ canonibus ecclesiasticis sunt statuta & mandata ut bis quotannis convocentur. Quarta vero significatio est primaria & vere ecclesiastica, qua libri sacri, quia perpetuam vitæ & morum regulam præstant, canonici sunt dicti; à qua, ut supra memoratum, decreta ecclesiastica, quæ dogmata fidei vel ritus determinant, aut mores informant, canones sunt dicti, quod adinstar scripturæ vitam hominis Christiani dirigant. Non tamen pari virtute & obligatione. Major enim sine ulla comparatione scripturæ canonicæ est auctoritas, quam canonis ecclesiastici in concilio decreti; illius enim prætoria est, hujus nulla, nisi illi innitatur & cum ea consentiat. Illius infallibilis est, hujus fallibilis, quod multis canonibus vel unius concilii Tridentini firmari posset, si quis hospes in antiquitate Ecclesiastica de eo dubitaret. Non dant concilia ejusque canones nobis novas veritates in scriptura non revelatas, sed sunt tantum suffragia & sententiæ, de veritatibus antea revelatis, quas mali quidam, aut non satis docti detorserunt in pravum sensum, aut non recte intellexerunt. Hæc de dogmatibus fidei intelligimus, in quibus concilia ejusque
units.tr: The councils established by the Roman Church. But this canon means the provincial councils, which by ecclesiastical canons were appointed and ordered to be convened twice a year. The fourth meaning is the primary and truly ecclesiastical one, by which the sacred books are called canonical, because they provide the perpetual rule of life and morals. From this, as I have said above, ecclesiastical decrees that determine the doctrines of faith or rites, or shape morals, are called canons, because like Scripture they direct the life of a Christian. They do not, however, have the same force or obligation. The authority of canonical Scripture is far greater, beyond any comparison, than that of an ecclesiastical canon decreed in a council. Scripture is the court of final appeal; a canon has no such standing unless it rests on Scripture and agrees with it. Scripture is infallible; a canon is fallible. This could be confirmed by many canons, or by the Council of Trent alone, if some stranger to ecclesiastical antiquity doubted it. Councils and their canons do not give us new truths not revealed in Scripture. They are only votes and opinions about truths already revealed, which wicked or insufficiently learned men have twisted into a perverse sense, or have not rightly understood. We understand this of doctrines of faith, in which councils and their canons

units.la: §12. Unde proprie constitutiones ecclesiasticæ canones dictæ.
units.tr: §12. Whence constitutions of the Church are properly called canons.

units.la: §13. Diversa canonum efficacia. ejusque decreta, nobis non magis sunt norma fidei, quam Judicis sententia juris & justitiæ. Sed ut hæc secundum jus & justitiam ferri debet, ita illa scripturæ inniti, siquidem nos ad credendum obstringere velint. In ritibus autem Ecclesiasticis, quæ libertati Ecclesiæ Christus & Apostoli sæpe reliquerunt, magis proprie decreta concilio-rum canonem seu regulam vivendi & parendi præscribunt, quam quisque observare tenetur, dummodo generalis illa ordinis decentia, sit observata. Utraque tamen definitio conciliorum & de dogmatibus fidei, & de ritibus ecclesiasticis, non inconcinne nomine canonis toleratur, ut sint regula fidei ac morum, quatenus Scripturæ innituntur, & veritates illius comprobant, aut morale illud ordinis determinant. Placuit id nomen antiquis magis, quam illud juris nomen, aut juris ecclesiastici, aut juris canonici, quod serius, forte fastu & æmulatione Romani Pontificis introductum est; de quo postea pluribus. Exinde patet canones esse duplicis generis, quidam agunt de fidei capitibus eaque ex scriptura determinant, quidam vero tantum mores, disciplinam, ritusque ecclesiasticos respiciunt, quod & specialibus vocibus veteres videntur indicasse, eos enim canones conciliorum,
units.tr: §13. The different force of canons. Their decrees are for us no more the rule of faith than a judge's sentence is the rule of law and justice. But just as the judge's sentence must be given according to law and justice, so the decrees of councils must rest on Scripture, if they wish to bind us to belief. In ecclesiastical rites, however, which Christ and the Apostles often left to the freedom of the Church, the decrees of councils more properly prescribe a canon or rule of living and obeying, which each person is bound to observe, provided that the general decency of order is kept. Yet both definitions of councils, concerning doctrines of faith and concerning ecclesiastical rites, are not unfittingly covered by the name canon, so that they are a rule of faith and morals insofar as they rest on Scripture and prove its truths, or determine the moral order. The ancients preferred this name to the name of law, or ecclesiastical law, or canon law, which came into use later, perhaps through the pride and emulation of the Roman Pontiff; I will speak of this more fully later. From this it is clear that canons are of two kinds: some deal with the heads of faith and determine them from Scripture, while others concern only morals, discipline and ecclesiastical rites. The ancients seem to have marked this with special terms, for they called the canons of councils

units.la: 15. Differentia seu species canonum. ciliorum, quibus fidei capita determinant δόγματα, latini decreta; quibus vero mores & disciplina Ecclesiae regitur,canones appellarunt. Illustre hujus rei documentum habemus in Imperat. Noftri Justiniani Novell. 131. quae inscribitur ὡς τῶν ἐκκλησιαστικῶν κανόνων, καὶ θεσμοιμίων τ εἰς τὰς ἁγιοτάτας ἐκκλησίας: quod in rubrica vertitur, de Ecclesiasticis titulis & privilegiis: in proœmio vero, de regulis ecclesiasticis & privilegiis, melius. In hac Novella capite primo, dilertim δόγματα & κανόνες distinguuntur à se invicem, & tamen in principio omnes sub nomine canonum ecclesiasticorum continentur. Cape Verba Imperatoris Graeca. Θεοπίζομεν τοίνυν, τάξιν νόμων ἐπέχειν τὰς ἁγίας ἐκκλησιαστικὰς πανόνας, τὰς ὑπὸ τῶν ἁγίων πατέρων συνόδων ἐκτεθέντας ἢ βεβαιωθέντας, τουτέστι τῆς ἐν Νικαίᾳ τῶν πη. καὶ τῆς ἐν Κωνσταντινουπόλει τῶν ἁγίων εν. πατέρων. ἡ τὲ ἐν Εφέσῳ πρώτης, ἐν ᾗ Νεστόριος κατεκρίθη· καὶ τῆς ἐν Καλχηδόνι, καθ' ἣν Εὐτύχης μετὰ Νεστορίου ἀνεθεματίσθη· τῶν γὰρ θεοφρυμένων ἁγίων συνόδων ἡ τὰ δόγματα, καθάπερ τὰς θείας γραφάς, δεχόμεθα, ἡ τὰς κανόνας ὡς νόμως φυλάττομεν. Quae ita vulgo versa leguntur, sive à Berguntio Pisano, ut vult Anton. Augustl. sive ab alio; dubitat enim Contius in Dedicatione Novellarum ad Jacobum CamCambræum. Sancimus igitur vicem legum obtinere sanctas ecclesiasticas regulas, quæ à sanctis quatuor conciliis expositæ sunt, aut firmatæ, hoc est in Nicæna trecentorum decem & octo, & in Constantinopolitana sanctorum centum quinquaginta patrum, & in Ephesina prima, in qua Nestorius est damnatus, & in Calchedonia in qua Eutyches cum Nestorio anathematizatus est. Prædictarum enim quatuor synodorum dogmata sicut sanctas scripturas accipimus, & regulas sicut leges observamus. Manifeste Imperator ecclesiasticos canones in principio vicem legum vult obtinere, sub quibus illa de fide capita, & de moribus & ritibus regulas simul complectitur, quæ postea distinguit, illa dogmata (quam vocem interpres quoque retinuit, cum potuisset vertere decreta) has canones vocans. Apud Eusteb. quoque lib. 6. cap. 35. H. E. ubi de Concilio Romano contra Novatum agit, in quo doctrina ejus: non dandam esse pœnitentiam lapsis tempore calamitatis & persecutionis fratribus, damnatur; quod Episcopi cæterique decreverunt, δόγμα vocatur: δόγμα, inquit, πεπεισμένω τοῖς πᾶσι. quod Christophorsonus reddit à quibus omnibus tandem decernitur nimis generaliter, ita ut emphasis vocis pereat: melius, decretum ab omnibus factum est. Locum totum Eusebii paulo post adduco. Ipse etiam Lucas illa quæ in concilio Hierosolymitano Actor. 15. decreta erant δόγματα vocat, Actor. 16. v. 4. Ὡς δὲ διεπερῶντο τὰς πόλεις, παρεδίδουν αὐτοῖς Φυλάσσειν τὰ δόγματα τὰ κεκριμένα ὑπὸ τῶν Ἀποστόλων ἢ τῶν πρεσβυτέρων τῶν ἐν Ἰερουσαλήμ. ubi Beza δόγματα vertit, Placita; Piscator, Instituta; vulgatus retinet græcam vocem, quam tamen Act. 17. v. 7. vertit decreta. ut & Ephes. 2. 15. 2. Col. 2. 14. ubi Beza illud ἐν δόγμασι vertit in ritibus. Lucæ vero 2. uterque vertit δόγμα edictum, Glossa nomica à Labbæo editæ, δόγμα interpretantur θέσμισμα. Non tamen inficias imus istam differentiam inter canones & dogmata ubique forte non semper, neque tam accurate observari, quin unum pro alio positum inveniatur. Maxime posterioribus temporibus & conciliis, quibus indifferenter omnia decreta, sive dogmata fidei, sive ceremonias ecclesiasticas respiciant, canones vocarunt. Item decreta & capitula, probantibus id affatim conciliorum inscriptionibus. Primis tamen temporibus & postea diu adhuc, saltem ad tempora usque Justiniani Imperatoris Nostri, ut patet ex ejus supra addicta Novella 131. videtur distinctio decretorum seu dogmatum & canonum alicujus observationis fuisse, quamvis nec hoc affirmare ausim, perpetuum fuisse, ut non aliquando unum pro alio positum sit. Nunc ad originem canonum progrediendum. Primis Christianismi temporibus usque ad seculum tertium tantum scriptura in ecclesia audita est, nulli fere canones, quia paucissima concilia habita, velut Hierosolymitanum illud, quod actis Apostolicis insertum est; in quo actum de legibus ceremonialibus Mosaicis, & an Christianos obligarent; adserta in eo Christiana libertas, decreta facta, ut ob scandala Judaeorum in districtu Antiochiae, Syriae & Ciliciae, abstinerent ab idolothytis, sanguine, suffocato & scortatione. Seculo secundo conventus quidam in Asia, Syria, Palestina, in Occidente Romae & in Gallia habiti contra haereses Montani & Cataphrygum, & controversiam Paschalem. Dein medio fere seculo tertio & quod excurrit Romae contra Novatum, ejusque sequaces, in quo tamen canones non sunt editi, sed δόγμα istius refert Eusebius lib. 6. Hist. Eccles. cap. 35. ἐφῶ σωνόδῳ μεγίςης ἐπὶ Ῥώμης συνκροτηθείσης ἐξ ἡκοντα μὴ τ ἀριθμὸν ἐπισκώπων, πλεόνων ἢ ἐπὶ μᾶλλον πρεσβυτέρων ἡ Αλεκανδρῶν, ἰδίως πὲ τὰς λοιπὰς ἐπαρχίας τῶν ἡ χώρων ποιμένων περὶ ξ ωεγκπὶκ ἀροσπεψαμένων, δόγμα πειςατῳ &c. Ob quam rem concilium maximum
units.tr: 15. The difference or kinds of canons. By which councils determine the heads of faith, they called them dogmata (Latin decreta); but by which the morals and discipline of the Church are governed, they called them canons. We have a notable proof of this in our Emperor Justinian's Novel 131, which is headed [ὡς τῶν ἐκκλησιαστικῶν κανόνων, καὶ θεσμοιμίων τ εἰς τὰς ἁγιοτάτας ἐκκλησίας], which in the rubric is rendered On ecclesiastical titles and privileges, but in the preface, more accurately, On ecclesiastical rules and privileges. In the first chapter of this Novel, dogmata and canons are clearly distinguished from one another, and yet at the beginning all are included under the name of ecclesiastical canons. Hear the Emperor's Greek words: [Θεοπίζομεν τοίνυν, τάξιν νόμων ἐπέχειν τὰς ἁγίας ἐκκλησιαστικὰς πανόνας, τὰς ὑπὸ τῶν ἁγίων πατέρων συνόδων ἐκτεθέντας ἢ βεβαιωθέντας]. This is commonly read in Latin, whether by Berguntius of Pisa, as Antonius Augustinus holds, or by another; Contius doubts it in his dedication of the Novels to James of Cambray. The Latin runs: "We therefore decree that the holy ecclesiastical rules, which were set out or confirmed by the holy councils, hold the place of laws, namely the Nicene council of 318, the Constantinopolitan council of 150 holy fathers, the first Ephesine council, in which Nestorius was condemned, and the Chalcedonian council, in which Eutyches was anathematized along with Nestorius. For we receive the doctrines of these four synods as we receive the holy Scriptures, and we observe their rules as laws." The Emperor plainly wishes ecclesiastical canons at the beginning to hold the place of laws, and under this heading he comprehends both the heads of faith and the rules of morals and rites, which he afterwards distinguishes: calling the former dogmata (a word the translator also retained, though he could have rendered it decreta), and the latter canons. Eusebius also, in book 6, chapter 35 of his Ecclesiastical History, where he deals with the Roman council against Novatus, in which the doctrine that penance should not be granted to the brethren who had fallen in a time of calamity and persecution was condemned, calls what the bishops and others decreed a dogma: [δόγμα πεπεισμένω τοῖς πᾶσι], "a decree agreed by all." Christophorsonus renders this "finally decreed by all them," which is too general, so that the emphasis of the word is lost; better, "a decree made by all." I will quote the whole passage of Eusebius shortly after. Luke himself also calls the decisions of the Jerusalem council in Acts 15 dogmata, Acts 16:4: [Ὡς δὲ διεπερῶντο τὰς πόλεις, παρεδίδουν αὐτοῖς φυλάσσειν τὰ δόγματα τὰ κεκριμένα ὑπὸ τῶν Ἀποστόλων ἢ τῶν πρεσβυτέρων τῶν ἐν Ἰερουσαλήμ], where Beza renders dogmata as placita, Piscator as instituta, and the Vulgate retains the Greek word, though in Acts 17:7 it renders it decreta. So also Ephesians 2:15 and Colossians 2:14, where Beza renders the phrase [ἐν δόγμασι] as in ritibus. But in Luke 2 both render dogma as edictum ("edict"). The Greek glossary edited by Labbe explains dogma as [θέσμισμα]. Yet we do not deny that this distinction between canons and dogmata is perhaps not everywhere observed, nor so strictly, but that one may be found used for the other. Especially in later times and in councils, which indifferently called all decrees, whether they concern doctrines of faith or ecclesiastical ceremonies, canons. Likewise decreta and capitula, as the titles of the councils abundantly prove. In the earliest times, however, and for a long time afterwards, at least until the time of our Emperor Justinian, as is clear from the Novel 131 cited above, the distinction between decrees or dogmata and canons seems to have been observed to some degree, although I dare not affirm that it was constant, so that sometimes one was not used for the other. Now let us proceed to the origin of canons. In the first times of Christianity, down to the third century, only Scripture was heard in the Church, and there were almost no canons, because very few councils were held, such as the Jerusalem council recorded in the Acts of the Apostles, in which the Mosaic ceremonial laws were discussed, and whether they bound Christians; in it Christian liberty was asserted, and decrees were made that, because of the scandal of the Jews in the district of Antioch, Syria and Cilicia, they should abstain from things offered to idols, from blood, from what is strangled, and from fornication. In the second century there were some gatherings in Asia, Syria and Palestine, and in the West at Rome and in Gaul, held against the heresies of Montanus and the Cataphrygians, and over the Paschal controversy. Then, about the middle of the third century, there was the one at Rome against Novatus and his followers, in which, however, no canons were published, but Eusebius reports its dogma, Book 6, chapter 35 of his Ecclesiastical History: [ἐφῶ σωνόδῳ μεγίςης ἐπὶ Ῥώμης συνκροτηθείσης ἐξ ἡκοντα μὴ τ ἀριθμὸν ἐπισκώπων, πλεόνων ἢ ἐπὶ μᾶλλον πρεσβυτέρων ἡ Αλεκανδρῶν, ἰδίως πὲ τὰς λοιπὰς ἐπαρχίας τῶν ἡ χώρων ποιμένων περὶ ξ ωεγκπὶκ ἀροσπεψαμένων, δόγμα πειςατῳ] etc. For which reason the great council

units.la: 21. Concilium Romanum contra Novatum. €ximum Romæ cogitur, in quo sexaginta Episcopi & Presbyteri totidem & amplius, una cum diaconis in unum conveniunt. A Pastoribus etiam separatim per singulas cujusque regionis provincias, quid ea de re agendum esset, deliberantibus, colloquia fiunt. Ab omnibus δόγμα decretum constituitur, Novatum ejusque fautores tanta superbia inflatos & quotquot illius inhumanissimæ & à fraterna charitate alienissimæ opinioni assentirentur, in eorum numero, qui erant ab ecclesia exclusi haberi: Fratres autem qui casu infelici prolapsi fuissent, pœnitentiæ medicamentis curari, & ad sanitatem restitui. Aliæ quoque hoc seculo habitæ synodi passim in Africa, Asia, Occidente, sed nulli fere in his canones in diptycha ecclesiastica & ex his in Codicem Canonum relati. Primi canones, qui in eo exstant, scripti sunt in synodo Ancyrana provinciali, viginti quatuor; qui tantum genuini sunt; habita est hæc Ancyræ civitate Galatiæ, principio seculi quarti, ut quidam volunt sub Imp. Diocletiano, alii, sub Constantino Imperatore, & Silvestro Papa Romano, A. C. 314. inter quos est Baronius. Pontacus An. Chr. 302. habitam putat. Hanc excepit & supplevit synodus Neocæsarienses, itidem provincialis Neocæsariæ habita, ut quidam conjiciunt, (de tempore enim certi quid statui vix potest, test, neque etiam multum nostra interest ad præsentem tractationem) Sub Constantino & Miltiade Pontifice, Anno 318; Baronius in Annum 314. conjicit. Canones habet quatuordecim, qui quoque in Codicem canonum conjecti. Post has synodos quidam censent habitam synodum Laodicenam, in quâ LIX. canones scripti, qui etiam leguntur in codice canonum Ecclesiæ universæ. Hujus sententiæ est Baronius qui Laodicenam locat inter Neocæsariensem & Nicenâ ad annū 319. velut ejus epitomator eam recenset An. 314. quam tamen alii rejiciunt in Annum 364. Pontacus in Annum 368. alii 355. ut recte Doctissimus Lydius de tempore hujus concilii dixerit, Oedipum illud non facile divinare posse. Baronii rationes ante Nicenam habitam hanc synodum valde probabiles sunt. Apparent quoq; in Codice Canonum antiquissimo Ecclesiæ Catholicæ viginti canones synodi Gangrensis, cujus quoque certum tempus ignoramus, quia vero per Osium Gangris Civitate Paphlagoniæ habita fuit, ex tempore quo Osius in Oriente ab Imperatore Constantino ex Hispania evocatus, hæsit, recte conjicit Baronius Anno 319. circiter habitam esse, Pontacus rejicit in annum seculi quarti XXVIII. alii in 36tum. alii longius. Est hæc quoque provincialis ut præcedentes. Eam excipit famosissima illa Nicæna, Synodus Oecumenica 318. Episcoporum, à plerisque in annum C. 325. conjecta, in qua xx. Canones scripti, teste vel unico codice canonum Ecclesiæ universæ, quos plerique antiqui & recentiores tantum pro authenticis habent, rejectis octuaginta, quos Turrianus & Pisanus ex Arabico Latinos secerunt & orbi obtrudunt, cujus erroris causam postea sumus detecturi. Hi quia in synodo Oecumenica scripti, primo loco in codice canonum Ecclesiæ universæ, seu catholicæ comparent. Quam rationem etiam ipse codex canonum Catholicæ Ecclesiæ adducit post canones Nicænos, τῆς ἐν Ἀγχυρᾳ συνόδῳ κανόνες νέ. οἱ τινες φθεγγένεται τῶν ἐν Νικαίᾳ ἐκτεθέντων κανόνων, δὲ τερευσοι δὲ ἀρ̃ πω τῆς οἰκουμενικῆς οἰωόδε αὐθεντείαν. Concilii Ancyrani canones xxv. qui quidem priores Nicæn is, sed ideo postpositi sunt propter auctoritatem synodi Oecumenicæ. & iterum post hos canones. Concilii Neocæsariensis canones xiv. qui quidem sunt Ancyranis posteriores, Nicænis vero antiquiores. Ab hoc tempore probabile est, coeptam esse collectionem canonum, ita ut canones Nicæni primo loco ponerentur, iisque subnecterentur canones, Nicænis anteriores, jam relati Ancyrani, Neocæsarienses, Gangrenses & Laodiceni ; hoc enim ordine in codice sæpæ citato canonum Ecclesiæ Catholicæ comparent. Nisi quod Laodicenis, præmittantur Antiocheni xxv. scripti in synodo Antiochiæ habita à provincialibus Episcopis in causa Athanasii potissimum; sub Constantio & constante Imperatoribus & Julio Papa Romano anno Christi 341. Tum sequuntur in eodem Codice, septem Canones Concilii Oecumenici secundi, Constantinopolitani vero primi, quod habitum sub Theodosio Imperatore, anno Christi 381 juxta Baronum, juxta alios 383. vel 386 contra Macedonium. Hos excipiunt Ephesini concilii Oecumenici tertii, Canones octo, quæ habita est seculi quarti anno xxxi contra Nestorium sub Theodosio secundo. Claudunt tandem codicem canonum xxix. canones Concilii œcumenici quarti Calchedonensis, sub Martiano Imperatore habiti, seculo quinto medio fere contra Eutychen. Ex horum conciliorum canonibus conflatus est Codex Canonum Ecclesiæ Catholicæ, quorum tantum ideo placuit facere mentionem, quia faciunt ad institutam à nobis Historiam Juris Ecclesiastici. Sunt quidem alia concilia, synodique & in iis scripti canones, antiquiores quiores relatis ; veluti concilium Eliberinum, quod in Hispania in principio seculi quarti, anno nimirum, ut melior fert sententia, quarto vel quinto ad restituendam collapsam lapsorum disciplinam in occidente habitum. Cui rei quoque in oriente Petrus Alexandrinus Episcopus eodem tempore scripserat suos canones poenitentiales, qui & hodie perennant, & leguntur in bibliotheca Patrum tomo septimo, & apud Theod. Balsamonem in Nomocanonis fine. Habita item Arelatensia concilia, primum & secundum, sed quia horum canones in codicem ecclesiae universae non sunt relati, ideo consulto praeterimus, & inquirimus potius, quando habuerit initia sua iste codex canonum Ecclesiae universae. Valde verisimile est, ut jam dictum, initia ejus fuisse statim post concilium Nicænum, cujus quisque Episcopus exemplar ad ecclesiam suam & ibidem in dyptycha ecclesiastica retulit. Non vero solos tantum canones Nicænos, sed etiam memoratos supra, Nicænis anteriores, quia itidem ad disciplinam ecclesiasticam faciebant, & à Nicænis patribus adoptati & confirmati esse videntur; probante id non obscure Novella Imperatoris Nostri 131, in qua per βεβαιωθέντας, intelligit Imperator canones priorum concilium. liorum. Ex quibus verofimile, quod primus codex canonum habuerit tantum canones, CXXXVIII. viginti nempe Nicænos, 25. Ancyranos, XIV. Neocæsarien-ses, LIX. Laodicenos, & XX. Gangrenses. Qui postea crevit ad tempora concilii Chalchedonensis, à quo ut & Imperatoris Justiniani Novell. 131. confirmatus est, ad canones CCVII. accedentibus Antiochenis XXV. Constantinop. VII. Ephesinis VIII. & Calchedonensibus XXIX. Ordo horum conciliorum in concilio Constantinopol. in Trullo canone Φπισφεχχιζομψ est idem, qui in Codice universæ Ecclesiæ invenitur observatus. Post tempora itaque synodi Nicænæ primæ, ecclesia duplici jure cœpit regi, divino, quod in sacris literis, & canonico, quod in Codice canonum continebatur. Qui codices ambo in conciliis in medio consessus ponebantur, ut ex iis dogmata pietatis explorarentur, obortæ hæreses refutarentur, & controversiæ ad disciplinam ecclesiasticam, sacramque politiam, pertinentes, dirimerentur. De sacris propositis literis, testimonium habemus in Epistola synodica concilii Aquilejensis, tom. 1. concil. cui præfuit Ambrosius Mediolanensis Episcopus, ad Gratianum Valentinianum & Theodosium Impp. Proposita, inquit; divina ip ne in medio scriptura; item in Apologia Cyrilli ad Theodos. de synodo Ephesina Oecumenica tertia, & passim in actis concilii Calchedonensis, Constantinopolitani in Trullo, Nicaeni secundi, quorum loca Doctissimus Christophor. Justellus, optime de jure & antiquitate ecclesiastica meritus, in Praefatione ad Codicem canonum Ecclesiae universae refert. De propositio codice canonum habemus testimonia concilii Calchedonensis, quod ex eo canones citat, & de controversiis ex iis pronunciat. Sic actione IV. Aetius Archidiaconus Constantinopolis, dixit; Regula est haec cum aliis posita a sanctis Patribus, quam custodientes sanctissimi Episcopi, docent & Clericos & Monachos & omnes Christum colentes; si autem inveniant aut insultantes, aut acquiescere non volentes, hac utuntur, regula: & ex Codice relegit haec (nempe canonem v. concilii Antiocheni) si quis Presbyter aut Diaconus suum contemnens Episcopum &c. Omnes Episcopi clamaverunt, haec justa regula, haec regula patrum. Iterum actione XI. Stephanus Episcopus Ephesi dixit; supplico ut canones relegantur, qui dicunt: ut is, qui in alia civitate ordinatus est, constitui non possit in altera. Gloriosissimi judices dixerunt: relegantur hi canones: Leontius reverendissimus Episcopus Magnesiae ex Codice relegit regulam nonagesimam quintam (est iste canon 16. concilii Antiocheni, in codice vero canonum Ecclesiae universae, canon xcv.) si quis Episcopus vacans, super ecclesiam vacantem &c. Idem Reverendissimus Leontius ex eodem Codice legit regulam nonagesimam sextam. Si quis Episcopus Ordinationem acceperit Episcopatus &c. tandem Actione XIII. Gloriosissimi judices dixerunt: Canones legantur. Beronicianus Secretarius divini Consistorii ex codice legit: Episcopos oportet quidem praecipue ab omnibus Episcopis provincialibus ordinari &c. qui est canon quartus synodi Nicaenae. Exinde patent duo, primum, quod volebamus probare, etiam codicem canonum in conciliis praesto fuisse, & ex eo diremtas controversias; Item alterum, quod quaedam collectio canonum, post concilium Nicaenum facta fuerit; quod ex eodem Calchedonensi concilio etiam odoratus est; Baronius tomo 3. Ann. 341. n. 34. Illud compertum est, inquit, ex quadam antiquiori nobis incomperta collectione (quae nunc edito Codice Canonum Ecclesiae catholicae Graeco notissima est) in concilio Calchedonensi duos canones Antiochenae synodi, in actione iv. atque xi. ad verbum esse citatos, sed absque titulo Antiocheni concilii, quorum quidem in eo codice, qui in synodo probatus & lectus est, actione xi. prior nonagesimus quintus, alter nonagesimus nagesimus sextus erat numero consignatus; cum tamen iidem in concilio Antiocheno sextus decimus & septimus decimus ordine describantur. Ut plane appareat non ex ipso Antiocheni concilii codice editos esse, sed ex quadam ante jam facta collectione, communi majorum auctoritate probata. Hujus concilii Calchedonensis beneficio, modum restituendi Codicem antiquum expiscatus est Auctor anonymus, sed Doctissimus, consultationis de controversia inter Paulum Quintum Papam Romanum & Remp. Venetam, qui est Jacobus Leschassierius, ubi docte multa de hac codice commentatur. Eoque concilii Calchedonensis testimonio Noster Antonius Augustinus, lib. I. dial. XI. nostrae editionis pag. 175. probat Canones Antiochenos esse authenticos & probatos. Receptos, inquit, esse constat, & in Corpore Canonum positos ante concilium Calchedonense, ut in ejus concilii actione XII. Graecis, Latinis XI. apparet: ex libro etiam Latino, quem eodem nomine, Corpus Canonum dicimus, quem aperte Leo IV. in Epist. ad Episcopos Britanniae approbat. Vocat Augustinus librum illum Corpus Canonum, quem nos cum antiquis rectius, Codicem canonum dicimus, adstipulantibus citationibus plerisque sequentibus. βιβλίον κανόνων Graecis appellatur. Hujus etiam mentionem Justellus in doctissima sua Præfatione, fieri testatur in synod. Bracharensi prima, can. XVIII. Toletana IV. can. III. apud Nicolaum & Leonem quartum Papas Romanos, quos citat Gratianus, c. si Romanorum dist. 19. & de libellis dist. 20. Burchardus quoque memorat eum inter libros, quibus in sua collectione est usus, & Gratianus. c. hæ vero 27. q. 1. item Gregorius Pontifex Romanus in inscriptione. c. non liceat. x. de præbend. & dignitat. Tribus manuscriptis exemplaribus hujus codicis ex vaticana bibliotheca depromptis, usos se testantur in Præfatione, selecti seculo anteriore viri ad emendationem Gratiani. Putat Doctiss: Justellus editum fuisse hunc codicem primum Moguntiæ seculi anterioris anno XXV. dein Lutetiæ anno superiori (id est nono hujus seculi) quam is ea scriberet, sed is, quod & credo de Exemplaribus Manuscriptis Vaticanis, non est Codex ecclesiæ universæ, sed Ecclesiæ Romanæ, qui Moguntiæ 1525. & Parisiis 1609. est editus, attamen ex illo codice Ecclesiæ universæ depromptus, quod & confitentur ipsi Recognitores Romani, de quo postea, ubi ad collectionem Dionysii Exigui pervenero. Græce primus seculi superioris anno quadragesimo ex antiquiss. Ecclesiæ Hilarianæ Pictaviensis codex dice, hunc Canonum codicem edidit Joh. Tilius, Lutetiæ, qui post hanc editionem, quam Cardinali Turnonio dicaverat, Episcopus Meldensis est factus, sedulus in hisce antiquitatis ruderibus eruendis & publicandis; dedit quippe & Codicem Theodosianum; item auro contra caros, libros Caroli Magni, de imaginibus, quos ipse primus sub nomine Eli Phili in Gallia publicavit, seculi anterioris anno 1549. addita sua præsatione, cujus authenticum exemplar adservamus in bibliothecula nostra, contra Pontificiorum vanos conatus, hunc fœtum ποθεías incusantium & exemplaria bonæ notæ in Gallia edita, abolentium. vid. sis Amicum nostrum Virum Nobilissimum & Consultissimum Dn. Vincentium Placcjum JC. Hamburgensem, quem honoris causa Nomino, in Tractatu nuper edito, de Scriptoribus Anonymis & Pseudonymis detectis, in Caroli Magni Imperat. scriptis. pag. 174. Cœpit postea hic Codex canonum vocari Corpus canonum, observante id Ant. Augustino nostro, loco jam adducto. & c. si Romanorum. dist. 19. ubi corpus Codicis canonum appellatur, item Innocentio III. in Epistola ad Petrum Compostellanum tom. 2. concil. Emeritense, sunt verba ejus, concilium authenticum esse, multis rationibus adstruebas, tum quia cum aliis conciliis conticontinetur libro, qui CORPVS CANONVM appellatur. Vocatus etiam est Liber canonum vide infra Bedam & Gregor. Turon. Inscriptio Codicis M. S. Chr. Juftelli. Incipit liber, qui appellatur, Corpus canonum, qui tamen fuit Isidori Mercatoris, Item Patrum canones & canonicarum constitutionum liber. synod. Nicæna. II. act. II. Tharasius sanctissimus Patriarcha inquit: legatur canonicarum constitutionum liber. Quare autem in corpus vel volumen certum compactum à veteribus fuerint Canones; tradit Leschasserius, in laudata consultatione; Voluerunt, inquit, Patres, Ecclesiam habere corpus certum regularum sui juris, quas ex certis conciliis collegerint, & concilia certo ordine disposuerint, certoque & immutabili numero canones illorum complexi sint, cui neque addi neque detrahi à quoquam posset, ut hoc quasi vallo & muro septum juris corpus adversus falsi crimen undique tutum esset. Neque tantum ut falsum prævenirent solebant veteres jura sua in certa corpora colligere, sed etiam ut vim omnem juribus extra collectiones publica authoritate factas vagantibus & dispersis adimerent.
units.tr: 21. A Roman council against Novatus. A very great council is gathered at Rome, in which sixty bishops and as many presbyters again, and more, together with deacons, come together in one place. Separately, the ministers also hold consultations province by province in each region, deliberating what should be done in this matter. From all of them a decree [δόγμα] is set down, that Novatus and his followers, puffed up with such pride, and all who assented to that most inhuman opinion, which is most alien to brotherly love, should be counted among those excluded from the Church; but brothers who had fallen by unhappy accident should be cured with the remedies of repentance and restored to health. Other synods were also held in this century here and there in Africa, Asia and the West, but almost none of them issued canons; these were entered in the ecclesiastical diptychs, and from them carried over into the Code of Canons. The first canons that survive in it were written at the provincial synod of Ancyra, twenty-four in number; these alone are genuine. This was held at Ancyra, a city of Galatia, at the beginning of the fourth century, as some hold under the Emperor Diocletian, others under the Emperor Constantine and Pope Silvester of Rome, in 314, among them Baronius. Pontacus thinks it was held in 302. This was followed and supplemented by the synod of Neocaesarea, likewise a provincial synod, held at Neocaesarea, as some conjecture (for nothing certain can be fixed about the time, nor does it much concern our present treatment), under Constantine and Pope Miltiades, in 318; Baronius conjectures 314. It has fourteen canons, which were also incorporated into the Code of Canons. After these synods some think a synod was held at Laodicea, in which fifty-nine canons were written, which are also read in the Code of Canons of the universal Church. Baronius holds this view, placing Laodicea between Neocaesarea and Nicaea around 319; as his epitomiser he lists it under 314. Others, however, reject that date for 364, Pontacus for 368, others for 355, so that the most learned Lydius rightly said that this riddle could not easily be divined as to the time of this council. Baronius's arguments for holding this synod before the Nicene one are very probable. There also appear in the most ancient Code of Canons of the Catholic Church twenty canons of the synod of Gangra, whose date we likewise do not know for certain; but since it was held through Osius at Gangra, a city of Paphlagonia, from the time when Osius, summoned from Spain to the East by the Emperor Constantine, stayed there, Baronius rightly conjectures it was held around 319. Pontacus puts it in the twenty-eighth year of the fourth century, others in the thirty-sixth, others later. This too is a provincial council, like the preceding ones. It is followed by that most famous Nicene synod, the ecumenical synod of 318 bishops, dated by most to 325, in which twenty canons were written, attested by the one codex of the canons of the universal Church alone. Most ancient and recent writers hold only these to be authentic, rejecting the eighty which Turrianus and Pisanus made into a Latin version from the Arabic and foisted on the world; we shall later disclose the cause of this error. Because these were written at an ecumenical synod, they stand first in the Code of Canons of the universal or catholic Church. The Code of Canons of the Catholic Church itself gives this reason after the Nicene canons: "the canons of the synod of Ancyra, twenty-five, which are indeed earlier than the Nicene, but are placed after them on account of the authority of the ecumenical synod"; and again after these: "the canons of the synod of Neocaesarea, fourteen, which are indeed later than Ancyra but earlier than Nicaea." From this time it is probable that the collection of canons began, so that the Nicene canons were placed first and to them were attached those earlier than Nicaea, already mentioned: Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Gangra and Laodicea; for in this order they appear in the often-cited Code of Canons of the Catholic Church. Except that before the Laodicene canons are placed the twenty-five Antiochene canons, written at the synod of Antioch, held by provincial bishops chiefly in the cause of Athanasius, under the Emperors Constantius and Constans and Pope Julius of Rome, in the year of Christ 341. Then follow in the same Code seven canons of the second ecumenical council, the first of Constantinople, held under the Emperor Theodosius in the year of Christ 381 according to Baronius, and according to others 383 or 386, against Macedonius. These are followed by the eight canons of the third ecumenical council, that of Ephesus, held in the year 431 against Nestorius under Theodosius the Younger. The Code of Canons closes with the twenty-nine canons of the fourth ecumenical council, Chalcedon, held under the Emperor Marcian about the middle of the fifth century against Eutyches. It is from the canons of these councils that the Code of Canons of the Catholic Church was compiled; I have thought fit to mention them only because they bear on the history of ecclesiastical law that we have set ourselves. There are indeed other councils, synods and canons written in them, older or later than those related; for example the council of Elvira, held in Spain at the beginning of the fourth century, in the year, as the better opinion has it, 304 or 305, to restore the discipline of the lapsed in the West. To the same end, in the East at the same time, Peter, bishop of Alexandria, had written his penitential canons, which survive even today and are read in the Bibliotheca Patrum, volume seven, and in Theodore Balsamon at the end of the Nomocanon. There were also the Arelatensian councils, the first and second; but since their canons were not included in the Code of the universal Church, we deliberately pass them over, and inquire rather when this Code of Canons of the universal Church began. It is very likely, as already said, that its beginnings came immediately after the Nicene synod, from which each bishop brought a copy to his church and recorded it there in the ecclesiastical diptychs. Not only the Nicene canons, however, but also those mentioned above, earlier than Nicaea, since they likewise pertained to ecclesiastical discipline and seem to have been adopted and confirmed by the Nicene fathers. Our Emperor's Novella 131 clearly proves this, in which by "confirmed" the Emperor understands the canons of the earlier councils. From this it is probable that the first Code of Canons had only 138 canons: twenty of Nicaea, twenty-five of Ancyra, fourteen of Neocaesarea, fifty-nine of Laodicea and twenty of Gangra. It later grew, down to the time of the council of Chalcedon, by which it was confirmed, as also by the Emperor Justinian's Novella 131, to 207 canons, with the addition of the twenty-five Antiochene, seven Constantinopolitan, eight Ephesine and twenty-nine Chalcedonian. The order of these councils in the Quinisext council in Trullo, in its canon ..., is the same as is observed in the Code of the universal Church. After the time of the first Nicene synod, therefore, the Church began to be governed by a twofold law: the divine, which is contained in the sacred letters, and the canonical, which was contained in the Code of Canons. Both these codes were placed in the middle of the assembly in councils, so that doctrines of piety might be tested from them, arising heresies refuted, and controversies pertaining to ecclesiastical discipline and the sacred polity settled. As for the sacred Scriptures placed in the midst, we have testimony in the synodal letter of the council of Aquileia, in the first volume of the councils, over which Ambrose, bishop of Milan, presided, addressed to the Emperors Gratian, Valentinian and Theodosius: "The divine Scripture itself being set forth," it says; likewise in Cyril's Apology to Theodosius concerning the third ecumenical synod of Ephesus, and throughout the acts of the councils of Chalcedon, Constantinople in Trullo, and the second Nicene, whose passages the most learned Christophe Justellus, who deserved well of the law and antiquity of the Church, cites in his Preface to the Code of Canons of the universal Church. Concerning the Code of Canons being set forth we have testimony from the council of Chalcedon, which cites canons from it and pronounces on controversies by them. Thus in the fourth session, Aetius, archdeacon of Constantinople, said: "This rule has been laid down with the others by the holy Fathers; the most holy bishops, keeping it, teach both clergy and monks and all who worship Christ; but if they find some who are insolent or unwilling to submit, they use this rule"; and from the Code he read out this (namely canon 5 of the council of Antioch): "If any presbyter or deacon, despising his own bishop, etc." All the bishops cried out: "This is the just rule, this is the rule of the Fathers." Again in the eleventh session, Stephen, bishop of Ephesus, said: "I beg that the canons be read, which say that one who has been ordained in one city cannot be appointed in another." The most glorious judges said: "Let these canons be read." Leontius, the most reverend bishop of Magnesia, from the Code read out the ninety-fifth rule (this is canon 16 of the council of Antioch, but in the Code of Canons of the universal Church it is canon 95): "If any bishop, while vacant, over a vacant church, etc." The same most reverend Leontius read from the same Code the ninety-sixth rule: "If any bishop has received ordination to the episcopate, etc." Finally, in the thirteenth session, the most glorious judges said: "Let the canons be read." Beronicianus, secretary of the divine consistory, read from the Code: "A bishop must indeed be ordained chiefly by all the bishops of the province, etc." which is the fourth canon of the Nicene synod. From this two things are plain: first, what we wished to prove, that the Code of Canons too was at hand in the councils, and that controversies were settled by it; second, that some collection of canons was made after the Nicene council, which the same Council of Chalcedon also suggests. Baronius, in volume 3, year 341, n. 34: "It is established," he says, "from a certain older collection unknown to us (which is now very well known in the printed Greek Code of Canons of the Catholic Church), that in the Council of Chalcedon two canons of the Antiochene synod were cited word for word, in the fourth and eleventh sessions, but without the title of the Antiochene council; of these, in that codex which was approved and read in the synod, the former in the eleventh session was numbered ninety-fifth, the latter ninety-sixth; yet in the Antiochene council they are described in order as the sixteenth and seventeenth. So it plainly appears that they were not taken from the codex of the Antiochene council itself, but from some collection already made, approved by the common authority of our elders." By the help of this council of Chalcedon, the anonymous author, but a most learned one, of a consultation on the controversy between Pope Paul V and the Venetian Republic, who is Jacques Leschassier, traced the manner of restoring the ancient Code, and comments learnedly on much concerning this code. By this testimony of the council of Chalcedon our own Antonius Augustinus, in the first book of his Dialogues, eleventh dialogue, page 175 of our edition, proves that the Antiochene canons are authentic and approved. "It is established," he says, "that they were received and placed in the Body of Canons before the council of Chalcedon, as appears in its twelfth session in Greek and the eleventh in Latin; and also from the Latin book, which we call by the same name, the Body of Canons, which Leo IV plainly approves in his letter to the bishops of Britain." Augustinus calls that book Corpus Canonum, which we more rightly call, with the ancients, the Code of Canons, as most later citations agree. It is called in Greek βιβλίον κανόνων [book of canons]. Justellus also attests in his most learned Preface that mention of it is made in the first synod of Braga, canon 18, the fourth of Toledo, canon 3, and by the Roman popes Nicholas and Leo IV, whom Gratian cites in c. si Romanorum, dist. 19, and de libellis, dist. 20. Burchard too mentions it among the books he used in his collection, and Gratian in c. hae vero, 27, q. 1; likewise Pope Gregory in the inscription of c. non liceat, X, de praebendis et dignitatibus. The learned men selected in the earlier century for the emendation of Gratian testify in their Preface that they used three manuscript copies of this code taken from the Vatican library. Justellus thinks this codex was first published at Mainz in the year 1525 of the earlier century, and then at Paris in the year before (that is, the ninth of this century) when he wrote it; but this, as I also believe of the Vatican manuscript copies, is not the Code of the universal Church but of the Roman Church, which was published at Mainz in 1525 and at Paris in 1609; yet it was taken from that code of the universal Church, as the Roman revisers themselves confess, of whom more later, when I come to the collection of Dionysius Exiguus. The Greek codex of this Code of Canons was first published in the earlier century, in the year 1540, from a very ancient codex of the Church of Hilary of Poitiers, by John Tilius at Paris, who after this edition, which he dedicated to Cardinal Turnonius, was made bishop of Meaux, zealous in digging up and publishing these ruins of antiquity; indeed he also gave the Theodosian Code, and likewise the Libri Carolini, on images, which he first published in Gaul under the name of Elipandus, in the year 1549 of the earlier century, with his own preface added. An authentic copy of it we keep in our little library, against the vain attempts of the Papists, who accuse this offspring of ποθεία [forgery] and abolish the good-quality editions printed in Gaul. See our friend, the most noble and most learned Mr. Vincentius Placcius, J.C. of Hamburg, whom I name out of respect, in his recently published treatise on anonymous and pseudonymous writers detected, in the writings of the Emperor Charles the Great, page 174. Afterwards this Code of Canons began to be called the Corpus canonum, as our Antonius Augustinus observes in the passage already cited, and in c. si Romanorum, dist. 19, where it is called the corpus of the Code of Canons; likewise Innocent III, in his letter to Peter of Compostela, in volume 2 of the Council of Mérida: his words are, "he argued that the council was authentic on many grounds, since it is contained together with other councils in the book which is called the BODY OF CANONS." It is also called the Liber canonum; see below in Bede and Gregory of Tours. The inscription of Justellus's manuscript Code reads: "Here begins the book which is called the Body of Canons," which however was Isidore Mercator's. Likewise "the canons of the Fathers and the book of canonical constitutions," Second Nicene synod, act 2, where the most holy Patriarch Tarasius says: "Let the book of canonical constitutions be read." Why the Canons were gathered by the ancients into a certain body or volume is explained by Leschassier in the consultation already cited: "The Fathers wished," he says, "that the Church should have a fixed body of rules of its own right, which they had gathered from certain councils, and had arranged the councils in a certain order, and had embraced their canons in a certain and unchangeable number, to which nothing could be added or taken away by anyone; so that this body of law, as if fenced by a rampart and wall, would be safe on every side against the crime of forgery." Nor did the ancients gather their laws into fixed bodies only to forestall forgery, but also to take away all force from laws wandering and scattered outside the collections made by public authority.

units.la: Ob easdem causas Theodosius Imperator Novella de confirmatione corporis suarum Novellarum, ait se in corpus unius codi-cis eis constitutiones præcessorum suorum redegisse: ne aliter nisi ex ipso codice in judicio proferrentur. Eandem rationem & consilium sequutus Justinianus codicem suum fecit, constitutiones in multa volumina dispersas in unum corpus colligendo, quod ipse testatur l. unic. C. de emendatione codicis Justiniani: unde jura extravagantia posteritas appellavit quæ non in corpore codicis, sed extra corpus divagarentur, ut Justiniani verba usurpem, quibus eodem loco usus est. Ea fuit primum, antequam componeretur codex Theodosianus, providentia & vigilantia Patrum Ecclesiæ catholicæ quæ collectionem suam Corpus codicis canonum nuncupavit, quemadmodum & Imperatores Corpus codicis constitutionum suarum dixerunt. Quare etiam in more habebat Ecclesia alia jura quæ illi obtrudebantur codice suo non comprehensa, velut notha & adulterina nulliusque authoritatis rejicere, quod Gallicani Episcopi factitarunt, teste acerrimo authoritatis Romanæ defensore Nicolao I. Papa, qui in epistola quam ad illos scripsit relata in codicem Gratiani can. si Romanorum distin. 19. hæc illorum verba recenset, Quanquam, inquit, quidam vestrum scripserint haud illa decretalia priscorum pontificum in toto corpore codicis dictis canonum inveniri descripta. Neque illud negligendum canones Ecclesiasticos in diptycha Ecclesiastica & quidem speciatim ad banc rem comparata, fuisse conjectos. Fidem faciet Justiniani l. 7. C. de summ. Trinit. §. 5. Μηδεὶς τοίνων μάτλω ἡμᾶς ταφεξαί-τω ἐλπίδι ματαίᾳ κεφατεμένῳ ἐπι ἡμεῖς ἐναντίον τ εἰρημένων. ἀ. σωώδων ἐπεάξαμεν ἡ πεά-ξομεν ἡ τεφεχθῆναι πῶς πού συγχωρήσομεν ἡ φειαιρεθῶν τὸν τ αὐτῶν ἁγίων. ἀ. σωώδων ὀσίαν μνήμην ἐκ τῶν εἰρημένων τ ἐκκλησίας διπτύχων ἀνεξόμεθα. Nullus itaque frustra nos turbet spe vana invixus, quasi nos contrarium à supradictis quatuor conciliis fecerimus aut faciamus, aut fieri à quibusdam permittamus, aut aboleri eorundem sanctorum quatuor conciliorum piam memoriam ex dictis Ecclesiæ diptychis sustinemus. Quod confirmatur sexta synodo collat. 2. Nam sanctas quatuor synodos Majestas ipsius (Justinianum intelligit) sacris diptychis inseri & publicari fecit: quod ante imperium ei divinitus concessum non procedebat. Hocque forte denotat verbum ἀναπυάσεσθαι in Novell. 115. cap. 4. §. 14. pr. quod tum per peram verteretur amplecti & recitare, melius diptychis inserere vel inscribere, tumque hæc verba ejus Novellæ, ἐν ᾗ πάντες οἱ μα-καριώτατοι Πατριάρχαι τὰς ἁγίας συνόδους, τὴν ἐν Νικαίᾳ καὶ πὶ ἐν Κωνσαντι-νουπόλει
units.tr: For the same reasons the Emperor Theodosius, in his Novel on the confirmation of the body of his Novels, says that he gathered the constitutions of his predecessors into the body of a single code, so that they should not be produced in court except from that code itself. Following the same reasoning and purpose, Justinian made his code by collecting constitutions scattered through many volumes into one body, as he himself attests in l. unic. C. de emendatione codicis Justiniani: whence posterity called the laws outside the code "extravagant," that is, laws that wander outside the body of the code, to use Justinian's own words from the same passage. This practice came first, before the Theodosian code was compiled, from the foresight and vigilance of the Fathers of the catholic Church, who called their collection Corpus codicis canonum, just as the Emperors called theirs Corpus codicis constitutionum. Accordingly, the Church also had the custom of rejecting as spurious, illegitimate and of no authority those other laws that were forced upon it but were not included in its code. The Gallican bishops did this, as the fiercest defender of Roman authority, Pope Nicholas I, testifies. In his letter to them, which is quoted in Gratian's code at can. si Romanorum, dist. 19, he recounts their words: "Although," he says, "some of you have written that those decretal letters of the early popes are not found described in the whole body of the code of canons." Nor should it be overlooked that the ecclesiastical canons were also placed in the ecclesiastical diptychs, and especially prepared for this purpose. Justinian's l. 7, C. de summ. Trinit. §. 5 bears witness to this: Μηδεὶς τοίνυν μάτην ἡμᾶς ταραξαι τολμάτω ἐλπίδι ματαίᾳ κεχρημένος, ὡς ἐπὶ ἐναντίον τῶν εἰρημένων ἁγίων τεσσάρων συνόδων ἐποιήσαμεν ἢ ποιήσομεν ἢ γενέσθαι πως ποτὲ συγχωρήσομεν ἢ ἀφαιρεθῆναι τὴν τῶν αὐτῶν ἁγίων τεσσάρων συνόδων ὁσίαν μνήμην ἐκ τῶν ἐκκλησιαστικῶν διπτύχων ἀνεξόμεθα. [Let no one, relying on a vain hope, presume to trouble us, as if we had done or would do anything contrary to the four holy synods mentioned above, or as if we would permit it to happen in any way, or would tolerate the pious memory of these same four holy synods being removed from the ecclesiastical diptychs.] This is confirmed by the sixth synod, collation 2: "His Majesty (he means Justinian) caused the four holy synods to be inserted and published in the sacred diptychs, which before the empire was divinely granted to him did not take place." This perhaps is what the word ἀναπυάσεσθαι denotes in Novel 115, ch. 4, §. 14 pr., which is wrongly rendered as "to embrace and recite"; it is better rendered "to insert or inscribe in the diptychs." And the words of that Novel, ἐν ᾗ πάντες οἱ μακαριώτατοι Πατριάρχαι τὰς ἁγίας συνόδους, τὴν ἐν Νικαίᾳ καὶ τὴν ἐν Κωνσταντινουπόλει, τὴν ἐν Ἐφέσῳ πρώτην καὶ τὴν ἐν Χαλκηδόνι, ἐπιβάσεως, ἤγουν ἀναφέρειν γινώσκοντες,
