units.la: ᾱ γραπόλει, τῳ ἐν Εφέσῳ πεῶτῳ ψῇ τῳ ἐν Χαλκηδόνι, ῷεπιϐάσεως, ἤγαν ἀναφέρεν γινώσκωντες; melius sic verterentur: in qua beatissimos Patriarchas sanctas quatuor synodos Nicenam, Constantinopolitanam, Ephesinam primam & Calchedonensem in diptychis describere & publice recitare compertum est. Quod, ut & morem hunc observavit quoque Philippus Bertherius πηξων diatrib. 2. cap. 6. pag. 226. Confirmatus est Codex ille, canone primo concilii Calchedonensis, sexcentorum & triginta Episcoporum seculo quinto medio fere. Canones sanctorum Patrum per unamquamque synodum nunc usque constitutos obtinere statuimus. Postea eundem confirmavit Imperator noster Justinianus Novella 131. Ex qua merito cum clarissimo Eichelio praefatione, ad Procopii ἀνέκδοτα colligimus, Codicem hunc esse partem nostri juris Justinianaei. Meritoque istam novellam constitutionem sequeretur, utpote qui Justiniani auctoritate confirmatus, vim legis obtinet. Verba Constitutionis supra sunt relata. Maxime cum statim ex synodi sextae collatione 2. adsertum, hoc primum ab Imperatore Justiniano introductum, ut prima quatuor concilia Oecumenica in diptycha Ecclesiastica referrentur, publice recitarentur, vim legis haberent; quod quando factum sit, indicat victor Tunnunensis in Chronico. Justiniano Augusto Cos. Orientales Ecclesiae ejusdem Principis jussione quatuor synodos præsentibus sacrificiis publica voce suscipiunt recitari. Notandum porro Imperatorem mentionem facere in d. Nov. 131. canonum τῶν ἁγίων πατέρων συνῳδῶν ἐκτεθέντων, ἢ βεβαιωθέντων constitutorum, aut confirmatorum per constitutos canones intelligit canones in ipsis quatuor conciliis sancitos, per confirmatos intelligit canones priorum conciliorum ante Nicænum primum, qui in eo sequentibus sunt suscepti & confirmati; nempe synodorum Ancyranæ, Neocæsariensis, Gangrensis, Antiochenæ, Laodicensis. Quorum canones pari passu, in iisdem diptychis asservabantur, in quibus ipsi canones quatuor conciliorum. Ex hoc codice passim depromsit suas constitutiones Ecclesiasticas Imperator noster Justinianus, qui in Codice & Novellis extant, quod demonstrat passim in notis Christophorus Justellus doctissimis, quas ad hunc codicem scripsit. Post Justinianum Imperatorem Græci quædam huic codici addiderunt, quæ enumerantur in synodo sexta Oecumenica, can. II. Anno 681. celebrata. Canones nempe Apostolorum LXXXV. de quibus postea dicemus,
units.tr: (…) are better translated thus: in which it is known that the most blessed Patriarchs describe and publicly recite in the diptychs the four holy synods, the Nicene, the Constantinopolitan, the first Ephesine, and the Chalcedonian. Philippus Bertherius also observed this custom, in his πηξων, diatrib. 2, ch. 6, p. 226. That code was confirmed by the first canon of the Council of Chalcedon, of about 630 bishops, in the middle of the fifth century: "We decree that the canons of the holy Fathers, constituted by each synod up to now, shall be kept." Later our Emperor Justinian confirmed the same code in Novel 131. From this Novel, together with the preface of the most distinguished Eichel to Procopius's Anecdota, we rightly conclude that this code is part of our Justinianic law; and that Novel rightly follows that constitution, since, being confirmed by the authority of Justinian, it has the force of law. The words of the constitution have been quoted above. The more so since it is asserted immediately after collation 2 of the sixth synod that this was first introduced by the Emperor Justinian, so that the first four ecumenical councils should be entered in the ecclesiastical diptychs, publicly recited, and have the force of law. When this was done is indicated by Victor of Tunnuna in his Chronicle: "In the consulship of Justinian Augustus, the Eastern churches, by the command of that prince, receive the four synods to be recited with a public voice during the sacrifices." It must further be noted that in the said Novel 131 the Emperor mentions the canons of the holy Fathers τῶν ἁγίων πατέρων συνῳδῶν ἐκτεθέντων, ἢ βεβαιωθέντων, meaning by constituted (constitutorum) the canons enacted in the four councils themselves, and by confirmed (confirmatorum) through constituted (constitutos) canons, and confirmed (confirmatos) the canons of the earlier councils before the first Nicene, which were received and confirmed in it by the following ones: namely of the synods of Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Gangra, Antioch and Laodicea. Their canons were kept in the same diptychs, side by side with the canons of the four councils themselves. From this code our Emperor Justinian drew his ecclesiastical constitutions, which are found in the Code and the Novels, as Christophorus Justellus shows throughout his most learned notes that he wrote on this code. After Justinian, the Greeks added certain items to this code, which are enumerated in the sixth ecumenical synod, can. II, celebrated in 681: namely the eighty-five canons of the Apostles, of which we shall speak later.

units.la: 54. Quid additum post Justiniani tempora. dicemus, Sardicensis concilii canones xxi. item Africæ concilia, sanctorumque Patrum canones sive Canonicas quasdam Epistolas, Theophili, Dionysii, Petri, Athanasii, Timothei Alexandrinorum Episcoporum; Gregorii Neocæsarienses, Basilii Cæsareæ Cappadociæ, Gregorii Nysseni, Gregorii Theologi, Amphilochi, Iconii & Gennadii Patriarchæ Constantinopolitani. Quem postea sic auctum confirmat synodus Nicæna secunda anno 787; citat enim ex eo canonem LIIII. Apostolorum, & VIII. synodi Nicænæ I. Videatur ejus actio II. & Christophori Fuftelli Præfat. ad Codicem illum sæpius jam laudata, ubi recte ab hoc Codice jus canonicum quod nunc vocamus, dicit, originem duxisse; atque antiquissima illa canonum collectione, utramque cum orientis, tum occidentis Ecclesiam diu usam fuisse. Ex oriente quippe canones & eorum collectiones in Occidentem & Africam transiverunt; Ita ut orienti originem juris canonici merito tribuamus. Occidentalis Ecclesia, ante concilium Nicænum nullos canones noverat, sed sacræ scripturæ auctoritate, moribus seu jure non scripto utebatur; post Nicænum concilium, ejus canones solos recepit, usque ad tempora Innocentii Primi, qui seculo quinto ineunte seu anno secundo ad Episcopatum Romanum pervenit, quod probat ejus Epistola ad Clerum Constantinopolitanum apud Sozomenem. lib. 8. c. 26. relata his verbis: ὅτι καὶ ὠς̓ἐι τ̓ς τῶν κανόνων φυλακῆς τύποις δεῖν ἐπεσθαι γεγέψομεν, οἵτινες ἐν Νικαίᾳ εἰσὶν ὡρισμένοι, οἷς μόνοις ὀφείλει ἐξανηθλυθῆναι ἡ Καθολικὴ Ἐκκλησία, καὶ τύπως γνωρίζειν· εἰ δὲ ἐπέροι ὑπό τινων προσφέροντες εἰσὶν ἀπὸ τῶν κανόνων ἐν Νικαίᾳ ἀλλοφωνῆσαι, καὶ ὑπὸ αἱρετικῶν ἐλέγχοντες συντετυχηκέναι, ὅτι ἀπὸ τῶν καθολικῶν ἐπισκόπων ὑποβάλλοντες &c. Nos enim quantum ad canonum observantiam attinet, illis obsequendum esse scribimus, qui Nicæa determinati sunt, quibus solis obtemperare & suum suffragium addere Ecclesia Catholica debet. Si qui vero & alii quibusdam proferuntur, qui à canonibus Nicænis discrepant, & ab hæreticis compositi deprehenduntur, hi vero ab Episcopis Catholicis rejiciuntur. Hæreticorum enim commenta catholicis canonibus adsuere non licet, semper enim vel per contraria, vel per illicita, labefactare student voluntatem concilii Nicæni. Non solum igitur his non obtemperandum esse dicimus, sed ipsa potius una cum hæreticis ac schismaticis dogmatibus esse condemnanda: Quomodo & antea in Sardicensi synodo ab Episcopis prædecessoribus nostris factum est. Ita ex recitato loco Sozomenis arbitratur Petrus de Marca, lib. 3. cap. 2. de concord. sacerd. & Imperii. Vereor tamen ne sub Nicænis canonibus in hac Epistola Innocentii, etiam lateant ii, qui ante synodum Nicænam in particularibus conventibus sunt sancti, quos supra retulimus esse confirmatos & receptos à synodo Nicæna, ut & hos habuerit Ecclesia Romana, cum Nicænis primos in diptychis suis Ecclesiasticis, seu in corpore suo canonum. Quanquam eos conetur removere cap. 3. l. cit. Petr. de Marca. Quod mihi ideo probabilius videtur, quia ut supra adsertum n. 28. & 34. post Nicæna tempora cœptum est studium colligendi canones atque in Corpus seu codicem congerendi, & in prima conceptione fuerunt præter Nicænos, Synodorum provincialium anteriorum canones, probati & suscepti à patribus Nicænis, quos per βεβαιωθέντας intellexit Justinianus Novella 131; Si itaque Romana Ecclesia recepit Nicænos canones, oportet quoque eos qui in eodem corpore, seu libro cum Nicænis edebantur Ancyranos, Neocæsarienses, Gangrenses & Laodicenos receperit, quia hi omnes apud antiquos sæpe nomine Nicænorum tanquam primorum & principalium veniebant; ut patebit ex fraude Zosimi, qui studens eminentiæ Episcopi Romani, collecollegit Nicænos canones, iisdemque Sardicenses subjecit, hosque etiam sub Nicænis vendere voluit; quam collectionem quia à Nicænis orsus fuerat, ab iis quoque sequentes denominaverat omnes, de qua fraude postea. Illud hic inserendum est, quod supra post numerum Marginalem trigesimum septimum poni debuisset; Istam primam collectionem materiam sequentibus vel collectionibus vel additionibus dedisse, primamque illam Nicæni concilii & in eo adsumtorum canonum non habuisse certum autorem, nulliusque collectoris nomen; sed postea cum cresceret illa collectio, ab illis qui sequentia addiderunt, aliquando accepisse nomen. Sic cum Stephanus Episcopus quidam Ephesinus, tempore Theodosii Magni, post Concilium Constantinopolitanum primum, canonibus Nicænis, Ancyranis, Neocæsariensibus, Gangrensibus, Antiochenis & Laodicensibus, addidisset Constantinopolitani primi canones septem, suum quoque nomen praefixit, quod praetulit Codex vetus bibliothecae eheu! quondam Palatinae, quem vidit Christophorus Justellus, ut refert Petrus de Marca, Archiepiscopus Tholosanus. Ex quo male deducere mihi videtur, Henri- cus Justellus, Christophori filius, qui patris bibliothecam juris Pontificii veterem, cum Guillielmo Voello Parisiis ante quatuordecim annos edidit, in Præfatione bibliothecæ isti præmissa; Codicem Ecclesiæ universæ, coepisse demum post concilium Constantinopolitanum primum, id est post annum 381. sub Theodosio Magno, ejusque collectorem esse Stephanum illum Ephesinum Episcopum, idque ob memoratam inscriptionem codicis, quondam Palatini; cum ille Nicænis canonibus, & qui cum Nicænis ambularunt, tantum septem Constantinopolitani concilii, aut forte etiam xxv. Laodicenos provinciales addere potuerit, Nicæni vero cum quatuor conciliis anterioribus, in unum collecti corpus ante eum fuerint. Stephanum illum postea imitati sunt Episcopi sequentes, qui suo tempore, addiderunt canones concilii Ephesini & Calchedonenses. Isque fuit Codex Ecclesiæ universæ, seu Catholicæ, quo usus Orientis & quem Occidens in Latinum vertit. Quem Justellus seculi hujus anno x. vulgavit & restituit, iterumque publicavit filius anno 1661. in bibliotheca juris canonici veteris, additis canonibus Ephesinis & Calchedonensibus. Qui paulo obscuratus fuit, postquā Græci habita synodo Constantinopoli in Trullo ediderunt alium Codicem, qui fuit Codex Ecclesiæ orientalis, paulo diversus, à Codice Ecclesiæ universæ. Quæ neglecta & ignorata distinctio, impulit Cardinalem Perronium in responsi. ad Magnæ Britaniæ Regem. lib. 1. c. 53; ut imperitiæ & malæ fidei sine causa Christophorum Justellum arguerit, quod in Codicem universæ Ecclesiæ Sardicenses canones non admiserit. Cum certissimum sit, sunt verba filii patrem excusantis, in præfat. bibliothecæ juris canonici præfixa, Ut omnes eruditi norunt, Codicem Ecclesiæ universæ, non debere confundi cum eo, qui nunc orientalis Ecclesiæ Codex dicitur, qui à Joh. Tilio (ex quibus rogo, ut explices, quæ supra num. 46. de Tilii editione dicta sunt) editus est primum Lutetiæ, Anno 1540. ex M. S. Codice Ecclesiæ Pictavienfis, illius summi viri tota argumentationis strues corruat necesse est, cum falso innitatur fundamento; Et certe non erat cur in Justello genuinum infringeret ob canones Sardicenses; cum inter emunctæ naris viros compertissimum sit, Synodi Sardicensis Canones in illo primario codice non extitisse. Hujus assertionis testis idoneus est Dionysius Exiguus, qui Codicem Græcum versione nova donavit, dum in Præfatione ad Stephanum Episcopum ait, in Chalcedonensis synodi decretis finem esse Græcorum canonum, quibus se subjicere Sardicensis & Africani concilii decreta, quas ta, quæ Latine sunt edita, declarat. Ex quibus verbis colligimus synodum Sardicensem à Græcis inter Orientales synodos non fuisse relatam, quippe cujus canones non Græce sed Latine primum editi fuissent; Sed alia eaque potissima ratio extitit, cur statim ab initio illius synodi canones ab Orientalibus Ecclesiis non fuerint admissi; nimirum ob canones de appellationibus ad Romanam sedem, qui è Diametro canonibus Antiochenis adversabantur, quos Episcopi Orientales ediderant, qui appellationes extra diœcesim graviter & iniquo animo ferebant. Quemadmodum & Africani patres, qui eandem ob causam Sardicenses Canones neglexerunt, nec appellationes transmarinas lubenter admittebant, quippe qui eadem qua orientales prærogativa se tuebantur, ut ex variis Codicis Ecclesiæ Africanæ canonibus palam est. Vindicandus etiam hic est titulus, Codicis Canonum, qui dicitur esse Ecclesiæ universæ seu Catholicæ, quem perstringit Franciscus Florens in dissert. de orig. jur. Canonic. part. 2. Idque verbis ejusdem Justelli, quia nobis non licuit inspicere istam Florentis dissertationem, etiamsi longe lateque conquisitam. Rationes, inquit, quas ad adstruendum, decorari Codicem illum, titulo specioso & nimis generali ECCLESIÆ UNIVERSÆ, adsumit Fr. Florens, adeo leves sunt, ut per se facile dissolvantur. Non enim enim necesse est, ut illa collectio codicis universa Ecclesia titulo gaudeat, ut omnes conciliorum canones à singulis Ecclesiis receptos & editos complectatur; sed sufficere videtur, quod primis Ecclesiæ temporibus quibus editus fuit hic Codex, illo solo, nec alio uteretur Ecclesia universalis in disceptandis de disciplina controversiis, quemadmodum à concilio Calchedonensi factum legimus. Sed è diverticulo in viam; Certum est non diu Ecclesiam Romanam solis Nicænis, & qui cũ Nicænis ambulabant canonibus, usam fuisse. Sed eam eodem studio cũ Orientalibus collegisse canones, quibus cum iisdem hostibus, qui utramque impugnabant Ecclesiam pugnaret. Eos autem conquisivit ex Oriente, & in Latinam Linguam vertit. Fuisse enim Codicem Canonum in Ecclesia Romana, ante versionem Dionysii Exigui, apparet affatim, Primo ex fraudente illa Collectione Zosimi Pontificis Romani, qui seculi quinti anno decimo septimo, ad synodum sextam Carthaginensem 227. Episcoporum Faustum Potentiæ Episcopum, Philippum & Asellum Ecclesiæ Romanæ presbyteros misit, potissimum ut Episcopi Africæ ad Romanum appellarent. Quod ut probaret allegavit Canones synodi Nicænæ, sed ex sua Collectione quæ continebat Nicænos canones xx. Ancyranos xxv. Neocæsarienses exsarienses xiv. Sardicenses xxi; qui simul computati faciunt canones lxxxx. Hanc collectionem Zosimus nomine Canonum Nicaenorum protrusit patribus; à potiori parte nempe canonibus Nicaenis, & Nicaena synodo probatis, quibus adjunxit Sardicenses ab orientalibus ut statim adsertum & Africanis patribus repudiatos, iisque tanquam Nicaenis adstruere appellationes ad Romanam sedem voluit. Tantum etiam negotii patribus illis fecit, ut pro detegenda fraude ad Constantinopolitanum, Alexandrinum & Antiochenum Episcopos mitterent, petitum canones authenticos Nicaenos. Vide totam rem accurate narratam & examinatam, à Doctissimo Mornaeo in Mysterio Iniquitatis. mihi pag. 51. edit. Daventrienf. Inde natus error de lxxx. canonibus Nicaenis,& disputatio de numero canonum Nicaenorum. Quorum tamen constat, viginti tantum esse genuinos, quos probant, praeter Codicem canonum Ecclesiae universae, ejus versiones variae & historia Ecclesiastica verior. Vide Theodoretum itemque Socratem. Stephanum Papam cap. 13. dist. 16. quam rem disquisitioni accuratiori reservabimus, & nunc monemus istos lxxx, quos Alphonsus Pisanus & Franciscus Turrianus Jesuitae ediderunt ex Arabico translatos, esse spurios & suppositos. Acceperunt autem illos, ut fertur, ab Alexandrino Patriarcha duo Legati quos ad eum miserat Pius Quartus, ut ad concilium Tridentinum invitarent. Secundo patet versionem antiquam Codicis Canonum, usque ad Calchedonensem synodum habuisse Ecclesiam Romanam, ex justis Dionysii Exigui querelis, ad Stephanum Episcopum Salonitanum, cujus hortatu suam versionem suscepit; in qua se prisca translationis confusione offensum dicit, quod & Magnus Baronius ad Annum 527. n. 72. adserit; Dionysium ideo Græcos canones transtulisse, non quod Latina Ecclesia hactenus caruisset iisdem canonibus latinitate donatis, sed quod sive vitio interpretis, sive librariorum incuria iidem reperirentur valde mendosi. Sed quid opus est conjecturis, cum ipsam versionem antiquam habeamus ex bibliotheca Christophori Justelli, quam filius ejus in bibliotheca juris canonici veteris tomo primo pag. 277. repræsentavit. Est illa à cæteris editionibus editis latinis diversa. Edita ex Codice M. S. literis majusculis & bene quadratis, quod antiquitatem istius Codicis demonstrat. Conjicit enim Justellus septingentorum annorum fuisse. Continet canones conciliorum Ancyrani, Neocæsariensis, Ni-cæni, æni, Sardicensis, Gangrensis, Antiocheni, Laodicensis,Calchedonensis,&Constantinopolitani I. Perierant injuria temporis in isto Codice canones Laodiceni omnes, maxima pars Sardicensium, & pars postrema subscriptionum concilii Nicæni. Justellus putat hunc interpretem & collectorem non dignitatem conciliorum, sed ordinem temporis secutum fuisse, quod Ordo enumeratus conciliorum qui & sic in editione invenitur, satis probat: neque obstat, quod Calchedonensis synodus ante Constantinopolitanam ponatur, & canon xxviii. Calchedonensis, inter Constantinopolitanos, hoc enim magis descriptori quam collectori imputandum esse videtur, ut & errata quæ passim in isto libro occurrunt, & ex religiosa antiquitatis observantia, ut invenerat, à Justello sunt typis expressa, additis sphalmatis in margine. Putat Petr. de Marca in Concordia sacerdot: & imperii lib.3. pag. 414. Post synodum Calchedone habitam Canones Græcos Latinitate donatos esse, & Occidentibus communicatos, interpretatione in eam rem elaborata, cujus meminit Dionysius Exiguus; Meminit ibidem exemplaris quod extat in antiquissima bibliotheca vaticana, & alterius quem habuit Justellus, quem editum esse diximus. Ex allato supra Innocentii primi testimonio, vereor ne aliter statuendum, nempe jam ante tempora Calchedonensis synodi in Ecclesia Romana receptos canones Nicænos, & cum iis à Nicæna synodo adoptatos, itemque versos ex Græco, & post concilium Calchedonense tantum sequentium conciliorum canones additos & versos fuisse. Usa est Ecclesia Romana antiqua codicis Græci versione minus accurata, usque ad tempora Imperatoris Justiniani, quibus vixit Dionysius Exiguus Abbas Romanus, qui rogatu Stephani Episcopi Salonitani (male Sixtus Bibliothecarius. libr. 2. observante idem Cl. Justello, putat id fecisse Stephanum urbis Episcopum, cum temporibus Justiniani neque duobus seculis post ea sederit Romæ Ste-phanus) vertit ex græco Codicem Canonum. Fuit autem hic Dionysius ex Scythia oriundus, Exiguus cognominatus, instituto Monachus, dignitate Abbas. Elogium Bellarmini de eo est hoc. Dionysius Exiguus, natione Scytha, sed moribus Romanus, quemadmodum cognomento Exiguus, sed doctrina & sanctitate Maximus. Sub Theodorico Rege & successoribus claruit, & scripsit, & quidem primo Cyclum Paschalem, ab an. 525. in quo, omissa profana numeratione annorum Æræ Diocletiani Imp.
units.tr: 54. What was added after the time of Justinian. We shall discuss the twenty-one canons of the Council of Sardica, likewise the councils of Africa, and the canons or canonical letters of the holy Fathers: Theophilus, Dionysius, Peter, Athanasius and Timothy, bishops of Alexandria; Gregory of Neocaesarea; Basil of Caesarea in Cappadocia; Gregory of Nyssa; Gregory the Theologian; Amphilochius of Iconium; and Gennadius, patriarch of Constantinople. This collection, enlarged in this way, was then confirmed by the Second Council of Nicaea in 787, for it cites from it the fifty-fourth canon of the Apostles and the eighth canon of the First Council of Nicaea. See its second action, and the preface of Christophorus Justellus to that codex, cited so often already, where he rightly says that the canon law which we now call by that name took its origin from this Code, and that the Eastern and Western Churches both used that most ancient collection of canons for a long time. Indeed, canons and their collections passed from the East into the West and Africa, so that we rightly attribute the origin of canon law to the East. The Western Church, before the Council of Nicaea, knew no canons; it used Holy Scripture's authority, custom, or unwritten law. After the Council of Nicaea it received its canons alone, up to the time of Innocent I, who came to the Roman episcopate at the beginning of the fifth century, in the second year, as his letter to the clergy of Constantinople, related in Sozomen, Book 8, chapter 26, proves, in these words: "Ὅτι καὶ ὡς ἐπὶ τῆς τῶν κανόνων φυλακῆς τύποις δεῖν ἐπεσθαι γεγράψαμεν, οἵτινες ἐν Νικαίᾳ εἰσὶν ὡρισμένοι, οἷς μόνοις ὀφείλει ἐξανηθλυθῆναι ἡ Καθολικὴ Ἐκκλησία, καὶ τύπως γνωρίζειν· εἰ δὲ ἕτεροί τινες ὑπό τινων προσφέρονται, ἀπὸ τῶν κανόνων ἐν Νικαίᾳ ἀλλοφωνοῦντες, καὶ ὑπὸ αἱρετικῶν ἐλέγχονται συντετυχηκέναι, ὅτι ἀπὸ τῶν καθολικῶν ἐπισκόπων ὑποβάλλονται &c." [Ὅτι καὶ ὡς ἐπὶ τῆς τῶν κανόνων φυλακῆς τύποις δεῖν ἐπεσθαι γεγράψαμεν, οἵτινες ἐν Νικαίᾳ εἰσὶν ὡρισμένοι, οἷς μόνοις ὀφείλει ἐξανηθλυθῆναι ἡ Καθολικὴ Ἐκκλησία, καὶ τύπως γνωρίζειν· εἰ δὲ ἕτεροι ὑπό τινων προσφέροντες εἰσὶν ἀπὸ τῶν κανόνων ἐν Νικαίᾳ ἀλλοφωνῆσαι, καὶ ὑπὸ αἱρετικῶν ἐλέγχοντες συντετυχηκέναι, ὅτι ἀπὸ τῶν καθολικῶν ἐπισκόπων ὑποβάλλοντες &c.] Translated: "For we have written that, as far as the observance of the canons is concerned, we must follow those which were determined at Nicaea, to which alone the Catholic Church ought to adhere and give its assent. If others are brought forward by some which differ from the Nicene canons, and are found to be compiled by heretics, these are rejected by the Catholic bishops. For it is not lawful to attach the inventions of heretics to the Catholic canons, since they always strive to undermine by contrary or unlawful means the will of the Council of Nicaea. Therefore we say not only that these must not be obeyed, but that they should rather be condemned together with the heretical and schismatic doctrines; just as was formerly done at the Council of Sardica by our predecessor bishops." Thus Peter de Marca, in On the Concord of Priesthood and Empire, Book 3, chapter 2, takes this passage of Sozomen. I fear, however, that under the Nicene canons in this letter of Innocent there are also hidden those saints who, before the Nicene Council, were confirmed in particular assemblies, whom we mentioned above as confirmed and received by the Nicene Council, so that the Roman Church also had them, placing the Nicene canons first in its ecclesiastical diptychs, or in its own body of canons. Yet Peter de Marca tries to remove them, in the cited chapter 3. This seems to me more probable, because, as we asserted above at numbers 28 and 34, after the Nicene period the study of collecting canons and gathering them into a body or code began; and in the first conception there were, besides the Nicene canons, the canons of earlier provincial synods, approved and accepted by the Nicene Fathers, which Justinian in Novella 131 understood by the term "confirmed." If therefore the Roman Church received the Nicene canons, it must also have received those Ancyrene, Neocaesarean, Gangrene and Laodicene canons which were published in the same body or book with the Nicene ones, since all of these were often called by the name of the Nicene canons among the ancients, as the first and principal ones. This will be clear from the fraud of Zosimus, who, eager for the prestige of the Roman bishop, gathered the Nicene canons, added the Sardican canons to them, and wished to sell these as Nicene too. Since that collection began with the Nicene canons, he named all the following ones after them, as we shall say later about this fraud. It must be inserted here what ought to have been put above after marginal number thirty-seven: that this first collection gave material to the later collections or additions, and that this first collection of the Nicene Council and of the canons adopted in it had no certain author and no collector's name; but later, as that collection grew, it sometimes received a name from those who added what followed. Thus when Stephen, a certain bishop of Ephesus, in the time of Theodosius the Great, after the First Council of Constantinople had added the seven canons of the First Council of Constantinople to the Nicene, Ancyrene, Neocaesarean, Gangrene, Antiochene and Laodicene canons, he also prefixed his own name, which appeared in an old codex of the library, alas once Palatine, which Christophorus Justellus saw, as Peter de Marca, archbishop of Toulouse, reports. From this, I think, Henricus Justellus, son of Christophorus, wrongly concludes, who published with William Voellus at Paris fourteen years ago his father's old library of pontifical law, in the preface prefixed to that library, that the Code of the universal Church began only after the First Council of Constantinople, that is after the year 381, under Theodosius the Great, and that its collector was that Stephen, bishop of Ephesus, on account of the mentioned inscription of the once Palatine codex. Yet he could have added to the Nicene canons, and to those which went with the Nicene ones, only the seven of the Council of Constantinople, or perhaps even the twenty-five Laodicene provincial canons, whereas the Nicene canons together with the four earlier councils had already been gathered into one body before him. Later bishops imitated that Stephen, and in their time added the canons of the Council of Ephesus and of Chalcedon. That was the Code of the universal or Catholic Church, which the East used and which the West translated into Latin. Justellus published and restored it in the tenth year of this century, and his son published it again in 1661 in the library of old canon law, with the canons of Ephesus and Chalcedon added. It was somewhat obscured after the Greeks, having held a council at Constantinople in Trullo, published another codex, which was the code of the Eastern Church, somewhat different from the code of the universal Church. This neglected and unknown distinction led Cardinal Perron, in his Response to the King of Great Britain, Book 1, chapter 53, to accuse Christophorus Justellus without cause of ignorance and bad faith, because he did not admit the Sardican canons into the code of the universal Church. "Since it is most certain," says the son, excusing his father, in the preface prefixed to the library of canon law, "that, as all learned men know, the code of the universal Church must not be confused with that which is now called the code of the Eastern Church, which was first published by John Tilius at Paris in 1540 from a manuscript codex of the Church of Poitiers (on this matter I ask you to explain what was said above at number 46 about Tilius's edition), the whole structure of that most eminent man's argument must necessarily collapse, since it rests on a false foundation. And certainly there was no reason for him to find fault with Justellus's text on account of the Sardican canons, since it is most thoroughly known among men of keen judgment that the canons of the Council of Sardica did not exist in that primary codex." A competent witness to this assertion is Dionysius Exiguus, who gave a new Latin version of the Greek codex, when in his preface to Bishop Stephen he says that the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon are the end of the Greek canons, to which the decrees of the Councils of Sardica and of Africa were subjoined, and declares that these were published in Latin. From these words we gather that the Council of Sardica was not counted by the Greeks among the Eastern councils, since its canons were first published in Latin and not in Greek. But another and quite the chief reason existed why from the very beginning the canons of that council were not admitted by the Eastern Churches: namely, the canons on appeals to the Roman see, which were directly opposed to the Antiochene canons that the Eastern bishops had published, and which the Eastern bishops took badly and with ill will, since they opposed appeals beyond their own diocese. Just as the African Fathers, who for the same reason neglected the Sardican canons, also did not willingly admit transmarine appeals, since they defended themselves by the same prerogative as the Eastern Churches, as is plain from various canons of the African Church's code. The title "Code of Canons," which is said to be that of the universal or Catholic Church, must also be defended here, and it is attacked by Francis Florens in his dissertation On the Origin of Canon Law, part 2. I quote it in the words of Justellus himself, since I have not been able to consult that dissertation of Florens, although sought far and wide. "The reasons," he says, "which Fr. Florens adopts to establish that this code is adorned with the specious and too general title of THE UNIVERSAL CHURCH are so weak that they are easily dissolved by themselves. For it is not necessary that that collection of the code should bear the title of the universal Church, as though it embraced all the canons of the councils received and published by the individual Churches; but it seems sufficient that in the first times of the Church, when this code was published, the universal Church used it alone, and no other, in disputing about disciplinary controversies, as we read was done by the Council of Chalcedon." But to return from this digression to the road: it is certain that the Roman Church did not for long use only the Nicene canons and those which went together with the Nicene ones. Rather, with the same zeal as the Eastern Churches, it gathered canons, by which it fought against the same enemies who attacked both churches. It sought these out from the East and translated them into Latin. That there was a code of canons in the Roman Church before the version of Dionysius Exiguus is clear enough. First, from that fraudulent collection of Zosimus, Roman bishop, who in the seventeenth year of the fifth century sent Faustus, bishop of Reggio, and the Roman presbyters Philip and Asellus to the sixth Council of Carthage, attended by two hundred and twenty-seven bishops, chiefly so that the bishops of Africa might appeal to Rome. To prove this he cited the canons of the Council of Nicaea, but from his own collection, which contained twenty Nicene canons, twenty-five Ancyrene, fourteen Neocaesarean, twenty-one Sardican, and so on, which, all counted together, make ninety canons. Zosimus foisted this collection on the Fathers under the name of the Nicene canons, namely because the greater part of it consisted of Nicene canons, approved by the Nicene Council, to which he added the Sardican canons, which, as we have already said, were rejected by the Eastern and African Fathers, and he wished to establish appeals to the Roman see from them as if they were Nicene. He also caused those Fathers so much trouble that, to detect the fraud, they sent to the bishops of Constantinople, Alexandria and Antioch to ask for the authentic Nicene canons. See the whole matter accurately narrated and examined by the most learned Mornaeus in The Mystery of Iniquity, my edition, page 51, Deventer. From this arose the error about the eighty Nicene canons, and the dispute about the number of the Nicene canons. Yet it is established that only twenty of them are genuine; the Code of the universal Church's various versions and the truer ecclesiastical history prove this, besides them. See Theodoret and also Socrates; Pope Stephen, chapter 13, distinction 16. We shall reserve this matter for a more careful inquiry, and now we warn that those eighty, which Alphonsus Pisanus and Francis Turrianus, Jesuits, published, translated from Arabic, are spurious and forged. They received them, as is said, from the Alexandrian patriarch, through two legates whom Pius IV had sent to him to invite him to the Council of Trent. Second, it is clear that the Roman Church had the old version of the Code of Canons up to the Council of Chalcedon, from the just complaints of Dionysius Exiguus to Bishop Stephen of Salona, at whose urging he undertook his version; in it he says he was offended by "the confusion of the earlier translation," which Cardinal Baronius also asserts at the year 527, number 72. Dionysius therefore translated the Greek canons not "because the Latin Church had hitherto lacked these canons given Latin form," but because they were found to be very faulty, either through the fault of the translator or the carelessness of the copyists. But why need conjectures, since we have the old version itself from the library of Christophorus Justellus, which his son presented in the library of old canon law, volume 1, page 277. It differs from the other Latin editions published. It was edited from a manuscript written in capital letters, neatly squared, which shows the antiquity of that codex. Justellus conjectures that it was seven hundred years old. It contains the canons of the councils of Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Nicaea, Sardica, Gangra, Antioch, Laodicea, Chalcedon and the First Council of Constantinople. By the injury of time all the Laodicene canons, the greater part of the Sardican ones, and the last part of the subscriptions of the Council of Nicaea had perished from this codex. Justellus thinks that this translator and collector followed not the dignity of the councils but the order of time, which the enumerated order of the councils, found also in the edition, sufficiently proves. Nor does it count against this that the Council of Chalcedon is placed before the Council of Constantinople, and the twenty-eighth canon of Chalcedon among the Constantinopolitan canons, for this seems more to be imputed to the copyist than to the collector, as do the errors which occur everywhere in this book; and Justellus printed them as he had found them, from a religious observance of antiquity, with corrections added in the margin. Peter de Marca, in On the Concord of Priesthood and Empire, Book 3, page 414, thinks that "after the Council of Chalcedon had been held, the Greek canons were given Latin form and communicated to the West, by a translation worked out for that purpose, of which Dionysius Exiguus makes mention." He mentions in the same place a copy which exists in the most ancient Vatican library, and another which Justellus had, which we said was published. From the testimony of Innocent I cited above, I fear that it must be judged otherwise: namely, that the Nicene canons, and those adopted with them by the Nicene Council, were already received in the Roman Church before the time of the Council of Chalcedon, and were translated from the Greek; and that after the Council of Chalcedon only the canons of the later councils were added and translated. The ancient Roman Church used a less accurate version of the Greek codex until the time of the Emperor Justinian, in whose time Dionysius Exiguus, a Roman abbot, lived, who at the request of Bishop Stephen of Salona translated the code of canons from Greek. (Sixtus the Librarian, Book 2, is wrong, as the same Justellus observes, when he thinks that Stephen, bishop of the city, did this; for in Justinian's time, and not two centuries later, a Stephen sat at Rome.) This Dionysius was born in Scythia, was surnamed Exiguus, was a monk by profession and an abbot by rank. Bellarmine's praise of him is this: "Dionysius Exiguus, a Scythian by nation but Roman in manners, as he was small in name, so was he greatest in learning and holiness." He flourished and wrote under King Theodoric and his successors, and first wrote the Paschal cycle from the year 525, in which, omitting the profane numbering of the years of the Era of Diocletian the Emperor,

units.la: 73. Quis fuerit Dionysius Exiguus; & quæ ille Codici in sua versione addidexit. Imp. computari annos coepit à nativitate Domini Nostri; Illustre est ejus elogium apud Cassiodor. ejus fynchronum de Divin. lect. cap. 23. quod affabre virum hunc depingit; Generat etiam hodieque Catholica Ecclesia viros illustres probabilium dogmatum decore fulgentes: fuit enim nostris temporibus, & Dionysius monachus, Scytha natione, sed moribus omnino Romanus, in utraque lingua valde doctissimus, reddens actionibus suis, quam in libris Domini legerat æquitatem, qui scripturas divinas tanta curiositate discusserat, atque intellexerat, ut undecunque interrogatus fuisser, paratum haberet competens sine aliqua dilatione responsum, qui mecum Dialecticam legit, & in exemplo gloriosi magisterii plurimos annos vitam suam Domino præstante transegit. Pudet me de conforte dicere, quod in me nequeo reperire. Fuit enim in illo cum sapientia magna simplicitas, cum doctrina humilitas, cum facundia loquendi parcitas: ut in nullo se vel extremis famulis anteferret, cum dignus essET Regum sine dubitatione colloquiis. Interveniat pro nobis, qui nobiscum orare consueverat: ut cujus hic sumus oratione suffulti, ejus possimus, nunc meritis adjuvari. Qui petitus à Stephano Episcopo Solonitano, Ionitano, ex Græcis exemplaribus canones Ecclesiasticos moribus suis, ut erat planus atque disertus, magnæ eloquentiæ luce composuit, quos hodie usu celeberrimo Ecclesia Romana complectitur. Hos etiam oportet vos assidue legere, ne videamini tam salutares Ecclesiasticas regulas culpabiliter ignorare. Alia quoque multa ex Græco translulit in Latinum, quæ utilitati possunt Ecclesiæ convenire. Qui tanta Latinitatis & Græcitatis peritia fungebatur: ut quoscunque libros Græcos in manibus acciperet, Latine sine offensione transcurreret, iterumque Latinos Attico sermone legeret, ut crederes hoc esse conscriptum, quod os ejus inoffensa velocitate fundebat. Longum est de illo viro cuncta retexere, qui inter reliquas virtutes hoc habuisse probatur eximium, ut cum se totum Deo tradidisset, non aspernaretur secularium conversationib. interesse. Castus nimium, cum alienas quotidie videret uxores, mitis cum fere gentium vesano turbine pulsaretur. Fundebat lachrimas motus compunctione, cum audiret garrula verba lætitiæ: jejunabat sine exprobratione prandentium, & ideo conviviis gratanter intererat, ut inter corporales epulas inquisitus spirituales copias semper exhiberet.
units.tr: 73. Who Dionysius Exiguus was, and what he added to the Code in his version; he began to count the years from the birth of Our Lord. His distinguished eulogy is found in his contemporary Cassiodor., de Divin. lect. cap. 23, which portrays the man admirably: "The Catholic Church still produces illustrious men who shine with the grace of sound doctrines. For in our own times there lived also Dionysius the monk, a Scythian by birth but wholly Roman in character, very learned in both languages, who expressed in his conduct the equity he had read in the books of the Lord. He had examined the divine Scriptures with such care and understood them so well that, whoever questioned him, he had a competent answer ready without delay. He read Dialectic with me, and by the Lord's help he spent many years of his life as an example of a glorious teaching office. I am ashamed to speak of his character, since I cannot find it in myself. For in him great wisdom was joined with simplicity, humility with learning, and restraint with eloquence. He never set himself above even the lowest servants, though he was worthy to converse with kings without hesitation. May he intercede for us, since he used to pray with us, so that we who are supported by his prayer may now be helped by his merits. At the request of Stephen, bishop of Salona, he composed ecclesiastical canons from Greek copies. He did this in a plain and clear style, with the brilliance of great eloquence, and the Roman Church now embraces them in very widespread use. You too ought to read them diligently, lest you seem culpably ignorant of such wholesome ecclesiastical rules. He also translated many other things from Greek into Latin which may be useful to the Church. He had such skill in Latin and Greek that whatever Greek books he took up he read in Latin without stumbling, and he read Latin books in Attic speech, so that you would think what he poured out in his effortless flow had been written down beforehand." It would be long to unfold everything about that man, who among his other virtues is shown to have had this outstanding one: though he had given himself wholly to God, he did not disdain to take part in secular company. He was very chaste, though he saw other men's wives every day; gentle, though the mad whirlwind of the peoples almost beat against him. He shed tears moved by compunction when he heard cheerful, chattering words. He fasted without reproaching those who dined, and so he gladly attended feasts, so that among bodily banquets, when he was asked, he might always set out spiritual riches.

units.la: Quod si tamen aliquando comederet, parvo quidem cibo, sed tamen escis communibus utebatur. Unde summum genus æstimo patientiæ, inter humanas esse delicias, & abstinentiæ custodire mensuram. Sed, ut bona mentis ejus infucata laude referamus, erat totus Catholicus, totus paternis regulis perseveranter adjunctus, & quicquid possunt legentes per diversos quærere, in illius scientia cognoscebatur posse fulgere. Cujus nomini aliqua pravi homines calumniose nituntur ingerere, unde sua videantur errata aliquatenus excusare. Sed ille jam seculi perversitate derelicta, præstante Domino, in Ecclesiæ pace sepultus, inter Dei famulos credendus est habere consortium, dicerem adhuc fortasse reliqua de sancto viro quæ nobis totius probationis veritate comperta sunt, sed necesse est ut propositum nostrum potius exequamur, ne cum simus debitores alterius promissionis, aliud diu referre importuna loquacitate videamur. Addo aliud Bedæ, de temp. rat. cap. 45. Primi decennalis circuli cursu temporum ordo præfigit; quem Græci calculatores à Diocletiani principis annis observavere: sed Dionysius venerabilis Abbas Romanæ urbis & utriusque linguæ Græcæ videlicet & Latinæ non ignobili præditus scientia, Paschales scribens circulos, noluit eis (sicut ipse testatur) memoriam impii persecutoris innectere. innectere, sed magis elegit ab incarnatione Domini Nostri Jesu Christi tempora prænotare; quatenus exordium spei nostræ notius nobis existeret, & causa reparationis humanæ, id est, passio redemptionis nostræ evidentius eluceret. De eo Joh. Trithemius quoque & ejus operibus in lib. de scriptor. Eccles. hæc habet. Dionysius, Abbas Romanus, cognomento Exiguus, Vir ingenio & scientia Magnus atque Clarissimus, in scripturis sanctis eruditus, & in disciplina secularium literarum nobiliter doctus, Græco & Latino Eloquio Clarus, computista & calculator temporum egregius, scripsit latino sermone nonnulla opuscula. De quibus Ego tantum reperi subjecta. Annorum DXXXII. Cyclum Paschalem Magnum. Transtulit de Græco in Latinum vitam sancti Pacomii Abbatis, librum quoque Gregorii Emisseni de conditione hominis & scripta Proterii Alexandrini Episcopi ad Leonem Papam, & quædam alia. Inchoavit autem Cyclum suum anno Domini DXXXI. claruit sub Justiniano Magno anno DXL. Hæc ex supra relatis sunt emendanda. Romæ ejus summam æ-stimationem fuisse, adserit Baron. ad ann. 533. n. 30. sin. Scripta ejus in Bibliotheca sua fuisse, testatur, Cassiodorus in divin. instit. cap. 23. Quid autem Dionysius hic præsti-terit cerit in versione canonum, id ex ejus Epi-stola ad Stephanum Episcopum Salonita-num patebit, quam ex collectione canonum Cresconii subjicimus. Habet eam quoque Baronius in annal. ad Annum 527. n. 73. Et edita est cum Indice canonum collectionis ipsius ex manuscripto Viri eruditissimi N. Fabri, tandemque inserta bibliothecæ Juris Pontificii Henrici Justelli.
units.tr: If, however, he at some time did eat, it was indeed a small amount of food, yet he used ordinary foods. Hence I count it the highest kind of patience to live amid human pleasures and yet keep the measure of abstinence. But, to speak of his good mind without undeserved praise, he was wholly Catholic, wholly and steadfastly bound to the rules of the Fathers, and whatever readers seek through various authors could be seen to shine in his learning. Some wicked men maliciously strive to fasten his name upon their errors, so that they may seem to excuse their own mistakes to some extent. But he, having now abandoned the perversity of the age, has by the Lord's gift been buried in the peace of the Church, and is to be believed to share fellowship among the servants of God. I might perhaps still say the remaining things about this holy man, which have been ascertained with full truth of proof, but it is necessary that we rather pursue our purpose, lest, since we are debtors of another promise, we seem to be spending a long time reporting another matter with tiresome chatter. I add another item from Bede, On the Reckoning of Time, ch. 45. In the course of the first ten-year cycle the order of the years is laid out, which the Greek calculators observed from the years of the emperor Diocletian: but Dionysius the venerable Abbot of the city of Rome, endowed with no ignoble learning in both Greek and Latin, when writing the Paschal cycles, was unwilling (as he himself testifies) to attach to them the memory of the impious persecutor. to attach, but rather chose to note the times from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that the beginning of our hope might be better known to us, and the cause of human restoration, that is, the passion of our redemption, might shine more clearly. Concerning him, John Trithemius also, in his book on ecclesiastical writers, has the following: Dionysius, Abbot of Rome, surnamed Exiguus, a man great and most distinguished in talent and learning, learned in the holy Scriptures and nobly taught in the discipline of secular letters, famous in Greek and Latin eloquence, an outstanding computist and calculator of times, wrote some small works in Latin. Of these I have found only the following listed: the Great Paschal Cycle of 532 years. He translated from Greek into Latin the life of the holy Abbot Pachomius, also the book of Gregory of Nyssa on the condition of man, and the writings of Proterius, Bishop of Alexandria, to Pope Leo, and certain other things. He began his cycle in the year of the Lord 531, and flourished under the Emperor Justinian the Great in the year 540. These things must be corrected from what has been related above. That his reputation at Rome was very high, Baronius asserts, Annals at the year 533, n. 30, near the end. That his writings were in his library, Cassiodorus testifies in Divine Institutions, ch. 23. What Dionysius accomplished in the translation of the canons will appear from his letter to Stephen, Bishop of Salona, which we subjoin from the collection of canons of Cresconius. Baronius also has it in the Annals at the year 527, n. 73. It was published together with the index of the canons of that collection from the manuscript of the most learned man N. Faber, and was finally inserted into the library of Pontifical Law of Henry Justel.

units.la: Domino venerabili mihi, patri Stephano Episcopo Dionysius Exiguus in Do-mino salutem.
units.tr: To my venerable lord, Father Stephen, Bishop: Dionysius Exiguus sends greetings in the Lord.

units.la: Quamvis charissimus frater noster Laurentius assidua & familiari cohortatione parvitatem nostram regulas Ecclesiasticas de Græco transferre impuleris, confusione credo priscæ translationis of-sensus: nihilominus tamen ingestum tuæ beatitudinis consideratione suscepi, cui Christus omnipotens Deus, solita populo pietate prospiciens, summi sacerdotis contulit dignitatem; ut inter plurima virtutis ornamenta, quibus Ecclesiam Domini mo-rum sanctitate condecoras, etiam sacratissima ju-ra Pontificalibus per Dei gratiam digestis conven-tibus intemerata conservans, perfecto regimine cle-rum plebemque moderareris; nullatenus nostri seculi more contentus, quo pronius desidetamus re-cta nosse quam facere: sed divino junctus auxi-lio, quæ fieri præcipis, ante perficias, ut efficacissimo Fidelibus prosis exemplo. Magna est siquidem dem jubentis auctoritas, eadem primitus jusse complentis: quatenus inconvulsa Ecclesiastici ordinis disciplina inviolabilis permanens, ad capessendum perenne præmium Christianis omnibus præstat accessum: per quem & sancti Præsules paternis muniantur regulis & obedientes populi spiritualibus imbuantur exemplis.
units.tr: Although our very dear brother Laurentius, by his constant and familiar urging, has compelled our humble self to translate the ecclesiastical rules from the Greek, I believe that you were offended by the confusion of the earlier translation. Nevertheless, I have taken up the task laid upon me in consideration of your blessedness, to whom Christ almighty God, looking upon his people with his customary piety, has granted the dignity of the high priest. So that, among the many ornaments of virtue with which you adorn the Church of the Lord by the holiness of your conduct, you may also keep the most sacred laws, arranged by the grace of God in pontifical assemblies, inviolate, and by perfect governance guide the clergy and the people. Being by no means content with the custom of our age, by which we are readier to know what is right than to do it, but joined with divine help, I may first accomplish what you command, so that by the most effective example I may benefit the faithful. For great indeed is the authority of the one who commands, when it is the same who first carries out what he has ordered; so that the undisturbed discipline of the ecclesiastical order, remaining inviolable, may give all Christians access to the everlasting reward; through which both holy prelates are fortified by paternal rules and obedient peoples are imbued with spiritual examples.

units.la: In principio itaque canones, qüi dicuntur Apostolorum, de Græco transtulimus: quibus quia plurimi consensum non præbuere facilem, hoc ipsum ignorare vestram noluimus sanctitatem: quamvis postea quædam constituta Pontificum ex ipsis canonibus assumpta esse videantur. Deinde regulas Nicænæ Synodi, & deinceps omnium Conciliorum, sive quæ ante eam, sive quæ postmodum facta sunt usq; ad Synodum centum quinquaginta Pontificum, qui apud Constantinopolim convenerunt, sub ordine numerorum, id est, à primo capitulo usque ad centesimum sexagesimum quintum, sicut habetur in Græca auctoritate, digessimus. Tum sancti Chalcedonensis Concilii decreta subdentes, in his Græcorum canonum finem esse declaramus.
units.tr: In the beginning, therefore, we have translated from the Greek the canons which are called those of the Apostles; since many have not readily given their assent to these, we did not wish your holiness to be ignorant of this, although certain decrees of the Pontiffs seem afterwards to have been drawn from these same canons. Next, we have arranged the rules of the Nicene Synod, and then those of all the Councils, whether those held before it or those held afterwards, down to the Synod of the one hundred and fifty Bishops who assembled at Constantinople, under the order of numbers, that is, from the first chapter to the one hundred and sixty-fifth, just as they are found in the Greek authority. Then, adding the decrees of the holy Council of Chalcedon, we declare that this is the end of the Greek canons.

units.la: Ne quid præterea notitiæ vestræ videamur velle subtrahere, statuta quoque Sardicensis Concilii, atque Africani, quæ Latine sunt edita, suis à nobis numeris cernuntur esse distincta. Universarum vero definitionum titulos post hanc præfationem strictius ordinantes, ea quæ in singulis passim passim sunt promulgata Conciliis, sub uno aspectu locavimus, ut ad inquisitionum cujusque rei compendium aliquod attulisse videmur.
units.tr: Lest we seem to wish to withhold anything further from your knowledge, the statutes of the Council of Sardica and of the African Council, which have been published in Latin, are marked off by us with their own numbers. Moreover, having arranged the titles of all the decrees more concisely after this preface, we have placed under a single view those things which have been promulgated scattered through individual Councils, so that we seem to have provided a kind of summary for the inquiry into any matter whatever.

units.la: Ex qua patet Dionysium Exiguum suæ interpretationi, in qua Græcos canones continua, nec interrupta serie numerorum computavit ad modum codicis Græci, addidisse Canones qui vocantur Apostolorum, Sardicense concilium, item Africana quædam concilia. Cujus codex in eo diversus est à Codice Romano, qui Moguntiæ & Parisiis est editus, ut supra notatum, quod hic non numeret canones una serie, seu non interrupto ordine; sed cuique concilio suos adsignet, atque novo incipiente concilio, novos quoque incipiat numeros; decurrit autem Dionysii Codex usque ad numerum CLXV. qui est tertius canon concilii Constantinopolitani primi, cujus septem inveniuntur in Codice Ecclesiæ Universæ Græco, tres vero etiam tantum in Codice Canonum Romano. Postea apud Dionysium nova numeratione sequuntur XXVI. canones concilii Calchedonensis, & nova item numeratione canones synodi Sardicensis, qui tantum Latine editi sunt. Tandem claudunt agmen ex variis Africanis conciliis, itidem nova numeratione ejus Canonicam collectionem CXXXVIII. canones Africani. Adeo ut Dionysianus hic codex partim ex Græcorum partim ex Occidentalium synodis collectus & compilatus fuerit. Meminit hujus collectionis Hincmarus Remensis Archiepiscopus, in opusculo LV. capit. adversus Hincmarum Laudunensem Episcopum cap. 43. Qui sunt, inquit, quos & Apostolica sedes, & omnes Episcopi per universum Orbem, & omnis Ecclesia Catholica canones appellat? Quique à Nicæno concilio, quod primum in nostris codicibus, quos ab apostolica sede majores nostri acceperunt sequendos, per ordinem usq; ad Africanum concilium, pro canonibus recipiendis, venerandis & observandis, retinent. Hisce conciliorum canonibus Dionysius Exiguus Romanorum Pontificum decreta, quotquot inveniri potuerunt, sub una numerorum serie, eodem quo patrum canones digesserat modo, & primus collectioni canonum subjunxit. Antiquiores enim Collectores, decretales Pontificum Romanorum Epistolas omiserunt, synodorum contenti regulis. Incipit autem à Siricio, quod indicium, eum antiquiores non reperisse: in Anastasio desinit. Quæ vero ab Hilario ad Gregorium Juniorem visuntur, ad hanc primam Collectionem Dionysii non pertinent, sed ab aliis Dionysio posterioribus addita sunt. Est vero hæc collectio Decretalium inscripta Juliano presbytero, tero, titulo S. Anastasiæ, à Dionysio; qui Presbyter subscripsit synodis Romæ celebratis, sub Felice Papa Dinamio & Siphidio Coss. an. Christi 488. & sub Symmacho post Cos. Paulini, an. 499. Hocque nobis monstrat tempus collectionis Dionysianæ, nempe vel sub finem seculi quinti, vel principio seculi sexti factam esse, & quidem primo eum vertisse canones Græcos, postea collegisse Decretales; Ipsa Epistola ad Julianum præmissa est à Justello Patre & Filio, collectioni Decretalium ejus. Hæc est collectio, quam Zacharias Papa in Epistola ad Pipinum Majorem Domus, & Episcopos Galliæ LIBRUM DECRETORUM vocat, atque ex eo citat quædam capitula Siricii, Innocentii, Leonis & Gelasii. Observanda quoque obiter differentia inter codicem Dionysii Exigui, & Codicem Ecclesiæ Universæ, nam Canones, i. iv. v. xvi. & xvii. concilii Antiocheni, quod ex concilio Calchedonensi probatur, in veteri Græco Codice xxc. xxciii. xxciv. xcv. & xcvi. fuere, qui in Latino Dionysii Exigui Codice lxxix. xxciv. xxcv. xcvi. & xcvii. sunt. Verum hæc disseritas, orta videtur, quod Ancyranum concilium in Græco canonum Codice, habeat viginti quinque canones, & Neocæsariense quinde-
units.tr: From this it is clear that Dionysius Exiguus, in his translation, in which he counted the Greek canons in a continuous and unbroken series of numbers after the manner of the Greek codex, added the Canons which are called those of the Apostles, the Council of Sardica, and likewise certain African councils. His codex differs in this from the Roman Code, which has been published at Mainz and Paris, as noted above, in that it does not number the canons in one series or uninterrupted order, but assigns to each council its own numbers, and when a new council begins, begins new numbers as well. The codex of Dionysius runs on to the number CLXV, which is the third canon of the First Council of Constantinople, of which seven are found in the Greek Code of the Universal Church, but only three in the Roman Code of Canons. Afterwards, in Dionysius, the twenty-six canons of the Council of Chalcedon follow with a new numbering, and likewise the canons of the Synod of Sardica, which were published only in Latin, with a new numbering. Finally, the African councils bring up the rear, likewise with a new numbering, and in his Canonical Collection there are one hundred and thirty-eight African canons. So that this Dionysian codex was gathered and compiled partly from the Greek synods and partly from the Western synods. Hincmar, Archbishop of Reims, makes mention of this collection, in the little work of fifty-five chapters against Hincmar, Bishop of Laon, chapter 43. "Who are they," he says, "whom both the Apostolic See and all the Bishops throughout the whole world, and the whole Catholic Church, call canons? And who retain, from the Nicene Council, which stands first in our codices, which our forefathers received from the Apostolic See to be followed, in order down to the African Council, for receiving, venerating and observing as canons." To these canons of the Councils, Dionysius Exiguus added, as the first to do so, the decrees of the Roman Pontiffs, as many as could be found, under one series of numbers, in the same manner in which he had arranged the canons of the Fathers. For the earlier collectors omitted the decretal letters of the Roman Pontiffs, being content with the rules of the synods. He begins, however, with Siricius, which is an indication that the earlier collectors did not find them; he ends with Anastasius. But those which are seen from Hilary to Gregory the Younger do not belong to this first collection of Dionysius, but were added by others later than Dionysius. This collection, moreover, is inscribed by Dionysius to Julian, presbyter, of the title of St. Anastasia; who, as a presbyter, subscribed to the synods celebrated at Rome under Pope Felix, in the consulship of Dynamius and Syphidius, in the year of Christ 488, and under Symmachus, after the consulship of Paulinus, in the year 499. This shows us the time of the Dionysian collection, namely that it was made either at the end of the fifth century or at the beginning of the sixth, and that he first translated the Greek canons and afterwards collected the Decretals. The letter to Julian prefixed to it has been published by Justellus, father and son, with his collection of Decretals. This is the collection which Pope Zacharias, in his letter to Pippin, Mayor of the Palace, and to the Bishops of Gaul, calls the BOOK OF DECREES, and from which he cites certain chapters of Siricius, Innocent, Leo and Gelasius. The difference between the codex of Dionysius Exiguus and the codex of the Universal Church should also be noted in passing: for the canons i, iv, v, xvi and xvii of the Council of Antioch, which is proved from the Council of Chalcedon, were in the old Greek codex numbered xc, xciii, xciv, xcv and xcvi, which are in the Latin codex of Dionysius Exiguus lxxix, xciv, xcv, xcvi and xcvii. But this discrepancy seems to have arisen because the Council of Ancyra in the Greek codex of canons has twenty-five canons, and the Council of Neocaesarea has fifteen;

units.la: 77. Differentia inter codicem Dionysii Exigui, & Ecclesiæ Universæ in dinumeratione canonum. quindecim ; in Latina vero Dionysii collectione quatuordecim & viginti quatuor tantum. Canonesque quartus & quintus Ancyrani concilii , item tertius & quartus decimus Neocæsariensis pro unico habeantur ; ut ex codicum collatione facile est observare. Vide sis , Doctissimum Leschasserium in consultatione de controv. inter Paul. V. & Remp. Venetam. & Henr. Justell. Præfat. in codicem Dionysii Exigui. Illud de collectione & versione Dionysii observandum ex ejus συγγραφῶ Cassiodoro supra relato, eam potissimum ab Ecclesia Romana esse probatam & receptam, quare etiam absolute CORPUS CANONUM appellari meruit c. 1. dist. 19, eoque nomine à posterioribus laudari solet. Quod confirmant Gratiani emendatores Romani , in Præfat. quam Gratiani decreto præfixerunt. Hæc ab Adriano I. Papa Carolo Magno ad ordinandas Ecclesias occidentis Romæ data est. Quod quando factum disquirit Doctiss. Sirmund. in Tomo II. conciliorum Galliæ pag. 117. ubi probat non epitomen canonum Orientalium & Africanorum , quæ edita Ingolstadii primum tomo II. Antiq. Lect. Canisii, deinde Coloniæ tom. III. conciliorum , ut ibidem dicitur ; sed integram collectionem canonum & Decretalium Dionysii Exigui , quæ codex canonum vocatur, Carolo Magno oblatam esse. Hoc declarant plurima, quæ in Bibliothecis Galliæ visuntur, Collectionis hujus exemplaria: quorum in fronte, velut oblati muneris dedicatio præfixa est, Hadriani ad Carolum epistola, quæ primis singulorum versuum litteris hunc titulum reddit, Domino Excell. Filio Carulo Regi Hadrianus Papa. Epistola autem ipsa sic habet, tum in aliis passim, tum in vetustissimo S. Germani codice, Caroli ipsius Magni temporibus exarato, anno regni ejus xxxvii. id est Christi DCCCV.
units.tr: 77. Difference between the codex of Dionysius Exiguus and that of the Universal Church in the numbering of the canons. ...fifteen; but in the Latin collection of Dionysius, only fourteen and twenty-four. And the fourth and fifth canons of the Council of Ancyra, likewise the third and fourth of the Council of Neocaesarea, are regarded as one; as it is easy to observe from a comparison of the codices. See, I pray, the most learned Leschassier, in his consultation on the controversy between Paul V and the Venetian Republic, and Henri Justel, Preface to the codex of Dionysius Exiguus. This must be observed concerning the collection and translation of Dionysius, from the writing [συγγραφῶ] of Cassiodorus cited above: that it was chiefly approved and received by the Roman Church, for which reason it has deserved to be called absolutely the BODY OF CANONS, c. 1, dist. 19, and it is customarily cited by later writers under that name. This is confirmed by the Roman emendators of Gratian, in the Preface which they prefixed to Gratian's Decretum. This was given by Pope Hadrian I to Charlemagne at Rome, for ordering the Churches of the West. When this was done is investigated by the most learned Sirmond, in Volume II of the Councils of Gaul, p. 117, where he proves that what was given to Charlemagne was not an epitome of the Eastern and African canons, which were first published at Ingolstadt in volume II of Canisius's Antiquae Lectiones, and then at Cologne in volume III of the Councils, as is said there; but the entire collection of canons and Decretals of Dionysius Exiguus, which is called the Codex of Canons. This is declared by the many copies of this collection which are seen in the libraries of Gaul; at the front of which, as a dedication of the gift offered, is prefixed the letter of Hadrian to Charles, which by the first letters of the individual verses gives this title: To the most excellent Lord, Son Charles the King, Hadrian the Pope. The letter itself reads thus, both in many other places and in the most ancient codex of St. Germain, written in the time of Charlemagne himself, in the year 37 of his reign, that is, of Christ 805.

units.la: EPISTOLA HADRIANI PAPÆ AD CAROLUM MAGNUM REGEM,
units.tr: THE LETTER OF POPE HADRIAN TO CHARLES THE GREAT, KING

units.la: Quæ in antiquis exemplaribus Codici Canonum præponitur.
units.tr: Which is placed at the head of the Codex of Canons in the old copies.

units.la: DIVINA fulgens doctrina sceptra præcellit regni, Origo regum felix, semper genitura beata, Molem perspicimus legis gratiam laudis habere. Iusto gignitur rege Ecclesiæ almæ defensor, Numquam enim vinci potest disciplina cælestis, Olim jam fumens paterni triumphans regni Exemplum, quo devota fides victoria gaudet, Christo juvante, ac beato clavigero Petro, Cunctas adversas gentes regalibus subdit plantis. En radix beata instar contulit prole. Læta Deum colere, legem semper amare divinam, Laudabilem servare fidem, sanctamque defendere vitam, Fautorem prorsus habens janitorem in triumphis cæli. Ipsius freta virtute victrice persistit semper. Lumen sequens doctrinæ fidei Apostolicæ Sedis, In hanc sanctam sedem magnus Rex Carulus splendet. Omnibus per eum ditata bonis triumphat ubique, Cœleste semper in his habere meruit regnum. Arma sumens divina gentes calcavit superbas. Reddidit prisca dona Ecclesiæ matri suæ, Urbesque Magnas, fines simul & castra diversa. Langobardam & Erulam virtute divina prostravit gentem, Ovans amplectitur fidem, quam suscepit ab avis. Magna prosapia hæc in toto rutilat mundo: Altus, nobilis, nitens, regit diversa regna. Gaudens celer ad limina venit Apostolorum sospes, Nimis laudibus hymnisque populo celebratur ab omni. Obnixe pro se summum orare Antistitem poscit, Redimi sibi noxas a juventute commissas. Exutus suffragiis almis spondebat lingua magistro Genium servare sanctæ Ecclesiæ in ævo Romanæ, Iustitias almi Petri sui protectoris tueri Habilem ut super donans in ejus Confessione libavit. Adhæc Hadrianus Præsul Christi prædixit triumphos, Dextera protegi diu divina Petro comitante Pauloque. Romphæam victoriæ donantes, atque pro te dimicantes, Inlæsus cum tuis victor manebis, nempe per ipsos Aditum petunt urbis Papiæ te ingredi victorem. Nefa perfidi regis calcabis Desiderii colla, Vires ejus prosternens merges baratro profundi. Septus Langobardorum regno, munus reddes tuum Pollicita sacra dona clavigeri aulæ Petri, Amplius donans tibi victoriam, simulque honorem Per sæcla regnare cum tuis hic, in futuroque soboli. A lege nunquam discede, hæc observans statuta.
units.tr: Divine doctrine, shining, surpasses the sceptre of the kingdom. Happy origin of kings, always a blessed offspring, we see that grace brings the mass of the law into praise. By a just king is born the defender of the nourishing Church. For heavenly discipline can never be conquered. Now already triumphant, taking up the example of his father's kingdom, in which a devoted faith rejoices in victory, with Christ helping and blessed Peter the key-bearer, he subdues all hostile nations under his royal feet. Behold, a blessed root has brought forth offspring like itself. Joyfully he worships God, always loves the divine law, keeps a praiseworthy faith and defends a holy life, having as his patron the doorkeeper of the heavenly triumphs. Relying on his victorious virtue, he persists always. Following the light of the doctrine of the apostolic see, King Charles the Great shines upon this holy see. Enriched with all good things through him, he triumphs everywhere, and he has deserved always to possess the heavenly kingdom in these things. Taking up divine arms, he trampled proud nations. He restored the ancient gifts to his mother the Church, and great cities, and borders together with various camps. By divine virtue he laid low the Lombard and the Heruli nation. Rejoicing, he embraces the faith which he received from his grandfathers. This great lineage shines throughout the whole world: lofty, noble, gleaming, he rules diverse kingdoms. Rejoicing, he came swiftly to the threshold of the Apostles, safe, and he is celebrated by all the people with exceeding praises and hymns. He earnestly asks the supreme Pontiff to pray on his behalf, that the sins committed by him from his youth might be redeemed. Stripped of his nourishing supports, with his tongue he pledged to the master to keep the genius of the holy Church in the Roman age, to guard the justices of blessed Peter, his protector, able to bestow them above, and he offered a libation at his Confession. Moreover, Hadrian, the Prelate of Christ, foretold your triumphs: that the divine right hand would protect you for a long time, with Peter and Paul accompanying. Granting you the sword of victory and fighting for you, you will remain a victor unharmed with your own people; indeed, through them they seek the entrance for you into the city of Pavia, to enter it as a victor. You will tread on the proud necks of the faithless king Desiderius, overthrowing his powers and sinking them into the deep abyss. Surrounded by the kingdom of the Lombards, you will render your gift, promising the sacred gifts of the key-bearer of Peter's court; giving you further victory, and at the same time honour, to reign here through the ages with your offspring, and in the future. Never depart from the law, observing these statutes.

units.la: Hactenus Hadriani Epistola, ut ex corruptis exemplaribus elici potuit. Est ea monumentū vergentis ad barbariem seculi. Quod vero ad tempus attinet, cum Carolus ter in urbem Hadriano superstite venerit, anno nimirum DCCLXXIV, cum Papiam obsideret, anno iterum DCCXXCI, cum ejus filii Pippinus Italiæ, Ludovicus Aquitaniæ Reges ab Hadriano inuncti sunt, anno denique DCCXXCVII, cum inde Capuam quoque, ac Beneventum adversus Grimoaldum Ducem profectus est: nos, tametsi res incerta est, Codicem Hadriani ad postremam potius profectionem referendum diximus, quam quod aliis placuit ad primam, cui multa, quæ in ejus Epistola leguntur, convenire vix possint. Præter Sirmondum in Gallia multa exemplaria manuscripta profstare testatur Anonymus, in Præfatione Breviarii canonum Fulgentii Ferrandi, quam præfixit editioni Parisiensi Anni 1609. Insertæ sunt postea huic Codici ut dictum Epistolæ Paparum Romanorum, Syricii, Innocentii, Zosimi, Cœlestini, Leonis & Gelasii; Quorum etiam meminit Cresconius in suo Breviario, item Hilarii Symmachi, Hormisdæ, Simplicii, Gregorii Junioris, qui Episcopatum Romanum seculo quarto decurrente usque ad octavum incipiens, administrarunt; Hoc ordine quoque recenset seriem Codicis hujus Leo IV. Papa. Apud Gratianum c. de libellis. dist. 20. De libellis, inquit, & commentariis aliorum non convenit aliquem judicare, & sanctorum conciliorum canones relinquere, vel decretalium regulas, id est, quæ habentur tur apud nos simul cum canonibus, quibus autem in omnibus ecclesiasticis utimur judiciis, sunt canones Apostolorum, Nicænorum, Ancyranorum, Neocæsariensium, Gangrensium, Antiochensium, Laodicensium, Constantinop. Ephes. Chalcedonensium, Sardicensium, Africanensium, Carthaginensium, & cum illis regulæ præsulum Romanorum, Sylvestri, Syricii, Innocentii, Zozimi, Cælestini, Leonis, Gelasii, Hilarii, Symmachi, Hormisdæ, Simplicii, & Gregorii junioris. Qui ordo comparet quoque in Codice Canonum Romano, Moguntiæ & Lutetiæ edito, nisi quod ille Codex non habeat Epistolam decretalem quæ Sylvestro tribuitur, & synodi Ephesinæ canones octo; Sed loco eorum Johannes Wendelstinus, qui istum Codicem Moguntiæ primus Anno 1525. edidit, se synodicam Epistolam Ephesini concilii, cum xii. capitulis contra Nestorium huic adjunxisse scribit. Quod facile condonandum homini, qui isto seculo quod potuit præstitit, & non animadvertit istos anathematismos non esse concilii Ephesini, sed esse Cyrilli & synodi Diœcæseos Ægypti. Quod inscriptio epistolæ, quæ actis concilii Ephesini inserta legitur in editione Romana anni 1608. sat probat, & observavit Doctiss;
units.tr: Thus far the Letter of Hadrian, as far as it could be drawn out from corrupt copies. It is a monument of an age tending towards barbarism. As for the date, since Charles came to the city three times while Hadrian was alive, namely in the year 774, when he was besieging Pavia; again in the year 781, when his sons Pippin, king of Italy, and Louis, king of Aquitaine, were anointed by Hadrian; and finally in the year 787, when he set out from there against Duke Grimoald, also to Capua and Benevento: we, although the matter is uncertain, have said that the Codex of Hadrian should be referred to the last of these journeys rather than, as others have preferred, to the first, to which many things read in his Letter can hardly apply. Besides Sirmond, the Anonymous author, in the Preface to the Breviary of the canons of Fulgentius Ferrandus, which he prefixed to the Paris edition of the year 1609, testifies that many manuscript copies exist in Gaul. Afterwards there were inserted into this Codex, as has been said, the letters of the Roman Popes: Siricius, Innocent, Zosimus, Celestine, Leo and Gelasius. Cresconius also mentions these in his Breviary, likewise those of Hilary, Symmachus, Hormisdas, Simplicius, and Gregory the Younger, who began to administer the Roman see in the fourth century and continued down to the eighth. Leo IV, the Pope, also recounts the series of this Codex in this order. In Gratian, c. de libellis, dist. 20: "Concerning libels and the commentaries of others," he says, "it is not proper to judge anyone, nor to leave aside the canons of the holy councils, or the rules of the decretals, that is, those which are held by us together with the canons; and the canons which we use in all ecclesiastical judgements are: the canons of the Apostles, of Nicaea, of Ancyra, of Neocaesarea, of Gangra, of Antioch, of Laodicea, of Constantinople, Ephesus, Chalcedon, Sardica, Africa, Carthage; and with these the rules of the Roman prelates: Sylvester, Siricius, Innocent, Zosimus, Celestine, Leo, Gelasius, Hilary, Symmachus, Hormisdas, Simplicius, and Gregory the Younger." This same order also appears in the Roman Codex of Canons, published at Mainz and Paris, except that this Codex does not have the decretal letter ascribed to Sylvester, and the eight canons of the Synod of Ephesus; but in their place Johannes Wendelstinus, who first published this Codex at Mainz in the year 1525, writes that he added to it the synodal letter of the Council of Ephesus, with twelve chapters against Nestorius. This is easily to be pardoned in a man who did what he could in that century, and did not notice that those anathematisms are not of the Council of Ephesus but of Cyril and of the synod of the Egyptian diocese. The inscription of the letter, which is read inserted among the acts of the Council of Ephesus in the Roman edition of 1608, sufficiently proves this, as the most learned man observed.

units.la: Note: Conveniantia & dissensus codicis Romani cum ordine memorato Leonis Papæ.
units.tr: Note: The agreements and disagreements of the Roman Codex with the aforementioned order of Pope Leo.

units.la: Doctiss: Justellus ad Canonem 171. Cod. Eccles. univerf. cujus filius istam Epistolam cum anathematismis in Bibliotheca juris Pontificii, Gr. & Lat. Codici Dionysii Exigui, ex ejus interpretatione subjecit, cum Præsatione ad Petrum quendam Episcopum; vid. sis Præfat. Henr. Justelli ad Cod. Dionys. Exig. in fine. Habet deinde iste Codex Bonifacii I. & Anastasii secundi Epistolas, quarum nec Cresconius, neque Leo in citato C. de libellis meminit. Est & alia levis differentia, quam observavit Anonymus ille in consultatione de controv. inter Paulum Quint. & Remp. Venetam, quem diximus esse Doctiss: Jacob: Leschafferium. Quod nimirum canon XVI. synodi Antiocheni, in codice canonum, quo usa est synodus Calchedonensis, sit nonagesimus quintus in codice vero Romano, si suo nimirum loco restituatur omissum concilium Ephesinum (quod tamen non animadvertit, saltem non monuit Leschafferius) nonagesimus quartus, & in Codice Græco quem edidit Tilius, sit nonagesimus sextus, unde differitas illa promanet, ipse Leschafferius late disquirit, & causas indicat, quæ eædem fere sunt, quas nos retulimus supra, num. 77. Hæc initia & progressus sunt Codicis Canonum in Ecclesia Romana, nunc lustrandæ aliæ Occidentis Ecclesiæ,
units.tr: Most learned: Justellus on Canon 171 of the Codex of the universal Church, whose son appended this Letter together with the anathematisms to the Bibliotheca of the Pontifical law, Greek and Latin, to the Codex of Dionysius Exiguus, from his translation, with a Preface to a certain bishop Peter; see besides the Preface of Henry Justellus to the Codex of Dionysius Exiguus at the end. Then this Codex contains the Letters of Boniface I and Anastasius II, of which neither Cresconius nor Leo, in the cited C. de libellis, makes mention. There is also another slight difference, which was observed by that anonymous author in the consultation on the controversy between Paul V and the Venetian Republic, whom we have said to be the most learned Jacob Leschassier. Namely, canon XVI of the Synod of Antioch, in the codex of canons used by the Council of Chalcedon, is the ninety-fifth; but in the Roman codex, if it is restored to its proper place the omitted Council of Ephesus (which nevertheless Leschassier did not notice, or at least did not point out), it is the ninety-fourth; and in the Greek Codex which Tilius edited, it is the ninety-sixth. Whence this difference arises, Leschassier himself discusses at length and indicates the causes, which are nearly the same as those we related above, no. 77. These are the beginnings and progress of the Codex of Canons in the Roman Church; now let us survey the other churches of the West.

units.la: 80. Aliæ Ecclesiæ Occidentis Ecclesiæ, videndumque quæ fata in iis habuerit. In Galliam eum deportandum dedisse Carolo Magno Adrianum Papam Romanum seculi octavi an. 773. ut vult Justellus, anno vero 787. ut voluit supra Sirmondus, dictum. Sed ante hæc tempora Galliam habuisse Codicem Latinum, vel ex antiqua versione, vel ex versione Dionysii Exigui probat illustris locis ex Gregorio Turonensi, seu potius acta concilii Parisiensis An. 580, in causa Pratextati Episcopi Rothomagensis, à Gregorio relata. Ipse vero (Rex Chilpericus) ad metatum discessit, transmittens Librum Canonum, in quo erat quaternio novus adnexus, habens canones quasi Apostolicos, continentes hæc: Episcopus in homicidio, adulterio & perjurio deprehensus, à sacerdotio divellatur. Est ille canon apostolicus 25. Ita censet Doctissimus Justellus. Mihi ex hoc loco valde probabile, imo certum videtur, Ecclesiam Gallicam habuisse versionem antiquam primo, non illam Dionysii Exigui; Quia Gregorius dicit librum illum canonum, habuisse adsutum quaternionem novum, in quo continebantur canones quasi Apostolici. Hi enim in versione antiqua non continebantur; ex Præfatione enim Dionysii Exigui supra relata, patet, eum primum eos vertisse, & suæ collectioni inseruisse.
units.tr: 80. The other churches of the West, and what fortunes it had among them must be considered. That Pope Hadrian of Rome, in the eighth century, gave this Codex to Charles the Great to be carried into Gaul, in the year 773, as Justellus holds, but in the year 787, as Sirmond above preferred to say.
