But that before these times Gaul had a Latin Codex, either from the old version or from the version of Dionysius Exiguus, is shown by an illustrious passage from Gregory of Tours, or rather the acts of the Council of Paris of the year 580, in the case of Pratextatus, bishop of Rouen, related by Gregory: "He himself (King Chilperic) departed for the mall, sending on the Book of Canons, in which there was a new quire attached, containing canons as if Apostolic, which said these things: a bishop caught in homicide, adultery and perjury is to be torn from the priesthood." That is the Apostolic canon 25. So the most learned Justellus thinks. To me, from this passage it seems very probable, indeed certain, that the Gallican Church had at first the old version, not that of Dionysius Exiguus; because Gregory says that book of canons had a new quire attached, in which the canons "as if Apostolic" were contained. For these were not contained in the old version; for from the Preface of Dionysius Exiguus related above, it is clear that he first translated them and inserted them into his own collection.

units.la: Ecclesiæ praeter Romanam, habuerunt quoque olim Codicem Canonum, habuit Gallia.
units.tr: Apart from the Roman one, the Church of Gaul also once had a code of canons.

units.la: 81. Cujus versionis disquisitio. feruisse. Ita ut probabile sit Chilpericum Codici illo antiquo & in Gallia recepto (novum enim nunc concilio obtrudere non audebat) addidisse ex versione Dionysii istos canones quos vocat Gregorius quasi Apostolicos, ad hæc usque tempora in Gallia incognitos, saltem non receptos. Imo circa tempora Dionysii Exigui mentio Gallicanorum canonum invenitur: refert Gratianus. c. si quis Diaconus. dist. 50. testimonium Hormisdæ Episcopi Romani, anni 515. Secundum titulos antiquorum Patrum sancto spiritu suggerente conscriptos, & secundum sententias CCCXVIII. Episcoporum, quas etiam GALLICANI CANONES continere videntur, clerici in adulterio deprehensi &c. Facit & horum mentionem canon XI. concilii Tarraconen-sis Anno 517. habiti. Vt nullus Monachorum Forensis negotii susceptor vel executor existat, nisi id quod monasterii poscit utilitas, Abbate sibi nihilominus imperante. Canonum ante omnia Gallicanorum de eis constitutione servata. An vero per Gallicanos illos canones sit intelligendus Codex Canonum Ecclesiæ universæ, ambigo, probo hac in re Doctissimi Justelli sententiam, qui (quod etiam in plerisque aliis Ecclesiis videmus factum, ut postea patebit) duplicem codicem Ecclesiæ Gallicanæ agnoscit, unum quem cum Ecclesia universa recepit; alterum, qui Gallicanos canones habuit, id est eos qui in conciliis Galliæ erant decreti. Quod non obscure collegit ex duobus Agobardi Lugdunensis Episcopi locis, qui sub Ludovico Caroli M. Filio vixit. Primus est ex libro de dispens. Eccles. Sunt, inquit, qui Gallicanos canones aut aliarum regionum putent non recipiendos, eo quod Legati Romani seu Imperatoris in eorum constitutionibus non interfuerint. Ex quo clarum loqui illum de Galliæ conciliis, & hos eum vocare Canones Gallicanos. In œcumenicis enim conciliis & legati Imperatoris, & Episcopus Romanus vel ipse vel legati ejus comparebant. Alter est ex Epistola ad Imperator. de duello. Huc accedit quod pia consideratione dignum videtur de canonibus scilicet Gallicanis, qui quasi superflui aut inutiles à quibusdam reputantur, eo quod Neoterici Romani eos non commendaverint, cum antiqui religiose eos venerati sint; neque hoc idcirco dicitur, ut passim omnium Episcopalium conventuum sanctiones æquali auctoritate recipienda credantur, ut Nicæni, Calchedonensis & cæterorum Generalium ex totius Mundi consensu congregatorum & receptorum; sed quia congrua veneratione pro causis necessariis, quarum definitiones in illis generalibus non inveniuntur, fides sit eis adhibenda religione debita. Quod idem videtur confirmare concilium Vasense II. anni 529. canone primo, dum distinguit, inter canones antiquos & novellos. ubi per antiquos Canones indicatur Codex canonum Ecclesiae universae, per novellos vero ii, qui proprii sunt conciliorum Galliae. Successu temporis in hunc Codicem Gallicum adoptati etiam canones exterorum conciliorum. Veluti Africani, qui & in codicem Ecclesiae Romanae sunt recepti. Colligi id potest ex Concilii Matisconensis II, quod celebratum an. 588. canone VI. Jam enim (sunt verba canonis) de tali causa, & in conciliis Africanis definitum est, quam definitionem nostro quoque dignam duximus sociare decreto & adlocare: ut sacramenta altaris, non nisi a jejunis celebrentur. Receptas etiam quasdam decretales epistolas Pontificum Romanorum, esse, probat concilii Agathensis celebrati anno 506. canon ix. ubi Siricii decretalis adsumitur, & canonibus inseritur. Quae est Siricii epistola ad Himerium Tarraconensem, quae legitur in Codice canonum Romanae Ecclesiae. Ut valde probabile sit, antiquum illum Codicem Gallicum ambulasse pari passu cum Romano, eo crescente etiam crevisse. Quod non obscure quoque probant Capitularia Caroli Magni, quae varia capitula ex Codice Romano & epistolis decretalibus Episcoporum Romanorum in eo contentis, laudant. Quod tamen verum tantum de Decretalibus, in codicem Romanum antiquum relatis, non de iis quas postea Isidorus Mercator, (de quo infra dicemus) collegit, vel finxit & suppoluit à Clemente ad Silvestrum: de quibus verum, quod Episcopi Gallia scribunt ad Nicolaum primum urbis Episcopum Anno 860. Decretalia priscorum Pontificum in toto corpore Codicis canonum non inveniri descripta, contra quos insurgit Nicolaus Papa in c. si Romanorum. 1. dist. 19; Sed ut dictum, id accipiendum de Decretalibus à Siricio usque ad Gregorium Juniorem, quousq; comparent quoque in Codice Canonum Romanæ Ecclesiæ. Patet id ex citatione Hincmari Rhemensis Archiepiscopi, qui temporibus Nicolai primi vixit; qui passim illas tantum decretales citat; Exemplum præbeat Epist. 6. cap. 23. ubi Innocentii Papæ Romani laudat epistolam ad Victricium Rothomagensem Archiepiscopum, ex sacris canonibus promulgatam. Improbat vero Sylvestri decreta, Epistol. 8. cap. 22. & 23. Caeterum, inquit, quoniam quidam quasi in auctoritatem proferunt S. Sylvestrum Papam decrevisse talia quæ Catholica Ecclesia inter synodalia decreta non computat, quæ majores nostri inde nobis tenenda suis posteris posteris reliquerunt, hic necessarium ponere duximus. Scriptum namque est in quodam sermone sine exceptoris nomine de gestis S. Sylvestri excepto, quem Isidorus Episcopus (Hispalensis) collegit cum Epistolis Romanae sedis pontificum à S. Clemente usque ad B. Gregorium, eundem Sylvestrum decrevisse, ut nullus laicus crimen clerico audeat inferre, &c. quae dicta quam adversa sibi & quam diversa à sanctis canonibus, & sacris legibus sint, nemo est qui dubitet, qui & haec dicta cum ratione attenderit, & sacras regulas, ac leges diligentius legit. Ubi per Isidorum intelligendus Isidorus Mercator, de quo postea. Ex Gallia in Hispaniam transeamus, ubi quoque Codex canonum receptus, & quidem ut in Gallia duplex. Antiquus ille, Ecclesiae universae, quem probabile est, eos accepisse à Romanis. Eum habere primo potuerunt ex antiqua Latina, postea etiam ex nova Dionysii Exigui versione, usque ad Martini Bracharensis Episcopi interpretationem; Quamquam non valde probabile, eos Dionysii Exigui versionem habuisse aut recepisse, quia ea satis accurata erat, ut nova versione Martini Bracharensis potuissent superseedere; Utraque enim eodem seculo adornata est, nempe sexto, illa Dionysii Exigui paulo ante, vel sub Justiniano Imperatore, altera Martini tini Bracharensis septimo anno post mortem Justiniani, nempe anno 572. Solet is Codex Hispanicus Ecclesiæ universæ, citari sub titulo Priscorum canonum, ut censet Doctissimus Justellus, in sua sæpius allegata Præfat. Cod. canon. item antiquorum canonum. Veluti in subscriptione concilii Toletani secundi, quod habitum fere circa ea tempora, quibus Dionysius Exiguus suam interpretationem adornavit, Salva auctoritate priscorum canonum. Imo & Codicis canonum mentio fit, in concilii Bracharensis primi canone XVIII; quod Novennio ante versionem Martini Bracharensis est habitum, secundum quosdam. Canonis verba sunt hæc: Lucretius Episcopus dixit: Necessarium arbitror si vestræ fraternitati videtur, ut institita sanctorum Patrum, recensitis antiquis canonibus, innotescant: quæ etsi non omnia, certe pauca vel quædam, quæ ad instructionem clericalis disciplinæ sustinent, relegantur. Omnes Episcopi dixerunt: placet quod dictum est, congrua res est; ut quibus fortasse per incuriam abolita sunt ecclesiastica constituta, audiant sanctorum canonum regulam & observent, Relecti sunt ex CODICE coram concilio, tam generalium synodorum canones, quam localium. & canone XL. Placuit ut præcepta antiquorum canonum, quæ modo in concilio recitata sunt, nullus audeat præterire: Fit quo-que que mentio Codicis Canonum in concilio Toletano quarto, seculi septimi anno trigesimo tertio habiti, Can. III. Diaconus, CODICEM CANONUM in medio proferens, capitula de conciliis agendis pronunciat. Alter Codex Canonum Hispaniæ specialis; & collectus fuit ex conciliis potissimum Hispaniæ. Quibus Clariss: Justellus addita probat quædam ex conciliis Galliæ, item epistolis decretalibus Pontificum Romanorum. Concilium Tarraconense anni 517. can. xi. jubet observari canones Gallicanos. Ilerdense concilium habitum anno 524. & Valentinum can. 2. synodi Agathensis & Rheginensis meminere; plura testimonia vide apud Justellum. Decretalium pontificum Romanorum facit mentionem concilium Toletanum III. canon. i. Anno 589. & Barcinonense can. III. Anno 599. Quas itidem Justellus probat esse eas epistolas, quæ in codice canonum Ecclesiæ Romanæ leguntur. Quia Canone xvi. Concilii Toletani iv. dicitur. Synodica Præsulum Romanorum decreta apocalypsin Johannis inter divinos libros recipiendum constituere, idque factum apparet Epistola Innocentii I. ad Exuperium Tholosanum Episcopum. Deinde quia in concilio Toletano vi. anni 638. laudatur Leonis I. Papæ Romani sententia, ex Epistola ad Rusticum Narbonensem Episcopum scripta. Utraque autem & Innocentii & Leonis Epistola in Codice canonum Ecclesiæ Romanæ legitur. Oceanum si trajiciamus in Britanniam, cognitus ibidem fuit codex canonum, sed qualis ille fuerit, an Ecclesiæ universæ, an vero particularis quidam proprius,non ita clarum;Item nec quo tempore collectio illa facta, aut recepta. In Antiquitatibus Britannicæ Eccles. proditum est, Theodorum Archiepiscopum librum protulisse, qui Patrum canones vocabatur, quem & in concilio Herefordiensi anno 673. probatum esse, ex lib. 4. Hist. Eccles. venerab. Bedæ conjicere licet. Anno tertio, inquit, Ecgfridi Regis Theodorus cogit concilium Episcoporum, una cum eis qui canonica Patrum statuta diligerent & nossent magistris ecclesiæ pluribus &c. Subjicit postea Theodori, præsidis hujus concilii verba: Rogo dilectissimi Fratres ut quæque decreta ac diffinita sunt à sanctis ac probabilibus Patribus, incorrupta ab omnibus nobis serventur. Hæc & alia quamplura, quæ ad charitatem pertinebant, unitatemque Ecclesiæ conservandam persecutus sum. Cumque explessem prolocutionem, interrogavi unumquemque eorum per ordinem, si consentirent ea quæ à Patribus canonice sunt antiquitus decreta custodire; ad quod omnes consacerdotes nostri dixerunt; optime omnibus bus placet, quaeque definiverunt sanctorum canones Patrum, nos quoque omnes alacri animo libentissime servare. Quibus statim protuli eundem Librum Canonum, & ex eodem libro decem capitula, quae per loca notaveram, quia nobis maxime necessaria sciebam, illis coram ostendi. Hactenus ille. Ut vero gustus istius codices exhibeatur, ex eodem Beda, decem illa capitula subjicimus.
units.tr: 81. On the inquiry into which version this was. ...have had. So it is probable that Chilperic, to that ancient code received in Gaul (for he did not then dare to impose a new one on the council), added from Dionysius's version those canons which Gregory calls as it were Apostolic, unknown in Gaul until these times, or at least not received. Indeed, around the time of Dionysius Exiguus, mention is found of the Gallican canons. Gratian, c. si quis Diaconus, dist. 50, cites the testimony of Hormisdas, bishop of Rome, from the year 515: According to the titles of the ancient Fathers written under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, and according to the sentences of the 318 bishops, which the GALLICAN CANONS also seem to contain, clerics caught in adultery etc. Canon XI of the council of Tarragona, held in 517, also mentions them: That no monk become a handler or executor of worldly business, unless what the needs of the monastery require, the abbot nevertheless commanding; the canons of the Gallicans above all things being observed concerning this. Whether by those Gallican canons the code of the universal Church is to be understood, I am in doubt; in this matter I approve the opinion of the most learned Justellus, who (as we see was also done in many other Churches, as will later appear) recognises a twofold code of the Gallican Church: one which it received together with the universal Church, and another which had the Gallican canons, that is, those which were decreed in the councils of Gaul. He gathered this clearly from two passages of Agobard, bishop of Lyons, who lived under Louis, son of Charlemagne. The first is from his book on the dispensation of the Church: There are, he says, some who think that the Gallican canons, or those of other regions, are not to be received, because the Roman legates or the emperor's were not present at their enactments. From this it is clear that he is speaking of the councils of Gaul, and calls these the Gallican canons. For at the ecumenical councils both the emperor's legate and the Roman bishop, either in person or through his legates, were present. The second is from his Letter to the Emperors on the duel: To this is added that it seems worthy of pious consideration concerning the canons, namely the Gallican ones, which are regarded by some as superfluous or useless, because the modern Romans have not commended them, although the ancients revered them with reverence; nor is this said so that the decrees of every episcopal assembly should be believed to be received with equal authority, as those of Nicaea, Chalcedon and the other general councils gathered and received from the consent of the whole world; but so that, for necessary causes whose definitions are not found in those general councils, they may be given faith with due reverence. The council of Vaison II of 529, canon one, seems to confirm the same thing, when it distinguishes ancient and newer canons: by the ancient canons is meant the code of canons of the universal Church, and by the newer those which are peculiar to the councils of Gaul. In the course of time the canons of foreign councils were also adopted into this Gallican code, for example the African canons, which were also received into the code of the Roman Church. This can be gathered from the second council of Mâcon, held in 588, canon VI: For already (these are the words of the canon) concerning such a case it has been defined in the African councils, a definition which we also have thought worthy to join to our decree and to append: that the sacraments of the altar be celebrated only by those who are fasting. That certain decretal letters of the Roman pontiffs were also received is proved by canon IX of the council of Agde, held in 506, where a decretal of Siricius is taken up and inserted among the canons. This is the letter of Siricius to Himerius of Tarragona, which is read in the code of canons of the Roman Church. So it is very probable that that ancient Gallic code kept pace with the Roman one, and grew as it grew. The Capitularies of Charlemagne also obscurely prove this, since they cite various chapters from the Roman code and from the decretal letters of the Roman bishops contained in it. Yet this is true only of the decretals brought into the ancient Roman code, not of those which Isidore Mercator (of whom we shall speak below) later collected, or invented and foisted in from Clement to Sylvester; concerning these is true what the bishops of Gaul write to Nicholas I, bishop of the city, in the year 860: The decretals of the early popes are not found written out in the whole body of the code of canons, against which Pope Nicholas rises up in c. si Romanorum, 1, dist. 19. But, as has been said, this must be understood of the decretals from Siricius down to Gregory the Younger, since these also appear in the code of canons of the Roman Church. This is clear from the citation of Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, who lived in the times of Nicholas I, and who cites only those decretals in passing. Let Epistle 6, chapter 23 serve as an example, where he praises the letter of the Roman pope Innocent to Victricius, archbishop of Rouen, promulgated from the sacred canons. But he rejects the decrees of Sylvester, Epistle 8, chapters 22 and 23: Moreover, he says, since some bring forward as if on authority that St Sylvester the pope decreed such things as the Catholic Church does not count among the synodal decrees, which our elders left to their successors to be held by us from them, it seemed necessary to us to set this down here. For it is written in a certain sermon, without the name of the scribe, concerning the deeds of St Sylvester, which Isidore the bishop (of Seville) collected together with the letters of the Roman see's pontiffs from St Clement down to Blessed Gregory, that the same Sylvester decreed that no layman should dare to bring a charge against a cleric, etc. How hostile to themselves these statements are, and how different from the holy canons and the sacred laws, no one doubts who has weighed these statements with reason and read the sacred rules and laws more diligently. Here by Isidore must be understood Isidore Mercator, of whom later. Let us pass from Gaul into Spain, where the code of canons was also received, and indeed, as in Gaul, twofold. The ancient one is that of the universal Church, which it is probable they received from the Romans. They could have had it first from the ancient Latin version, afterwards also from the new version of Dionysius Exiguus, down to the translation of Martin, bishop of Braga; although it is not very probable that they had or received the version of Dionysius Exiguus, since it was accurate enough that they could have dispensed with the new version of Martin of Braga. For both were made in the same century, the sixth: the former of Dionysius a little before, or under the emperor Justinian, the latter of Martin of Braga in the seventh year after Justinian's death, that is, in the year 572. This Spanish code of the universal Church is usually cited under the title of the ancient canons, as the most learned Justellus thinks, in his Preface to the Code of Canons, which he often cites; likewise of the ancient canons. As in the subscription of the second council of Toledo, which was held about the time when Dionysius Exiguus prepared his translation: Saving the authority of the ancient canons. Indeed mention is also made of the code of canons in canon XVIII of the first council of Braga, which, according to some, was held nine years before the version of Martin of Braga. The words of the canon are these: Lucretius, bishop, said: I think it necessary, if it seems good to your brotherhood, that the institutions of the holy Fathers be made known by reviewing the ancient canons; and though not all of them, at least a few or some which bear on the instruction of clerical discipline be read over. All the bishops said: What has been said pleases us; it is a fitting matter; so that those to whom perhaps through carelessness the ecclesiastical constitutions have been abolished may hear the rule of the holy canons and observe it. There were read out from the CODE before the council, the canons of the general synods as well as of the local ones. And in canon XL: It has pleased that the precepts of the ancient canons, which have just been recited in the council, no one dare to pass over. Mention of the Code of Canons is also made in the fourth council of Toledo, held in the thirty-third year of the seventh century, canon III: The deacon, holding up the CODE OF CANONS, announces the chapters concerning the holding of councils. The other code is the special code of Spain, and it was collected chiefly from the councils of Spain. To these the most distinguished Justellus shows that certain things from the councils of Gaul were added, and likewise decretal letters of the Roman pontiffs. The council of Tarragona of 517, canon XI, orders the Gallican canons to be observed. The council of Lérida held in 524, and that of Valence, canon 2, and the synods of Agde and Riez make mention of them; see more testimonies in Justellus. The third council of Toledo, canon I, of 589, and that of Barcelona, canon III, of 599, make mention of the decretal letters of the Roman pontiffs; Justellus likewise proves these to be the letters which are read in the code of canons of the Roman Church. For canon XVI of the fourth council of Toledo says: The synodal decrees of the Roman prelates have established that the Apocalypse of John is to be received among the divine books, and this appears to have been done in the letter of Innocent I to Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse. Next, because in the sixth council of Toledo, of 638, the opinion of Leo I, pope of Rome, is praised, taken from the letter written to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne. Both the letter of Innocent and that of Leo are read in the code of canons of the Roman Church. If we cross the ocean into Britain, the code of canons was known there too; but what it was, whether that of the universal Church or some particular code of its own, is not so clear; nor is it clear at what time that collection was made or received. In the Antiquities of the British Church it is reported that Archbishop Theodore brought forward a book which was called the canons of the Fathers, which one may gather from Bede's Ecclesiastical History, book 4, to have been approved also in the council of Hertford in 673. In the third year, he says, of King Ecgfrith, Theodore convened a council of bishops, together with those who loved the canonical statutes of the Fathers and knew them, many teachers of the church... He subjoins afterwards the words of Theodore, the president of this council: I ask, most beloved brothers, that whatever decrees and definitions have been made by the holy and approved Fathers be kept by us all uncorrupted. These and many other things, which pertained to charity and to preserving the unity of the Church, I have pursued. And when I had finished my address, I asked each of them in turn whether they consented to keep those things which have been canonically decreed of old by the Fathers; to which all our fellow priests said: it pleases everyone very much, and whatever the holy canons of the Fathers have defined, we all also gladly and with eager spirit are glad to keep. Then at once I produced before them the same Book of Canons, and from the same book I showed them ten chapters, which I had marked in place, because I knew them to be most necessary for us. So far he. To show a sample of that code, we subjoin those ten chapters from the same Bede.
The First Chapter.

units.la: Ut sanctum diem Paschae in communi omnes servemus dominica post xiv. Lunam primi mensis.
units.tr: That we all observe the holy day of Easter together, on the Sunday after the fourteenth moon of the first month.
The Second.

units.la: Ut nullus Episcoporum parochiam alterius invadat, sed contentus sit gubernatione creditae sibi plebis.
units.tr: That no bishop encroach on another's parish, but be content with governing the people entrusted to him.
The Third.

units.la: Ut quaeque monasteria Deo consecrata, nulli Episcoporum liceat ea in aliquo inquietare: nec quicquam de eorum rebus violenter abstrahere.
units.tr: That no bishop be permitted to disturb any monasteries consecrated to God, or violently to take anything from their property.
The Fourth.

units.la: Ut ipsi Monachi non migrent de loco ad locum, hoc est de monasterio ad monasterium, nisi per missionem proprii Abbatis: sed in ea permaneant obedientia, quam tempore suae conversionis promiserunt.
units.tr: That the monks themselves not move from place to place, that is, from monastery to monastery, unless sent by their own abbot, but remain in the obedience they promised at the time of their conversion.
The Fifth.

units.la: Ut nullus Clericorum relinquens proprium Episcopum, passim quolibet discurrat, nec alicubi veniens absque commendatitiis literis sui præsulis suscipiatur. Quod si semel susceptus est, & noluerit invitatus redire, & susceptor & is qui susceptus est, excommunicationi subjacebit.
units.tr: That no cleric who leaves his own bishop wander about anywhere he likes, and that he not be received anywhere without letters of recommendation from his prelate. If he has been received, and refuses to return when invited, both the one who received him and the one who was received shall be subject to excommunication.
The Sixth.

units.la: Ut Episcopi atque Clerici peregrini contenti sint hospitalitatis munere oblato, nullique eorum liceat ullum officium sacerdotale absque permissu Episcopi, in cujus parochia cognoscitur, agere.
units.tr: That bishops and clerics who are foreigners be content with the hospitality offered, and that none of them be allowed to perform any priestly office without the permission of the bishop in whose parish he is found.
The Seventh.

units.la: Ut bis in anno synodus congregetur. Sed quia diversæ causæ impediunt, placent omnibus in communi ut Kal. Augusti in loco qui appellatur Clofaes semel in anno congregetur.
units.tr: That the synod be convened twice a year. But since various causes hinder this, it pleases all in common that it be convened once a year, on the first of August, in the place called Clofaes.
The Eighth.

units.la: Ut nullus Episcoporum se præferat alteri per ambitionem, Sed omnes agnoscant tempus & ordinem consecrationis suæ.
units.tr: That no bishop put himself before another out of ambition, but that all acknowledge the time and order of their consecration.
The Ninth Chapter.

units.la: In communi tractatum est, ut plures Episcopi crescente numero fidelium augerentur; sed de hac re adpræsens silemus.
units.tr: It was discussed in common that several bishops should be appointed as the number of the faithful grows; but on this matter we are silent for the present.
Decii
The Tenth.

units.la: Pro conjugiis, ut nulli liceat nisi legitimum habere connubium. Nullus incestum faciat, nullus conjugem propriam, nisi, ut sanctum Evangelium docet, fornicationis causa relinquat. Quod si quisquam propriam expulerit conjugem, legitimo sibi matrimonio conjunctam, si Christianus esse recte voluerit, nulli alteri copuletur. Sed ita permaneat, aut propriæ reconcilietur conjugi.
units.tr: Concerning marriages: that no one be permitted to have any marriage except a lawful one. No one shall commit incest, and no one shall leave his own wife except, as the holy Gospel teaches, on account of fornication. If anyone has put away his own wife, joined to him in lawful marriage, and wishes to be a Christian rightly, let him not join himself to another; but let him remain so, or be reconciled to his own wife.

units.la: His itaque capitulis in communi contractis ac definitis, ut nullum deinceps ab aliquo nostrum orietur contentionis scandalum, aut alia pro aliis divulgarentur; Placuit ut quæque diffinita sunt, unusquisque nostrum manus propriæ subscriptione confirmaret. Quisquis igitur contra hanc sententiam juxta decreta canonum, nostra etiam consensione ac subscriptione manus nostræ confirmatam quoquo modo vivere vel venire, eamque infringere tentaverit, noverit se ab omni officio sacerdotali & nostra societate separatum. Divina nos gra-tia in unitate sanctæ Ecclesiæ suæ viventes custodiat incolumes; Facta autem est hæc Synodus anno ab incarnatione Domini DCLXXIII.
units.tr: Therefore, these chapters having been agreed upon and decided in common, so that no scandal of contention may arise among us from now on, nor one thing be published in place of another, it has pleased us that each of us confirm what has been decided by the subscription of his own hand. Whoever, therefore, contrary to this decision made according to the decrees of the canons, and confirmed by our consent and the signature of our hands, shall attempt in any way to live or act, and try to break it, let him know that he is cut off from every priestly office and from our fellowship. May the divine grace, keeping us living in the unity of its holy Church, preserve us unharmed. This synod was held in the year of the incarnation of the Lord DCLXXIII.

units.la: Hactenus specimen Codicis Canonum BritanBritannicorum ex Beda. Fuit autem hic Theodorus Roma missus in Angliam, ut Archiepiscopus Doruvernensis esset, Patria Tharsensis, seculari & divina literatura & Græce instructus & Latine, ut de eo refert Beda eod. lib. 4. cap. I. Valde itaque probabile, illum Librum canonum quem ille protulit in concilio Herefordiensi, fuisse Codicem Canonum Ecclesiæ Romanæ; In allocutione enim ad Episcopos, rogat, si consentirent ea quæ à PATRIBUS CANONICE sunt ANTIQVITVS decreta; Respondent illi. Optime omnibus placere, quæ definiverunt SANCTORUM CANONES PATRUM. Quibus verbis satis innuere videntur eos intelligere antiquorum conciliorum canones; qui continebantur libro illo, quem Theodorus protulit in concilio. Illud unde habeat Justellus Præf. ad Cod. can. Eccles. univers. scripsisse Theodorum hunc Librum canonum, invenire non potui, saltem Beda ex quo sua probat, nil de eo tradit, & ex dictis magis probabile illum, ut jam conjectum, fuisse Codicem Romanæ Ecclesiæ; Deinde etiam ausim affirmare nec Theodorum hunc fuisse collectorem istius Codicis vel Libri; Idque ex eo conficio, quod in allocutione jam memorata Theodorus roget Episcopos, de iis, quæ à Patribus Canonice sunt ANTI-
units.tr: Thus far a specimen of the Code of the British canons, taken from Bede. This Theodore was sent from Rome into England to be Archbishop of Canterbury; he was a native of Tarsus, instructed both in secular and in sacred literature, in Greek and in Latin, as Bede reports in the same work, book 4, chapter 1. It is therefore very probable that the book of canons which he produced at the council of Hereford was the Code of canons of the Roman Church. For in his address to the bishops he asks whether they agreed to the decrees which had been canonically established by the ANCIENT FATHERS; they replied: It pleases us all well, what the HOLY CANONS OF THE FATHERS have decided. By these words they seem sufficiently to indicate that they understood the canons of the ancient councils, which were contained in that book which Theodore produced at the council. Where Justellus, in his Preface to the Code of the Canons of the Universal Church, got the claim that this Theodore wrote this book of canons, I have been unable to find; at least Bede, on whose testimony he rests his case, says nothing of it. And from what has been said, it is more probable, as conjectured already, that it was the Code of the Roman Church. Furthermore, I would venture to affirm that this Theodore was not the compiler of this Code or book either. I infer this from the fact that in the address already mentioned Theodore asks the bishops about those things which have been ANCIENTLY decreed canonically by the Fathers

units.la: 91. De Auctore hujus Codicis disquisitum, ubi negatur esse eū Theodorum Archiepiscopum
units.tr: 91. On the author of this Code, where it is denied that this Theodore was the Archbishop.

units.la: 92. Asseritur eum esse Codicem Ecclesiæ Romanæ;
units.tr: 92. It is asserted that it is the Code of the Roman Church.

units.la: 93. Probatur neque esse ab eo collectum.
units.tr: 93. It is proved that it was not compiled by him.

units.la: ANTIQVITVS DECRETA; Illis annuentibus, dicit significanter Beda, eum protulisse eundem Librum Canonum. Quæ antea antiquitus à Patribus decreta nominaverat, postea dicit se proferre in libro, aut eundem Librum se proferre qui continebat quæ à patribus antiquitus canonice sunt decreta. Neque etiam ausus fuisset Theodorus alium Codicem quam Romanum Ecclesiæ Britannicæ obtrudere, quia Inspector ei additus erat Adrianus Monachus; ut Doctrina, ait Beda l. c. cooperator existens, diligenter attenderet, ne quid ille contrarium veritati, fidei Græcorum more, in Ecclesiam cui præerat, introduceret. Ipsi etiam canones supra memorati satis conveniunt, ratione materiæ, cum canonibus antiquis, quod facile demonstrari posset, si quidem id otium & properans typographus nunc permitterent. Colligunt alii etiam aliquid de Codice Anglicanæ Ecclesiæ ex Leonis IV. Epistola in c. ex libellis, dist. 20, adi Justellum in Præfat. allegata. Ex Anglia in Germaniam properemus. Qualem hæc habuerint Codicem,& quam collectionem, non usque adeo clarum est. Certe pars ejus mature ad fidem Christianam conversa est, quo autem codice canonum usa sit primis temporibus, ob historicorum penuriam & silentium vix potest determinari. c Temporibus Riculphi Episcopi Moguntini, Isidori Mercatoris compilatio vel potius suppositio in Germaniam delata est, de qua re dicemus postea, ubi ad Isidori collectionem pervenerimus. Africa nobis quoque adeunda est, Ibi quoque Codex Canonum duplex in usu, ille universæ Ecclesiæ; deinde particularis quidam ex synodis Africanis compilatus. De Codice universæ Ecclesiæ in Ecclesiis Africanis usitato, facit fidem Collectio Fulgentii Ferrandi, Diaconi Ecclesiæ Carthaginiensis, de quo infra dicemus, quam ille ex conciliis supra memoratis, quæ in Codice Ecclesiæ Catholicæ continentur, composuit ac digessit; Habuit autem Latinam antiquam versionem, floruit enim Ferrandus cum Dionysio Exiguo sub Justiniano, qui novam Latinam ex Græco fonte fecit. Specialis Collectio canonum Ecclesiæ Africanæ, est ex conciliis propriis Africanis facta sequentibus.
units.tr: ANCIENT DECREES. When they had agreed, Bede significantly says that he produced the same Book of Canons. What he had earlier named decrees anciently made by the Fathers, he afterwards says he produces in a book, or that he produces the same Book which contained what the Fathers anciently decreed canonically. Nor would Theodore have dared to force upon the British Church another Code than the Roman one, since an overseer was assigned to him, Hadrian the monk; that he, as a co-worker, might carefully attend to the teaching, says Bede in the place cited, lest he introduce into the Church over which he presided anything contrary to the truth, in the manner of the Greeks in matters of faith. The canons mentioned above also agree well, in their subject matter, with the ancient canons, which could easily be demonstrated, if leisure and the hurrying printer permitted it now. Others also gather something about the Code of the English Church from the letter of Leo IV, in c. ex libellis, dist. 20; see Justellus in the Preface cited. Let us hasten from England into Germany. What Code and what collection these churches had is not so very clear. Certainly a part of them was converted early to the Christian faith, but what code of canons they used in the earliest times can hardly be determined, because of the scarcity and silence of the historians. In the times of Riculf, bishop of Mainz, the compilation or rather forgery of Isidore Mercator was brought into Germany; we shall speak of this matter later, when we come to the collection of Isidore. We must also visit Africa. There too two Codes of canons were in use: one of the universal Church, and then a certain particular one compiled from the African synods. The collection of Fulgentius Ferrandus, deacon of the Church of Carthage, of whom we shall speak below, attests to the Code of the universal Church used in the African churches; he composed and arranged it from the councils mentioned above, which are contained in the Code of the Catholic Church. He had the ancient Latin version, for Ferrandus flourished together with Dionysius Exiguus under Justinian, who made a new Latin version from the Greek source. The special collection of the canons of the African Church is made from the following councils of Africa itself.

units.la: I. Concilio Carthaginensi, post Conf. Honorii XII. & Theodosii VIII. an. Christi 419. cujus canones xxxiii. præmittuntur, idque ideo, quia in hoc concilio confirmatus est hic Codex Particularis Africanus.
units.tr: I. The Council of Carthage, held in the consulship of Honorius (for the twelfth time) and Theodosius (for the eighth), in the year of Christ 419, whose thirty-three canons are prefixed; and this for the reason that in this council this particular African Code was confirmed.

units.la: II. Concilio Hipponensi, Theodosio III. & Abundantio Coss. Anno Christi 393. habito. III. Car-
units.tr: II. The Council of Hippo, held in the consulship of Theodosius (for the third time) and Abundantius, in the year of Christ 393. III. Car-

units.la: III. Carthaginensi, Arcadio III. & Honorio II. Coss. Anno Christi. 394.
units.tr: III. The Council of Carthage, in the consulship of Arcadius (for the third time) and Honorius (for the second time), in the year of Christ 394.

units.la: IV. Carthaginensi, Cæsario & Attico Coss. Anno Christi 397, cujus memorantur canones xxiii.
units.tr: IV. The Council of Carthage, in the consulship of Caesarius and Atticus, in the year of Christ 397; its canons mentioned are twenty-three.
V. Another Council of Carthage, in the same consulship.

units.la: VI. Carthaginensi, post Conf. Honorii IV. & Eutychiani V. Anno Christi 399.
units.tr: VI. The Council of Carthage, in the consulship of Honorius (for the fourth time) and Eutychianus (for the fifth time), in the year of Christ 399.

units.la: VII. Carthaginensi, post Conf. Fl. Stilico-nis. Anno Christi 401. cujus sunt canones ix.
units.tr: VII. The Council of Carthage, in the consulship of Flavius Stilicho, in the year of Christ 401; its canons are nine.

units.la: VIII. Carthaginensi, Vincentio & Flavito Coss: eodem anno Christi, cujus sunt canones xx.
units.tr: VIII. The Council of Carthage, in the consulship of Vincentius and Flavitus, in the same year of Christ; its canons are twenty.

units.la: IX. Milevitano, Arcadio & Honorio V. Coss. Anno Christi 402. cujus memorantur canones v.
units.tr: IX. The Council of Milevis, in the consulship of Arcadius and Honorius (for the fifth time), in the year of Christ 402; its canons mentioned are five.

units.la: X. Carthaginensi, Theodosio & Rumori-do Coss. Anno Christi 403. cujus sunt canones vi.
units.tr: X. The Council of Carthage, in the consulship of Theodosius and Rumoridus, in the year of Christ 403; its canons are six.

units.la: XI. Carthaginensi, Honorio VI. Coss. Anno Christi 404. cujus tantum unicus est canon.
units.tr: XI. The Council of Carthage, in the consulship of Honorius (for the sixth time), in the year of Christ 404; of it only a single canon is extant.

units.la: XII. Carthaginensi, Stilicone II. & Anthemio Coss. Anno Christi 405. cujus quoque unicus tantum recensetur canon.
units.tr: XII. The Council of Carthage, in the consulship of Stilicho (for the second time) and Anthemius, in the year of Christ 405; of it likewise only a single canon is recorded.

units.la: XIII. Carthaginensi, Honorio VII. & Theodosio II. Coss. Anno Christi 407. cujus numerantur canones xii.
units.tr: XIII. The Council of Carthage, in the consulship of Honorius (for the seventh time) and Theodosius (for the second time), in the year of Christ 407; its canons are counted as twelve.

units.la: XIV. Carthaginensi, Basso & Philippo Coss. Anno Christi 408.
units.tr: XIV. Carthaginian council, with Bassus and Philippus as consuls, in the year of Christ 408.

units.la: XV. Carthaginensi, Honorio VII. & Theodosio III. Coss. Anno Christi 409.
units.tr: XV. Carthaginian council, with Honorius (for the seventh time) and Theodosius (for the third time) as consuls, in the year of Christ 409.

units.la: XVI. Carthaginensi, post Consulatum Honorii VIII. & Theodosii III. anno Christi 410.
units.tr: XVI. Carthaginian council, after the consulship of Honorius (for the eighth time) and Theodosius (for the third time), in the year of Christ 410.

units.la: XVII. Carthaginensi, Honorio XII. & Theodosio VIII. Coss. Anno Christi 418.
units.tr: XVII. Carthaginian council, with Honorius (for the twelfth time) and Theodosius (for the eighth time) as consuls, in the year of Christ 418.

units.la: XVIII. Carthaginensi, post Consulatum Honorii XII. & Theodosii VIII. Anno Christi 419. cujus sunt canones VII.
units.tr: XVIII. Carthaginian council, after the consulship of Honorius (for the twelfth time) and Theodosius (for the eighth time), in the year of Christ 419. It has seven canons.

units.la: Quæ concilia memorantur in actis concilii Carthaginensis supra primo loco positi, in quo hic Codex Africanus à CCXVII. est confirmatus. In fine enim primæ sessionis, quæ VIII. Kal. Jun. habita est, in qua etiam editi canones XXXIII. hæc leguntur.
units.tr: These councils are mentioned in the acts of the Council of Carthage placed first above, in which this African Code was confirmed by 217 bishops. For at the end of the first session, which was held on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, and in which thirty-three canons were also issued, the following is read.

units.la: Recitata sunt etiam in ista synodo diversa concilia universæ provinciæ Africæ transactis temporibus Aurelii Carthaginensis Episcopi celebrata.
units.tr: Also recited in this synod were the various councils of the whole province of Africa, celebrated in past times under Aurelius, bishop of Carthage.

units.la: Fuit itaque ante hæc tempora Codex ille, sed ab hoc tempore confirmatus auctoritate CCXVII. Episcoporum Africæ & publice receptus in tota Provincia, & actis concilii insertus, in quibus etiam hodie extat. Cardinalis Perronius in Respons. ad Magnæ Britanniæ Regem in utramque partem disquirit, an hæc collectio sit privati alicujus industria facta, an vero sit concilium aliquod, & prius magis probat, cum tamen posterius verius sit, probantibus id satis Editoribus Bibliothecæ juris Canonici veteris, in Præfatione. Ex eo, quod Dionysius Exiguus in Præfatione suæ collectionis, hosce canones Africanos, vocet Concilium Africanum, & in contextu incipit synodus apud Carthaginem Africanorum quæ constituit Canones CXXXVIII. Deinde quia in Capitularibus Caroli Magni & in aliis collectionibus Anonymis iidem canones sub titulo hoc, ex concilio Africano citati leguntur, quem titulum manuscripti codices, itemque codex Ecclesiæ Romanæ retinuerunt. Tertio Cresconius etiam in utraque collectione sua, cap. xxx. & CLIV. hanc synodum Africanam vocat, Concilium Carthaginense universale, non quod concilium totius Africæ dicœceseos velit indicare, tum enim omnia Carthaginensia potuisset vocare universalia, sed quia hoc ex pluribus conciliis Africanis compactum & compilatum erat. Porro nil evidentius dici potest, quam quod supra ex actis concilii Carthaginensis adductum est, esse hanc collectionē post illud concilium publicatam; quibus tandem addi potest, quod ante triginta canones hujus concilii dicitur: Deinde quæ in conciliis Africanis promulgata sunt, actis præsentibus inserta noscuntur. Græci etiam, ut postea patebit, & ex Photio, Zonara, Balsamone constat, hanc collectionem semper concilium Carthaginense vocant. Illud facile concesserim, ante concilium illud Carthaginense, in quo probata hæc collectio, à privato quodam vel potius à singulis Episcopis ad usum Ecclesiasticum factam esse; postquā autem in concilio probata fuit, non amplius pro privata collectione censeri debet. Scriptus est hic Codex, primum Lingua Latina, postea ex ea in Græcam ductus, quo auctore incertum est. Quamquam alii aliter censeant, arbitrantes Græce Africanos sua concilia scripsisse. Sed illi falluntur, quod satis ostendit Dionysius Exiguus, in Epistola suæ collectioni præmissa supra relata, ubi statuta dicit Sardicensis concilii atque Africani, quæ Latine sunt edita suis numeris cerni distincta, Dionysius quoque Alexandrinus Episcopus, synodicam Epistolam concilii Carthaginensis anno 254. tempore Cypriani habiti contra Novatum, Latine scriptam dicit apud Eusebium lib. 6. H. E. cap. 35. Epistolæ quidem Cornelii Episcopi Romani scriptæ ad Fabium Episcopum Ecclesiæ Antiochenæ, ad nos pervenerunt, quæ tum, illa quæ acta sunt in concilio Romæ habito, tum quæ ab omni-bus bus in Italia, in Africa, inque aliis locis de eo errore decreta fuerant, evidenter declarant, aliæ item extant Epistolæ Latino sermone à Cypriano & aliis, qui cum illo erant, in Africa compositæ. Lingua quoque Latina magis in Africa usitata quam Græca, quæ videtur cum Imperio Romano recepta esse cum lingua Punica, quæ postea rarior fuit ipsa Latina, quod vel unus Augustini locus, de verb. Apost. serm. 25. satis probat. Proverbium notum Panicum, quod quidem Latine vobis dicam, quia punice non omnes nostis; quod pluribus demonstratum vide apud Christ. Fustell. in Præfat. Codicis Canonum Ecclesiæ Africanæ, prope finem. Quando versus sit hic Codex in Græcum idioma incertum est. Postquam autem versus fuit, sub titulo Concilii Carthaginensis insertus est codici Ecclesiæ Orientalis, teste concilii Constantinopolitani VI. Oecumenici, anno 692. habiti, canone II; in quo concilia recepta in Oriente, interque ea Africana recensentur, quem ordinem etiam repræsentat Codex canonum Ecclesiæ Orientalis Joh. Tilii anno 1540. Græce editus. Facit quoque ad auctoritatem hujus codicis Africani particularis, quod in Codicem canonum Ecclesiæ Romanæ sit relatus & receptus. Fecit hoc primum Dionysius Exiguus, qui suæ versioni ex Græco Africana concilia, eodem ordine & numerorum serie distincta, inseruit, & codici Ecclesiæ universæ notabile hoc augmentum addidit. Justellus loco citato, putat Græcam versionem post tempora Dionysii Exigui factam esse, sed nullam suæ conjecturæ rationem adfert, potest dari ea, quod Dionysius Exiguus in sæpe laudata præfatione, dicat expresse post canones Calchedonenfis, Græcorum Canonum finem esse; se addere statuta Sardicensis concilii atque Africani. Ordo varius invenitur in hoc codice; In Dionysii Exigui editione ut & editione Græco Latina, omnes numeri canonum decurrunt, à primo usque ad centesimum trigesimum octavum. In Codice vero Ecclesiæ Romanæ, primo ponuntur xxxiii. canones concilii Carthaginensis, tum nova numeratione anteriorum conciliorum, in hoc concilio confirmatorum, canones recensentur centum & tres, qui cum memoratis triginta tribus juncti, eundem numerum centum & triginta octo canonum efficiunt. Græce & Latine edidit hunc codicem Christophorus Justellus primum anno 1614. Parisiis, doctissimasque notas adjecit; postea secundum filius, in bibliotheca juris canonici veteris, anno 1661. Editus autem est ex vetustissimo codice manuscripto Nicolai Fabri, quem suprema voluntate Justello commiserat, ut post editionem Magno Jacobo Augusto Thuano restitueretur, ut testatur Justellus in Epistola dedicatoria ad memoratum Thuanum, qua ei quoque suam editionem & notas inscribit. Graeca repraesentavit Justellus ex codice Tilii, quibus Manuscriptis usus sit, ostendit in principio notarum. Atque haec sunt fata codicis canonum Ecclesiae universae, cujus quanta fuerit auctoritas ex praedictis patet, quae evincunt fuisse quasi jus aliquot gentium receptum utrobique; Imo Justinianus in Novell. 131. tantam agnoscit quatuor synodorum Oecumenicarum, quae in codice canonum universae Ecclesiae habebantur, auctoritatem, ut non vereatur dicere. Τῶν γὰρ θεοφορημένων ἁγίων συνόδων καὶ τὰ δόγματα καθάπερ τὰς θείας γραφὰς δεχόμεθα καὶ τοὺς κανόνας ὡς νόμους φυλάττομεν. Praedictorum conciliorum dogmata, sicut divinas scripturas accipimus, & canones sicut leges servamus. Neque novum est, ut propter excellentiam haec concilia quatuor oecumenica prima comparentur scripturae sacrae, non quasi ejusdem plane auctoritatis cum scriptura habita sint, sed quod post eam maximum momentum & pondus habuerint in decidendis controverfiis religionis & ordinandis ritibus Ecclefiasticis. Ideoque Isidorus lib. 7. Etymol. cap. 16. quasi quatuor Euangelia, vel totidem Paradisi flumina, quatuor venerabiles synodos, totam principaliter fidem complectentes, esse dicit; non simpliciter euangelia, sed quasi euangelia, quod similitudinem quandam infert, nominat. Nimium progreditur Gregorius Papa Romanus, relatus in cap. sicut sancti dist. 15. Qui se, sicut sancti Euangelii quatuor libros, sic quatuor concilia suscipere & venerari fatetur. Itaque recte Doctiss. Rittershusius part. 1. Nov. cap. 2. n. 17. monet verba Imp. Justin. in d. Nov. 131. cum grano salis accipienda esse; ne scilicet ob id parem auctoritatem per omnia tribuamus quorumlibet conciliorum decretis, illa veneratione quae sacris debetur. Nam conciliis & horum canonibus credimus propter scripturam: sed scripturae sacrae, quae sit αὐτόπιστος propter se ipsam, quia divinitus est inspirata: Deinde Scriptura sacra infallibilem habet certitudinem; concilia vero non aliter, nisi quatenus ejus vestigiis insistunt, appositae Salvianus Massiliensis lib. 3. de provid. seu gubernatione Dei. in edit. Rittershusii. p. 68. Alia omnia, id est humana dicta, argumentis ac testibus indigent, Dei autem sermo ipse sibi testis est: quia necesse est, quidquid incorrupta veritas loquitur, incorincorruptum sit testimonium veritatis. Potissima tamen auctoritas concilio Nicæno delata, cujus venerabilis quædam & decisoria vis in singulis fere id sequentibus conciliis est firmata & repetita. Quare etiam merito ab eo exordium collectionis canonum constituitur. Quod agnovit quoque non obscure Isidorus, quando canones à temporibus Constantini cœpisse adserit. lib. 7. Etymol. c. 16. relatus à Gratiano in c. canones. dist. 15. Canones, inquit, generalium conciliorum à temporibus Constantini cœperunt. In præcedentibus namque annis persecutione fervente, docendarum plebium minime dabatur facultas. Inde Christianitas in diversas hæreses scissa est: quia non erat licentia Episcopis in unum conveniendi, nisi tempore supradicti Imperatoris. Ipse enim dedit facultatem Christianis libere congregari, sub hoc etiam sancti patres in concilio Nicæno, de omni orbe terrarum convenientes, juxta fidem Euangelicam & Apostolicam, secundum post Apostolos symbolum tradiderunt. Sed magnam nobis controversiam faciunt illli, qui non à Nicænis temporibus, ut à nobis factum, sed à temporibus Apostolicis canones deduci volunt, idque famosis, si non fumosis, Constitutionibus Apostolorum (quarum libros octo sub nomine Clementis, Romani Episcopi obtrudunt) dunt) deinde etiam 85. vel 90. canonibus Apostolorum, probare nituntur. Quare antequam ad alias digestiones & compilationes canonum transeamus, hæc collectio constitutionum Apostolicarum primum, dein & hi canones Apostolici ad examen revocandi sunt; Esse utrumque opus supposititium, falsique nominis & falsæ antiquitatis, evicit singulari commentario, invictisque in eo argumentis demonstravit, antiquitatis Ecclesiasticæ promus condus, Johannes Dalæus, in Pseudepigraphis Apostolicis, libris tribus. Quare nos summa capita tantum tangemus, & quæ in adversariis collegimus variorum judicia subnectemus; plura desiderantem lectorem ad ipsius Dalæi commentarios ablegantes. Adscribuntur autem constitutiones iltæ Apostolicæ Clementi Episcopo Romano; Primo (siquidem Petrus non fuit Romæ aut Episcopus Romanus) an tertio hic non longe disquiremus, quia non conveniunt hic historici, probamus interea opinionem adferentium, hunc Clementem cum Lino, & Cleto, eodem tempore suisse Romæ Compresbyteros, tanquam magis verisimilem. Esse eum cujus facit mentionem Paulus Apostolus in Epistol. ad Philip. c. 4. verf. 3. quidam censent. Annos eum tradunt in Episcopatu Romano transegisse novem & dimidium. Scripta varia ei tribuuntur pleraque adfinguntur. Epistolæ binæ ad Jacobum Fratrem Domini, qui septennio ante Petri Martyrium fatis jam concesserat. Deinde tres aliæ adhuc, quas omnes tot argumentis invincibilibus νοθείας convicit & peregit Magnus Blondellus, in Pseud- Isidoro & Turriano vapulante à pag. 1. usque ad 101. (ubi quoque ipsæ Epistolæ legi possunt) ut nemo amplius contra mutire possit. Præterea tribuuntur ei Epistolæ encyclicæ tres. Interpretatio Epistolæ S. Pauli Apostoli ad Hebræos; liturgia, Disputatio Petri & Appionis, Disputatio Petri contra falsitatem Simonis Magi, Libri decem Recognitionum, quæ & Odeporicon, vel circuitionum, vel periodorum, vel itinerarium Petri, vel à Beda Historiæ Clementis vocantur. Item constitutionum Apostolicarum seu præceptionum libri octo; quibus solent accedere Canones Apostolorum, Concionum Petri in populo suo habitarum compendium; De Responsionibus Petri ad interrogata Tripolitanorum, quæ pleraque in censum Apocryphorum sunt relata à Gelasio, in c. sancta Romana dist. 15. ab Hieronymo, Honorio Augustodunensi olim, postea etiam à plerisque Pontificiis, & Protestantibus, Riveto
units.tr: There was, then, a codex of this kind even before these times, but from this time it was confirmed by the authority of 217 bishops of Africa and was publicly received throughout the province. It was also inserted into the acts of the council, where it still stands today. Cardinal Perron, in his Response to the King of Great Britain, argues both sides of the question whether this collection was made by the diligence of some private person or whether it is the work of a council. He favours the first view, though the second is in fact the truer, as the editors of the Library of Ancient Canon Law, in their preface, sufficiently prove. First, Dionysius Exiguus, in the preface to his own collection, calls these African canons the African Council, and in the text he begins, "the synod at Carthage of the Africans, which enacted canons," (the canons numbering 138). Second, because in the Capitularies of Charlemagne and in other anonymous collections the same canons are cited under this title, from the African Council, a title which the manuscript codices as well as the codex of the Roman Church have retained. Third, Cresconius too, in both of his collections, chapters 30 and 154, calls this African synod the universal Council of Carthage. He did not mean that it was a council of the whole diocese of Africa, for in that case he could have called all the Carthaginian councils universal, but because it was put together and compiled from several African councils. Moreover, nothing can be said more clearly than what was cited above from the acts of the Council of Carthage, namely that this collection was published after that council. To these may finally be added the statement made before the thirtieth canon of this council: Then, the things that have been promulgated in the African councils are known to have been inserted in the present acts. The Greeks, too, as will be shown later, and as is established from Photius, Zonaras and Balsamon, always call this collection the Council of Carthage. I readily grant that before that Council of Carthage, in which this collection was approved, it was made by some private person, or rather by individual bishops, for ecclesiastical use. But once it was approved in the council, it ought no longer to be regarded as a private collection. This codex was written first in the Latin language and afterwards turned from it into Greek, by an author who is uncertain. Others, however, think otherwise, supposing that the Africans wrote their councils in Greek. But they are mistaken, as Dionysius Exiguus sufficiently shows in the epistle prefixed to his collection, cited above, where he speaks of the decrees of the Council of Sardica and of Africa, which were published in Latin, and are seen to be distinguished by their own numbers. Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, likewise says that the synodal letter of the Council of Carthage, held in the year 254 in the time of Cyprian against Novatus, was written in Latin. This is in Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book 6, chapter 35: Indeed the letters of Cornelius, bishop of Rome, written to Fabius, bishop of the church of Antioch, have come down to us, which clearly declare both what was done at the council held at Rome and what was decreed about that error by all the bishops in Italy, in Africa and in other places. There are also other letters, written in Africa in the Latin tongue by Cyprian and others who were with him. Moreover, the Latin language was more commonly used in Africa than Greek, which seems to have been received together with the Roman Empire alongside the Punic language. The Punic language later became rarer than Latin itself, as a single passage of Augustine, On the Words of the Apostle, sermon 25, sufficiently proves: a well-known Punic proverb, which I will tell you in Latin, since not all of you know Punic. This is demonstrated at greater length by Christophe Justel, in the preface to the Code of the Canons of the African Church, near the end. It is uncertain when this codex was translated into the Greek language. But after it was translated, it was inserted under the title Council of Carthage into the codex of the Eastern Church, as attested by canon 2 of the Sixth Ecumenical Council, held in the year 692, in which the councils received in the East are listed, and among them the African. The Codex of the Canons of the Eastern Church, published in Greek by John Tilius in 1540, also reproduces this order. The authority of this African codex in particular is also supported by the fact that it was carried over and received into the codex of canons of the Roman Church. This was first done by Dionysius Exiguus, who inserted the African councils into his Latin version of the Greek, in the same order and distinguished by the same series of numbers, and so added this notable enlargement to the codex of the whole Church. Justel, in the place cited, thinks the Greek version was made after the time of Dionysius Exiguus, but he offers no reason for his conjecture. It may be answered that Dionysius Exiguus, in the preface so often praised, says expressly after the canons of Chalcedon that this is the end of the Greek canons; he adds the decrees of the Council of Sardica and of Africa. The order is varied in this codex. In the edition of Dionysius Exiguus, as also in the Greek-Latin edition, all the numbers run on from the first to the hundred and thirty-eighth. In the codex of the Roman Church, however, the thirty-three canons of the Council of Carthage come first, and then, with a new numbering, the earlier councils confirmed in this council are listed, one hundred and three canons. These, joined with the thirty-three mentioned, make the same total of one hundred and thirty-eight canons. Christophe Justel first published this codex in Greek and Latin in Paris in 1614, and added most learned notes. Later his son published a second edition in the Library of the Ancient Canon Law in 1661. It was published from the very old manuscript codex of Nicolas Fabri, which Justel had entrusted to him by his last will, so that after the edition it might be returned to Jacques-Auguste de Thou, as Justel testifies in the dedicatory epistle to the said de Thou, in which he also dedicates to him his edition and notes. Justel reproduced the Greek from the codex of Tilius, and he shows which manuscripts he used at the beginning of the notes. These are the fortunes of the codex of canons of the universal Church, and the extent of its authority is clear from what has been said. These facts prove that it was in a sense received as a law of certain peoples on both sides. Indeed, Justinian in Novel 131 acknowledges so great an authority in the four ecumenical synods, which were held in the codex of canons of the universal Church, that he does not hesitate to say: [Τῶν γὰρ θεοφορημένων ἁγίων συνόδων καὶ τὰ δόγματα καθάπερ τὰς θείας γραφὰς δεχόμεθα καὶ τοὺς κανόνας ὡς νόμους φυλάττομεν] We accept the decrees of the holy synods, which were inspired by God, just as the divine Scriptures, and we keep their canons as laws. It is not new that, on account of their excellence, these four first ecumenical councils are compared to the Holy Scripture. This is not to say that they have been held to have exactly the same authority as Scripture, but that after it they have had the greatest weight and importance in deciding controversies of religion and in ordering ecclesiastical rites. Therefore Isidore, Etymologies, book 7, chapter 16, says that they are as if they were four Gospels, or as many rivers of Paradise, four venerable synods, which embrace the whole faith principally. He does not simply call them Gospels, but as if Gospels, since he names them by way of a certain likeness. Gregory the Pope of Rome goes too far, as cited in the chapter Sicut sancti, distinction 15, where he confesses that he receives and venerates the four councils just as the four books of the holy Gospel. Hence the most learned Rittershusius, Novels, part 1, chapter 2, number 17, rightly warns that the words of the emperor Justinian in the said Novel 131 must be taken with a grain of salt. We must not, that is, on that account attribute equal authority in every respect to the decrees of any councils, with that reverence which is owed to the sacred books. For we believe the councils and their canons on account of Scripture; but Scripture, which is self-credible [αὐτόπιστος] because of itself, since it is divinely inspired. Further, Holy Scripture has infallible certainty; the councils, however, have it only in so far as they follow its footsteps. Salvian of Marseilles, On the Providence or Government of God, book 3, in Rittershusius's edition, page 68, adds: All other things, that is, human sayings, need arguments and witnesses, but the word of God is itself its own witness, because whatever the uncorrupted truth speaks must be an uncorrupted testimony of the truth. Yet the chief authority was given to the Council of Nicaea, whose venerable and decisive force was confirmed and repeated in almost all the councils that followed it. Therefore the collection of canons rightly takes its beginning from that council. Isidore also clearly recognised this, when he asserts that the canons began from the times of Constantine, book 7 of the Etymologies, chapter 16, cited by Gratian in canones, distinction 15: The canons of the general councils began from the times of Constantine, he says. For in the preceding years, while persecution was raging, there was by no means an opportunity of teaching the people. Hence Christianity was split into various heresies, because bishops had no liberty to meet together, except in the time of the aforesaid emperor. For he himself gave Christians the opportunity to gather freely. Under him also the holy fathers, meeting in the Council of Nicaea from the whole world, delivered, in accordance with the Gospel and Apostolic faith, the creed, second after the Apostles. But those who want the canons to be derived not from the Nicene times, as we have done, but from the Apostolic times, cause us great controversy. They try to prove this by the notorious, if not smoky, Apostolic Constitutions, of which they foist eight books under the name of Clement, bishop of Rome, and then by the eighty-five or ninety canons of the Apostles. Therefore, before we pass to other arrangements and compilations of canons, this collection of Apostolic constitutions must first be brought to examination, and then these Apostolic canons. That both are spurious works, of false name and false antiquity, was proved by John Daillé, the storehouse of ecclesiastical antiquity, in a singular commentary, On the Apostolic Pseudepigrapha, in three books, with invincible arguments. Therefore we shall touch only the main points here, and subjoin the judgements of various writers, collected in our notes, sending the reader who desires more to the commentaries of Daillé himself. These Apostolic constitutions are ascribed to Clement, bishop of Rome. First (since Peter was neither at Rome nor bishop of Rome), I shall not discuss at length here whether this Clement was third, since the historians do not agree on this point. Meanwhile we approve, as more probable, the opinion of those who assert that this Clement was at Rome together with Linus and Cletus, at the same time, as co-presbyter. Some think he is the one whom the Apostle Paul mentions in the epistle to the Philippians, chapter 4, verse 3. They record that he spent nine and a half years in the Roman bishopric. Various writings are attributed to him, most of which are falsely fathered on him. Two letters are addressed to James, the brother of the Lord, who had already departed this life seven years before the martyrdom of Peter. Then three others, all of which Magnus Blondel refuted and destroyed by so many invincible arguments of spuriousness [νοθείας] in his Pseudo-Isidore and Turrianus being thrashed, from page 1 to page 101 (where the epistles themselves can also be read), so that no one can any longer murmur against it. Besides, three encyclical epistles are attributed to him; an interpretation of the Epistle of the Apostle Paul to the Hebrews; a liturgy; the Disputation of Peter and Apion; the Disputation of Peter against the falsehood of Simon Magus; the ten books of the Recognitions, which are also called the Odeporicon, or Of Circuits, or Of Periods, or Itinerary of Peter, or, by Bede, the History of Clement. Likewise the eight books of the Apostolic constitutions or commandments, to which the Canons of the Apostles usually belong; an epitome of Peter's sermons delivered to his people; and the Answers of Peter to the questions of the Tripolitans. Most of these were placed by Gelasius, in the chapter Sancta Romana, distinction 15, among the Apocrypha, and by Jerome, by Honorius of Autun formerly, and afterwards by most Papists and Protestants, and by Rivet

units.la: 108. Quæ ejus scripta, supposita & genuina lib. 1. Crit. sacr. c. 7. & 8. Rob. Coco. aliis̃que bene multis; Unicum adhuc genuinum cunctis, praeter Gathakerum Cinni pag. 19. hujus Auctoris monumentum superesse creditur, Epistola ejus prior ad Corinthios scripta, quam & laudat Hieronymus in Catalogo, eamque valde utilem & nonnullis locis publice lectam dicit, quaeque ei videtur Characteri epistolae quae sub Pauli nomine ad Hebraeos fertur, convenire. Laudant eam quoque Euseb. lib. 3. c. 12. Iren. lib. 3. c. 3. Clemens Alexandrin. lib. 4. 6. & 7. strom. Quam Baronius, Bellarminus, Miraeus, aliique periisse arbitrati sunt; sed cum fragmento secundae, A. 1633. Oxoniae in lucem producta est, ex reliquiis vetustissimi exemplaris Bibliothecae Regiae Anglicanae, notisque illustrata a Patritio Junio Viro Clariss: Regis Britanniarum Bibliothecario. Postea secundum edita & adserta est a Joach. Joh. Madero Helmaestadii 1654. quorum praefationes inspici possunt. Nobis cum constitutionibus & Canonibus Apostolicis nunc res est, quibus historica nostra collectio canonum impetitur. Hosce foetus esse suppositios nobis probandum. Varia de hisce constitutionibus sunt Doctorum judicia, quibusdam probantibus, quibusdam improbantibus & rejicientibus, quibusdam interpolatas
units.tr: 108. Of his writings, which are genuine and which spurious, see lib. 1. Crit. sacr. c. 7 and 8, Rob. Cocus, and many others. Only one genuine monument of this author is believed to survive for all, apart from Gathaker's Cinni, p. 19: his first epistle, written to the Corinthians, which Jerome also praises in his Catalogue, saying it is very useful and was read publicly in some places, and which seems to match the character of the epistle that is ascribed to Paul to the Hebrews. Eusebius, lib. 3 c. 12, Irenaeus, lib. 3 c. 3, and Clement of Alexandria, lib. 4, 6 and 7 Stromata, also praise it. Baronius, Bellarmine, Miraeus and others thought it had perished. But together with a fragment of the second, it was brought to light at Oxford in 1633, from the remains of a very old copy in the Royal Library of England, and illustrated with notes by Patrick Junius, most distinguished librarian to the King of Britain. Afterwards it was published a second time and defended by Joachim Johann Mader at Helmstedt in 1654; their prefaces may be consulted. Now we have to deal with the Apostolic Constitutions and Canons, on which our historical collection of canons is attacked. We must prove that these offspring are spurious. Learned men have varied judgments on these Constitutions: some approve them, some disapprove and reject them, and some cry out that they have been interpolated.

units.la: 105. Varia judicia de constitutionibus Apostolicis tas clamantibus. Inter Euangelicos uno ore hæc sententa resedit, & invictis argumentis adserta est, mentiri has constitutiones nomen & ætatem Apostolicam. Pontificiorum quidam probant, quidam in totum rejiciunt. Probantium sunt paucissimi, & plerique vel obscuri vel quos partium studium adversus nos agit præcipites. Inter hos præcipui sunt & alicujus nominis Carolus Bovius Episcopus Ostunensis, qui eas in Latinum transtulit, & anno LXIII. seculi superioris edidit. Franciscus Turrianus Jesuita, Famosus defensor istiusmodi quisquiliarum, qui easdem Latine vertit. Item Th: Stapletonus Jesuita; qui quod parum à blasphemia abest, in def. Eccl. author. lib. 2. c. 11. non veretur de iis adserere, Librum harum constitutionum, Spiritu Apostolico plenissimum esse. & in princ. fid. doct. contr. 5. q. 2. art. 5. nullam rationem obstare, quin si præsens Ecclesia referret has Constitutiones Apostolicas, à Clemente editas in canonem sacræ scripturæ; nos eas pro canonicis admittere debeamus, æque atque Epistolam Jacobi. Ejusdem tenoris sunt hæc Alani Copi. dial. 3. c. 5. pag. m. 232. Summo Dei beneficio Clementis διαταξεις & Cyrilli καταχρησεις, multis seculis recondita, ad reprimendam Magdeburgensium & Apologeticorum istam contra sanctos insolentiam in lucem prodierunt. runt. Quorum certe testimonia, etiamsi alii deessent, homini non nimis præfracto, ad hanc notam, qua de agitur, quæstionem sufficere possent. Alios qui superstitiones iis fulcire conantur, easque probant, vid. apud Rob. Cocum. in Censura scriptorum veterum, non longe à principio. Alii contra Doctiores & emunctioris in literis nasi è Pontificiis, nobiscum sentiunt esse supposititias. Inter quos est Bellarminus de script. Eccles. in Clemente, ubi Clementis Recognitiones cum inter Apocrypha retulisset, subjicit. De libris con-stitutionum Apostolicarum, quæ Clementi auctori tribuuntur, idem fere judicium fieri debet, ac de libris recognitionum. addit porro: Mul-ta in illis utilia sunt, & à Græcis veteribus magni fiunt; sed in Ecclesia Latina nullum fere nomen habere, ipsosque etiam posteriores Græcos in concilio Trullano can. 2. improbare has constitutiones, ut ab hæreticis depravatas. Audio Æthiopes his constitutionibus uti, ut vere A-postolicis, & ea de causa in erroribus versari circa cultum Sabbati & diei Dominicæ, & circa ministrum Sacramenti baptismi, & in aliis qui-busdam dogmatibus. Nam lib. 7. cap. 24. jubent servari diem Sabbati & Dominicæ, & lib. 5. constit. cap. 10. prohibetur absolute, ne laici baptizent, & lib. 6. cap. 15. jubent rebaptizari eos, qui baptizantur ab hæreticis, ea de causa, quia haeretici non sunt Sacerdotes. Ac ne forte objiceretur, quod Philippus Diaconus baptizabat, ut dicitur Act. 8. in iisdem constitutionibus lib. 6. cap. 7. dicitur Philippum, qui baptizavit Simonem magum, fuisse Apostolum, quod manifeste falsum est. Habentur in iisdem Constitutionibus alia non pauca, quae abhorrere videntur à veritate: ut quod lib. 3. cap. 2. quartas nuptias appellent manifestam fornicationem. lib. 5. cap. 6. distinguant Mariam Magdalenam à Maria sorore Lazari. lib. 8. cap. 14. Jacobum fratrem Domini velint esse Apostolum ex duodecim, & lib. eodem c. 26. 27. & 28. velint imponi manum Subdiacono, & Lectori, & ipsi etiam Diaconissae, dum ordinantur: & lib. eodem cap. 32. dicant, Exorcistas non ordinari, & cap. 38. dicant, ancillam soli domino obsequentem recipi; si cum aliis intemperans fuerit, rejici. In eadem sententia est Baronius, ad ann. 32. §. 18. Ubi quaedam cum sibi ex his libris de Maria Magdalena objecisset, tanquam diversa à Maria Lazari sorore. Uno verbo, inquit, his liberari possemus, si apocryphum esse librum exciperemus. Sane quidem, si haec dicta sunt à Clemente, quomodo ea latere potuerunt tot antiquos Patres, qui de ea re scripserunt? Cum praesertim tanti Auctoris praecipua fuerit auctoritas in Ecclesia; ut licet ejus Epistola ad Corinthios scripta penitus exciderit; tamen quod saepius citata reperiatur, pene revivisçat integra in fragmentis. Idem quoque ad ann. 44. §. 36. Apocryphis accenset. adde eum ad annum 102. §. 9. Neque abit ab his judicium Jacobi Davii Perronii Cardinalis, lib. 2. c. 1. de Eucharistia pag. 174. ubi hæc de opere constitutionum habet. Hoc opus à multis gra-vibus auctoribus veteris ac recentioris memoriæ in dubium vocatur. Epiphanius Hæres. Audian. libri meminit id nomen præferentis, aitque multos suo tempore in dubium revocare, se vero eum nequaquam rejicere. Synodus Constantinopoli in Trullo, multis post Epiphanium temporibus sub Justiniano Rhitnotmeto habita, opus condemnat. Photius in Bibl. cod. 113. ipsa illa synodo recen-tior, vix Arianismo purgari posse ait. Quod suspicari cogit librum hunc vel non eundem esse, cum eo qui Epiphanii tempore hoc nomine censebatur, vel certe ab Arianis postea corruptum adulteratumque fuisse. Sane multa apud veteres inde descripta reperiuntur, quæ cum iis quæ nunc circumferuntur exemplaribus non congruunt. Cardinalis Bessario Marco Ephesio, Sixt. Senens. in biblioth. sanct. quendam ex his Constitutionibus locum objectanti, respondet opus esse Apocryphum. Idem lib. 1. Replic. cap. 24. Quæ Clementis nomine Apostolicæ constitutiones circumferuntur, non sunt ejus fidei, ut in rebus ad religionem pertinentibus, auctoritatem habeant decisivam sive sive enim ab initio Clementis nomine suppositus, sive ab haereticis postea interpolatus atque adulteriatus fuerit hic liber, constat suspectam ejus esse auctoritatem. Margarinus de la Bigne, editor bibliothecae Patrum, tomo 3. in Anast. Nic. q. in script. col. 44. in margine pro Apocryphis habet has constitutiones Clementis, & Gabriel Albaspinaeus obs. Eccles. lib. I. c. 13. p. 37. Non tantum Apocryphas censet, sed insuper eos, qui aliter sentiunt, stultitiae insimulat, tacite supramemoratos perstringens. Haec autem sunt ejus verba. Certe si quis esset qui canones Apostolorum, & Divi Clementis Constitutiones Apostolorum auctoritate sancitas publicatasve certo affirmaret, imperitus censeretur. Nam qui antiquarum consuetudinum gnari, quo quidque tempore, aut loco observari desitum sit, aut mutari coeptum norunt, de iis ne quidem dubitare possunt. Quod ille postea pluribus ostendit, & nos infra ostendemus. Eandem sedisse Doctissimo Jesuitae Petavio sententiam patet, quia ad locum Epiphanii agnoscit alias fuisse constitutiones illas Apostolorum, quam quae hodie libris octo circumferuntur, quae tamen etiam dubiae habitae sunt; nec ea etiam in hodiernis, imo contraria inveniri. Et ad eundem Epiphan. in Expos. Fid. pag. 349. & 360. expresse Pseudodiataxin Clementis vocat. & in Dogmatis Theolog. tom. 2. lib. i. de Trinit. c. 3. §. 7. pag. 15. Potestat, inquit, ante omnes illos, nempe Athenagoram Tatianum, Theophilum, Ireneum, vetustatis unius nomine commemorari Clemens Romanus; siquidem Germana essent, quæ illius inscripta nomine circumferuntur, sed non sunt. Hic igitur in constitutionibus Apostolicis ridiculum nescio quid & hæreticum posuit. Quod nos postea in argumentis adducemus. Non necesse est, plures ex recentioribus addere, è choro Pontificorum, isti memorati eruditione & nominis claritate omnes vincunt. Hi itaque si constitutiones has Clementis nomen mentientes, pro dubiis, incertis, a-pocryphis, falsis, corruptis, adulteratis, & nullius in religionis fidei, vel auctoritatis adserant, & merito nos è numero canonum & juris Ecclesiastici dejicimus, nec ab iis nostram Historiam & Canonum collectionem ordimur. Antiquorum judicia etiam addemus, Humbertus Cardinalis, Episcopus Sylvæ Candidæ, qui vixit seculi xi. anno liv. fuitque legatus Pontificis Constantinopolim, Nicætæ Pectorato, in Tractatu contra hunc Nicetam scripto tom. 4. biblioth. Patr. part. 2. p. 243. a. b. & in append. tom. 11. Annal. Bar. quædam loca ex his constitutionibus objicienti, respondet, eum sua adserere ex Apocryphis libris, & canonibus pari sententia sancto-
units.tr: 105. Varied judgments on the Apostolic Constitutions. Among the evangelical writers this opinion has settled with one voice, and it has been asserted with unconquered arguments: that these Constitutions falsely claim the name and the apostolic age. Few of the Papists approve them, and some reject them altogether. Those who approve them are very few, and most of them are obscure, or are headlong partisans who act against us out of party zeal. Among these the chief is Carolus Bovius, bishop of Ostuni, a man of some reputation, who translated them into Latin and published them in the sixty-third year of the last century. Franciscus Turrianus, a Jesuit, a famous defender of this sort of trifle, also translated them into Latin. Likewise Thomas Stapleton, a Jesuit, who, in Def. Eccl. author. lib. 2. c. 11., is not ashamed (coming close to blasphemy) to assert about them: that the book of these Constitutions is most full of the Apostolic Spirit, and, in princ. fid. doct. contr. 5. q. 2. art. 5.: that there is no reason why, if the present Church were to receive these Apostolic Constitutions, published by Clement, into the canon of Sacred Scripture, we should not admit them as canonical, just as we admit the Epistle of James. Of the same tenor are these words of Alanus Copus, dial. 3. c. 5. p. 232.: By the great goodness of God, the διαταξεις of Clement and the καταχρησεις of Cyril, hidden away for many centuries, have come to light to repress the insolence of the Magdeburgians and Apologists against the saints. Their testimonies, even if there were no others, could certainly suffice to settle the question at issue for a man not too obstinate. As for those who try to prop up superstitions with them and approve them, see Rob. Cocus, in Censura scriptorum veterum, not far from the beginning. Others, on the contrary, among the more learned Papists, of more discerning taste in letters, agree with us that they are spurious. Among these is Bellarmine, de script. Eccles. in Clemente, where, after listing Clement's Recognitions among the Apocrypha, he adds: Concerning the books of the Constitutions of the Apostles, which are attributed to Clement as author, roughly the same judgment should be made as for the books of the Recognitions. He adds further: Many useful things are in them, and they are held in high regard by the ancient Greeks; but in the Latin Church they have almost no reputation, and even the later Greeks in the Council in Trullo, canon 2, disapproved these Constitutions as corrupted by heretics. I hear that the Ethiopians use these Constitutions as truly apostolic, and for this reason they err concerning the observance of the Sabbath and the Lord's Day, concerning the minister of the sacrament of baptism, and in certain other doctrines. For book 7, chapter 24, orders that the Sabbath and the Lord's Day be kept; and book 5, chapter 10, absolutely forbids laymen to baptize; and book 6, chapter 15, orders those baptized by heretics to be rebaptized, for the reason that heretics are not priests. And lest someone object that Philip the deacon baptized, as is said in Acts 8, the same Constitutions, book 6, chapter 7, say that Philip, who baptized Simon the magician, was an Apostle, which is manifestly false.
