Many other things in the same Constitutions seem far removed from the truth: for example, book 3, chapter 2, calls fourth marriages manifest fornication; book 5, chapter 6, distinguishes Mary Magdalene from Mary, the sister of Lazarus; book 8, chapter 14, wants James the brother of the Lord to be one of the twelve Apostles; and in the same book, chapters 26, 27 and 28, wants the hand to be laid on the subdeacon, the reader, and even the deaconess when they are ordained; and in the same book, chapter 32, says that exorcists are not ordained; and chapter 38 says that a maidservant who serves only the master is received, but if she is intemperate with others, she is rejected. Baronius is of the same opinion, ad ann. 32. §. 18. When someone objected to him some things from these books about Mary Magdalene, as different from Mary the sister of Lazarus, he said: In a word, we could be freed from these difficulties if we declared the book to be apocryphal. Indeed, if these things were said by Clement, how could they have remained hidden from so many ancient Fathers who wrote on that matter? Especially since the authority of so great an author was pre-eminent in the Church; so that, although his epistle to the Corinthians has entirely perished, yet because it is found cited so often, it is almost revived whole in its fragments. Baronius also counts it among the Apocrypha ad ann. 44 §. 36; add that he does so ad annum 102 §. 9. Nor does the judgment of Cardinal Jacques Davy du Perron differ from these, lib. 2 c. 1 de Eucharistia p. 174, where he says this about the work of the Constitutions: This work is called into doubt by many grave authors of old and recent memory. Epiphanius, Haer. Audian., mentions a book bearing this name and says that many in his time called it into question, though he himself by no means rejects it. The Council of Constantinople in Trullo, held many years after Epiphanius under Justinian Rhinotmetus, condemns the work. Photius, in Bibl. cod. 113, says that even that council, more recent than the time of Epiphanius, could hardly be purged of Arianism. This compels us to suspect that this book is either not the same one that bore this name in Epiphanius's time, or certainly that it was later corrupted and adulterated by the Arians. Indeed many passages drawn from it are found in the ancient writers which do not agree with the copies now in circulation. Cardinal Bessarion, against Marcus of Ephesus, and Sixtus of Siena, in the Bibliotheca sancta, when someone objected a passage from these Constitutions, replied that the work is apocryphal. The same, lib. 1 Replic. cap. 24: The Constitutions circulating under Clement's name are not of such trustworthiness that they have decisive authority in matters pertaining to religion; for whether this book was from the beginning falsely ascribed to Clement, or was later interpolated and adulterated by heretics, it is agreed that its authority is suspect. Margarinus de la Bigne, editor of the Bibliotheca Patrum, tomo 3, in Anast. Nic. q. in script. col. 44, in the margin lists these Constitutions of Clement among the Apocrypha; and Gabriel Albaspinaeus, Obs. Eccles. lib. 1 c. 13 p. 37, not only judges them apocryphal, but also charges with folly those who think otherwise, tacitly striking at the authors just mentioned. His words are these: Certainly, if anyone were to affirm for certain that the canons of the Apostles and the Constitutions of the Apostles of St. Clement were sanctioned or published by apostolic authority, he would be judged ignorant. For those who know the ancient customs, and know at what time and place each practice ceased to be observed or began to be changed, cannot even doubt about them. This he later showed at greater length, and we shall show below. It is clear that the most learned Jesuit Petavius held the same opinion, since at the passage of Epiphanius he acknowledges that there were other Constitutions of the Apostles than those which today circulate in eight books, and that even these were regarded as doubtful, nor are they found in the present text, indeed the contrary. And at the same Epiphanius, in Expos. Fid. p. 349 and 360, he expressly calls them the spurious Diataxis of Clement; and in Dogmatis Theolog. tom. 2, lib. 1, de Trinit. c. 3 §. 7 p. 15, he says: Before all those, namely Athenagoras, Tatian, Theophilus and Irenaeus, Clement of Rome is mentioned for the sake of his antiquity alone; for if the works circulating under his name were genuine, they would be; but they are not. He therefore put in the Apostolic Constitutions I know not what ridiculous and heretical matter. Which we shall afterwards adduce in our arguments. It is not necessary to add more from the recent writers of the company of the Papists: those men mentioned above surpass all others in learning and in reputation. If, then, these men assert that the Constitutions which falsely bear Clement's name are doubtful, uncertain, apocryphal, false, corrupted, adulterated, and of no authority in matters of religion and faith, and rightly we cast them from the number of canons and ecclesiastical law, and we do not base our history and collection of canons on them. We shall also add the judgments of the ancients. Humbert, Cardinal and Bishop of Silva Candida, who lived in the eleventh century, in the year 1054, and was the Pope's legate at Constantinople, when Nicetas Pectoratus objected certain passages from these Constitutions, in his treatise against this Nicetas, written and printed in tom. 4, Bibl. Patr., part 2, p. 243 a, b, and in the appendix to tom. 11, Annal. of Baronius, replies that he asserts these things from apocryphal books, and rejects them with a like judgment of the holy

units.la: {1} Antiquorum judicia Latinorum. sanctorum Patrum repudiatis ; Nam Clementis Librum, id est, Itinerarium Petri, & canones Apostolorum numeravere inter Apocrypha, exceptis capitulis quinquaginta, quae decreverunt regulis Orthodoxiae adjungenda. Unde nos quoque omne Apocryphon abjicientes dedignamur audire eorum fabulosas traditiones, quia non sunt ut Lex Domini. Ex quo loco & id videtur notandum, Humbertum non recognitionum opus, & itinerarium Petri, nomine Clementis editum, ut fecit & censet Bellarminus; sed libros constitutionum & itinerarium Petri, ut vocatur, pro iisdem habere, & à Gelasio inter apocrypha relatum putare. Quod quidem numerus librorum confirmare videtur; nam recognitionum libri referuntur decem, Itinerarii ut & Constitutionum Libri octo. Quod si verum, jam pateret saeculi quinti anno 94, ab Ecclesia Romana inter Apocrypha relatas has Constitutiones Pseudapostolicas Humbertum censuisse; quam ejus sententiam videntur innuere haec verba jam citata: Pari sententia sanctorum Patrum repudiatis. Ante haec Gelasii tempora, nulla extat memoria constitutionum harum Apostolicarum sub nomine Clementis editarum: non apud Hieronymum in Catalogo; quod satis arguit ei notas non fuisse; ut vana & falsa sit conjectura Bovii & Turriani in Præfa-tione ad has Constitutiones, quando hos libros ab Hieronymo, ut concilient eis au-ctoritatem, versos suspicantur. Cum apud omnes in confesso sit, à nato Christo usque ad Hieronymum in quatuor seculis in-ter Latinos nullum fecisse harum constitu-tionum mentionem, quod tamen fieri de-buisset, si auctor fuisset Clemens, isque Episcopus Romanus. Æthiopes habent has constitutiones pro vere Apostolicis, teste Bellarm. de script. Eccles. A. D. 29. in Cle-mente. Quod firmat Alvares in suo de Abyssinis libro. c. 81. extr. in vol. navig. di Gioan. Batt. Ramusio, ubi narrat Æthiopes habere librum in octo partes divisum, quem ab universis Apostolis Hierosolyma congregatis scriptum ferunt: quemque ipsi vulgo Manda & Abetilis vocant. Quæ bene conveniunt cum constitutionibus Pseudapostolicis, quarum etiam feruntur libri octo. Sed an idem sit liber ille apud Æthiopes, & eadem referat, quæ Constitutiones Apostolicæ à Bovio & Turriano versæ, illud non est proditum.
units.tr: {1} The judgments of the Latin ancients: rejected by the holy Fathers. For they counted the Book of Clement, that is, the Itinerary of Peter, and the canons of the Apostles among the Apocrypha, except for fifty chapters, which they decided were to be added to the rules of orthodoxy. Hence we too, rejecting every apocryphal writing, disdain to hear their fabulous traditions, because they are not like the Law of the Lord. From this passage it also seems worth noting that Humbert did not take the work of the Recognitions and the Itinerary of Peter, published under the name of Clement, as Bellarmine does and holds; rather, he regarded the books of the Constitutions and what is called the Itinerary of Peter as the same work, and thought that Gelasius had listed it among the apocrypha. The number of books seems to confirm this, for the books of the Recognitions are reckoned at ten, while the Itinerary and the books of the Constitutions are both eight. If this is true, it would be plain that Humbert judged these Pseudo-Apostolic Constitutions to have been listed among the Apocrypha by the Roman Church in the year 494, in the time of Gelasius; and the words already cited, rejected by the holy Fathers in the same way, seem to hint at this view. Before the time of Gelasius there is no trace of these Apostolic Constitutions published under Clement's name: not in Jerome's Catalogue, which sufficiently shows that he did not know them. So the conjecture of Bovius and Turrianus in the Preface to these Constitutions is vain and false, when they suspect that Jerome translated these books in order to lend them authority. It is agreed by all that from the birth of Christ down to Jerome, through four centuries, no Latin made any mention of these Constitutions, although they should have done so if Clement, who was Bishop of Rome, had been their author. The Ethiopians hold these Constitutions to be truly Apostolic, according to Bellarmine, On Ecclesiastical Writers, under Clement, number 29. Alvares confirms this in his book on the Abyssinians, chapter 81 near the end, in the volume of voyages of Giovanni Battista Ramusio, where he relates that the Ethiopians have a book divided into eight parts, which they say was written by all the Apostles gathered together at Jerusalem, and which they commonly call Manda and Abetilis. These agree well with the Pseudo-Apostolic Constitutions, of which eight books are also reported. But whether that book among the Ethiopians is the same, and contains the same things as the Apostolic Constitutions translated by Bovius and Turrianus, has not been reported.

units.la: Græci nunquam hasce constitutiones æstimarunt; ut falsus sit Bellarminus l. c. qui Græcis veteribus magni fieri scribit, apud Latinos nullius esse nominis. Antiquissima constitutionum Apostolicarum mentio apud Epiphanium, phanium, qui floruit seculi quarti, anno 75. Hic variis locis eas laudat; quas tamen ipse Hæresi 70. §. 10. dubias apud multos, fidei fuisse, dicit. Loca ipsa congessit & examinat late Doctissimus Dalæus in Pseudepigraphis Apostol. lib. 1. cap. 2. probatque cum Petavio, quia multa ex citatis ab Epiphanio in hodiernis Bovii & Turriani constitutionibus non, imo contraria inveniuntur, non esse easdem Epiphanii & Bovianas constitutiones Apostolicas; Ideoque turpiter abuti & fallere incautos Turrianum, auctoritate Epiphanii, dum adserit in proœmio versionis suæ Latinæ. Tales habere nostram ætatem Apostolorum Constitutiones, sanas scilicet & incorruptas, quales Epiphanii ætas habuit. Probat deinde multis invictissimis argumentis, neque Constitutiones Apostolicas quas Epiphanius habuit, pro Apostolicis esse habendas, aut receptas ab Ecclesia aut pro apostolicis habitas, sed & ipsas falsas & Apostolis adfictas esse. Producit quoque Bovius pro suis Constitutionibus Cyrillum Hierosolymitanum, qui in Catechef. 18. p. 213. ex Clemente recenset fabulam Phœnicis, quasi hæc ex quinto libro Constitutionum apostolicarum sit decerpta: sed & is in eo falsus est. Invenitur enim hæc fabula in genuina & ab Hieronymo nymo aliisque sæpius laudata Clementis epistola ad Corinthios priore, ex qua desumsit auctor Catecheseos eam, quod ex collatione phrasium & verborum satis patet ; utitur enim sæpe iisdem verbis, quæ reperiuntur apud Clementem in Epistola ad Corinthios, non vero iis quæ in constitutionibus Bovianis leguntur ; quare, sola hac diversitate observata, Doctissimus Rigaltius in obs. ad lib. Tertull. de resurrectione, diversos auctores Epistolæ & Constitutionum facit. Etsi, inquit, ejusdem Phœnicis historia exemplum reperiatur etiam in Constitutionibus supra citatis, tamen ex earum cum epistola Clementis comparatione hoc videmur adsequi, vix esse, ut ejusdem auctoris utrumque opus censeri debeat. Aliud testimonium ex Athanasio & Eusebio detortum de libro, qui διδαχὴ τῶν ἀποστόλων olim vocatus, apud quosdam in usu, communiter tamen pro spurio habitus & reprobatus fuit, nil facit ad Constitutiones Apostolicas Bovianas, quoniam ex ipso Athanasio patet, Clementis opera & haec διδαχὰς ἀποστόλων esse diversas, nec etiam Eusebium lib. 3. c. 25, edit. Gr. Christophorsoni. c. 19. eas adscribere Clementi, quia in aliis locis ubi expresse de Clementinis scriptis genuinis & spuriis agit, haec διδαχὰς ἀποστόλων ei non adscribit. vid. eum lib. 3. c. 57. 58. & 59. Verum itaq; est, quatuor primis seculis nullam fieri mentionem apud quenquam Græcorum Constitutionum Apostolicarum ; deinde quarum meminit Epiphanius, eas non fuisse receptas & probatas pro apostolicis, neque etiam esse easdem cum Bovianis. Antiquissima mentio occurrit in Concilio Constantinopolitano in Trullo, habito an. 692; in quo à patribus ibidem congregatis, can. 2. rejiciuntur. Canonis verba sunt hæc: Ταῖς τ᾽ ἁγίων Ἀποστόλων Διατάξεις πάλαι ὑπὸ τ᾽ ἑτεροδόξων ὅπὶ λύμῃ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας νόθα πινὰ ἢ ξένα τῆς εὐσεβείας παρενετέθησαν, τὸ ἀπηχεπὲς καὶ λῶν τῶν θείων δογμάτων ἡμῖν ἀμαυρώσαντα, τῶν τοιούτων Διατάξεων ἀποφόρως ἀποβολῶ πεπιστεύμεθα πρὸς τὸ ἢ χρισιανικωτάτης ποιμνίς οἰκοδομὴν καὶ ἀσφάλειαν, ἱδαμῶς ἐγκεῖνοντες τὰ τ᾽ αἱρετικῆς ψιθυρολογίας κινήματα, καὶ τῇ γνησίᾳ τῶν Ἀποστόλων καὶ ὁλοκλήρῳ διδαχῇ παρενείροντες. His Apostolorum per Clementem Constitutionibus jam olim ab iis qui à fide aliena sentiunt, ad Labem Ecclesiæ aspergendam, adulterina quedam & à pietate aliena introducta sunt, quæ divinorum nobis decretorum elegantem at decoram speciem obscurarunt, has Constitutiones ad Christianissimi gregis ædificationem ac securitatem conducibiliter REJECIMUS, hæretica falsitatis fœtus. fœtus nequaquam admittentes, & germanæ ac integræ Apostolorum doctrinæ inserentes. Post hos Patres earum meminit Photius in Bibloth. Cod. 113. qui vera argumenta, quare rejicienda essent vidit, sed studio partium contra Latinos, qui ex iis oppugnari poterant, excusari posse contendit. Post hunc plerique omnes Græci rejiciunt, uno aut altero excepto, qui ob idem partium studium contra Romanos iis utuntur. Balsamo, qui in fine seculi duodecimi scripsit, ad Canon. 85. Pseudapostol. hæc de iis habet. Συ δὲ γινώσκεις ὡς εἰ καὶ γέγεγραπται ἐντευθεν ἀναγινώσκειν ἡμᾶς τὰς Διαταγὰς τῶ Κλήμεντος, ὥλιω μὴ δημοπιδεῖν αὐτὰς, ἀλλ' ὁ δὲ κανὼν τῆς ἑκτης συνόδου ἀπηγόρευσε τὴν τῶν ἀναγνώσιν, ᾿Διὸ τὸ γενέσθαι παρωμοίωσιν ἐν αὐτοῖς. Tu autem intelligas, quod etsi hic scriptum est, Constitutiones Clementis legi à nobis, sed non divulgari debere, synodi tamen sextæ canon secundus earum lectionem prohibuit, quod in eis adulteratio facta sit. In eundem Canonem Zonaras hæc habet. Αὕτη τῶν κανονδόξων τινῶν, ἐνοφευτησάν τε καὶ παρεφθάρησαν. διὸ ἡ ἀναγινώσκεσθαι ὅλως αὐτὰς ἀπηγόρευσεν ἡ εκκλησιαστικὴ ἕκτη συνόδῳ. Ab heterodoxis & sectariis quibusdam adulteratæ & corruptæ fuerunt. Quapropter istas omnino legi vetuit Oecumenica sexta synodus. Similia habet Alexius Aristenus apud Usserium disser. de Ignat. ὁ δευτερ⸗ κανὼν τῆς ἐν Τρέλλῳ γνωμένης ἕκτης συνόδῳ παντελῶς ἀποβάλλειν τὰς ποιεῖτας διαταγάς, ἃ ἐν αὐταῖς ὑπὸ τ᾽ ἑτεροδόξων ψευδῶς ἐγκεῖ- σθαί τινα νόθα καὶ ξένα τῆς εὐσεβείας. Secundus canon synodi sextae in Trullo habitae, hasce Constitutiones omnino rejicit, propterea quod iis non- nulla adulterina ab heterodoxis adjecta fuerint atque à pietate aliena. Ut quoque sciamus quid Moderni Græci de hisce sentiant, ado Heremiæ Patriarchæ Constantinop. judicium ex ejus Resp. I. c. 13. p. 103. ad Wirtenbergenses. νενοθεύσθαι τὰς Κλημεντείας διατάξεις, adulteratas fuisse Clementinas Constitutiones. Ex quibus testimoniis videmus quid de hisce Pseudapostolicis Constitutionibus censuerint Græci quid Latini, quid Antiqui, quid recentiores; nempe esse eas spurias, confictas, suppositas, depravatas, heterodoxiis maculatas, & uno verbo apocryphas, inter quas etiam habet noster Antonius Augustus in Dialogo 6. lib. primo, pag. edit. nostræ 99. & seqq. ex quo pete ejus de hisce Constitutionibus judicium, quod omittendum hic nec negligendum erat. Quodnam sit Cardinalis Bonæ lib. 1. liturg. cap. 8. §. 5. de hisce Constitutionibus judicium id commodius infra referemus, ubi de tempore suppositionis aliquid dicemus. Alios bene multos Magni Nominis Viros, Salma-sium, Vossium, Usserium, Filesacum, Voetium, & innumeros præterea præterimus; qui omnes in censum scriptorum supposititiorum & quæ sunt dubiæ fidei hasce constitutiones retulerunt, quorum testimonia ex adversariis adducere possemus, nisi superiora sufficere censeremus. Ne vero auctoritatibus sed & rationibus cadat auctoritas harum Constitutionum Pseudapostolicarum, ex bene multis quas Doctissi-mus Dalæus coacervavit paucas adducemus. Magnum argumentum exinde peti potest, esse has constitutiones alicujus Im-postoris, non Apostolorum, quod cum Apostolorum nomen referant, tamen nunquam cum aliis Apostolorum scriptis in canonem scripturæ, neque à Græcis neque à Latinis receptæ sint; quod certe oportuisset fieri si verè essent apostolicæ & oporteret eos facere, qui pro Apostolicis constitutionibus Orbi audent obtrudere. Quanquam enim Auctor falsarius in Canone 85. seu ultimo, ut suæ inserviret causæ, eas ante acta Apostolorum, inter Canonicos libros Novi Testamenti collocaverit, attamen ipse Bovius, qui eas edidit & vertit, in Præfatione fatetur, nunquam obtinuisse, ut in canonem sacrarum Scripturarum referren-tur. tur, nec se iis tantam auctoritatem tribuere, quo velut una litura delet, quidquid constitutionum Apostolicarum Orbi sub Clementis nomine ausus est obtrudere. Pro Apostolorum constitutionibus habere, & non in canonem scripturæ referre, apud Theologos implicat contradictionem; ut & pro apostolico aliquid protrudere, nec auctoritatem tantam, id est sacræ scripturæ, ei attribuere. Hoc argumentum urget, in repudianda Christi ad Abgarum Epistola, Bellarminus, de scriptor. Eccles. in Petro init. Ea (inquit Epistola) nunquam fuit admissa ab Ecclesia inter scripturas canonicas, inter quas sine dubio admissa fuisset, si ab ipso domino scriptam fuisse constaret. units.tr: The Greeks never esteemed these Constitutions, so Bellarmine, in the passage cited, is wrong when he writes that they were held in high regard by the ancient Greeks but are of no standing among the Latins. The earliest mention of the Apostolic Constitutions is in Epiphanius, who flourished in the fourth century, about the year 375. He cites them at various points, yet in Heresy 70, §10, he says they were regarded as doubtful by many and were held in faith by some. The most learned Dalaeus, in Pseudepigrapha Apostolorum, book 1, chapter 2, has gathered the passages and examined them at length. Along with Petavius, he shows that many of the passages Epiphanius cites are not found in the present Constitutions of Bovius and Turrianus, and some are even contrary to them. So these are not the Constitutions of Epiphanius, and Turrianus disgracefully abuses and deceives the unwary when, on the authority of Epiphanius, he asserts in the preface to his Latin version that our age has Apostolic Constitutions of the same kind, sound and uncorrupted, as Epiphanius's age had. Dalaeus then proves by many very strong arguments that the Constitutions Epiphanius had should not be held as Apostolic, nor were they received by the Church or regarded as apostolic. He shows that they too are spurious and falsely attributed to the Apostles. Bovius also cites Cyril of Jerusalem in Catechesis 18, p. 213, where he recounts from Clement the fable of the Phoenix, as if it had been taken from the fifth book of the Apostolic Constitutions. But Cyril is wrong here too. This fable is found in the genuine first epistle of Clement to the Corinthians, which Jerome and others often cite. The author of the Catechesis took it from there, as a comparison of phrases and words makes plain. He often uses the same words that are found in Clement's Epistle to the Corinthians, not those read in the Constitutions of Bovius. For this reason alone, the most learned Rigaltius, in his notes on Tertullian's book on the resurrection, makes the author of the Epistle and the author of the Constitutions different men. Although, he says, the same story of the Phoenix is also found in the Constitutions cited above, yet from comparing them with Clement's Epistle we seem to gather that it can scarcely be held that both works come from the same author. Another testimony, twisted from Athanasius and Eusebius, concerns the book once called the Teaching of the Apostles [διδαχὴ τῶν ἀποστόλων], which was in use among some but was commonly regarded as spurious and rejected. It has nothing to do with Bovius's Apostolic Constitutions, since Athanasius himself makes clear that the works of Clement and this Teaching of the Apostles [διδαχὰς ἀποστόλων] are different. Nor does Eusebius, book 3, chapter 25, Greek edition of Christophorson, chapter 19, ascribe them to Clement, because in other places, where he expressly treats of the genuine and spurious writings of Clement, he does not attribute this Teaching to him. See book 3, chapters 57, 58 and 59. It is therefore true that in the first four centuries no Greek anywhere mentions the Apostolic Constitutions. Further, the Constitutions that Epiphanius mentions were not received or approved as apostolic, nor are they the same as those of Bovius. The earliest mention occurs in the Council of Constantinople in Trullo, held in the year 692, where the fathers gathered there rejected them in canon 2. The words of the canon are these: "Since adulterous and foreign things, alien to piety, were long ago inserted into the Apostolic Constitutions of the holy Apostles by heterodox men to defile the Church, obscuring for us the elegant and fitting appearance of the divine decrees, we have believed that these Constitutions must be utterly cast out, for the building up and security of the most Christian flock, in no way admitting the movements of heretical babbling, and inserting [in their place] the genuine and whole teaching of the Apostles." [Ταῖς τ᾽ ἁγίων Ἀποστόλων Διατάξεις πάλαι ὑπὸ τ᾽ ἑτεροδόξων ὅπὶ λύμῃ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας νόθα πινὰ ἢ ξένα τῆς εὐσεβείας παρενετέθησαν, τὸ ἀπηχεπὲς καὶ λῶν τῶν θείων δογμάτων ἡμῖν ἀμαυρώσαντα, τῶν τοιούτων Διατάξεων ἀποφόρως ἀποβολῶ πεπιστεύμεθα πρὸς τὸ ἢ χρισιανικωτάτης ποιμνίς οἰκοδομὴν καὶ ἀσφάλειαν, ἱδαμῶς ἐγκεῖνοντες τὰ τ᾽ αἱρετικῆς ψιθυρολογίας κινήματα, καὶ τῇ γνησίᾳ τῶν Ἀποστόλων καὶ ὁλοκλήρῳ διδαχῇ παρενείροντες.] The Latin of this is: these Constitutions of the Apostles, which through Clement were long ago corrupted by men of other opinions, we REJECT, as the offspring of heretical falsehood, in no way admitting them, and inserting in their place the genuine and whole doctrine of the Apostles. After these fathers, Photius also mentions them in the Bibliotheca, Codex 113. He saw the true arguments for why they should be rejected, but he contends, out of partisan zeal against the Latins, who could be attacked with them, that they may be excused. After him nearly all Greeks reject them, with one or two exceptions, who use them for the same partisan reason against the Romans. Balsamon, who wrote at the end of the twelfth century, on Canon 85 of the Pseudo-apostolic canons, says this about them: "You know that although it is written that we should read the Constitutions of Clement, they should not be published, for the second canon of the sixth synod forbade their reading, because interpolation was made in them." [Συ δὲ γινώσκεις ὡς εἰ καὶ γέγεγραπται ἐντευθεν ἀναγινώσκειν ἡμᾶς τὰς Διαταγὰς τῶ Κλήμεντος, ὥλιω μὴ δημοπιδεῖν αὐτὰς, ἀλλ' ὁ δὲ κανὼν τῆς ἑκτης συνόδου ἀπηγόρευσε τὴν τῶν ἀναγνώσιν, ᾿Διὸ τὸ γενέσθαι παρωμοίωσιν ἐν αὐτοῖς.] Zonaras says the same on that canon: "They were adulterated and corrupted by heterodox and sectarian persons. For this reason the sixth ecumenical synod forbade them to be read at all." [Αὕτη τῶν κανονδόξων τινῶν, ἐνοφευτησάν τε καὶ παρεφθάρησαν. διὸ ἡ ἀναγινώσκεσθαι ὅλως αὐτὰς ἀπηγόρευσεν ἡ εκκλησιαστικὴ ἕκτη συνόδῳ.] Alexius Aristenus says similar things, cited by Ussher in his dissertation on Ignatius: the second canon of the sixth synod held at Trullo entirely rejects the Apostolic Constitutions, because certain adulterine and foreign things, alien to piety, were falsely inserted into them by heterodox men. [ὁ δευτερ⸗ κανὼν τῆς ἐν Τρέλλῳ γνωμένης ἕκτης συνόδῳ παντελῶς ἀποβάλλειν τὰς ποιεῖτας διαταγάς, ἃ ἐν αὐταῖς ὑπὸ τ᾽ ἑτεροδόξων ψευδῶς ἐγκεῖ- σθαί τινα νόθα καὶ ξένα τῆς εὐσεβείας.] So that we may also know what the modern Greeks think of these, here is the judgment of Jeremiah, Patriarch of Constantinople, from his Response, chapter 13, p. 103, to the Württembergers: the Clementine Constitutions have been adulterated. From these testimonies we see what the Greeks, the Latins, the ancients and the more recent have judged about these Pseudo-apostolic Constitutions: namely, that they are spurious, fabricated, forged, corrupted, stained with heterodoxy, and in a word apocryphal. Among them our Antonius Augustinus also counts them, in Dialogue 6 of the first book, page 99 and following of our edition, from which his judgment on these Constitutions may be sought. It should not be omitted or neglected here. We will report more conveniently below the judgment of Cardinal Bona on these Constitutions, Liturgies, book 1, chapter 8, §5, when we say something about the time of their forgery. We pass over many other men of great name, Salmasius, Vossius, Ussher, Fabricius (Filesacus), Voetius and countless more, who all placed these Constitutions among spurious writings and works of doubtful faith. Their testimonies could be adduced from our opponents, were we not judging the above sufficient. But so that the authority of these Pseudo-apostolic Constitutions may fall by arguments as well as by authorities, we will adduce a few of the many that the most learned Dalaeus has gathered. A great argument can be drawn from this: these Constitutions are the work of some impostor, not of the Apostles. Although they bear the name of the Apostles, they were never placed in the canon of Scripture alongside the other writings of the Apostles, neither by Greeks nor by Latins. That certainly would have had to happen if they were truly apostolic, and those who dare to thrust Apostolic Constitutions upon the world ought to have made it happen. For although the false author, in Canon 85, or the last, to serve his cause, placed them before the Acts of the Apostles among the canonical books of the New Testament, yet Bovius himself, who published and translated them, confesses in his Preface that they never obtained that they should be counted in the canon of the sacred Scriptures, nor does he himself grant them such authority that by one stroke he could erase whatever Constitutions of the Apostles were presumed to be thrust upon the world under Clement's name. To hold something as Apostolic and yet not to place it in the canon of Scripture involves a contradiction among theologians, just as it does to put something forward as apostolic without attributing to it the authority of Scripture itself. Bellarmine presses this argument in rejecting the Epistle of Christ to Abgarus, in his On Ecclesiastical Writers, under Peter, at the beginning: (the Epistle says) it was never admitted by the Church among the canonical Scriptures, among which it would undoubtedly have been admitted, had it been established that it was written by the Lord himself. Furthermore, the style and certain expressions of these Constitutions are foreign to the character of the Apostles. I list a few by way of example. In book 2, chapter 10, and elsewhere, the word neophytus [νεοφὁτιςος] is used for one recently baptized; mysis [μύησις] for baptism; in book 8, chapter 7, katechoumenos [κατηχούμενος] and akroumenos [ἀκροώμενος] for catechumen and hearer. Thysia [Θυσία] and thysia anaimaktikē [Θυσία ἀναιμακτικὴ] are used for the Eucharist. In book 8, chapter 12, archiereus [ἀρχιερεὺς] is used for bishop, a pontiff. In book 8, chapter 13, hiereis [ἱερεῖς] is used for bishops and presbyters, as priests. In book 3, chapter 15, hieroprepes katalogos [ἱεροπρεπὲς καταλόγος] means the catalogue of priests or the diptychs. In book 8, chapter 12, thysiasterion [θυσιαστήριον] means altar, for the Lord's table. Words of this kind, with these meanings, are not found among the Apostles but among writers of later centuries, and so they prove that these works were written in later centuries and not by the Apostles. The writer's style also betrays this sufficiently. It is sometimes inflated and rhetorical, not humble and plain, and even his manner of speaking, which belongs to those who lived after the Apostles, shows it. See examples at book 2, chapter 41 and book 5, chapter 16, where the controversy over celebrating Easter also makes clear that the writer lived at least after the second century. See also book 6, chapter 10. But what surpasses all foolishness is what occurs at book 7, chapter 47: "But concerning the bishops who were ordained by us while we lived, or in our lifetime, we make you aware." [Εἰ δὲ τὰ ὑφ' ἡμῶν χειροποιηθέντων ἀποστόλων ἐν τῇ ζωῇ τῇ ἡμετέρᾳ γνωρίζομεν ὑμῖν.] These things sufficiently show that they were written after the death of the Apostles. To these may be added, thirdly, what these Constitutions say about the Son of God, whom they deny to be God, contrary to the doctrine of the Apostles. Book 6, chapter 6: "Others of them (the heretics) suspect that Jesus himself is God over all." [Ἕτεροι δὲ ἐξ αὐτῶν, αὐτὸν εἶναι τὸ Ἰησοῦν τὸ ὑπὲρ πάντων θεὸν ὑποπιλάζουσιν.] These are words of Arians, Photinians or Ebionites rather than of the Apostles. Add to these, of much the same kind, passages from book 5, chapters 6 and 10, book 8, chapter 12, book 2, chapter 44, and no better things concerning the Holy Spirit in book 2, chapter 26, book 3, chapter 17, book 8, chapter 37 at the beginning, and elsewhere. This is why Petavius, mentioned above, says in Theological Dogmas, vol. 2, p. 15, that Clement set forth I know not what ridiculous and heretical notion about the Trinity, book 2, chapter 26. For the Constitutions say that the bishop in the Church is like God the Father; the deacon likewise like Christ, who stands by the Father and ministers in all things. If Christ is considered as man, these things may not seem improperly said. But it is pestilential that they add that the deaconess has the figure of the Holy Spirit, who ought to do or say nothing without the deacon, just as the Paraclete does nothing and speaks nothing of himself, but glorifying Christ awaits his will. This indeed savours of Macedonian poison and venom. Photius, discussing Clement's works in Codex 113, asserts that certain traces of Arian impiety are present in the Constitutions, which cannot be excused except by force. What kind of passage this was, which we have cited, no other passage involved in a similar stain is found. So Petavius. What follows from it, which still bears on this point, may be drawn from him, and other passages of this impiety from those mentioned above may be suggested, chiefly from book 6, chapter 25. Bovius himself confesses in the Preface to the Constitutions that their author speaks meagrely about the Holy Spirit, and at times pours forth certain harsher expressions about the Word also. Yet with the greatest impudence he does not hesitate to thrust these upon the world as Apostolic Constitutions, and to attach to them expressions meagre and harsh where they speak of the mysteries of faith. The Constitutions are no fairer on marriage. Book 3, chapter 2: "They say that a third marriage is a sign of intemperance, and a fourth marriage and beyond is manifest fornication and undoubted impurity." No milder and no truer is what they say about fornication, book 8, chapter 38, edition of Bovius and Lambert Gruter: "An unbelieving concubine, who serves only her master, is to be received; if she is intemperate with others, she is to be rejected." Bovius, in excusing these things, like those who wrote them as their Apostles or as impostors, says: Since the maidservant does not have power over her own body, the fault is rightly to be laid not on her but on the master. But if interpreters of the divine law like this had been present in Joseph's time, he too could have gratified his mistress with impunity, because he was her servant, and could have cast the blame on her. In baptism, book 3, chapters 15, 16 and 17, book 7, chapter 23, they require oil besides water, and after baptism they order anointing with chrism. This was neither instituted by the Apostles nor belongs to the Apostolic age, and it would not have been added unless these things had been added. Book 7, chapter 45: "They say that the one baptized goes down into the water alone, so that he may lay aside the filth not only of the body but also of the soul, like a Jew." Nor does it belong to the Apostolic age to give the Eucharist to infants or children, but to the third and later centuries; nor does that frequent distinction between bishops and presbyters, which were names of one office among the Apostles, belong to the Apostolic age, but was made only in the third century, according to Blondel. Book 2, chapters 25; book 3, chapter 11; book 8, chapters 28 and 46. Words and offices unheard of in the time of the Apostles, subdeacons, acolytes, exorcists, readers, doorkeepers, occur everywhere in these Constitutions. Unheard of too is that power which they everywhere attribute to bishops, book 2, chapters 11, 12, 14, 20, 26, 28, 30 and 52, and the tithes granted to them, book 2, chapter 34, and ibid. and chapter 35. Concerning the marriage of ecclesiastical persons, the Constitutions teach that bishops and presbyters, once ordained and in the ministry, may not take wives, nor pass to second marriages. These things contradict the true Apostolic Constitutions revealed in Holy Scripture, book 6, chapter 17. Against these they also introduce the distinction of foods, book 5, chapter 18, fixed fasts, book 5, chapters 12, 14, 19, 20; book 7, chapter 24, festival days, book 5, chapters 12, 17, 19, 20; book 8, chapter 33, and the observance of the Sabbath and the Lord's Day, ibid., book 8, chapter 33; book 7, chapter 24, fasting before baptism, book 7, chapter 23, and prayer toward the east by the one baptized. This ceremony belongs to the fourth century, as Cyril testifies, and not to the Apostolic age, book 7, chapter 46, and book 2, chapter 57. Further, the rites of catechumens and penitents, which were known and established in the Church only in the third and fourth centuries, sufficiently prove that these Constitutions falsely bear the Apostles' names and their age. See them at book 8, chapter 6. It is absurd that they forbid a believer to pray at home together with a catechumen, book 8, chapter 34, near the end, and that one who has eaten the Eucharist unawares should be baptized at once, book 5, chapter 19; book 7, chapter 26. Ridiculous are the things commanded for the celebration of the Eucharist: book 8, chapter 12: "Two deacons, on either side of the altar, are to hold fans made of thin parchment, or of peacock feathers, or of linen, to drive away small flying creatures, so that they do not fall into the cups." It belongs to idle men, not to Apostles, to pursue such trifles, and to prescribe so laboriously the form of the basilicas, book 2, chapter 57. False, and contrary to the historical truth recorded in the Acts of the Apostles, is the claim that the seven deacons of Jerusalem, gathered together with the Apostle Paul, are pretended book 8, chapter 4 to have written these Constitutions, since Stephen had already been removed before Paul's apostleship. That stupid impostor, in this same book, before the writing of these Constitutions, mentions that Stephen gave his life for Christ. See chapter 46, and add book 5, chapter 7, and book 8, chapter 33. Of the same kind is the claim that James, son of Zebedee and brother of John, who had been put to death with the sword by Herod, Acts 12:2, is pretended to have been present at the Council of Jerusalem seven years after his death, Acts 15, and to narrate its history, book 6, chapter 22, though he had been counted among the martyrs in book 5, chapter 7. Likewise, these Constitutions are said to have been sent by Clement, Bishop of Rome, who certainly could not have been converted before the death of James in the year of Christ 44. It is also most charming, and most apt to provoke laughter, that in book 2, chapter 57 the Apostles prescribe as follows concerning the reading of their books: "Then let our Acts be read, likewise the Epistles of Paul our fellow-worker, and afterwards the deacon or presbyter should read what I, Matthew and John, have handed down to you, and what Mark and Luke, the fellow-workers of Paul, have received and left to you." Yet the Gospel of John was written only after his recall from Patmos, that is, in the year of the Lord 97, when almost all the Apostles had already departed this life. Of the same sort is their mention, book 6, chapter 6, of the Ebionites, who, according to Epiphanius, Heresy 30, §2, and Baronius, ad annum 74, §6, began after the destruction of Jerusalem. At that time, all agree, not only James but also Peter and Paul, and likewise the other Apostles, had passed from life, yet these men are feigned to be writing these Constitutions. In book 7, chapter 48 they narrate that Simeon, son of Cleophas, succeeded James in the bishopric of Jerusalem. According to Halloix, in his notes to the Life of Ignatius, chapter 2, Simeon lived after our Clement, yet he is pretended to have been present at these Constitutions. In book 6, chapter 8 they mention the heretics Marcion, Basilides and Saturninus, whom we know from Irenaeus to have arisen after the death of Clement and the Apostles. See Irenaeus, Against Heresies, book 3, chapter 3, and Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book 4, chapter 6, Greek edition, and in the Chronicle, where he places Basilides in the year 136. Theodoret, Heretical Fables, book 1, chapter 2, and Clement of Alexandria, Stromata, book 7, agree with him. To prove the resurrection they also adduce ten Sibylline verses, book 5, chapter 6, though the Sibylline works were fabricated and published only under Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius, thirty or forty years after the death of all the Apostles. Book 6, chapter 24, they say that the Romans believed in God and turned away from the multitude of gods and from injustice, which did not happen before the reign of Constantine in the fourth century. To these add the testimonies of the Apocryphal books and their praises: Susanna, book 2, chapter 51; Judith, book 3, chapter 17; Baruch, book 5, chapter 2; Ecclesiasticus, book 4, chapter 11, which it is clear the true Apostles did not do. Likewise there is the false etymology and meaning of the name Israel as "the one who sees God" [ὁ ὁρῶν Θεόν], book 7, chapter 37, and book 8, chapter 15. Against this, Jerome, in his Hebrew Questions on Genesis, chapter 32, vol. 3, p. 220 of my edition of Froben, Basel, 1553, hands down the correct view. False also is the assertion, book 6, chapter 7, about Philip the Apostle, who was only a deacon, and about James the brother of the Lord, whom they deprive of the apostleship and say was ordained by themselves as bishop of Jerusalem. Book 6, chapters 14 and 12; book 8, chapter 4; book 7, chapter 48. Against this see Bellarmine, On Ecclesiastical Writers, under Clement, and Baronius, ad annum 44, §§36 and 37. Further, it is false that they make Mary, sister of Lazarus, different from Mary Magdalene, book 3, chapter 6, against which Baronius rises up, ad annum 32, §19, and Bellarmine, loc. cit. False too is what they assert, book 6, chapter 24, that Moses forbade the Jews to place Aram outside Jerusalem and to read the law outside the borders of Judaea, and book 5, chapter 20, that the Jews were accustomed to read Baruch. False too is the citation, book 6, chapter 2, where they cite "Adadan" [Ἀ′ Ἐεδαδαὰν], which in 2 Samuel 20:1 is called Sheba. That forger seems to have drawn this from the pseudo-Ignatian Epistle to the Masuesians. From all these things it is abundantly plain that these Constitutions are not the Apostles' work. Nor were they written by Clement, Bishop of Rome. This is shown first from the Constitutions themselves, which say that they were written not by Clement but by the Apostles themselves, and mention Clement only as a courier or minister, who conveys them to the bishops and churches. See book 6, chapter 14, book 8, chapter 4, and book 6, chapter 18. Epiphanius also, who, as above…

units.la: 116. Non sunt scriptae à Clemente. dicúnt, Clementis vero tamquam portitoris vel ministri, qui ad Episcopos & Ecclesias deferat, meminerunt. vid. eas lib. 6. c. 14. lib. 8. c. 4. & lib. 6. c. 18. Epiphanius etiam, qui, ut supra dictum, sæpius meminit Διαταξέων τ̈ Αποστόλων, nunquam tamen eas Clementinas vocat, aut Clementi adscriptas refert, sed simpliciter aut Αποστόλων Διάταξεις, vel singulari numero Διάταξιν appellat. vid. eum Haref. 80. §. 7. Haref. 70. §. 10. & Haref. 75. §. 6. Haref. 45. §. 2. Neque etiam Athanasii & Eusebii Διδαχὴ τῶν Αποστόλων ullibi adscribitur Clementi. Itaque non immerito dubitat Dalæus, an non illa Διὰ Κλήμεντος addita fuerint titulo ab alia manu; temporibus Trullani Concilii Constantinopolitani, videntur jam habuisse id nomen; in ejus enim Canone secundo eas Patres vocant τὰς τῶν Αποστόλων Διὰ Κλήμεντος Διατάξεις. Neque negligenda hic nobis ejusdem Dalæi conjectura, lib. 1. cap. ult. Pseudepigraphōn Apost. ex antiquis Constitutionibus Apostolorum, Epiphanii temporibus notis, & Διδαχὴ τῶν Αποστόλων Athanasio & Eusebio memoratis, hoc quod Bovius opus propinavit forte potuisse esse consarcinatum, & majoris auctoritatis causa Clementi inscriptum. Verum hæc tantum conjectura est. Id majori attentione tentione dignum; quod libro secundo latissime & solidissime probat, neque ipsi Clementi, cui adfinguntur cognitas fuisse ex ejus genuina epistola; neque postea Justino Martyri & Philosopho, neque Athenagorae, neque Irenaeo, neque Clementi Alexandrino, Tertulliano, Orgeni, Cypriano, Dionysio vel Petro Alexandrinis, neque Patribus Eliberitani, aut Nicaeni concilii quidquam de his innotuisse, neque Arrianos aut Catholicos quarti seculi, neque Laodicenos Patres, neque Basilium, neque quinto seculo nisi decurrente Graecos vel Latinos, eorum notitiam habuisse: sequentibus autem seculis apud Latinos usque ad undecimum, imo ante Bovii editionem vix innotuisse, nunquam receptas fuisse. Si quis conjecturae tamen locus ex ritibus tertii, quarti & quinti seculi, qui in iis obvii, censet Dalaeus in fine seculi quinti esse scriptas & suppositas, non post quintum, quia quae post id seculum recenter sunt inducta, non memorantur in iis: nil de imaginibus & reliquis ritibus invectis. Ab hac sententia non abludere videtur, quod eodem tempore quo scriptae propter multas absurditates in nativitate quasi oppressae videantur, a Gelasio & 70. Episcopis in concilio Romano, in quo damnatae, inter apocrypha relatae tamdiu delituerunt, donec
units.tr: 116. They were not written by Clement. They say that they were written by the Apostles themselves, and they mention Clement only as a carrier or minister who delivers them to the bishops and churches. See them book 6, chapter 14; book 8, chapter 4; and book 6, chapter 18. Epiphanius too, who, as said above, often mentions the Ordinances of the Apostles [Διαταξεις τῶν Αποστόλων], never calls them Clementine or refers them to Clement, but simply calls them the Ordinances of the Apostles [Αποστόλων Διάταξεις], or in the singular, the Ordinance [Διάταξιν]. See him Haer. 80 §7; Haer. 70 §10; Haer. 75 §6; Haer. 45 §2. Nor is the Teaching of the Apostles [Διδαχὴ τῶν Αποστόλων] mentioned by Athanasius and Eusebius ascribed to Clement anywhere. So Dalaeus doubts, not without reason, whether the words "through Clement" [Διὰ Κλήμεντος] were added to the title by another hand. In the time of the Council in Trullo, the Council of Constantinople, they seem already to have borne that name, for in its second canon the Fathers call them "the Ordinances of the Apostles through Clement" [τὰς τῶν Αποστόλων Διὰ Κλήμεντος Διατάξεις]. Nor should Dalaeus's conjecture be neglected here, in book 1, last chapter, Pseudepigrapha of the Apostles: that the work which Bovius has put forward may perhaps have been patched together from the ancient Constitutions of the Apostles, known in Epiphanius's time, and from the Teaching of the Apostles mentioned by Athanasius and Eusebius, and, for greater authority, been inscribed to Clement. But this is only a conjecture. What deserves closer attention is what he proves most fully and solidly in book two: that neither Clement himself, to whom they are falsely attributed, knew of them from his genuine epistle; nor afterwards Justin Martyr and Philosopher, nor Athenagoras, nor Irenaeus, nor Clement of Alexandria, Tertullian, Origen, Cyprian, Dionysius or Peter of Alexandria, nor the Fathers of Elvira or of the Council of Nicaea, knew anything of them; nor did the Arians or the Catholics of the fourth century, nor the Fathers of Laodicea, nor Basil; nor did the Greeks or Latins of the fifth century have knowledge of them until its end; and in the following centuries, among the Latins down to the eleventh, indeed even before Bovius's edition, they were scarcely known and never received. If anyone nonetheless finds some room for conjecture in the rites of the third, fourth and fifth centuries that occur in them, Dalaeus thinks they were written and foisted on at the end of the fifth century, and not later than the fifth, because rites introduced after that century are not mentioned in them: nothing about images and the other rites introduced later. This view does not seem to differ from the view that, at the same time as they were written, they were crushed at birth, as it were, on account of many absurdities, condemned by Gelasius and seventy bishops in the Roman council, and, listed among the apocrypha, lay hidden for so long until
117. Note on the Fathers of the first three centuries.

units.la: 118. Vix notae Latinis usque ad Bovii editionem.
units.tr: 118. Scarcely known to the Latins until Bovius's edition.

units.la: 119. Conjectura de tempore scriptionis & suppositionis. donec iterum in lucem à Bovio revocarentur. Materiam impostor insicetus ex scriptura, Ecclesiasticis ritibus & disciplina, suo tempore usitata, tum etiam libris quibusdam ritualibus, veluti Epiphanii tempore notis Constitutionibus Apostolicis, & doctrina Apostolorum Athanasio & Eusebio memorata forte hausit, & stultissime digessit. Quod eo magis probabile, saltem de Constitutionibus Apostolorum, quia & ab iis titulum mutuatus videtur, & quædam quæ Epiphanius ex iis recenset, hodie in Bovianis constitutionibus leguntur; quædam vero, ut supra quoque dictum, non com-parent. Hæreticum & Arriana labe infe-ctum fuisse harum constitutionum scriptoré, ex iis satis superque colligi potest, quæ de filii & Spiritus sancti persona ex eo in medium produximus. Rectissime itaque suam crisin Magnus Dalæus hisce finit, vix ullum aliud esse opus Apocryphum quod sic undique ab omni parte laboret, ut Boviana Διαταξεις. Hanc etiam causam esse arbitror, quare in editione conciliorum anni 1636. Parisiis facta Constitutiones hæ Pseudapostolicæ penitus ex opere isto exturbatæ sint. Ex quibus, hactenus disputatis, judicare lector poterit quid de judicio Cardinalis Bonæ sit statuendum, & quo id loco habendum, quod ille, ut suam fulciret Missam Pseudoclementinam, de hisce Constitutionibus Pseudapostolicis, in lib. I. liturgicōν cap. 8. §. 4. pag. mihi 52. edit. Parisiensi. prodidit. Recenseri item, inquit, potest inter Apostolicas sancti Clementis Romani Liturgia in Libro Constitutionum descripta & ab Apostolis accepta, ut ille ait, à qua paucis me expediam. Testimonium de illa perhibet Proclus initio tract. de traditione Missæ, asserens B. Clementem Apostolis dictantibus eam edidisse: cujus sententiæ adhærent Baronius anno 102. num. 23. Bellarminus lib. de Scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis, & alii, qui eam legitimam esse putant, sed auctam à successoribus. Sicut enim formulam Symboli ab Apostolis traditam Patres deinde auxerunt, ut fidei mysteria clarius exprimerent; ita Liturgiæ ab illis prout ferebant tempora contextæ, ab aliis postea amplificatæ fuerunt. Alii tamen non infimi subsellii scriptores, qui negant Clementem apostolicarum Constitutionum auctorem esse, ab eo consequenter Missam abjudicant, quæ pars illarum notabilis est. Photius Cod. 112. tria capita ipsis Constitutionibus opponi ait, sed quæ facile dilui possint. Epiphanius hæresi 70. num. 10. citat Librum Constitutionum Apostolicarum, tum ait: Qui Liber tametsi dubia apud nonnullos nonnullos fidei sit, non est tamen improbandus. Nam in eo quæ ad Ecclesiæ disciplinam attinent omnia comprehenduntur; neque quidquam aut in fide ac Catholica professione depravatum, aut Ecclesiæ administrationi ac decretis contrarium continet. Sed has Constitutiones quas Epiphanius citat, diversas videri ab his quæ octo libris comprehensæ circumferuntur, observat Petavius in suis animadversionibus: quædam enim illarum sententiæ ab Epiphanio citatæ in vulgatis non extant. At hæc Petavii conjectura est, qua non obstante haud improbabile existimo easdem esse, sed interpolatas, & aliquibus in locis vel librariorum incuria, vel hæreticorum fraude depravatas. Quidam putant ad eas alludere Dionysium Alexandrinum in epistola quam refert Eusebius lib. 7. cap. 7. in qua nihil prorsus deprehendo, quod ad Clementem referri possit. Quicquid autem sit de Auctore harum Constitutionum, certum apud omnes & exploratum nunc est, quod si ab Apostolis immediate dictatæ non fuerunt, Concilio tamen Nicæno antiquiores sunt, & his continetur disciplina Ecclesiastica, qua Orientalis Ecclesia sub Ethnicis Imperatoribus ante Magnum Constantinum regebatur, ut Vir eruditissimus Joannes Morinus docet Parte 2. de sacris Ordinat. pag. 20. pag. 20. Cui adstipulatur Joannes Fronto in prænotatis ad Kalendarium Romanum §. 5. Petrus item de Marca lib. 3. Concordiæ cap. 2. ejus libri Auctorem saltem sæculo tertio floruisse ait, idque omnibus hodie persuasum esse. Est igitur Missa Clementis antiquissima, ejusque testimonio sæpius utar, si non præcise ut ab Apostolis editæ, & à successoribus auctæ, quod valde probabile est; saltem ut à Patribus secundi vel tertii sæculi usurpatæ. Hæc ille. Oscitanter inspectas Constitutiones oportet esse à Cardinale, qui ait, Clementem dicere in Constitutionibus istis Pseudapostolicis, se liturgiam ab Apostolis accepisse, quod ille in toto opere non scribit. Sed paucissima tantum verba hæc. lib. 8. c. 46. profatur. Et ego Clemens: con- stitutus sum ab Apostolis Episcopus. Ubi autem Clementis fit mentio, ea tanquam de ministro fit, ut supra dictum. vid. lib. 6. cap. 18. const. Pseud-Apost. Sed his diutius non est opus immorari, quia alii sufficienter probarunt omnes istas liturgias veteres esse aut suppositas, aut saltem depravatas, quod posterius vel ipse Bona, de sua Clementis Liturgia fatetur. Ut possit itaque jactata hæc alicujus auctoritatis esse, accessiones tolli primum debent, & probari quæ sint genuina; quod Cardinalis Bona non magis in hac Clementis, quam in aliis liturgiis ipse vel quisquam alius unquam facere poterit. Iis vero quæ adfert de interpolatione istarum Constitutionum, opponimus ea quæ in eadem materia contra Trullanos Patres, easdem interpolatas & depravatas adserentes solidissime disseruit, sæpius jam laudatus D: Dalæus in Pseudepig. Apost. lib. 2. cap. 15. & iis quæ ille de ætate harum Constitutionum profert, quasi Concilio Nicæno sint antiquiores, eundem lib. eod. capitib. octo prioribus, & quæ jam disputata sunt. Nunc ad Canones Apostolorum, ut vocantur, transimus. Sunt hi pars libri octavi Constitutionum Pseudapostolicarum secundum Turrianum cap. 1. pro Canonib. Apost. contra Magdeburg. in cujus editione, post ultima capitis XLVI. verba, sequuntur, Canones Ecclesiastici, ut ibidem vocantur, illi qui vulgo appellantur Apostolorum; quod & videtur firmare canon eorum ultimus, ubi ipsi Apostoli ita ad Episcopos se convertunt. Hæc vobis, Episcopi, constituimus &c. Inde forte totum opus hoc Constitutionum Apostolicarum Auctor Operis imperfecti in Matthæum, antiquus quidem sed tamen hæreticus, vocat Libros Canonum Apostolorum, & citat librum octavum Homil. 53. cujus citata inveniuntur libri 8. const. cap. 2. Hoc si verum, rum, quod anterioris operis, latissime refutati, partem faciant, hi canones; non opus foret, pluribus contra eos exprofesso agere: sed videtur verius & ptobabile magis Impostorem quendam canones & constitutiones, duo diversa opera combinasse, & novos quosdam iis addidisse, quod vel iistud solum evincere potest, quod ea quæ in canonibus leguntur,pleraque in ipsis constitutionibus fusissime inveniuntur. Adde, quod canon ultimus Pseudapostolicus etiam satis indicet esse diversum opus illud canonum à Constitutionibus Pseudapostolicis, & quod Gelasius in c. sancta Romana. dist. 15. distinguat hæc duo opera. Item Photius in Bibliotheca Cod. 112. & 113. Quare,& quia hi canones magis adhuc, quam præcedentes Constitutiones Apostolicæ, ad Historiam nostram Juris Ecclesiastici facere videntur, & quia jam à multis retro seculis, collectionibus Juris Ecclesiastici additi sunt, opus ut seorsim eos examinemus. Diversæ sunt hic quoque Doctorum sententiæ. Turrianus homo ferrei stomachi, & æneæ frontis in propugnandis apocryphis singulari volumine eos defendit contra Magdenburgenses Centuriatores, & omnes pro Apostolicis habet. Quem sequitur Lambertus Gruterus, in sua Clementis Romani operum rum editione, quæ prodiit Colon. anno 1570. Baronius, ad An: 102. § 14. & Bellarmin de Script. Eccles. in Clemente, quinquaginta pro genuinis agnoscunt, cæteros xxxv. vel secundum alios xxxiv. repudiant. Hisce subscribit Possevinus in apparatu. verb. Clemens. & Binius quoq; ita tamen ut & cæteri, excepto lxv. & ultimo per eum inter authenticos haberi jure meritoque possint. vid. ejus not. in tit. Can. Apost. tom. i. concil. & miraberis judicium, quod eodem halitu probet eos canones, & à Gelasio Papa inter apocrypha relatos confitetur. Apostolis certo adscribere nemo audet, Baronius l. cit. Incertum esse, ait, ab ipsis Apostolis esse conscriptos, neque id ipsum, Turrianum contendere. Qui diserte id negat. tract. pro iis in princ. Quis, inquit, unquam ex Catholicis scriptos ab Apostolis dixit. Postea tamen à Clemente omnes scriptos contendit, & quidem impudentissime fingit ab Apostolis post decretū de legalibus factum Hierosolymæ constitutos, à Clemente exceptos, idq; anno Christi xlv. Claudii VI. P. Valerio Asiatico II. Cos. Binius, incertum relinquit, quis quinquaginta priores scripserit, quos maxime pro certis & indubitatis habent, hos traditione Apostolica vult ad nos dimanasse. De cæteris dubitat, an sint ex Apostolorum Canonum Codice à Pontificibus conciliis ac Patribus accepti, an potius ex ipsorum sententiis in hunc Codicem translati. Aliud est Judicium de auctoritate, nomine & auctoribus Gabrielis Albaspinaei lib. 1. observat. c. 15. ubi pro imperitis habet, qui canones istos Apostolorum auctoritate sancitos publicatosve certo adfirmant. Tum Ab antiquitate eos Apostolicos appellatos esse existimant. Nam, addit, cum eorum aliquot ab Apostolorum successoribus, qui teste Tertulliano de Praescriptionibus Apostolici Viri nominabantur, facti essent, Apostolicorum primum canones; deinde nonnullorum Latinorum ignorantia aliquot literarum detractione, Apostolorum dicti sunt. Et apud Græcos quoque res ita processisse videtur. Aucti sunt postea, cum adjecti essent, & eodem volumine comprehensi Græcæ Ecclesiæ canones. Græci hos canones, non priores quinquaginta tantum, sed & posteriores triginta quinque jam ultra mille & quod excurrit annos, habuerunt pro apostolicis. Patet id ex Canone 2. Synodi Constantinopolitanæ in Trullo, seculo septimo decurrente habitæ. Cujus verba hæc sunt. Ἔδοξε καὶ τῷ τῇ ἁγίᾳ ταύτῃ συνόδῳ καλλισά τε ἡ ἀσ-[?]
units.tr: 119. Conjecture about the time of writing and of the forgery. Until they were brought back into the light again by Bovius. The impostor, who was a clumsy fellow, drew his material from Scripture, from the ecclesiastical rites and discipline in use in his own time, and perhaps also from certain ritual books, such as the Apostolic Constitutions, which were well known in Epiphanius' day, and from the teaching of the Apostles mentioned by Athanasius and Eusebius, and he arranged it very foolishly. This is the more probable, at least for the Apostolic Constitutions, because he seems to have borrowed the title from them, and some things that Epiphanius lists from them are read today in the Bovian constitutions, while others, as was said above, do not appear. That the writer of these constitutions was a heretic, infected with the Arian taint, can be gathered sufficiently and more than sufficiently from those points which we have brought forward about the person of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Magnus Dalaeus therefore rightly ends his judgment of them with these words: there is hardly any other apocryphal work that is so flawed on every side as the Bovian Διαταξεις. I also think this is the reason why these Pseudo-apostolic constitutions were entirely thrust out of the work in the edition of the councils made at Paris in 1636. From what has been argued so far, the reader will be able to judge what is to be decided about the opinion of Cardinal Bona, and what weight is to be given to what he published about these Pseudo-apostolic constitutions in order to support his Pseudo-Clementine Mass, in book I of the Liturgies, chapter 8, section 4, page 52 of my edition, Paris. He says: among the apostolic liturgies may also be counted that of St Clement of Rome, described in the Book of Constitutions and received from the Apostles, as he says, from which I shall extricate myself in a few words. Proclus, at the beginning of his tract on the tradition of the Mass, bears witness to it, asserting that Clement published it while the Apostles dictated it. Baronius, in the year 102, number 23, agrees with this opinion, as do Bellarmine in his book on ecclesiastical writers, and others, who think it is genuine but was enlarged by later successors. For just as the Fathers afterwards enlarged the formula of the creed handed down by the Apostles, so that they might express the mysteries of the faith more clearly, so the liturgies were composed by the Apostles as their times then required, and were afterwards amplified by others. Yet other writers of no mean standing, who deny that Clement was the author of the Apostolic Constitutions, consequently deny that the Mass, which is a notable part of them, is his. Photius, in Codex 112, says that three chapters are objected to the Constitutions themselves, but these can easily be answered. Epiphanius, in heresy 70, number 10, cites the Book of the Apostolic Constitutions and then says: This book, although it is doubtful to some, is not on that account to be rejected. For in it are contained all things that pertain to the discipline of the Church; nor does it contain anything either corrupted in the faith and the Catholic profession, or contrary to the administration and decrees of the Church. But Petavius, in his notes, observes that the Constitutions which Epiphanius cites appear to differ from those that circulate in the eight books: for some of the sayings of those Constitutions cited by Epiphanius are not found in the printed texts. This, however, is merely Petavius' conjecture, and notwithstanding it I think it not improbable that they are the same, but interpolated, and in some places corrupted either by the carelessness of copyists or by the fraud of heretics. Some think that Dionysius of Alexandria alludes to them in the letter that Eusebius reports in book 7, chapter 7, but in it I find nothing at all that could be referred to Clement. Whatever may be the case about the author of these Constitutions, it is now certain and established for all that, even if they were not dictated immediately by the Apostles, they are nevertheless older than the Council of Nicaea, and in them is contained the ecclesiastical discipline by which the Eastern Church was governed under the heathen emperors before Constantine the Great, as the most learned man Jean Morin teaches in part 2, on sacred ordinations, page 20. Jean Fronto agrees with him in his notes prefixed to the Roman Calendar, section 5. Pierre de Marca likewise, in book 3 of the Concord, chapter 2, says that the author of that book flourished at least in the third century, and that this is now believed by all. The Mass of Clement is therefore very ancient, and I shall often make use of its testimony, if not precisely as published by the Apostles and enlarged by their successors, which is very probable, at least as used by the Fathers of the second or third century. So far he. It must be said that the Cardinal read the Constitutions carelessly, for he says that Clement, in these Pseudo-apostolic Constitutions, says that he received the liturgy from the Apostles, which he does not write anywhere in the whole work. Yet these few words are spoken in book 8, chapter 46: And I, Clement, was appointed bishop by the Apostles. Where Clement is mentioned, it is said of him as a minister, as was said above; see book 6, chapter 18, of the Pseudo-apostolic Constitutions. But there is no need to dwell longer on these matters, because others have sufficiently proved that all those ancient liturgies are either spurious, or at least corrupted, as Bona himself later admits about his own Liturgy of Clement. So that this much-vaunted work may have any authority, its accretions must first be removed and it must be shown which parts are genuine; and this Cardinal Bona, or anyone else, will never be able to do, in this Clementine liturgy any more than in the others. As for what he brings forward about the interpolation of these Constitutions, we oppose to it what the learned Dalaeus, already often praised, argued most solidly on the same subject against the Trullan Fathers, who asserted that these same Constitutions were interpolated and corrupted, in Pseudepigrapha of the Apostles, book 2, chapter 15; and also what he sets out in the same book, in the eight preceding chapters, about the age of these Constitutions, as if they were older than the Council of Nicaea, together with what has already been argued. We now pass to the so-called Canons of the Apostles. These are, according to Turrianus, chapter 1, in defence of the Apostolic Canons against the Magdeburg Centuriators, part of the eighth book of the Pseudo-apostolic Constitutions; in his edition, after the last words of chapter 46 there follow Ecclesiastical Canons, as they are called there, those which are commonly called the Apostles'. This seems to be confirmed by their last canon, where the Apostles themselves address the bishops: These things we have laid down for you, bishops, etc. Hence perhaps the author of the Opus Imperfectum on Matthew, an ancient but nonetheless heretical writer, calls the whole work of the Apostolic Constitutions the Books of the Canons of the Apostles, and cites the eighth book, Homily 53, whose citations are found in book 8 of the Constitutions, chapter 2. If this were true, that these canons formed part of the earlier work, which has been very widely refuted, there would be no need to argue at length against them in a separate treatment. It seems more likely and probable that some impostor combined two different works, the canons and the constitutions, and added some new ones to them; and this alone can prove, that most of the things read in the canons are found very fully in the constitutions themselves. Add that the last Pseudo-apostolic canon also sufficiently indicates that this work of canons is different from the Pseudo-apostolic Constitutions, and that Gelasius, in c. Sancta Romana, dist. 15, distinguishes these two works. Likewise Photius, in the Bibliotheca, Codices 112 and 113. Therefore, and because these canons bear even more on our history of ecclesiastical law than the preceding Apostolic Constitutions, and because for many centuries now they have been added to collections of ecclesiastical law, we should examine them separately. Here too the opinions of the learned are divided. Turrianus, a man of iron stomach and brazen forehead in defending apocryphal works, defended them in a separate volume against the Magdeburg Centuriators, and holds them all to be Apostolic. Lambert Gruter follows him, in his edition of the works of Clement of Rome, which appeared at Cologne in the year 1570. Baronius, in the year 102, section 14, and Bellarmine, on ecclesiastical writers, under Clement, acknowledge fifty as genuine and reject the remaining thirty-five, or according to others thirty-four. Possevinus agrees with these in his Apparatus, under the word Clement, and Binius too, though in such a way that the rest, except the sixty-fifth and the last, can rightly and justly be regarded by him as authentic; see his notes on the title of the Apostolic Canons, volume 1 of the councils; and you will be astonished at the judgment that in the same breath he approves those canons and confesses that they were listed among the apocrypha by Pope Gelasius. No one dares to ascribe them with certainty to the Apostles. Baronius, in the place cited, says: It is uncertain whether they were written by the Apostles themselves, nor does Turrianus himself contend this. Turrianus plainly denies it, in his tract defending them, at the beginning: Who, he says, ever among Catholics said that they were written by the Apostles? Afterwards, however, he maintains that all were written by Clement, and indeed he shamelessly invents that they were set down by the Apostles after the decree about the legal observances had been made at Jerusalem, were received by Clement, and this in the year of Christ 45, in the sixth year of Claudius, when Publius Valerius Asiaticus was consul for the second time. Binius leaves it uncertain who wrote the first fifty, which they hold above all as certain and indubitable; these he wishes to have come down to us by apostolic tradition. About the rest he doubts whether they were received by the Pontiffs, councils and Fathers from the Code of the Apostolic Canons, or whether they were rather transferred into this Code from the opinions of the Apostles themselves. Another is the judgment about the authority, name and authors of Gabriel Albaspinaeus, in book 1 of his Observations, chapter 15, where he holds that those are unskilled who firmly affirm that those canons were sanctioned or published by the authority of the Apostles. Then, they think that they were called Apostolic from antiquity. For, he adds, since several of them were made by the successors of the Apostles, who, as Tertullian witnesses in his book On Prescription, were called apostolic men, the canons first became apostolic; then, through the ignorance of some Latins, who by omitting a few letters called them Apostolic. And it seems that the matter went the same way among the Greeks too. They were afterwards increased, when the canons of the Greek Church were added and included in the same volume. The Greeks have held these canons to be apostolic for more than a thousand years, not only the first fifty but also the later thirty-five. This is clear from Canon 2 of the Synod of Constantinople in Trullo, held in the course of the seventh century. Its words are these: It also seemed good to this holy synod that the most beautiful [...] ἔδοξε καὶ τῷ τῇ ἁγίᾳ ταύτῃ συνόδῳ καλλισά τε ἡ ἀσ

units.la: δαιότατα, ὥστε μένειν καὶ ἀπὸ ξ νῦν βεβαίως καὶ ἀσφαλεῖς πρὸς ψυχῶν θεσωπείαν, ἢ ἰα-[?] τείαν παθῶν τὲς ὑπὸ τῶν περὶ ἡμῶν ἁγίων τῇ ἐνδόξων Ἀποστόλων οψδοήκοντα πέντε κανόνας-[?]
units.tr: most beautifully and most honourably, so that from now on they remain firm and secure for the care of souls and the healing of the passions: the eighty-five canons handed down by the holy and glorious Apostles.

units.la: Hoc quoque huic sancta synodo pulcherrime & honestissime placuit, ut deinceps ad animarum medelam & perturbationum curationem firmi stabilesque maneant, qui ab iis qui nos praecesserunt, Sanctis & gloriosis Apostolis traditi sunt octuaginta quinque canones. Ipse etiam Justinianus Imperator noster in Constitutione ad Epiphanium Patriarcham Constantinopol. hisce canonibus perhibet testimonium luculentum Novell. 6. quae etiam refertur in princ. nomocanon. Joh. Scholastici. Κα- λῶς δ' ἂν ἅπαντα πεάτῆοιτο, ἢ ᾳεσηκόντως, εἴωεϱ ἡ τᾶ πεϕγματ@ ἀρχὴ γένοιτο πεέπνσοα ἢ Φίλη Θεῷ. τῶτο δὲ ἐστᾷυ πισδίομῳ, εἴπερ ἡ τῶν ἱερῶν κανόνων ϕατηρήσις ϕυλάττοιτο, ὧ οἱ τε δικαίως ὑμνούμενοι καὶ ᾳεσηκωυσύμνοι, καὶ αὐτόπλαι ἢ ὑπηρέτη τὸ Θεῦ λόγυ ϕαδδε- δώκασιν ἀποσολοι, καὶ οἱ ἅγιοι πατέρες ἐφυλά- ξαντό τε, καὶ ὑφηγήσαντο. Recte, inquit, atque congruenter omnia agerentur, si ipsum rei initium gratum Deo esset, quod quidem certe futurum credimus, si sacri illi canones (vulgatus interpres habet regulas) diligenter observentur, quos nunquam satis laudati, adorationeque digni, & qui ipsi filium Dei conspexerunt, illique ministrarunt Apostoli nobis reliquerunt, ac sancti Patres custodiverunt & interpretati sunt. Intelligi autem hic Canones Apostolorum octuaginta quinque à Justiniano Doctissimus
units.tr: This also seemed most fitting and honourable to this holy synod: that from now on those eighty-five canons, handed down to us by the holy and glorious Apostles who went before us, remain firm and stable for the healing of souls and the cure of disorders. Our own Emperor Justinian also bears clear witness to these canons in his constitution addressed to Epiphanius, Patriarch of Constantinople, Novell. 6., which is also cited at the beginning of the Nomocanon of John Scholasticus. The Greek reads: all things would turn out well and acceptably if the beginning of affairs were pleasing to God. We believe this will surely be so if the sacred canons, which the Apostles who saw the Son of God and ministered to him handed down to us, and which the holy Fathers guarded and expounded, are diligently observed. Rightly and fittingly, he says, would everything be done, if the very beginning of the business were pleasing to God; and this we surely believe will be the case if those sacred canons (the Vulgate translator has rules) are diligently observed, which are never sufficiently praised or worthy of reverence, and which the Apostles, who themselves saw the Son of God and served him, have left to us, and which the holy Fathers guarded and interpreted. That these canons are the eighty-five Canons of the Apostles, as cited by Justinian, the most learned Ussher seeks to prove.

units.la: Usserius dissert. ad Ignat. cap. 6. pag. 37. & seq. evincere conatur. Primo quod totidem in Nomocanonem ab ipso Justiniano confirmatum, & eidem Epiphanio commendatum relatos fuisse fides sit ex Arabico illius Codicis interprete, qui in Oxoniensi bibliotheca habetur, à Thoma Roe, ex Oriente allatus, & donatus. Deinde quia idem numerus à Johanne Scholastico, de quo postea, relatus est in ejus Nomocanonem, qui vixit sub Justiniano, quam causam esse arbitror quare in corpus nostrum juris relati sint hi Canones Apostolici, non tamen suo loco: vel enim post hanc Novellam sextam, ut Codex canonum Ecclesiæ Catholicæ post Novellam 131. vel saltem post novellas Justiniani Constitutiones collocari debuissent, non in fine ante consuetudines feudales. Tanti hos fecit Johannes Damascenus, quod nullus Græcorum ausus est, ut lib. 4. c. 18. de orthodoxa fide eos retulerit in canonem sacræ Scripturæ. Ita enim ille. Παύλς Α᾿ποστόλς ἐπιστολαὶ δεκατεσαρες, Α᾿ποκάλυψις Ἰωάννς εὐανγελισ᾿. Κανόνες τῶν ἁγίων Α᾿ποσόλων διὰ κλήμεντ᾿ος.
units.tr: Ussher, dissert. ad Ignat. cap. 6. pag. 37. & seq., seeks to prove this. First, because it is credible from the Arabic interpreter of that codex, held in the Bodleian library at Oxford and brought from the East and given by Thomas Roe, that the same number was confirmed and recorded in the Nomocanon of Justinian himself, and commended to this Epiphanius. Second, because the same number is reported by John Scholasticus, of whom more later, in his Nomocanon, who lived under Justinian. I think this is the reason why these Apostolic canons were incorporated into our body of law, though not in their proper place. For they ought to have been placed either after this sixth Novel, as the Codex of the canons of the Catholic Church is placed after Novel 131, or at least after the other constitutions of Justinian, and not at the end, before the feudal customs. John of Damascus esteemed them so highly that, as in book 4, chapter 18, of the Orthodox Faith, no Greek has dared to place them in the canon of Holy Scripture. For he writes thus: Fourteen Epistles of Paul the Apostle, the Revelation of John the Evangelist, the Canons of the holy Apostles through Clement.

units.la: Pauli Apostoli Epistolæ quatuordecim, Apocalypsis Johannis Evangelistæ. Canones sanctorum Apostolorum per Clementem. Hujus singulare est judicium, ut & Photii, qui unus fere Græco-
units.tr: The fourteen Epistles of Paul the Apostle, the Apocalypse of John the Evangelist, the Canons of the holy Apostles through Clement. His judgement on this is singular, as is that of Photius, who almost alone among the Greeks

units.la: Note: the marginal note reads "128. Canones apostolici pars corporis juris." Græcorum, quantum quidem nobis compertum est, quosdam de hisce canonibus dubitasse scribit, in Prolegomenis Nomocanonis sui in principio fere, quæ nunc ex Bibliotheca Justelli edidit Filius, in Bibliotheca juris Canonici veteris. Tom. 2. p. 790. ἀλλὰ τὰς λεγομένας τῶν ἁγίων Ἀποστόλων, εἰ καί τινες αὐτὰς ἀμφιβόλως διά τινας αἰτίας ἡγήσαντο. Nec non (digessimus) etiam eos canones, qui sanctorum Apostolorum esse dicuntur. Quamvis nonnulli quibusdam causis moti, produbiis eos habuerint. Quos ille putet, qui dubitaverint de hisce canonibus, incertum est. Putat Dalæus eum forte intelligere Latinos; quod non est necesse, quia ex Græcis aliqui & forte ipse Photius, librorum censor accuratissimus dubitavit. Latinis tantum cogniti canones quinquaginta, quod satis patet ex Dionysii Exigui versione, qui primus, ut supra ex ejus Præfatione indicatum, quinquaginta Canones Apostolicos suæ versioni præmisit, & tot agnoscit quoque codex Romanæ Ecclesiæ Moguntiæ & Parisiis editus, qui fere idem cum Dionysii Codice, exceptis quibusdam, quæ supra sunt indicata. Idem confirmat c. Clementis dist. 16. quod falso inscribit Gratianus Leoni IX. cum sit Humberti Cardinalis; de quo vid. Ant. August. lib. 1. dial. 6. a. pag. 98. nostræ edit. & seqq. Neque plures Isidorus Mercator, Impostor ille, suæ collectioni inseruit; Hi quinquaginta qui Latinis noti fuerunt, apud eos non ejusdem fuerunt auctoritatis, qua apud Græcos: nullo apud eos, ut Græcos concilio sanciti aut recepti, sed manifeste jam seculo quinto exeunte à Gelasio & 70. Episcopis reprobati & inter Apocrypha relati c. sancta Romana. dist. 15. Cui concinit Isidorus Hispalensis, qui seculi septimi anno 39. vita functus est, relatus à Gratiano in c. Canones. dist. 16. Canones qui dicuntur Apostolorum, seu quia eosdem nec sedes apostolica recepit, nec sancti Patres illis adsensum præbuerunt, pro eo quod ab hæreticis sub nomine Apostolorum compositi dignoscuntur, quamvis in eis utilia inveniantur: tamen ab auctoritate canonica atque Apostolica eorum gesta placet esse remota, atque inter Apocrypha deputata. Quem Isidorum dubie separant ab Isidoro Mercatore in notis Emendatores Gratiani, qui in eadem distinctione c. placuit contraria dicit; quod mascule facit l.c. Anton. Augustinus noster, quem vide. Notabile est hoc Isidori testimonium, quo ademta est omnis auctoritas hisce canonibus Pseudapostolicis. Quos enim Turrianus, ab Apostolis conditos, à Clemente scriptos mentitur, ille ab hæreticis sub nomine Aposto-lorum lorum compositos dicit. Quos ille receptos per-suadere conatur, Isidorus, receptos vel à Pa-tribus probatos negat; quos ille pro legitimis & Ecclesiasticis obtrudit, hos Isidorus, inter Apocrypha deputatos & ab auctoritate Canonica, atque Apostolica remotos fuisse, adserit. Quod certum indicium seculi septimi principio, non fuisse alicujus apud Latinos auctoritatis hos canones Pseudapostolicos, quare etiam Ferrandus Diaconus Carthag. qui eodem tempore fere, quo Dionysius Exiguus vixit, suum Breviarium canonum scripsit, eos suæ digestioni non inseruit. Agnovit hoc quoque Dionysius Exiguus, qui idcirco hæc præfationi supra relatæ inseruit; In principio itaque canones QVI DICUNTVR, Apostolorum de Græco transtulimus, quibus quia PLVRIMI CONSENSVM NON PRÆBVERE FACILEM, hoc ipsum vestram noluimus ignorare sanctitatem; quamvis postea constituta Pontificum ex ipsis canonibus adsumta esse videantur. Quibus suam versionem videtur voluisse mitigare & munire, cum sciret non ita diu à Gelasio damnatos esse hos canones, & ut conciliaret quondam iis auctoritatem subjecisse: postea Constituta Pontificum ex ipsis canonibus adsumta videri. In quo certe non omnino falsus fuit, posteri enim, quanquam semper cum odii cujusdam contestatione & timide, eos admiserint, & aliquo loco habuerint, nunquam tamen tanti æstimarunt, ut quod inscriptio cantat pro Apostolicis reputaverint. Ex his patent fata horum canonum apud Latinos. Nempe primo inter apocrypha relatos esse à Gelasio, mox à Dionysio Exiguo versos, & canonibus conciliorum additos, attamen adhuc, ut constat ex Isidoro supra relato, reprobatos esse; donec tandem à Leone IV. seculo nono medio admitterentur. Turrianus ut Gelasii auctoritatem eluderet, homo in fabulis comminiscendis major Æsopo fabulatore celeberrimo, fingit sine ulla antiqui testis auctoritate, canones Apostolicos à Priscillianistis suppositos, eosque damnare Gelasium. Isidori auctoritatem fœdissima ignorantia eludere conatur, opponendo Isidorum Isidoro in cap. 1. & 4. dist. 16. tanquam eundem; quos tamen recte Antonius Augustinus noster ut supr. monstratu, agnoscit esse diversos, unum Hispalensem, & alterum Mercatorem. Vide accuratissime Turriani commenta refellentem Dalæum in Pseudepigr. Apostol. lib. 3. cap. 3. pag. 442. & multis seqq. Aliter enervat auctoritatem Gelasii Bellarminus, de Script. Eccles. qui cum Humberto seculi undecimi medii scriptore & legato Pontificis, agnoscit quinquaginta genuinos; triginta quinque spurios, & de posterioribus vult loqui Gelasium. Sed hoc commentum ipse Gelasius in d. c. sancta Romana. dist. 15. inspectus abunde refellit; qui totum librum Canonum Apostolorum inter Apocrypha refert, nullos genuinos aut priores, à spuriis & posterioribus distinguit.
