Deinde etiam Dionysius Exiguus, qui eodem fere cum Gelasio tempore vixit, & quinquaginta canones Codici canonum primus adjunxit, ille de his quinquaginta dicit; plurimos his consensum facilem non præbuisse; porro ipse Isidorus Mercator, qui etiam quinquaginta tantum conciliis præposuit, eos à quibusdam Apocryphos dici scribit. d. c. 4. dist. 16. Neque plures quam quinquaginta agnoscit Gratianus ante. c. 1. dist. 16. neque plures noti aut compositi fuerunt tempore Gelasii. Certum itaque est hos ab eo & patribus septuaginta fuisse damnatos, cæteri enim xxxv. postea confecti sunt, & à Justiniano Imperatore & Johanne Scholastico in Nomocanonem relati. Quod vel ex eo patet, quod Dionysius non longe post Gelasium vivens, tantum quinquaginta verterit, cæteros certe etiam versurus, si extitissent, quod non obscure agnoscit Baronius ad Ann. 102. §. 11. qui tantum quinquaginta ginta reperiße Dionysium Exiguum ingenue refert, & confitetur hos quinquaginta canones à Gelasio inter apocryphos esse relatos; Sed alio effugio,ejus damnationem evitare, aut interpretari conatur. Ea, inquit, ratione, canones isti, quod cum Apostolorum nomine censerentur non essent in Canone librorum Novi Testamenti, merito sunt Apocryphorum censura signati; Quod vero à sanctis Patribus, privatim & à sacris Synodis publice sunt recepti, merito authentici dici debent. Sed & hoc commentum abscondendæ vel obvelandæ veritaris causa fictum, ipsum decretum Gelasii satis refellit, quod prima parte præter scripturas sacras recenset etiam ea scripta, quibus Ecclesia Catholica uteretur, sed infra sacræ Scripturæ auctoritatem. Posteriori vero parte enumerat scripta, quæ repudiata sunt, iisque diserte accenset Librum Canonum Apostolorum, adeoque nec sacris, nec Ecclesiasticis libris annumerari vult eos; imo quod magis est ipse Gelasius accenset libris quæ ab hæreticis sive scismaticis conscripti, vel prædicati sunt, quos nullatenus recipit Catholica & Apostolica Ecclesia; è quibus pauca, quæ ad memoriam venerunt, & à Catholicis vitanda sunt, credit esse subdenda. Post recensionem istorum librorum, & inter hos canonum Apostolicorum subdit. Hæc & cætera his bis similia, quæ Simon Magus, &c. nec non & omnes hæretici eorumque discipuli, sive schismatici docuerunt, vel conscripserunt, quorum nomina minime retinentur, non solum repudiata, verum etiam ab omni Romana Catholica & Apostolica Ecclesia eliminata atque cum suis auctoribus auctorumque sequacibus sub anathematis indissolubili vinculo in æternum confitemur esse damnata. Ejusmodi vero libros Baronius nobis pro Ecclesiasticis obtrudere conatur, quos diserte Gelasius in æternum damnatos dicit,& cum aliis pessimæ notæ libris apocryphis accenset; quæ sola vox apocryphi Baronii fucum eludit & eliminat, concinente vel ipso Bellarmino, lib. 1. de verb. Dei. c. 20. cujus verba rei præsenti aptissima recensebo. Interdum vocant apocryphos libros eos, qui errores admixtos habent. Sic utitur hac voce Origenes homil. 1. in Cantic. Hieronymus in Epistola ad Letam de institutione filiæ, & Augustinus lib. 15. de civit. Dei. c. 23. Quam significationem secutus Gelasius, in decreto de libris Ecclesiasticis, eos libros vocat Apocryphos, qui sunt editi ab auctoribus hæreticis, vel certe suspectis. Neque quidquam Turrianum juvare potest figmentum, quasi ipse Gelasius multa ex hoc Apostolicorum canonum libro laudet in Epistolis suis, quoniam hoc aperte falsum est, & clarum, quod ille sua vel ex sacris Scripturis, vel ex Concilii Nicæni scitis hauserit, quæ Turrianus impudenter eum ex hoc ab ipso damnato libro adferre fingit. vid. sis Dalæi Pseudep. Apost. lib. 3. c. 4. Zepherini Papæ Epistolam summa cum impudentia à Gelasio probatam adserere audet Turrianus, quam infra ab Isidoro Mercatore septem seculis post Zephyrinum confictam demonstrabimus. Verum itaque est de his Canonibus judicium Magni Dalæi. lib. 3. Pseudepigr. Apost. cap. 4. pag. 479. & seqq. quod adscribo; Profligatis ergo quacunque ad hunc locum à Turriano, Bellarminoque & Baronio objecta, vel excogitata sunt; firmum ac verum stat Gelasii in Romana 70. episcoporum Synodo decretum, Liber Canonum Apostolicorum apocryphus. Unde clarum certumque fit primo Dionysium Exiguum quinquaginta Apostolorum Canones à se in Græcis exemplaribus inventos, temere ac inscite & præter dissertissimam Episcopi, Conciliique Romani sententiam Ecclesiastico codici primum omnium inseruisse; multo pejus, atque periculosius paulo post peccasse Justinianum, & Joannem ex Scholasticis, qui eundem canonum Apostolicorum librum, & quidem triginta quinque capitulis auctiorem, in publicum Nomocanonem retulerunt; gravissime omnium peccasse Damascenum, qui non modo falsos ac nuperos, sed etiam à Papa & Concilio Romano Romano damnatos canones divinis libris per intolerabilem, planeque sacrilegam audaciam exæquavit; peccasse & Trullanos Patres, qui eundem librum firmare & authoritate summa donare non dubitarunt, eodemque in flagitio hærere reliquos omnes Græcos, qui hujus Synodi placita sequuntur; errasse postremo Leonem IV. & Nicolaum I. & cæteros Latinos, quotquot Dionysiacæ collectionis specie decepti, adversus sacra canitie veneranda Gelasii & majorum statuta, ac contra luculentissimam Isidori Hispalensis admonitionem, damnatos, qui Apostolorum dicuntur, canones, inter Ecclesiasticas regulas habere ac recensere ausi sunt. Horum omnium quotcunque, ac quanticunque de cætero sint, authoritatem omnem obterit antiquius Gelasii, Romanaque Synodi decretum; neque ullis posterorum sententiis convalescere possunt, quæ jam tot ante sæculis legitimo, ac canonico, non Romani modo Præsulis, & quidem ejus, qui inter sapientissimos habetur, sed & Romanæ, & quidem LXX. Episcoporum Synodi, statuto convulsa & ex Ecclesiæ Catholicæ finibus exterminata fuerunt. Hoc ego Romanæ veteris Ecclesiæ decretum omnibus recentiorum scitis, ac disputationibus oppono; hoc unum pluris facio, quam & Trullanæ Synodi, & Græculorum omnium canones & psephismata. Neque satis mirari possum degenerem Turriani & aliorum ignaviam, qui in tota hac causa Romani nominis dignitate fœdissime prodita, unius Scythæ nugas, & Græcorum levitatem sui Gelasii, suaque Synodi authoritati anteponunt. Ac illis quidem, si moribus, quos jactant, Romanis vere essent, hæc ad contemnendos, & ad Apocrypha relegandos Apostolorum, quotquot dicuntur, Canones, satis esse deberent. Non satis potest mirari degeneres Latinorum animos Dalæus, quod tanquam pro aris & focis propugnent Constitutiones & Canones Pseudapostolicos; ego desino hoc mirari, quando video eos præcipua sua dogmata ex iis confirmare. Constitutiones citat Bellarminus lib. 1. de clericis. c. 12. pro antiquitate ordinum Ecclesiasticorum. lib. 2. de Monach. c. 26. pro voto continentiæ. lib. 1. de purg. cap. 6. pro oratione pro mortuis lib. 3. de cultu sanct. cap. 7. pro aqua lustrali. lib. 4. c. 4. de Euchar. pro reservatione sacramenti. & cap. 10. ibid. pro mistione vini & aquæ in sacramento Eucharistiæ. lib. 2. c. 15. de Missa. pro lotione manuum ante consecrationem. lib. 2. de confir. cap. 3. pro confirmationis sacramento. Anglo-Remenses citant easdem, ut probent ab Apostolis institutum esse quadragesimæ jejunium, in annot. ad Luc. 4. 1. Canones Apostolorum adducuntur fere ab omnibus Pontificiis. Bellarminus canonem primum laudat, lib. 1. de Cler. cap. 3. & lib. 4. de not. de not. Eccles. cap. 8. ut probet, Episcopum non nisi à tribus Episcopis ordinandum esse. Canonem item 3. & 4. idem pro ritu altarium, ut probet Missam esse sacrificium proprie dictum. de Missa. lib. 1. c. 16. Canon. 12. 13. & 15. pro distinctione Clericorum & Laicorum. lib. 1. de Cler. c. 1. Canonem 27. pro coelibatu ordinibus initiatorum. ibid. c. 19. Canon. 48. pro insolubilitate matrimonii quoad vinculum. de matrim. lib. 1. c. 26. Canon. 68. pro jejunio quadragesimali. lib. 2. c. 14. de bon. operib. Canon. 2. adducit Stapleton. relect. contr. 2. q. 4. art. 3. ut probet Presbyterum ab uno Episcopo esse ordinatum. Canon. 34. pro appellationibus ad Pontificem Romanum. ibid. contr. 3. q. 7. Alanus Cardinalis canonem ultimum profert, ad probandam auctoritatem canonicam librorum Machabaeorum lib. de suffragio pro defunct. c. 3. Alii alios laudant, ut suas quisquilias colorent; Atque haec est causa quare hasce Apocryphas delicias ita affectent, ut ex orco, in quem damnatae sunt à Gelasio & 70. Patribus, revocent, quo fucum multis faciant & novis inventis antiquitatis speciem & faciem conciliënt. Non abs re itaque erit, larvas paucis detrahere his Apocryphis quoque canonibus; Bellarminus in Clemente de script. Eccles. itemque
units.tr: Marginal note: 128. The Apostolic Canons are part of the body of canon law. The Greeks, as far as we have learned, wrote that some of them doubted these canons, in the opening part of the Prolegomena to his Nomocanon, which his son has now published from the library of Justellus, in Bibliotheca juris Canonici veteris, vol. 2, p. 790: "but those called the canons of the holy Apostles, even if some have considered them doubtful for certain reasons" [ἀλλὰ τὰς λεγομένας τῶν ἁγίων Ἀποστόλων, εἰ καί τινες αὐτὰς ἀμφιβόλως διά τινας αἰτίας ἡγήσαντο]. Nor have we (arranged) also those canons which are said to be of the holy Apostles. Although some, moved by certain causes, have regarded them as doubtful. It is uncertain whom he means by those who doubted these canons. Dalaeus thinks he perhaps means the Latins; but that is not necessary, since some of the Greeks, and perhaps Photius himself, the most careful critic of books, doubted them. Among the Latins only fifty canons were known, as is quite clear from the version of Dionysius Exiguus, who was the first, as indicated above from his Preface, to place the fifty Apostolic Canons at the head of his version. The codex of the Roman Church published at Mainz and Paris also recognizes this number; it is almost the same as the codex of Dionysius, apart from certain differences already noted above. The same is confirmed by the chapter of Clement, dist. 16, which Gratian wrongly ascribes to Leo IX, since it is by Cardinal Humbert. On this see Antonius Augustinus, lib. 1, dial. 6, from p. 98 of our edition and following. Nor did Isidore Mercator, that impostor, include more in his collection. These fifty, which were known to the Latins, did not have among them the same authority as among the Greeks. They were never sanctioned or received by any council among them, as among the Greeks; and already at the end of the fifth century they were plainly rejected by Gelasius and seventy bishops and listed among the Apocrypha, in the chapter Sancta Romana, dist. 15. Isidore of Seville agrees with this. He died in the thirty-ninth year of the seventh century, and is cited by Gratian in the chapter Canones, dist. 16: "The canons which are said to be of the Apostles, since neither the apostolic see has received them nor the holy Fathers given assent to them, because they are known to have been composed by heretics under the name of the Apostles, although useful things are found in them, nevertheless their acts are held to be removed from canonical and apostolic authority and reckoned among the Apocrypha." The editors of Gratian, in the notes, doubtfully separate this Isidore from Isidore Mercator, who in the same distinction, chapter placuit, says the opposite; our Anton. Augustinus does this well in the passage cited, and see him. This testimony of Isidore is notable, since it takes away all authority from these Pseudo-apostolic canons. For what Turrianus lies about, that they were founded by the Apostles and written by Clement, he calls "composed by heretics under the name of the Apostles." What he tries to persuade us were received, Isidore denies were "received or approved by the Fathers"; what he pushes forward as legitimate and ecclesiastical, Isidore asserts were "reckoned among the Apocrypha and removed from canonical and apostolic authority." This is a sure sign that at the beginning of the seventh century these Pseudo-apostolic canons had no authority among the Latins. For this reason Ferrandus the Deacon of Carthage, who wrote his Breviary of canons at about the same time as Dionysius Exiguus lived, did not include them in his collection. Dionysius Exiguus also recognized this, and therefore inserted into his Preface the words quoted above: "At the beginning, then, we have translated from the Greek the canons which are called of the Apostles, to which, because very many have not given easy assent, we did not wish your holiness to be ignorant of this very fact; although it seems that the decrees of the Pontiffs were later taken from these same canons." By these words he seems to have wished to soften and fortify his version, since he knew that these canons had not been condemned by Gelasius very long before, and so to win them some authority by adding that the decrees of the Pontiffs were later seen to be taken from the canons themselves. In this he was certainly not altogether wrong. For later generations, although always with some protest of dislike and timidly, admitted them and gave them some place; yet they never valued them so highly as to regard as Apostolic what the title proclaims. From this the fate of these canons among the Latins is clear. First they were listed among the apocrypha by Gelasius; soon afterwards they were translated by Dionysius Exiguus and added to the canons of the councils; yet they were still, as appears from the Isidore cited above, rejected; until at last Leo IV in the middle of the ninth century admitted them. Turrianus, to evade the authority of Gelasius, a man greater in inventing fables than the famous fabulist Aesop, makes up, without any witness of antiquity, that the Apostolic canons were forged by the Priscillianists, and that Gelasius condemned them. He tries to evade the authority of Isidore with the most shameful ignorance, by setting Isidore against Isidore in chapters 1 and 4, dist. 16, as if they were the same man; yet our Antonius Augustinus, as above, has shown that they are different, one the Sevillian and the other Mercator. See the most careful refutation of Turrianus's inventions by Dalaeus in his Pseudepigrapha Apostolorum, lib. 3, cap. 3, p. 442, and many following pages. Bellarmine weakens the authority of Gelasius in another way, in his De scriptoribus ecclesiasticis. Together with Humbert, a writer and legate of the Pontiff in the middle of the eleventh century, he acknowledges fifty as genuine and thirty-five as spurious, and wishes Gelasius to be speaking of the latter. But Gelasius himself, examined in the chapter Sancta Romana, dist. 15, thoroughly refutes this invention. He lists the whole book of the Apostolic Canons among the Apocrypha, and does not distinguish any genuine or earlier ones from spurious and later ones. Then also Dionysius Exiguus, who lived at about the same time as Gelasius and was the first to add the fifty canons to the collection of canons, says of these fifty that very many have not given them easy assent. Further, Isidore Mercator himself, who also placed only fifty before the councils, writes that they are called apocryphal by some (chapter 4, dist. 16). Nor does Gratian, before chapter 1, dist. 16, acknowledge more than fifty, and no more were known or composed in the time of Gelasius. It is therefore certain that these were condemned by him and by the seventy Fathers; for the other thirty-five were composed afterwards, and were included in the Nomocanon by the Emperor Justinian and John the Scholastic. This is clear also from the fact that Dionysius, living not long after Gelasius, translated only fifty; he would certainly have translated the rest too, if they had existed, which Baronius acknowledges plainly in his note to the year 102, §11. He honestly reports that Dionysius Exiguus found only fifty, and admits that these fifty canons were listed by Gelasius among the apocryphal books. But he tries to escape or explain away their condemnation by another evasion. "For this reason," he says, "these canons, because they were reckoned under the name of the Apostles and were not in the canon of the books of the New Testament, were rightly marked with the censure of the Apocrypha; but because they were received privately by the holy Fathers and publicly by the sacred Synods, they ought rightly to be called authentic." But this invention, made to hide or veil the truth, is itself sufficiently refuted by the decree of Gelasius, which in its first part enumerates, besides the sacred Scriptures, also those writings which the Catholic Church uses, but beneath the authority of Holy Scripture. In its latter part it lists the writings that have been rejected, and expressly counts among them the Book of the Canons of the Apostles; so he does not wish them to be numbered either among the sacred or among the ecclesiastical books. Indeed, what is more, Gelasius himself counts among the books those written or proclaimed by heretics or schismatics, which the Catholic and Apostolic Church nowhere receives; of which few, which have come to memory, and which are to be avoided by Catholics, he believes should be subjoined. After the list of these books, and among them the Apostolic canons, he adds: "These and other things like them, which Simon Magus, etc., and also all heretics and their disciples, or schismatics, have taught or written, whose names are not at all kept, not only are rejected, but are also removed from the whole Roman Catholic and Apostolic Church, and we confess that they, together with their authors and the followers of their authors, have been condemned forever under the indissoluble bond of anathema." But Baronius tries to force upon us as ecclesiastical books those which Gelasius expressly says were condemned forever, and he counts them among the apocryphal books, of very bad repute. This single word apocryphal Baronius uses to cover up and eliminate the trick; and Bellarmine himself agrees, in lib. 1, De verbo Dei, cap. 20, whose words I shall quote as most suited to the present matter: "Sometimes they call apocryphal those books which contain mixed errors. Origen uses this word so in Homily 1 on the Song of Songs, Jerome in his Letter to Leta on the education of a daughter, and Augustine in De civitate Dei, lib. 15, cap. 23. Following this meaning, Gelasius in the decree on ecclesiastical books calls apocryphal those books which have been published by heretical or at least suspect authors." Nor can the fiction of Turrianus help him, as if Gelasius himself praised many things from this book of the Apostolic canons in his letters; for this is plainly false and clear, since he drew his material either from the sacred Scriptures or from the decisions of the Council of Nicaea, which Turrianus shamelessly pretends he took from this book that was itself condemned. See the Pseudepigrapha Apostolorum of Dalaeus, lib. 3, cap. 4. Turrianus dares to assert, with the greatest shamelessness, that the letter of Pope Zephyrinus was approved by Gelasius; below we shall show that it was forged by Isidore Mercator seven centuries after Zephyrinus. The judgment of the great Dalaeus on these canons is true, and I adopt it: "Therefore, when whatever has been objected or devised at this point by Turrianus, Bellarmine and Baronius has been overthrown, there stands firm and true the decree of Gelasius in the Roman Synod of seventy bishops: the book of the Apostolic Canons is apocryphal. Whence it becomes clear and certain: first, that Dionysius Exiguus, having found fifty canons of the Apostles in Greek copies, rashly and foolishly, and against the very clear judgment of the Bishop and the Roman Council, was the first of all to insert them into the ecclesiastical code; far worse and more dangerously, a little afterwards, Justinian and John the Scholastic sinned, who brought the same book of Apostolic canons, indeed enlarged by thirty-five chapters, into the public Nomocanon; most gravely of all, Damascene sinned, who, with intolerable and plainly sacrilegious audacity, put on a par with the divine books canons that were not only false and recent but were condemned by the Pope and the Roman Council; the Trullan Fathers also sinned, who did not hesitate to confirm the same book and give it the highest authority, and all the other Greeks who follow the decisions of this Synod remain in the same disgrace; finally Leo IV, Nicholas I, and all the other Latins erred, as many as, deceived by the appearance of the Dionysian collection, dared to hold and list among the ecclesiastical rules the canons called Apostolic, which had been condemned against the venerable authority of Gelasius and the decrees of our fathers, and against the most clear admonition of Isidore of Seville."* Whatever and however many, from now on, these authorities may be, the older authority of Gelasius and the decree of the Roman Synod overthrow them all; nor can they gain strength from any opinions of later men, which were already overturned many centuries ago by a lawful and canonical statute, not only of a Roman Pontiff, and indeed of one counted among the wisest, but also of a Roman Synod of seventy bishops, and so driven out of the bounds of the Catholic Church. I set this decree of the ancient Roman Church against all the decisions and disputations of more recent men; this one thing I value more than both the Trullan Synod and all the canons and decrees of the Greeklings. Nor can I sufficiently wonder at the degenerate cowardice of Turrianus and others, who, in this whole cause, with the dignity of the Roman name shamefully betrayed, prefer the trifles of one Scythian and the lightness of the Greeks to the authority of their own Gelasius and Synod. If they were truly Romans in the customs they boast of, these considerations should be enough to despise and relegate to the Apocrypha the canons, however many, that are called Apostolic." I cannot sufficiently wonder at the degenerate spirit of the Latins, that, as if fighting for altars and hearths, they defend the Pseudo-apostolic constitutions and canons, says Dalaeus; I cease to wonder at this, since I see them confirm their chief doctrines from them. Bellarmine cites the Constitutions, lib. 1, De clericis, cap. 12, for the antiquity of the ecclesiastical orders; lib. 2, De monachis, cap. 26, for the vow of continence; lib. 1, De purgatorio, cap. 6, for prayer for the dead; lib. 3, De cultu sanctorum, cap. 7, for lustral water; lib. 4, De Eucharistia, cap. 4, for the reservation of the sacrament; and cap. 10, ibid., for the mixing of wine and water in the sacrament of the Eucharist; lib. 2, De missa, cap. 15, for the washing of hands before consecration; lib. 2, De confirmatione, cap. 3, for the sacrament of confirmation. The Anglo-Rhemish annotators cite the same Constitutions to prove that the fast of Lent was instituted by the Apostles (note on Luke 4:1). The Apostolic canons are adduced by almost all the Papists. Bellarmine praises the first canon, lib. 1, De clericis, cap. 3, and lib. 4, De notis ecclesiae, cap. 8, to prove that a bishop must be ordained by three bishops only. He cites the third and fourth canons likewise, for the rite of the altars, to prove that the Mass is a sacrifice properly so called (De missa, lib. 1, cap. 16). Canons 12, 13 and 15 for the distinction between clergy and laity (lib. 1, De clericis, cap. 1); canon 27 for celibacy of those initiated into orders (ibid., cap. 19); canon 48 for the indissolubility of marriage as to the bond (De matrimonio, lib. 1, cap. 26); canon 68 for the Lenten fast (lib. 2, De bonis operibus, cap. 14). Stapleton cites canon 2 (Relectiones contra, 2, q. 4, art. 3) to prove that a presbyter is ordained by one bishop. Canon 34 is cited for appeals to the Roman Pontiff (ibid., contr. 3, q. 7). Cardinal Allen brings forward the last canon to prove the canonical authority of the books of the Maccabees (De suffragiis pro defunctis, cap. 3). Others praise others, to colour their trifles. And this is the reason why they so eagerly cherish these apocryphal delicacies, that they call them back from the underworld into which Gelasius and the seventy Fathers condemned them, so that they may deceive many and lend to new inventions the appearance and face of antiquity. It will not be out of place, then, briefly to strip away the masks of these Apocryphal canons too. Bellarmine, in Clement, De scriptoribus ecclesiasticis, and likewise Possevinus, cite the testimony of Tertullian in his book Against Praxeas in support of the authority of the Apostolic canons. But Sixtus of Siena deceived both of them, Bibliotheca, lib. 2. For Tertullian, as Magnus Ussher has already observed, De scriptis Ignatii, cap. 6, p. …

units.la: 132. Auctoritates & argumenta itemque Possevinus, laudant pro Canonibus Apostolorum, testimonium Tertulliani in libro adversus Praxeam. Sed utrumque decepit Sixtus Senensis lib. 2. Bibliothec. Tertullianus enim ut jam antea observavit Magnus Usserius, in Dissert. de script. Ignatii. cap. 6. pag. 35. & seqq. neque in libro adversus Praxeam, neque in aliis libris meminit canonum Apostolicorum, aut dicit eos esse nobis per manus Apostolorum traditos, quod Bellarm. & Possevinus asserunt. Quinimo certum est Tertulliano nullos suisse istiusmodi canones cognitos; multa enim alias ex eorum auctoritate firmasset, aut aliter quam fecit, decidisset. Falsa quoque est allegata à Sixto & Bellarmino auctoritas Athanasii, vel alius auctoris synopseos, qui nullibi meminit Canonum Apostolicorum, sed tantum τὰ Κλημεντίνα Clementina refert inter ea Novi Testamenti, quibus contradicitur cum Petri, Joannisque & Thomæ periodis, sive itinerariis. Per Clementina autem non intelligi posse canones Apostolorum, vel ex eo patet, quod multis demum post Clementem annis sint scripti & congesti, ut postea patebit. Testimonia primorum Urbis Romæ Episcoporum, Anacleti, Alexandri, Julii, Eleutherii, Marcelli, Fabiani, Eusebii, Aniceti, Callixti, Lucii, Eutychiani, pro Canonibus Apostolicis, nemo cordatus, qui in antiquitate Ecclesiastica non est totus Hospes, etiam ex Pontificiis, pro genuinis habet, sed impudentis seculi noni ineuntis impostoris, quod postea, ubi de Isidoro Mercatore, ejusque collectione nobis sermo erit, pluribus demonstrabimus. Mentitur porro strenue Turrianus, pro Canonibus istis contr. Magdeb. pag. 69. & Binius, in canon. 51. Apost. tom. 1. Bibl. Patr. quando notos & citatos origini dicunt canones istos lib. 8. & 3. contra Celsum, quia quædam refert, quibus similia leguntur in Canonibus Apostolorum; cum vel pueri sciant nullum legitimum argumentum inde duci posse; mores quidam in usu tertio seculo decurrente, laudati ab origine, inveniuntur quoque in Canonibus Pseudapostolicis, ergo Origini illi fuerunt noti, & ab eo citati. Eodem modo adducit Turrianus quædam ex Cypriano, & synodis quarti seculi, quæ certe si doceret Turrianus patres illos ex Canonibus Apostolicis hausisse, aut hausta dicere, jam probaret, quod sibi adsumserat. Magisque verum, imo forte certum est, quod Impostor ille, qui seculo quinto exeunte (ut probabile est) hos canones Apostolis suppositit, sua ex conciliis aut Patribus, quam Patres aut concilia sua ex his canonibus, quos ignorarunt, sumferint. Maxime cum nullibi sua Patres muniant auctoritate Canonum Apostolorum, quod religiosi certe non praeteriissent, si scivissent tales extare. Neque etiam Nicaeni Patres passim τ κανόνας simpliciter can. 1. 2. 15. citassent, sed illud Ἀποστόλων, vel illud Ἀποστόλων σὺν Κλήμεντος, itemque numerum procul dubio subjecissent, si Apostolos tradidisse, & extare illos canones iis compertum fuisset. Verum hic mos est Turriani, si apud quendam ex Patribus, aut in concilio tantum legatur: secundum canonem, regulam, morem Ecclesiasticum & simile quid inveniatur in Canonibus Pseudapostolicis, statim id sufficiens argumentum est, & probatio, Patrem illum, vel Synodum respexisse vel citasse canones Apostolicos. Sic adducit cap. 12. pro canonibus hisce pag. 31. & seqq. ex seculo quinto Epistolam Innocentii Romani Episcopi ad Victricium Rothomagensem, quae scripta est Anno 404; in qua tota ne χεῖρ invenitur pro hisce canonibus. Quaedam ex tredecim capitulis quae ibid. leguntur, inveniuntur quidem praecepta etiam in canonibus hisce, sed non dicit se ea hausisse ex iis Innocentius, nec horum auctoritate sua fulcit; quod certe non neglexisset, cum in capite primo mo & septimo citet synodum Nicænam, si habuisset eos cognitos. Qui neglectus firmius argumentum contra Turrianum præbet, tum incognitos fuisse, & postea ex hac Epistola in suam rapsodiam transtulisse quædam auctore istorum canonum; quam convenientia dictorum quorundā pro Turriano & canonibus. Nec magis patrocinatur synodus Ephesina, in cujus act. 7. Turrianus iis cap. 13. & 14. d. tract. præter fidem codicis canonum Ecclesiæ universæ, Latinæ versionis, & editiones conciliorum pro voce πατέρων legit Ἀπόστολων, quam lectionem editiones conciliorum Græco Latinæ in margine habent & notant, quę à Græcis hos canones probantibus, videtur efficta & excogitata. Ejusdem notæ sunt quæ ex synodo Calchedonensi, Cyrillo & Leone pro canonibus istis à Turriano proferuntur, quæ recensione & refutatione indigna sunt, qui ea desiderat, adeat Dalæi Pseudepigrah. Apost. lib. 3. cap. 10. Sufficiat demonstrasse non esse istos canones Apostolicos, neque ab Apostolis, neque à Clemente constitutos aut scriptos. Quod de posterioribus triginta quinque Latini contra Græcos tam veteres quam recentiores præter Turrianum fere omnes, saltem celebriores defenderunt, Humbertus, Ant. Augustinus noster, lib. I. dial. 6. pag. nostr. edit. 99. & seqq. Bellarminus; nus, Baronius, qui omnes post Turrianum scripserunt. Quod & probant illi ex Latinis, qui tantum quinquaginta agnoscunt; Dionysius nempe Exiguus, item Cresconius Afer in concordia canonum seculo sexto, Hadrianus primus seculo octavo, Isidorus Mercator seculi noni scriptor, Impostor volebam dicere, Gratianus compilator Decreti seculo duodecimo. Neque scio quod quisquam, praeter unum Turrianum, intra quindecim & quot excurrit secula, usque dum ille suam infelicem Apologiam seculi superioris anno 73. pro his canonibus edidisset, dissentiat. Probat falsitatem posteriorum 35. canonum primus, alias in ordine 51mus, qui lapsos promiscue recipiendos sanxit; quod ante seculi tertii medium, quo tempore de lapsis dispensari coepit, ignotum fuisse, ipse agnoscit sagax rupator antiquitatis Ecclesiasticae Albaspinaeus, lib. 1. obs. cap. 13; deinde ante Cyprianum rigor ille in lapsos idolatras nondum fuit remissus, hoc est anno Christi 254. Pater idem ex canone nono, supra quinquagesimum, in quo τὰ Ψευδεπιγεγραφα τῶν ἀποστόλων βιβλία, falso inscripti libri impiorum publicari ab Ecclesia prohibentur. Intelligit autem edita Apostolorum nomine scripta suppositicia (de quibus nos, Deo volente, ad famosum Gelasii & 70. Episcopo-
units.tr: 132. Possevinus and others also cite, in support of the Canons of the Apostles, the testimony of Tertullian in his book against Praxeas. But Sixtus of Siena was misled on both points, Bk. 2 of the Bibliotheca. For Tertullian, as the great Usher has already observed, in his Dissertation on the writings of Ignatius, ch. 6, p. 35 and following, mentions the Canons of the Apostles neither in the book against Praxeas nor in any of his other books, and he does not say that they were handed down to us by the hands of the Apostles, as Bellarmine and Possevinus assert. Indeed it is certain that Tertullian knew of no canons of this kind. For he would have confirmed many matters by their authority, or else decided them differently from how he did. The authority alleged by Sixtus and Bellarmine from Athanasius, or from some other author of the synopsis, is also false. That writer nowhere mentions the Canons of the Apostles, but only lists the Clementine writings [τὰ Κλημεντίνα] among the books of the New Testament that are rejected, together with the Acts of Peter, John and Thomas, or itineraries. That the Clementine writings cannot be understood as the canons of the Apostles is clear from the fact that they were written and compiled many years after Clement, as will be shown later. No sensible person who is not wholly a stranger to ecclesiastical antiquity, even among the Papists, regards as genuine the testimonies of the first bishops of the city of Rome, Anacletus, Alexander, Julius, Eleutherius, Marcellus, Fabian, Eusebius, Anicetus, Callixtus, Lucius and Eutychianus, in favour of the Apostolic Canons. These are the work of an impostor of the early ninth century, as we shall demonstrate at length later, when we come to speak of Isidore Mercator and his collection. Moreover Turrianus boldly lies, in his work for these canons against Magdeburg, p. 69, and so does Binius, on canon 51 of the Apostles, vol. 1 of the Bibliotheca Patrum, when they say that these canons were known and cited by Origen, Bks. 8 and 3 against Celsus, because he reports some things that are also read in the Canons of the Apostles. Even children know that no legitimate argument can be drawn from this. Some customs praised by Origen, which were in use in the third century, are also found in the Pseudo-Apostolic Canons; therefore, they say, Origen knew them and cited them. In the same way Turrianus adduces certain things from Cyprian and from the synods of the fourth century. If Turrianus could show that those Fathers drew these things from the Canons of the Apostles, or said that they had done so, he would already prove what he has taken upon himself. Much more probable, indeed perhaps certain, is that the impostor who foisted these canons upon the Apostles at the end of the fifth century (as is likely) took his material from the councils or the Fathers, rather than that the Fathers or councils took theirs from these canons, which they did not know. This is especially so since the Fathers nowhere support their own positions by the authority of the Canons of the Apostles, which they certainly would not have passed over had they known that such canons existed. Nor did the Fathers of Nicaea simply cite the canons [κανόνας] in passing, as in canons 1, 2 and 15, but would undoubtedly have added either of the Apostles or of the Apostles, with Clement, together with the number, if it had been known that the Apostles had handed them down and that these canons existed. But this is Turrianus's habit: if something is read in one of the Fathers, or only in a council, as according to the canon, rule, Ecclesiastical custom, and something similar is found in the Pseudo-Apostolic Canons, he immediately takes this as a sufficient argument and proof that the Father or synod had regard to or cited the Apostolic Canons. Thus he adduces, ch. 12, for these canons, p. 31 and following, from the fifth century, the letter of Innocent, bishop of Rome, to Victricius of Rouen, written in 404. In the whole of that letter there is not a word in favour of these canons. Some of the thirteen chapters read there are indeed found as precepts in these canons as well, but Innocent does not say that he drew them from those canons, nor does he support his own position by their authority. He would certainly not have neglected to do so, since in chapters 1, 6 and 7 he cites the Nicene synod, if he had known these canons. This neglect provides a stronger argument against Turrianus, both that these canons were then unknown and that the author of these canons later transferred some things from this letter into his own patchwork. Nor does the Synod of Ephesus support him any better. In its Act 7, Turrianus, ch. 13 and 14 of the same tract, reads Ἀποστόλων [of the Apostles] instead of πατέρων [of the Fathers], contrary to the testimony of the manuscripts of the canons of the universal Church, the Latin version, and the printed editions of the councils. The Greek-Latin editions of the councils note this reading in their margins, and it seems to have been invented and devised by the Greeks who defend these canons. Of the same kind are the things that Turrianus brings forward for these canons from the Council of Chalcedon, and from Cyril and Leo. They are not worth examining or refuting. Whoever wants them may consult Daillé, Pseudepigrapha of the Apostles, bk. 3, ch. 10. It is enough to have shown that these canons are neither of the Apostles, nor established or written by Clement. Almost all Latins, apart from Turrianus, both ancient and recent, have defended this against the Greeks with regard to the later thirty-five canons, at least the more famous among them: Humbert, our Antonius Augustinus, Bk. 1, dialogue 6, p. 99 of our edition and following, Bellarmine, Baronius, all of whom wrote after Turrianus. The Latins who acknowledge only fifty canons also prove this: namely Dionysius Exiguus, likewise Cresconius of Africa in his concord of canons in the sixth century, Hadrian I in the eighth century, Isidore Mercator, a writer of the ninth century (I meant to say impostor), and Gratian, the compiler of the Decretum in the twelfth century. I know of no one, apart from Turrianus alone, who has disagreed with this in the fifteen or so centuries that have run their course, until he published his unhappy apology for these canons in the year 73 of the last century. The falsity of the later thirty-five canons is proved first by the fifty-first canon, which in the order is otherwise the fifty-first, and which decrees that the fallen should be received indiscriminately. Albaspinaeus, a shrewd breaker of ecclesiastical antiquity, Bk. 1, observations, ch. 13, himself acknowledges that this was unknown before the middle of the third century, when the granting of dispensations to the fallen began. Then, before Cyprian, that severity towards idolatrous apostates had not yet been relaxed, that is, in the year of Christ 254. The same is proved by the ninth canon, after the fiftieth, in which the spurious books of the Apostles [τὰ Ψευδεπιγεγραφα τῶν ἀποστόλων βιβλία], books falsely inscribed with the names of the impious, are forbidden to be published by the Church. He means by this writings put out under the names of the Apostles and spurious in origin (about which, God willing, we shall comment at length on the famous chapter of Gelasius and the 70 Bishops, which Gratian cites in dist. 15, c. sancta Romana). Such writings could not have been published or prohibited at all except after the Apostles' time. This is also demonstrated by canon 62 …

units.la: Note: the Greek phrase in the running text is reproduced as printed. piscoporum capitulum, relatum à Gratiano dist.15. c.sancta Romana, aliquid commentabimur,) quæ sane non nisi post Apostolos fuerunt vel potuerunt publicari aut prohiberi. Evincit hoc etiam in canone 62. adducta ratio prohibiti esus sanguinis, quæ hæc est: quia lex id prohibuit. Quæ sane non est ratio Apostolorum; qui ob scandalum Judæorum ad tempus id prohibuerunt. Lex enim, utpote ceremonialis, abrogata jam erat; scandalum autem temporalem abstinentiam adhuc suadebat, vid. Apost. I. ad Corinth. 10. v. 25. & 27. Quod latissime executus est præter alios contra Schookium & Curcellæum. Johan. Henr. Heideggerus in Hist. Patriarcharum & tractatu proprio. Canonem 65: non esse Apostolicum, evincet pro nobis Baronius, ad Annum 102. §. 15. & cum eo Bellarmin. de Pontif. Roman. lib.2. c.27. Possevinus In apparat. sac. verb. Clemens. Binius in not. ad istum canonem, Petavius & alii. Canonis verba sunt hæc: Si quis Clericus inventus fuerit jejunare die Dominico vel Sabbatho, præterquam uno solo, deponatur; sin autem Laicus segregetur. Ad hæc notat Baronius; Quomodo quaso, tot tamque disertos antiquos Patres, qui de jejunio Sabbathi instituerunt Disputationem canon ille præteriit, ut à nemine citatus reperiatur? Vel quonam pacto, obsecro, Romana Ecclesia clesia contra omnium Apostolorum canonem Sabbathi jejunium suscepisset, vel eorum Episcopus Clemens, id fieri permisisset, qui quod statuissent Apostoli & ipse scripsisset, perquam optime sciret? vel quomodo ex traditione Petri & Pauli Apostolorum Principum, ejusmodi dies Sabba-thi jejunii sibi vendicari est solita eadem Ecclesia observantiam, quam Apostolorum Canoni penitus adversari nosset. Petavius ad Epiphanium pag. 359, rejicit hunc canonem tanquam spurium, negatque fieri potuisse, ut is ab Apostolis communi decreto constitueretur, ob illam Augustini, præscriptionem neque scriptura auctoritate, neque universalis Ecclesiæ traditione determinatum esse, sabbatho ne jejunare deceat an prandere, sed ejus in qua versaris Ecclesiæ consuetudini obtemperandum esse. Quod probat Tertullianus quoque de coron. milit. capit. 3. & latius exequitur tractatu singulari Doctiss: Dalæus de jejunio, & in Pseudepigraph. Apostolicis. lib. 3. cap. 12. pag. 562. Eadem ratione se prodit canon 58. qui quadragesimæ jejunium sancit, quod temporibus Apostolorum incognitum, nec ab Apostolis institutum fuit. Ita nec Apostolos aut eorum ætatem redolent, quæ canone 71. leguntur: Si quis vel Clericus vel Laicus ceram vel oleum à sancta Ecclesia abstulerit, segregandus est. Nullum enim oleum nulla cera cognita Apostolis in usum Ecclesiæ, uti nec aurea vel argentea vasa vel vela sanctificata, de quibus loquitur canon. 72. Insipidus quoque & contra plerosque Patres est ille canon sacræ scripturæ, qui in canone ultimo, 85. aliis penultimo & ultimo legitur. In quo libri Machabaici omnes, contra Eusebium, Athanasium, Gregorium Nazianzenum, Amphilochium Iconiensem, Cyrillum Hierosolymitanum, Epiphanium Damascenum, Hilarium, Philastrium, Russinum, Hieronymum in Canonem admittuntur. In quo etiam contra omnium sententiam, etiam ipsam Synodum Tridentinum admittitur & canonizatur (ut hac voce hic utar) liber tertius Machabæorum. Porro Constitutiones Pseudapostolicæ, supra repudiatæ in censum Apocryphorum, etiam in numerum sacrorum voluminum cum summa impudientia adsumuntur; in quo articulo etiam ipsi Græci, alias horum canonum propugnatores acerrimi hos respuunt. Tertio duæ Epistolæ Clementis pro divinis scripturis obtrudūtur, quas nec vetus nec recentior ecclesia pro talibus agnovit. Quarto in canone omittit Esdram in Veteri, in Novo Testamento Apocalypsin. Illud, ne omnia sectemur, ridiculum est, quod cum hi Apostoli, & quidem ut supra Turrianus rianus voluit An. 45. æræ Christianæ, constituant canonem Novi Testamenti, in eum etiam referant Euangelia, actus Apostolorum & Epistolas, quorum omnium nil, aut fere nihil eo tempore scriptum fuit. Saltem non Euangelium Johannis, quod constans fama vult scriptum esse in fine vitæ ejus, & sic quinquaginta annis post hujus canonis constitutionem, in quo tamen tanquam jam scriptum recensetur, & quidem ab omnibus Apostolis, cum tempore scriptionis ejus nullus præter Johannem superesset. Quibus ineluctabilibus argumentis moti Latini omnes, præter unicum impudentissimum Turrianum, huncce trigesimum quintum canonem, in Apocryphorum numerum lubentes meritoque ablegarunt, videatur unus pro omnibus Baronius ad Ann. 102. §. 15. & 16. Neque magis genuini sunt quinquaginta priores, quos Græci pariter & Latini pro Apostolicis recipiunt & defendunt: Gelasius vero & septuaginta cum eo Episcopi in synodo Romana damnant, & in Apocryphorum censum referunt. Dionysius Exiguus supra in Epistola ad Stephanum, qui fere circa natales horum canonum vixit, multos fatetur iis non præbuisse consensum facilem. Postea septimo seculo Isidorus Hispalensis testis classicus, negat ab Apostolica sede recep-ptos esse, negat à sanctis Patribus esse probatos seculo nono præcipite Hincmarus. lib. quinquaginta quinque cap. c. 24. pag. 473. ait de his canonibus, non credi ab Apostolis esse conscriptos, quædam in iis esse non servanda, eos duntaxat ad instructionem propter vulgatam famam scilicet ante concilia in canonum libris poni; sic legendos, ut sequamur cautelam à Gelasio (intelligit. c. Sancta Romana. dist. 15. de Apocryphis) præmonitam; Cum hæc ad Catholicorum manus advenerint, B. Pauli Apostoli præcedere debere sententiam: Omnia probate, quod bonum est retinete.Istud vero non tantum testes, sed & rationes evincunt. Ex can. 1. & 2. videmus distingui Presbyteros & Episcopos, quæ duo vocabula synonymōs veris Apostolis usurpata fuerunt, & demum seculo tertio ceperunt distingui, de quo latissime Blondellus de Episcopis, Salmasius de primatu & de Episcopis, Seldenus & alii; Clerici quoque non fuerunt noti Apostolis, præter Episcopos, Presbyteros & Diaconos; quibus tamen canon secundus alios Clericos addit. Ejusdem notæ sunt, primitiæ, quas canon quartus jubet solvi Episcopo & Clericis. Incognitum Apostolis quoque est ϑυμίαμα seu incensum, quod tempore sanctæ oblationis offerri jubet canon non tertius, in Dionysii editione quartus: quod etiam notum non fuit tempore Tertulliani, cujus hæc sunt Apologet. cap. 24. Thura plane non eminus; si Arabiæ quæruntur, scient Sabæi pluris & carioris suas merces Christianis sepeliendis profligari, quam aliis fumigandis. Canon septimus de celebratione Paschæ prodit se ipsum, qui jubet celebrari Pascha post vernale æquinoctium, non ante cum Judæis; quæ controversia est tertii seculi; & contrariam traditionem Apostolicam refert Epiphanius, quæ tamen utraq; falsa est, nil enim Apostoli de Paschate celebrando statuerunt unquam.
units.tr: The Greek phrase in the running text is reproduced as printed. Dist. 15, c. Sancta Romana, which Gratian cites, but we will comment on it at some point, God willing. These texts could certainly not have been published or prohibited except after the Apostles. This is also proven by canon 62, where the reason given for forbidding the eating of blood is this: because the law forbade it. That is certainly not the reasoning of the Apostles, who forbade it for a time on account of the offence it gave the Jews. For the law, being ceremonial, was already abrogated; but the offence still urged abstinence for a time. See 1 Corinthians 10, vv. 25 and 27. This has been pursued at length, among others, against Schookius and Curcellaeus by Johann Heinrich Heidegger, in his History of the Patriarchs and in a separate treatise. That canon 65 is not Apostolic will be shown on our side by Baronius, at the year 102, §15, and with him Bellarmine, On the Roman Pontiff, book 2, chapter 27; Possevinus, in the Apparatus sacer, under Clemens; Binius in his notes on that canon; Petavius and others. The words of the canon are these: If any cleric is found fasting on the Lord's day or on the Sabbath, except only one, let him be deposed; but if a layman, let him be excommunicated. On this Baronius remarks: How, I ask, did that canon pass over so many and such eloquent ancient Fathers who wrote disputations on the fast of the Sabbath, so that it is found cited by no one? Or in what way, I beg you, could the Roman Church have undertaken a fast on the Sabbath against the canon of all the Apostles, or would its bishop Clement have permitted it, who would have known perfectly well what the Apostles had decreed and had himself written? Or how, from the tradition of the Apostles Peter and Paul, the chief Apostles, would that same Church have been accustomed to claim for itself the observance of such a Sabbath fast, which it would have known to be utterly opposed to the canon of the Apostles? Petavius, on Epiphanius, page 359, rejects this canon as spurious and denies that it could have been established by the Apostles by a common decree, on account of that prescription of Augustine, that it is determined neither by the authority of Scripture nor by the universal tradition of the Church whether one ought to fast or to dine on the Sabbath, but that one must obey the custom of the Church in which one lives. Tertullian also proves this, On the Crown of the Soldier, chapter 3, and the most learned Dalaeus pursues it more fully in a separate treatise On Fasting, and in Pseudepigrapha Apostolica, book 3, chapter 12, page 562. By the same reasoning canon 58 betrays itself, which enjoins the fast of Lent, a practice unknown in the times of the Apostles and not instituted by them. Nor do those things that are read in canon 71 smell of the Apostles or their age: If any cleric or layman takes wax or oil from the holy Church, let him be cut off. For no oil and no wax was known to the Apostles for use in the Church, any more than the sanctified gold or silver vessels or veils of which canon 72 speaks. That canon on Scripture, which is read as canon 85 in the last place (in others, the penultimate and last), is also insipid and contrary to most of the Fathers. In it all the books of the Maccabees are admitted into the canon, against Eusebius, Athanasius, Gregory Nazianzen, Amphilochius of Iconium, Cyril of Jerusalem, Epiphanius of Damascus, Hilary, Philastrius, Rufinus and Jerome. In it too, against the judgment of all, even the Council of Trent is admitted, and (to use the word here) the third book of the Maccabees is canonized. Furthermore, the Pseudo-Apostolic Constitutions, rejected above, are taken with the greatest impudence into the number of the sacred volumes; on this point even the Greeks themselves, otherwise the most fierce defenders of these canons, reject them. Thirdly, two Epistles of Clement are thrust upon us as divine Scripture, which neither the older nor the more recent Church has acknowledged as such. Fourthly, the canon omits Ezra from the Old Testament and the Apocalypse from the New. That the canon says, lest we follow everything, is ridiculous: since these Apostles, and indeed (as Turrianus above wished) in the year 45 of the Christian era, were to establish the canon of the New Testament, they also include in it the Gospels, the Acts of the Apostles and the Epistles, of all of which nothing, or almost nothing, had been written at that time. At least the Gospel of John was not, which constant report says was written at the end of his life, and so fifty years after the establishment of this canon, in which nonetheless it is listed as already written, and indeed by all the Apostles, although when it was written no one survived except John. Moved by these unanswerable arguments, all the Latins, except the single most shameless Turrianus, have gladly and rightly relegated this thirty-fifth canon to the number of the Apocrypha; let Baronius alone stand for all, at the year 102, §§15 and 16. Nor are the first fifty genuine, which the Greeks equally and the Latins receive and defend as Apostolic. Gelasius, indeed, and the seventy bishops with him in the Roman synod condemn them and count them among the Apocrypha. Dionysius Exiguus, above in his Epistle to Stephen, who lived about the time when these canons were born, confesses that many did not readily give their consent to them. Later, in the seventh century, Isidore of Seville, the classic witness, denies that they were received by the Apostolic See, denies that they were approved by the holy Fathers; and in the ninth century Hincmar, book 55, chapter 24, page 473, says of these canons that they are not believed to have been written by the Apostles, that some things in them are not to be observed, and that they are placed in the books of canons only for instruction, on account of the common report, namely before the councils; they are to be read so that we follow the caution warned of by Gelasius (he means c. Sancta Romana, dist. 15, on the Apocrypha), namely that when these things come into the hands of Catholics, the judgment of the blessed Apostle Paul must go before: Prove all things; hold fast that which is good. But not only witnesses but also reasons prove this. From canons 1 and 2 we see that presbyters and bishops are distinguished, two words that were used synonymously by the true Apostles, and that they began to be distinguished only in the third century, on which Blondel On Bishops, Salmasius On Primacy and On Bishops, Selden and others have written at great length. Clerics, too, besides bishops, presbyters and deacons, were unknown to the Apostles; yet canon 2 adds other clerics. Of the same character are the first-fruits, which canon 4 orders to be given to the bishop and the clerics. Also unknown to the Apostles is the incense [θυμίαμα], or incense, which canon 3 (in Dionysius's edition the fourth) orders to be offered at the time of the holy oblation; nor was it known in the time of Tertullian, whose words are these in the Apology, chapter 24: Incense, to be sure, not from afar; if they seek it from Arabia, the Sabaeans will know that their wares are sold for more and at a higher price to Christians for burying than to others for burning. Canon 7 on the celebration of Easter betrays itself, for it orders that Easter be celebrated after the vernal equinox, not before, along with the Jews; this controversy belongs to the third century, and Epiphanius reports a contrary Apostolic tradition, which however is false in both forms, for the Apostles never decreed anything about the celebration of Easter.

units.la: De octavo Canone, in quo communione privantur Clerici, qui facta oblatione non communicant, pro me loquatur Binius ad istum canonem. Totum hoc, inquit, decretum non divino sed humano jure constitutum, jam contraria consuetudine est abrogatum. quæ satis probant non esse eum Apostolicum. Eadem consuetudo apud Romanos nonum abrogavit, qui Dionysio est decimus, utpote apud quos plerique sunt ingredientes Ecclesiam, auditores verbi, pauci communicantes, quod est contra canonem, qui severissime non communicantes, communione privat. Pariter abolitus est decimus sextus canon, vel 17. Dionysio, in quo Bigami & concubinarii sunt irregulares, ut loquuntur nunc canônistæ, quod hodie de concubinariis secus est, & teste Binio secundum Magnum illum JurisC: Covarruvium Clement. si furiosus. part. 1. §. 2. n. 2. usu nunc revocatum & sublatum. Ea quoque quæ can. 21. 22. 23. vel aliis 22. 23. 24. de Eunuchis & qui seipsos castrant, leguntur, magis factum Origenis cujusdam, ejusdemque, vel quod adhuc probabilius est, posteriorem ætatem, quam Apostolos eorumque tempus redolent, uti quoq; quæ 33. canone aliis 35. de Metropolitanis eorumque juribus statuuntur, qui seculo tertio cœperunt demum innotescere, & quarto in synodo Nicæna sanciri & fulciri; de quibus synodus ipsa provocat ad antiquam tantum consuetudinem, can. 6. nullius Apostolicæ legis vel canonis meminit; quod certe non intermisisset illa, si ipsi cognitus fuisset iste canon Apostolicus: firmius quippe sanctione Apostolica expressa, quam consuetudine fulcirentur jura Metropolitanorum. Tandem ex canone penultimo 49, aperte constat non esse canones hos Apostolicos, in quo præcipitur depositio istius Episcopi vel Presbyteri, qui sine trina mersione quenquam baptizaverit. Quod plerique Patres, qui ejus meminerunt, adscribunt antiquæ traditioni. Tertullian. de Coron. Milit. c. 3. inter eas observationes, quas sine ullius scriptu-ra instrumento, solius traditionis titulo, & exinde consuetudinis titulo vindicabant, numerat diserte, ter mergitamur. Basilius de Sp. Sanct. c. 27. quaerit, τὸ τὴς βαπτίζεσθαι ἡ ἄνθρωπον, πόθεν; jam illud ter immergi, unde est? Id est ut ex antecedentibus patet ἐκ ποίας λόγῳ γεγραμμένης; ex qua scriptura? quod facete quaereretur, si extaret scriptus à Clemente canon Apostolicus. Huc quoque faciunt haec, quae habet Hieronym. dialog. ad verf. Lucifer. Multa alia, quae per traditionem in Ecclesiis observantur, auctoritatem sibi scriptae legis usurpaverunt, veluti in lavacro ter caput mergitare. Qua de re latissime videatur, Clariss: Vossius. de Baptismo disp. 2. thes. 1. & seq. à pag. 41. & Vicecomes de antiquis ritibus. Baptismo. lib. 4. cap. 8. quod his verbis incipit. Utrum vero unica an trina immersio fieret, nihil certi responderi posset, utrovis enim modo quondam in Ecclesia baptismum vere confectum esse, ex S. Gregorii Epist. 41. ad Leandrum Episcopum & concilio Toletano 4. cap. 5. satis apparet. Postea tamen pag. 612. impudenter vel imprudenter haec, de trina immersione effudit. Quidquid autem sit, de traditione vel praecepto, nemini dubium esse debet, quin ab ipsis Apostolis saepe idem traditum fuerit. Nam canon. 49. Episcopos vel Presbyteros, qui qui simplam mersionem usurpaverint, sacerdotali honore spoliari jubent. Ex quibus patet, quam frivole & sine reverentia, isti homines Apostolicos canones & traditiones habeant; quando neglecta ista, de qua nemini dubium esse dicit, traditione Apostolica, utroque modo baptismum rite administratum veteribus esse, in principio capitis supra citato, adserit; quod etiam Gregorius Magnus & concilium Toletanum quartum probat. Sed ad canones revertamur, ipsa oratio, phrasis & voces etiam, probant eos non esse seculi Apostolici. Invenitur enim Κληρικὸς, pro eo qui in functione Ecclesiastica est, item ἀναγνώστης & ψάλτης, ἱερεύς, ἱερατικὸς καταλόγος, ἱερατικὴ διοίκησις, quae denotant lectorem, cantorem, sacerdotem, sacerdotalem catalogum, sacerdotii administrationem; legitur & καταλόγως τῶν κληρικῶν, catalogus clericorum, θυσιαστήριον altare, pro mensa Eucharistiae, can. 3. c. 30. θυσία sacrificium pro Eucharistia, can. 45. & προσφορὰ oblatio pro eadem; πρῶτος ἐν ἐπισκόποις, primus inter Episcopos. can: 33. (35.) est ille Metropolitanus. Τὰ κυριακὰ, Dominica, pro rebus ab Ecclesia possessis, c. 39. quas & vocant τὰ τῆς ἐκκλησίας πράγματα Res Ecclesiae. can.37. (39.) Ὑπερθέρετai October. can. 38. (36.) Quae voces ab Apostolis ista signifisignificatione non leguntur usurpatæ, sed à patribus sequentium seculorum, & liquido probant, sequentibus seculis hos canones etiam esse effictos & Apostolis suppositos. In dogmate de rebaptizandis iis, qui ab hæreticis sunt baptizati ab orthodoxa, itemque Romana Ecclesia dissentiunt, utpote, qui rebaptizari semel ab hæreticis baptizatum volunt; Can. 45. (46.) & can. 67, cujus jam ab ultima antiquitate, & Episcopatu Stephani, anno nempe 254. Ecclesia Romana contrarium observavit, & can: 19. Nicænus, tantum à Paulianistis rebaptizandos sancit. Ex quo certissimum ducitur argumentum Cyprianum & Patres synodi Carthaginiensis ignorasse hos canones, qui quidem eandem cum hisce fictitiis canonibus Apostolicis sententiam fovent, attamen nullibi eorum auctoritate utuntur, quæ sola alias sufficisset ad hujus controversiæ decisionem; Neque etiam Donatistæ, qui Cypriani sententiam hac in parte sequuti sunt, Augustino ullibi canonum Pseudapostolicorum auctoritatem objiciunt, quod indicium quinto seculo ineunte, non fuisse illos cognitos. Quibus argumentis adductus, negat Albaspinæus, hos esse Apostolorum canones. Obser. lib. 1. c. 13. pag. 37. Si Canones, inquit, isti constitutionesque ab Apostolis probatæ, sancitæque fuissent, quis existimet ea in dubium fuisse revocata, quæ ab Apostolis decreta sancitaque fuissent? An adeo ignorantes erant illius ætatis Patres, ut si extitissent, illi Apostolorum canones eos continuo non produxissent? Adde Possevinum, qui ob canon. 67. in apparatu verbo Clemens omnes triginta quinque posteriores spurios esse adserit; & tacite simul quinquaginta priores; utpote qui eadem de rebaptizandis ab hæreticis baptizatis constituunt, quos tamen ille omnes probat. Eodem modo errat Bellarminus de script. Eccles. in Clemente. verf. at contra. Adde his, ut absolvamus hoc de canonibus Pseudapostolicis examen, neminem Patrum in quatuor seculis prioribus facere ullam horum tanquam ab Apostolis sancitorum, & à Clemente scriptorum mentionem; & cum jam exeunte seculo quinto compositi & suppositi essent, non fuisse probatos, teste Dionysii Exigui supra relata Præfatione; Ideoque nec à Ferrando in Breviarium, nec à Martino Bracarensi in collectionem Orientalium canonum relatos. Repete quoque huc supra num. 81, adductum testimonium Gregorii Turonensis, quod probat in Gallia anno 580. ignotos fuisse, Quaternione novo codici canonum annexos, & ad imminuendam eorum fidem & auctoritatem vocari Quasi Apostolicos. Huc quoque facit Hincmari in libro quinquaginta quinque capitulor. cap.43. testimonium seculi noni decurrentis, quod clare probat, neque tunc temporis in codice canonum Gallico probatos fuisse & receptos. Adserit ille ibidem esse canones, quos & Apostolica sedes & omnes Episcopi per universum orbem à prima sedis Pontificie, usque ad illum, qui novissime etiam post Te (Hincmarum Laudunensem putat) est ordinatus Episcopus; imo & omnis Catholica Ecclesia canones appellant, quique à Nicæno concilio, quod primum in nostris Codicibus (quos ab Apostolica sede majores nostri acceperunt) sequendos per ordinem usque ad Africanum Concilium pro canonibus recipiendis, venerandis & observandis retinent; & Innocentius, Zosimus, Bonifacius, Cœlestinus, Leo, Hilarius, Symmachus, Gelasius, Hormisda, Gregorius & cateri quique observandos canones nominant. His itaque abunde satis confectum censemus, esse istos Canones opus spurium, futile, quod nunquam Apostolos, vel Clementem Apostolorum discipulum habuit auctores, aut Apostolicis temporibus, aut etiam primis quatuor seculis natales; sed in fine seculi quinti à tenebrione & haeretico quodam Graeco quinquaginta primos ex variis conciliis, moribus ritibus Ecclesiæ esse corrasos, atque ut auctoritatem sibi nomine suo magnam statim conciliarent, vocatos esse Apostolicos. Quos statim in natalibus, tanquam ab hæreticis fictos, & Apostolis falso suppositos, Gelasius Episcopus Romanus inter Apocrypha merito damnavit. Post hoc decretum damnationis, probabile est accessisse posteriores triginta quinque, vel ab eodem nebulone vel alio, qui istiusmodi nugis delectatus fuit: deinde ab Imperatore Justiniano commendatos, & à Johanne Scholastico in nomocanonem omnes 85. susceптos esse, quod factum paulo post annum 560, quo tempore ille Johannes floruit, ut infra demonstrabimus. Quare nullius momenti est Albaspinæi judicium, Magni alias in antiquitate Ecclesiastica Viri, lib. 1. Obs. cap. 13. qui censet, non uno tempore esse conditos istos canones, sed alios primo, alios secundo seculo ab Apostolicis Viris, quos vult esse Apostolorum successores, postea alios successive esse additos seculo tertio, retento tamen Apostolicorum Canonum nomine, quod postea oscitantia vel ignorantia Latinorum in Apostolorum degeneravit; Nihilque aliud esse hanc farraginem, quam Breviarium & epitomen privatorum conciliorum & rerum ab Episcopis privatis sancitarum, qui Ecclesiæ ecclesias Græcas ante Concilium Nicænum administrarunt. Illud primo à vero videtur alienum, quod hic codex Albaspinæo videtur esse epitome privatorum conciliorum & rerum ab Episcopis Græcis sancitarum, cum manifeste contineat contraria Græcis dogmata, quod vel ille canon sacræ scripturæ in ultimo canone relatus liquido demonstrat. Deinde si ante Nicænam synodum, fuisset id Breviarium Ecclesiasticorum Decretorum, proculdubio Codici Canonum Ecclesiæ Universæ fuisset insertum, tanquam antiquitatis illustre monumentum; aut saltem citassent Ancyrani, Neocæsarienses, Nicæni aut Antiocheni Patres, idque sub certis numeris, siquidem hoc Breviarium collectum fuisset: quemadmodum videmus factum à Patribus Calchedonensibus, qui sub suis numeris laudant Codicis Ecclesiæ Catholicæ canonem quartum, octuagesimum tertium & quartum; item nonagesimum quintum & sextum, ut supra indicatum est. Porro si fuisset id Breviarium, quod Albaspinæus ex eo facit, ab apostolicis Viris compositum & ab Episcopis sancitum ante concilium Nicænum, certe à Gelasio & Episcopis lxx. cum eo congregatis, Apocryphis accenseri non debuisset; deinde etiam in hoc Breviario, seu collectione. ctione, ut in aliis Græcorum omnibus, habita fuisset ratio temporis, si non ab uno, nec uno tempore, quod vult Albaspinæus, sed successive coaluisset, auctores quoque & concilia, ex quibus desumti essent hi canones, nominata fuissent, ut in aliis quoque factum collectionibus diversorum auctorum videmus. Inspiciatur solummodo Codex Ecclesiæ Catholicæ, & Codex Ecclesiæ Orientalis; ubi novæ synodi canones incipiunt, id semper solet indicari, item si ex Basilio aut alio quid sit depromptum. Sed manifeste refutant ipsi canones Albaspinæi sententiam, qui non plures sibi succedentes auctores, diversisque seculis scriptos, sed Apostolos auctores agnosci volunt, quod etiam argumentum est, non esse à Clemente conscriptos; Quod non tantum ex calce & peroratione, sed ipsis etiam canonibus, apparet tam prioribus, quam posterioribus triginta quinque. Canone 28. (30.) qui est contra Simoniacum, Petrus nominatur unus ex auctoribus, & sancit. Dejiciatur & ipse & ordinator ejus & à communione modis omnibus excindatur, ut Simon Magus à me Petro. Iterum Canon. 49. (50) ex versione Dionysii. Non enim dixit NOBIS (Apostolis) Dominus in morte mea baptizate, sed euntes docete omnes gentes, baptizantes etc. Item
units.tr: Concerning the eighth canon, by which clergy who do not communicate after the oblation is made are deprived of communion, let Binius speak for me on this canon. The whole of this decree, he says, was established by human and not divine law, and has now been abrogated by contrary custom. These words sufficiently show that it is not Apostolic. The same custom abrogated the ninth canon among the Romans, which is the tenth in Dionysius, since among them many enter the Church, are hearers of the Word, and few communicate. This is contrary to the canon, which most severely deprives of communion those who do not communicate. Likewise the sixteenth canon, or the seventeenth in Dionysius, has been abolished. In it bigamists and concubinaries are declared irregular, as the canonists now put it. Today the rule regarding concubinaries is otherwise, and according to Binius, following that great jurist Covarruvias, Clement. si furiosus, part. 1, §2, n. 2, it has now been revoked and abolished by use. Those things also which are read in canons 21, 22 and 23 (or 22, 23 and 24 in other numbering), concerning eunuchs and those who castrate themselves, smell rather of the deed of a certain Origen, or, what is more probable, of a later age than the Apostles and their time. So too what is laid down in canon 33 (or 35 in other numbering) concerning Metropolitans and their rights. These began to become known only in the third century, and were sanctioned and supported at the Nicene synod in the fourth. Concerning them the synod itself appeals only to ancient custom, can. 6, and mentions no Apostolic law or canon. It would certainly not have omitted this if that Apostolic canon had been known to it, for the rights of Metropolitans would be supported more firmly by an express Apostolic sanction than by custom. Finally, from the penultimate canon, the 49th, it is plainly evident that these are not Apostolic canons. In it the deposition is commanded of that bishop or presbyter who has baptized anyone without a threefold immersion. Most of the Fathers who mention this ascribe it to ancient tradition. Tertullian, de Corona militis c. 3, expressly counts among those observances, which they claimed without the instrument of any Scripture, by the title of tradition alone, and thence by the title of custom, we are dipped three times. Basil, de Spiritu Sancto c. 27, asks: whence comes the being baptized as a man? Whence is the threefold immersion? That is, as appears from what precedes, from what written word [ἐκ ποίας λόγῳ γεγραμμένης], from what Scripture? This would be a witty question to ask if an Apostolic canon written by Clement were extant. These words of Jerome in the Dialogue against the Luciferians also bear on the point: many other things observed in the Churches by tradition have usurped for themselves the authority of written law, as for example dipping the head three times in the bath. On this matter see at length the most distinguished Vossius, de Baptismo, disp. 2, thes. 1 and following, from p. 41, and Vicecomes, de antiquis ritibus Baptismi, lib. 4, cap. 8, which begins with these words: Whether the immersion was single or threefold, nothing certain could be answered, for it appears sufficiently from Gregory's Epistle 41 to Bishop Leander, and from the fourth Council of Toledo, cap. 5, that baptism was once truly completed in either way in the Church. Afterwards, however, on p. 612, he shamelessly or thoughtlessly poured out these words about the threefold immersion: Whatever it may be, concerning tradition or precept, there ought to be no doubt that the same was often handed down by the Apostles themselves. For canon 49 orders bishops or presbyters who have used a single immersion to be stripped of sacerdotal honour. From this it is plain how frivolously and irreverently these men hold the Apostolic canons and traditions, when at the beginning of the chapter cited above he asserts that baptism was rightly administered by the ancients in either way, neglecting that Apostolic tradition about which he says there is no doubt. Gregory the Great and the fourth Council of Toledo also prove this. But let us return to the canons. The very language, style and even the words prove that they do not belong to the Apostolic age. For klērikos [Κληρικὸς] is found for one who holds an ecclesiastical office; likewise anagnōstēs [ἀναγνώστης] and psaltēs [ψάλτης], hiereus [ἱερεύς], hieratikos katalogos [ἱερατικὸς καταλόγος], hieratikē dioikēsis [ἱερατικὴ διοίκησις], which denote reader, cantor, priest, the sacerdotal catalogue and the administration of the priesthood. One also reads katalogōs tōn klērikōn [καταλόγως τῶν κληρικῶν], the catalogue of clergy; thysiastērion [θυσιαστήριον], altar, for the table of the Eucharist, canon 3, c. 30; thysia [θυσία], sacrifice, for the Eucharist, canon 45; and prosphora [προσφορὰ], oblation, for the same. Prōtos en episkopois [πρῶτος ἐν ἐπισκόποις], first among bishops, canon 33 (35), is that Metropolitan. Ta kyriaka [τὰ κυριακὰ], the Dominical things, is used for property possessed by the Church, c. 39, which they also call ta tēs ekklēsias pragmata [τὰ τῆς ἐκκλησίας πράγματα], the affairs of the Church, canon 37 (39). Hyperberetaios [Ὑπερβερεταῖος], October, canon 38 (36). These words are not found used in this sense by the Apostles, but by the Fathers of later centuries, and they clearly prove that in the following centuries these canons too were fabricated and foisted on the Apostles. On the dogma about rebaptizing those baptized by heretics, the Orthodox Church and likewise the Roman Church disagree with these canons, since they want one baptized by heretics to be rebaptized once, canons 45 (46) and 67. The Roman Church has observed the contrary since the earliest antiquity, and from the episcopate of Stephen, namely in the year 254. The Nicene canon 19 sanctions rebaptism only for the Paulianists. From this a most certain argument is drawn that Cyprian and the Fathers of the Synod of Carthage did not know these canons, which indeed foster the same opinion as these fictitious Apostolic canons, yet nowhere use their authority, which alone would otherwise have sufficed to decide this controversy. Nor do the Donatists, who followed Cyprian's opinion in this part, ever object to Augustine the authority of the pseudo-Apostolic canons, a sign that at the beginning of the fifth century these were not known. Moved by these arguments, Albaspinaeus denies that these are the canons of the Apostles. Obser. lib. 1, c. 13, pag. 37. If these canons and constitutions, he says, had been approved and sanctioned by the Apostles, who would think that things decreed and sanctioned by the Apostles had been called into doubt? Or were the Fathers of that age so ignorant that, had these existed, they would not at once have produced those canons of the Apostles? Add Possevinus, who, on account of canon 67, under the word Clement in his Apparatus, asserts that all thirty-five later canons are spurious, and tacitly at the same time the first fifty, since they lay down the same things about rebaptizing those baptized by heretics, which yet he approves in full. Bellarmine errs in the same way, de scriptoribus ecclesiasticis, under Clement, verse "at contra". To these, to complete this examination of the pseudo-Apostolic canons, add that none of the Fathers of the first four centuries makes any mention of these as sanctioned by the Apostles and written by Clement. Since they were composed and foisted on the Church at the close of the fifth century, they were not approved, as the preface of Dionysius Exiguus cited above witnesses. Therefore they were included neither by Ferrandus in his Breviary nor by Martin of Braga in his collection of Eastern canons. Repeat here also the testimony of Gregory of Tours, cited above at no. 81, which proves that in Gaul in the year 580 they were unknown, appended to the codex of canons on a new quire, and were called "Apostolic" in order to diminish their faith and authority. The testimony of Hincmar from the ninth century, in the book of fifty-five chapters, chap. 43, also bears on this, and clearly proves that not even then were they approved and received in the Gallic codex of canons. He asserts there that these are canons which both the Apostolic See and all bishops throughout the world, from the first see of the Pontiff down to him who most recently, even after you (he thinks Hincmar of Laon), was ordained bishop, and indeed the whole Catholic Church call canons, and which, from the Nicene council, which is first in our codices (which our forefathers received from the Apostolic See), they keep in order down to the African council, to be received, revered and observed as canons. Innocent, Zosimus, Boniface, Celestine, Leo, Hilary, Symmachus, Gelasius, Hormisdas, Gregory and the rest name the canons to be observed. Therefore we think it has been sufficiently established by these arguments that these canons are a spurious and worthless work, which never had the Apostles, or Clement the disciple of the Apostles, as its authors, and which was not born either in the Apostolic times or even in the first four centuries. Rather, at the end of the fifth century, the first fifty were scraped together from various councils, customs and rites of the Church by some Greek forger and heretic, and in order to win great authority at once under their name, they were called Apostolic. Gelasius, bishop of Rome, rightly condemned these among the Apocrypha at their very birth, as fabricated by heretics and falsely foisted on the Apostles. After this decree of condemnation it is probable that the later thirty-five were added, either by the same scoundrel or by another who delighted in such trifles. Then they were commended by the Emperor Justinian, and John Scholasticus received all eighty-five into his Nomocanon, which happened shortly after the year 560, when that John flourished, as we shall demonstrate below. Hence the judgment of Albaspinaeus, otherwise a great man in ecclesiastical antiquity, lib. 1, Obs. cap. 13, is of no weight. He thinks these canons were not composed at one time, but that some were made in the first, others in the second century, by Apostolic men whom he wants to be successors of the Apostles, and that others were afterwards added successively in the third century, the name Apostolic canons being retained, which afterwards through the carelessness or ignorance of the Latins degenerated into of the Apostles. He holds that this farrago is nothing other than a breviary and epitome of private councils and of matters decreed by private bishops, who governed the Greek churches before the Nicene Council. The first point seems far from the truth: that this codex should appear to Albaspinaeus to be an epitome of private councils and of matters decreed by Greek bishops, when it manifestly contains doctrines contrary to the Greeks. That canon, which is related in the last canon from Holy Scripture, clearly demonstrates this. Next, if before the Nicene synod there had been such a Breviary of Ecclesiastical Decrees, without doubt it would have been inserted into the Codex of Canons of the Universal Church as an illustrious monument of antiquity, or at least the Fathers of Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Nicaea or Antioch would have cited it, and that under definite numbers, if indeed this Breviary had been collected. Just as we see was done by the Fathers of Chalcedon, who under their own numbers cite canons 4, 83 and 84 of the Codex of the Catholic Church, likewise 95 and 96, as indicated above. Further, if that Breviary which Albaspinaeus makes of it had been composed by Apostolic men and sanctioned by bishops before the Nicene council, then certainly Gelasius and the seventy bishops gathered with him would not have counted it among the Apocrypha. Next, in this Breviary or collection, as in all other Greek collections, account would have been taken of time. If it had grown together not from one author and at one time, as Albaspinaeus wants, but successively, the authors and councils from which these canons were taken would have been named, as we see done also in other collections of various authors. Let the Codex of the Catholic Church and the Codex of the Eastern Church alone be inspected. Where the canons of a new synod begin, this is always usually indicated, and likewise if something has been taken from Basil or another. But the canons of Albaspinaeus themselves manifestly refute his opinion, for they want not several successive authors writing at different ages, but the Apostles acknowledged as authors. This is also an argument that they were not written by Clement, which appears not only from the close and peroration, but from the canons themselves, both the earlier and the later thirty-five. In canon 28 (30), which is against Simony, Peter is named as one of the authors and sanctions: Let both him and his ordainer be cast down, and be cut off from communion in every way, as Simon Magus was by me, Peter. Again, canon 49 (50), in the version of Dionysius: For the Lord did not say to us (the Apostles), in my death baptize, but go and teach all nations, baptizing etc. Likewise

units.la: Item canon. 81; in quo de servo sermo, atque hæc leguntur. Qualis noster quoque Onesimus visus est. Ex quibus satis patet, Impostorem illum voluisse & intendisse hos canones tanquam ab ipsis Apostolis profectos orbi obtrudere. Quod si itaque Albaspinæus velit suam defendere sententiam, unum ex duobus confiteri debet, vel canones ipsos mentiri, quod verissimum est; vel si veraces sint, ab ipsis Apostolis, non à Clemente aut Patribus sequentium seculorum, scriptos esse; & sic perit quoque ejus somnium de Viris Apostolicis, à quibus scriptos putat, & oscitantia Latinorum qui eos in Apostolos levi mutatione verterunt. Vide hæc latius contra Albaspinæum exequentem Dalæum d. l. c. 21. & si plura desideras de hisce Canonibus & eorum voθεíα, præter Dalæi libros sæpius laudatos, Pseudepigraphῶν Apostolorum, adi Criticos sacros: Rivetum, in crit. sacr. lib. 1. cap. 1. Cocum. in Censur. in princ. fere. Doctiss: Usserium in accurata dissert. de scriptis Ignatii Polycarpi, Apostolicis constitutionibus & canonibus Clementi Romano tributis, quæ præfixa Polycarpi & Ignatii Epistolis ex editione ejus Anni 1644. Melchiorem Canum celebrem inter Pontificios Episcopum, in locis Theolog. lib. 2. cap. XI. ubi pro Apostolicis non habet eos, nec inter ter sacros libros numerari vult lib. 5. c. 5. item Casp. Zieglerum Dissert. praemis. Lancel. Instit. Jur. can: §. 8. & seqq. & multos alios. Novissime Joh. Cabassutium in Notitia Concilior. pag. 16. ubi iis detrahit auctoritatem Apostolicam; cujus utpote Pontificii judicium,quod consensu superiorum, ut illi dicunt, nuper est editum adscriberem, quia liber iste adhuc paucis est cognitus, nisi prolixius esset, & jam refutatio nostra Constitutionum & Canonum Pseudapostolicorum sub manibus nimium crevisset. De numero hæc tantum addo, neminem agnoscere plures quam octuaginta quinque: unicus Lambert. Gruterus, in editione operum Clementis Romani, quæ prodiit Coloniæ An. 1570. post dedicationem & præsationem,ubi Elenchum in editione ista contentorum exhibet, LXXXX.
