Canonum Apostolorum, conscriptore Clemente meminit; qui tamen in ipso volumine, ut alii, tantum LXXXIV. repræsentat Græce & Latine, postea vero cum scholiis Balsamonis Latinos LXXXV. Ut arbitrer priorem numerum nonaginta canonum, esse mendum typographicum; Hæc autem est causa quare supra §. 105. consulto duplicem numerum expressterim, 85. vel 90. canonum; quamquam sciam, ab omnibus, qui posteriores
units.tr: Likewise canon 81, in which a servant is spoken of and these words are read: "Such was our Onesimus also, as he seemed to be." From these things it is clear enough that that impostor wanted and intended to thrust these canons upon the world as if they had come from the Apostles themselves. But if Albaspinaeus wishes to defend his opinion, he must concede one of two things: either the canons themselves are lying, which is most true, or, if they are genuine, they were written by the Apostles themselves and not by Clement or by the Fathers of later centuries. In that case his dream about the Apostolic men, by whom he thinks they were written, also falls apart, as does the carelessness of the Latins who turned them into "the Apostles" with a slight change. See these matters argued more fully against Albaspinaeus by Dallaeus, who follows him, in the place cited, chapter 21. If you want more on these canons and their spuriousness, besides the often-cited books of Dallaeus, see Pseudepigrapha Apostolorum, and consult the sacred critics: Rivetus, in Critici sacri, book 1, chapter 1; Cocus, in Censura, at the beginning; the most learned Usher, in his careful dissertation on the writings of Ignatius and Polycarp, and on the Apostolic Constitutions and canons ascribed to Clement of Rome, which is prefixed to the edition of the Epistles of Polycarp and Ignatius published by him in 1644; Melchior Cano, the famous Bishop among the Papists, in Loci theologici, book 2, chapter 11, where he does not regard them as Apostolic and does not wish them counted among the sacred books (book 5, chapter 5); likewise Caspar Ziegler, in the preliminary dissertation to Lancelot's Institutes of Canon Law, §8 and following, and many others. Most recently, John Cabassut, in the Notitia Conciliorum, page 16, where he takes away their Apostolic authority. I would add the judgment of this Papist, which has lately been published with the consent of their superiors, as they say, were it not that this book is still little known, and were it not that our refutation of the Apostolic Constitutions and canons has already grown too long under our hands. As to the number, I add only this: no one recognises more than eighty-five. The only exception is Lambert Gruter, in the edition of the works of Clement of Rome which appeared at Cologne in 1570. After the dedication and preface, where he gives the list of contents of that edition, he speaks of ninety canons of the Apostles written by Clement. Yet in the volume itself, like others, he presents only eighty-four in Greek and Latin, and later, with the scholia of Balsamon, eighty-five in Latin. I think the former number of ninety canons is a typographical error. This is why above, in §105, I deliberately expressed the double number, 85 or 90 canons, although I know that by all who recognise the later ones, not more than 85 are acknowledged, and by others only 84.

units.la: {a} Canonum Apostolorum error: Lambert. Gruteri notatus. riores etiam agnoscunt, non ultra 85. agnosci, ab aliis tantum octuaginta quatuor. Alios insuper impudentissime sinxit, vel saltem fictos obtrudit nobis canones Apostolicos novem Antiochenos, quos Apostolos in Synodo Antiochena, in antiquitate Ecclesiastica inaudita, à nullo historico fide digno memorata, vult constituisse & sancivisse ; non alio fini, quam ut hisce fulciat improbum imaginum cultum ; Hos operose refellere non est operæ pretium, sufficit altissimum quindecim & quod excurrit seculorum, usque ad Turriani somnia silentium, deinde abunde sufficiunt quæ contra hos solide disseruit Magnus Dalæus, in Pseudepigraphis Apostolicis, lib. 3. cap. 22. & seqq.
units.tr: {a} Error in the canons of the Apostles, noted by Lambert Gruter. Besides these, he has shamelessly invented, or at least foisted upon us as false, nine Apostolic canons of Antioch, which he wishes the Apostles to have laid down and enacted in a Synod at Antioch, a thing unheard of in ecclesiastical antiquity, recorded by no trustworthy historian. He did this for no other purpose than to support with them the wicked worship of images. It is not worth the trouble to refute them at length. It is enough that they are attested only from a late period, some fifteen centuries after the events, and that they then fall into the silence of Turrianus' dreams. Moreover, what Magnus Dallaeus has solidly argued against them is more than sufficient: Pseudepigrapha Apostolica, book 3, chapter 22 and following.

units.la: Refutatis itaque iis, quæ contra certa initia collectionis Canonum ex constitutionibus & canonibus Apostolicis adferri poterant, persequamur Historiam nostram & collectiones sequentes, quæ multæ & variæ fuerunt, ideoque quædam de varia colligendi & digerendi methodo vel modo sequentium Canonistarum præmittenda; tum observato ordine temporis singulos eorumque collectiones & opera persequemur & attexemus. Genera colligendi & digerendi potissimum quinque observo, quæ sequentes collectiones confirmabunt. Primum & simplicissimum genus est, enumerare & recensere tantum nude canones, eo ordine quo in conciliis sunt scripti & subscripti, hocque vel est unius tantum concilii, veluti Nicæni Constantinopolitani, vel diversorum conciliorum, habita tantum ratione temporis, sub una serie numerorum: & hæc collectio vocata fuit corpus, vel codex canonum, de quo supra late. Inter quæ duo tamen, quod obiter hic addo, Doctissimus Capellus in tractatu, de sedis Romanæ fide, seu stellionatu cap. 5. hanc agnoscit differentiam. Ex canonibus, inquit, ad disciplinam pertinentibus conflatum syntagma minus & vetustius dicebatur corpus, ubi augescere cœpit codex dictus est. Quod speciose quidem dictum, sed veritati mihi consonum non videtur, à Græcis enim primùm collectiones factas supra docuimus, hi autem βιβλον κανόνων, ut supra quoque observavimus, appellarunt collectionem istam, quod vel unica Synodus Calchedonensis affatim probat, quæ sæpius meminit βιβλις τ κανόνων. Action. 4. καὶ ἀπὸ βιβλίς ἀνέγνω ταῦτα. & ex Codice relegit hæc. & iterum καὶ λαῶν τῶ βίβλον Αἰτως Αρχιδιάκονον ἡ πρωτοπρεσβύτερος τῆς μεγάλης Ἐκκλησίας ἀνέγνω. Sumtoque Codice Actius Archidiaconus & Primicerius Magnæ Ecclesiæ. Ecclesiæ legit. Iterumque sic occurrit actione xi. & act. xiii. ejusdem synodi pag. 377. & 388. tom. 2. edit. Roman. Apud Latinos passim sine differentia legas ; Codicem canonum, Corpus canonum, & Corpus codicis canonum, ut supra notatum & probatum est. Hoc genus posterius, quando plurium conciliorum canones una serie numerorum decurrunt, Græci vocarunt ἀκολουθίαν κανόνων. Concil. Ephesin. act. 2. Cum δὲ τῶν ἐκκλησιαστικῶν θεσμῶν ἀκολουθίαν, Per Ecclesiasticarum Sanctionum CONSEQUENTIAM controversias in medium positas examinari oporteat. & postea. Cum animadverteremus causa sua defensioni diffidere, quæ temere παρὰ τὰ τῶν κανόνων ἀκολουθίαν, contra CANO-NUM CONSEQUENTIAM adversus Cyrillum & Memnonem scripto mandaverat ea irrita & prorsus vana judicavimus. Ita quoque apud Georg. Alexandrin. in vita Joh. Chry-sostomi, ἢ δὲ παροικούμενοι ἐπίσκοποι καὶ μητροπολίται, κατὰ τὴν κανόνων ἀκολουθίαν ἐκείνῳ-νησαν τῷ Ἰωάννῃ, Advenientes autem Episcopi & Metropolitani, juxta Canonum consequentiam, Joanni communicarunt. & concil: Calchedonens. act. 3. ἀγιωτάτη καὶ οἰκουμενικὴ σωνόδος, τέλεων ἤδη κλῆσιν ταύτῃ πισμένη, κατὰ τὴν ἀκολουθίαν τῶν ἁγίων κανόνων. Sancta & universalis synodus tertiam jam hanc voca-tionem tionem faciens, secundum consequentiam sanctorum canonum. Addo unum locum adhuc ex collectione Canonum Johannis Antiocheni Presbyteri Scholastici, ex quo constat ratio denominationis, qui hanc ἀκολυθίαν seu consequentiam se omisisse, dicit. Τὰ, inquit, ἐφειθέντες ἐν καιρῷς διελόντες εἰς πίτλας ν'. ἢ τάξιν τινὰ τὴν ἀκολουθίαν ἀριθμῶν ἐφυλάξαμεν. Quae pro tempore definita sunt, (canonica nimirum decreta) in titulos quinquaginta distribuimus, non servato ordine, ut vides, & consequentia numerorum. Quia numeri se consequuntur sine interrupta serie, ideo haec collectionis species vocata est ἀκολυθία. Quam ECCLESIASTICAM CONSEQUENTIAM vocant Episcopi Provinciae Europae tom. 2. concil. pag. 477. edit. Roman. Eos qui in damnationem, inquiunt, locus ab eo (Timotheo) sunt constituti, sive Episcopi sint, sive Archimandritae, sive Presbyteri, sive Diaconi, sive quilibet in Clero humiliori consistens, hos indignos graduum, in quibus sunt praeter ECCLESIASTICAM CONSEQUENTIAM ordinati, decrevimus. Vocatur & alibi passim haec species τάξις τῶν κανόνων, series canonum ex eadem ratione. Actione prima Concilii Ephesini. tom. 1. pag. 327. edit. Rom. Proinde quae jam prae manibus sunt ea capessantur, riteque τὴν τῶν κανόνων τάξιν, secundum SERIEM RIEM
units.tr: Therefore, having refuted those objections that could be brought against the certain beginnings of the collection of canons from the Apostolic constitutions and canons, let us pursue our history and the following collections, which were many and various. So some remarks on the varied method and manner of collecting and arranging used by the later canonists must be set down first. Then, observing the order of time, we shall follow and set out the individual collections and their works. I observe mainly five kinds of collecting and arranging, which the following collections will confirm. The first and simplest kind is merely to list and recount the canons bare, in the order in which they were written and subscribed in the councils. This was done either for a single council only, such as Nicaea or Constantinople, or for several councils, taking account only of time, under one series of numbers. This collection was called a corpus or a codex canonum, about which I have spoken at length above. Between these two, however, I add in passing that the most learned Capellus, in his treatise On the Faith of the Roman See, or Stellionatus, chapter 5, recognises this difference: a collection put together from canons pertaining to discipline was called a syntagma, which was smaller and more ancient; when it began to grow it was called a codex. This is said with some show, but it does not seem to me to agree with the truth. For I have shown above that the collections were first made by the Greeks, and they called that collection βιβλον κανόνων, as I also observed above. The Council of Chalcedon alone proves this abundantly, for it often mentions the βιβλις τῶν κανόνων (book of canons). In Action 4: and from the book he read these things [καὶ ἀπὸ βιβλίς ἀνέγνω ταῦτα], and he read these things from the Codex. Again: and Aetius, the archdeacon or first presbyter of the Great Church, read from the book [καὶ λαῶν τῶ βίβλον Αἰτως Αρχιδιάκονον ἡ πρωτοπρεσβύτερος τῆς μεγάλης Ἐκκλησίας ἀνέγνω]; taking the Codex, Aetius the Archdeacon and Primicerius of the Great Church read. So it occurs again in Action 11 and Action 13 of the same synod, pages 377 and 388 of volume 2 of the Roman edition. Among the Latins you will read everywhere, without distinction, Codex canonum, Corpus canonum, and Corpus codicis canonum, as noted and proved above. This second kind, when the canons of several councils run in one series of numbers, the Greeks called ἀκολουθίαν κανόνων (a sequence of canons). Council of Ephesus, Action 2: since the sequence of ecclesiastical ordinances [τῶν ἐκκλησιαστικῶν θεσμῶν ἀκολουθίαν] ought to be used to examine the controversies put forward; and afterwards: when we observed that his defence lacked confidence, since he had rashly written against Cyril and Memnon contrary to the sequence of the canons [παρὰ τὰ τῶν κανόνων ἀκολουθίαν], we judged those writings void and utterly vain. So also in Georgius Alexandrinus, in the life of John Chrysostom: the bishops and metropolitans who arrived, according to the sequence of the canons, communicated with John [κατὰ τὴν κανόνων ἀκολουθίαν ἐκοινώνησαν τῷ Ἰωάννῃ]. And in the Council of Chalcedon, Action 3: the most holy and ecumenical synod, making this now its third summons, according to the sequence of the holy canons [κατὰ τὴν ἀκολουθίαν τῶν ἁγίων κανόνων]. I add one more passage from the collection of canons of John, Presbyter and Scholastic of Antioch, which shows the reason for the name, since he says he did not keep this sequence or consequence. What was defined at various times, we have distributed into fifty titles [Τὰ ἐφειθέντες ἐν καιρῷς διελόντες εἰς πίτλας ν'. ἢ τάξιν τινὰ τὴν ἀκολουθίαν ἀριθμῶν ἐφυλάξαμεν], without keeping the order, as you see, and the sequence of numbers. Because the numbers follow one another without interrupted series, this kind of collection was called ἀκολουθία. The bishops of the province of Europe call it the ecclesiastical sequence in volume 2, page 477 of the Roman edition: we have decreed that those who have been ordained by him (Timothy) to the damnation of those in their places, whether bishops, archimandrites, presbyters, deacons, or anyone in the lower clergy, are unworthy of the degrees in which they are, contrary to the ecclesiastical sequence. This kind is also everywhere else called τάξις τῶν κανόνων, the order of the canons, for the same reason: in the first action of the Council of Ephesus, volume 1, page 327 of the Roman edition. Therefore let what is now at hand be taken up, and let the canons be set out properly in the order of the canons, according to the series of canons [τὴν τῶν κανόνων τάξιν]. In Council of Chalcedon, Action 3, volume 2, page 243, and in Evagrius, Ecclesiastical History, book 2, chapter 2: the things done by Dioscorus, once Bishop of the Church of the great city of Alexandria, were made manifest [Manifesta facta sunt, quae à Diofcuro quondam Alexandriae Magnae civitatis Ecclesiae Episcopo commissa sunt].

units.la: 142. τάξις τῶν κανόνων. RIEM CANONVM constituantur. In Concil. Calchedon. act. 3. tom. 2. pag. 243. & apud Euagr. Hist. Eccles. lib. 2. cap. 2. Manifesta facta sunt, quae à Diofcuro quondam Alexandriae Magnae civitatis Ecclesiae Episcopo commissa sunt, ἢ τῆς τῶν κανόνων τάξεως καὶ τῆς ἐκκλησιαστικῆς καταστάσεως, contra CANONUM SERIEM & Ecclesiasticam disciplinam. Et in Epistola Mappini Archiep. Remensis ad Nicetium Episcopum Trevirensem. in concil. Galliae tom. I. pag. 293. Licet nihil novi vos de his rebus invenire cognoscimus, quod prisca Patrum solertia non potuit reperire, tamen absurdum esse videtur, ut à nobis recipiantur, quia vobis secundum SERIEM CANONUM Ecclesiastica severitate abdicantur.Secundus collectionis & digestionis modus est eorum, qui acta cum canonibus colligunt & recitant, non nudos tantum canones; & hic modus multum facit ad historiam, & seriem rei gestae, itemque dogmata Ecclesiastica. In actis enim plerumque recensentur disputationes & argumenta de dogmatibus fidei, quae ab haereticis & contra haereticos sunt ventilata. Istiusmodi collectores fuerunt noti jam ab ultima antiquitate. Socrates lib. I. Hist. Eccles. cap. 5. ἐκυρῶτο τε ἤδε καὶ ἐγγεγράφως δι' ὑποπμειώσεως ἐπάσῃ τὰ κοινὴ δεδογμένα. Jam vero quae communi omnium sententia decreta
units.tr: 142. τάξις τῶν κανόνων [the order of the canons]. The series of the canons to be established. In the Council of Chalcedon, act 3, vol. 2, p. 243, and in Evagrius, Ecclesiastical History, book 2, chapter 2: The things that were once committed by Dioscorus, bishop of the Church of the great city of Alexandria, were made manifest, [namely] the order of the canons and the ecclesiastical constitution [τῆς τῶν κανόνων τάξεως καὶ τῆς ἐκκλησιαστικῆς καταστάσεως], against the series of the canons and ecclesiastical discipline. Also in the letter of Mappinus, archbishop of Reims, to Nicetius, bishop of Trier, in the Councils of Gaul, vol. 1, p. 293: Although we know that you can discover nothing new in these matters that the ancient diligence of the Fathers could not have discovered, nevertheless it seems absurd that they should be received by us, when by you they are rejected with ecclesiastical severity according to the series of the canons. The second mode of collecting and arranging is that of those who gather and recite the acts together with the canons, not the canons alone. This mode contributes much to history, to the sequence of the events, and likewise to ecclesiastical doctrines. For in the acts the disputations and arguments about the doctrines of the faith, which were raised by heretics and against heretics, are usually recorded. Collectors of this kind were already known from the earliest antiquity. Socrates, book 1 of the Ecclesiastical History, chapter 5, says that those things which were agreed upon by the common judgment of all were ratified and recorded in writing by subscription [ἐκυροῦτο τε ἤδε καὶ ἐγγεγράφως δι' ὑπογραφῆς]. Moreover, the decrees made by the common opinion of all were confirmed when each man's hand had subscribed them.

units.la: 143. Secundus modus collectionis creta erant cum cujusque manu subscripta essent; rata habebantur, & in commentarios referebantur. Exemplum statim subjicit in Sabino Socrates ibidem. Σαβῖν@ ὁ τῶν ἐν Ἡ͵ερακλείᾳ τῆ Θρᾳκης Μακεδονιαώων ἐπίσκοπ@, συνα-γωγὴν τῶν Ἀφφορι σωοδων ἐγγεγράφως ἐξέ-δωκαν, ποιησαμένος &c. Sabinus Macedonianorum qui Heracleam civitatem Thraicæ incolunt, Episcopus, tum ea quæ varia Episcoporum concilia scriptis ediderant, in unum volumen collegit. Ex quo duo patent: primum ante hunc Sabinum Episcopos jam varia concilia scriptis complexos edidisse; deinde hæc acta omnia & concilia in unum volumen compegisse Sabinum. Non tamen ex fide; subdit enim Socrates: Quinetiam nonnulla dedita opera prætermittit, quaedam etiam pervertit; quæ autem ad eum exitum, quem sibi proposuerat, facere videbantur, omnia diligenter excerpit. & postea libro 2. cap. 13. Σαβῖν@ μψῖοι ὁ τῆς Μακεδονίας αἱρέσεως, ὃ ἡ ἤδη πεώπρον ἐμνη-μονεύσαμεν; τὰς ἀφ᾽ Ιυλίῳ ἐπιστολὰς ἐν τῇ συναγωγῇ τῶν συνόδων ἐκ ἔθηκεν &c. Sabinus erroris Macedoniani propugnator; de quo jam antea mentionem feci, quanquam in libro ejus, qui rerum in conciliis gestarum collectio inscribitur, Epistolam Episcoporum Antiochiæ convocatorum ad Julium scriptam minime prætermisit, Epistolas tamen ipsius Julii in eodem neutiquam intexuit. texuit. Duplicem hunc modum colligendi facit Doctissimus Christ. Justellus, in Præsat. ad Codic. canon. Eccles. African. non longe à principio. Synodicarum autem collectionum, inquit, duo genera fuisse constat, quarū primum conciliorum acta, quæ ad dogmata, & fidei doctrinam spectant, continebat; Et συναγωγὴ τῶν συνόδων, vel συνοδικῶν, à Socrate vocatur libr. 3. Hist. Eccles. cap. 21. Alterum vero canones conciliorum, qui ad disciplinam Ecclesiasticam sacramque πολιτείαν pertinent, & βιβλίον κανόνων in Calchedonensi nuncupatur. Actione 4. 11. & 13. Hinc frequens Διαπτπώσεων & κανόνων distinctio apud Græcos Ecclesiasticæ historiæ scriptores. Ac synodalium quidem gestorum monumenta pauca exstant, permulta desiderantur, hæc Justellus. Nobis autem videtur posterior ille modus melius referri ad primum illum simplicem, quem supra retulimus; & debere distingui acta & sancita in conciliis à se invicem, ut qui sancita tantum referunt, ad primum modum referantur, qui vero acta & sancita conjungunt ad secundum. Quod faciunt operosa illa Generalium & Provincialium conciliorum volumina, quorum hodie habemus editiones varias, quarum præcipuas obiter hic recensemus, quia multum conferunt ad studium dium juris Ecclesiastici. Prima prodiit Coloniæ An. 1530. postea Petrus Crabbe edidit An. 1551. secundam duobus voluminibus; hunc excepit Surius, qui quatuor voluminibus concilia edidit, An. 1567. Dominicus Nicolinus quinque, Severinus Binius Canonicus Coloniensis Volum. octo Colon. 1606. & 1618. Romæ quoque Conciliorum Generalium Ecclesiæ Catholicæ; Græco Latina facta est editio jussu Sixti V. An. 1608. & novissime Collectio Regia Lutetiæ Parisiorum prodiit 37. voluminibus cum Indice separatim excuso anno 1636, cui cum decretalibus Romanorum Pontificum epistolis, inserta sunt concilia Gallica J. Sirmondi, Hispanica Garsiæ Loaysæ, Anglicana Henr. Spelmanni, Lemovicense è Bibliotheca Thuani, Florentinum Horatii Justiniani, &c. Sed hæc obiter. Ad modos colligendi revertimur. Tertius modus colligendi est magis artificiosus, priores illi magis naturales; Estque quando sub certos titulos & rubricas referuntur & digeruntur canones diversorum conciliorum, qui de iisdem rebus agunt, aut qui sunt ejusdem argumenti, veluti concilii Nicæni, Gangrensis, Calchedonensis. Hic modus est duplex iterum, aliquando enim Canones diversorum conciliorum unius tenoris & sententiæ, seu de iisdem rebus agentes, sub uno titulo aut rubrica digeruntur & citantur tantum, ut quis sciat esse concordantes, non vero recitantur verba; quod vocant veteres Breviationem Canonum, & istiusmodi opera seu collectiones Breviaria, quale Cresconii infra videbimus; aliquando vero insuper etiam recitantur verba canonum concordantium, & hoc appellant concordiam canonum; cujus exempla postea quoque occurrent. Quartus digerendi modus itidem artificialis est, & tertio modo insuper aliquid adjungit. Recitat nempe, aut citat canones diversorum conciliorum concordantes, sub certis titulis, tum etiam subjungit, concordes Imperatorum leges; quam collectionem, quia sociantur leges & canones, Nomocanonem appellare solent; cujus exempla præbebit infra Johannes Scholasticus & Photius. Tandem quinto latissime se diffundunt collectores, & canonibus, Leges Imperatorum, Decretales Epistolas Pontificum & Episcopum, sententias Patrum sub certos titulos seu rubricas corradunt & digerunt; quale opus exhibebunt postea plures, maximæ molis Gratianus. Possunt & aliæ collectionum differentiæ observari, nempe quod sint vel publicæ, quæ publica auctoritate fiunt; vel privatæ, quæ privatorum industria perficiuntur. Deinde & collectiones quædam sunt particulares, quæ tantum unius Ecclesiæ Canones colligunt, de quibus supra satis actum, & demonstratum plerasque Ecclesias habuisse collectionem Codicis Ecclesiæ Universæ, & insuper collectionem privatam suæ Ecclesiæ; inde diversitas codicum, Africani, Romani, Gallici, Hispanici, &c. Aliæ sunt Collectiones Universales, eaque iterum duplici respectu, ut supra observavimus, vel quod complectantur omnes omnium synodorum canones universalium & particularium; qualis collectio fortasse nondum extat; in hoc Genere perfectissima est Collectio Regia, cujus jam facta est mentio: vel ideo universalis dicitur, quod ubique recepta sit in Orbe Christiano, & ejusmodi habita fuit olim auctoritate & confirmatione Concilii Calchedonensis & Justiniani Imperatoris, Codex canonum Ecclesiæ Vniversæ seu Catholicæ.
units.tr: 143. They were held valid and were entered in the records. Socrates immediately gives an example of this in Sabinus, in the same place. Sabinus, bishop of the Macedonians who live in Heraclea, a city of Thrace, [συναγωγὴν τῶν συνόδων, the collection of the councils], made in writing. Sabinus, bishop of the Macedonians who inhabit the city of Heraclea in Thrace, collected into one volume both the things that various bishops had published in writing about the councils. From this two things are clear: first, that before this Sabinus, bishops had already published in writing the various councils, gathered together; and second, that Sabinus compiled all these acts and councils into one volume. Yet he was not trustworthy, for Socrates adds: Indeed, he deliberately omitted some things and even distorted others; but all those things that seemed to serve the end he had set for himself he diligently excerpted. And later, book 2, chapter 13: Sabinus, the champion of the Macedonian heresy, of whom I have already made mention, although in his book entitled the collection of the things done in the councils he did not omit the letter of the bishops of Antioch, convened to Julius, he by no means inserted in the same book the letters of Julius himself. Christian Justellus, in the preface to the Codex of the Canons of the African Church, not far from the beginning, makes this twofold mode of collecting. He says: "It is established that there were two kinds of synodal collections: the first contained the acts of the councils, which concern dogmas and the teaching of the faith, and it is called by Socrates, Ecclesiastical History, book 3, chapter 21, the collection of the synods [συναγωγὴ τῶν συνόδων] or of the synodal acts [συνοδικῶν]. The second contains the canons of the councils, which pertain to ecclesiastical discipline and the holy polity, and at Chalcedon it is called the book of canons [βιβλίον κανόνων], in acts 4, 11 and 13." Hence the frequent distinction among the Greek writers of ecclesiastical history between the acts and the canons. Of the synodal acts, few monuments survive; very many are lacking, so Justellus. But it seems to me that this latter mode is better referred to that first simple one which I set out above; and the acts and decrees of the councils should be distinguished from each other, so that those which report only the decrees are referred to the first mode, and those which join the acts and decrees to the second. This is what those laborious volumes of the General and Provincial Councils do, of which we today have various editions. I briefly list the chief of these here, because they contribute much to the study of ecclesiastical law. The first appeared at Cologne in 1530; afterwards Peter Crabbe published his edition in two volumes in 1551; Surius succeeded him, who published the councils in four volumes in 1567; Dominicus Nicolinus in five; Severinus Binius, canon of Cologne, in eight volumes, Cologne 1606 and 1618. At Rome, too, an edition of the General Councils of the Catholic Church, in Greek and Latin, was made by order of Sixtus V in 1608. And most recently the Royal Collection appeared at Paris in 37 volumes, with an index printed separately, in the year 1636; into it, along with the decretal letters of the Roman Pontiffs, have been inserted the Gallic councils of J. Sirmond, the Spanish of Garsias Loaysa, the English of Henry Spelman, the Limousin council from the library of Thuanus, the Florentine of Horatius Justinianus, etc. But these things in passing. We return to the modes of collecting. The third mode of collecting is more artful; the former ones were more natural. It is when the canons of various councils that deal with the same matters, or that are of the same subject, are referred and arranged under certain titles and headings, as of the Council of Nicaea, of Gangra, of Chalcedon. This mode is again twofold. For sometimes the canons of various councils of one tenor and sense, or dealing with the same matters, are arranged and merely cited under one title or heading, so that one may know that they agree, but the words are not recited. The ancients call this the abbreviation of the canons, and such works or collections are called breviaries, of which kind we shall see Cresconius below. Sometimes, however, the words of the agreeing canons are also recited, and this they call the concord of the canons; examples of this will also occur later. The fourth mode of arranging is likewise artful, and adds something to the third mode. It recites or cites the agreeing canons of various councils under certain titles, and then also adds the agreeing laws of the emperors. This collection, because laws and canons are joined, they are accustomed to call a Nomocanon; examples of which John Scholasticus and Photius will provide below. Finally, the fifth and most widely diffused kind of collectors gather and arrange under certain titles or headings the canons, the laws of the emperors, the decretal epistles of the Pontiffs and bishops, and the sayings of the Fathers. Several will later exhibit such a work of very great bulk, Gratian most of all. Other differences of collections can also be observed, namely that they are either public, which are made by public authority, or private, which are accomplished by the industry of private persons. Then, some collections are particular, which gather only the canons of one church, concerning which enough has been said above, and it has been shown that most churches had both the collection of the Code of the Universal Church and, in addition, a private collection of their own church; hence the diversity of codes: African, Roman, Gallic, Spanish, etc. Others are universal collections, and these again in a twofold respect, as we observed above: either because they comprise all the canons of all synods, universal and particular, a collection of which perhaps does not yet exist (in this kind the Royal Collection, already mentioned, is the most perfect); or because it is called universal for this reason, that it was received everywhere in the Christian world, and such a collection was formerly held by the authority and confirmation of the Council of Chalcedon and of the Emperor Justinian: the Code of the Canons of the Universal or Catholic Church.

units.la: His præli-batis, ipsas collectiones aggrediamur, habita ratione tantum temporis, quo sibi successerunt. Post primæ istius collectionis, quæ post concilium Nicænum cœpit, & lente ut dictum, per sequentia concilia progressa est, confirmationem, cœpit magis magisque studium colligendi canones inclarescere. scere, ut plerumque fieri solet, progressu tem-poris, quando utilitatem, laudem, & favorem studia conciliant; tum quilibet animum ad ea solet applicare. Maxime hic fervor se coepit exserere tempore Justiniani, à quo non tantum confirmatus Codex Ecclesiæ Universæ, & laudati atque commendati ex facilitate quadam, quam passim in hoc Imperatore taxant interpretes nostri, canones Pseudapostolici: Sed sub eo etiam multi collectores & compilatores canonum floruere; fortè accensi famosa illa digestione juris civilis. Prima hoc tempore est collectio Dionysii Exigui, de qua supra abunde dictum; qui primus canones Apostolorum Latinos fecit, & Codici canonum Ecclesiæ Universæ adjecit. Hic duas fecit Collectiones, unam canonum, alteram vero Decretalium Epistolarum Romanæ urbis Præsulum, ut supra notatum: quibus hoc tantum adjicimus, recte Justellum Patrem & filium utramque collectionem distinguere, & Præfationibus quas singulis præmisit Dionysius ornare, ut videri potest in Bibliotheca juris Canonici veteris tom. I. Excipiat hanc Dionysii collectionem ea, quam adornavit Fulgentius Ferrandus Ecclesiæ Carthagi-niensis Diaconus; quæ si non præcessit eam, saltem simul aut paulo post adornata est, ita ut alterum alterius labores non vidisse; sit verosimile ; De Ferrandi enim Collectione Henr. Justellus filius adserit, nullam esse apud Latinos antiquiorem, floruit enim Justini & Justiniani temporibus in Ecclesia Carthaginiensi, in qua Diaconatus officio functus est, ut ex Chronico Victoris Tununensis constat, qui eum claruisse refert, anno sexto post consulatum Basilii, id esset, anno Christi 547. Cum Fulgentio Ruspensi Episcopo vixisse, eumque Magistrum agnovisse & se discipulum ejus, ex scriptis ejus constat. Excessit autem vita Fulgentius Ruspensis anno 529; De Ferrando nostro haec refert Auctor incertus, de XII. script Ecclesiast. qui Isidoro & Ildefonso subjici solet, cap. XI. Ferrandus, Carthaginiensis Ecclesiae Diaconus, multum in Scripturis sacris floruisse adseritur; multasque cum beato Fulgentio propositiones alteriis epistolis habuisse narratur. Iste ad Pelagium & Anatolium Romanos Diaconos, consulentes eum utrum liceat quenquam damnare post mortem, edidit rescriptum, ubi inter alia sic locutus est, dicens: Quid prodest dormientibus Ecclesiam perturbare? Si quis in corpore mortis hujus accusatus & damnatus, antequam mereretur absolvi, de Ecclesia raptus est, absolvi ulterius non potest humano judicio. Si quis accusatus & absolutus ante diem sacri examinis, examinis, repentina vocatione praeventus est, intra sinum matris Ecclesiae constitutus, divino intelligendus est judicio reservari. De hoc nullus homo potest manifestam proferre sententiam: cui si Deus indulgentiam dedit, nihil nocet nostra severitas, sed si supplicium praeparavit, nihil prodest nostra benignitas. Meminit ejus quoque cum honore, Facundus Episcopus Hermianensis, pro defensione trium capitulorum concil. Calchedonensis ad Justinian. Imperat. nostrum. lib. 4. cap. 3. pag. mihi 169. edit. Jac. Sirmondi. Nam venerabilis Pelagius & Anatolius Romani Diaconi, debitam officio suo & loco sollicitudinem pro Ecclesia Dei gerentes, Laudabilis in Christo memoriae Ferrando Carthaginensi Diacono scripserunt, ut habito de causa diligenti tractatu, cum Reverendissimo ejusdem Ecclesiae Carthaginensis Episcopo, vel aliis, quos & zelum fidei, & divinae scripturae scirent habere notitiam consulentibus responderet, quid observandum in commune omnibus videretur: & quibusdam interjectis: sed & ille qui consultus fuerat, rescribens interrogantibus, retractandam non esse docuit epistolam, quam universalis synodus approbavit. Prodiere hi libri Facundi, ut tradit Victor Tunnunensis in Chronico, anno x. post Consulatum Basilii, id est Christi 551. quo tempore jam mortuus fuit noster Ferrandus, qui sexto anno post Consulatum Basilii, ut supra ex eodem Victore observatum adhuc floruit. Meminit quoque reverenter Ferrandi Cresconius in Praefatione sui Breviarii, ubi reverendissimum Carthaginis Ecclesiae Diaconum vocat, & postea Virum sapientissimum. Scripta ejus memorant varia. Paraeneticum ad Reginum Comitem, qui in Bibliotheca Patrum extat, item Epistolam amplam ad Anatolium Diaconum urbis Romae, & alias duas ad Fulgentium Episcopum Ruspensem, aliam adhuc ad Eugypium Abbatem, Thesauri ex operibus S. Augustini concinnatorem, quae primum Romae sunt publicatae, postea insertae tomo 6. Bibliothec. Patr. edit. Colon. Sunt quoque qui eum censent auctorem esse vitae S. Fulgentii Ruspensis, Episcopi, quam habemus in vit. sanct. inter quos est Justel: Pater in Praefatione ad Ferrandi nostri Breviationem; & Miraeus in notis ad incerti script. opusculum de XII. scriptor. jam citatum in Biblioth. Eccles. p. 106. Scripsit quoque Breviationem Canonum, quae pertinet ad institutum nostrum. Eam primo edidit cum Cresconii Breviario, Petr. Pithoeus ex Codice MS. Ecclesiae Trecensis, Lutetiae An. 1588; quod falso Altaserranus Nicolao Fabro adscribit; edita est postea cum codice canonum Ecclesiae Romanae Parisiis an. 1610; à Chiffletio vero Augustoriti Pictonum anno 1630, & ab Altaœrrano Divione 1649, tandem vero in Bibliothecam juris Canonici veteris retulerunt Voellus & Justellus Filius, ex destinatione tamen Patris. Non sequitur in hac Collectione Ferandus canonum consequentiam ut Dionysius, sed, habita materiarum ratione, canonicam omnem disciplinam capitibus ducentis & triginta duobus, inclusit, & singulis capitibus concordantes canones & decreta subjecit. Duplex vel triplex error Baronii ex his cavendus. Primus, quod Ferrando trecenta tribuat capitula. tom. 5. ad. Ann. 419. n. 90. his verbis: Ferrandus Diaconus Carthaginensis Ecclesiæ in hujus seculi fine magno splendore claruit non Carthagine tantum, sed in Universa Ecclesia Africana, hic quidem in suo Breviario, seu concordantia Canonum, quam diligenter elucubratam trecentis distinxit capitibus, eorundem (Sardicensium) canonum mentionem habet, recensens eos sub titulo concilii Sardicensis. Citat tum in margine Breviarium Ferrandi, c. 149. 153. apud Crescomium. Pergit porro. Immo ipse recte interpretatus, alteri hujusmodi præfixit titulum: De provinciali synodo retractanda per vicarios Episcopi Urbis Romæ, si ipse decreverit. In margine citat. Conc. Sard. 6. 7. Secundus, quod hic & tom. 7. Anno Christi 527. n. 76: Ferrandi & Cresconii Breviarium confundat; & censeat, Cresconium suæ collectioni subjecisse eam, quam eodem ferme tempore elaboravit Ferrandus, sed alio plane ordine dum sub unoquoque collegii capite & citando eos, non recitando, qui diversorum conciliorum de eadem re tractantes reperirentur canones, collocavit; quod opus jure Cresconius Breviarium appellandum putavit. Tertius, quod Cresconium faciat æqualem Fulgentio, qui fere duobus seculis post eum vixit, ut postea videbimus, ubi de eo ex professo agendum est; Observarunt hoc Voellius & Justellus in Bibliotheca juris Canonici veteris præfatione. In qua post indicatos errores, hæc, quæ multa singularia de utriusque collectione continent, subjiciunt. Etenim licet in methodo & ratione tradendi conveniant, Ordo tamen Ferrandi multo spectabilior est & accuratior, quam Cresconii. Si de materia item quæstio sit, non parum inter se differunt, quippe multa habent propria & peculiaria. Ferrando certe propria sunt, quæcunque refert ex conciliis Constantinopolitano, Zellensi seu Tiellensi, Suffetulensi, Septimunicensi, Macrianensi, Juncensi, Mazaranensi seu Maradianensi, Thenitano & Thusdritano, seu Thusduritano, quorum ne meminit quidem Cresconius. Similiter
units.tr: Having made these preliminary remarks, let us now turn to the collections themselves, bearing in mind only the period in which they succeeded one another. After the confirmation of the first of these collections, which began after the Council of Nicaea and advanced slowly, as I have said, through the later councils, the zeal for gathering canons began to grow brighter and brighter, as usually happens with the passage of time, since usefulness, praise and favour commend such studies, and then everyone is wont to apply his mind to them. This ardour first showed itself strongly in the time of Justinian. Under him the Code of the Universal Church was not only confirmed, but the so-called Pseudapostolic canons were also praised and commended, owing to a certain easiness that our writers generally charge against this emperor. Under him, too, many collectors and compilers of canons flourished, perhaps kindled by that famous digest of civil law. The first collection of this period is that of Dionysius Exiguus, of which we have spoken fully above. He was the first to render the canons of the Apostles into Latin and to add them to the Code of the Universal Church. He made two collections, one of canons and the other of the Decretal Epistles of the bishops of the city of Rome, as noted above. To these points we add only that the elder and the younger Justellus rightly distinguish the two collections, and that the prefaces which Dionysius prefixed to each may be seen in the Bibliotheca juris canonici veteris, vol. I. Following this collection of Dionysius is the one compiled by Fulgentius Ferrandus, deacon of the Church of Carthage. If it did not precede that of Dionysius, it was at least compiled at the same time or a little later, so that it is likely the one did not see the other's labours. For Henry Justellus the younger asserts that there is no older collection among the Latins than that of Ferrandus. He flourished in the times of Justin and Justinian in the Church of Carthage, where he served as deacon, as is clear from the Chronicle of Victor of Tunnuna, who reports that he was active in the sixth year after the consulship of Basilius, that is, in the year of Christ 547. That he lived with Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, and acknowledged him as his teacher and called himself his disciple, is clear from his writings. Fulgentius of Ruspe died in 529. The anonymous author On the Twelve Ecclesiastical Writers, which is usually appended to Isidore and Ildefonsus, says of our Ferrandus, in chapter 11: "Ferrandus, deacon of the Church of Carthage, is said to have flourished greatly in the holy Scriptures; and he is reported to have had many propositions with the blessed Fulgentius in other letters." To Pelagius and Anatolius, Roman deacons, who consulted him whether it is lawful to condemn anyone after death, he issued a reply, in which among other things he speaks thus: "What good does it do to disturb the sleeping Church? If someone who has been accused and condemned in this body of death has been snatched from the Church before he deserved to be absolved, he cannot be absolved any further by human judgement. If someone who has been accused and absolved before the day of the holy examination has been overtaken by a sudden summons, and has been placed within the bosom of mother Church, he is to be understood as reserved for the divine judgement. No man can pronounce a clear sentence concerning him. If God has granted him indulgence, our severity does him no harm; but if He has prepared punishment for him, our kindness does him no good." Facundus, bishop of Hermiane, also mentions him with honour, in his defence of the Three Chapters of the Council of Chalcedon, addressed to our emperor Justinian, book 4, chapter 3, page 169 of the edition of Jacques Sirmond. For, he says, the venerable Pelagius and Anatolius, Roman deacons, bearing the care for the Church of God that was due to their office and station, wrote to Ferrandus, deacon of Carthage, of blessed memory in Christ, that after a diligent treatment of the case he should reply, with the most reverend bishop of the same Church of Carthage or others whom they knew to have zeal for the faith and knowledge of divine Scripture, to those who consulted him, what seemed to be observed by all in common; and after some intervening matter: "But he too who had been consulted, writing back to those who asked, taught that the letter, which the universal synod had approved, was not to be retracted." These books of Facundus appeared, as Victor of Tunnuna reports in his Chronicle, in the tenth year after the consulship of Basilius, that is, in the year of Christ 551, by which time our Ferrandus was already dead, though he was still flourishing in the sixth year after the consulship of Basilius, as noted above on the authority of the same Victor. Cresconius also mentions Ferrandus with reverence in the preface to his Breviarium, where he calls him "the most reverend deacon of the Church of Carthage," and afterwards "a most wise man." His writings are recorded in various places: a Paraenetic to Count Reginus, which is extant in the Bibliotheca Patrum; likewise a long letter to Anatolius, deacon of the city of Rome, and two others to Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, and yet another to the abbot Eugippius, compiler of the Thesaurus from the works of St Augustine. These were first published at Rome and afterwards inserted in vol. 6 of the Bibliotheca Patrum, Cologne edition. There are also those who think he is the author of the Life of St Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, which we have in Vitae sanctorum; among them is Justellus the father, in the preface to his edition of our Ferrandus's abridgement, and Miraeus, in his notes to the anonymous little work On the Twelve Writers already cited, in the Bibliotheca ecclesiastica, p. 106. He also wrote an Abridgement of the Canons, which pertains to our present purpose. It was first published with the Breviarium of Cresconius by Pierre Pithou, from a manuscript codex of the Church of Troyes, at Paris in 1588. This Altaserranus wrongly ascribes to Nicolas Faber. It was afterwards published with the codex of the canons of the Roman Church at Paris in 1610; by Chifflet at Poitiers in 1630; and by Altaserranus at Dijon in 1649. Finally, Voellus and Justellus the younger included it in the Bibliotheca juris canonici veteris, though in accordance with their father's intention. In this collection Ferrandus does not follow the order of Dionysius, but, having regard to the subject matter, he included all canonical discipline under two hundred and thirty-two chapters, and subjoined to each chapter the agreeing canons and decrees. Baronius's double or triple error must be guarded against here. The first is that he attributes three hundred chapters to Ferrandus, vol. 5, year 419, n. 90, in these words: "Ferrandus, deacon of the Church of Carthage, flourished with great brilliance at the end of this century, not only at Carthage but throughout the whole African Church. He, in his Breviary, or concordance of canons, which he carefully elaborated and divided into three hundred chapters, has a mention of the canons of the Sardican council, recording them under the title of the Council of Sardica." In the margin he cites the Breviary of Ferrandus, chapters 149 and 153, in Cresconius. He goes on: "Indeed he himself, interpreting rightly, prefixed to another such chapter this title: On a provincial synod to be retracted through the vicars of the bishop of the city of Rome, if he himself has decided so." In the margin he cites Council of Sardica, canons 6 and 7. The second error is that here and in vol. 7, year of Christ 527, n. 76, he confuses the Breviaria of Ferrandus and Cresconius, and thinks that Cresconius subjoined to his collection the one that Ferrandus had composed at about the same time, but in an entirely different order, since under each chapter of the collection he placed, by citing and not reciting, the canons of various councils which were found to treat the same matter; which work Cresconius rightly thought should be called a Breviary. The third error is that he makes Cresconius contemporary with Fulgentius, who lived almost two centuries after him, as we shall see later, where we must treat of him expressly. Voellus and Justellus observed this in the preface to their Bibliotheca juris canonici veteris. In that preface, after pointing out these errors, they subjoin the following, which contains many singular points about both collections: "For although they agree in method and in the manner of presentation, the order of Ferrandus is much more distinguished and accurate than that of Cresconius. If the question also concerns the material, they differ not a little from one another, for they have many things that are their own and peculiar. Certainly the following are peculiar to Ferrandus: whatever he reports from the councils of Constantinople, Zelle or Tiellum, Suffetula, Septimunca, Macriana, Iuncca, Mazara or Maradi, Thenae and Thusdrus or Thusduros, of which Cresconius does not even make mention." Likewise

units.la: Similiter Cresconio proprii sunt Canones Apostolorum & Calchedonensis concilii, decreta item Romanorum Pontificum, Siricii, Innocentii, Zosimi, Cœlestini, Leonis & Gelasii, quæ à Ferrando nusquam laudantur. Ferrando quidem & Cresconio communes sunt canones Nicæni, Ancyrani, Neocæsarienses, Gangrenses & Antiocheni, Laodicenses & Sardicenses; Sed cum hoc discrimine, quod Cresconius has septem synodos ex editione Dionysii Exigui iisdem verbis & numeris exhibeat, non item Ferrandus, qui codicibus usus est in utroque plane diversis & Dionysiana editione vetustioribus. Quod indicium esse potest, Ferrando labores Dionysii Exigui fuisse ignotos, & nunquam visos; ideoque non diu unum ante alium suam collectionem perfecisse. In Ferrando quoque diversi sunt numeri canonum Carthaginiensium, à Dionysianis & Cresconianis. Quæ diversitas ex eo nata est, quod omnes pariter collectione Canonum Carthaginiensium usi non sunt; Græci enim, itemque Dionysius Exiguus omnes CXXXIII. una serie numerarunt, tanquam unius synodi, ut revera sunt. Alii vero ex una synodo quasi duas secerunt, nec eodem plane modo. Nam Codex vetus canonum Ecclesiæ Romanæ edi-tus tus Moguntiæ Anno 1525. prius exhibet primos xxxiii. canones sub nomine concilii Africani. Eadem divisione usus est Cresconius, qui canones illos xxxiii. priores adscribit concilio quod Carthaginense ἀσωλῶς nuncupat, sed alios centum velut ex altero concilio refert, quod cap. 30. & 154. Carthaginense Universale appellat. At Ferrando minus placuisse illam collectionem verosimile est; sive quod in ea quædam deesse, quædam redundare, alia inconcinne sejuncta vel connexa esse deprehenderit: sive quod ipsos fontes adire, quam ipsos revulos sectari maluerit. Quapropter ex toto illo concilio anni CDXIX. ex quo Africana Collectio emanavit, sex tantum ultimos canones, qui soli sunt ejus proprii, spectavit, & ex eis titulos 2. 3. 4. & 6. capitulis suis 73. 195. 196. & 197. inseruit, reliquos canones, ex quibus Africana constat Collectio, non ex ipsa Collectione, sed ex singulorum conciliorum Africæ integris actis retulit.
units.tr: Similarly, Cresconius has his own the Canons of the Apostles and of the Council of Chalcedon, and likewise the decrees of the Roman bishops Siricius, Innocent, Zosimus, Celestine, Leo and Gelasius, which Ferrandus nowhere cites. Ferrandus and Cresconius share the canons of Nicaea, Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Gangra, Antioch, Laodicea and Sardica. But there is this difference: Cresconius gives these seven councils in the same words and numbering as the edition of Dionysius Exiguus, whereas Ferrandus does not, since he used manuscripts quite different from one another and older than the Dionysian edition. This may be an indication that Ferrandus did not know the labours of Dionysius Exiguus and had never seen them, and so he did not finish his own collection long after the other. The numbering of the Carthaginian canons also differs in Ferrandus from the Dionysian and Cresconian. This difference arises because not all of them used the same collection of Carthaginian canons. The Greeks, and Dionysius Exiguus likewise, numbered all 133 in one series, as belonging to one council, which in fact they are. Others, however, divided one council into two, and not in exactly the same way. For the old codex of the canons of the Roman Church, published at Mainz in 1525, first gives the first thirty-three canons under the name of the African council. Cresconius used the same division: he assigns those first thirty-three to the council that he calls the Carthaginian "without qualification," but he cites the other hundred as if from a second council, which in chapters 30 and 154 he calls the Universal Carthaginian council. It is likely, however, that Ferrandus did not much care for that collection, either because he found in it some things missing, some things superfluous, and other things awkwardly separated or joined, or because he preferred to go to the sources themselves rather than follow their streams. Therefore, from the whole of that council of 419, from which the African Collection emerged, he looked only at the last six canons, which alone are proper to it, and from these he inserted the titles 2, 3, 4 and 6 under his chapters 73, 195, 196 and 197. The remaining canons, of which the African Collection consists, he took not from the Collection itself but from the complete acts of the individual councils of Africa.

units.la: Plures convenientias & differentias ostendet duplex ille index, quem in Fulgentium & Cresconium publicarunt Voellius & Justellus in sæpius laudata Bibliotheca juris Canon. veter. ex manuscripto Guillielmi Blueti, in Senatu Parisiensi Advocati, quorum unus Materiam canonum, alter vero consonantiam & difcrepantiam inter utrumque declarat.
units.tr: The double index that Voellus and Justellus published in the often-cited Bibliotheca juris canonici veteris, on Fulgentius and Cresconius, from the manuscript of Guillaume Bluet, advocate in the Parisian Senate, will show more agreements and differences. One of its parts sets out the subject matter of the canons, the other the agreement and disagreement between the two.

units.la: Ferrandum sequitur Johannes Antiochenus Presbyter, qui Scholasticus vocatur, quod quidam volunt fuisse officii cujusdam Ecclesiastici nomen, & idem cum Protonotarii esse, sed falso. Temporibus enim Justiniani & anterioribus Scholastici vocabantur Advocati & Patroni, qui in foro causas dicebant. Probat hoc vel unicus Agathias, quem Suidas Scholasticum vocat. Ἀγαθίας σχολαστικὸς Σμυρναῖος, ὁ γεγράψας τὴν μετὰ Προκόπιον ἱστορίαν τὴν Καισαρέα. Agathias Scholasticus Smyrnaeus scripsit historiam post Procopium Caesariensem. Agathias autem ipse cujus fuerit professionis docet lib. 1. Histor. Ἀγαθίας μὲν ὄνομα, Μύεινα δὲ πατρίς, Μεμνόνιος πατὴρ, τέχνη δὲ τὰ Ῥωμαίων νόμιμα, ᾗ οἱ τῶν δικαστηρίων ἀγῶνες. Agathias mihi nomen est, Murrina patria, Memnonius Pater, ars quam profiteor, jura Romana & judiciorum certamina; Quod iterum testatur libro 3. vide quoque Synesii Epistolas, in quibus causidici passim vocantur Scholastici. Epist. 105. 155. & 156. ad Domitianum Scholasticum. Hoc quoque nomine judices per Provincias sunt appellati. Sigebert. in Chronico: Franco Scholasticus Leodicensium & scientia literarum & morum probitate claret. Walafridus Strabo de reb. EccleEcclesiasticis cap. xxv. Quales composuerunt Ambrosius, Hilarius, & Beda Anglorum Pater, & Prudentius Scholasticus Hispaniarum. Scholæ tum temporis erant Collegia Jurisperitorum. Vid. Joh. Meurs. Glossar. Græco-barbar. voce Σχολαστικὸς, & Vossium de Histor. Græc. lib. 2. cap. 22. in vita Agathiæ. Fuerunt & alii Scholastici dicti, sed hos nunc, quia ad institutum nostrum nil faciunt, prætermittimus. Noster Johannes inde quoque est dictus χολαστικὸς, quia in foro ex Scholasticorum seu advocatorum numero erat. Fuit primum Presbyter Antiochiæ, & Apocrisiarius, quales vocabantur, qui legati Ecclesiæ negotia tractabant. Justin. Novell. 6. c. 2. δ᾽ ἐὰν τῶν τὰ πεάγματα τῶν προσθέντων τ᾽ ἀμοτώτων ἐκκλησιῶν, ὡς ἀποκελισθέντος καλῶσιν. Propterea sancimus, si propter ecclesiasticam occasionem inciderit necessitas, hanc aut per eos qui res agunt sacrarum ecclesiarum, quos Apocrisiarios vocant &c. Postea tamen indifferenter pro quovis legato positum legitur. Incepit hoc munus & nomen temporibus Constantini Magni. Hincmarus Epist. 3. cap. 13. Cujus (Apocrisiarii) ministerium co tempore sumsit exordium, quando Constantinus Magnus Imperator Christianus effectus propter amorem & honorem sanctorum Apostolorum Petri, quorum doctrina ac ministerio
units.tr: Ferrandus is followed by John of Antioch, a presbyter who is called Scholasticus. Some think this was the name of a certain ecclesiastical office, and the same as that of protonotary, but this is false. For in the time of Justinian and earlier, scholastici were advocates and patrons who pleaded causes in the courts. This is shown by Agathias alone, whom Suidas calls Scholasticus: Agathias the Scholasticus of Smyrna, who wrote the history after Procopius of Caesarea [Ἀγαθίας σχολαστικὸς Σμυρναῖος, ὁ γεγράψας τὴν μετὰ Προκόπιον ἱστορίαν τὴν Καισαρέα]. Agathias himself tells what his profession was in book 1 of the Histories: Agathias is my name, Murrina my homeland, Memnonius my father; my craft is Roman law and the contests of the courts [Ἀγαθίας μὲν ὄνομα, Μύεινα δὲ πατρίς, Μεμνόνιος πατὴρ, τέχνη δὲ τὰ Ῥωμαίων νόμιμα, ᾗ οἱ τῶν δικαστηρίων ἀγῶνες]. He says the same again in book 3. See also the letters of Synesius, in which advocates are everywhere called scholastici: Letters 105, 155 and 156, to Domitian the Scholasticus. In this sense judges in the provinces were also so called. Sigebert, in the Chronicle: Franco the Scholasticus of Liège shines both in learning and in integrity of life. Walafrid Strabo, On ecclesiastical affairs, chapter 25: such as Ambrose, Hilary, and Bede the Father of the English, and Prudentius the Scholasticus of Spain have written. At that time the scholae were colleges of jurists. See John Meursius, Glossarium Graeco-barbarum, under the word Σχολαστικός, and Vossius, On Greek Historians, book 2, chapter 22, in the life of Agathias. There were others also called scholastici, but these we now pass over, since they have nothing to do with our purpose. Our John was called Σχολαστικός for the same reason: he was in the forum, among the number of the scholastici or advocates. He was first presbyter at Antioch and apocrisiarius, the name given to those who conducted the business of the Church as envoys. Justinian, Novel 6, chapter 2: If, on account of an ecclesiastical matter, necessity arises, let it be settled through those who manage the affairs of the holy churches, whom they call apocrisiarii [δ᾽ ἐὰν τῶν τὰ πράγματα τῶν προσθέντων τ᾽ ἀμοτώτων ἐκκλησιῶν, ὡς ἀποκελισθέντος καλῶσιν]. Afterwards, however, the word is found applied indiscriminately to any envoy. This office and name began in the time of Constantine the Great. Hincmar, Letter 3, chapter 13: The ministry of the apocrisiarius took its beginning at the time when Constantine the Great, an emperor made Christian, out of love and honour for the holy Apostles Peter, by whose teaching and ministry

units.la: {164} Fuit Presbyter & Apocrysiarius; & quale hoc officium. rio ad Christi gratiam baptismatis sacramenti pervenit, &c. Habuerunt honorem hunc primum Episcopi; postea, quia satius ut illi ecclesias curarent, plerumque adhibiti Presbyteri aut Diaconi. Officium eorum erat regere omnem palatii Clerum; habebant adjunctum Protocapcellarium: dicti quoque fuerunt Capellani, & custodes Pallatii. Videatur Hincmarus d.l. Ex Apocrisiario Johannes noster factus est per Justinianum Imperatorem Patriarcha Constantinopolitanus, idque in Eutychii locum, qui in exilium ejectus fuit. Factum id an. 564. vid. Baron. ad istum Annum num. 14. ubi hoc ei tribuit elogium vel potius vituperium. Ubi primum autem de exilio Eutychii sententia lata est: continuo de successore eligendo actum delectusque fuit Johannes cognomento Scholasticus ex apocrisiario Ecclesiae Antiochenae, homo plane servus gloriae & nundinator rerum sacrarum, quique pretio adulationis eam mercatus est dignitatem. Quod tamen elogium ille nullius auctoritate probat. Sedit in Episcopatu usque ad annum 578, quo tempore revocatus est Eutychius, post mortem Justiniani. Hujus est duplex opus in jure ecclesiastico elaboratum, primum praefert titulum συναγωγὴ κανόνων, Collectionis canonum, alterum Nomocanonis. In collectione omnium conciliorum canones in codice Ecclesiæ Universæ se secundum temporis rationem consequentes, in quinquaginta titulos digerit, & eos qui sunt ejusdem argumenti, sub eadem capita seu titulos refert, ὁ τάξιν τινὰ, ἢ ἀναλυθίων ἀριθμῶν ἐφυλάξαμεν, inquit ipse in Præfatione collectioni præfixa, ἀλλὰ ὅμοια τοῖς ὁμοίοις ὡς οἷόντε συναρμόσαντες, κεφαλαίῳ συμπλέξαντες, Non ordinem quendam & seriem numerorum servavimus: sed similia similibus, quantum fieri potuit, copulantes, & par pari capiti connectentes &c. Inseruit suæ collectioni primus inter Græcos Canones Apostolicos LXXXV; ante semi fere seculum effictos & suppositos, Sardicenses XXI. eosque præmittit Antiochenis antiquioribus, & Basilii LXVIII; quos omnes non summatim recenseт, sed longe lateque descripsit. Ad hanc Collectionem respexisse videtur Nicolaus I. Papa, eamque vocare concordiam canonum, quia unius argumenti canones, sub eodem titulo in concordiam rediguntur; ita enim scribit ad Photium, Patriarcham Constantinopol. Quomodo non sunt penes vos canones Sardicenses, quando inter quinquaginta titulos, quibus CONCORDIA CANONUM apud vos texitur, ipsi quoque reperiuntur. Alterum ipsius opus est Nomocanon, isque est epitome Collectionis quinquaginta quaginta istorum capitum seu titulorum, omissis integris canonibus, notata tantum sententia & numero, quibus concordes leges, τὰ συνᾴδοντα νόμιμα, potissimum Justiniani Imperatoris Novellas Constitutiones subjicit. Ad hunc Nomocanonem Johannis Scholastici putat Justellus Pater Præfatione ad eum, respexisse Theodorum Balsamonem ad canonem I. Concil. Constantinopol. in Trullo habiti, in exemplari Græco Joh. Tilii, quo olim usus Gentianus Hervetus, in cujus Latina interpretatione hæc verba reperiuntur, quæ in Græca editione Parisiensi desiderantur. Nomocanonum autem, inquit, quod in quinquaginta titulos leges & canones redegit, & reliquas Justiniani Novellas, quæ exoleverunt, ut quæ in Imperio non sunt recepta, & alias quasdam leges ex Digestis & Codice. Hinc facile est colligere Johannem Scholasticum, cum adhuc Presbyter esset Antiochiæ Collectionem suam Canonum quinquaginta titulis distinctam composuisse, Nomocanonem autem postquam Patriarcha Constantinopolitanus designatus est. Sunt qui συναγωγὴν κανόνων, seu Collectionem canonum non Johanni Scholastico, sed Theodoreto Cyri Episcopo adscribunt, qui centum & triginta annis nostrum Joh. Scholasticum præcessit, inter quos est, auctor in jure Canonico alias non hospes; Francisc: Florens, de origine Juris Canonici. part. 2. qui deceptus est à codice Manuscripto Bibliothecæ Regiæ, in quo Nomocanon habetur, qui præfert auctorem Theodoretum Episcopum Cyri, quasi Johannes Scholasticus tantum leges subjecisset. Hunc titulum Justellus d. l. vocat adjectitiam, & suppositititiam epigraphen, & subdit, Nec enim alibi unquam, ab ullo quovis auctore Græco, ejus Nomocanonis, sub Theodoreti nomine, mentio facta est, sed Joh. Scholastico tribuunt omnes codices MSS. Sic enim habet Codex Illustrissimi Franciæ Cancellarii Petri Seguierii. Ἰωάννης Ἐπισκόπος Κωνσταντινουπόλεως τῆς μήσου Εὐτυχίᾳ, συναγωγὴ κανόνων εἰς ν'. τίτλους διῃρημένη; Codex vero Claromontensis. Ἰωάννης πρεσβύτερος Ἀντιοχείας, ἀπὸ φολασικῶν [?] συντάττει τὰς ὅλας καινόνας εἰς ν'. τίτλους. Et Codex Oxoniensis. Συναγωγὴ κανόνων ἐκκλησιαστικῶν εἰς πεντήκοντα τίτλους διῃρημένη, & postea: Ἰωάννης ἀρχιεπίσκοπος Κωνσταντινουπόλεως εἰς τὸ νομοκανόνα σχόλιον. Quinimo ipse Codex Manuscriptus Regius in fine exprimit, nomen Ἰωάννης ἀρχιεπισκόπως Κωνσταντινουπόλεως, τῆς ἀπὸ φολασικῶν. Unde planum est, subdit Justellus, & indubium, utramque hanc collectionem esse ejusdem auctoris, Joh. videlicet Scholastici. Nec sane Theodoreto digna digna est hæc Collectio, cujus stylus non redolet gravitatem tanti Viri, planeque Doctissimi. Nec verosimile est Theodoretum inseruisse canones Apostolicos & Sardicenses, sua ætate à Græcis nondum receptos (adde quoad canones Apostolicos, nondum effictos aut suppositos) nec veteri Codici canonum, quo usa est Ecclesia universa in concilio Calchedonensi, cui ipse interfuit insertos, & quos Joh. Scholasticus, Collectionis quinquaginta titulorum & Nomocanonis auctor, suæ Collectioni primus inseruit, & postea Ecclesia Orientalis in synodo Trullana probavit, & confirmavit, anno demum DCCVII. sub Justiniano II. Imp. Sunt & multa alia quæ eam collectionem non esse Theodoreti, atque post ejus obitum, factam indicare videantur: sed in tanta luce sufficit hæc adnotasse. Conatur nihilominus Fr. Florens dicto loco suam sententiam adstruere, esse collectionis auctorem Theodoretum, quia concilii quinti Oecumenici sub Justiniano celebrati collectio illa mentionem non facit. Praterea quod Theodoretus conciliorum & Patrum canones non integros referat, sed sententiam tantum brevissimo verborum compendio certis titulis includat. Denique quod ex duabus Basilii Epistolis tantum xxvii. non plures canones auctor collectionis adducat. Quæ omnia si vera essent, attamen non evince-rent,
units.tr: {164} He was presbyter and apocrisiarius, and what kind of office this was. came to the grace of Christ through the sacrament of baptism, etc. The first bishops held this honour; later, since it was more fitting that they look after their churches, presbyters or deacons were usually employed. Their duty was to govern the whole clergy of the palace; they had as an assistant the protochancellor. They were also called capellani and custodes palatii. See Hincmar, as above. From apocrisiarius John our man was made Patriarch of Constantinople by the Emperor Justinian, in place of Eutychius, who had been driven into exile. This happened in 564; see Baronius at that year, number 14, where he gives him this description, or rather this reproach: As soon as sentence was passed on the exile of Eutychius, at once a successor was to be chosen, and John, surnamed Scholasticus, was chosen from the apocrisiarius of the Church of Antioch, a man altogether a slave to glory and a haggler in sacred things, who bought that dignity with the price of flattery. Yet he proves this description by the authority of no one. He held the episcopate until 578, when Eutychius was recalled after the death of Justinian. He produced a twofold work on ecclesiastical law. The first bears the title Synagogue of canons [συναγωγὴ κανόνων], a collection of canons, the second Nomocanon. In the collection he arranges the canons of all the councils, following the order of their time, in the code of the universal Church, into fifty titles, and he brings together under the same chapter or title those that are on the same subject. We have not kept some order or series of numbers, he says himself in the preface prefixed to the collection, but joining like things to like as far as possible, and connecting them under one head, and matching equal with equal, etc. Among the Greeks he was the first to insert into his collection the Apostolic Canons, eighty-five in number, drawn up and fabricated some half century before, and the twenty-one of Sardica. He puts these before the older canons of Antioch and the sixty-eight of Basil. He does not recount all of these briefly, but sets them out at length and in full. Pope Nicholas I seems to have had this collection in view, and to call it concord of canons, because canons on one subject are brought into concord under one title. He writes thus to Photius, Patriarch of Constantinople: How is it that you do not have the Canons of Sardica, since they too are found among the fifty titles, by which the CONCORD OF CANONS is woven among you? His other work is the Nomocanon, which is an epitome of that collection of fifty titles or chapters, with the complete canons omitted, the sense and number only noted, to which he adds the laws that agree with them, ta synadonta nomima [τὰ συνᾴδοντα νόμιμα], chiefly the Novels of the Emperor Justinian. Justellus the father, in his preface to it, thinks that Theodore Balsamon, in his commentary on the first canon of the Council of Constantinople held in Trullo, had this Nomocanon in view, in the Greek copy of John Tilius, which Gentianus Hervetus once used. In his Latin translation these words are found, which are missing from the Greek Paris edition: The Nomocanon, which reduced laws and canons into fifty titles, and the remaining Novels of Justinian, which have fallen out of use, since they were not received in the Empire, and certain other laws from the Digest and the Code. From this it is easy to conclude that John Scholasticus composed his collection of canons, divided into fifty titles, while he was still presbyter at Antioch, but the Nomocanon after he had been designated Patriarch of Constantinople. Some ascribe the Synagogue of canons, or collection of canons, not to John Scholasticus but to Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrus, who preceded our John Scholasticus by a hundred and thirty years. Among these is Francis Florens, On the origin of canon law, part 2, who is otherwise no stranger in canon law. He was deceived by a manuscript codex of the Royal Library, in which the Nomocanon is found, and which gives Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrus, as the author, as if John Scholasticus had only added the laws. Justellus, in the passage cited, calls this title an added and supposititious inscription, and adds: For nowhere else, at any time, from any Greek author, is there any mention of this Nomocanon under the name of Theodoret, but all the manuscript codices give it to John Scholasticus. For so the codex of the most illustrious Chancellor of France, Pierre Séguier, has it: John, Bishop of Constantinople, surnamed Eutychius, a collection of canons divided into fifty titles [Ἰωάννης Ἐπισκόπος Κωνσταντινουπόλεως τῆς μήσου Εὐτυχίᾳ, συναγωγὴ κανόνων εἰς ν'. τίτλους διῃρημένη]. The Clermont codex has: John, presbyter of Antioch, from the Scholastici, compiles all the canons into fifty titles [Ἰωάννης πρεσβύτερος Ἀντιοχείας, ἀπὸ φολασικῶν συντάττει τὰς ὅλας καινόνας εἰς ν'. τίτλους]. And the Oxford codex: A collection of ecclesiastical canons divided into fifty titles [Συναγωγὴ κανόνων ἐκκλησιαστικῶν εἰς πεντήκοντα τίτλους διῃρημένη], and afterwards: John, archbishop of Constantinople, commentary on the Nomocanon [Ἰωάννης ἀρχιεπίσκοπος Κωνσταντινουπόλεως εἰς τὸ νομοκανόνα σχόλιον]. Indeed the royal manuscript codex itself gives at the end the name John, archbishop of Constantinople, of the Scholastici [Ἰωάννης ἀρχιεπισκόπως Κωνσταντινουπόλεως, τῆς ἀπὸ φολασικῶν]. Hence it is plain, adds Justellus, and beyond doubt, that both collections are by the same author, namely John Scholasticus. Nor indeed is this collection worthy of Theodoret, whose style does not smell of the gravity of so great and truly most learned a man. Nor is it likely that Theodoret inserted the Apostolic and Sardican canons, which in his day were not yet received by the Greeks (add: as to the Apostolic canons, not yet made or fabricated) nor into the old code of canons which the universal Church used in the Council of Chalcedon, at which he himself was present; and which John Scholasticus, author of the collection of fifty titles and of the Nomocanon, first inserted into his collection; and afterwards the Eastern Church approved and confirmed it in the Council of Trullo, at last in 707 under the Emperor Justinian II. There are also many other things which seem to indicate that this collection is not Theodoret's and was made after his death; but in so great a light it is enough to have noted these. Nevertheless Francis Florens, in the passage cited, tries to establish his own opinion, that Theodoret is the author of the collection, because the collection makes no mention of the fifth Ecumenical Council held under Justinian. Besides, Theodoret does not give the canons of the councils and Fathers whole, but only summarises their sense in very brief words under certain titles. Finally, the author of the collection cites only twenty-seven canons from two Letters of Basil, and no more. All of which, even if true, would not prove what Florens intends, namely that Theodoret, and not John Scholasticus, is the author of that collection. Moreover, his first argument rests on the false supposition that that synod under Justinian issued canons, which in fact it issued none; and the two following will appear from inspection itself to be...

units.la: m rent, quod Fr. Florens intendit, nempe Theodoretum, non Joh. Scholasticum esse auctorem istius collectionis. Tum etiam nititur falso supposito primum argumentum, quasi synodus illa sub Justinirno ediderit canones, quæ nullos edidit; tandem duo sequentia ex ipsa inspectione apparebunt esse falsa. Quod indicium est, Florentem non vidisse labores Joh. Scholastici, qui tum adhuc in bibliothecis delitescebant. Produxit eos primus Justellus Pater, & Filius in Bibliotheca juris Canonici veteris, in cujus tomo secundo utrumque opusculum primum occupat locum Græcè & Latinè versum. Tria, ut Nomocanonis jam recensita, sic etiam συναγωγὴς κανόνων, seu Collectionis Canonum memorantur manuscripta; Unum perquam vetustum Romæ in Bibliotheca Vaticana, Heidelberga allatum, insigne quidem & eximium, sed exesum & mutilum. Alterum æque antiquum, sed integrum in Bibliotheca Franciæ Cancellarii Petri Seguierii, Tertium in Bibliotheca Collegii Claromontani Parisiensis, quod à Jacobo Sirmondo accepit Justellus, & typis exprimi curavit. Collectiones hæ Johannis Scholastici ab initio fuerunt magni usus & auctoritatis, utpote quæ in suo genere diu apud Græcos solæ fuerunt. Deinde Magnus
units.tr: ...prove what Fr. Florens intends, namely that Theodoret, and not John Scholasticus, is the author of this collection. Moreover, his first argument rests on the false assumption that the synod under Justinian issued canons, when it issued none; and the two that follow will, on inspection, prove to be false too. This shows that Florens had not seen the works of John Scholasticus, which still lay hidden in libraries at that time. They were first brought to light by Justellus the father and son in their Bibliotheca juris canonici veteris, where both works take the first place in the second volume, printed in Greek and Latin. Three manuscripts of the Nomocanon, as already noted, and likewise of the synagoge kanonon, or Collection of Canons, are recorded. One, very old, is in the Vatican Library at Rome; it was brought from Heidelberg, is remarkable and excellent, but is worn and incomplete. The second is equally old but complete, in the library of the Chancellor of France, Pierre Séguier. The third is in the library of the Clermont College at Paris, which Justellus received from Jacques Sirmond and had printed. These collections of John Scholasticus were from the beginning of great use and authority, since in their kind they were for a long time the only ones among the Greeks. Then Magnus...
170. The authority of the Collections of John Scholasticus.

units.la: Magnus Usserius in disser. de script. Ignatii. cap. 6. pag. 37. & seq. prodidit, ejus Nomocanonem ab Imperatore Justiniano fuisse confirmatum, & Epiphanio Patriarchæ, ad quem Nov. 6. scripta est, commendatum. Sed tum ante Patriarchatum debet supponi scriptus Nomocanon, contra quam supra Justellus censuit. Verba Usserii subjicimus.
units.tr: Magnus Usserius, in his dissertation on the writings of Ignatius, chapter 6, page 37 and following, reported that his Nomocanon was confirmed by the Emperor Justinian and commended by him to Epiphanius, Patriarch of Constantinople, to whom Novel 6 was written. But in that case the Nomocanon must be supposed to have been written before the patriarchate, contrary to what Justellus thought above. We add Usher's own words.

units.la: Cum igitur, inquit, sub sexti seculi, ut diximus initia, quinquaginta tantum extiterint Canones, iidemque à pluribus habiti apocryphi: triginta quinque alios à falsario, de quo nunc agimus, mox adjectos animadvertimus; Justiniani Imperatoris temporibus & primum natos, & in Ecclesiasticum Nomocanonem unâ cum reliquis mox admissos. tum illum, quem à se confirmatum Epiphanio Constantinopolitano Patriarchæ commendavit ipse Justinianus (si qua fides Arabico hujus Codicis interpreti adhibenda, quem Viri clarissimi & optimi D. Thomæ Roe, equitis aurati & Serenissimi Regis nostri apud Turcarum Imperatorem nuper Oratoris, beneficio Bibliotheca Oxoniensis jam possidet:) tum alterum, à Johanne Epiphaniensi Scholastico (qui Eutychio in Patriarchatu Constantinopolitano, sub finem imperii Justiniani, est suffectus) concinnatum; cui in quibusdam exemplaribus Theodoreti Cyrensis Episcopi nomen perperam est adscriptum. Hac ille. Postea vero testan-
units.tr: "Since, then," he says, "at the beginning of the sixth century, as we have said, there were only fifty canons, and these were regarded by many as apocryphal, we observe that thirty-five others were afterwards added by the forger of whom we are now speaking. These were both first produced in the times of the Emperor Justinian and at once admitted, together with the rest, into the ecclesiastical Nomocanon. Then came that Nomocanon which Justinian himself, as the Arabic translator of this codex should be trusted (the one that the most distinguished and excellent Sir Thomas Roe, knight, and our most serene King's ambassador lately at the court of the Emperor of the Turks, has now brought to the Bodleian Library at Oxford), confirmed and commended to Epiphanius, Patriarch of Constantinople; and then the other, compiled by John Scholasticus of Epiphania, who was appointed to the patriarchate of Constantinople under Eutychius, near the end of Justinian's reign, and whose name is wrongly ascribed in some copies to Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus." So far he. But afterwards, as Balsamon testifies in his supplement

units.la: [Page ends mid-word; catchword "testan-" follows.] te Balsamone in supplem. per Photii Nomocanonem pleniorem & uberiorem hi Johannis labores penitus sunt offuscati, & memoria fere plane deleta. Ex eo quod octuaginta quinque canones Apostolicos non ita diu fictos & Apostolorum nomine ornatos, à nullo adhuc probatos vel receptos, statim ille admiserit, & collectionibus suis inseruerit, forte etiam Justiniano eorum commendationem persuaserit, videtur colligi posse, fuisse Hominem non magni judicii: (alias facile hos canones deprehendisset, nil minus quam Apostolos auctores aut aetatem spirare) sed ingenii Graeci, quae facilia sunt in admittendis istiusmodi nugis. Quamobrem non obscure, nec immerito nostrum hunc Scholasticum taxat, Doctissimus Dalaeus de Pseudepigraph. Apostolicis. lib. 3. cap. 3. pag. 456. & cap. 21. sin. pag. 686.
units.tr: [Page ends mid-word; catchword "testan-" follows.] ...as Balsamon testifies in his supplement, these labours of John were entirely overshadowed by the fuller and more abundant Nomocanon of Photius, and their memory was almost wholly wiped out. From the fact that he at once admitted the eighty-five Apostolic canons, which had been fabricated not long before and adorned with the name of the Apostles, and which no one had yet approved or received, and inserted them into his collections, and perhaps even persuaded Justinian to commend them, it seems we may infer that the man was not of great judgement (otherwise he would easily have detected that these canons breathe nothing less than Apostolic authorship or antiquity), but that he had a Greek temperament, which readily admits such trifles. Hence our Scholasticus is rightly and not obscurely censured by the most learned Dalaeus, On the Pseudepigraphic Apostolic Writings, book 3, chapter 3, page 456, and chapter 21, near the end, page 686.

units.la: Ordo temporis nunc exigit, ut Martinum, primum Dumiensis Monasterii Abbatem, postea Episcopum Bracarensem in scenam producamus. Fuit is natione Pannonius, teste Gregor. Turonensis. Hist. Franc. lib. 5. c. 38. Errat itaque Garsias Loaysa, Praefat. ad Mart. Bracar. capit. in collect. concil. Hispan. qui eum Graecum fuisse bis terve affirmat, & ne existimes eum id de cognitione linguae Graecae intellexisse, diserte homi- hominem Græcum vocat. En Elogium ejus. Martinus Bracarensis Episcopus capitula edidit synodorum Græcarum quæ citantur à Gratiano cap. propter Ecclesiasticas distinct. 18. Erat Græcus & hæc capitula Græca Latina fecit, vocatur liber Capitulorum Martini. Hic cum esset Græcus ad utilitatem Ecclesiarum Hispaniæ hæc capitula Græca Latina fecit, & alia quædam ex Latinis addidit, & à Græcis aliqua detraxit, ut est in cap. propter Ecclesiasticas, quod desumptum est ex concilio Antiocheno. cap. 20. Alia etiam ex Toletanis conciliis posuit Græcus homo, & ad mores nostrorum hominum Græcos ritus sanctè & prudenter accommodavit. Ex patria in Orientem progressus, bonas literas & scientias ibidem hausit, & tantos in iis profectus fecit, ut doctissimos sui temporis æquaret, aut superaret. Ex Oriente in Galliciam trajecit, ibique conversis ab Arriana impietate Suevorum populis, regulam fidei & sanctæ religionis constituit. Ecclesias confirmavit, Monasteria condidit; vid. Isidor. Hispal. de Viris Illustr. cap. 22. alias 35. Qui etiam in Histor. sive Chro. Gothor. hæc de eo refert. Post multos deinde Reges regnum Suevorum suscepit Theudemirus, qui fidem Catholicam adeptus, Arriana impietatis errore destructo, Suevos unitati fidei reddidit. Hujus temporibus Martinus, Monasterii Dumiensis Episcopus, fcopus, fide & sanctitate claruit; cujus studio & pax Ecclesia reddita est, & multa monasteria condita. Ipsius quoque Dumiensis Monasterii conditor dicitur, vid. Concil. Toletani. X decret. 3. cujus fuit primum Abbas, & ex Abbate factus est Episcopus Braccarensis; in quo sacerdotio eum plus minus triginta annis exegisse, & plenum virtutibus ad Dominum migrasse dicit Gregor. Turon. cit. loc. & Aimoinus Monach. de gestis Francor. lib. 3. c. 38. alias 39. Ea tempestate, inquit, B. Martinus Gallicensis migravit ad Dominum. Hic Pannonia oriundus loca in Oriente circumiens, abunde se illis litteris imbuit, & per Galliciam revertens, in basilica, quæ prima apud Hispanos in honore S. Martini dedicata est, Pontifex ordinatus, triginta in hoc officio explevit annos. Anno 7. Childeberti Regis, qui fuit 21. Chilperici atque Guntranni, &c.
