Testamenti ejus fit mentio in Concilii Toletani X. decret. 3. Scripta ejus recenset Isidorus, loc. cit. à quo omissa supplet Miræus in Bibliotheca Ecclesiast. Hæc recenset Isidorus. Copiosa præcepta piæ institutionis composuit. Cujus quidem ego (ipse) legi librum de Differentiis quatuor virtutum, & aliud volumen Epistolarum, in quibus hortatur vitæ emendationem, & conversationem fidei, orationis in-stantiam, eleemosynarum distributionem, & su-per per omnia cultum virtutum omnium, & pietatem. Floruit regnante Theodemiro Rege Suevorum, temporibus illis, quibus Justinianus in Republica, & Athanagildus in Hispaniis impe-rium tenuerunt. Eadem fere ad verbum habet Honorius Augustodun. de luminaribus Ecclesiæ, sive de Scriptoribus Ecclesiast. lib. 3. cap. 4. Quæ hisce supplet Miræus. Martinus Dumiensis in Galæcia monasterii primum Abbas & conditor, postea Bracarensis in Lusitania Episcopus anno 572. floruit, ÆRA 598. Bracarensi synodo primæ, & ÆRA 610. secundæ præfuit. Baronius existimat ipsum anno 573. obiisse. Scripsit librum de quatuor virtutibus, falso Senecæ a nonnullis attributum, sive Formulam honestæ vitæ, quæ tomo VI. Bibliothecæ Patrum extat. Isidorus huic libro dat titulum de quatuor virtutum Cardinalium differentia. Idem Collectionem Canonum ex Græcis synodis adornavit, quæ in Tomis Conciliorum legitur. In appendice ad vitas Patrum typis Plantinianis 1628. editas, extant sententiæ ÆGYPTIORUM Patrum ab homine Graeco anonymo collectæ, & à Martino Dumiensi in Latinum translatæ. Fuit autem natione Pannonius, ut ex ejus epitaphio constat. Interrogationes illæ, quarum in fine meminit Miræus, translatæ sunt per manum Paschasii Diaconi. ut refert Sigebertus, de Scriptor. Eccles. cap. 117. Martinus, inquit, Episcopus transtulit transstulit per manum Paschasii Diaconi interrogationes & responsiones plurimas sanctorum Ægyptiorum Patrum, in Dumiensi Monasterio. Idem librum de quatuor virtutibus, inscriptum docet; Honestæ vitæ formulam. cap. 19. de iisd. script. Eccles. Ad nostrum institutum tantum pertinet Collectio Canonum ejus,quæ facta est eodem fere tempore, quo Dionysius Exiguus Romæ suam Collectionem & versionem;& in Africa & quidem Carthagini suam Digestionem adornaret Ferrandus: utrique tamen posterior est. Nam Ferrandus, ut supra notatum ex Facundo Hermianensi anno 551. jam vita excesserat, & Dionysius Exiguus in principio Iustinianæi Imperii, seculi sexti anno trigesimo præter propter suam versionem adornavit, aut etiam citius adhuc, ut supra ex eo ostendimus, quod decretales, quæ post versionem canonum sunt collectæ, Iuliano Presbytero sint inscriptæ, vid. num: marg. 76. Martinus autem noster, si triginta annis in Hispania, ut supra probatum, exegit, & anno 573. secundum Baronium, vel 580. secundum Dalæum vita excessit, anno 43. vel 50. in Hispaniam venit. Propius ad eam accedit συναγωγὴ κανόνων Ioh. Scholastici, quæ facta ante annum 564. ut supra quoque observavimus. Collectionem suam fecit cit eandem ob causam, ob quam Diony- sius Exiguus suam versionem adornavit, nempe, ob antiquæ versionis incommoditatem; quod ille in Præfatione, quam suæ collectioni præmisit satis innuit. Canones, inquit, qui in partibus Orientis ab antiquis Patribus constituti sunt, Græco prius sermone conscripti sunt; postea autem succedenti tempore in Latinam linguam translati sunt. Et quia difficile est, ut simplicius aliquid ex alia lingua transferatur in aliam; simulque & illud accidit, ut in tantis temporibus scriptores, aut non intelligentes, aut dormitantes multa prætermittant, & propterea in ipsis canonibus aliqua simplicioribus videantur obscura. Ideo visum est ut cum omni diligentia, & ea quæ per translationes obscurius dicta sunt, & ea quæ per scriptores sunt imminuta, simplicius & emendatius restaurarem. Quod tamen non satis accurate observavit aut præstitit. Pleraque quidem ex Græco vertit, aliqua tamen immiscuit ex conciliis Occidentalibus, Africanis, item Hispanicis, veluti Toletano I. & Bracarensibus, quia ibidem erat antistes. Aliquando etiam non ita Latina facta sunt, ut habentur in Græcis, sed ex duobus aut tribus capitibus diversorum conciliorum unum ille facit caput, quod observat Anton. Augustinus. in judicio de Collectoribus canonum, quod extat, part.2. Epit.jur. Pontif. Opus ejus bipartitum est, & aliqua arte & methodo pollet. Prima pars continet canones, qui de personis, rebus & ritibus Ecclesiasticis agunt, altera res ad Laicos, ut vocant, pertinentes, complectitur. Quod & ipse in statim laudata Praefat. indicat. Id primum, inquit, observans, ut illa quae ad Episcopos vel universum Clerum pertinent, una in parte conscripta sint: similiter & quae ad Laicos pertinent, simul sint adunata, ut de quo capitulo scire aliquis voluerit, possit celerius invenire. Hujus collectionis duae sunt editiones, una vulgaris & vetus, quam omnes conciliorum collectiones exhibent; Altera recens, quam ex antiquis Manuscriptis dicit se edidisse Garsias à Loaysa in collectione conciliorum Hispaniae. Veterem illam & vulgarem exhibuere Editores saepius laudatae Bibliotheca juris Canonici veteris, Voellius & Justellus Filius in appendice tomi I. ita tamen ut novum opus, ut illi praefantur, jure censeri ac dici mereatur, ut quae singulari cura ab eruditissimo Viro Johanne Doviatio sacrorum Canonum interprete Regio cum caeteris editionibus & libris Manu exaratis collata sit, annotatis, ad marginem versionibus tum variis lectionibus, tum conciliis ex quibus, tanquam fontibus suos Martinus canones depromsit. In quo
units.tr: The order of the story now requires us to bring Martin, first abbot of the monastery of Dume and afterwards bishop of Braga, onto the stage. He was by birth a Pannonian, according to Gregor. Turonensis, Hist. Franc. lib. 5. c. 38. So Garsias Loaysa is wrong, Praefat. ad Mart. Bracar. capit. in collect. concil. Hispan., when he says two or three times that Martin was a Greek. Lest you think he meant this of knowledge of the Greek language, he plainly calls him "a Greek man." Here is his eulogy: Martin, bishop of Braga, published the chapters of the Greek synods that are cited by Gratian in the chapter "propter Ecclesiasticas," dist. 18. He was a Greek, and he rendered these Greek chapters into Latin for the good of the churches of Spain. He added some things from the Latin and left out some things from the Greek, as is found in the chapter "propter Ecclesiasticas," which is taken from the council of Antioch, can. 20. This Greek man also set down some things from the Toledan councils, and he adapted the Greek rites to the customs of our people wisely and piously. Having set out from his homeland for the East, he drank in good letters and learning there, and made such progress in them that he equalled or surpassed the most learned men of his time. From the East he crossed into Galicia, and there, when the Suevi had been turned from the Arian impiety, he established a rule of faith and of holy religion. He confirmed churches and founded monasteries; see Isidor. Hispal. de Viris Illustr. cap. 22., alias 35. In his Historia sive Chronica Gothorum Isidore also reports this about him: After many kings, Theudemir received the kingdom of the Suevi. Having embraced the Catholic faith and destroyed the error of Arian impiety, he restored the Suevi to unity of faith. In his time Martin, bishop of the monastery of Dume, shone forth in faith and holiness; through his zeal peace was restored to the Church, and many monasteries were founded. He is also said to be the founder of the monastery of Dume; see Concil. Toletani X, decret. 3. He was its first abbot, and from abbot he was made bishop of Braga. Gregory of Tours, in the place cited, and Aimoin the monk, de gestis Francorum lib. 3. c. 38., alias 39., say that he spent about thirty years in that office and, full of virtues, departed to the Lord. Aimoin says: At that time the blessed Martin of Galicia departed to the Lord. Born in Pannonia, he wandered through the regions of the East, and imbued himself abundantly with those letters; returning through Galicia, he was ordained bishop in the basilica which was the first among the Spaniards dedicated in honour of St Martin. He spent thirty years in this office. In the seventh year of King Childebert, who was the twenty-first after Chilperic and Guntram, etc. Mention of his will is made in Concil. Toletani X, decret. 3. Isidore, in the place cited, lists his writings, and Miraeus in the Bibliotheca Ecclesiastica supplies what Isidore omitted. Isidore lists them thus: He composed copious precepts of pious instruction. I myself have read his book on the differences of the four virtues, and another volume of letters, in which he urges the amendment of life, the conversation of faith, instancy in prayer, the distribution of alms, and above all the cultivation of all the virtues and piety. He flourished in the reign of Theudemir, king of the Suevi, in the times when Justinian held power in the commonwealth and Athanagild in Spain. Honorius of Autun, de luminaribus Ecclesiae, sive de Scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis lib. 3. cap. 4., has almost the same words. Miraeus supplements these: Martin of Dume, first abbot and founder of the monastery in Galicia, afterwards bishop of Braga in Lusitania, flourished in the year 572, era 598, and presided over the first Synod of Braga and in the year 610, era, the second. Baronius thinks he died in the year 573. He wrote a book on the four virtues, wrongly attributed to Seneca by some, or the Formula of an Honourable Life, which is found in volume VI of the Bibliotheca Patrum. Isidore gives this book the title On the Difference of the Four Cardinal Virtues. He also compiled a collection of canons from the Greek synods, which is read in the volumes of the Councils. In the appendix to the Lives of the Fathers, printed by the Plantin press in 1628, there are extant sayings of the Egyptian Fathers collected by an anonymous Greek and translated into Latin by Martin of Dume. He was a Pannonian by birth, as is clear from his epitaph. Those questions which Miraeus mentions at the end were translated by the hand of Paschasius the deacon, as Sigebert reports, de Scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis cap. 117. Martin, the bishop, translated through the hand of the deacon Paschasius many questions and answers of the holy Egyptian Fathers, in the monastery of Dume. The same Sigebert teaches that the book is entitled Formula of an Honourable Life, cap. 19. de iisdem Scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis. For our present purpose only his Collection of Canons is relevant. It was made at about the same time as Dionysius Exiguus was preparing his collection and translation at Rome, and as Ferrandus was drawing up his digest at Carthage in Africa. Yet Martin's is later than both. For Ferrandus, as noted above from Facundus of Hermiane, had already died in the year 551, and Dionysius Exiguus prepared his translation at the beginning of the reign of Justinian, about the thirtieth year of the sixth century, or even earlier, as we have shown above from the fact that the decretals, which were collected after the translation of the canons, are addressed to the presbyter Julian; see num. marg. 76. Our Martin, however, if he spent thirty years in Spain, as we have shown above, and died in the year 573 according to Baronius, or 580 according to Dalaeus, came to Spain in the year 43 or 50. Nearer to him is the collection of canons [συναγωγὴ κανόνων] of John Scholasticus, which was made before the year 564, as we also observed above. Martin made his collection for the same reason for which Dionysius Exiguus made his translation, namely the inadequacy of the old translation, which Dionysius sufficiently hints at in the preface he prefixed to his collection: The canons which were laid down in the East by the ancient Fathers were first written in the Greek language, and afterwards in later times were translated into Latin. And because it is difficult for anything to be translated from one language into another with perfect simplicity, and because it also happens that in such long periods writers, either not understanding or nodding, omit many things, some things in the canons themselves seem obscure to the simpler sort. Therefore it seemed good to me to restore, with all diligence, both what has been said more obscurely through translations and what has been diminished through the copyists, in a simpler and more correct form. Yet he did not observe or achieve this with sufficient accuracy. He translated most of his material from the Greek, but he mixed in some things from Western councils, African councils, and likewise Spanish ones, such as the first Council of Toledo and the Councils of Braga, since he was bishop there. Sometimes the chapters were not rendered as they stand in the Greek, but he made one chapter out of two or three chapters of different councils; Anton Augustinus observes this in his judgement on the Collectors of Canons, which is extant in part 2 of the Epitome iuris pontificii. His work is in two parts and is distinguished by a certain skill and method. The first part contains the canons which deal with persons, things and ecclesiastical rites; the second embraces matters pertaining to the laity, as they are called. He himself indicates this in the preface already cited: I observed this first, that those things which pertain to the bishops or to the whole clergy should be written in one part; likewise those which pertain to the laity should be gathered together, so that whoever wishes to know about a given chapter may find it more quickly. There are two editions of this collection: one common and old, which all collections of councils exhibit; and another recent one, which Garsias de Loaysa says he published from ancient manuscripts in his collection of the councils of Spain. The older and common edition was exhibited by the editors of the often cited Bibliotheca iuris canonici veteris, Voellus and Justellus the son, in appendix to volume I. Yet the work deserves to be regarded and called a new work, as they state in their preface, because it was collated with the other editions and with manuscript books by the most learned man John Doviatius, royal interpreter of the sacred canons, with notes in the margin giving both variant readings and the councils from which Martin drew his canons, as from their sources. On this point the reader must be warned not to trust Doviatius, or whoever added the sources in the edition of Voellus and Justellus, when in indicating the sources they also mention the Pseudo-apostolic canons; Martin never included these in his Collection, nor does he mention them.

units.la: 278. Editionum diversitas. quo id monendus es lector, ne credas Doviatio, aut ei, qui in editione Voelli & Justelli fontes adjecit, quando in indicandis fontibus etiam memorat canones Pseudapostolicos; hos nunquam in suam Collectionem retulit, nec eorum meminit, neque etiam eo tempore quo is in Oriente fuit, ante nimirum seculi quinti medium ficti aut Apostolis suppositi fuerunt, ut patet ex iis quae late supra disputata sunt. Faciunt huc quae refert Doctiss: Dalaeus. in Pseudepig. Apostolic. lib. 3. cap. 19. pag. 653. fine. Itaque, inquit, non Latinis magis, quam Graecis, quarto seculo, quintoque jam ad annum 51. adulto cogniti erant isti Apostolorum canones. Ac tametsi sexto ineunte seculo quinquaginta Dionysiaci jam extarent, ne tum quidem inter regulas Ecclesiasticas ab omnibus admissi sunt. Nam neque iis Ferrandus Ecclesiae Carthaginensis Diaconus locum ullum in Breviario canonum dedit, quod circa sexti seculi principia concinnavit, atque publicavit; neque qui in Hispania a. D. 580. obiit, Martinus Bracarensis, eos vel memoravit, vel usurpavit, aut inseruit in sua illa Graecorum Canonum interpretatione, quam Collectionis Orientalium Canonum nomine ad Nitigesium a. D. 572. missam edidit. Quod & observavit & fatetur Antonius Augustinus, statim adducendus. Illud hic non negligendum
units.tr: 278. Diversity of editions. Here the reader must be warned not to believe Doviatius, or whoever added the sources to the edition of Voellus and Justellus, when in indicating sources he also mentions the Pseudo-Apostolic canons. Doviatius never included these in his Collection, nor did he mention them, not even at the time when he was in the East. Clearly they were invented, or foisted upon the Apostles, before the middle of the fifth century, as is evident from what has been argued at length above. Relevant here is what the very learned Dalaeus reports: in Pseudepigr. Apostol. bk. 3, ch. 19, p. 653, near the end. Therefore, he says, these canons of the Apostles were known to the Latins no more than to the Greeks in the fourth century, and even by the fifth century they had not yet grown to the age of fifty-one. And although fifty Dionysian canons were already extant at the beginning of the sixth century, they were still not admitted by all among the ecclesiastical rules. For Ferrandus, deacon of the Church of Carthage, gave them no place at all in his Breviary of canons, which he put together and published around the beginning of the sixth century; nor did Martin of Braga, who died in Spain in the year of our Lord 580, either mention them, use them, or insert them in that translation of Greek canons which he sent to Nitigisius in the year of our Lord 572 under the title of a Collection of Eastern Canons. Antonius Augustinus also observed and admitted this, as will be shown shortly. This point should not be neglected here.

units.la: 179. Canones Apostolici Martino Ignoti, error Doviatii cavendus. gligendum sed monendum, quod ante Antonii Democharis editionem Decreti Gratiani, Collectio hæc Martini Bracharensis, citata sit, quasi essent capitula Martini Papæ Romani, qui tamen multis annis posterior est Martino nostro. Hosce errores Gratiani correxit in sua editione Democharesque & Contius, qui in margine quando Gratianus scribit: Ex concilio Martini Papæ, notant: Martini Bracharensis nomen, ex capitulis Græcarum synodorum. Latissime hac de re agit Ant. Augustinus noster, Dialogorum lib. I. Dialog. X. XI. & XII. quorum primus sic incipit, & hæc quæ potissimum ad rem præsentem faciunt, habet. Credo vos non ignorare, si Gratiani librum ab Ant. Demochare, vel ab Ant. Contio editum legistis: in omnibus fere capitibus, quæ habent hanc inscriptionem: Ex concilio Martini Papæ: additum esse in margine Martini Bracarensis nomen, ex capitulis Græcarum synodorum. Quod à Democharc factum est, sumitur ex libris conciliorum, in quibus post secundum Bracarense concilium, illa capita sunt Martini Episcopi, qui se ex Orientis conciliis ea sumere dicit, ofsensus varia interpretatione eorum. Unde autem singula capita sumantur, non adscripsit, quod sciam? sed ego ea conferens cum Græcis inveni, paucis exceptis, quæ non in Græcis, sed in Latinis conciliis reperta sunt. Concilium Martini Papæ insigne fuit contra Monothelitas habitum ante sextam synodum, in quo non hi canones editi fuerunt, neque confirmati. Tamen nescio quomodo à collectoribus referri solent, ut Martini Papæ in synodo. Sic fit, ut à Gratiano Martini Papæ appellentur, & cum Græcis conjungantur quasi diversi. Exemplum sumamus à concilio Nicæno; nam canones Apostolorum prætermitos ab eo esse video. Idem observavit in secunda parte Epitom. juris Pontificii Ant. Augustt. Baronius ad ann. 572. num. 14. postquam ipsam Martini Præfationem recitasset, subjungit. Extat ipsa collectio canonibus octoginta quinque locupletata. Intelligit, nisi fallor, Canones Apostolicos, qui sunt additi collectioni Martini, ab ipso autem, ut dictum, neglecti.
units.tr: 179. The Apostolic canons attributed to Martin the Unknown; the error of Doviatius is to be avoided. It should not be neglected here, but it must be pointed out, that before the edition of Decretum Gratiani by Antonius Demochares, this Collection of Martin of Braga was cited as though its chapters were those of Martin, Pope of Rome, who nonetheless lived many years after our Martin. Demochares and Contius corrected these errors of Gratian in their edition; where Gratian writes in the margin: From the Council of Pope Martin, they note: the name of Martin of Braga, from the chapters of Greek synods. Our Antonius Augustinus treats this matter at length in Dialogues, book 1, Dialogues 10, 11 and 12, the first of which begins thus and contains what bears most directly on the present subject. I believe you are not unaware, if you have read Gratian's book as edited by Antonius Demochares or by Antonius Contius, that in almost all the chapters bearing the heading From the Council of Pope Martin, the name of Martin of Braga has been added in the margin, taken from the chapters of Greek synods. What Demochares did comes from the books of councils, in which, after the second Council of Braga, those chapters are by Martin, bishop, who says he took them from the councils of the East, though they differ in various renderings. Where each chapter is taken from, he did not record, as far as I know; but comparing them with the Greek texts I found them, with a few exceptions, not in the Greek councils but in Latin ones. The Council of Pope Martin was a famous council held against the Monothelites before the sixth synod, and these canons were neither issued nor confirmed in it. Yet somehow the compilers are accustomed to report them as of Pope Martin in synod. Thus it happens that Gratian calls them the canons of Pope Martin, and joins them with the Greeks as if they were a different body. Let us take an example from the Council of Nicaea; for I see that the canons of the Apostles were passed over by it. The same point was noted by Antonius Augustinus in the second part of the Epitome of Pontifical Law, and by Baronius at the year 572, number 14, who, after reciting Martin's own preface, adds: The collection itself is enriched with eighty-five canons. He means, unless I am mistaken, the Apostolic canons which were added to Martin's collection, but which, as has been said, he himself neglected.

units.la: Nunc ad Cresconium transeamus, ejusque Collectionem. Fuit ille Episcopus Africanus, Eruditissimis Viris annumeratus ætate Leontii Imperatoris. Carmine panxit historiam eorum quæ Johannes Patricius gessit in Africa, cujus libri summam ex Cedreno cognoscere possumus; qui refert, quod, cum Arabes tertio Leontii anno (is erat Christi 696.) Africam occupassent, Leontius Imperator eo miserit Joannem Patricium Virum Strenuum, qui hostes suderit, castraque eorum in Africa ceperit universa. Vid. Vossium de Histor. Latin. lib. 3. cap. 3. quem miror Cresconium neglexisse in Poëtarum Latinorum historia. Eadem testatur inscriptio Codicis MSti Bibliothecæ Vaticanæ, quam adducit Baron. ad Ann. 527. num. 76: quæ est hæc. Concordia Canonum à Cresconio Africano Episcopo digesta, sub capitibus trecentis. Iste bella & victorias, quas Johannes Patricius apud Africam de Saracenis gessit, hexametris versibus descripsit. In jure Canonico duplex ejus fertur opus, vel ut alii volunt, unius operis duæ partes. Una, quæ Canonum Breviarium vocatur. Cujus epigraphe est hæc in editione Parisiensi quæ Codici Ecclesiæ Romanæ est annexa, & in Bibliotheca Juris Canonici Veteris.
units.tr: Now let us turn to Cresconius and his Collection. He was an African bishop, numbered among the most learned men in the age of the emperor Leontius. He wrote in verse a history of what John the Patrician did in Africa, a summary of whose book we can learn from Cedrenus. Cedrenus reports that when the Arabs occupied Africa in the third year of Leontius (which is the year of Christ 696), the emperor Leontius sent thither John the Patrician, a vigorous man, who routed the enemy and captured all their camps in Africa. See Vossius On Latin Historians, bk. 3, ch. 3, whom I am surprised Cresconius neglected in his History of Latin Poets. The same is attested by the inscription of a manuscript codex of the Vatican Library, which Baronius cites at the year 527, number 76, and which reads thus: A Concord of Canons digested by Cresconius, bishop of Africa, under three hundred headings. He described in hexameter verses the wars and victories which John the Patrician waged against the Saracens in Africa. In canon law his work is said to be twofold, or, as some would have it, two parts of one work. One is called the Breviary of Canons. Its title is this, in the Paris edition which is appended to the Codex of the Roman Church, and in the Bibliotheca Juris Canonici Veteris:

units.la: CRESCONII. EPISCOPI. AFRICANI. BRE- VIARIUM. CANONICUM. HIC. HABETUR. CONCORDIA. CANONUM. CONCILIORUM. INFRASCRIPTORUM. ET. PRÆSULUM. RO- MANORUM. ID. EST. CANONUM. APOSTO- LORUM. NICÆNORUM. NOVÆCÆSARIEN- SIUM. GANGRENSIUM. ANTIOCHENSIUM. LAODICENSIUM. CALCHEDONENSIUM. SARDICENSIUM. CARTHAGINENSIUM. ITEM. PRÆSULUM. SIRICII. INNOCENTII.
units.tr: The Canonical Breviary of Bishop Cresconius of Africa, containing the concord of the canons of the councils listed below and of the Roman pontiffs, that is, of the canons of the Apostles, the Nicene, Neocaesarean, Gangra, Antioch, Laodicea, Chalcedon, Sardica and Carthage councils, and likewise of the pontiffs Siricius, Innocent,

units.la: TII. ZOSIMI. CELESTINI. LEONIS. ET GELASII.
units.tr: Zosimus, Celestine, Leo and Gelasius.

units.la: In hoc opere disciplinam Ecclesiasticam ad exemplum Fulgentii Ferrandi, trecentis titulis vel summulis inclusit, citatis tantum canonibus aut Pontificum decretis, non recitatis verbis.Quem modum supra Breviarium Canonum vocari diximus. Ipse Cresconius, in Præfatione sua, Fulgentii opus vocat Breviatum. Alterum opus ejus, seu altera pars operis eodem ordine, iisdem numeris & titulis decurrit usque ad trecentesimum, & iidem canones conciliorum, & decreta Pontificum citantur non tantum, sed δἰχ̀ πλατέων etiam recitantur. Quod opus in Manuscriptis inscribitur Concordia Canonum, vel Liber Canonum. Ita docti hactenus censuerunt, & opus vel opera Cresconii distinxerunt: mihi ruminanti accuratius, suspicio oritur Cresconium tantum scripsisse posterius opus, in quo canones integri recensentur; Idque ex eo conjicio, quod ille in Fulgentii Breviario taxet, quod illud magis ad recolligendam memoriam sit scriptum, quam ad instructionem & doctrinam imperitorum: quoniam citabantur quidem capitula & decreta ex variis libris, quibus multi carebant, aut in quibus citata quærere nec invenire poterant. Huic difficultati occurrere volens Cresco-
units.tr: In this work, following the example of Fulgentius Ferrandus, he arranged the church discipline under three hundred titles or short summaries, citing only the canons or the decrees of the pontiffs without reciting their words. We said above that this method is called the Breviarium Canonum. Cresconius himself, in his Preface, calls the work of Fulgentius a Breviatum. His other work, or the second part of the same work, runs in the same order, with the same numbers and titles, up to the three hundredth title. In it the canons of the councils and the decrees of the pontiffs are not only cited but also quoted in full [δἰχ̀ πλατέων]. In manuscripts this work is entitled the Concordance of Canons, or the Book of Canons. Learned men have hitherto judged so and distinguished the work or works of Cresconius in this way. But on closer reflection I suspect that Cresconius wrote only the later work, in which the canons are set out in full. I infer this from the fact that, in his criticism of Fulgentius's Breviary, he says that it was written more to jog the memory than to instruct and teach the unlearned, since the chapters and decrees were cited from various books, which many people lacked, or, when they were cited, readers could not look them up and find them. Wishing to meet this difficulty, Cresco-

units.la: {a} 184. Disquisitio de opere Cresconii accuratior. Cresconius, non tantum, quemadmodum Ferrandus citavit concordes canones, verum etiam ipsa canonum verba subjecit. Res magis aperta fiet ex ipsius Cresconii verbis, quae ex praefatione ad Liberinum, vel ut alii libri habent Liberium Pontificem, Breviario praefixa (quam tamen secundum dicta Concordia vel Libro canonum praemitti potius debere censemus) haec sunt. Caelesti auxilio praemanitus, obsequi malui imperatis, vestrisque votis, Deo favente, libentissime subservire, illa maxime invitatus ex parte, quod antefatus venerabilis Vir (Ferrandus) ad conversationem memoriae eorum hoc effecisse noscitur Breviatum, quia illa ipsa jam bene cognita perceperant, quo per eum cum voluerint, quae cupiunt recordentur; Indoctorum vero, quorum est maxima multitudo, in eodem opere studium probatur, ut ita dixerim, sequestrasse, dum eos ad inquisitionem earum rerum praemisit, quae nec ab omnibus reperiuntur, nec repertae sine fastidio perleguntur. Nulli siquidem dubium est, quam molestissime perferat Lector, dum avidius cujusque rei cognitionem, expectat, & ad librum praemittitur, quem aut forte non legit, aut ubi reperiat non novit. Quamobrem antefati Viri laude praelata, necessarium duxi profectui subserviens parvulorum, juxta vestrum imperium, cuncta ecclesiastica, ut dictum est, constituta, constituta, quæ ad nostram notitiam pervenerunt, in hoc opere sub titulorum serie prænotare; & ea condiscere valentibus, & volentibus dubitationis ambagem auferre; ut eorumplena instructio non ex difficultate scriptoris, sedex desidia jam dependeat Lectoris. Ex quibusapparet illum voluisse aliquid corrigere, quod Ferrandus neglexerat, nempe, ne tantum doctis, sed insuper quoque indoctis & rudibus novam scriberet suam collectionem: deinde quoque succurrere eis qui sub certistitulis, tantum nude citatos canones velnon poterant ob defectum librorum, & investigandi imperitiam, aut nolebant ob desidiam quandam requirere & investigare; huic fini observata methodo Fulg. Ferrandi,conquisivit ex variis libris integros ipsos ca-nones. Sed quid tum fiet Breviario? Potestid esse decerptum ab alio, cui Cresconiiopus prolixum nimis, vel qui nudam no-titiam tantum memoriæ causa habere voluit. Quod & in aliis videmus factum. Exemplum potest præbere syllabus & tituliilli canonum Dionysii Exigui, qui seorsimsunt editi, & ab opere seu versione & collectione Dionysii avulsi; quod præter aliademonstrat satis editio Parisiensis Codiciscanonum Ecclesiæ Romanæ, in cujus finecum Præfatione Dionysii Exigui, subjiciuntur tantum lemmata & tituli canonum; ex quo tamen nemo dixerit duo opera Dionysium edidisse, unum quod titulos canonum, alterum quod ipsos canones contineret. Si quis tamen aliter verba Cresconii supra adducta interpretari, & utrumque opus Cresconio adscribere velit, non multum repugnabo. Est haec tantum conjectura nostra; non enim inficias imus, posse etiam haec: Necessarium duxi, subservientes profectui parvulorum, cuncta Ecclesiastica constituta in hoc opere sub titulorum serie praenotare, & ea condiscere valentibus & volentibus dubitationis ambagem auferre. &c. Ad utrumque opus applicari, ita ut praenotare illud denotet Breviarium Canonum, ad colligendam tantum memoriam juxta exemplum Ferrandi factum; caetera Concordiam Canonum indicent, qua condiscere valentibus & volentibus dubitationis ambagem voluit auferre, ut eorum plena instructio non ex difficultate scriptoris, sed ex desidia jam dependeat lectoris. Quae supra de convenientia & differentia, item de confusione Ferrandi & Crescònii, & tandem de erroribus Baronii dicta sunt, non opus est hic repetere, videantur numeri marginales 160. 161. Illud monendum adhuc, in Concordia Canonum, seu Libro Canonum Cresconii initium non esse ipsius Crescconii, tonii, sed ab aliena manu profectum & additum ipsi libro, post Cresconii scriptionem. Videtur autem præmissum titulo primo, de ordinatione Episcopi, quia cum isto titulo affinitatem habet. Monuerunt hoc quoque editores Bibliothecæ juris Canonici veteris in margine. Incipit illud adsumentum, ob res quas continet non quidem contemnendum; Qui Episcopus ordinandus est: exit: sed Patrum diffinitionibus acquiescat. Solet addi Cresconii Breviarium, ob materiæ adfinitatem, Ferrandi Breviario, cujus variæ editiones supra memoratæ sunt. vid. num. marg. 159. commendanda imprimis, ea quæ est in Bibliotheca juris Canonici veteris, & ea quam Petrus Franciscus Chifletius Jesuita Divione anno 1649. cum suis notis emisit. Concordiam vero canonum, vel Librum canonum Cresconii anno hujus seculi LXI. in publicam lucem Editores sæpius laudati Bibliothecæ juris Canonici veteris, in appendice tomi primi, ex Manuscripto antiquo Bibliothecæ Collegii Claromontani, beneficio Caroli Labbæi Jesuitæ, primùm protulerunt, & contulerunt cum Manuscripto Bibliothecæ Thuanæ, qui Cresconii quidem nomen præferebat; sed multis canonibus & decretis interpolatus, & diversa methodo abs vero & genuino Cresconii foetu conscriptus erat. Illud etiam non prætereundum, Cresconium primum Romanorum Pontificum Epistolas, inter Canones retulisse, & eas eo canonizasse, ut ita loquar, seu iis auctoritatem canonicam addidisse, quæ antea non majoris fuerunt valoris, quam aliorum Episcoporum Responsa; Decretales hæ Epistolæ à consulendo habent originem, quemadmodum enim in civilibus Imperatores Sacratissimi, ita in spiritualibus & sacris consulebantur Episcopi. Inter quos cum emineret Romanus, is quoque præ aliis consultus sæpius, ejusque responsa majorem præ cæteris auctoritatem acquisiverunt, & diligentius etiam adservata sunt; reliquorum vero Episcoporum non tanti æstimata, perierunt pleraque. Hæc causa Cresconium forte movit, quare Decretalibus Romanorum Pontificum, tantam detulerit auctoritatem, ut inter canones conciliorum ausus sit eos locare. Verum quidem est, quod Dionysius Exiguus primus cœperit colligere Decretales, orsus à Syricio; Sed ille tantam iis auctoritatem non detulit, ut inter canones recensuerit; verum speciali volumine vel opere hanc collectionem, ut supra memoratum, digessit, quod postea incuria, vel potius quia ejusdem auctoris, cum Codice canonum ex conciliis versorum coaluit, aut cum eo editum est; non tamen in eum finem, ut ejusdem cum canonibus conciliorum auctoritatis essent. Hoc forte Cresconium, qui non bene Canonum & Decretalium differentiam distinguebat se duxit; ut, cum Codicem Dionysii, qui tantum ordinem temporis, tam in canonibus quam in decretalibus sectabatur, in concordiam canonicam redigere vellet, utramque Dionysii collectionem sine distinctione inexcusabili audacia vel imprudentia digesserit. Ad hoc exemplu postea in Orientali Ecclesia coeperunt valere, adservari & colligi responsa Patriarchalia, uti postea patebit ex codice Ecclesiae Orientalis. Haec hic obiter monenda fuerunt; de Decretalibus vero & eorumque collectoribus postea expresso tractabimus.
units.tr: {a} 184. A more exact inquiry into the work of Cresconius. Cresconius did not merely cite the agreeing canons as Ferrandus did; he also added the very words of the canons. The matter will become clearer from Cresconius's own words, which are found in the preface to Liberinus, or, as other books have it, to Pope Liberius, prefixed to the Breviary (which, however, we judge should rather be placed before the said Concordance or Book of Canons). They are these: Forewarned by heavenly help, I preferred to obey your commands, and, with God's favour, most willingly to serve your wishes. I was especially moved to this by the fact that the aforesaid venerable man (Ferrandus) is known to have made the Breviary for the refreshing of their memory, since they had already well understood those very things, so that through it they might recall whatever they wished, when they wished. But for the unlearned, who form the greatest multitude, the work shows, so to speak, a concern to set them apart, in that it sends them ahead to search out those matters which are not found by all, and which, when found, are not read through without weariness. For there is no doubt how very grievously the reader bears it, when, eagerly expecting knowledge of each thing, he is sent to a book which perhaps he does not read, or does not know where to find. Therefore, the aforesaid man being duly praised, I thought it necessary, serving the progress of little ones according to your command, to set down in this work, under the sequence of titles, all the ecclesiastical constitutions, as has been said, which have come to our notice; and to take away the winding doubt from those who are able and willing to learn them, so that their full instruction may depend not on the difficulty of the writer but now on the sloth of the reader. From these words it appears that he wished to correct something that Ferrandus had neglected: namely, to write a new collection not only for the learned but also for the unlearned and rude. Then, too, he wished to help those who, under certain titles, could not look up the canons merely cited, because of a lack of books and their own inexperience in searching, or who were unwilling, out of a certain sloth, to seek and investigate them. To this end, keeping the method of Fulgentius Ferrandus, he gathered the whole canons themselves from various books. But what then becomes of the Breviary? It could have been extracted by someone else, for whom the work of Cresconius was too lengthy, or who wished to have only a bare notice of the matter for the sake of memory. We see this also happening in other cases. The syllabus and titles of the canons of Dionysius Exiguus can serve as an example, which were published separately and detached from Dionysius's work, version and collection. This is sufficiently shown, besides other things, by the Paris edition of the Codex of the canons of the Roman Church, at the end of which, along with the Preface of Dionysius Exiguus, only the lemmata and titles of the canons are added. Yet from this no one would say that Dionysius published two works, one containing the titles of the canons and the other the canons themselves. If anyone, however, wishes to interpret the words of Cresconius cited above otherwise, and to ascribe both works to Cresconius, I will not argue much. This is only our conjecture; for we do not deny that these words may also be read thus: I thought it necessary, serving the progress of little ones, to set down in this work, under the sequence of titles, all the ecclesiastical constitutions, and to take away the winding doubt from those who are able and willing to learn them, etc. These may be applied to both works, so that to set down beforehand denotes the Breviary of Canons, made only to gather the memory after the example of Ferrandus; and the rest indicates the Concordance of Canons, by which he wished to take away the winding doubt from those who are able and willing to learn, so that their full instruction may depend not on the difficulty of the writer but now on the sloth of the reader. What has been said above about the agreement and difference, likewise about the confusion of Ferrandus and Cresconius, and finally about the errors of Baronius, need not be repeated here; let the marginal numbers 160 and 161 be consulted. This still needs to be warned: in the Concordance of Canons, or Book of Canons of Cresconius, the beginning is not by Cresconius himself but was added to the book by another hand, after Cresconius wrote it. It seems to have been placed before the first title, on the ordination of a bishop, because it has affinity with that title. The editors of the Library of Old Canon Law also noted this in the margin. That addition begins: Who is to be ordained bishop? and ends: but let him submit to the definitions of the Fathers. The Breviary of Cresconius is usually appended to the Breviary of Ferrandus because of the affinity of subject matter; of the various editions of the latter we have mentioned above (see marginal number 159), the one in the Library of Old Canon Law is especially to be recommended, and also the one that the Jesuit Petrus Franciscus Chifletius published at Dijon in 1649 with his notes. The Concordance of Canons, or Book of Canons, of Cresconius was first brought to light in the year 1661 of this century, in the appendix to the first volume of the Library of Old Canon Law, by the editors just often praised, from an ancient manuscript of the library of the Clermont College, through the kindness of the Jesuit Charles Labbe; and they compared it with a manuscript of the Thuanus library, which bore the name of Cresconius but was interpolated with many canons and decrees and was composed by a method differing from the true and genuine offspring of Cresconius. Nor must it be passed over that Cresconius was the first to include the Epistles of the Roman pontiffs among the canons, and so, as I may put it, to canonize them, or add canonical authority to them, which before were of no greater value than the replies of other bishops. These Decretal Epistles take their origin from consulting; for just as in civil matters the most sacred emperors were consulted, so in spiritual and sacred matters the bishops were consulted. Among them, since the Roman bishop stood out, he was consulted more often than the others, and his replies acquired greater authority than the rest and were kept more carefully; but the replies of the other bishops, not being valued so highly, mostly perished. This perhaps moved Cresconius to grant such authority to the Decretals of the Roman pontiffs that he dared to place them among the canons of the councils. It is true that Dionysius Exiguus was the first to begin collecting the Decretals, starting from Siricius; but he did not give them such authority that he counted them among the canons. Rather he arranged this collection in a special volume or work, as mentioned above; later, through carelessness, or rather because it was by the same author, it grew together with the code of canons translated from the councils, or was published along with it. Yet this was not done to the end that they should have the same authority as the canons of the councils. Perhaps Cresconius, who did not distinguish well between the difference of canons and decretals, was led to this; so that, when he wished to reduce into a canonical concord the code of Dionysius, which followed only the order of time in both the canons and the decretals, he arranged both of Dionysius's collections without distinction, through inexcusable boldness or imprudence. After this example, in the Eastern Church later, the patriarchal responses began to be valued, kept and collected, as will later become clear from the Code of the Eastern Church. These things had to be noted here in passing; but we will treat of the Decretals and their collectors more fully later.

units.la: Cresconii Collectionem sequitur Codex Ecclesiae Orientalis; de quo jam aliquid dictum supra numero marg. 54. qui in concilio sexto Oecumenico Trullano anno 681. vel potius in quini-sextae synodi canone secundo confirmatus & approbatus est. Constat autem ex Codice Canonum Ecclesiae Universae, deinde additionibus iis, quas ipse Canon 2. refert, quem Latine subjicimus, ut eum editio Parisiensis, Gr. Latin. repraesentat. Hoc quoque huic sanctae Synodo pulcherrimè & honestissimè placuit, ut ab hoc nunc tempore deinceps ad animarum medelam, & perturbationum curationem firmi stabilesque maneant, qui à sanctis Patribus, qui nos præcesserunt, suscepti ac confirmati, atque adeo nobis etiam traditi sunt, sanctorum & gloriosorum Apostolorum nomine, LXXXV. canones. Quoniam autem in his canonibus nobis præceptum est, ut eorundem SS. Apostolorum per Clementem ordinationes susciperemus, quibus jam olim ab iis qui à fide aliena sentiunt, adulterina quædam & à pietate aliena introducta sunt, quæ divinorum nobis decretorum elegantem ac decoram speciem obscurarunt; has constitutiones ad Christianissimi gregis ædificationem ac securitatem conducibiliter rejecimus, hæreticæ falsitatis fœtus nequaquam immiscentes, & germanæ ac integræ Apostolorum doctrinæ inserentes. Obsignamus etiam reliquos omnes canones, qui à sanctis & beatis nostris Patribus expositi sunt, id est, à trecentis decem & octo sanctis ac divinis Patribus, qui Nicæa convenerunt: iisque qui Ancyræ, & iis etiam qui Neocæsareæ: similiter & qui Gangris: præterea & iis qui in Antiochia Syriæ, atque iis etiam qui in Laodicea Phrygiæ: præterea autem & CL. Patribus, qui in hac Dei cultrice & Imp. civitate convenerunt; & ducentis, qui in Ephesiorum Metropoli prius coacti sunt: & sexcentis triginta sanctis & beatis Patribus, qui Calchedone: similiter & iis qui Sardicæ, & qui qui Carthagine, & qui rursus in hac Dei cultrice & Imp. urbe convenerunt sub Nectario, qui Imperiali huic civitati praesidebat; & Theophilo, qui fuit Alexandriae Archiepiscopus. Quinetiam canones Dionysii, qui fuit Archiepiscopus magnae Alexandrinorum civitatis: & Petri, qui fuit Alexandriae Archiepiscopus & martyr: Gregorii Neocaesareae Episcopi, qui Θαυματουργὸς, id est, mirabilium operum effector, dictus est: Athanasii Alexandrini Archiepiscopi, Basilii Archiepiscopi Caesarea Cappadociae, Gregorii Episcopi Nyssae, Gregorii Theologi, Amphilochii Iconii, Timothei Archiepiscopi Alexandrini, Cyrilli ejusdem Alexandriae Archiepiscopi, & Gennadii, qui fuit Patriarcha hujus Dei cultricis & Imp. civitatis. Praeterea vero, & à Cypriano, qui Afrorum regionis fuit Archiepiscopus & martyr, & synodi quae sub eo fuit, emissum canonem, qui in praedictorum Praesulum locis, & solum secundum traditam eis consuetudinem, servatus est. Et nulli licere prius declaratos canones adulterare vel abolere, vel alios praeter prius hic propositos canones admittere, à quibusdam falsa adjecta inscriptione compositos, qui veritatem cauponari nati sunt. Si quis autem, quod praedictorum canonum aliquem innovare vel subvertere conetur, convictus fuerit, reus erit secundum eum canonem, ut ipse pronuntiat Canon, poenam luens, & per ipsum in eo,
units.tr: Following the Collection of Cresconius comes the Code of the Eastern Church, of which something has already been said above at marg. no. 54. It was confirmed and approved at the sixth Ecumenical Council, the Trullan council of 681, or rather in the second canon of the Quinisext Synod. It consists of the Code of Canons of the Universal Church, and then of the additions which that second canon itself records. We give them here in Latin, as the Paris edition of the Greek and Latin text presents them. It has also seemed most fitting and proper to this holy Synod that the eighty-five canons, which were received and confirmed by the holy Fathers who went before us and have been handed down to us in the name of the holy and glorious Apostles, should from now on remain firm and stable for the healing of souls and the cure of disturbances. Since in these canons we are commanded to receive the ordinances of the same holy Apostles through Clement, into which some adulterine things and things alien to piety were long ago introduced by those who think contrary to the faith, things which have obscured the elegant and seemly appearance of the divine decrees, we have profitably rejected these constitutions for the edification and safety of the most Christian flock, mixing in nothing of heretical falsehood and inserting them into the genuine and unimpaired teaching of the Apostles. We also seal all the remaining canons which were set forth by our holy and blessed Fathers, that is, by the three hundred and eighteen holy and divine Fathers who assembled at Nicaea; and those at Ancyra, and those at Neocaesarea; likewise those at Gangra; besides those at Antioch in Syria, and those also at Laodicea in Phrygia; moreover the 150 Fathers who assembled in this God-fearing and imperial city; and the two hundred who were first gathered in the metropolis of the Ephesians; and the six hundred and thirty holy and blessed Fathers at Chalcedon; likewise those at Sardica, and those who at Carthage, and who again assembled in this God-fearing and imperial city under Nectarius, who presided over this imperial city, and Theophilus, who was archbishop of Alexandria. Moreover the canons of Dionysius, who was archbishop of the great city of the Alexandrians; and of Peter, who was archbishop and martyr of Alexandria; of Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea, who was called Thaumaturgus [Θαυματουργὸς], that is, the worker of wonders; of Athanasius, archbishop of Alexandria; of Basil, archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia; of Gregory, bishop of Nyssa; of Gregory the Theologian; of Amphilochius of Iconium; of Timothy, archbishop of Alexandria; of Cyril, likewise archbishop of Alexandria; and of Gennadius, who was patriarch of this God-fearing and imperial city. Besides these, also the canon issued by Cyprian, who was archbishop and martyr of the region of Africa, and by the synod which met under him, which has been kept in the places of the aforesaid prelates, and only according to the custom handed down to them. And it is not lawful to corrupt or abolish canons previously declared, or to admit canons other than those proposed here, composed by certain persons with a false added inscription, who were born to peddle the truth. If anyone is convicted of trying to renew or overturn any of the aforesaid canons, he will be liable under that canon, as the canon itself pronounces, paying the penalty and being healed through it in the very matter in which he offended.

units.la: in quo offendit, medelam suscipiens. Ex quo canone patet, quod multa sint addita à Trullanis Patribus Codici Ecclesiæ Universæ, post Justinianum Imperatorem: nempe, canones Pseudapostolici, (quam temere supra abunde dictum) item canones Sardicenses, Africanorum conciliorum, de quibus supra, ubi de Codice Ecclesiæ Africanæ actum est. Deinde etiam Episcoporum & Patrum & Patriarcharum quorundam canones & Epistolæ, quia idem factum videbant ab Occidentalibus. Quæ additamenta ex editione Parisiensi anni 1620. cum Balsamonis commentariis in Codicem hunc Canonum Ecclesiæ Orientalis, ad intellectum allegati Nicæni canonis omnia subjicimus. Sunt autem isthæc: Beati Dionysii Archiepiscopi Alexandrini Epistola ad Basilidem de diversis capitibus, ad quæ per Epistolam Dionysius responsa dedit, quæ tanquam canones sunt admissa. Canones Beati Petri Archiepiscopi Alexandrini & Martyris, qui feruntur in sermone de pœnitentia. Epistola Canonica sancti Gregorii Archiepiscopi Neocæsariensis, qui Thaumaturgus dictus est, de iis qui in barbarorum incursione idolothyta comederant, & alia quædam peccata commiserant. Sancti Athanasii Archiepiscopi Alexandrini epistola stola ad Ammum monachum. Ejusdem ex xxxix. festiva epistola. Ejusdem epistola ad Ruffinianum. Sancti Patris nostri Basilii Archiepiscopi Cæsareæ Cappadociæ, ad Amphilochium Iconii Episcopum Epistola Canonica prima. Ad eundem Canonica epistola ii. Ejusdem alia epistola ad Amphilochium, de differentia ciborum. Ejusdem ad Diodorum, de eo qui duxit duas sorores in matrimonio. Ejusdem Epistola ad Gregorium Presbyterum, ut separetur à muliercula cum qua habitat. Ejusdem ad Chorepiscopos, ne sine ipso fiant ministri præter canones. Ejusdem ad Episcopos qui ei suberant, ne pecuniis ordinent. Ejusdem ex xxvii. capite, eorum quæ de sancto Spiritu ad beatum Amphilochium scripta sunt, & ejusdem ex xxix. cap. ejusdem operis excerpta. Epistola canonica sancti Gregorii Nysseni Episcopi ad sanctum Letoium Melitines Episcopum. Responsa canonica Timothei sanctissimi Alexandrini Episcopi, qui fuit unus ex cl. Patribus qui Constantinopoli convenerunt. Edictum Theophili Archiepiscopi Alexandrini, cum Theophania in die Dominico instarent. Ejusdem commonitorium quod accepit Ammon propter Lyco. Ejusdem expositio de iis qui dicuntur Cathari, Ejusd. Ep. ad Agathone Episcopum,
units.tr: in which he offended, receiving the remedy. From this canon it is clear that many things were added by the Trullan Fathers to the Code of the Universal Church after the Emperor Justinian, namely: the Pseudo-apostolic canons (which, as was said rashly and at length above); likewise the canons of Sardica and of the African councils, of which we spoke above, where the Code of the African Church was discussed. Then also the canons and epistles of certain bishops, Fathers and patriarchs, since they saw the same thing done by the Westerners. All these additions, from the Paris edition of 1620 together with Balsamon's commentaries on this Code of the Eastern Church, to the extent needed for understanding the cited Nicene canon, we set out in full. They are as follows. The Epistle of the blessed Dionysius, archbishop of Alexandria, to Basilides, concerning various chapters, to which Dionysius gave answers by the epistle, which have been admitted as canons. The canons of the blessed Peter, archbishop and martyr of Alexandria, which are found in his sermon on repentance. The canonical epistle of the holy Gregory, archbishop of Neocaesarea, who was called Thaumaturgus, concerning those who ate sacrificial meat during the barbarian invasion and committed certain other sins. The letter of Athanasius, holy archbishop of Alexandria, to Ammon the monk. The same author's festal letter of the thirty-ninth year. The same author's letter to Rufinianus. Our holy father Basil, archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia: the first canonical epistle to Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium. To the same, the second canonical epistle. The same author's other letter to Amphilochius, concerning the difference of foods. The same author's letter to Diodorus, concerning the man who took two sisters in marriage. The same author's letter to the presbyter Gregory, that he should separate from the little woman with whom he lives. The same author's letter to the chorepiscopi, that they should not make ministers without him contrary to the canons. The same author's letter to the bishops who were under him, that they should not ordain for money. The same author's excerpts from the twenty-seventh chapter of what was written about the Holy Spirit to the blessed Amphilochius, and excerpts from the twenty-ninth chapter of the same work. The canonical epistle of the holy Gregory of Nyssa, bishop, to the holy Letoius, bishop of Melitene. The canonical responses of the most holy Timothy, bishop of Alexandria, who was one of the 150 Fathers who assembled at Constantinople. The edict of Theophilus, archbishop of Alexandria, when the Epiphany was approaching on the Lord's day. The same author's admonition which Ammon received on account of Lyco. The same author's exposition concerning those who are called Cathari. The same author's letter to Agathon, bishop,

units.la: & & altera ad Menam Episcopum. Sancti Patris Cyrilli Archlepiscopi Alexandrini Epistola canonica & altera ad Episcopos qui sunt in Libya & Pentapoli. Sancti Patris nostri Gregorii Theologi ex metricis ejus poëmatibus quinam libri sint legendi veteris & novi testamenti. Sancti Amphilochii Episcopi Iconii ex Iambis ad Seleucum de eodem argumento. Gennadii Patriarchæ Constantinopolitani & sanctæ cum eo congregatæ Synodi ad sanctissimos omnes Metropolitanos, & ad Papam urbis Romæ epistola circularis, quæ incipit. Religiosissimo & sanctissimo in sacris comministro Gennadius, & quæ in Christi amante regia civitate Constantinopoli coacta est sancta synodus. Ex epistola Magni Basilii ad Nicapolitanos quædam. Post Trullanam approbationem, quæ facta seculi octavi anno septimo, accesserunt canones ipsi Trullani in synodo quini-sexta sanciti C11. & canones XXII. synodi Nicænæ secundæ anno 787. habitæ. Ex quibus omnibus constat codex canonum Ecclesiæ Orientalis à Nicæna prima, ad Nicænam secundam synodum, cui titulus est Κανόνες τὐ ἁγίων Ἀποστόλων, ἢ τῶν πωόδων; & hic est Codex ille, quem supra diximus editum esse seculi superioris anno XL. à Joh. Tilio, Græcè ex Bibliotheca Canonicorum Divi Hilarii Pictaviensis, quem postea Elias Ehingerus ex Bibliotheca Augustana Witebergæ, A. MDXIV. iterum edidit, ad quem Zonaras & Balsamo suas interpretationes fecerunt. Illud de hoc codice Orientali observandum, in eum primum sententias patrum esse receptas & canonibus exæquatas; ad modum Cresconii, qui in Occidente decretales Pontificum Romanorum, canonibus immiscuerat primus; nisi quod antea etiam Joh. Scholasticus Basilii canones suo Nomocanoni addiderit.
units.tr: and another to Menas, bishop. The canonical epistle of the holy Father Cyril, archbishop of Alexandria, and another to the bishops who are in Libya and Pentapolis. Of our holy father Gregory the Theologian, from his metrical poems, which books of the Old and New Testament are to be read. Of the holy Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium, from his iambics to Seleucus on the same subject. The circular epistle of Gennadius, patriarch of Constantinople, and of the holy synod gathered with him, to all the most holy metropolitans, and to the Pope of the city of Rome, which begins: To the most religious and most holy fellow minister in sacred things, Gennadius, and the holy synod which has been gathered in the royal city of Constantinople, lover of Christ. Some passages from the epistle of Basil the Great to the Nicopolitans. After the Trullan approval, which was made in the seventh year of the eighth century, there were added the Trullan canons themselves, sanctioned in the Quinisext Synod, one hundred and eleven, and the twenty-two canons of the second Nicene Synod, held in 787. From all these it is established that the Code of Canons of the Eastern Church, from the first Nicene Synod to the second, bears the title Canons of the Holy Apostles, or of the Fathers [Κανόνες τῶν ἁγίων Ἀποστόλων, ἢ τῶν πατέρων]. This is the Code which we said above was published in the last century, in the year 1540, by John Tilius, in Greek, from the library of the canons of St. Hilary of Poitiers; and which Elias Ehinger afterwards published again at Wittenberg, in 1614, from the Augsburg library. Zonaras and Balsamon made their interpretations on it. It should be noted about this Eastern Code that the sayings of the Fathers were first received into it and placed on a level with the canons, in the manner of Cresconius, who was the first to insert the decretals of the Roman Pontiffs among the canons in the West; except that John Scholasticus had earlier added the canons of Basil to his Nomocanon.

units.la: Eodem tempore fere, quo in Oriente in synodo Nicæna secunda confirmatus Codex Ecclesiæ Orientalis, & in Occidente sua incrementa habuit Jus Canonicum. Hadrianus enim primus Papa Carolo Magno misit collectionem canonum & Epistolarum Decretalium, ad usum Ecclesiarum Occidentis: quam olim Dionysius Exiguus concinnarat, qua de re supra num. marg. 78. Hanc quoque in Germaniam nostram, si non antea, saltem tum transiisse valde probabile, usque ad tempora Ricolphi Episcopi Moguntini, qui Isidori Mercatoris, Impostoris volebam dicere, collectionem in eam pertulit, ut infra, ubi Mercatoris collectio examinanda est, observabimus. Hujus Collectionis auctor non fuit Hadrianus, quare ideo nec inter Collectores canonum locum cum aut laudem meretur. Sed alia est ejus Collectio Canonum aliquot, in gratiam Ingelrami Episcopi Metensis seu Mediomatricæ urbis, ex Græcis & Latinis Canonibus & Synodis Romanis atque Decretis Præsulum & Principum Romanorum facta & tradita Ingelramo An. 785. Indict. 9. 13. Cal. Octobr. Complectitur canones septuaginta duos quos collectioni suæ inseruit Isidorus Mercator. Eosque forte intelligendos esse conjicit Doctissimus Blondellus, in Pseudo-Isidoro & Turriano vapulante, quorum idem Impostor meminit in suppositá Epistola Zepherini Papæ prima. Ita ille in censura istius Epistolæ in fine pag. 246. Si quis, inquit, in re obscura conjectandi locus esse debeat, suspicari non immerito quis possit, non alias 70. Apostolorum sententias Mercatori nostro in mentem venisse, quam quas A. D. 785. Indict. 9. 13. Cal. Octob. in gratiam Ingelramni Metensium Episcopi, ex Græcis & Latinis canonibus, & synodis Romanis, atque decretis Præsulum ac Principum Romanorum collegisse dicitur Adrianus primus urbis Episcopus. Sunt enim numero 72. eas semper in ore habet impostor, præter 6. 12. 28. 35. 36. 38. 40. 41. 44. 45. 46. 52. 55. 57. 58. 59. 60. 61. 62. 64. 68. 72. quas vel silentio præterire, vel oblique tantum tangere videtur; reliquas liquas 50. citat sub nomine Apostolorum, quorum hic 70. sententias memorat; & synodi Nicaenæ, cui totidem canones tribuit. Vide Epist. PseudoAthanasii ad Marcum, Pseudo-Marci, Pseu-Julii secundam, & Pseudo-Felicis secundi primam. Nisi quis velit præferre sententiam Magni Usserii, in Disert. de script. Ignatii. cap. 6. pag. 39, qui mendosum locum Pseudo-Zepherini Epistolæ de can. Apost. intelligit & corrigit ex Gregorii Presbyteri Polycarpo, ubi non septuaginta sententiæ, sed quinquaginta leguntur, quam sententiam ut simpliciorē & vero magis similem probat Doctiss: Dalæus de Pseudepigraph. Apost. lib. 3. cap. 4. pag. 478. Hanc Adriani collectionem Ludovicus Jacob à S. Carolo, Cabilionensis Burgundus Ordinis Carmelitarum Alumnus (auctor futilis, qui in omnibus fere paginis errores cumulat, maxime ubi de Scriptoribus protestantibus loquitur) in Bibliothecæ Pontificiæ libro I. in vita Hadriani, pag. mihi 102. vocat: Conciliorum volumen. & hæc de ea refert. Scripsit Hadrianus primus, Conciliorum volumen, ubi præfixit præfationem & epigramma Acrostichis versibus, seu Collectionem canonum octoginta à se elaboratam, quam dedit Ingelramo vel Angeranno Episcopo 38. Metensi, tunc Romæ commoranti. Extat ex versione Dionysii Exigui. De quorum veritate & pondere ex jam dictis judicare æquus Lector poterit.
units.tr: At about the same time that the Code of the Eastern Church was confirmed in the second Nicene Synod in the East, Canon Law gained its growth in the West as well. For Pope Hadrian I sent to Charlemagne a collection of canons and decretal epistles for the use of the churches of the West, which Dionysius Exiguus had once put together, on which matter see above at marg. no. 78. It is also very probable that this collection passed into our Germany, if not earlier, at least then, and it was brought in until the time of Bishop Riculf of Mainz, who brought in the collection of Isidore Mercator (I wanted to say, the impostor's), as we shall observe below, where the collection of Mercator is to be examined. Hadrian was not the author of this collection, and therefore he does not deserve a place or praise among the compilers of canons. But there is another collection of his, of some canons, made for the sake of Ingelram, bishop of Metz, or of the city of the Mediomatrici, from Greek and Latin canons and Roman synods and decrees of Roman prelates and princes, and handed over to Ingelram in the year 785, indiction 9, on the 13th before the October Kalends. It contains seventy-two canons, which Isidore Mercator inserted into his collection. The most learned Blondel conjectures that these are perhaps what is meant, in his work Against Pseudo-Isidore and the battered Turrian, where the same impostor mentions them in the forged first epistle of Pope Zephyrinus. Thus he writes in his criticism of that epistle, at the end of page 246: If there ought to be room for conjecture in an obscure matter, one may reasonably suspect that it was not any other seventy sayings of the Apostles that came into the mind of our Mercator, than those which, in the year 785, indiction 9, on the 13th before the October Kalends, Hadrian I, bishop of the city, is said to have collected in favour of Ingelram, bishop of the Metensians, from Greek and Latin canons, Roman synods, and decrees of Roman prelates and princes. For the impostor always has in his mouth seventy-two of them, except 6, 12, 28, 35, 36, 38, 40, 41, 44, 45, 46, 52, 55, 57, 58, 59, 60, 61, 62, 64, 68, 72, which he seems either to pass over in silence or to touch on only obliquely; the remaining fifty he cites under the name of the Apostles, of which he mentions here seventy sayings; and he assigns as many canons to the Synod of Nicaea. See the pseudo-Athanasius's epistle to Marcus, the pseudo-Marcus, the second pseudo-Julius, and the first pseudo-Felix the Second. Unless someone prefers the opinion of Ussher, in his dissertation on the writings of Ignatius, chapter 6, page 39, who takes the faulty passage in the pseudo-Zephyrinus epistle on the apostolic canons to be, and corrects it from Gregory the Presbyter's Polycarp, where not seventy sayings but fifty are read. The most learned Daillé approves this view as simpler and more like the truth, in his work on the pseudepigrapha of the Apostles, book 3, chapter 4, page 478. This collection of Hadrian is called by Ludovicus Jacob à S. Carolo, a Burgundian of Châlons, a pupil of the Order of Carmelites (a futile author who piles up errors on almost every page, especially when speaking of Protestant writers), in his Bibliotheca Pontificia, book 1, in the life of Hadrian, page 102 by my count, the volume of Councils. He reports of it: Hadrian I wrote a volume of Councils, in which he prefixed a preface and an epigram in acrostic verses, or a collection of eighty canons which he himself had compiled, which he gave to Ingelram or Angelram, bishop of Metz, then staying at Rome. It survives in the translation of Dionysius Exiguus. On the truth and weight of these matters the fair reader will be able to judge from what has already been said.

units.la: Temporibus Hadriani vixit quoque Carolus Magnus Gloriosissimus Imperator, cujus multæ extant leges Ecclesiasticæ, ut & successorum ejus; quæ postea collectæ sunt ab Ansegiso Abbate Lobiense, & Benedicto Levita. Ad Imperium pervenit Carolus Magnus Longobardis devictis seculo nono incipiente, & usque ad annum decimum & quartum imperavit. Magnam rei ecclesiasticæ curam gessit: concilia, & synodos varias habuit; de quibus multa passim vitæ ejus scriptores, ita Reghino Abbas Prumiensis in Chronico. sub ann. 813. de eo refert. Concilia jussu ejus super statu Ecclesiarum per totam Galliam ab Episcopis celebrata sunt, quorum unum Moguntiæ, alterum Remis, tertium Turonis, quartum Cabillone, quintum Arelate congregatum est, & constitutiones, quæ in singulis factæ sunt, ab Imperatore confirmatæ sunt; quas qui nosse voluerit, in supradictis civitatibus invenire poterit, quanquam & earum exemplaria in archivo Palatii habeantur. Memorabilis quoque est synodus Francofurtensis ab eodem celebrata, ubi contra Græcorum synodum Imaginum adoratio est damnata, unde profecti libri illi de imaginibus sacris, qui Caroli Magni nomen præferunt à Tilio editi, de quibus supra aliquid in transitu dictum. Has leges Eccle-
units.tr: Hadrian's time also saw the reign of Charles the Great, the most glorious emperor, under whom many ecclesiastical laws were issued, as were those of his successors. These were later collected by Ansegisus, abbot of Lobbes, and by Benedict the Levite. Charles came to the empire at the beginning of the ninth century, after he had conquered the Lombards, and he reigned for forty-four years. He took great care over church affairs and held various councils and synods. Many of his biographers record them in various places. So Regino, abbot of Prüm, in his Chronicle under the year 813, reports of him: By his command councils were held by the bishops throughout all of Gaul on the state of the churches. One was gathered at Mainz, another at Reims, a third at Tours, a fourth at Chalon, and a fifth at Arles. The decrees made at each were confirmed by the emperor. Whoever wishes to know them can find them in the cities named, although copies of them are also kept in the palace archive. The synod of Frankfurt, held by the same emperor, is also memorable, where the adoration of images was condemned in opposition to the Greek synod. From this came those books on sacred images that bear the name of Charles the Great, published by Tilius, about which something was said in passing above.

units.la: Ecclesiasticas Caroli Magni, ut & Ludovici Pii ejus filii, & Lotharii ejus Nepotis collegit Ansegisus Abbas Laubiensis, vel Lobiensis, (quod est Benedictinorum illustre coenobium ad Sabin Fluvium in diœcesi Cameracensi, sed sub ditione Leodicensi) postea Archiepiscopus Senonensis, & in duos & seculares leges itidem in duos libros retulit, publicavitque anno Christi 827, Imperii Ludovici Pii Anno XIII. Indict. quinta. ut ipse testatur in Præfationis initio, quam capitulis præmisit: in qua quia totius operis rationem reddit & modum digestionis, eam subjicere operæ pretium duximus. Dominante per secula infinita omnium dominatore Christo salvatore nostro, creatore universæ creaturæ, Anno incarnationis ipsius DCCCXVII. indictione v. anno vero XIII. Imperii gloriosissimorum Principum domini Ludovici Augusti Christianæ religionis magni propagatoris, & Lotharii Cæsaris filii ipsius, Ansegisus nullis præcedentibus meritis, sed gratia omnipotentis Dei abba, pro amore bonæ memoriæ domini Caroli Magni Imperatoris Christianorum, atque præcellentissimi ac piissimi domini Ludovici Augusti filii ipsius sincera dilectione, necnon & præclari Lotharii Cæsaris filii piissimi Ludovici Imperatoris, hac subter descripta adunavi capitula. Quae proculdubio quia ad sancta Ecclesia
units.tr: Ansegisus, abbot of Lobbes, or Laubach (which is the famous Benedictine monastery on the Sambre river, in the diocese of Cambrai but under the jurisdiction of Liège), later archbishop of Sens, collected the ecclesiastical laws of Charles the Great, of his son Louis the Pious, and of Louis's nephew Lothar. He arranged them in two books, and likewise the secular laws in two books, and published them in the year of Christ 827, the thirteenth year of the reign of Louis the Pious, fifth indiction, as he himself testifies at the beginning of the Preface that he placed before the chapters. Since in it he gives the plan of the whole work and the method of its arrangement, we have thought it worth while to add it here. With Christ our Saviour, lord of the ages, creator of every creature, ruling for endless ages, in the year of his incarnation 817, fifth indiction, and in the thirteenth year of the reign of the most glorious princes, Lord Louis Augustus, great propagator of the Christian religion, and Lothar Caesar, his son, I, Ansegisus, abbot, not by any previous merit but by the grace of almighty God, for love of the good memory of Lord Charles the Great, emperor of the Christians, and out of sincere affection for the most excellent and most pious Lord Louis Augustus, his son, and also for the illustrious Lothar Caesar, the most pious son of Emperor Louis, have gathered the chapters written below. Since these have undoubtedly been made for the advancement of the holy Church, they are to be firmly observed as useful law.

units.la: Ecclesiæ eclesiæ profectum facta sunt, pro utili firmiter tenenda sunt lege. Fuerant nanque quondam tempore prædicti magni domini Caroli Imperatoris, necnon & nunc præfatorum Principum hoc in tempore domini piissimi Ludovici Augusti, & præclari Lotharii Cæsaris jussu per intervalla temporum ad Christianam religionem conservandam, atque ad concordiam pacis & dilectionis in Ecclesia Catholica tenendam edita : sed quia in diversis sparsim scripta membranulis per diversorum spatia temporum fuerant, ne oblivioni traderentur pro dilectione nimia, ut præfatus sum, prædictorum gloriosissimorum Principum, & pro amore sanctissimæ prolis eorum, sed & pro sanctæ ecclesiæ statu, placuit mihi prædicta in hoc libello adunare, quæ invenire potui, capitula prædictorum Principum jussu descripta : ut ad sanctæ ecclesiæ statum longævis conservandum temporibus, atque ad meritum præfatorum Principum gloriosius in vita perpetua augmentandum proficiant. Amen.
units.tr: For there were formerly, in the time of the aforesaid great Lord Charles the Emperor, and now in this time of the aforementioned princes, the most pious Lord Louis Augustus and the illustrious Lothar Caesar, decrees issued at various intervals by command, for keeping the Christian religion and for maintaining the concord of peace and love in the Catholic Church. But since they had been written in scattered little parchments at different times, lest they be forgotten, I have, as I said, out of great love for those most glorious princes, and for love of their most holy offspring, and also for the state of the holy Church, been pleased to gather into this little book the chapters of these princes, which I could find, written down by their command, so that they may serve to preserve the state of the holy Church for long ages, and to increase the merit of the said princes more gloriously in eternal life. Amen.

units.la: Sed hoc notum sit Lectori, quia prædictæ capitula quæ per intervalla temporum à præfatis sunt principibus edita, in quatuor distinxi libellis. Illa scilicet quæ dominus Carolus Imperator fecit ad ordinem pertinentia ecclesiasticum in primo adunavi libello. Ea vero ecclesiastica, quæ dominus ac piissimus Ludovicus Imperator & Lotharius Cæsar filius ipsius ediderunt, in secundo descripsi. Illa autem quæ dominus Carolus in diversis fecit temporibus ad mundanam pertinentia legem, in tertio adunavi. Ipsa vero, quæ dominus Ludovicus præclarus Imperator & Lotharius Cæsar filius illius fecerunt ad augmentum mundanæ pertinentia legis, in quarto congressi. Præmittitur libro primo ipsius Caroli Magni præfatio, quæ est suasoria & confirmatoria capitulorum, lectu sane digna, quæ merito subjici deberet, nisi nimium cresceret hæc tractatio, & festinatio operarum aliud juberet. Complectitur liber ille primus capitula CLXVIII. Secundum incipit Anfegisus alia, sed brevi præfatione, in qua tantum monet se in eum librum conjecisse capitula Ecclesiastica, quæ dominus Ludovicus Cæsar piissimus & Lotharius Imperator filius ipsius condiderunt, complectiturque iste capitula XLVII; quorum primum est præfatio ipsius Imperatoris. Tertium librum itidem nova præfatione ut & quartum orditur Anfegisus, monens se tertio illa ad mundanæ augmentum legis pertinentia, quæ Dominus Karolus Imper. edidit, & quarto ejusdem argumenti, quæ præclarissimus Dominus Ludovicus Augustus & Lotharius Cæsar fecerunt, capitula adunavisse libello. Continet tertius capitula LXXXIX. quartus vero LXXV. Post librum IV. sequuntur tres appendiculæ. De hisce libris, seu collectione pendiculæ. De hisce libris, seu collectione Sige-
units.tr: But let this be known to the reader: I have divided the chapters issued by the aforesaid princes at various intervals into four books. I have gathered into the first book those decrees made by Lord Charles the Emperor that pertain to the ecclesiastical order. Those ecclesiastical decrees which the Lord and most pious Emperor Louis and his son Lothar Caesar issued I have written out in the second. Those which Lord Charles made at various times pertaining to secular law I have gathered into the third. Finally, those which the illustrious Lord Emperor Louis and his son Lothar Caesar made for the increase of secular law I have brought together in the fourth. The first book is prefaced by a preface of Charles the Great himself, which is persuasive and confirmatory of the chapters and is certainly worth reading; it ought rightly to be added, were this treatment not growing too long and the haste of the printers not demanding otherwise. That first book contains 168 chapters. Ansegisus begins the second with another, but brief, preface, in which he only remarks that he has put into that book the ecclesiastical chapters which Lord Louis the most pious Caesar and his son Lothar the Emperor issued. It contains 47 chapters, the first of which is the preface of the Emperor himself. Ansegisus begins the third book, and likewise the fourth, with a new preface, noting that in the third he has gathered together those chapters pertaining to the increase of secular law which Lord Charles the Emperor issued, and in the fourth those of the same subject which the most illustrious Lord Louis Augustus and Lothar Caesar made. The third contains 89 chapters, the fourth 75. After the fourth book follow three appendices. Concerning these books, or collection, Sige-

units.la: Sigebertus Gemblacensis Monachus in Chro-nico an. 827. Ansegisus, inquit, Abbas Lobien-sis Edicta Imperatorum Karoli Magni & Ludovici filii ejus ad Ecclesiasticam legem pertinentia duobus libellis digessit. Idem eorum etiam edicta ad Mundanam legem pertinentia in duobus aque libellis digessit, Longævum fuisse & alia de eo scimus ex Odoranni Monachi Senonensis Chronico. Anno ab incarnatione Christi DCCCLXXXII. obiit Ansegisus venerabilis Senonum Archiepiscopus, totius Galliæ & Germaniæ Papa secundus feliciter, VII. Kalend. Decemb. & sepultus est in monasterio S. Petri. Hic Karolum Calvum unxit in regem, & postquam primatum totius Galliæ obtinuit, & superna moderatione secundus Papa appellari meruit, in synodo habita in loco qui dicitur Pontigonis XVI. Kal. Augusti. ann. DCCCLXXVI. Indict. IX. Judæos certi causa & moniales ab urbe Senonica expulit, & ne ulterius in ea habitaculum manendi haberent, sub anathematis jugulo interdixit. Mortuo Epitaphium hoc scriptum est. Antistes Senonum, reverentia magna potentum Ansegisus in hoc conditus est tumulo. Ut primas fieret Gallorum, Papa Joannes Instituit, meritis hoc tribuendo suis. Karli Romana cinxit caput iste corona, Et dedit in cunctos imperium populos. Gregorii Papæ secum caput abstulit inde.
units.tr: Sigebert of Gembloux, a monk, in his Chronicle under the year 827, says: Ansegisus, abbot of Lobbes, arranged in two books the edicts of the emperors Charles the Great and his son Louis that pertain to ecclesiastical law. He likewise arranged their edicts that pertain to secular law in two books of equal size. We know other things about him too from the Chronicle of Odoranus, a monk of Sens. In the year from the incarnation of Christ 882, Ansegisus, the venerable archbishop of Sens, the second Pope of all Gaul and Germany, died happily on the seventh day before the Kalends of December, and was buried in the monastery of St Peter. He anointed Charles the Bald as king. And after he had obtained the primacy of all Gaul, and by heavenly direction had deserved to be called the second Pope, at a synod held in the place called Pontigny on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the year 876, ninth indiction, he expelled the Jews and the nuns from the city of Sens for a certain cause, and forbade them under pain of anathema to have any dwelling in it again. After his death this epitaph was written: The bishop of Sens, held in great reverence by the mighty, Ansegisus, is laid in this tomb. That he might become first of the Gauls, Pope John appointed him, attributing this to his merits. He bound the Roman crown on the head of Charles, and gave him rule over all peoples. Thence he carried away the head of Pope Gregory with him.

units.la: Hic locus ossa fovet, spiritus astra tenet.
units.tr: This place holds his bones; his spirit holds the stars.

units.la: His quatuor libris ab Ansegiso non satis diligenter, aut potius satis plenè collectis, postea Benedictus Levita libros tres, quintum nempe, sextum & septimum adjecit, in quos non tantum supra memoratorum Impp. capitula, sed alia insuper inseruit, quorum rationem ipse optimè, quanquam paulo prolixius, sequente præfatione, reddit. Præcedentes, inquit, libelli nonnulla gloriosissimorum Karoli atque Ludovici Imperatorum continent capitula, quæ eorum tempore ab Ansegiso abbate sunt collecta, atque in prædictis coacta libellis, sicut in eorundem proœmio continetur. Sed quia ab eo nec media, ut rati sumus, sunt forsitan inventa vel collecta, necesse erat, ut à fidelibus ubicumque inveniri potuissent, quærerentur, & ob recordationem tantorum principum, vel eorundem capitum, ita emendo, utilitatem coadunarentur, & membranis insererentur, atq; à fidelibus memoriæ commendarentur.
