Qua propter ea, quæ ille aut invenire nequivit, aut inserere fortasse noluit, & illa quæ postmodum à fidelibus sanctæ Dei Ecclesiæ, & Pipini ac Karoli atque Ludovici didicimus in jam dictis libellis minimè esse inserta, pro Dei omnipotentis amore, & sanctæ Dei Ecclesiæ ac servorum ejus, atque totius populi utilitate fideliter investigare curavimus: & in tribus subsequentibus libellis distinctè
units.tr: To these four books, which Ansegisus collected not very carefully, or rather not fully enough, Benedict the Levite afterwards added three books, namely the fifth, sixth and seventh. In these he inserted not only the chapters of the emperors mentioned above, but also others besides. He himself explains his reasons very well, though somewhat at length, in the following preface: The preceding books contain some chapters of the most glorious emperors Charles and Louis, which were gathered in their time by Abbot Ansegisus and put together in the books already mentioned, as is set out in the preface to those same books. But since, as we believe, he perhaps did not find or collect everything, it was necessary that they be sought out from the faithful wherever they could be found, and gathered together, and inserted into parchments and commended to the faithful memory, both for the remembrance of such great princes and of their chapters, and for the profit of correcting them. Therefore, we have diligently taken care, for love of almighty God and of the holy Church of God and of his servants, and for the good of the whole people, to investigate faithfully those things which he either could not find or perhaps did not wish to insert, and those which we have since learned from the faithful of the holy Church of God, and from Pepin, Charles and Louis, were not at all inserted in the books already mentioned; and we have set them out distinctly in three following books
195. The Collection of Benedict the Levite.

units.la: 196. Præfatio ejus collectionis præmissa. distincte cum titulis suis coadunare. Ac Ludovico, Lothario[que], atque Karolo nobilissimis regibus, filiis videlicet Ludovici piissimi Imperatoris habenda & omnium Christianorum fidelibus tradenda scribere non distulimus, ut scirent qualiter juxta normam avi, proavi, ac genitoris, secundum Domini scilicet voluntatem, sicut & illi fecerunt, clerum & populum sibi commissum Domino opem ferente regere mererentur. Haec vero capitula quae in subsequentibus tribus libellis coadunare studuimus, in diversis locis, & in diversis schedulis, sicut in diversis synodis, ac placitis generalibus edita erant, sparsim invenimus. maxime sanctae Magontiacensis metropolis Ecclesiae scrinio à Riculfo ejusdem sanctae sedis metropolitano recondita, & demum ab Autcario secundo ejus successore atque consanguineo inventa reperimus, quae in hoc opusculo tenore suprascripto inserere maluimus. Monemus ergo Lectores, ut si eadem capitula duplicata vel triplicata repererint, non hoc nostrae imperitiae reputent, quia ut diximus, diversis ea in schedulis invenimus. Et ob id tam cito haec emendare nequivimus: sed cunctis scientia repletis Lectoribus haec corrigenda dimisimus. Invenimus insuper quedam ex his paria initia habentia, & imparem finem: quaedam vero pares fines: sed non paria initia. In quibusdam autem minus, & in quibusdam plus. Et propterea illa sic dimisimus: sicut invenimus. Precamur etiam omnes, ut si deinceps plura ex his invenerint, quæ memoratus Ansegisus non inseruit, nec nos potuimus hactenus invenire, ut ea illis in quarto aut quinto libello distincte inserere non pigeat, quatenus ipsi ex hoc gratiam Dei habeant, & clerus ac populus eorum utilitatibus non careat. Quoniam valde sunt utilia hæc capitula, & scire volentibus oppido profutura: quæ pro lege tam Ecclesiastica, quam & seculari jure firmissimo sunt tenenda. Primò igitur in loco posuimus nonnullos versiculos in laudem prædictorum Principum metrice compositos: deinde sequuntur capitula primi libelli subjectis numeris suis, ut facilius inveniri possit sententia quæ quaeritur. His ita peractis, est in fronte primi libelli posita Zachariæ Papæ epistola omnibus Episcopis, ac reliquis Ecclesiastici ordinis gradibus, & cunctis ducibus atque comitibus, omnibusque Deum timentibus per Gallias, & Francorum provincias constitutis directa, sicut in ea continetur. Quam sequuntur duo synodales conventus, quos sanctæ Romanæ & Apostolicæ ecclesiæ legatus Bonifacius memoratæ Magontiacensis Ecclesiæ Archiepiscopus vice supradicti Zachariæ Papæ una cum Carlomanno Francorum principe canonicè tenuit, ut agnoscant omnes hæc prædictorum Principum capitula maxime Apostolica auctoritate fore firmata. Post ista quoque quæ sequuntur, eadem auctoritate maxima, ut diximus, ex parte, & omnium Francorum utriusque ordinis virorum assensu sunt roborata. Secundò vero in libello post capitulorum numerum prima fronte posita sunt quædam ex lege divina excerpta capitula, sicut ea sparsim in eo-rum mixta capitulis reperimus, ut omnes hæc capitula legibus divinis, regulisque canonicis con-cordare non ignorent. Tertio siquidem in libello post ejusdem libelli capitulorum numerum quædam ex canonibus à Paulino Episcopo, & Albino magistro, reliquisq; jussione Karoli invictissimi Principis magistris sparsim collecta sunt incerta capitula, & quibusdam interpositis sequuntur alia regulæ monasticæ congruentia, & demum ea quæ sequuntur ad sancta Dei Ecclesia servorumque ejus atque totius Christiani populi utilitatem sunt conscripta capitula, sicut in eodem continentur libello. Precamur quoque lectores o-mnes, cunctosque judices & sapientes, ut non ea sinistra interpretatione ullo unquam tempore dignentur exponere: aut quemquam injustè judicare, vel eo quod non sint quædam ex his juxta regulam Grammaticæ artis composita reprehendere, sed pro ipsis Principibus eorumque & sanctæ Dei Ecclesiæ fidelibus, qui hæc eadem simul cum eis tractaverunt, atque pro nobis, qui ea colligere ac describere certavimus, orare studeant: & jam dicta capitula pariter nobiscum & cum illis amplecti, venerari, amare, legibusque tenere decer-tent, annuente Domino, ut parem omnes ex hoc mercedem habere mereamur. Amen. Quare in Ansegisi Praefatione nomen Lotharii adjectum sit, cum tamen in ista collectione nil sit Lotharii proprium, illud explicat Pithoeus in Praefatione ad capitularia his verbis. Sane quod in Ansegisi praefationibus Lotharii nomen adjectum est, datum id scias exemplarium quorundam antiquati, quae sub ejus ditione, ut verisimile est, primum descripta, non hoc solum ipsius honori tribuerant, sed & ex versibus qui Benedicti collectionem praecedunt, in Lotharii sui gratiam illos de Ludovici filiis ita permutatos habuerunt: Ex quo prosequitur soboles veneranda per orbem Ipsius insigni nomine digna patris. Lotharius primum regnum sortitus avitum Arduinae nemoris incola factus ovat. Hinc Hludovicus heros Rheni cis littora genti Imperat, & populis effera colla terit. Tum Karolus cari species genitoris amata Gallorum coetus ordinat atque domat. Illis nos qui fata tenent loca partibus aequis Haec ferimus.
units.tr: 196. Preface to this collection, placed in front. to arrange distinctly under their own titles. And we did not delay in writing to the most noble kings Lothair, Louis and Charles, namely the sons of the most pious Emperor Louis, to be kept by them and handed to all the faithful Christians, so that they might know how to rule the clergy and people committed to them, with the Lord bringing help, according to the norm of their grandfather, great-grandfather and father, and in accordance with the will of the Lord, as they also did. The chapters which we have striven to arrange in the following three little books we found scattered in various places and on various slips, just as they had been issued in various synods and general assemblies. Chiefly we found them stored in the chest of the holy church of Mainz, laid up by Riculf, metropolitan of that holy see, and afterwards discovered by Autcharius the Second, his successor and kinsman. These we preferred to insert in this little work in the form stated above. We therefore warn the readers that if they find the same chapters doubled or tripled, they should not put this down to our inexperience, since, as we said, we found them on different slips. For this reason we could not correct them so quickly, and we have left them for the learned readers to correct. We have also found some of these with like beginnings but unlike endings, and some with like endings but unlike beginnings; in some cases there are fewer, in some more. For this reason we have left them as we found them. We also beg everyone: that if in future they find more of these which the aforementioned Ansegisus did not insert, and which we have not yet been able to find, they would not hesitate to insert them distinctly in the fourth or fifth little book, so that they may have the grace of God from this, and their clergy and people may not lack their benefits. For these chapters are very useful and will greatly profit those who wish to know, and they are to be held as most firm law, both ecclesiastical and secular. First, then, we have placed at the front some verses composed in metre in praise of the aforesaid princes. Then follow the chapters of the first little book with their numbers attached, so that the passage sought may be found more easily. This done, at the front of the first little book is placed a letter of Pope Zachary, addressed to all bishops and the remaining grades of the ecclesiastical order, and to all dukes and counts, and all who fear God, established in Gaul and the provinces of the Franks, as it is contained in it. It is followed by two synodal assemblies, which Boniface, legate of the holy Roman and Apostolic church and archbishop of the aforesaid church of Mainz, held canonically in place of the aforesaid Zachary, together with Carloman, prince of the Franks, so that all may acknowledge that these chapters of the aforesaid princes are confirmed especially by apostolic authority. After these, which follow, they were strengthened by the same very great authority, as we said, and by the assent of men of both orders of all the Franks. Secondly, in the book, after the number of chapters, there are placed at the very front certain chapters excerpted from divine law, as we found them scattered and mixed among their chapters, so that everyone may know how these chapters agree with divine laws and canonical rules. Thirdly, in the book, after the number of its chapters, there are certain uncertain chapters gathered scattered from the canons by Paulinus the bishop and Albinus the master, and the other masters, by command of Charles, most invincible prince. With some interposed, others follow that agree with monastic rule, and finally those which follow are chapters written for the benefit of the holy Church of God, its servants and the whole Christian people, as they are contained in the same book. We also beg all readers, all judges and wise men, that they would never deign to expound these in a sinister sense, or unjustly condemn anyone, or find fault with some of them on the ground that they are not composed according to the rules of the art of grammar. Rather, let them be eager to pray for the princes themselves and their faithful in the holy Church of God, who discussed these matters together with them, and for us who laboured to gather and copy them; and let them strive, together with us and with them, to embrace, venerate, love and keep by law the aforesaid chapters, the Lord granting that we may all deserve an equal reward from this. Amen. Why the name of Lothair was added in Ansegis's preface, although nothing in this collection is peculiar to Lothair, Pithoeus explains in his preface to the capitularies in these words: Indeed, you should know that the name of Lothair was added in the prefaces of Ansegis in some old copies, which, as is likely, were first written out under his rule. Those copies not only paid this honour to him, but also, in the verses which precede Benedict's collection, changed the lines about the sons of Louis so as to favour Lothair, and so had them thus: From whom there follows a venerable offspring throughout the world, worthy of their father's famous name. Lothair, having first received the ancestral kingdom, becomes a dweller of the Ardennes forest and rejoices. Hence Louis the hero rules the peoples on this side of the shores of the Rhine, and crushes the proud necks of the nations. Then Charles, the beloved image of his dear father, orders and tames the assembly of the Gauls. To those of us who hold the fates in equal parts, we bring these things.

units.la: Et tamen Lotharii ejus inter haec nihil proprium esse putamus, cujus tantum nomine extant quaedam ex his ipsis decerpta Capitula ad Italiae regnum, quae jam olim Langobardicarum legum libris inserta & Ka-roli ,,roli cujusdam Cotti Siculi, sive is Toccus ,,fuit, commentario ante annos CCCLXXX. ,,exposita leguntur. Sed neque Karoli fratris ,,(quem nostrum, id est, Francorum Gallo,,rumve regem verè proprieq; dixeris)quic,,quam hic adjectum reperias, præter ea Ca,,pitula quæ circa initia regni sui in Sparnaco ,,probaverat observarique præceperat. Hæc Pithœus. Continet quintus capitula CCLI. sextus CCCXXX, septimus CCCLXXII. Sequuntur tunc appendices, prima capitulorum LXXX. quæ anno Christi 817. Imperii vero Ludovici Principis IV. Sexto Idus Julii Aquisgrani in domo Pallatii, quæ Lateranis dicitur, communi consilio inviolabiliter à regularibus conservari decreverunt, ut habet inscriptio hæc in meo Codice, pag. 339. Anno incarnationis Domini nostri Jesu Christi DCCC.XVII. Imperii vero Gloriosissimi Principis Ludovici IV. VI. Idus Julii, cum in domo Aquisgrani Palatii, quæ Lateranis dicitur, Abbates cum quampluribus una suis resedissent monachis, quæ subsequuntur capitula communi consilio ac pari voluntate inviolabiliter à regularibus conservari decreverunt. Secunda capitulorum xxv. quorum hæc est inscriptio.
units.tr: And yet we do not think that anything in these is peculiar to that Lothair, whose name alone is attached to certain chapters excerpted from these same texts for the kingdom of Italy, which were long ago inserted in the books of the Lombard laws and are read explained in a commentary of a certain Cotto the Sicilian, or Toccus, composed some 380 years ago. Nor do you find the name of Charles's brother added here, who could truly and properly be called our king, that is, king of the Franks or the Gauls, except for those chapters which he had approved about the beginning of his reign at Sparnacum and had ordered to be observed. Thus Pithoeus. The fifth contains 251 chapters, the sixth 330, the seventh 372. Then follow the appendices, the first of 80 chapters, which in the year of Christ 817, in the fourth year of the reign of Prince Louis, on the sixth Ides of July at Aachen, in the palace hall called the Lateran, they decreed by common counsel should be inviolably kept by the regular clergy, as this inscription in my codex, page 339, has it: In the year of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 817, in the reign of the most glorious Prince Louis the Fourth, on the sixth Ides of July, when the abbots, together with many of their monks, were sitting at Aachen in the palace hall called the Lateran, they decreed by common counsel and with equal consent that the following chapters should be inviolably kept by the regular clergy. The second, of 25 chapters, whose inscription is this: The chapters which follow were not, as they stand below, found, gathered, arranged and inserted here at the time when they were written, but were afterwards discovered by the faithful on this slip, as they had been done, and inserted, so that they might more easily be found by the faithful whenever necessary.

units.la: Capitula quæ deinceps sequuntur non tunc quando præscripta, velut in subsequentibus habentur, inventa, collecta, ordinata, hucque inserta esse noscuntur, sed postmodum à fidelibus reperta hac in scedula, sicut acta erant sunt inserta, ut facilius à fidelibus quotiens necesse fuerit reperiantur. Tertia, continet capitula LXXIX. quibus hæc præmittuntur. Hæc capitula proprie sunt ad Episcopos vel ad ordines Ecclesiasticos pertinentia, quæ non solum observari, sed etiam sibi subjectos, vel commissos facienda perdocere debent. Quarta capitulorum CVIII. cujus etiam capitula in vetustis quibusdam exemplaribus cum præcedentibus numeris continuata sunt. Inscriptio eorum est hæc. Sequentia quædam capitula ex sanctorum Patrum decretis & Imperatorum edictis colligere curavimus, atque inter nostra capitula lege firmissima tenenda generali consultu Erchembaldo Cancellario nostro inserere jussimus. Claudunt hoc volumen capitula xx. Caroli Imp. Ludovici filii, quorum hæc est inscriptio. Hæc quæ sequuntur capitula excerpta sunt à Domno Rege Karolo Domni Hludowici Imp. filio & Principibus ejus ex capitulis quæ anno DCCCXLVI. ediderant Episcopi in synodis, Wenilo scilicet cum suffraganeis suis, Guntboldus cum suffraganeis suis, Ursmarus cum suffraganeis suis, Hincmarus cum suffraganeis suis, Amalo cum suffraganeis suis: & oblata sunt eidem Principi, sicut ipse jusserat, collecta ad relegendum in Sparnaco villa Remensis Ecclesia. Et quia factione quorundam motus est animus ipsius Regis contra Episcopos, dissidentibus regni sui primoribus ab eorundem Episcoporum ammonitione & remotis ab eodem concilio Episcopis, ex omnibus illis capitulis hac tantum observanda & complacenda sibi collegerunt, & Episcopis scripto tradiderunt, dicentes, non amplius de eorum capitulis acceptasse quam ista, & ista se velle cum Principe observare. Videtur Pithoeus in ea opinione esse, quasi libri isti tres posteriores diversos habuerint præter Benedictum, collectores & post eum diversis temporibus diversa accrementa, non tantum ex capitulis Imperatorum, sed canonibus Gallicanis, pœnitentialibus libellis, Patrum sententiis, Juliani Antecessoris Novellis. Hæc enim habet in Præfatione: Illud etiam verendum est, ne nos quoque in hac rutuba non pauca fefellerint. quamquam nec fortassis fuerint illa tanti, præsertim quæ post Ansegisum pro cujusque collectoris ingenio & propositio, confuse nulloque ordine aut delectu, non certa etiam plerumque auctoritate & fide, ex Gallicanis canonibus ac pœnitentialibus libellis, SS. quoque Patrum sententiis, quædam etiam ex Juliani Antecessoris CP. Novellis & Alarici breviario Anianique ad illud interpretationibus, quin & ex Wisigothorum Langobardorumque legibus
units.tr: The chapters which follow were not, as they are written below, found, gathered, arranged and inserted here at the time when they were written, but were afterwards discovered by the faithful on this slip, as they had been done, and inserted, so that they might more easily be found by the faithful whenever necessary. The third, containing 79 chapters, is prefaced by these words: These chapters properly pertain to bishops or to the ecclesiastical orders, who must not only observe them but also thoroughly teach them to those subject or committed to them. The fourth, of 108 chapters, whose chapters in some old copies are also continued with the preceding numbers. Its inscription is this: We have taken care to gather the following chapters from the decrees of the holy Fathers and the edicts of the emperors, and by general counsel we have ordered them to be inserted among our chapters, to be held as most firm law, through Erchembald our chancellor. The volume closes with twenty chapters of Charles, son of Emperor Louis, whose inscription is this: The following chapters were excerpted by Lord King Charles, son of Lord Emperor Louis, and his princes, from the chapters which the bishops had published in synods in the year 846: namely Wenilo with his suffragans, Guntbold with his suffragans, Ursmar with his suffragans, Hincmar with his suffragans, and Amalo with his suffragans. They were offered to the same prince, as he himself had ordered, gathered for reading at Sparnacum, a village of the Church of Reims. And because the mind of the same king was moved against the bishops by the faction of certain men, his chief men dissenting from the admonition of those bishops, and the bishops having been removed from the same council, they gathered from all those chapters only these to be observed and pleasing to him, and handed them in writing to the bishops, saying that they had received no more of their chapters than these, and that they wished these to be observed with the prince. Pithoeus seems to hold the opinion that these three later books had collectors other than Benedict, and that after him various additions were made at different times, not only from the chapters of the emperors but also from Gallican canons, penitential books, sayings of the holy Fathers, the Novels of Julian the Antecessor, and the breviary of Alaric with Anianus's interpretations of it, and even from the laws of the Visigoths and Lombards. For he says in his preface: It must also be feared lest these have deceived us in this rustic work too. Yet perhaps they were not of such great importance, especially those which after Ansegis were put together by the wit and purpose of each collector, confusedly and without any order or selection, often not with certain authority or reliability, from Gallican canons and penitential books, also from the sayings of the holy Fathers, and some from the Novels of Julian the Antecessor of Constantinople and the breviary of Alaric with Anianus's interpretations of it, and even from the laws of the Visigoths and Lombards.

De Benedicto Levita hoc habemus incerti scriptoris elogium, quod præmisit Pithœus editioni primæ Capitularis Caroli Magni: Benedictus Moguntiacensis Ecclesiæ levita, Capitula quædam „Regalia, synodalia, & alia collegit ex iis „quæ in scriniis ejusdem Metropolis reponi fecerant Ricolfus Archiepiscopus qui „monasterium S. units.tr: 200. From these, the later books were drawn and collected. Readers will easily recognise that some additions have been made to them, by those to whom these matters are of concern. We have not wished to leave these out either, lest anyone should miss them or look for them. Concerning Benedict the Deacon we have this account by an unknown writer, which Pithou prefixed to the first edition of the Capitularies of Charlemagne: "Benedict, deacon of the Church of Mainz, collected certain capitularies, royal, synodal and others, from those which Archbishop Ricolf, who restored the monastery of St Alban and presided over the synod of Mainz under Lord Charles, had ordered to be deposited in the archives of that metropolis; and Otgar, his kinsman and the second successor after Haistulf, both of whom were most diligent in such capitularies and very devoted to the Holy See of Rome, so much so that the Apostolic Gregory once entrusted his own functions in Germany to Otgar. Otgar favoured the sons of Emperor Louis against their father, but was later reconciled, and died in the year 847. He had as successor in the archbishopric, under Emperor Lothar VII, Lord Rhabanus, abbot of Fulda. From these facts it is clear, as the preface quoted above also shows at length, that this Benedict the Deacon greatly favoured and was attached to the Roman See." Concerning the joining together of the collections of Ansegis and Benedict, the following verses are read in old manuscripts:

units.la: hi leguntur in antiquis codicibus versiculi: Quattuor explicitis Lector venerande libellis, Qui canonum recitant jura tenenda satis. Quosque Pater quondam collegit nobilis aptè, Ansegisus ovans, ductus amore Dei. Otgario, ita emendo, demum, quem tunc Magontia summum Pontificem tenuit, præcipiente pio. Post Benedictus ego ternos levita libellos Adnexi, legis queis recitatur opus. Quos patet inventos præfatio pandit ut ipsa, Distinctim titulis subpositisque suis. Hos igitur relegens devoto pectore biblos, Gratanter studeas fundere posco preces. Quatenus æterno donentur munere cælo, Hæc pia sanxerunt qui quoque jura piè.
units.tr: Four books, reader, you have now been shown, / which set out the laws of the canons that must be kept. / These noble Father Ansegis once collected with skill, / rejoicing, moved by love of God. / Then, at the command of the pious Otgar, whom Mainz then held as its chief bishop, / I, Benedict the deacon, added three further books, / the work of law which they recite. / The preface shows these books to have been found as it does, / each distinguished by its own titles and subheadings. / Reading these books with a devout heart, / gladly study them; I ask you to pour out prayers / that they may be granted the eternal gift of heaven, / those who have also piously upheld these pious laws.

units.la: Vide quoque de hoc capitulari, quæ breviter & accurate satis disserit Ant. nosterAugustinus, de emend. Gratiani, lib.2. dial.10. & seq. ubi de ratione ordinis hæc habet: pag. 444. nostræ editionis, vel 238. edit. Parisiens. Ordinem noli ab eo exposcere, contenti sinus ipso collectionis opere, & ut ajunt, quod dant, accipiamus. Omnia fere sine ulla inscriptione proponuntur, etiam si ex aliis libris intelligamus cujus sint. Et paulo post pag. sequent. hæc de auctoritate subjungit. Quia de auctoritate Capitularium dubitabas, licet verum sit, hæc fragmenta esse constitutionum trium Imperatorum
units.tr: See also what our Antonius Augustinus discusses briefly and quite accurately on this capitulary, On the Emendation of Gratian, book 2, dialogue 10 and following, where he says the following about the order: page 444 of our edition, or 238 of the Paris edition. Do not ask him for an order; be content with the collection's work itself, and, as they say, let us take what they give. Almost everything is set out without any heading, although from other books we can tell whose they are. And a little later, on the following page, he adds the following about authority: Because you doubted the authority of the Capitularies, although it is true that these fragments are the constitutions of three Emperors

units.la: 204. Collectiones hæc confusè facta & nullo ordine.
units.tr: 204. This collection was made in a confused way and without any order.

Ut capitula ecclesiastica ,,à Domno Carolo Magno Imp. nec non & à Do,,mno Ludovico Pio Aug. promulgata, obnixe obser,,vari præcipiantur, sicut & legalia observanda esse ,,noscuntur. & cap. LXXX. ad Carolum Calvum ,, Ludovici Pii filium. Capitula patris vestri si- ,,ne refragatione de cetero conserventur, ac capi,,tulis vestræ religionis ab exiguitatis nostræ mi- ,,nisterio oblatis hoc diploma, si complacet, adne,,ctatur. Sic multa capita referuntur hujus ,,collectionis in concilio Trosleiano, in Ti,,cinensi, & in Coloniensi sub Carolo tertio. ,,Leonis IV. ex epist. ad Lotharium Aug. ,,verba referunt Ivo,& Gratian. & liber Cæ,,saraug. De capitulis vestris, vestrorumq; prede,,cessorum irrefragabiliter custodiendis, & conser,,vandis, quanto valuimus, & valemus Christo ,,propitio, & nunc, & in ævum conservaturos, ,,modis omnibus profitemur. De integritate capitularium quæ sequuntur, apud eundem Augustin. illa ex supradictis emendari debent. Multa, pergit, desiderantur, ut notatur in triplici appendice post librum quartum, & libro VI. post caput CCLXXXXIIX. usque ad CCCXXX. & lib. VII. post caput CCCCLXXXIIX. ad DLIIX. Adjecta sunt postea duabus collectionibus capita XXVIII. & capita CCXCVI. Ex quo evenit, ut non omnia, quae Ivo, & Anselmus, & Deusdedit, & alii collectores in Capitularibus esse referunt, inveniantur. Habuit Augustinus codices mutilos, nec videre editionem Parisiensem Pithoei anni 1588. potuit, biennio antea jam sublatus, in qua Lacunæ libri sexti expletæ, & in libro septimo quædam quæ bis aut sæpius posita erant, sunt sublata, ideoque iste non excurrit ultra numeros supra memoratos, cum Augustinus adscribat ei capitula 558. Testatur hoc posterius ipse Pithoeus in Præfatione his verbis: Nos jam ex pluribus nostris alienisque codicibus plura & integriora edi curavimus, bona saltem fide, Tilii exemplum judiciumque sequuti, qui non ex Benedicti modo, sed & ex Ansegisi ipsius collectione eadem non semel posita sustulerat, similibus tantum quibusdam relictis, numeris etiam capitulorum consequenter mutatis. Quod eo monere visum est, ne quis eadem post hac ex iisdem aut aliis etiam exemplaribus augere aut supplere conetur, frustra. Quantæ auctoritatis fuerint Capitularia in Gallia non tantum ex dictis patet, sed magis patebit, si inspiciantur testimonia illa, quæ Pithoeus suæ editioni præmisit: ita ut Codex ecclesiæ Gallicæ, si non per ea absorptus, saltem valde obscuratus fuerit. Primus de restituendis Capitularibus superiori seculo sollicitus fuit Johan. Tilius, cujus supra facta mentio, verum ille morte sublatus perficere non potuit, pauca folia post obitum ejus prodierunt, quibus usi recognitores & emendatores Gratiani. Perfecit opus ex pluribus exemplaribus, Petrus Pithœus, de literis optime meritus, atque seculi anterioris anno 88. cum Gloffario vocum obscurarum in capitularibus repertarum Lutetiæ edidit, quod ibidem recussum est, anno tertio hujus seculi. Non præfert quidem editio nomen Pithœi, attamen ex Miræi Bibliotheca Ecclesiastica, pag. 143 & 229. & Præfatione Sirmondi ad Capitula Caroli Calvi scimus eum edidisse, & Præfationem præmisisse; sub Pithœi quoque nomine citat Justellus istam Præfationem, in fine suæ Præfationis, quam Codici Canonum Ecclesiæ universæ præmisit, ubi de Capitularibus adserit, omnia in iis fere desumta esse ex Codice Canonum Ecclesiæ Romanæ & Isidori collectione: subdit deinde hæc de Ludovici Pii libro: Nescio, inquit, an inter collectiones Gallicanas Canonum recensendus sit liber Ludovici Pii in concilio Aquisgranensi anno DCCCXVI. celebrato, confirmatus, cujus exemplar habemus Coloniæ editum anno MDXLIX, cum cum hac inscriptione: Reformationis abusuum Cleri formula per Ludovicum cognomento Pium, Romanorum Imperii Imperatorem optimum, Karoli Magni filium. Ipseque Ludovicus Imperator testatur, in Epistola ad Arnulphum Saltzburgensem Episcopum, quae etiam inter constitutiones Imperiales a V. C. Melchiore Goldasto nuper editas, extat. Hisce capitulis Caroli Magni & Ludovici Pii, accessit aliud capitulare Caroli Calvi, primum Regis Galliae, post mortem Ludovici Secundi, etiam Imperatoris, in qua dignitate paucos annos tantum exegit. Fuit ille Caroli Magni Nepos, ex Ludovico Pio & Judita filia Welphi Suevi secunda Ludovici uxore. Hic ad exemplum Avi & Patris rei ecclesiasticae curam habuit, & Avi & Patris capitula, in conventu apud Carisiacum Anno DCCCLXXVII. tit. 43. confirmavit; quod caput, quia praebet quoque illustre testimonium ipsius Caroli Calvi capitulari, subjicimus. Capitula quae Avus & Pater noster pro statu & munimine sanctae Dei Ecclesiae ac ministrorum ejus & pro pace ac justitia populi & quiete regni constituerunt, & quae nos cum fratribus nostris Regibus & nostris ac eorum fidelibus communiter constituimus; sed & quae nos consilio & consensu Episcoporum & caeterorum Dei & nostrorum fidelium, pro supradictis causis in diversis placitis placitis nostris conservanda statuimus, permanere inconvulsa decernimus, similiter & à filio nostro inconvulsa conservari volumus & mandamus.
units.tr: 205. The authority of the capitularies, though collected by private individuals, is nevertheless, as Benedict says, confirmed by apostolic authority. Read also the words of the Council of Meaux, chapter 78: that the ecclesiastical capitularies promulgated by Lord Charles the Great, Emperor, and also by Lord Louis the Pious, Augustus, be strictly observed, just as the secular laws are known to be to be observed. And chapter 80, to Charles the Bald, son of Louis the Pious: Let the capitularies of your father be kept henceforth without objection, and let this charter, if it pleases you, be attached to the capitularies of your religious observance offered through the ministry of our meagre self. In the same way, many chapters of this collection are cited in the Council of Troyes, in the Council of Ticino, and in the Council of Cologne under Charles the Third. Ivo and Gratian give the words of Leo IV from his letter to the Emperor Lothar, and the book of Caesaraugusta: We profess in every way that we have valued, and still value, with Christ being propitious, that we will preserve, both now and forever, your capitularies and those of your predecessors, to be kept and conserved irrefragably. Concerning the completeness of the capitularies that follow, in the same Augustinus, those things should be corrected from what was said above. Much, he goes on, is lacking, as is noted in the threefold appendix after the fourth book, and in book 6 after chapter 290 up to chapter 330, and in book 7 after chapter 488 to 558. Chapters 28 and 296 were later added to two collections. As a result, not all the things that Ivo, and Anselm, and Deusdedit, and the other collectors report as being in the Capitularies are found. Augustinus had mutilated manuscripts, and could not see the Paris edition of Pithou of 1588, which had already been withdrawn two years before, in which the gaps of book 6 were filled and in book 7 some things that were placed twice or more often were removed; therefore this one does not go beyond the numbers mentioned above, since Augustinus assigns to it 558 chapters. Pithou himself testifies to this latter point in his Preface in these words: We have now had more and fuller material published from many of our own and others' manuscripts, following in good faith the example and judgment of Tilius, who had removed from the collection not only that of Benedict but also that of Ansegis himself the things that had been placed more than once, leaving only certain similar ones, with the numbers of the chapters consequently changed. This has been thought worth noting so that no one may vainly try to add to or supplement these things afterwards from the same or other copies. How great the authority of the Capitularies was in Gaul is clear not only from what has been said, but will be clearer still if one examines those testimonies that Pithou prefixed to his edition, so that the Code of the Gallican Church, if not wholly absorbed by them, was at least greatly obscured. The first to be concerned with restoring the Capitularies in the previous century was Johannes Tilius, whose work I have mentioned above; but, carried off by death, he could not finish it, and a few leaves appeared after his death, which the revisers and emenders of Gratian used. Petrus Pithoeus, a man who deserved well of letters, completed the work from several copies, and in the year 1588 of the previous century published it at Paris with a glossary of obscure words found in the capitularies, which was reprinted there in the third year of this century. The edition does not indeed bear Pithou's name, but from Miraeus's Ecclesiastical Library, pages 143 and 229, and from Sirmond's Preface to the Capitularies of Charles the Bald, we know that he published it and prefixed the Preface. Under Pithou's name, Justellus also cites this Preface, at the end of his own Preface, which he prefixed to the Code of the Canons of the Universal Church, where, concerning the Capitularies, he asserts that almost everything in them is taken from the Code of the Canons of the Roman Church and the collection of Isidore. He then adds this about the book of Louis the Pious: I do not know, he says, whether the book of Louis the Pious, confirmed at the council of Aachen celebrated in the year 816, is to be counted among the Gallican collections of Canons, of which we have a copy printed at Cologne in 1549, with this heading: The formula for the reform of abuses of the clergy, by Louis, surnamed the Pious, the best Emperor of the Roman Empire, son of Charles the Great. Louis the Emperor himself also testifies to this in his letter to Arnulf, Bishop of Salzburg, which is also extant among the imperial constitutions recently published by the most learned Melchior Goldast. To these capitularies of Charles the Great and Louis the Pious was added another capitulary of Charles the Bald, first King of France, and after the death of Louis II, also Emperor, in which dignity he held office for only a few years. He was a grandson of Charles the Great, the son of Louis the Pious and Judith, daughter of Welf the Swabian, second wife of Louis. Following the example of his grandfather and father, he took care of ecclesiastical affairs, and in the assembly at Quierzy in the year 877, title 43, he confirmed the capitularies of his grandfather and father; since this chapter also provides a notable testimony to the capitulary of Charles the Bald himself, we subjoin it. The capitularies which our grandfather and father established for the state and protection of the holy Church of God and its ministers, and for the peace and justice of the people and the tranquillity of the realm, and which we with our brother kings and our own and their faithful men have jointly established; and also those which we, with the counsel and consent of the bishops and of the other faithful men of God and of ours, have decided to be kept in our various assemblies for the aforesaid causes, we decree shall remain unshaken, and we likewise wish and command that they be kept unshaken by our son.

units.la: Edidit hæc ac digessit capitula inter Jesuitas Doctissimus & Magni in literis & antiquitate nominis, Jacobus Sirmondus, cum aliorum successorum capitulis, hujus seculi anno xxiiii. Parisiis, in qua editione præter Caroli Calvi memorata, habentur Ludovici II. Caroli filii, Carolomanni Regis Ludovici II. filii, Caroli Simplicis Regis capitula, & tum sequuntur Coronationes Caroli Calvi, & Ludovici ejus filii Regum, Judithæ item filiæ & Hermintrudis conjugis Caroli. Quibus omnibus doctas suas, ut solet, notas adjecit. Collegit hæc ex diversis locis & quinque Codicibus manuscriptis antiquis, quorum primi duo, unus ex bibliotheca Joh. Tilii, alter ex bibliotheca Thuani, ultra titulum xvi. non progrediebantur; sequentes vero usque ad xliii, partim ex Belluacensis, partim ex Laudunensis Ecclesiæ libris, partim ex Metensi desumta sunt. Coronationes vero Regum, quæ capitulis subjiciuntur, ex Mohasterii Laurentiani Leodicensis exemplari solo descripsit. Ipse Sirmondus titulorum numeros & nomina, in longioribus Manuscriptorum titulis commodioris usus gratia prænotavit. Tituli Capitulorum Caroli Calvi sunt xliii. Ludovici Balbi iii. Carolomanni ii. Caroli Simplicis ii. Coronationes iv. Illud interest inter Capitularia quæ edidit Pithœus, & quæ edidit Sirmondus, quod in Ansegisi & Benedicti collectionibus, Regum tantum leges sint nullo fere ordine digestæ, nullaque temporum vel locorum nota distinctæ. In illis quæ Sirmondus edidit, synodi & conventus ipsi regales, in quibus constituta sunt exhibentur; & quo quisque conventus anno ac loco, quas ad res, & per quos coacti celebratique sunt, exprimitur. Vide sis Sirmondi Præfationem Capitulis Caroli Calvi præmissam, à quo etiam discès, constitutum fuisse Pithœo post capitula Caroli Magni & Ludovici edere quoque, ea quæ à sequentibus Regibus profecta sunt. Capitularia autè vocantur, à capitulis, hæc à capitibus, qua voce notabant leges Regum, ut observat Sirmondus, in Præfat. jam laudata. In Ansegisi, inquit, Abbatis & Benedicti Levitæ Collectionibus, nudæ Regum ac meræ leges sunt, quæ CAPITULA vocabant; Quod & factum in jure nostro videmus, in l. 28. §. 5. C. de administr. tutorum, quanquam & aliter ibidem capitulum interpretari possimus, nempe pro certo articulo, sententia, puncto rei, de qua tractamus & agimus. Dicta autem Capitula propter brevitatē, quia concisè cardinem, summam & caput rei proponebant. Appositè Papias. Capitulum brevis multorum complexio, sic dictum, quod breviter capiat totam summam, sive quod quasi alterius sententiæ caput. Item Catholicon. Capitulum primo parvum caput. Secundo ille parvus locus, in quem conveniunt claustrales. Tertio illa congregatio claustralium. Quarto aliqua distinctio in quolibet libro; unde versus; distinguit, minuit, locat & collectio fertur. & iterum: Capitula librorum dicta, quod breviter capiant & continent aliquam sententiam: sive quasi caput & titulus majoris scripti. Græci etiam in oratione κεφάλαια vocant, quæ Latini capita & summas. Isocrates ad Nicoclem. κεφάλαιον δὲ τῶν εἰρημένων, Summa vero supradictorum. Sic quoque Apostolus ad Hebr. cap. 8. vers. 1. κεφάλαιον δὲ ἐπὶ τοῖς λεγομένοις, τοιοῦτον ἔχομεν ἀρχιερέα. quod vulgatus vertit: Capitulum autem super ea quæ dicuntur. Beza vero. Eorum quæ dicimus hæc summa est. adde ejus notas ibid. Æschines contra Ctesiphontem; ταῦτα κεφάλαια λέγω βεβαιῶν ἐγὼ προερῶ. Plinius lib. 2. cap. 12. Hist. nat. effert appositè: De iis breviter & capitulatim attingam. Inde & capitula, nervosæ summulæ, quæ breviter referunt contenta tractationis majoris. ris. Hinc & nostris capitularibus nomen esse inditum, probabile est, quia concise exhibent summam ejus quod constitutum est. Capitula enim Caroli Magni, non sunt integra acta aut totæ leges, sed cardo & medulla seu potius sententia legis, paucis verbis expressa; ideo capitula distinguuntur ab ipsis integris actis. Alii capitula dicta volunt, quia in capitulis, id est locis ubi Ecclesiastici conveniunt, à capitularibus constituuntur. Alii capitularia, capitulares libros dictos volunt, quia libri illi multa capita complectuntur. Ita forte Glossa in authent. Cassa. C. de Sacros. Eccles. Capitularia interpretatur libros statutorum; quod sequitur Gothofred. ibid. Audi Anton. Augustinum, de emendat. Gratian. lib. 2. dial. 11. pag. nostræ editionis 451.
units.tr: The most learned Jacob Sirmond, a Jesuit and a man of great reputation in letters and antiquity, edited these chapters together with the chapters of later successors in the year 1624 at Paris. That edition, besides the cited capitularies of Charles the Bald, contains those of Louis II, son of Charles, of Carloman, son of King Louis II, and of Charles the Simple, the King, and then follow the coronations of Charles the Bald and of his son Louis, as kings, and also of Judith, daughter, and Hermintrude, wife of Charles. To all of these he added his learned notes, as is his custom. He gathered them from various places and from five old manuscript codices. Of these, the first two, one from the library of John Tilius and the other from the library of Thuanus, went no further than title xvi. The following ones, up to xliii, were taken partly from the books of the Church of Beauvais, partly from those of the Church of Laon, and partly from Metz. The coronations of the kings, which are appended to the chapters, he transcribed from the single copy of the monastery of Lorsch at Liège. Sirmond himself noted in advance the numbers and names of the titles, taken from the longer titles of the manuscripts, for the sake of easier use. The titles of the capitularies of Charles the Bald are xliii; of Louis the Stammerer, iii; of Carloman, ii; of Charles the Simple, ii; the coronations, iv. There is this difference between the Capitularia that Pithou edited and those that Sirmond edited: in the collections of Ansegisus and Benedict there are only the laws of the kings, arranged in almost no order and marked with no note of time or place. In those which Sirmond edited, the synods and the royal assemblies themselves, at which the decrees were made, are set out, and it is stated in what year and place each assembly was held, on what business, and by whom it was summoned and conducted. Please see Sirmond's Preface prefixed to the Capitularies of Charles the Bald, from which you will also learn that Pithou had determined, after the capitularies of Charles the Great and Louis, to publish also those that came from the later kings. Capitularia are so called from capitula, and these from capita, a word by which they marked the laws of the kings, as Sirmond observes in the preface already cited. "In the collections of Ansegisus the abbot and Benedict the Levite," he says, "there are simply the laws of the kings and nothing else, which they called CAPITULA." We see that this was also the practice in our law, in l. 28 §5 C. de administratione tutorum, although there too we could interpret capitulum otherwise, namely as a certain article, opinion, or point of the matter we are treating and discussing. The chapters are so called for brevity, because they set out concisely the hinge, sum and head of the matter. Papias aptly says: "A capitulum is a brief summary of many things, so called because it briefly takes in the whole sum, or because it is, as it were, the head of another opinion." Likewise the Catholicon: "A capitulum is first a small head; second, that small place in which the cloistered brothers meet; third, that assembly of the cloistered brothers; fourth, some division in any book; whence the verse: 'it distinguishes, divides, places, and a collection is produced.'" And again: "Chapters of books are so called because they briefly take in and contain some opinion, or are as it were the head and title of a larger writing." The Greeks too in oratory call kephalaia what the Latins call heads and summaries. Isocrates, to Nicocles: [κεφάλαιον δὲ τῶν εἰρημένων] "and the sum of what has been said." So also the Apostle, to the Hebrews, chapter 8, verse 1: [κεφάλαιον δὲ ἐπὶ τοῖς λεγομένοις, τοιοῦτον ἔχομεν ἀρχιερέα]; which the Vulgate renders: "Now the chief point of the things that are said." But Beza: "This is the sum of what we are saying." Add his notes on the same place. Aeschines, against Ctesiphon: [ταῦτα κεφάλαια λέγω βεβαιῶν ἐγὼ προερῶ]. Pliny, Natural History, book 2, chapter 12, aptly puts it: "I shall touch on these briefly and by way of heads." Hence also capitula are sinewy little summaries, which briefly report the contents of a larger treatment. It is probable that our capitularies were named from this, because they concisely present the sum of what has been enacted. For the chapters of Charles the Great are not complete acts or whole laws, but the hinge and marrow, or rather the sense of the law, expressed in a few words; therefore the chapters are distinguished from the complete acts themselves. Others want the chapters so called because they are enacted by the capitulars in chapters, that is, in the places where churchmen meet. Others want the capitularies, capitulares, to be books so called because those books embrace many chapters. Perhaps this is how the gloss on authent. Cassa, C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis interprets capitularia as "books of statutes," which Gothofredus follows in the same place. Hear Antonius Augustinus, On the emendation of Gratian, book 2, dialogue 11, page 451 of our edition.

units.la: C. Latinam ne vocem, an barbaram esse dicemus Capitulare: sive Capitularia? A. An non recte deducitur à capite capitale crimen, & capitalis homo. C. Recte. A. Sic igitur à capitulo capitularis, & capitulare pro capitulalis quod ineptum esset. sic etiam à sæculo sæcularis, ab angulo angularis dicitur. C. Quis ex veterib. Latinis hac voce usus est? A. Non omnium veterum libros habemus: ex illis deperditis existima hanc erutam vocem fuisse. Acta capituli multi capitularia dicunt, & syndicum capituli
units.tr: C. Shall we say that the word Capitulare, or Capitularia, is Latin, or barbarous? A. Is it not rightly derived from caput, whence capitale, a capital crime, and capitalis, a man deserving death? C. Rightly. A. So then from capitulum comes capitularis, and capitulare rather than capitulalis, which would be awkward. Likewise sæcularis from sæculum, and angularis from angulus. C. Which of the old Latin writers used this word? A. We do not have the books of all the ancients; from those that are lost, judge that this word was dug up from somewhere. Many call the acts of a chapter capitularia, and the syndic of the chapter
