De eo hæc habet Ludovicus Jacob à S. Carolo, in Bibliotheca Pontif. lib. i. pag. 88. Capitulare Gregorii II. datum Martiniano Episcopo, Geor-
units.tr: "...of the chapter, capitularem: that is certainly not the most absurd thing." C. Those who call a book capitulare because it belongs to the chapter seem to err less than those who call a volume capitulare because it is divided into many capitula, and is as it were a collection of many chapters. A. So was the question not whether the word itself was Latin, but about the use of the word in this sense? And indeed I think it was introduced by barbarians, in the times of Charles, Ansegisus and Theodulf. But to return to Gratian: he uses this word in Causa 11, chapter 39. For after citing two constitutions he says: "If anyone contends that these things are obsolete, because they are not found inserted thus in the Code of Justinian, let him know that they were renewed by Charles, who in his Capitularies among other things says: 'We will and command,' etc." Anselm also headed his work: "In the Capitularies of the Emperor Charles." Antonius Augustinus is mistaken, who thinks the word was invented in the time of Charles the Great, Ansegisus and Theodulf, who lived in the ninth century; for at the beginning of the eighth century the Capitulare of Gregory II occurs, who was raised to the Roman bishopric in the year 714. Of him Louis Jacob of St Charles has this, in Bibliotheca Pontificia, book 1, page 88: "The Capitulare of Gregory II, given to the bishop Martinianus and to the presbyter George, who were sent into Bavaria,"

units.la: 216. Capitulare Gregorii secundi Papæ. gio Presbytero &c. in Bavariam ablegatis, legitur etiam tomo 5. Concil. Binii, ex Codice M.S. membranaceo vetustissimo Monasterii Veingarcensis, & ab Eruditissimo Marco Velsero Duumviro Augustano communicato. Extat M.S. in Bibliotheca Bodlejana, ut ex librorum indice edito, colligo. In quo & ego illud observo. Est itaque antiquior Carolo Magno ista denominatio; superioribus enim temporibus & apud Græcos & Latinos κεφάλαια & capita, ut jam probatum, designabant summulas, sententias, concisa dicta, & aliorum longius dictorum compendia; sæpe occurrit vox apud Ciceronem, sed alia atque alia significatione. Item adhibitæ voces capitis & capituli in distinctionibus librorum, quod in Gellio, aliisq; observamus. Sed diu satis nos capitula & capitularia detinuerunt, alii nos vocant collectores, aliæ collectiones; hoc tamen adhuc de Capitulari Caroli Magni & Collectione Ansegisi addendum, eum capitula collegisse mandato & instinctu Otgarii (qui & Odogarius & Audegarius vocatur) Archiepiscopi Moguntini, qui ab an. 826. vel 827. usque ad 847. in Archiepiscopatu Moguntino sedit; de quo Serrarius in rerum Moguntinar. lib. 4. pag. m. 620. Colligo hoc ex versibus istis supr: n: 203. de conjunctione collectionis Ansegisi & Benedicti nedicti Levitae positis; quorum hic reddenda ratio emendatorum. Leguntur vulgo sine sensu: Quosque Pater quondam, collegit nobilis apte Ansegisus ovans, ductus amore Dei. Aut cario demum, quem tunc Maguntia summum Pontificem tenuit, praecipiente pio.
units.tr: "216. The Capitulare of Pope Gregory II." It is also read in volume 5 of the Councils of Binius, from a very old membranous manuscript codex of the monastery of Weingarten, communicated by the most learned Marcus Welser, duumvir of Augsburg. The manuscript is in the Bodleian Library, as I gather from the printed index of books. In this I also observe the following. That name is therefore older than Charles the Great; for in earlier times both among the Greeks and the Latins kephalaia and capita, as already shown, denoted short summaries, sentences, brief sayings, and compendia of longer sayings by others. The word often occurs in Cicero, but with one meaning and another. Likewise the words caput and capitulum were used for the divisions of books, as we observe in Gellius and others. But the chapters and capitularies have held us long enough. Some call us collectors, others collections. Yet this must still be added concerning the capitulary of Charles the Great and the collection of Ansegisus: he gathered the chapters at the command and instigation of Otgar (also called Odogar and Audegar), archbishop of Mainz, who held the see of the archbishopric of Mainz from the year 826 or 827 until 847; of him Serrarius, Rerum Moguntinarum, book 4, page 620. I gather this from the following verses above, n. 203, placed about the joining of the collection of Ansegisus and of Benedict the Levite, in which the reason for the corrections is to be rendered. They are commonly read without sense: "Which the father Ansegisus, a noble man, long ago gathered aptly and joyfully, moved by love of God. Or at last Mainz, which then held the chief bishop, with the pious man commanding."

units.la: Illa aut cario, sunt nullius momenti, & relicta à Pithoeo, qui antiquam scripturam in prima editione (secundam enim non vidi) non satis percepit, aut examinavit, itaque restitui veram, de quo nullus dubito lectionem Otgario demum, quem tum Maguntia &c.
units.tr: Those readings aut cario are of no importance. They were left by Pithoeus, who did not sufficiently perceive or examine the old writing in the first edition (I have not seen the second). So I have restored the true reading, about which I have no doubt: Otgario demum, quem tum Maguntia &c.

units.la: Cui emendationi tempus concinit, vixerunt enim eodem tempore Ansegisus & Otgarius seculo nono, saltem usque ad annum quadragesimum septimum. Deinde ex Praefatione Benedicti Levitae, supra recitata scimus, Riculphum & Otgarium, (qui ibidem, quod magis adhuc ad veterem scripturam accedit Autcarius vocatur) studiosos fuisse in colligendis istiusmodi Legibus & Capitulis ecclesiasticis. Illud quoque ex Pithoei praefatione observavimus, capitularia antiqua non habuisse titulum. Qui in Pithoei editione est, illum Joh. Tilius, ex non adeo vetusto codice editioni suae imperfectae praefixit, quem etiam Pithoeus retinuit, tinuit. Non est animus contra Baronium multis hic excurrere, an capitula hæc Imperatorum & Regum Galliæ,quod ille vult, cum consensu & approbatione summi Pontificis scripta & promulgata sint, hoc enim ad historiam quam texi mus nil facit. Negant id Galli in hodiernum usque diem. Dicit quidem Benedictus Levita in Præfatione sua fuisse auctoritate Apostolica (sic tum temporis sedes Romana vocabatur) firmata, sed & absque ista auctoritate valuissent. Verum hoc ideo Benedictus Levita,sedi Romanæ addictus, ut supra quoque monitum, suæ Præfationi inseruit, ut & ex hoc capite capitulis alibi auctoritatem conciliaret; deinde etiam observandum hac in re faciliorem fuisse Ludovicum Pium sub quo, vixit Benedictus, quam Carolum ejus Patrem. Sed ut dixi, hæc sunt alterius loci. Habet multa huc facientia Nobilissimus Mornæus in Mysterio iniquitatis, quod Baronio oppositi; quæ legisse non pœnitebit.
units.tr: This emendation agrees with the period, for Ansegisus and Otgarius lived at the same time in the ninth century, at least until the year 847. Then, from the preface of Benedict the Levite quoted above, we know that Riculphus and Otgarius (who there, coming even closer to the old reading, is called Autcarius) were zealous in collecting such laws and ecclesiastical chapters. We have also observed from Pithoeus' preface that the ancient capitularies had no title. The one in Pithoeus' edition was prefixed by Johannes Tilius to his imperfect edition, taken from a not very old manuscript, and Pithoeus kept it. It is not my intention to range at length here against Baronius, over whether these chapters of the emperors and kings of Gaul were written and promulgated with the consent and approval of the supreme Pontiff, as he maintains; for that has nothing to do with the history I am weaving. The Gauls deny it to this very day. Benedict the Levite indeed says in his preface that the chapters were confirmed by apostolic authority (so the Roman see was then called), but they would have had force even without that authority. Benedict the Levite, however, devoted to the Roman see, as noted above, inserted this into his preface so that from this point he might also win authority for the chapters elsewhere. Further, it should be observed in this matter that Louis the Pious, under whom Benedict lived, was more easygoing than Charles his father. But as I said, these are matters for another place. The most noble Mornaeus has much that bears on this in his Mystery of Iniquity, written against Baronius; you will not regret reading it.

units.la: Hoc eodem tempore, nempe seculo nono incipiente, in lucem prodiit Collectio Impostoris nequissimi, qui se Isidori nomine tegere ausus fuit. De quo verissimum est elogium Magni Blondelli. Erepsit, inquit, ante annos 800. è solo Iberico, lumbricus nescio quis Isidori Hispalensis larva tectus, qui pilissimas vilissimas fæces, pretiosissimis antiquorum urbis Episcoporum titulis appositis, sempiternæ gloriæ, (si divina providentia pateretur) commendaret, octo propemodum seculorum decurrit ordo, tantisper dum Latinorum omnium patientia abuteretur, excæcatique orbis oculum suis sublineret offuciis, ingenio hebes, vita turpis, existimatione damnatus, impudentia atque audacia, super quam dici potest, fretus, projectæ nequitiæ rabula; & postea, vocat, nebulonem perditissimum, eorum omnium qui scientiam ex conscientiæ puritate æstimant, cauterio inustum. & ejus collectionem, mendaciorum mercem. Collegit Impostor ille vel potius supposuit Pontificibus Romanis primis à Clemente usque ad Siricium epistolas Decretales; cum vel unica compilatio Dionysii, primi Decretalium & seduli conquisitoris, demonstret, ultra Siricii tempora eum nullas invenisse ab Episcopis Romanis scriptas. Simile audaciæ exemplum in omni antiquitate reperiri non memini; posset quidem comparari cum hoc nebulone, Johannes Annius Viterbiensis Monachus, qui Berofo libros quinque antiquitatum, Manethoni supplementorum ad Berofum librum unum, Xenophonti Æquivoca, Fabio Pictori de aureo seculo & origine urbis Romæ libros duos, Myrsilo Lesbio de Bello pelasgico librum, M. Catoni fragmenta. gmenta de originibus, Archilocho librum de temporibus, Antonino Pio Cæsari Augusto itinerarium, C. Sempronio de divisione Italiæ librum, Matasthani (Megastheni volebat dicere) de judicio temporum & annalium Persarum librum, Philoni Breviarium de temporibus suppositit, & suppositia commentariis illustravit; vide sis de hac fraude præ multis aliis Amicum nostrum Clariss: & Consultiss: Dn. Vincent. Placcium, JC. in Notis ad Johan. Rhodii auctores supposititios, quos præmisit Syntagmati nuper edito de Scriptoribus anonymis & pseudonymis, pag. 12. & seqq. & multos ab eo ibidem citatos. Sed quanto periculosius est errare in sacris, quam in profanis; ita multo gravior in iis quoque est impostura & suppositio. Quare & multis parasangis Isidori illius suppositititii fraudulentia præcellit illam Annii Viterbiensis, quia ejus fraus tantum circa historiam, Isidori vero circa religionem, illius circa ethnicas, hujus vero circa Christianas res occupata est. Epistolas autem decretales, ut vocant, suppositit nebulo ille sequentibus Episcopis Romanis. Clementi quinque; Aniceto tres; Euaristo duas; Alexandro tres; Sixto duas; Telesphoro unam; Hygino duas; Pio quatuor; Aniceto unam; Soteri duas; Eleutherio unam; Victori duas; ZephyZephyrino duas; Callisto duas; Urbano unam; Pontiano duas; Anterio unam; Fabiano tres; Cornelio duas; Lucio unam; Stephano duas; Dionysio duas; Felici tres; Eutychiano duas; Cajo unam; Marcellino duas; Marcello duas; Eusebio tres; Melchiadi Epistolam unam, de primitiva Ecclesia, & Munificentia Constantini Magni Imperatoris erga eandem, dein quoque decretalem Epistolam unam. Synodo Nicæna Epistolam ad Sylvestrem Papam, & Sylvestri rescriptum ad eam; Ægyptiis ad Marcum Papam Epistolam, & Marco responsoriam ad eandem; Julio Epistolam unam; Orientalibus ad Julium unam, & Julio responsionem; Liberio Epistolam XII. Athanasio & Episcopis Ægypti Epistolam ad Liberium, & Liberio responsoriam ad eam Epistolam. Athanasio & Ægyptiis ad Felicem secundum Epistolam, & Felici secundo responsoriam, deinde eidem alteram quoque suppositi; Damaso Pontifici Epistolam tertiam ad Hieronymum, & Hieronymo rescriptionem; Africano concilio epistolam ad Damasum, Damaso responsoriam, quartam epistolam, eidem quintam de Chorepiscopis, & septimam ad Episcopos Italiæ. Aurelio Carthaginensi Episcopo ad Damasum, & Damaso rescriptum; Siricio Papæ quartam Epistolam. Anastasio Papæ, duas; Sixto III. Epistolam tertiam; Leoni epistolam lxxxviii. Joanni primo Epistolas duas. Felici quarto Epistolas duas; Bonifacio secundo, epistolam unam, Justino & Justiniano exemplar precum; Johanni secundo Epistolam unam; Agapeto Epistolam quintam, Silverio epistolam unam; Amatori Epistolam ad Silverium, & Silverio responsoriam ad eam, quæ est epistola secunda; Pelagio primo epistolam unam; Johanni tertio epistolam unam; Benedicto primo Epistolam decretalem; Pelagio secundo epistolam primam, secundam, octavam, nonam; Gregorio Magno privilegium Medardi Monasterio collatum; Felici Siciliæ Episcopo Epistolam ad Gregorium Magnum; Gregorioque Magno rescriptionem, quæ est lib. xii. epistol. 32. Deusdedit Papæ Epistolam unam. Hæ sunt merces Impostoris quas supposuit, & orbi pro genuinis veterum urbis Episcoporum epistolis impudenter obtrusit: quas sunt, qui defendunt collegisse Isidorum Hispalensem Episcopum; inter quos est Possevinus, in apparat. sacr. parum tamen sibi constans, imo contrarius, utpote qui in verbo Isidorus Hisp. eum facit auctorem. In verbo Burchardus, contrariam sententiam tuetur, eos nempe errare, qui hanc (compilatorum canonum) laudem S. Isidoro Hispalensi tribuunt. Nititur primo Posse-
units.tr: At this same time, that is, at the beginning of the ninth century, there came to light the collection of a most wicked impostor, who dared to hide behind the name of Isidore. Of him the words of Magnus Blondellus are very true: There crept forth, he says, some earthworm or other, about 800 years ago, from the Spanish soil, shrouded in the mask of Isidore of Seville, who would have commended the vilest dregs to everlasting glory (if divine providence had allowed it) by attaching the most precious titles of the ancient bishops of the city. A span of almost eight centuries ran on while he abused the patience of all Latins and smeared his cosmetics over the eye of the blinded world; dull of wit, foul of life, condemned in reputation, relying on an impudence and audacity beyond what can be said, a wrangling peddler of cast-off wickedness; and afterwards, a most desperate scoundrel, branded with the cautery of all those who judge learning by the purity of conscience. And his collection he calls a merchandise of lies. This impostor, or rather forger, put forward as the letters of the Roman Pontiffs, from Clement to Siricius, the Decretal Epistles. Yet the single compilation of Dionysius, the first collector of Decretals and a diligent searcher, shows that beyond the time of Siricius he found no letters written by Roman bishops. I do not recall finding a similar example of audacity in all antiquity. One could indeed compare this scoundrel with John Annius of Viterbo, a monk, who forged five books of antiquities under the name of Berosus, one book of supplements to Berosus under Manetho, the Equivocals under Xenophon, two books on the golden age and the origin of the city of Rome under Fabius Pictor, a book on the Pelasgian war under Myrsilus of Lesbos, fragments on origins under M. Cato, a book on times under Archilochus, an itinerary under the emperor Antoninus Pius Augustus, a book on the division of Italy under C. Sempronius, a book on the judgement of times and the annals of the Persians under Matasthenes (he meant to say Megasthenes), and a breviary on times under Philo; and he illustrated these supposititious works with commentaries. On this fraud, among many others, see our friend the most distinguished and most learned Dr. Vincent Placcius, JC, in his notes to the supposititious authors of Johann Rhodius, which he prefixed to his recently published Syntagma on anonymous and pseudonymous writers, p. 12 and following, and the many authors he cites there. But as it is more dangerous to err in sacred matters than in profane ones, so the imposture and forgery is much graver in the sacred sphere. Hence the fraud of that supposititious Isidore far surpasses that of Annius of Viterbo by many parasangs, because the latter's fraud concerns only history, and the former's religion; Annius' concerns the pagan matters, Isidore's the Christian. The scoundrel forged the so-called Decretal Epistles under the following Roman bishops: five under Clement; three under Anicetus; two under Evaristus; three under Alexander; two under Sixtus; one under Telesphorus; two under Hyginus; four under Pius; one under Anicetus; two under Soter; one under Eleutherius; two under Victor; two under Zephyrinus; two under Callistus; one under Urban; two under Pontianus; one under Anterus; three under Fabian; two under Cornelius; one under Lucius; two under Stephen; two under Dionysius; three under Felix; two under Eutychian; one under Caius; two under Marcellinus; two under Marcellus; three under Eusebius; one letter to Miltiades, on the primitive Church and the munificence of the emperor Constantine the Great toward it, and then one decretal letter as well; to the Synod of Nicaea a letter to Pope Sylvester, and Sylvester's rescript in reply; to the Egyptians a letter to Pope Mark, and Mark's answer to the same; one letter to Julius; to the Eastern bishops one letter to Julius, and Julius' reply; twelve letters to Liberius; to Athanasius and the bishops of Egypt a letter to Liberius, and Liberius' answer to that letter; to Athanasius and the Egyptians a second letter to Felix, and a reply to Felix the second, then another likewise forged for the same; to Pope Damasus a third letter to Jerome, and Jerome's reply; to the African council a letter to Damasus, Damasus' answer, a fourth letter, a fifth to the same on the chorepiscopi, and a seventh to the bishops of Italy; to Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, a letter to Damasus, and Damasus' rescript; to Pope Siricius a fourth letter; to Pope Anastasius, two; to Sixtus III, a third letter; to Leo, letter eighty-eight; to John I, two letters; to Felix IV, two letters; to Boniface II, one letter; to Justin and Justinian, a copy of prayers; to John II, one letter; to Agapetus a fifth letter; to Silverius, one letter; to Amator a letter to Silverius, and Silverius' reply to it, which is the second letter; to Pelagius I, one letter; to John III, one letter; to Benedict I, a decretal letter; to Pelagius II, the first, second, eighth and ninth letters; to Gregory the Great, a privilege granted to the monastery of Medard; to Felix, bishop of Sicily, a letter to Gregory the Great; and to Gregory the Great, a reply, which is book twelve, letter thirty-two; to Pope Deusdedit, one letter. These are the wares of the impostor which he forged and shamelessly thrust upon the world as the genuine letters of the ancient bishops of the city. Some defend that Isidore, bishop of Seville, compiled them, among whom is Possevinus in his Sacred Apparatus, though he is scarcely consistent with himself, indeed contrary, since under the heading Isidorus Hispalensis he makes him the author; under the heading Burchardus he holds the opposite view, namely that those err who ascribe this praise (of compiling the canons) to St. Isidore of Seville. Possevinus first relies on this flimsy argument, that many of the words read in the preface of this collection are found in the fifth book of the Etymologies of Isidore of Seville. This argument presses the contrary view more strongly, unless we are willing to say that Isidore of Seville, a learned man, was an empty babbler who without need…

units.la: Possevinus hoc futili argumento, quod multa verba, quæ in Præfatione collectionis hujus leguntur, extant in libro quinto etymologiarum Isidori Hispalensis. Quod argumentum fortius stringit pro contraria sententia, nisi velimus dicere Isidorum Hispalensem Hominem Doctum, esse inanem blateronem, qui sine necessitate recoctam crambem bis lectoribus apponat. Tum etiam constat, libros etymologiarum non esse editos ab ipso Isidoro, sed à Braulione post mortem Isidori, teste Ildephonso, ad finem libri Isidori de Viris illustribus, & Braulione in Catalogo operum ipsius Isidori, qui ambo cum Isidoro vixerunt. Idem quoque colligi potest ex ipsius Isidori Epistola ad Braulionem, quæ libris originum est præfixa. Cum itaque post mortem demum Isidori editi sint libri etymologiarum, qui eos descripsit, id necessario debet post mortem ejus fecisse. Alterum argumentum Possevini adhuc futilius est: quod non solum perantiquus sit hic Isidorus, qui Mercator dicitur, cujus collectio protenditur à canonibus Apostolorum, usque ad concilium Hispalense secundum, habeturque in duobus codicibus Vaticanæ Bibliothecæ, & uno Monasterii Dominicani S. Mariæ supra Minervam; verum etiam quod eidem ipsi concilio Hispalensi interfuit, ac primas tenuit. Præter enim illud, quod nulla vis concludens Logica huic argumento insit, illud perabsurdum imo impossibile est; quod collector ille Pseudisidorus, cum dicatur ad secundæ synodi Hispalensis tempora perduxisse collectionem, tamen faciat mentionem Gregorii secundi & tertii, item Zachariæ Pontificum Romanorum, eorumque epistolas laudet, qui omnes post annum DCC. post synodum Hispalensem secundam, & diu post mortem Isidori Hispalensis Episcopi vixerunt, utpote, quem qui longissime vitam ejus protendunt, mortuum dicunt anno 647. ut Vasæus in Chronic. vel anno 643. ut Rodericus Toletanus, lib. 2. Histor. c. 18. vel anno 635, ut officium sanctorum Hispaniæ, quod sequitur Andr. Schottus, cujus est anonymûs edita Bibliotheca Hispaniæ, tom. 2. classi. 1. pag. 183. vel anno 636, quæ verior est sententia, Æra nimirum 674, Cinthila regnum ineunte, Heraclii Augusti anno 26. ut Redemtus Diaconus de Obitu Isidori, testis oculatus & Braulio, Ecclesiæ Cæsaraugustanæ Episcopus, in catalogo operum Isidori Lucas Tudensis antistes lib. 3. Chron. & alii multi; Quod & probat Magnus Blondellus in Pseudisidori prolegumenis. cap. 2. In quo tractatu tam plene hunc Isidorum ejusque commenta, item Fr. Turriani hominis, ad propugnanda apocrypha nati, apologiam pro iftis decretalibus, feu potius nugis, refutavit, ut vix aliquid addi poffit. De quo veriffimum eft elogium, quod ei fcripfit Joh. Dalæus, de Pfeudepigraphis Apoftolicis. lib. 3. cap. 5. pag. 476. Itaque, funt verba ejus, nihil ad Gelafium quicquid bonus ille Zephyrinus in ftraminea fua epiftola delirat. Quæcunque vero pro ea conftituenda in hoc ipfo opere attulit Turrianus, ea accurate diffolvit Doctiffimus Blondellus nofter; ipfamque & cæteras ejusdem commatis priorum urbis præfulum ad Siricium usque Latinas epiftolas, ita plane, liquidoque demonftravit poft a. D. 800. à nequiffimo & imperitiffimo Impoftore fuiffe confictas; ut ne ex ipfis quidem adversariis quisquam in eum totis his viginti annis, à quo fcilicet ipfius liber lucem vidit, pro epiftolis certator furrexerit. & poftea pag. 493. Neque nos necesse eft in confodiendis iftis Decretalibus immorari; quas eruditiffimus Blondellus noster proprio ac fingulari opere copiosiffime atque accuratiffime impugnavit, ac profligavit, sigillatim confutatis iis omnibus, quæ pro illis Turrianus totis quatuor verbosiffimis libris attulerat; clariffimeque oftendit, eas omnes epiftolas ex ejusdem Impoftoris officina circa noni fæculi initia prodiiffe. Tertium, quo pugnat Possevinus, argumentum est, Quod constans ferme fama per omnia tempora percrebuerit, auctorem collectionis stionis ctionis ejus fuisse Isidorum Hispalensem. Hincmarus Rhemensis Archiep. in libro de synodis, Joh. Gerson, Trithemius testantur ab eodem Isidoro Librum Decretorum fuisse conscriptum: Quartum vero argumentum ducit inde, quod expurgatores atque emendatores Decreti ac Decretalium Gregorii decimi tertii Pont. Maximi jussu editarum, in hanc ipsam videntur sat liquido propendere sententiam, sicuti initio ante corpus decreti significarunt, quamobrem & Collector sive Compilator, est dictus. Quibus addere poterat Possevinus Pighium Hierarch. Eccles. lib. 6. c. 6. Coccium Thesauri Catholi. tom. 1. lib. 7. art. 6. Bellarminum de Roman. Pont. lib. 2. cap. 14. Turrianum pro Sramineis illis & suppositititiis epistolis lib. 5. cap. 23. Pamelium, in Tertullian. de pudic. cap. 1. si plus recentibus novisque testibus deferre & iis pugnare voluisset; quam ab oculatis Braulione & Ildephonso, qui cum ipso Isidoro vixerunt, ejusque operum catalogos reliquerunt, veritatem petere; qui nullibi collectionem hanc, aut ullam aliam ei adscribunt. Ex quibus assatim apparet, non fuisse hujus collectionis auctorem Isidorum Hispalensem antistitem, sed alium esse ab eo diversum, qui vel idem cum eo nomen habuit, vel ejus nomen per fraudem & falsi crimen adsumsit & cognomine distinguitur. stinguitur;est autem illud in quibusdã libris, Peccatoris,quod ex facto in eum quadrat; vel ut alii libri manuscripti ferunt,Mercatoris.vid. Baron. ad Martyrol. 4. Aprilis. & Ant.Augusti. lib. 1. de emend. Grat. dial.6. pag.101. & 102. nostrae editionis. Prius illud adsumere potuisse conjicit Blondellus, quia sæpius exquisitis phrasibus peccata deploravisse pœnitentem Isidorum Hispalensem, cujus nomine se tegere voluit,compererat; vel quia alios id ex modestia epitheton in subscriptionibus suis addidisse legerat. Sic in concilio sexto Toletano Silva; in septimo Basconius, Gotomarus, Farus, Sona; duodecimo Julianus & Liuba, alii in aliis subscripserunt, quos forte imitari voluit; & quid ni nunc retineret homo peccator, qui tam multa peccavit, finxit, mentitus est & alios decepit; cui ludus fuit Dei & hominum patientiam tentare? Mercatoris vero denominatio unde proficiscatur in obscuro est; fatente ipso Blondello; subnectit tamen. l. c. Quidni Mercator dicatur, qui tot scorias conquisivit, quas specioso titulorum augustiorum velamine circumtectas Christianis venales obtruderet, & callidiorum quos prisca tulit ætas surum vota nuncupare è re sua duxisse videtur, Sancta Laverna, da mihi fallere, da Sanctum justumque videri? Creditum fuit Hispanum fuisse & ex Hispania allatas has merces, quia Hispani Antistitis nomen habuit, vel adsumsit. Sed hoc displicet Clarissimo Blondello, primum quia isto seculo, nempe Caroli Magni Hispani durissimo barbarorum jugo presli, si non oppressi fuerunt, ita ut de supponendis Canonibus & Decretalibus non, sed magis de vita & quali quali cura Ecclesiae atque exercitio religionis solliciti fuerint; Deinde, quia parce nimis Hispaniae ejusque Provinciarum meminit, aut pau- cissimas decretales ad Hispanicas provincias commentus est, cum tamen plurimas ad Gallos Italosque dictatas mentiatur. Bis me- minit tantum Hispaniae, nempe Pseudo- Sixtus II. in Ep. 2. & PseudoMelchiades; bis Beticae, Pseudo Anterus scilicet, & Pseu- doEutychianus epist. 1. semel Cordubensis provinciae, PseudoDionysius nempe epist. 2, quod non credendum fecisse Hispanum, etiam de patriae gloria ex Pseudepigraphis scriptoribus paranda sollicitus. Tertio, quia in turbulenta harum epistolarum congerie, multi GalloFrancorum & Longobardorum Idiotismi leguntur, Hispanorum vero, quales ex Eterii & Eulogii scriptis annotari possunt a curiosis nulli. Conjicit itaque eum fuisse GermanoFrancum, vel GalloFrancum, idque primum ob sermonis barbari, & Idio- tismorum simorum affinitatem, quam habet cum scriptoribus temporum Caroli Magni, Stephani scilicet tertii & quarti, Adriani primi, Leonis tertii & successorum epistolis, Anastasii Bibliothecarii scriptis, GermanoFrancicis sub Pipino, Carolo & Ludovico Pio congregatis conciliis, & Capitularibus Caroli M. & Ludovici Pii & Caroli Calvi libris. Deinde si spurcissimi sermonis vitia abessent, absurdissima illa commenta imperitissimum historiæ politiæque non modo primitivæ Ecclesiæ, sed etiam veteris Romanorum reipublicæ nebulonem produnt, non excedere eum Caroli Magni ætatem. In hunc censum refer priscorum Magistratuum confiēta nomina. Archiflamines, Primiflamines, primates legis seculi, primos legis,seculi Doctores. vide sis Pseudo-Clementis Epist. 1. Item, Primates, Archiepiscopos, Patriarchas etiam universales in Ecclesia ante seculum quartum ignotos; Huc quoque refer appellationes ex toto orbe ad Romanum Episcopum. Huc paradoxa vix opinabilia. Non licere populis, imo nulli fas esse Episcopos accusare; Concilia hæc sola rata esse, quæ Antistes Romanus rata habuerit; Licere quidem Metropolitis Episcoporum causas audire, at solius Papæ esse sententiam definitivam pronunciare; Tertiò, quoque videtur de patria conjectura duei
units.tr: Possevinus relies on this trivial argument: that many of the words read in the preface of this collection also occur in the fifth book of the Etymologies of Isidore of Seville. This argument actually weighs more strongly on the opposite side, unless we are willing to say that Isidore of Seville, a learned man, was an empty babbler who served up warmed-over hash to his readers for no reason. Moreover, it is established that the books of the Etymologies were not published by Isidore himself but by Braulio after Isidore's death, as witnessed by Ildephonsus at the end of Isidore's book On Illustrious Men, and by Braulio in the Catalogue of Isidore's own works. Both of them lived with Isidore. The same can be gathered from Isidore's own Letter to Braulio, which is prefixed to the books of the Origins. Since the books of the Etymologies were published only after Isidore's death, the one who copied them must necessarily have done so after his death. Possevinus's second argument is even more trivial: that this Isidore, who is called the Merchant, is very ancient, that his collection runs from the canons of the Apostles down to the Second Council of Seville, and that it is found in two manuscripts of the Vatican Library and in one of the Dominican monastery of Santa Maria sopra Minerva; and indeed that he himself took part in that same Council of Seville and held the first place. For apart from the fact that this argument has no conclusive logical force, the following is utterly absurd, indeed impossible: that this compiler, the pseudo-Isidore, is said to have brought his collection down to the times of the Second Council of Seville, and yet he mentions Gregory II and III, and likewise the Roman Pontiffs Zacharias, and quotes their letters. All of these lived more than 700 years after the Second Council of Seville and long after the death of Isidore, Bishop of Seville. Those who extend his life the furthest say he died in 647, as Vasaeus in Chronicon does, or in 643, as Rodericus of Toledo in Historia, book 2, chapter 18 does, or in 635, as the Office of the Saints of Spain, which Andreas Schott follows (Schott being the author of the anonymous Bibliotheca Hispana), vol. 2, class 1, p. 183 does; or in 636, which is the truer opinion, namely in the year of the Era 674, at the beginning of the reign of Sisenand, in the twenty-sixth year of the Emperor Heraclius. So say Redemptus the deacon On the Death of Isidore, an eyewitness, and Braulio, Bishop of the Church of Zaragoza, in the catalogue of Isidore's works, and Lucas, Bishop of Tuy, in Chronicon, book 3, and many others. Magnus Blondellus also proves this in the Prolegomena to the Pseudo-Isidore, chapter 2. In that treatise he has refuted so fully this Isidore and his inventions, and likewise the apology of Turrianus, a man born to defend spurious works, for those decretals, or rather trifles, that scarcely anything more can be added. Of him John Dallaeus wrote a most true tribute, On Apostolic Pseudepigrapha, book 3, chapter 5, p. 476. These are his words: nothing that the good Zephyrinus raves about in his straw-stuffed letter has any bearing on Gelasius. Whatever Turrianus brought forward in this very work to establish that, our most learned Blondellus has carefully dissolved. He has so plainly and clearly demonstrated that this letter and the other Latin letters of the early Roman bishops, down to Siricius, were fabricated after the year 800 by a most wicked and most ignorant impostor, that not one of the opponents themselves has come forward as a champion of these letters in all the twenty years since his book saw the light. And afterwards, p. 493: Nor is it necessary for us to dwell on demolishing those decretals, which our most learned Blondellus has attacked and overthrown most copiously and most accurately in his own separate work, refuting one by one all the things that Turrianus had brought forward for them in his four very wordy books. He has most clearly shown that all those letters came out of the workshop of that same impostor around the beginning of the ninth century. The third argument with which Possevinus fights is this: that a fairly constant report has spread through all ages that the author of the collection was Isidore of Seville. Hincmar, Archbishop of Reims, in his book On Councils, and John Gerson and Trithemius testify that the Book of Decrees was written by this same Isidore. The fourth argument he draws from the fact that those who corrected and emended the Decree and the Decretals published by order of Pope Gregory XIII seem fairly clearly to incline to this very opinion, as they indicated at the beginning, before the body of the Decree; for which reason the collector or compiler is also so called. To these he could have added Pighius Hierarchia Ecclesiastica, book 6, chapter 6, Coccius Thesaurus Catholicus, vol. 1, book 7, article 6, Bellarmine On the Roman Pontiff, book 2, chapter 14, Turrianus in defence of those straw and spurious letters, book 5, chapter 23, and Pamelius in Tertullian, On Modesty, chapter 1, if he had wished to bring forward more recent and newer witnesses and to set them against the truth sought from the eyewitnesses Braulio and Ildephonsus, who lived with Isidore himself and left catalogues of his works. They nowhere ascribe this collection, or any other, to him. From these things it is abundantly clear that the author of this collection was not Isidore, Bishop of Seville, but some other person, different from him, who either had the same name or assumed his name by fraud and the crime of forgery, and who is distinguished by a surname. In some books that surname is Peccator, which fits him because of what he did; or, as other manuscript books have it, Mercator. See Baronius on the Martyrology, 4 April, and Antonius Augustinus On the Emendation of Gratian, book 1, dialogue 6, pp. 101 and 102 of our edition. Blondellus conjectures that he could have assumed the former, because he had learned that Isidore of Seville, whose name he wished to conceal himself behind, often lamented his sins in exquisite phrases when he repented; or because he had read that others, out of modesty, added that epithet to their signatures. So in the Sixth Council of Toledo, Silva; in the Seventh, Basconius, Gotomarus, Farus, Sona; in the Twelfth, Julianus and Liuba, and others in others, signed in this way, and he perhaps wished to imitate them. And why should not the sinner, who sinned so much, invented, lied, and deceived others, and for whom it was a game to test the patience of God and of men, now keep it? As for the name Mercator, where it comes from is obscure, Blondellus himself admits; nevertheless he adds, loc. cit.: Why should he not be called Mercator, who gathered so many dregs, which he tried to foist on Christians as saleable goods, wrapped in the splendid covering of august titles; and who seems to have judged it to his advantage to make vows to the more cunning men of ancient times, saying: "Holy Laverna, grant me to deceive, grant me to seem holy and just"? It was believed that he was a Spaniard and that these wares came from Spain, because he had or assumed the name of a Spanish bishop. But this displeases the most distinguished Blondellus, first because in that century, in the time of Charlemagne, the Spaniards were pressed, if not crushed, under the very harsh yoke of the barbarians, so that they were concerned with the lives and the poor condition of the Church and the practice of religion, not with forging canons and decretals. Second, because he mentions Spain and its provinces too sparingly, or devises very few decretals for the Spanish provinces, although he falsely attributes very many to the Gauls and Italians. He mentions Spain only twice, namely in the pseudo-Sixtus II, Letter 2, and the pseudo-Melchiades; he mentions Baetica twice, namely the pseudo-Anterus, and the pseudo-Eutychianus, Letter 1; once the province of Cordoba, namely the pseudo-Dionysius, Letter 2. It is not to be believed that a Spaniard would have done this, even one anxious to win glory for his homeland from pseudepigraphic writers. Third, because in this turbulent heap of letters many idioms of the Gauls, the Franks, and the Lombards are read, but none of the Spanish idioms, such as curious readers can note from the writings of Eterius and Eulogius. He therefore conjectures that he was a German-Frank or a Gallo-Frank, and this first because of the affinity of his barbarous speech and very base idioms with the writers of the time of Charlemagne: the letters of Stephen III and IV, Hadrian I, Leo III and their successors, the writings of Anastasius the Librarian, the German-Frankish councils gathered under Pepin, Charles and Louis the Pious, the Capitularies of Charlemagne, Louis the Pious and Charles the Bald. Next, even if the vices of a most foul style were absent, those absurd inventions reveal a writer who was utterly ignorant not only of the history and politics of the primitive Church but also of the ancient Roman commonwealth, and that he did not live beyond the age of Charlemagne. To this category belong the invented names of ancient magistrates: archiflamines, primiflamines, primates of the age's law, the first teachers of the age's law; see the pseudo-Clement, Letter 1. Likewise primates, archbishops, patriarchs, even universal ones, unknown in the Church before the fourth century. To this too belong appeals from the whole world to the Roman bishop. To this belong paradoxes scarcely to be credited: that it is not permitted to the people, indeed that it is right for no one, to accuse bishops; that only those councils are valid which the Roman prelate has approved; that metropolitans may indeed hear the causes of bishops, but that only the Pope may pronounce the definitive sentence. Thirdly, a conjecture about his homeland also seems to be drawn from

units.la: Quod statim duci posse, quod cum quinque Epistolas ad Hispanos tantum, ad Italos & Campanos octo, ad Ægyptios tres, ad Afros & Mauros duas, ad Orientales quinque, ad Gallos Germanosque decem sinxerit, ut exinde Galliam Vetetibus urbis Episcopis charam forte ostenderet. Quartum argumentum Blondellus pro patria hujus nebulonis ducit, quod maleferiatus Impostor inter alia plurima, post annum 700. edita scripta, Bonifacii Moguntini Epistolam ad Ethibaldum Regem, post annum Domini 744. datam, & Cangith Abbatissæ Epist. aliam post annum 720. ad eundem Bonifacium scriptam deflorarit. Quæ familiares epistolæ vix eo seculo in Hispanorum, tam longe Moguntia dissitorum, nullum commercium cum iis habentium & vix animas trahentium manus venire, Germano-vero Franci eas habere poterant, quia inter eos Bonifacius ab anno 719. usque 754. vixit. Quintum pro hac sententia adducit, quod primi omnium Moguntini, epistolarum harum, Romanis Pontificibus suppositarum collectionem in medium protraxerint, & per totum orbem disseminaverint. Quod probat Præfatio Benedicti Levitæ, quam supra num: 196. retulimus, verba autem huc facientia, pag. 212, linea nona & sequentibus inveniuntur. Aliud hujus rei testimonium anonymi exhibuimus numero marg. 201. Quibus tertium adjungo ex Hincmari Rhemensis Archiepiscopi libro, adversus Hincmarum Laudunensem post annum 870. scripto cap. 24: hoc nimirum. Quia forte putasti neminem alium eosdem sententias vel ipsas epistolas praeter te habere, & idcirco talia libere te existimasti colligere, res mira est, cum de ipsis sententiis plena sit ista terra: Sicut & de libro collectarum Epistolarum ab Isidoro, quem de Hispania allatum Riculphus Moguntinus Episcopus, in hujusmodi, sicut & in capitulis Regiis studiosus (alii monent in M. S. curiosus legi) obtinuit, & ista regiones ex illo repleri fecit. Ex quibus testimoniis Blondellus concludit ex scriniis praesulum Moguntinorum promanasse primum & disseminatas esse hasce suppositicias merces primorum urbis Episcoporum; sive Riculphi, qui anno 786. vel 787. ad Episcopatum venit, & obiit anno 814. vel 815. vid. Serrarii Histor. rer. Mogunt. lib. 4. pag. 613. & seqq. sive, quod magis adhuc probat, aliorum qui Riculpho supervixerunt arte conquisitas fuisse. Non obstante Hincmari testimonio, qui credidit sub Riculpho innotuisse, & eum ex Hispaniis allatas, in vulgus sparsisse; Quia adsunt argu
units.tr: This can be inferred at once: he invented five letters to the Spanish alone, eight to the Italians and Campanians, three to the Egyptians, two to the Africans and Moors, five to the Orientals, and ten to the Gauls and Germans. Perhaps he meant to show that Gaul was dear to the ancient bishops of the city. Blondel draws a fourth argument for this rogue's homeland. The wicked impostor, among many other things, plundered writings published after the year 700, namely a letter of Boniface of Mainz to King Ethelbald, dated after the year of the Lord 744, and another letter written to that same Boniface by the abbess Cangith after the year 720. Such familiar letters could hardly have come into the hands of the Spanish in that century, since Spain was so far distant from Mainz, had no dealings with them, and scarcely had any contact with them. The Franks, however, could have had them, since Boniface lived among them from 719 to 754. The fifth argument Blondel adduces for this view is that the first of all the men of Mainz brought forth a collection of these letters, falsely ascribed to the Roman pontiffs, and spread them throughout the world. The preface of Benedict the Levite, which we quoted above at number 196, proves this, and the words relevant to it are found on page 212, line nine and following. We have given another testimony to this matter from an anonymous writer at marginal number 201. To these I add a third, from the book of Hincmar, Archbishop of Reims, written after the year 870 against Hincmar of Laon, chapter 24, which says: Perhaps you thought that no one else had these opinions or these very letters besides yourself, and so you thought you could freely collect such things. It is a strange matter, since this land is full of those same opinions, just as it is full of the book of collected letters by Isidore, which Riculf, bishop of Mainz, a man zealous in such matters as in the royal capitularies (others note that it is read in the manuscript as "curious"), obtained from Spain, and he had those regions filled with it. From these testimonies Blondel concludes that these spurious wares, the goods of the first bishops of the city, came first from the chests of the prelates of Mainz and were spread abroad, either from Riculf, who came to the episcopate in 786 or 787 and died in 814 or 815 (see Serrarius, Histor. rer. Mogunt. lib. 4. pag. 613. & seqq.), or, what proves it even more, from others who outlived Riculf and had been skilfully sought out. But there are arguments

units.tr: Digitized by Google arguments which suggest that Riculf knew either the whole collection of the Pseudo-Mercator or at least some letters such as we now have were unknown to him. We shall set out these arguments in Blondel's own words. He says: "Moreover, lest anyone suspect that Riculf was the author or the compiler either of the Pseudo-Isidorian compilation or of all the letters which that hodgepodge now contains, as others believed after Hincmar, we prove by a most clear argument, which no trickery can evade, that this cannot be. It is absurd that Riculf, who died in the year of the Lord 814, should have stitched together, or known, patchworks made from writings published over the following fourteen years. Likewise, no one can rightly doubt that Riculf could not have known certain letters, such as the letters of Pseudo-Urban and Pseudo-John III, in which the decisions of the council held at Paris under Louis the Pious in the year of the Lord 829 are read word for word, or at least could not have known them in the form they now have." units.tr: * The year of the Lord 829 is 15 years after Riculf's death, and 3 years after that of Aistulf, who succeeded Riculf in rule. 5, that the same reasoning ought to apply to it as to the letters of Pseudo-Urban and Pseudo-John III, since in it certain imitations of phrases can be noted, which Jonas of Orléans used in his letter to Charles the Bald. No one will deny that Charles began to reign 25 years after Riculf's death. Perhaps others will observe the same in other letters. Since it is clear from these matters that the Pseudo-Isidorian collection must have been made after Riculf's death (unless we want to say, as we often see happen in such collections, that it grew over time and was enlarged), the strongest suspicion falls on Benedict the Levite, of whom we spoke above, who collected the three later books of the Capitularies of the emperors Charles and Louis. For he was the first to divide up the letters and to place them, without mention of titles, into the Capitulary of Charles the Great and Louis the Pious. See Capitular. lib. 6. cap. 119. To this is added the identity of style in the spurious letters and in the three later books of the capitularies, likewise the similar sordidness of phrases and the clumsy construction of the periods. units.tr: * In the year 839 Louis the Pious died, on 12 kalends of July of that year. Mercator, an exile among the German Franks, lived indeed at Mainz, from which city the first dissemination, if not also the fabrication, of the letters took place. Benedict could have abused his name, whether Mercator was unaware or willing, which he explains at length. Blondel illustrates this conjecture in the often-cited Prolegum. cap. 6. pag. 28. & seqq., though he leaves it to the reader's judgement how much weight to give it. Whoever the author of the letters may be, not only many arguments but also witnesses prove that they are spurious. The Magdeburg Centuriators rightly say in cent. 2. cap. 7.: "They argue, beyond controversy, that the matters which the state of the times required are not the work of those first Roman bishops, since they have not a single word about the affairs and state of their times: nothing about persecutions, nothing about the dangers of the Church, nothing about doctrine, the episcopal office, the care of the flock, the consolation of martyrs, the refutation of heretics, and so on. And if they bring anything forward, it does not agree with the controversies and affairs of this second century; for example, this question, whether the Son is greater than the Father, or whether the Son alone has immortality, which was debated in the time of Arius, not in the second century." Turrian, the defender of these trifles, tries in vain to evade this, and the judgement of the most learned Englishman John Rainolds is very true of him. In tom. 1. Apocryphor. he says: "Francis Turrian the Jesuit tries with five books to prove that these letters were written by those bishops; but so shamelessly that I do not believe any work was ever written which could be a more striking and clearer proof of Jesuit impudence." Next, the false and erroneous consular dating at the end of the letters provides a great argument for a forged birth, so that to Baronius no more than ten agree with the true consular annotation, or at least with the one he follows. See him ad annum 69. §. 35. & seqq.; An. 80. §. 3; A. 103. §. 2; A. 121. §. 1; A. 142. §. 3; A. 158. §. 1; A. 167. §. 1; A. 175. §. 2, and for the other years of the following popes to which the letters are ascribed. The Annalist attributes the cause of this to the fact that the forger of these letters everywhere followed the very faulty chronology of the Liber Pontificalis. Third, the use of the Vulgate version proves the time, which follows the age of Jerome. Fourth, the same style shines through all the letters, from which it must certainly be concluded that these trifles were written not at different times, in the periods in which each of the bishops lived, but at one time by one and the same person. Fifth, the same barbarism, which smacks of the ninth century, can be observed everywhere. These little flowers will serve as a specimen: "Bishops are to be obeyed, not detracted from; they are to be borne and loved" (Pseudo-Eu­aristus, Letter 2); "to harm someone" (Pseudo-Victor, in his letter); "to speak" (Pseudo-Callistus, Letter 2); "to protect" (Pseudo-Sixtus I, Letter 2); "to persecute" used in the passive (Pseudo-Alexander, Letter 2); "to be made a partaker of another's evils" (again Pseudo-Alexander, Letter 3); "a continence of letters injuring paternal disciplines" (Pseudo-Marcellinus, Letter 2); "charitatively" (Pseudo-Stephen, Letter 2); "potestatively" (Pseudo-Felix, Letter 1); "rigorous," and likewise "to take care" (Pseudo-Eusebius, Letter 1). Sixth, the impostor everywhere betrays himself in that he plunders other authors who lived some centuries after those to whom he ascribed his letters. Blondel observes such anachronisms in all the letters: In prolegumenis Pseudo-Isidori cap. 13. This alone is enough to extract from even unwilling men the verdict that all these wares are the spurious goods of Mercator. Since we cannot go through all of them, we shall recount only one or two examples. Clement of Rome is said to have held the see from the year of the Lord 93 to 103. In the first letter ascribed to him there are read words from the version of the Bible corrected by Jerome after the year 372, some passages of the Recognitions rendered into Latin by Rufinus after

Hunc ita excepit Doctissimus Blondellus, quod jam occupatum est, ut nemo hactenus Turriani defensionem suscipere ausus fuerit; nec tantum Turriani istas, sed & alias quas antiquissimorum Urbis Episcoporum nomine vulgavit Mercator Isidorus, demonstravit spurias & suppositas esse. Varia praeterea argumenta contra has Epistolas & PseudoIsidorianam collectionē suggere possent canones illi Isagogici ad criticam Ecclesiasticam, quos nuper Clarissimus & Acutissimus Theologus & Historicus, Fridericus Spanhemius, Magni Spanhemii patrissans Filius, in celeberrimo Leidensi Lyceo Professor, quem honoris causa hic nomino, elegantissimae suae introductioni ad historiam & antiquitates Ecclesiasticas, majoris operis prodromo, (quod utinam publice promissum, publice hic interpellatus, monitus & rogatus bono reipublicae literariae repraesentaret) subjunxit; si ad eos Pseud-Isidori suppositos partus examinare vellemus; aut si cordatus quispiam de νοθεία harum mercium dubitaret amplius. Itaque missis argumentis ad testimonia digitum tantum intendemus, quae idem cum argumentis figmentum convincunt. Non desunt testes antiqui, nec recentiores. units.tr: It can be observed that the printed words are as above; the Greek-free text contains no marginal notes. Translated into Latin after the year 386; Cyril of Alexandria's apostrophe disputing against Theodore of Mopsuestia, A.D. 435; the sentence taken from the Fifth Roman Council, assembled under Pope Symmachus in A.D. 503; chapter four of the Rule of Benedict, written after A.D. 494, when he went into the desert; the opening of the exposition of the creed by Venantius Fortunatus, composed around A.D. 590; and extracts from Gregory's Morals on Job, published in A.D. 591, and from the sayings of Isidore of Seville, collected after the year 600. Of this letter there is indeed an ancient mention, and a translation by Rufinus exists, but that impostor appended it to his collection of decretals. We shall take another example from Anacletus. He is said to have held the Roman bishopric from A.D. 103 to 112. To him is ascribed the first letter, which borrows from the letter of Damasus to the bishops of Illyricum, dated A.D. 369; from chapter 3 of the little book On the Dignity of Man by Ambrose; from chapter 9 of the Third Council of Carthage, held in A.D. 397; from the Vulgate version of the Bible and the version of the Psalter from the Hebrew, published around A.D. 380 under Jerome as author; from the first epistle of Pseudo-Clement in the translation of Rufinus, around the year 380; from the second letter of Innocent, written in A.D. 404; from a letter of Leo, given shortly before A.D. 456; from the speeches 8, 9 and 11 of book 2 and letters 14, 19 and 22 of book 4, letters 4, 8, 9, 19 and 24, of Ennodius, who is known to have flourished from 490 to 521; from the translations of Aniane, published in A.D. 506; and from the Historia tripartita, compiled around the year 545. Cangius's letter of the Abbess to Boniface, written in A.D. 721, and Boniface of Mainz's letter to King Ethelbald, given in A.D. 745, he plucks from. So the most learned Blondel traces, through all the letters, the sources from which the anachronisms [ἀντιχρονισμοί] that teem in these letters were taken. To these we may add a seventh argument, that none of the ancients borrowed sentences from these letters and transferred them into their own writings, nor confessed that they had done so, nor cited these letters as authorities. The Fathers, otherwise devout praisers of the ancients, would certainly not have omitted this if the letters had existed, or if they had used their testimony. The Magdeburg Centuriators also press this argument: Centur. 2, chap. 7. On the authority, they say, of Eusebius, Jerome and other witnesses, the ancient bishops of the city are excused, so that they are not counted as authors of the letters to which their names are attached. And they are not only deprived of the authority of those named, but of all authority up to the year 830; for until that time those wretched prelates and these most excellent treasures lay hidden. Afterwards, however, they were admitted and praised without any judgment or inquiry by Ansegis the abbot, perhaps their parent or at least midwife as collector, and by Burchard, Anselm of Lucca and Ivo, as useful merchandise for their own workshops of decretals. Who praised and cited them from the year 830 onward, Blondel has diligently gathered in his often-cited Prolegomena, chap. 18, at the end of which he also lists some Protestants who were deceived by this crafty merchant Isidore: namely Beza, who in Against Saravia, chap. 24 cites letters on country bishops written in the names of Damasus and Leo; Francis Junius, in Against Bellarmine, On the Roman Pontiff, who cites the first Clementine letter; and John Rainolds, in Censura Apocryphorum, who praises the first letter of John I, though the Magdeburgers in Centur. 6, chap. 15 cite the later one. In the last century Fr. Turrianus, a Jesuit, defended them in a treatise issued in the year 733 against the Magdeburg Centuriators. He left undefended those attributed to Clement, Anacletus, Evaristus, Alexander, Sixtus, Telesphorus, Hyginus, Pius, Anicetus, Soter, Eleutherius, Victor and Zephyrinus, but the rest he defended. The most learned Blondel dealt with him in such a way that it has already been taken up, so that no one has hitherto dared to undertake Turrianus's defence. Blondel showed that not only Turrianus's letters but also the others which the merchant Isidore published under the names of the most ancient bishops of the city are spurious and falsely ascribed. Moreover, various arguments against these letters and the Pseudo-Isidorian collection could be furnished by those Isagogical canons on ecclesiastical criticism which the most distinguished and acute theologian and historian, Fridericus Spanhemius, son of the elder Spanheim and professor in the famous Leiden lyceum, whom I name here out of respect, recently appended to his most elegant introduction to ecclesiastical history and antiquities, a prelude to a larger work (which, if only it were publicly presented for the good of the literary commonwealth, as he was publicly challenged, warned and asked to do). These arguments would serve if we wished to examine those suppositious offspring of Pseudo-Isidore, or if some sensible person still doubted the spuriousness of these wares. Therefore, setting the arguments aside, we shall point only to the testimonies, which convict the fiction just as the arguments do. Ancient witnesses are not lacking, nor recent ones. The old Codex of canons of the Roman Church, of which much has been said above, which acknowledges only thirteen letters of the Popes, namely those of Siricius, Innocent, Zosimus, Boniface, Coelestine, Leo, Hilary, Simplicius, Gelasius, Anastasius II, Symmachus, Hormisdas and Gregory the Younger, abundantly establishes and proves that the older decretals were not received or known.
