Hoc argumentum urgebant Episcopi Galliæ circa annum 865. qui idcirco Isidori suppositam collectionem, pro canonibus admittere nolebant, quia in toto Codicis canonum corpore non continebantur descriptæ. Hincmarus Laudunensis, qui ex facilitate primo harum epistolarum testimonio usus fuit, postea cognito errore, earum auctoritatem destruere conatus est: Non enim tantum veris auctoribus restituit, quæ PseudIsidorus ex iis decerpserat, cap. 12. 23. 25. 36. in libro quinquaginta quinque capitum, sed etiam docuit, epistolas esse canonibus receptis & sibi contrarias, Scriptum est, inquit, in præfatis Epistolis, ut accusationes Episcoporum non recipiantur, & in eisdem habetur qualiter recipiantur, & ut à suis ovibus Episcopi accusari non valeant: lib. 55. cap. 20. cap. & paulo post: In iisdem epistolis scriptum est, non debere vel posse synodum sine jussione, vel consensu Romani Pontificis, Pontificis; & sacri Nicæni Canones dicunt: be-ve placuit annis singulis per unamquamque pro-vinciam bis in anno concilia celebrari. Et quamquam in d. c. conetur contradictio-nem excusare distinctione temporum, re-rum & causarum, attamen apud Flodoar-dum lib. 3. c. 22. diserte adserit, ab Hinc-maro Laudunensi collectas sententias inter se dissonas & contra Euangelicam & Apostolicam atque Canonicam & Apostolicæ sedis auctoritatem immissas; & cap. 24. libr. 55. capitum, observat ipsum Collectorem seu Impostorem, hasce epistolas reliquis decretalibus æquiparare non fuisse ausum: Differentiam quoque, inquit, inter Epistolas quas collegit & sacros canones, ex verbis B.Gelasii, quibus & sanctos verba interposuit, fecit. Nicolaus quoque primus, qui Gallicis Episcopis occurrere studuit, consulto tamen abstinet, citans Clementis epistolam 1. à Lacinia Pseudo-Isidorianam, ut & à cæteris Clementis, Anacleti & aliorum suppositis epistolis; quod & odoratus est Baronius, qui hæc notat ad an. D.865. §.7. Ab ipsa quidem Isidori, inquit, Collectione consulto visus abstinuisse, quippe cum in his controversiis frequens esset, in quibus de appellatione ad sedem Apostolicam ageretur, & ex illis epistolis multiplicia suppeterent eademque fortissima testimonia Sanctissimorum Pontificum eorundemque eorundemque Martyrum, quorum summa auctoritas in Ecclesia esse posset; abstinuit tamen ab illis penitus, quas saltem dubias intellexisse, non dubium sit; illis tantum usus de quibus nunquam in Ecclesia Dei fuerat dubitatum, quod illis adventitiis & recens-inventis, non egeret Ecclesia, cum eadem ex Germanis, sinceris, omnino legitimis securis, certisque, Romanorum Pontificum Epistolis abundanter accipere licuisset. Post haec tempora invalescente potentia Romana, invaluit quoque auctoritas; ut ad seculum decimum quintum vix duo inveniantur, qui se Pseudo-Isidorianis commentis opposuerint, nempe Marsilius Patavin. qui claruit anno 1324, defens. pacis, de re Imperatoria & Pontificia, cap. 27. part. 2. & Gobelinus in Cosmidromio. Post haec tempora coepta contra subdolas Pseudo-Isidori merces disputatio. videatur Nicolaus de Cusa Cardinalis, Concordia Catholica cap. 34. lib. 2. & libro 3. cap. 2. scripsit, anno 1432. Henricus Kaltheysen in Tractatu, an Imperium sit unquam a Romanis ad Graecos translatum, a Centuriatoribus allegatus, obiit iste A.D. 1465. Post hos catervatim docti abjecerunt haec figmenta, Joh. de Turrecremata Card. Erasmus, Driedo, Claud. Espencaeus, Didac. Covarruvias, Gregor. Cassand. in defens. libelli de offic. viri pii. pii. Anton. Contius in editione Corpor. Canonici. Qui in c. septuaginta. dist. 16. quæ manum censorum Belgicorum effugerunt, hæc habet. Multas supra in præfatione rationes adduxi, quibus omnes Pontificum, qui Sylvestrum præcesserunt, decretales falsas esse manifeste ostendi. Ipsa præfatio à censoribus suppressa est. Adde his Carol. Bovium Oltunens. Episcop. in præfat. præmiß. constit. Pseudapost. à se in Latinum versis. Bellarminus earum propugnator lib. 2. de Pont. Roman. cap. 14. hæc sibi tamen excidere passus est. Aliquos errores in has Epistolas irrepsisse non negaverim nec indubitatas esse affirmare audeam. Baronii judicia in annalibus variis locis sunt dispersa; excerpta tamen & cuique epistolæ subjecta à Clarissimo Blondello, digitum intendo in locum prolixiorem. Ad A. D. 865. §. 5. & in Notis ad Martyrol. ad 4. April. Vide & Edmundum Richerium, lib. de Eccles. & polit. potest; ex nostris Molinæum in Vate lib. 2. cap. ult. pag. 129. & 132. Claud. Salmasium de Coma pag. 186. & seq. Dalæum de jejunio & quadragesf. lib. 3. c. 10. & 12. pag. 537. & lib. 4. c. 6. pag. 751. In Pseudepigraphis Apostol. lib. 3. cap. 2. pag. 427. & pag. 434. & 448. posteriori, 476. & seq. 493. Ioh. Rainold. tom. 1. Apocryph. Magnum Iacob. Usser, de success. in Occid. Eccles. cap. 2. pag. 60. pag. 60. & 61. Robb. Cocum passim in censura. Rivetum in Critico sacro. lib. 1. cap. 8. Withakerum de Pontifice Rom. controverf. 4. quæst. 5. Ioh. Gerhardum. tom. 1. conf. catholi. lib. 1. part. 2. cap. 9. Caspar. Zieglerum, in diffært. de orig. & increm. jur. Can. quam præmisit Lancelotti Instit. jur. Can. §. 25. & seqq. Agmen claudat elogium, Cardinalis Iohan. Bonæ, quod de hac Collectione Pseudo-Isidoriana edidit nuper in liturgicis lib. 1. cap. 3. prin. Adstipulantur, inquit, Baronio Ioseph. Vicecomes, & Ioh. Baptista Scortia, in suis Tractatibus de sacrificio Missæ, & Stephanus Durantus, libro de ritibus Ecclesiæ, atque alii recentiores, qui ut probent Missæ nomen Apostolicæ ætatis esse, & Christianæ religioni coævum, ex Romanis Pontificibus primi & secundi seculi testimonia nullius roboris coacervant: dudum enim ab Eruditis observatum est illorum Epistolas decretales usque ad Siricium, suppositititias esse: à quodam Hispano sub nomine Isidori, quicunque ille fuerit sub finem septimi seculi (imo octavi vel initio noni, & forte non ab Hispano, sed Germano-Franco aut Franco-Gallo, ut supra latius dictum est) pia fraude (pace Card. Bonæ id liceat mutare in impiam impostluram) & ex sententiis veterum canonum, legum etiam civilium „ & Sanctorum Patrum, qui quarto & „quinto seculo floruerunt, turpi anachro„nismo, eodemque fere stylo ac dicendi „charactere, magna ex parte contextas; „quas primum ex Hispania in Galliam detulit (non detulisse dixit Hincmarus Remensis, ex quo id Cardinalis colligere forte potuit, sed delatas disseminasse, ut patet ex loco supra adducto) la„bente octavo seculo Riculphus Episcopus „Moguntinus; & inde in alias Regiones „disseminatae, ac communiter receptae sunt. „Sed tandem Impostura detecta est, & Ba„ronius de his epistolis differens anno 865, „earum falsitatem agnoscit, & aperte fa-„tetur, ne quis, inquit, calumniari pos„sit, ab Ecclesia Romana aliquid hujus„modi commentum esse. Earum igitur te„stimoniis tanquam falsis & inutilibus reje„ctis, certiora ex veris & legitimis Ponti„ficum ac Patrum scriptis proferenda sunt. Est hoc ingenuum Cardinalis testimonium, quod vel ex Blondello, vel alio ejusdem Sectae homine hausit, vel veritas extorsit. Adserta itaque affatim impostura improbissima, totius hujus compilationis auctoritas concidit; quae quid contineat ipse subdolus Impostor in praefatione collectioni praemissa ostendit. In principio, inquit, hujus volu-„minis, qualiter concilium apud nos celebratur
units.tr: {229} Witnesses who hold the collection of Isidore Mercator suspect, reject and condemn it: nis, Hilary, Simplicius, Gelasius, Anastasius II, Symmachus, Hormisdas and Gregory the Younger. It abundantly establishes and proves that the earlier decretals were neither received nor known. Leo IV, who came to the episcopate in A.D. 847, also attests only so much. Yet he mentions Silvester and omits Boniface and Anastasius, and this fault is due either to his forgetfulness or to the carelessness of copyists, c. de libellis, dist. 20. The bishops of Gaul urged this argument about the year 865. For this reason they refused to admit the collection attributed to Isidore as canons, because the decretals were not written down in the whole body of the Code of canons. Hincmar of Laon, who at first, from credulity, used the testimony of these letters, afterwards recognised his error and tried to destroy their authority. For he not only restored to their true authors the passages that Pseudo-Isidore had plucked from them (cap. 12, 23, 25, 36, in the book of fifty-five chapters), but also showed that the letters were contrary to the received canons and to themselves. It is written, he says, in the aforesaid letters, that the accusations of bishops are not to be received, and in the same place it is laid down how they are to be received, and that bishops cannot be accused by their own sheep (book 55, chapter 20). Shortly afterwards he adds: In the same letters it is written that a synod may not or cannot be held without the command or consent of the Roman Pontiff; and the holy canons of Nicaea say: it has pleased us that councils be celebrated twice a year in each province every year. Although in the said chapter he tries to excuse the contradiction by a distinction of times, matters and cases, nevertheless in Flodoard (book 3, chapter 22) he plainly asserts that the opinions collected by Hincmar of Laon are inconsistent with one another and are put forward against the Gospel, the Apostolic and canonical authority and the authority of the Apostolic See. And in chapter 24 of book 55 of the chapters he observes that the compiler, or impostor, himself did not dare to equate these letters with the other decretals: He made also a difference, he says, between the letters which he gathered and the sacred canons, from the words of Blessed Gelasius, into which he also inserted the words of the saints. Nicholas I also, who was eager to oppose the Gallican bishops, nevertheless deliberately refrains from citing the first letter of Clement from the Pseudo-Isidorian Lacinia, as well as the other spurious letters of Clement, Anacletus and others. Baronius also smelled this out, and he notes it at the year 865, §7. It seems, he says, that he deliberately abstained from the very collection of Isidore, since in these controversies, in which appeal to the Apostolic See was being discussed, there were frequent occasions, and from those letters many and very strong testimonies of the most holy Pontiffs and of their martyrs were available, whose authority could be supreme in the Church; yet he abstained entirely from those which it is beyond doubt he understood to be at least doubtful. He used only those about which there had never been doubt in the Church of God, because the Church did not need those adventitious and recently discovered ones, since it could have drawn abundantly from the genuine, sincere, wholly legitimate, certain letters of the Roman Pontiffs. After these times, as Roman power grew, authority grew too; so that down to the fifteenth century scarcely two are found who opposed themselves to the Pseudo-Isidorian fictions: namely Marsilius of Padua, who flourished in 1324 (Defensor pacis, on the Imperial and Papal matters, chapter 27, part 2), and Gobelinus in the Cosmidromium. After these times a dispute began against the crafty wares of Pseudo-Isidore. See Nicholas of Cusa, the cardinal, who wrote in 1432 (Catholic Concord, chapter 34 of book 2, and chapter 2 of book 3). Henry Kaltheysen, in the treatise whether the Empire was ever transferred from the Romans to the Greeks, cited by the Centuriators, died in 1465. After these men learned scholars in crowds rejected these fictions: John de Torquemada the cardinal, Erasmus, Driedo, Claude d'Espence, Diego Covarrubias, Gregory Cassander (in the defence of the little book On the duty of a godly man), and Anton Contius in the edition of the Corpus of Canon Law. He says in the chapter Septuaginta, dist. 16, which escaped the hand of the Belgian censors: I have brought forward many reasons in the preface above, by which I have clearly shown that all the decretals of the Pontiffs who preceded Silvester are false. The preface itself was suppressed by the censors. Add to these Charles Bovius, bishop of Oltuna, in the preface to the constitutions of the Pseudo-Apostles which he translated into Latin. Bellarmine, the defender of these letters, nevertheless allowed this to slip from him (book 2, On the Roman Pontiff, chapter 14): I would not deny that some errors have crept into these letters, nor dare to affirm that they are beyond doubt. Baronius's judgements are scattered in various places in his Annals; but Blondel, most distinguished man, gathered excerpts and placed them under each letter, and I point to the longer passage at A.D. 865, §5, and in the Notes on the Martyrology at 4 April. See also Edmund Richer (On ecclesiastical and political power); among our own writers Molinaeus in Vates (book 2, last chapter, pp. 129 and 132); Claude Salmasius on De coma, p. 186 and following; Daillé, On fasting and Lent (book 3, chapters 10 and 12, p. 537, and book 4, chapter 6, p. 751); On the Pseudepigrapha of the Apostles (book 3, chapter 2, p. 427, and pp. 434, 448, and in the later part 476 and following, 493); John Rainolds, vol. 1 of the Apocrypha; the great James Ussher, On the succession in the Western Church (chapter 2, pp. 60 and 61); Robert Cawdrey(?) and Robert Cocus passim in the Censure; Rivet in the Critici sacri (book 1, chapter 8); Withaker On the Roman Pontiff, controversy 4, question 5; John Gerhard, vol. 1 of the Confessio catholica (book 1, part 2, chapter 9); Caspar Ziegler in his dissertation On the origin and growth of canon law, which Lancelotti prefixed to his Institutes of Canon Law, §25 and following. The procession is closed by the eulogy of Cardinal John Bona, which he lately published on this Pseudo-Isidorian collection in his Liturgical book 1, chapter 3, at the beginning. Joseph Vicecomes and John Baptist Scortia, in their treatises On the sacrifice of the Mass, support Baronius, he says, and so does Stephen Durantus in his book On the rites of the Church, as do other more recent writers; they heap up testimonies of the Roman Pontiffs of the first and second centuries, of no weight at all, to prove that the name of the Mass belongs to the Apostolic age and is coeval with the Christian religion. For learned men have long observed that those decretal letters of these Pontiffs, down to Siricius, are spurious: they were written under the name of Isidore by a certain Spaniard, whoever he was, toward the end of the seventh century (or rather the eighth or the beginning of the ninth, and perhaps not a Spaniard but a German-Frank or Franco-Gaul, as was said more fully above), by a pious fraud (with Cardinal Bona's permission, let this be changed to impious imposture), and are for the most part woven together from sayings of the ancient canons, also of civil laws and of the holy Fathers who flourished in the fourth and fifth centuries, in a shameful anachronism, and in nearly the same style and manner of speaking. These they first brought from Spain into Gaul (Hincmar of Reims said they were not brought but spread abroad, as may be gathered from the place cited above), and when the eighth century was failing, Riculf, bishop of Mainz, spread them through other regions, and they were commonly received. But at last the imposture was detected, and Baronius, discussing these letters at the year 865, acknowledges their falsity and plainly confesses, lest anyone could allege that the Roman Church had devised anything of this kind: Therefore, with their testimonies rejected as false and useless, more certain things must be brought forward from the true and legitimate writings of the Pontiffs and Fathers. This is a frank testimony of the cardinal, which he drew either from Blondel or from another man of the same sect, or which truth wrung from him. Thus, with the most shameless imposture asserted in abundance, the authority of this whole compilation collapses; what it contains the crafty impostor himself shows in the preface placed before the collection. At the beginning of this volume, he says, we have set out how the council is celebrated among us.

units.la: 230. Quid Pseudo-Isidori collectio contineat. bratur posuimus, ut qui nostrum ordi-nem sequi voluerint, sciant qualiter hoc agere debeant. Denique propter eorum auctoritatem cæteris conciliis præposuimus, canones qui dicuntur Apostolorum, licet à quibusdam Apocryphi dicantur, quoniam plures eos recipiunt, & Sancti Patres eorum sententias synodali auctoritate roboraverunt, & inter canonicas posuerunt constitutiones. Deinde quarundam epistolarum decreta Virorum Apostolicorum interseruimus, id est Clementis, Anacleti, Euaristi, & cæterorum Apostolicorum, quas potuimus hactenus reperire epistolas, usque ad Silvestrum Papam. Postmodum vero Nicænam Synodum constituimus, propter auctoritatem ejusdem magni concilii, deinceps diversorum conciliorum Græcorum ac Latinorum, sive quæ ante seu quæ postmodum facta sunt, sub ordine numerorum ac temporum, capitulis suis distincte sub hujus voluminis adspectu locavimus; subjicientes etiam reliqua decreta Præsulum Romanorum usque ad Sanctum Gregorium &c. Vide sis. cap. placuit, dist. 16. in quod partem præfationis Pseudo-Isidorianæ conjecit Gratianus. Laudat M. S. suum codicem Justellus, in quo se protendit dit collectio usque ad concilium Toleta-num xii, quod celebratum anno 682. In-ferti quoque sunt canones ab Hadriano primo Papa Ingelramno dati, de quibus supra. Doctissimus Iustellus, in Praefat. quem codici canonum Ecclesiae universae praefixit, de hac Isidori collectione dicit, eam privatam fuisse, usque ad Alexandrum Papam Romanum, id est, annum 1061, ab eoque approbatam videri, ut Innocentius tertius in epistola ad Petrum Compostellanum tom. 2. concilior. testatur, cujus haec verba refert: Emeritense Concilium Authenticum esse multis rationibus adstruebas, tum quia cum aliis conciliis continetur in libro, qui CORPUS CANONUM appellatur, quem Alexander Papa per interlocutionem authenticum approbavit. Subdit dein Iustellus. Nec enim dubium est, hoc loco Corporis Canonum nomine, collectionem Isidori significari, quae aucta multorum canonum accessione in nomen illud transiit, ut etiam Liber seu Corpus canonum diceretur; Sic enim habet inscriptio in meo Codice M. S. Incipit Liber qui appellatur Corpus canonum. Nisi quis existimet his verbis apud Innocentium Codicem canonum Ecclesiae Hispanicae significari, cum Emeritense illud concilium in vulgatis Isidori codicibus nusquam reperiatur. riatur. Quæ sane certissima & evidentissima ratio est, non posse apud Innocentium intelligi Codicem canonum Isidori Mercatoris, cum in eo codice Emeritense concilium non legatur. Quæ causa forte est, quare Iustellus in curis secundis hæc omnia omiserit, in Præfatione Codicis Canonum Ecclesiæ universæ secundæ editionis, quam Filius præmisit Bibliothecæ juris canonici veteris. vide tom. I. pag. 26. & pag. 24. fine & seq. initio, ubi satis clare Iustellus refert Innocentii verba ad Codicem Hispanicum specialem, non vero ad Pseudo-Isidori collectionem. Usus vero est Pseudo-Isidorus versione canonum antiqua, non Dionysii Exigui, nec Martini Bracharensis, ut testatur editio conciliorum Coloniensis. Scopus quis huius collectionis fuerit, itidem defensionis Turriani, ex iis quæ hactenus disputata sunt, affatim patet: huic nempe fini epistolæ effictæ sunt, ne deessent Ecclesiæ Romanæ, aut potius Pontificibus Romanis antiquorum testimonia Episcoporum, potentiæ, eminentiæ & auctoritatis; item ut stabilirentur & fulcirentur jura appellationum ex toto orbe ad sedem, ut illi vocant, Apostolicam. Hoc enim argumentum tractant potissimum epistolæ, neglectis veris istorum seculorum rebus, ut supra observarunt Magdeburg
units.tr: 230. What the collection of Pseudo-Isidore contains. We have set it down, so that those who wish to follow our order may know how they ought to proceed. Then, on account of their authority, we have placed before the other councils the canons called those of the Apostles, although some call them apocryphal, since many accept them and the holy Fathers confirmed their judgments with synodal authority and counted them among the canonical constitutions. Next we have inserted decrees from certain letters of the apostolic men, namely Clement, Anacletus, Evaristus and the other apostolic men, as far as we have been able to find their letters, down to Pope Silvester. After that we set down the Nicene Synod, on account of the authority of that great council. Then, in order of numbers and times, we have arranged, each under its own chapter and before the eyes of this volume, the councils of the Greeks and Latins, whether held before or after. We have also added the remaining decrees of the Roman prelates down to Saint Gregory, etc. See, if you like, cap. placuit, dist. 16., into which Gratian threw part of the Pseudo-Isidorian preface. Justellus praises his manuscript codex, in which the collection extends to the twelfth Council of Toledo, held in the year 682. Also included are the canons which Pope Hadrian I gave to Ingelram, of which above. The most learned Justellus, in the preface he prefixed to the codex of canons of the universal Church, says of this collection of Isidore that it remained private until Pope Alexander of Rome, that is to the year 1061, and that it seems to have been approved by him, as Innocent III testifies in his letter to Peter of Compostela, vol. 2 of the councils, quoting his words: You argued that the Council of Mérida is authentic on many grounds, since it is contained with other councils in the book called THE BODY OF CANONS, which Pope Alexander approved as authentic by a decision. Justellus then adds: For there is no doubt that in this place by the name Body of Canons the collection of Isidore is meant, which, with the addition of many canons, came to bear that name, so that it was also called the Book or Body of canons. For so the inscription in my manuscript codex reads: Here begins the book which is called the Body of canons. Unless someone thinks that by these words in Innocent is meant a codex of the canons of the Spanish Church, since that Council of Mérida is nowhere found in the printed editions of Isidore. This is surely the most certain and evident reason: that in Innocent one cannot understand the codex of canons of Isidore Mercator, since in that codex the Council of Mérida is not read. This is perhaps why Justellus omitted all these things in the second edition, in the Preface to the Codex of Canons of the universal Church, which his son prefixed to the Library of ancient canon law; see vol. I, p. 26, and p. 24 at the end and beginning of the following, where Justellus quite clearly refers Innocent's words to the special Spanish codex, not to the collection of Pseudo-Isidore. Moreover, Pseudo-Isidore used the old version of the canons, not that of Dionysius Exiguus nor that of Martin of Braga, as the edition of the councils of Cologne testifies. What the aim of this collection was, and likewise of Turrianus's defence, is clear enough from what has been argued so far. To this end, namely, the letters were fabricated, so that the Roman Church, or rather the Roman Pontiffs, should not lack testimonies from ancient bishops to their power, eminence and authority; and likewise so that the rights of appeal from the whole world to the so-called Apostolic See might be established and supported. For the letters deal chiefly with this argument, neglecting the true events of those centuries, as the Magdeburg

Basil.) ignotum hominem, & annis sexaginta, Dominicæ æræ an. 1573. quo scripta est pro Decretalibus Epistolis defensio, superiorem fuisse opinatur. Quid memorem fœdos perpetuosque summiculosi sed φλυαρῆντ Theologi paralogismos, & frequentia ἀσυχήματα jactabundi Critici, quem nihil præter novas Lectiones, manuscriptos Codices, Bibliothecas, Vaticanam, Florentinam, Sancti Marci, Cryptæ ferratæ, cum incredibili antagonistarum, divinæq; quam vel renitente conscientia vellicat, veritatis contemptu, crepare audias. Cui elogio sis adde ea, quæ habet Dalæus in Pseudepigraph, graph. Apostolicis, pag. 22. 417. 419. 690. & seqq. & ex dictis liquido concludas rogo, quantæ auctoritatis sit collectio Pseudo-Isidoriana, & quid tot figmentis, quibus passim dogmata fidei stabiliuntur, sit deferendum.
units.tr: Magdeburg Centuriators have observed above, and as Baronius himself confesses, cited earlier, who says that many and very strong arguments can be drawn from them. This is perhaps the reason why Nicholas I tries to persuade the Gauls to accept them, though they refused, because they seemed suspect and recent, and were not read among the other decretals in the codex of canons. The Pontiff tries carefully to remove this objection; see him disputing at considerable length in Gratian, cap. si Romanorum, dist. 19. This was also the reason why Turrianus wrote his laborious defence against the Magdeburg men, as if the whole Roman cause stood or fell with this sly and spurious merchandise of Pseudo-Isidore. To this end he strains every sinew of his wit and spends all his diligence, so that by arguments and fabrications the authority of the Epistles, and above all that of the supreme Pontiff, might remain patched up and covered. To this end also new witnesses and new books are invented, which do not exist, and perhaps never professed, or could not be produced: such as the Sermons of Eusebius of Alexandria, bk. 1, on the Epistles, c. 21, and bk. 2, cc. 6, 12, and elsewhere; Eusebius of Caesarea, against Marcellus, bk. 5, c. 7; Hippolytus, martyr and Theban, bk. 2, c. 18; Magnes, against Theosthenes, bk. 1, c. 5, bk. 2, cc. 3 and 13, bk. 4, c. 7; Theodotus of Ancyra, bk. 2, c. 14; Severian of Gabala, on 1 Corinthians, bk. 5, c. 5; Apollinaris, on Numbers, bk. 4, c. 14; Leontius, on Matthew, bk. 4, c. 10; Eustratius of Constantinople, on the operation of the soul, bk. 4, c. 14; Damascene, on fasts and on the communion of the body, bk. 5, cc. 8 and 18, bk. 4, c. 1; Theodore of Antioch, he who ruled the Church of Mopsuestia, bk. 2, c. 20, bk. 4, c. 8, and bk. 5, c. 6; Theophanes, in the Harmony of the Old and New Testaments, bk. 2, c. 28, and bk. 4, c. 13; Constantine, out of the scholastics, bk. 1, c. 28; Photius, his Lexicon, Questions to Amphilochius, Commentaries on the Epistles, bk. 3, cc. 11 and 12, bk. 5, c. 18, bk. 2, c. 13, bk. 4, c. 12; Nilus, on Luke, bk. 5, c. 6; Pamphilus, Canons, bk. 1, c. 25. These Blondel excerpted and noted in his Pseudo-Isidore and in Turrianus under the lash, prolegomena, c. 1, p. 7, and he adds this judgment and specimens of errors: "Certainly a man of very wide reading, but of the most brazen brow and the slightest judgment, a harsh and wicked man, a creature of anger and glory, another Pyrgopolinices, who writes that Hincmar was bishop of the Church of Rheims in Belgic Gaul, bk. 1, c. 15, and bk. 3, c. 3, and a bishop of the German nation; who, bk. 2, c. 20, and so on, calls that infamous Theodore, whom the fifth Synod anathematized 126 years after his death, and, bk. 2, c. 15, bk. 3, cc. 16 and 18, bk. 5, cc. 12 and 16, a writer who invades the titles of Sixtus, whether the second or third, oozing with the pus of the Pelagian leprosy and marked with the black theta, he cites as witnesses. He who, bk. 5, c. 10, wants the Synod of Elvira, which is known to have been held in the year 305 under Marcellus, to have been convened under Silvester; he who, bk. 2, c. 13, believes that Theodosius the Elder, who died in 395, and the relics of Chrysostom, who died in 407, were transferred to Constantinople in 438; he who, ibid. and c. 9, bk. 5, c. 2, speaks of the bishops of Lérins in Gaul, of Paschasius at Rome, bk. 1, c. 21, of the bishops of Alexandria, Eusebius, and so on; bk. 5, c. 19, of the kings of the Picts in Britain, and bk. 5, c. 2, of the Church of Garolitana or Garopolitana, administered by regular canons down to this day in Scotland, which he invents. He who, bk. 2, c. 13, and bk. 5, c. 24, now says Rufinus was the translator of the first Clementine, now denies it; he who, bk. 5, c. 17, makes Victor, whom our opponents place in the year 203, sit more than 230 years before the Synod of Nicaea of 325; he who, bk. 5, c. 19, makes Rabanus, who died in 856, live more than 900 years before; Germanus, bk. 5, same chapter, whose last day Baronius put at 730, he writes died more than 900 years earlier; Henry Kaltheysen, bk. 5, cc. 20 and 23, whom Bernard of Luxemburg in his Catalogue of heretics (where he is called Inquisitor of heretical depravity, Professor of sacred theology in the most famous Academy of Cologne, who gave an oration before the Council of Basel on the free preaching of the Word of God, against Udabricus, presbyter of orphans, in the year 1433 over three wearisome days of the week; on whom see Bellarmine on ecclesiastical writers and Possevinus in the Apparatus, and the appendix to the Council of Basel) teaches was a man unknown, who, from the Papal palace first Master, then raised to the archbishopric of Nidaros and Caesarea, and present at the Council of Basel, he thinks lived sixty years earlier, in the year of the Lord 1573, in which the defence of the Decretal Epistles was written." Why should I mention the foul and endless syllogisms of the sophistical but chattering [φλυαρεῖν] theologians, and the frequent inanities [ἀσυχήματα] of the boastful critics, who, with nothing but new readings, manuscript codices, libraries, the Vatican, the Florentine, St Mark's, the Crypta ferrata, you would hear crackling with incredible contempt for their opponents and for divine truth, which their own conscience, even while resisting, plucks at? To this judgment add what Daille has in his Pseudepigrapha Apostolica, pp. 22, 417, 419, 690 and following. And from what has been said, I ask you to conclude clearly how great the authority of the Pseudo-Isidorian collection is, and how much it must be rejected because of the many fabrications by which doctrines of the faith are everywhere supported.

units.la: Vocat nos Ordo ad Photium Patriarcham Constantinopolitanum, celeberrimi inter collectores & digestores Juris Canonici nominis. Fuit ille nobili prosapia ortus; Protospatharius dignitate, ut refert Cedrenus, quæ dignitas magna, & inter Magnificas numerata, Glossæ Basilicorum, illustres interpretantur. Ἰλλύσεως· πεωτοπατἀρείῳ. Codino dicitur ὅτι λῶ μὲν τὸ παλαιὸν πεῶτος τ' ατα[?]ἀων τ[?]. Quod erat primus stationum Spathariorum. σπαθάριος Cedreno est σωματοφύλαξ. vide sis Joh. Meurs. in Glossario Græco-Barbaro. pag. mihi 463. & Jul. Cæsar. Bulenger. de imperio Romanorum. lib. 8. c. 26. pag. 662. Imperatori à secretis inserviisse Photiū; divitiis & scientia rerum secularium pollentem, & antiquis comparandum fuisse, dicit Nicetas. Zonaras eum appellat ἀνδρα τῶν Θαυμασίων πρωτοασηκρητης τότε τυγχάνοντα ἐν λόγοις ὀνομαστόν, Virum insignem, primarium à secretis, tunc eruditionis nomine celebrem, vixit sub Imp. Michaele tertio & Ludovico secundo. Ad PatriarPatriarchatum Constantinopolitanum pervenit anno 858. in locum Ignatii dejecti fraude Bardæ. Multæ ei lites cum Pontificibus Romanis fuere, quare durus in eum Baronius,qui ubique eum insectatur & prosscindit,videantur ejus annales ab anno 858, usque ad 886, quibus vita ejus & gesta sunt inclusa. Vir fuit multæ Lectionis, quod ejus Bibliotheca,quam Μυριόβιβλον inscripsit,satis demonstrat. Bellarm. eum in lib. de script. Eccl. vocat Virum Magnæ eruditionis. Sed addit,majoris nequitiæ,procul dubio ob lites quas habuit cum Romanis Pontificibus. Defendit tamen eum contra Baronium & Bellarminum Richardus Montacutius, Episcopus Norvicensis in Anglia; qui Epistolas ejus edidit Græce & Latine Londini an. 1651. in Bibliothecam seu Μυριόβιβλον retulit auctores omnes à se lectos & argumenta scriptionis, addidit etiam judicia. Fecit hoc opus rogatu Tarasii Fratris sui, cum ab Imperatore missus esset legatus in Syriam, ut ipse testatur in Præfatione. Edita est Bibliotheca Græcè Augustæ vindelicorum A. 1600. Græce & Latine edidit & notis illustravit Andr. Schottus, Rotomachi, seculi hujus anno quinquagesimo tertio, cujus de Photio vide Prolegumena. Adscribitur ei Etymologicum manuscriptum Græcum,
units.tr: The Ordo calls us to Photius, Patriarch of Constantinople, a name most famous among the collectors and arrangers of canon law. He was born of a noble family and held the rank of Protospatharius, as Cedrenus reports, a high dignity counted among the magnificent offices; the Glossae of the Basilica render it "illustrious." Codinus says that formerly it meant the first of the stations of the Spatharii. For Cedrenus the spatharius is a bodyguard [σωματοφύλαξ]. See Joh. Meursius, Glossarium Graeco-Barbarum, p. 463, and Jul. Caesar Bulenger, De imperio Romanorum, bk 8, c. 26, p. 662. Nicetas says that Photius served the emperor as secretary, was rich and learned in secular affairs, and could be compared with the ancients. Zonaras calls him "a man of remarkable distinction, then first secretary, famous for learning" [ἀνδρα τῶν Θαυμασίων πρωτοασηκρητης τότε τυγχάνοντα ἐν λόγοις ὀνομαστόν]. He lived under the Emperor Michael III and Louis II. He came to the Patriarchate of Constantinople in 858, in place of Ignatius, who had been deposed by the treachery of Bardas. He had many disputes with the Roman Pontiffs, which is why Baronius is harsh with him, attacking and tearing him apart everywhere; his Annals from 858 to 886, which contain his life and deeds, may be consulted. He was a man of wide reading, as his Bibliotheca, which he entitled Myriobiblon, sufficiently shows. Bellarmine, in De scriptoribus ecclesiasticis, calls him a man of great learning, but adds "of greater wickedness," doubtless because of his quarrels with the Roman Pontiffs. Yet Richard Montagu, Bishop of Norwich in England, defends him against Baronius and Bellarmine; he published his Epistles in Greek and Latin at London in 1651. In the Bibliotheca, or Myriobiblon, he recorded all the authors he had read, with the subjects of their writings, and he also added judgements. He did this work at the request of his brother Tarasius, when he had been sent by the Emperor as legate to Syria, as he himself testifies in the Preface. The Bibliotheca was published in Greek at Augsburg in 1600. Andreas Schottus of Rouen edited it in Greek and Latin with notes in the fifty-third year of this century; on Photius see his Prolegomena. The manuscript Greek Etymologicum is ascribed to him.

units.la: Scripta ejus cum, quod possidet Clariss: & Eruditiss: Marquardus Gudius, ut testatur, id allegans, Vir Nobiliss: & Clariss: Ezechiel Spanhemius, Serenissimorum Electorum Brandenburgici & Palatini Consiliarius intimus & in Ubiis, ut vocant, Residens, in elaboratissimis & politissimis dissertationibus de usu & praestant: numismatum antiquorum; editionis posterioris Amstelodamensis, disert. 4. pag. 358. Tribuitur quoque ei Liber de Spiritus sancti processione, & alius, quo probare nititur Spiritum sanctum à solo patre procedere, quos M. S. citat Blondellus in Iohanna Papissa, qui postea Londini sunt editi. Sed hos Maresius suspectos habet, an sint Photii, in Iohanna Papissa restituta, pag. 47. apud quem & loca Blondelli vide pag. 45. De his, quae ejus nomine laudavit Fr. Turrianus, Lexicon nempe, quaestiones adversus Amphilochium, & commentarios in Epistolas, supra dictum num. marg. 234. Ejus est quoq; opusculum de septem synodis Oecumenicis, Graece & Latine editum in Bibliotheca Juris canonici veteris. Ad Institutum nostrum tantum facit ejus Nomocanon; qui est quasi compendium aliquod seu qui continet elementa totius juris Canonici Graeci, & tanti fit à Graecis ut omnibus collectionibus eum praemittere soleant, etiam ipsi Codici canonum. nonum. Divisus est in quatuordecim titu-los, & hi iterum in certa capita. Congefsit in eum, ut docent prolegumena, nunc demum in Bibliotheca juris Canonici vete-ris vulgata, sequentes canones conciliorum, Patriarcharum, Episcoporum & Patrum.
units.tr: His writings, which the most distinguished and learned Marquard Gudius possesses, as he testifies, citing them, and which the most noble and distinguished Ezechiel Spanheim, privy councillor of the most serene Electors of Brandenburg and the Palatinate and resident at the so-called Ubii, has used in his most elaborate and polished dissertations on the use and value of ancient coins (later Amsterdam edition, diss. 4, p. 358). A book On the Procession of the Holy Spirit is also attributed to him, and another in which he tries to prove that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone. Blondel cites these in manuscript in his Pope Joan, and they were later published at London. But Maresius regards them with suspicion, whether they are Photius's, in the restored Pope Joan, p. 47, where see also Blondel's passages at p. 45. As for what Fr. Turrianus cited under his name, namely a Lexicon, Questions against Amphilochius, and Commentaries on the Epistles, mentioned above at marginal number 234. There is also a short work of his on the seven Ecumenical Synods, published in Greek and Latin in the Bibliotheca Juris Canonici Veteris. Only his Nomocanon is relevant to our purpose. It is a kind of compendium, containing the elements of the whole Greek canon law, and the Greeks value it so highly that they usually place it before all collections, even before the Code of Canons itself. It is divided into fourteen titles, and these again into particular chapters. As the Prolegomena teach, he compiled into it the following canons of councils, patriarchs, bishops and Fathers, now at last published in the Bibliotheca Juris Canonici Veteris.

units.la: His subjiciuntur tum leges Imperatorum Ecclesiasticæ, ad eosdem titulos & capita pertinentes; Canones sub titulis citantur tantummodo, non recitantur, Leges vero citantur & breviter recitantur. Compilationis rationem reddit ipse Photius in prologo. logo, qui diu desideratus tandem, ut dictum ex M.S. Bibliothecæ Oxoniensis, in lucem protractus est à Justello filio in Bibl. jur. Can. veter. ; ex cujus fine collectum cognoscimus Nomocanonem Anno Mundi, secundum Græcos, 6391 : is est æræ Christianæ 883. Hunc commentariis illustravit Balsamo, ut infra dicemus, ubi de eo inter Interpretes Græcos juris Canonici dissemus. Latinæ Nomocanonis versiones extant duæ; una, quam Gentianus Hervetus; alteram quam Henricus Agylæus elabora-vit, quæ tantum Latine primo prodierunt sine textu Græco, posterior illa Agylæi duplici nomine præ illa Herveti commendanda; quia plenior, utpote quæ ex pleniore exemplari Græco facta est; deinde quia magis accedit ad stylum Jurisconsultorum. Primus Græce ex Codice Bibliothecæ Palatinæ edidit Christophorus Justellus, anno 1615, postea Græce & Latine editus est Nomocanon Parisiis cum commentariis Balsamonis ex Typogr. Regia & interpretatione Gentiani Herveti; Patris labores repetivit Filius Henr. Justellus in bibliothe-ca juris Canon. veteris, qui accuratissime Græce & Latine ex interpretatione Agylæi cum Commentariis Balsamonis edidit, ad-[?]dicis diu desideratis Photii prolegomenis ab Usse-
units.tr: To these are added the ecclesiastical laws of the Emperors, relating to the same titles and chapters. The canons are cited under the titles only, not recited; the laws, however, are cited and briefly recited. Photius himself gives the reason for the compilation in his Prologue. This was long lost, but at last, as said above from the manuscript of the Bodleian Library at Oxford, it was brought to light by Justellus's son in the Bibliotheca Juris Canonici Veteris. From its end we learn that the Nomocanon was compiled in the year of the world 6391 according to the Greeks, that is, in the Christian era 883. Balsamon illustrated it with commentaries, as we shall say below, where we discuss the Greek interpreters of canon law. There are two Latin versions of the Nomocanon: one by Gentianus Hervetus, the other elaborated by Henricus Agylaeus. The first appeared in Latin only, without the Greek text. Agylaeus's version is to be preferred to Hervetus's for two reasons: it is fuller, being made from a fuller Greek copy, and it comes closer to the style of the jurists. Christophorus Justellus first published the Greek from a codex of the Palatine Library, in 1615. Afterwards the Nomocanon was published in Greek and Latin at Paris, with Balsamon's commentaries, from the royal press, with Gentianus Hervetus's translation. The son, Henricus Justellus, took up his father's labours in the Bibliotheca Juris Canonici Veteris, and published with great accuracy the Greek and Latin, using Agylaeus's translation, with Balsamon's commentaries, adding the long-desired Prolegomena of Photius from Ussher.
242. When it was compiled.
243. Its various translations.
244. Agylaeus's translation is the better one.

units.la: 245. Nova editio, quæ extat in bibliotheca juris canonici veteris commendata. ab Usserio & aliis ex Manuscriptis citatis; Quid præstiterit, illud cum suo socio, Guillielmo Voello in præfatione his verbis declarat; Photius inter præclara ingenii sui monumenta reliquit & hunc quem tibi exhibemus Nomocanonem. De quo cum multi eruditi & gravissimi Viri quererentur, quod in præcedentibus editionibus infinitis propemodum mendis scateret: quod in multis etiam deficeret, ac quamplurima confuse & interturbato ordine contineret, nec Latina cum Græcis ubique bene convenirent, tandem ad hoc præstantissimum antiquitatis monumentum integrum Græce & Latine typis & prælo committendum nos accingimus. Itaque in hac editione pro exemplari sumpsimus editionem, quam Justellus olim Lutetiæ emiserat è Codice MS. Bibliothecæ Palatinæ, quam cum alia subsequenti quæ Lutetiæ etiam Græce & Latine edita est anno 1620. diligenter contulimus, & utramque cum antiquissimis MSS. Bibliothecæ Eminentissimi Cardinalis Julii Mazarini, quos humanissimus Posterius hujus divitis & numerosæ supellectilis promuscondus nobiscum lubentissime communicavit; sicque illius beneficio opus illud insigne sanitati perfectæ, integritati pristinæ, nativoque splendori restituimus. Græco textui addidimus Latinam translationem, non eam quam Gentianus Hervetus, sed quam Henricus Agylaus olim elaboraverat; tum quod Agylaus me-liord liori usus est, & ampliori Codice Græco quam Hervetus; tum etiam quod Agylæi translatio magis ad stylum, & genium juris peritorum accedat, in quorum potissimum gratiam novus hic à nobis susceptus est labor. Ita tamen ut quæ in ea deficerent versione nova supplerentur, quæ cum Græco non omnimode congruerent emendarentur, mutatis etiam nonnullis, quæ minus proprie in rebus Theologicis viderentur expressa. Hoc tempore aut usque ad hoc tempus videtur Codex Dionysii Exigui accepisse accessiones sequentium eum Episcoporum Romanorum, & dictis Patrum major auctoritas dari, canonica nimirum & decisoria, ut colligimus ex Epistola Leonis quarti, (qui seculi noni anno quadragesimo septimo pervenit ad Pontificatum Romanum, & in eo fuit usque ad annum quinquagesimum quintum; ideoque Photio anterior, eique præmitti debuisset) ad Episcopos Britanniæ, relata à Gratiano, in c. 1. dist. 20. his verbis: De libellis & commentariis aliorum non convenit aliquem judicare, & sanctorum conciliorum canones relinquere, vel decretalium regulas, id est, quæ habentur apud nos simul cum canonibus, quibus autem in omnibus ecclesiasticis utimur judiciis, sunt canones Apostolorum, Nicænorum, Ancyranorum, Neocæsariensium, Gangrensium, Antiochensium, Laodicensium;
units.tr: 245. The new edition, which is found in the Bibliotheca juris canonici veteris, was recommended by Usher and others from manuscripts they cited. What it achieved, Usher declares in the preface together with his colleague William Voellus, in these words: Photius left behind, among the remarkable monuments of his genius, this Nomocanon which we offer you. Many learned and most serious men have complained about it, because in the earlier editions it swarmed with almost endless errors, because it was also deficient in many places, and because it contained very many things in a confused and disordered arrangement, and the Latin did not agree everywhere well with the Greek. At last we have set ourselves to commit this most excellent monument of antiquity, whole, in Greek and Latin, to the press. In this edition, therefore, we took as our exemplar the edition which Justellus had long before published at Lutetia from a manuscript of the Palatine Library. We carefully collated it with another later edition, also published in Greek and Latin at Lutetia in 1620, and we compared both with the very ancient manuscripts of the library of the most eminent Cardinal Jules Mazarin, whom the most obliging Posterius, the steward of this rich and extensive collection, most willingly shared with us. Thanks to his kindness we have restored that famous work to perfect health, its original integrity, and its native splendour. To the Greek text they added a Latin translation, not that of Gentianus Hervetus but the one which Henricus Agylaeus had long ago worked out, first because Agylaeus used a better and fuller Greek codex than Hervetus, and second because Agylaeus's translation keeps closer to the style and the genius of jurists, for whose sake this new labour was chiefly undertaken. Yet they did so on condition that what was missing in that version would be supplied by the new translation, that what did not fully agree with the Greek would be corrected, and that some things rendered too loosely in matters theological would be changed. At this time, or down to this time, it seems that the Code of Dionysius Exiguus received additions from the following Roman bishops, and that greater authority was given to the sayings of the Fathers, namely canonical and decisive authority, as we gather from the letter of Leo IV (who reached the Roman papacy in the forty-seventh year of the ninth century and remained in it until his fifty-fifth year; so he should have come before Photius and been placed before him) to the bishops of Britain, cited by Gratian in c. 1, dist. 20, in these words: Concerning the libels and commentaries of others, it is not fitting for anyone to pass judgment, and to set aside the canons of the holy councils, or the rules of the decretals, that is, those which are held among us together with the canons, by which we use in all ecclesiastical judgments: they are the canons of the Apostles, of Nicaea, of Ancyra, of Neocaesarea, of Gangra, of Antioch, of Laodicea;

units.la: Digitised by Google fium, Constantinopol. Ephef. Chalcedonensium, Sardicensium, Africanensium, Carthaginensium, & cum illis regulæ præsulum Romanorum, Sylvestri, Syricii, Innocentii, Zozimi, Cælestini, Leonis, Gelasii, Hilarii, Symmachi, Hormisdæ, Simplicii, & Gregorii junioris. Isti omnino sunt, & per quos judicant Episcopi, & per quos Episcopi simul judicantur, & clerici. Nam si tale emerserit, vel contigerit inusitatum negotium, quod minime possit per istos definiri: tunc si illorum, quorum meministis, dicta, Hieronymi, Augustini, Isidori, vel cæterorum similiter sanctorum doctorum similium reperta fuerint, magnanimiter sunt retinenda, ac promulganda; vel ad Apostolicam sedem referendum de talibus. Quam ob causam luculentius magna voce pronunciare non timeo: quia, qui illa, quæ diximus, sanctorum Patrum statuta, quæ apud nos canonum nomine prætitulantur, (sive sit ille Episcopus, sive Clericus, sive Laicus) non indifferenter recipere convincitur, nec catholicam, & Apostolicam fidem nec sancta quatuor Euangelia utiliter, & efficaciter ad effeCtum suum retinere, vel credere probatur. Puduit posteriorum hujus capitis verborum & tantæ auctoritatis, Anselmum, Deusdedit Cardinalem & Gregorium Presbyterum in Polycarpo, ideoque posteriora impia satis verba Leonis, ut monent quoque Correctores Romani in notis ad istud caput, ita legunt : Qui eandem indifferenter non recipit, ipse se convincit minime Catholicam & Apostolicam fidem ad effectum sua retinere salutis. Quae sane tolerabiliora sunt, quam Leonis verba, comparantis Epistolas Paparum, aliquando non satis pias neque saluti necessarias, cum quatuor Euangeliis, quae sane intolerabilis est audacia, & complementum eorum redolet, quae Paulus Apostolus praedixit 2. Thessal. 2. ℣. 4. Sed ad rem. Apparet exinde Codici aut Collectioni decretalium primae à Dionysio Exiguo factae, tempore Leonis quarti additas esse decretales Hilarii, Simplicii, Felicis, Symmachi, Hormisdae & Gregorii junioris ; quod bene in Editione Justelli est observatum, qui distinxit has collectiones in primam & secundam, primam incipit à Siricio usque ad Anastasium, octo Pontificum, quae à Dionysio Exiguo facta est; secundam ab Hilario ad Gregorium juniorem, cui hic titulus praefigitur.
units.tr: of Constantinople, of Ephesus, of Chalcedon, of Sardica, of Africa, of Carthage, and with them the rules of the Roman prelates: Sylvester, Siricius, Innocent, Zosimus, Caelestine, Leo, Gelasius, Hilary, Symmachus, Hormisdas, Simplicius, and Gregory the Younger. These are wholly the ones by which bishops judge, and by which bishops and clergy are judged together. For if some unusual matter should arise, or occur, which cannot be settled by these, then the sayings of those you have mentioned, of Jerome, Augustine, Isidore, or of other holy and similar teachers, if they are found, are to be retained and promulgated with magnanimity; or such matters are to be referred to the Apostolic See. For this reason I do not fear to declare more plainly and with a loud voice: whoever is shown not to receive without distinction those decrees of the holy Fathers which are prefixed with the name of canons among us, whether he be a bishop, a cleric, or a layman, is proved neither to believe in the Catholic and Apostolic faith nor to keep the holy four Gospels usefully and effectively to their purpose. Anselm, Deusdedit the Cardinal and Gregory the Presbyter in Polycarp were ashamed of the latter words of this chapter and of such great authority; and therefore the rather impious words of Leo, as the Roman correctors also note in their notes on that chapter, read thus: Whoever does not receive the same without distinction proves himself not to keep the Catholic and Apostolic faith for the effect of his salvation. These are certainly more tolerable than Leo's words, which compare the letters of the Popes, at times not sufficiently pious nor necessary for salvation, with the four Gospels, which is surely an intolerable audacity, and smells of the fulfilment of what the Apostle Paul foretold in 2 Thess. 2:4. But to the matter. It appears from this that the following were added at the time of Leo IV to the collection or code of decretals first made by Dionysius Exiguus: the decretals of Hilary, Simplicius, Felix, Symmachus, Hormisdas and Gregory the Younger. This was well observed in Justellus's edition, who distinguished these collections into a first and a second: the first begins with Siricius and runs to Anastasius, the eight Popes, and was made by Dionysius Exiguus; the second runs from Hilary to Gregory the Younger, under which title it is prefixed.

units.la: COLLECTIO II. DECRETORUM PONTIFI- CUM ROMANORUM AB HILARIO AD GREGORIUM II. COLLECTIONI I. DIO- NYSII EXIGUI ADDITA.
units.tr: COLLECTIO II. DECRETORUM PONTIFICUM ROMANORUM AB HILARIO AD GREGORIUM II. COLLECTIONI I. DIONYSII EXIGUI ADDITA.

units.la: Ex utraque putat Anton. Augustinus in Praefatione ad antiquas Decretalium Collectiones Codicem Romanum esse factum, & quidem eum qui Moguntiae primum est editus. An hae accessiones cessiones contigerint simul & semel temporibus hujus Leonis quarti, an sub singulis Pontificibus factæ sint, illud conjectu difficile est. Ex collatione memorati capitis cum Codice Canonum Romanæ Ecclesiæ Moguntiæ & Parisiis edito, patet, quod supra quoque observavimus, esse verum, eosdem esse Codices, illum qui à Leone quarto vel auctus vel probatus est, & illum qui in memoratis locis typis descriptus est; nisi quod Leo mentionem faciat Sylvestri, cujus decretales non extant in codice canonum Ecclesiæ Romanæ, ejusque nomen vitio ex scriptoris in textum irrepsisse, ideoque expungendum esse, quia ea tempestate Sylvestri canones recepti non erant, docet Petrus de Marca, de concordia Sacerdotii & Imper. lib. 3. c. 4. Dein Bonifacii I. & Anastasii II. nomina sunt omissa vel incuria Leonis, vel descriptorum, tandem & Felicis decretales comparent in editione Parisiensi, pag. 507. item in secunda post primam Dionysii Exigui collectione, cujus etiam non fit mentio in Epistola Leonis quarti. Post Leonem magis magisque literarum & scientiarum splendor decrescere, barbaries invalescere cœpit, ortaque sunt ista tempora & secula quæ obscura, barbara, ferrea, merito dixeris. De quibus gravissimi Scriptores conqueruntur, quorum querelas nunc mittimus. Quievere itaque per sesqui & quod excurrit seculum Collectiones Juris. Orientales Photii Nomocanone, & Basilicis; Occidentales vero Codice canonum, & Capitularibus Caroli & Ludovici aliorumque Imperatorum contenti vivebant, usque ad seculum undecimum & duodecimum, in quibus certatim iterum magno numero Collectores in canonum & juris Ecclesiastici studium incumbere ceperunt, tam in Oriente quam in Occidente. Primus seculo xi. occurrit Burchardus, Wormatiensis Episcopus, patria Hassus, & primum Lobii Monachus & discipulus Olberti, Monachi Lobiensis & postea Abbatis Gemblacensis. Ex Monacho factus est Burchardus, Episcopus Wormatiensis, anno 96, noni seculi, in quo sedit usque ad annum 1025. vel 1026; quo mortuus est. Hic, quia in sua diacæsi canones & pœnitentium jura confusa, imo discrepantia videret, ut aut ex toto neglecta, aut omni pene auctoritate destituta, vel modice in Ecclesiastica disciplina institutis apparere potuerint, ut ipse in Præfatione operis sui loquitur; rogatu Brunichonis præpositi Ecclesiæ Wormatiensis coepit congerere & digerere jura Ecclesiastica, ad utilitatem suæ Ecclesiæ, ob negligentiam & inscitiam, ut ipse loquitur sacerdotum; Fontes autem & partes sui operis, ipse recenset, in sin. memorata Praefationis. Synodalia, inquit, praecepta, sanctaque instituta, tam ex sanctorum Patrum sententiis, quam ex canonicis scriptis adjutore Deo in unum fasciem ex amplissimo orbe collegi; eaque, ut potui, uno veluti corpore connexa, viginti libris distinxi; Et quibusdam interjectis: Quantis autem hoc laboribus atque vigiliis praestiterim, Deus Optimus judicabit, quem quod pro nostra Ecclesia necessitate fecerim, non latet; Quare etiam si nostra Provincia limites non exierit nihil omnino ægre feremus, modo nostrorum ministrorum manibus teratur. Porro legentibus etiam id persuasum esse cupimus, nihil de meo in hoc opere additum esse, sed ex divinis testimoniis scripturarum, (quaenam hoc tempore hic & supra divinae scripturae & canonica scripta dicta fuerint, id proh dolor statim patebit) singula esse decerpta, ea sane fide, ut perpetuam auctoritatem habitura non dubitem. Ex quibus autem scriptis selegerem ordo sequens indicat.
units.tr: Antonius Augustinus, in his preface to the ancient collections of Decretals, thinks that the Roman Codex was made from both, and specifically from the one first published at Mainz. Whether these additions were made all at once, in the time of this Leo IV, or under the individual popes, is hard to guess. By comparing the chapter mentioned above with the Codex of the Canons of the Roman Church, published at Mainz and Paris, it is clear, as we also observed above, that these are the same codices: the one that was either enlarged or approved by Leo IV, and the one printed in the places cited. The only difference is that Leo mentions Sylvester, whose decretals do not appear in the codex of canons of the Roman Church, and that his name crept into the text through a copyist's error and so should be struck out, because the canons of Sylvester were not yet received in that age; Peter de Marca teaches this in his work on the concord of the priesthood and the empire, book 3, chapter 4. Then the names of Boniface I and Anastasius II have been omitted, either by Leo's carelessness or by the copyists. Finally the decretals of Felix also appear in the Paris edition, p. 507, and likewise in the second collection after the first collection of Dionysius Exiguus, which is not mentioned in the letter of Leo IV. After Leo, the splendour of letters and learning gradually declined, and barbarism grew strong, and those times and ages arose which one may rightly call dark, barbarous and iron. Serious writers complain about them, and I omit their complaints here. So for a century and a half or more the collections of law rested. The Eastern churches lived content with the Nomocanon of Photius and the Basilica; the Western churches with the Codex of canons and the capitularies of Charlemagne, Louis and other emperors, until the eleventh and twelfth centuries, when collectors in great numbers, vying with one another, again began to devote themselves to the study of canons and ecclesiastical law, both in the East and in the West. The first to appear in the eleventh century is Burchard, bishop of Worms, a native of Hesse, who was first a monk and pupil of Olbert, monk of Lobbes and later abbot of Gembloux, at Lobbes. Burchard was made bishop of Worms from a monk in the year 996, and sat in that see until 1025 or 1026, when he died. Because he saw that in his diocese the canons and the laws of penitents were confused, indeed conflicting, so that they were either wholly neglected, or stripped of almost all authority, or could scarcely appear in the institutions of ecclesiastical discipline, as he himself says in the preface to his work, at the request of Brunicho, provost of the church of Worms, he began to gather and arrange the ecclesiastical laws for the benefit of his church, on account of the negligence and ignorance, as he puts it, of the priests. He lists the sources and parts of his work himself, at the end of the aforementioned preface. "The synodal precepts and holy institutions," he says, "both from the opinions of the holy Fathers and from the canonical writings, I have gathered, with God's help, into one bundle out of a very wide world; and these, as far as I could, joined together as in one body, I have divided into twenty books; and after some intervening words: "How much labour and watchfulness I have spent on this, God the Best will judge, and that I did it for the need of our church is not hidden. Therefore, even if it goes beyond the limits of our province, I will take it in no way amiss, provided it is handled by the hands of our ministers. Moreover, I wish readers also to be persuaded that nothing of my own has been added to this work, but that each item has been plucked from the divine testimonies of the Scriptures (what writings are here and above called divine Scripture and canonical writings will at once become plain, alas), and I have no doubt that they will have a lasting authority, so surely have I trusted them. The order that follows shows from which writings I chose them."
From the Canons, which are called the Body of Canons.
From the Canon of the Apostles.
From the councils beyond the sea. He means the Eastern councils.

units.la: Ex conciliis in Germania, Gallia, Hispania ce-lebratis,
units.tr: From the councils celebrated in Germany, Gaul and Spain.
From the decrees of the Roman Pontiffs.
From the Gospels and the Apostolic Scriptures.
From the Old Testament.

units.la: Ex libris Sancti Gregorii. Ex Hieronymo, Augustino, Ambrosio, Benedicto, Basilio, Magno, Isidoro.
units.tr: From the books of Saint Gregory. From Jerome, Augustine, Ambrose, Benedict, Basil, Magnus, Isidore.

units.la: Hic tamen non omnes enumerat Burchardus.
units.tr: Burchard does not, however, list them all here.
From the Roman penitential.
From the penitential of Theodore.
From the penitential of Bede.

units.la: Distinxit Burchardus opus suum in libros viginti, quorum quilibet sua capita seu canones habet, quodlibet autem caput est tantum unius canonis; cuique tamen canoni titulus, seu summarium prænotatus legitur. Summam librorum hanc præmisit ipse Burchardus.
units.tr: Burchard divided his work into twenty books, each of which has its own chapters or canons, but each chapter is of one canon only; yet each canon is read with its title, or summary, prefixed. Burchard himself prefaced the following summary of the books.

units.la: Primus liber continet de potestate & primatu Apostolicæ sedis, Patriarcharum, cæterorumque primatuum, metropolitanorum, & de synodo celebranda, & vocatione ad synodum, De accusatis, & accusatoribus, & testibus, De expoliatis injuste, De judicibus ac de omni honore competenti, ac dignitate, & diverso negocio, & ministerio Episcoporum.
units.tr: The first book contains: on the power and primacy of the Apostolic See, of the patriarchs and the other primates and metropolitans; on holding a synod and summoning to a synod; on the accused, the accusers and the witnesses; on those unjustly despoiled; on judges, and on all the honour, fitting dignity, varied business and ministry of bishops.

units.la: Secundus liber continet de congruenti dignitate, & diversa institutione, ac nutrimento mento vel qualitate vitæ, & diverso negocio, & ministerio presbyterorum & diaconorum, seu reliquorum ordinum ecclesiasticorum.
units.tr: The second book contains: on the fitting dignity, the various appointment, the maintenance, the quality of life, the varied business and ministry of presbyters and deacons, and of the other ecclesiastical orders.

units.la: Tertius liber continet de divinarum domorum institutione, & cultu, & honore. De decimis, & oblationibus, & justitiis singulorum, & qui libri in sacro catalogo recipiantur, qui vero apocryphi, & quando apponendi sint.
units.tr: The third book contains: on the institution, worship and honour of the houses of God; on tithes, offerings and the dues of individuals; and which books are received in the sacred catalogue, which are apocryphal, and when they are to be added.

units.la: Quartus liber continet sacramentum baptismatis, & ministerium baptizandorum & baptizatorum, & consignandorum, & consignatorum.
units.tr: The fourth book contains: the sacrament of baptism, and the ministry to those to be baptized and those baptized, and to those to be confirmed and those confirmed.

units.la: Quintus liber continet de sacramento corporis & sanguinis domini, & de perceptione, & observatione eorum.
units.tr: The fifth book contains: on the sacrament of the body and blood of the Lord, and on the receiving and observing of them.

units.la: Sextus liber continet de homicidiis sponte & non sponte commissis, & de paricidiis, & de fratricidiis, & de illis qui uxores legitimas, & seniores suos interficiunt, & de occisione ecclesiasticorum, & de observatione, & de pœnitentia singulorum.
units.tr: The sixth book contains: on homicides committed wilfully and unwillingly, on parricides, fratricides, and those who kill their lawful wives and their elders, and on the killing of clergy; and on the observance and penance of individuals.

units.la: Septimus liber continet de incesta copulatione consanguinitatis, & in quo geniculo fideles, & conjungi, & separari debeant, & de revocatione & de pœnitentia singulorum.
units.tr: The seventh book contains: on incestuous marriage within the degrees of kinship, and in what degree the faithful may and may not be joined and separated; and on the revocation and penance of individuals.

units.la: Octavus liber continet de viris ac fœminis minis Deo dicatis, & sacrum propositum transgredientibus, & de revocatione, & de poenitentia eorum.
units.tr: The eighth book contains: on men and women dedicated to God who transgress their holy profession; and on their revocation and penance.

units.la: Nonus liber continet de virginibus & viduis non velatis, de raptoribus earum, & de separatione eorum, de conjunctione legitimorum connubiorum, de concubinis, & de transgressione & poenitentia singulorum.
units.tr: The ninth book contains: on virgins and widows not veiled, on their ravishers, and on their separation; on the joining of lawful marriages; on concubines; and on the transgression and penance of individuals.

units.la: Decimus liber continet de incantatoribus, de auguribus, de divinis, de sortilegis, & de variis illusionibus Diaboli, & de maledicis, & de contentiosis, & de conspiratoribus, & de poenitentia singulorum.
units.tr: The tenth book contains: on enchanters, augurs, diviners, sorcerers, and the various illusions of the devil; on slanderers, the quarrelsome and conspirators; and on the penance of individuals.

units.la: Undecimus liber continet de excommunicandis, & excommunicatis, de furibus, & de praedatoribus, & de praesumptione, & contemptu, & negligentia, & reconciliatione & poenitentia eorum.
units.tr: The eleventh book contains: on those to be excommunicated and the excommunicated; on thieves and robbers; on presumption, contempt and negligence; and on their reconciliation and penance.

units.la: Duodecimus liber continet de perjurio, & de poenitentia ejus.
units.tr: The twelfth book contains: on perjury and the penance for it.

units.la: Tertiusdecimus liber continet de veneratione, & observatione sacri jejunii.
units.tr: The thirteenth book contains: on the reverence for and observance of the holy fast.

units.la: Quartusdecimus liber continet de crapula, & ebrietate, & de poenitentia eorum.
units.tr: The fourteenth book contains: on gluttony and drunkenness, and their penance.

units.la: Quintusdecimus liber continet de Imperatoribus, de Principibus, & de reliquis laicis, & de ministerio eorum.
units.tr: The fifteenth book contains: on emperors, princes and the other laity, and on their ministry.

units.la: Sextusdecimus liber continet de accusatoribus, de judicibus, de defensoribus, de falsis testibus, & de poenitentia singulorum.
units.tr: The sixteenth book contains: on accusers, judges, defenders, false witnesses, and the penance of individuals.

units.la: Septimusdecimus liber continet de fornicatione, & incestu diversi generis, & de poenitentia utriusque sexus, & diversae aetatis.
units.tr: The seventeenth book contains: on fornication and incest of various kinds, and on the penance of both sexes and of every age.

units.la: Octavusdecimus liber continet de visitatione, & poenitentia, & reconciliatione infirmorum.
units.tr: The eighteenth book contains: on visiting, penance and reconciliation of the sick.

units.la: Nonusdecimus liber qui corrector vocatur, continet correctiones corporum, & animarum medicinas, & docet unumquemque sacerdotem, etiam simplicem quomodo vel qualiter unicuique succurrere valeat, ordinato vel sine ordine, pauperi, diviti, puero, juveni, seni, decrepito, sano, infirmo, in omni aetate, in utroque sexu.
units.tr: The nineteenth book, called the Corrector, contains corrections for bodies and remedies for souls. It teaches every priest, even an ordinary one, how and in what manner he may help each person, whether ordained or not: the poor, the rich, the boy, the youth, the old man, the decrepit, the healthy, the sick, at every age and in both sexes.

units.la: Vigesimus liber speculationum vocatur, Speculatur enim de providentia, & de praedestinatione divina, & de adventu Antichristi, de ejus operibus, de resurrectione, de die judicii, de infernalibus poenis, de felicitate perpetuae vitae.
units.tr: The twentieth book is called Speculations, for it speculates on the providence and predestination of God, on the coming of Antichrist and his works, on the resurrection, the day of judgement, the punishments of hell, and the happiness of eternal life.

units.la: Ubi & quibus auxiliantibus hoc opus Burchardus perfecerit, docet auctor Anonymus, qui post obitum ejus vitam scripsit, cum ipsius decreto editus.
