Praeterea multa alia congerit nescio unde hausta, quae tribuit Euaristo lib. 3. cap. 17. lib. 18. cap. 16. Alexandro lib. I. logo, qui diu desideratus tandem, ut di-ctum ex M. S. Bibliothecæ Oxoniensis, in lucem protractus est à Justello filio in Bibl. jur. Can. veter. ; ex cujus fine collectum cognoscimus Nomocanonem Anno Mundi, secundum Græcos, 6391: is elt æræ Christianæ 883. Hunc commentariis illustravit Balsamo, ut infra dicemus, ubi de eo inter Interpretes Græcos juris Canonici dissemus. Latinæ Nomocanonis versiones extant duæ; una, quam Gentianus Hervetus; alteram quam Henricus Agylæus elaboravit, quæ tantum Latinè primo prodierunt sine textu Græco, posterior illa Agylæi duplici nomine præ illa Herveti commendanda; quia plenior, utpote quæ ex pleniore exemplari Græco facta est; deinde quia magis accedit ad stylum Jurisconsultorum. Primus Græce ex Codice Bibliothecæ Palatinæ edidit Christophorus Justellus, anno 1615, postea Græce & Latine editus est Nomocanon Parisiis cum commentariis Balsamonis ex Typogr. Regia & interpretatione Gentiani Herveti; Patris labores repetivit Filius Henr. Justellus in bibliotheca juris Canon. veteris, qui accuratissimè Græce & Latinè ex interpretatione Agylæi cum Commentariis Balsamonis edidit, addicis diu desideratis Photii prolegumenis ab Ulleab Usserio & aliis ex Manuscriptis citatis; Quid præstiterit, illud cum suo socio, Guillielmo Voello in præfatione his verbis declarat; Photius inter præclara ingenii sui monumenta reliquit & hunc quem tibi exhibemus Nomocanonem. De quo cum multi eruditi & gravissimi Viri quererentur, quod in præcedentibus editionibus infinitis propemodum mendis scateret: quod in multis etiam deficeret, ac quamplurima confuse & interturbato ordine contineret, nec Latina cum Græcis ubique bene convenirent, tandem ad hoc præstantissimum antiquitatis monumentum integrum Græce & Latine typis & prælo committendum nos accingimus. Itaque in hac editione pro exemplari sumpsimus editionem, quam Justellus olim Lutetiæ emiserat è Codice MS. Bibliothecæ Palatinæ, quam cum alia subsequenti quæ Lutetiæ etiam Græce & Latine edita est anno 1620. diligenter contulimus, & utramque cum antiquissimis MSS. Bibliothecæ Eminentissimi Cardinalis Julii Mazarini, quos humanissimus Poterius hujus divitis & numerosæ supellectilis promuscondus nobiscum lubentissime communicavit; sicque illius beneficio opus illud insigne sanitati perfectæ, integritati pristinæ, nativoque splendori restituimus. Græco textui addidimus Latinam translationem, non eam quam Gentianus Hervetus, sed quam Henricus Agylaus olim elaboraverat; tum quod Agylaus me-liori
units.tr: Where, and with whose help, Burchard completed this work, the anonymous author who wrote his life after his death, and who was published by his order, informs us. Forestus is a forest, he says, two miles distant from Worms (Forestus himself is cited in the confirmation of Conrad, ch. 28, book 14, ch. 16, from the letter 2, book 3, ch. 216, book 5, ch. 11 and 14, from letter 3, book 2, ch. 93, book 3, ch. 59, book 4, ch. 15, from the Pseudo-Anacletus first, book 1, ch. 4, 59, book 2, ch. 154, book 3, ch. 71, 77, book 11, ch. 18, from the second letter, book 1, ch. 1 and 15, book 2, ch. 5, from the third, book 1, ch. 136, 152, 178, from the second of Pseudo-Eusebius, book 1, ch. 76, 99, 34, 40, book 11, ch. 9, from the second of Pseudo-Sixtus I, book 3, ch. 214, from the first of Pseudo-Alexander, book 1, ch. 129, 130, 132, book 2, ch. 52, book 5, ch. 5, from the letter of Pseudo-Telesphorus, book 3, ch. 63, from the former of Pseudo-Hyginus, book 1, ch. 65, from the second of Pseudo-Pius, book 11, ch. 29, from Pseudo-Anicetus, book 1, ch. 28, 63, from the latter letter of Pseudo-Soter, book 3, ch. 215, from Pseudo-Eleutherus, book 16, ch. 30, from the former of Pseudo-Victor, book 1, ch. 176, book 4, ch. 3, from the former of Pseudo-Zephyrinus, book 1, ch. 154, book 16, ch. 13, from the latter, book 2, ch. 3, from the former of Pseudo-Callistus, book 11, ch. 38, from the latter, book 1, ch. 66, 80, 135, 171, book 3, ch. 49, book 7, ch. 1, book 10, ch. 64; see also book 9, ch. 7, from Pseudo-Urban, book 3, ch. 3, 143, book 1, ch. 1, from Pseudo-Anterus, book 1, ch. 77, book 4, ch. 66, from the second of Pseudo-Fabian, book 1, ch. 147, 148, from the third, book 1, ch. 183, book 2, ch. 10, from the second of Pseudo-Cornelius, book 1, ch. 193, book 12, ch. 12, 19, from Pseudo-Lucius, book I, ch. 54, book II, ch. 19, from the former of Pseudo-Stephen, book I, ch. 173, from the latter, book I, ch. 142, 161, 177; see also book 16, ch. 19, from the latter of Pseudo-Sixtus II, book I, ch. 143, 192, from the second of Pseudo-Dionysius, book 3, ch. 43, from the first of Pseudo-Felix I, book I, ch. 157, 169, book 16, ch. 11, from the second, book I, ch. 174, from Pseudo-Eutychianus, book 5, ch. 7, from Pseudo-Caius, book I, ch. 139, from the first of Pseudo-Eusebius, book I, ch. 138, 165, from the second, book II, ch. 25, 27, from the third, book 4, ch. 63, from the former of Pseudo-Melchiades, book 3, ch. 2, 4, 5, from the latter, book I, ch. 2, book 4, ch. 61, from Pseudo-Marcus, book I, ch. 98, from the second of Pseudo-Julius, book I, ch. 144, 170, and from the first, book I, ch. 175, from the former of Pseudo-Felix II, book I, ch. 141, 163, 167, 180, 221, 222, book 16, ch. 11, from the fifth of Pseudo-Damasus, book I, ch. 153, 156, 172, 179, book 16, ch. 31, from the former of Pseudo-Anastasius, book 3, ch. 103, and from the latter, book 19, ch. 129, from the second of Pseudo-Felix IV, book 3, ch. 57, 58, from the former of Pseudo-John II, book 3, ch. 32, from the ninth of Pseudo-Pelagius II, book 3, ch. 69, from the letter of Pseudo-Gregory to Felix, book 7, ch. 19, from Pseudo-Deusdedit, book 17, ch. 44). Besides this, he gathers many other things, drawn from I know not where, which he attributes to Evaristus, book 3, ch. 17, book 18, ch. 16, and to Alexander, book I, the Logos, which, long desired, was at last brought to light, as stated, from a manuscript of the Bodleian Library at Oxford, by Justellus the son, in the Bibliotheca juris canonici veteris. From its end we learn that the Nomocanon was collected in the year of the world 6391 according to the Greeks, which is the year 883 of the Christian era. Balsamon illustrated it with commentaries, as we shall say below, where we discuss him among the Greek interpreters of canon law. There are two Latin versions of the Nomocanon. One was produced by Gentianus Hervetus, the other by Henricus Agylaeus. Those were the first published in Latin only, without the Greek text. Agylaeus's version is to be preferred to that of Hervetus for two reasons: first, because it is fuller, having been made from a fuller Greek copy; second, because it comes closer to the style of the jurists. The Nomocanon was first published in Greek by Christophorus Justellus in 1615, from a manuscript of the Palatine Library. Afterwards it was published in Greek and Latin at Paris with the commentaries of Balsamon, from the royal press, with the translation of Gentianus Hervetus. The son, Henricus Justellus, took up his father's labours in the Bibliotheca juris canonici veteris, and most accurately published the Greek and Latin text, with Agylaeus's translation and the commentaries of Balsamon, adding the long-desired prolegomena of Photius, from the manuscripts cited by Ussher and others. What he achieved he declares, together with his colleague Guillelmus Voellus, in the preface in these words: Photius left among the splendid monuments of his genius also this Nomocanon, which we now offer you. Since many learned and most serious men complained that in the earlier editions it swarmed with almost countless errors, that in many places it was incomplete, and that it contained very many things in confused and disordered arrangement, and that the Latin did not everywhere agree well with the Greek, we have at last set ourselves to commit this most excellent monument of antiquity, whole, in Greek and Latin, to the press and the printing house. In this edition, therefore, we took as our exemplar the edition which Justellus once issued at Paris from a manuscript of the Palatine Library, and we carefully collated it with another later edition, also published in Greek and Latin at Paris in 1620, and we compared both with the most ancient manuscripts of the library of the most eminent Cardinal Jules Mazarin, which the most courteous Poterius, the guardian of this rich and numerous collection, most willingly shared with us. Thus, by his kindness, we have restored that famous work to perfect soundness, to its original integrity, and to its native brilliance. To the Greek text we have added a Latin translation, not that of Gentianus Hervetus, but that which Henricus Agylaeus had once made, because Agylaeus used a better and fuller Greek codex than Hervetus, and also because the translation of Agylaeus comes closer to the style and genius of the jurists, for whose sake especially this new labour has been undertaken by us.

units.la: {2} liori usus est, & ampliori Codice Graco quam Hervetus; tum etiam quod Agylæi translatio magis ad stylum, & genium juris peritorum accedat, in quorum potissimum gratiam novus hic à nobis suscepsus est labor. Ita tamen ut quæ in ea deficerent versione nova supplerentur, quæ cum Graco non omnimode congruerent emendarentur, mutatis etiam nonnullis, quæ minus proprie in rebus Theologicis piderentur expressa.
units.tr: {2} He used a better and fuller Greek codex than Hervetus; and also because Agylaeus's translation comes closer to the style and spirit of lawyers, for whose benefit this new work was chiefly undertaken by us. Yet so that whatever was lacking in that version has been supplied by our new one, and whatever did not altogether agree with the Greek has been corrected, with some expressions also changed that seemed rendered less properly in theological matters.

units.la: Hoc tempore aut usque ad hoc tempus videtur Codex Dionysii Exigui accepisse accessiones sequentium eum Episcoporum Romanorum, & dictis Patrum major auctoritas dari, canonica nimirum & decisoria, ut colligimus ex Epistola Leonis quarti, (qui seculi noni anno quadragesimo septimo pervenit ad Pontificatum Romanum,& in eo fuit usque ad annum quinquagesimum quintum; ideoque Photio anterior, eique præmitti debuisset) ad Episcopos Britanniæ, relata à Gratiano, in c. 1. dist.20. his verbis: De libellis & commentariis aliorum non convenit aliquem judicare, & sanctorum conciliorum canones relinquere, vel decretalium regulas, id est, quæ habentur apud nos simul cum canonibus, quibus autem in omnibus ecclesiasticis utimur judiciis, sunt canones Apostolorum, Nicænorum, Ancyranorum, Neocæsariensium, Gangrensium, Antiochensium, Laodicensium; sium, Constantinopol. Ephef. Chalcedonensium, Sardicensium, Africanensium, Carthaginensium, & cum illis regulæ præsulum Romanorum, Sylvestri, Syricii, Innocentii, Zozimi, Cœlestini, Leonis, Gelasii, Hilarii, Symmachi, Hormisdæ, Simplicii, & Gregorii junioris. Isti omnino sunt, & per quos judicant Episcopi, & per quos Episcopi simul judicantur, & clerici. Nam si tale emerserit, vel contigerit inusitatum negotium, quod minime possit per istos definiri: tunc si illorum, quorum meministis, dicta, Hieronymi, Augustini, Isidori, vel cæterorum similiter sanctorum doctorum similium reperta fuerint, magnanimiter sunt retinenda, ac promulganda; vel ad Apostolicam sedem referendum de talibus. Quam ob causam luculentius magna voce pronunciare non timeo: quia, qui illa, quæ diximus, sanctorum Patrum statuta, quæ apud nos canonum nomine prætitulantur, (sive sit ille Episcopus, sive Clericus, sive Laicus) non indifferenter recipere convincitur, nec catholicam, & Apostolicam fidem nec sancta quatuor Euangelia utiliter, & efficaciter ad effeƈtum suum retinere, vel credere probatur. Puduit posteriorum hujus capitis verborum & tantæ auctoritatis, Anselmum, Deusdedit Cardinalem & Gregorium Presbyterum in Polycarpo, ideoque posteriora impia satis verba Leonis, ut monent quoque Correctores Romani in notis ad istud caput, ita legunt: gunt : Qui eandem indifferenter non recipit, ipse se convincit minime Catholicam & Apostolicam fidem ad effectum sua retinere salutis. Quæ sane tolerabiliora sunt, quam Leonis verba, comparantis Epistolas Paparum, aliquando non satis pias neque saluti necessarias, cum quatuor Euangeliis, quæ sane intolerabilis est audacia, & complementum eorum redolet, quæ Paulus Apostolus prædixit 2. Thessal. 2. ꝟ. 4. Sed ad rem. Apparet exinde Codici aut Collectioni decretalium primæ à Dionysio Exiguo factæ, tempore Leonis quarti additas esse decretales Hilarii, Simplicii, Felicis, Symmachi, Hormisdæ & Gregorii junioris ; quod bene in Editione Justelli est observatum, qui distinxit has collectiones in primam & secundam, primam incipit à Siricio usque ad Anastasium, octo Pontificum, quæ à Dionysio Exiguo facta est; secundam ab Hilario ad Gregorium junriorem, cui hic titulus præfigitur.
units.tr: At this time, or at least up to this time, the Collection of Dionysius Exiguus seems to have received additions from the successive Bishops of Rome, and the sayings of the Fathers seem to have been given greater authority, namely canonical and decisive authority. We gather this from the Epistle of Leo IV (who came to the Roman papacy in the forty-seventh year of the ninth century and remained in office until the fifty-fifth year, and so should have been placed before Photius) to the Bishops of Britain, which Gratian cites in c. 1. dist. 20. in these words: Concerning books and commentaries of others, it is not fitting for anyone to pass judgment and to set aside the canons of the holy councils or the rules of the decretals, that is, those which are held among us together with the canons, and which we use in all ecclesiastical judgments. These are the canons of the Apostles, of the Nicenes, of the Ancyrans, of the Neocaesareans, of the Gangrans, of the Antiochenes, of the Laodiceans, of the Constantinopolitans, of the Ephesines, of the Chalcedonians, of the Sardicans, of the Africans, of the Carthaginians, and with them the rules of the Roman prelates: Sylvester, Siricius, Innocent, Zosimus, Celestine, Leo, Gelasius, Hilary, Symmachus, Hormisdas, Simplicius, and Gregory the Younger. These are the ones by which bishops judge, and by which bishops and clergy are themselves judged. For if some unusual matter should arise or occur which cannot be settled by these, then, if the sayings of those you have mentioned, of Jerome, Augustine, Isidore, or of other similar holy teachers, are found, they are to be firmly retained and published; or such matters are to be referred to the Apostolic See. For this reason I do not hesitate to declare more clearly and loudly that whoever is shown to receive without discrimination those holy decrees of the Fathers which we have described, which are prefixed among us with the name of canons (whether he be bishop, cleric, or layman), is proved neither to believe the Catholic and Apostolic faith nor to hold the holy four Gospels usefully and effectively to their purpose. Anselm, Cardinal Deusdedit, and the Presbyter Gregory were ashamed of the latter part of this chapter and of words of such authority, and therefore, as the Roman Correctors also advise in their notes on this chapter, they read the impious and rather too harsh words of Leo as follows: He who does not receive the same without discrimination convicts himself of not in any way retaining the Catholic and Apostolic faith to the effect of his salvation. These are certainly more tolerable than the words of Leo, which compare the Epistles of the Popes, at times not sufficiently pious nor necessary for salvation, with the four Gospels, a boldness that is truly intolerable and smells of the fulfilment of what the Apostle Paul foretold in 2 Thess. 2:4. But to the matter. It appears from this that the decretals of Hilary, Simplicius, Felix, Symmachus, Hormisdas and Gregory the Younger were added, in the time of Leo IV, to the Collection or first collection of decretals made by Dionysius Exiguus; this was well observed in Justellus's edition, who divided these collections into a first and a second. The first begins with Siricius and runs to Anastasius, covering eight Popes, and was made by Dionysius Exiguus; the second runs from Hilary to Gregory the Younger, and bears this title.

units.la: COLLECTIO II. DECRETORUM PONTIFI- CUM ROMANORUM AB HILARIO AD GREGORIUM II. COLLECTIONI I. DIO- NYSII EXIGUI ADDITA.
units.tr: COLLECTION II OF THE DECRETALS OF THE ROMAN POPES, FROM HILARY TO GREGORY II, ADDED TO THE FIRST COLLECTION OF DIONYSIUS EXIGUUS.

units.la: Ex utraque putat Anton. Augustinus in Præfatione ad antiquas Decretalium Collectiones Codicem Romanum esse factum, & quidem eum qui Moguntiæ primum est editus. An hæ accessiones cessiones contigerint simul & semel temporibus hujus Leonis quarti, an sub singulis Pontificibus factæ sint, illud conjectu difficile est. Ex collatione memorati capitis cum Codice Canonum Romanæ Ecclesiæ Moguntiæ & Parisiis edito, patet, quod supra quoque observavimus, esse verum, eosdem esse Codices, illum qui à Leone quarto vel auctus vel probatus est, & illum qui in memoratis locis typis descriptus est; nisi quod Leo mentionem faciat Sylvestri, cujus decretales non extant in codice canonum Ecclesiæ Romanæ, ejusque nomen vitio ex scriptoris in textum irrepfisse, ideoque expungendum esse, quia ea tempestate Sylvestri canones recepti non erant, docet Petrus de Marca, de concordia Sacerdotii & Imper. lib. 3. c. 4. Dein Bonifacii I. & Anastasii II. nomina sunt omissa vel incuria Leonis, vel descriptorum, tandem & Felicis decretales comparent in editione Parisiensi, pag. 507. item in secunda post primam Dionysii Exigui collectione, cujus etiam non fit mentio in Epistola Leonis quarti. Post Leonem magis magisque literarum & scientiarum splendor decrescere, barbaries invalescere cœpit, ortaque sunt ista tempora & secula quæ obscura, barbara, ferrea, merito dixeris. De quibus gra-vissimi
units.tr: Anton. Augustinus, in his Preface to the ancient collections of Decretals, thinks the Roman Code was made from both, and indeed from the edition first published at Mainz. Whether these additions came together at one time, in the days of this Leo IV, or were made under individual popes, is hard to conjecture. A comparison of the chapter mentioned with the Code of Canons of the Roman Church, published at Mainz and Paris, shows, as we observed above, that it is true that these are the same codices: the one that was either enlarged or approved by Leo IV, and the one printed in the places mentioned. The only difference is that Leo mentions Sylvester, whose decretals are not found in the code of canons of the Roman Church; Petrus de Marca, in On the Concord of Priesthood and Empire, book 3, ch. 4, teaches that his name crept into the text through a copyist's error and must therefore be deleted, because the canons of Sylvester were not received at that time. Then the names of Boniface I and Anastasius II have been omitted, either through Leo's carelessness or that of the copyists. Finally the decretals of Felix appear in the Paris edition, p. 507, and also in the second collection placed after the first collection of Dionysius Exiguus, which is not mentioned in Leo IV's letter. After Leo, the brilliance of letters and learning began to fade more and more, and barbarism to grow strong; and there arose those times and centuries which you may rightly call dark, barbarous, and iron.

units.la: 247. Progressus ad seculum XI vissimi Scriptores conqueruntur, quorum querelas nunc mittimus. Quievere itaque per sesqui & quod excurrit seculum Collectiones Juris. Orientales Photii Nomocanone, & Basilicis; Occidentales vero Codice canonum, & Capitularibus Caroli & Ludovici aliorumque Imperatorum contenti vivebant, usque ad seculum undecimum & duodecimum, in quibus certatim iterum magno numero Collectores in canonum & juris Ecclesiastici studium incumbere ceperunt, tam in Oriente quam in Occidente.
units.tr: 247. Progress to the eleventh century. The most serious writers complain of these, and we now pass over their complaints. Thus for a century and a half and more the collections of law lay quiet. In the East they lived content with Photius's Nomocanon and the Basilica; in the West with the Code of Canons and the Capitularies of Charlemagne, Louis, and other emperors. Then, in the eleventh and twelfth centuries, many collectors in both East and West again eagerly turned in great numbers to the study of canons and ecclesiastical law.

units.la: Primus seculo xi. occurrit Burchardus, Wormatiensis Episcopus, patria Hassus, & primum Lobii Monachus & discipulus Olberti, Monachi Lobiensis & postea Abbatis Gemblacensis. Ex Monacho factus est Burchardus, Episcopus Wormatiensis, anno 996, noni seculi, in quo sedit usque ad annum 1025. vel 1026; quo mortuus est.
units.tr: The first to appear in the eleventh century is Burchard, Bishop of Worms, a Hessian by birth, who was first a monk and pupil of Olbert, monk of Lobbes and later abbot of Gembloux. From a monk Burchard was made Bishop of Worms in 996. He held the see until 1025 or 1026, when he died.

units.la: Hic, quia in sua diacæsi canones & pœnitentium jura confusa, imo discrepantia videret, ut aut ex toto neglecta, aut omni pene auctoritate destituta, vel modice in Ecclesiastica disciplina institutis apparere potuerint, ut ipse in Præfatione operis sui loquitur; rogatu Brunichonis præpositi Ecclesiæ Wormatiensis coepit congerere & digerere jura Ecclesiastica, ad utilitatem suæ Ecclesiæ, ob negligentiam & inscitiam, ut ipse loquitur sacerdotum; Fontes autem & partes sui operis, ipse recenset, in sin. memoratæ Præfationis. Synodalia, inquit, præcepta, sanctaque instituta, tam ex sanctorum Patrum sententiis, quam ex canonicis scriptis adjutore Deo in unum fascem ex amplissimo orbe collegi; eaque, ut potui, uno veluti corpore connexa, viginti libris distinxi; Et quibusdam interjectis: Quantis autem hoc laboribus atque vigiliis præstiterim, Deus Optimus judicabit, quem quod pro nostræ Ecclesiæ necessitate fecerim, non latet; Quare etiam si nostræ Provinciæ limites non exierit nihil omnino ægre feremus, modo nostrorum ministrorum manibus teratur. Porro legentibus etiam id persuasum esse cupimus, nihil de meo in hoc opere additum esse, sed ex divinis testimoniis scripturarum, (quænam hoc tempore hic & supra divinæ scripturæ & canonica scripta dicta fuerint, id proh dolor statim patebit) singula esse decerpta, ea sane fide, ut perpetuam auctoritatem habitura non dubitem. Ex quibus autem scriptis selegerem ordo sequens indicat.
units.tr: Burchard, seeing that the canons and the laws on penitents in his diocese were confused, indeed conflicting, so that they had either been wholly neglected or stripped of almost all authority, or could appear only slightly in the institutions of church discipline, as he himself says in his Preface, began at the request of Brunicho, provost of the church of Worms, to gather and arrange the ecclesiastical laws for the benefit of his church, on account of the negligence and ignorance, as he puts it, of its priests. He himself lists the sources and parts of his work at the end of the said Preface: "I have gathered into one bundle, with God's help, from the wide world the synodal precepts and holy institutions, both from the opinions of the holy Fathers and from canonical writings; and I have divided them, connected as far as I could into one body, into twenty books." And after some interjections: "God the Best will judge how much labour and vigil I have spent on this, and it is not hidden why I have done it, for the need of our Church. Therefore, even if it goes beyond the limits of our province, we shall bear it with no discomfort at all, provided it is handled by the hands of our ministers. Moreover we wish readers also to be persuaded that nothing of my own has been added to this work, but that the individual items have been excerpted from the divine testimonies of the Scriptures (what is here and above called divine Scripture and canonical writings will, alas, soon be plain), with such faith that I do not doubt they will have perpetual authority. The following order shows from which writings I chose them."

units.la: Ex Canonibus, qui Corpus canonum vocantur.
units.tr: From the Canons, which are called the Body of Canons.
From the Canon of the Apostles.
From the transmarine councils. He means the Eastern ones.

units.la: Ex conciliis in Germania, Gallia, Hispania celebratis,
units.tr: From the councils held in Germany, Gaul, and Spain.
From the Decrees of the Roman Popes.
From the Gospels and the apostolic Scriptures.
From the Old Testament.

units.la: Ex libris Sancti Gregorii. Ex Hieronymo, Augustino, Ambrosio, Benedicto, Basilio, Magno, Isidoro.
units.tr: From the books of St Gregory. From Jerome, Augustine, Ambrose, Benedict, Basil, Leo the Great, and Isidore.

units.la: Hic tamen non omnes enumerat Burchardus.
units.tr: Burchard does not list them all here.
From the Roman penitential.
From the penitential of Theodore.
From the penitential of Bede.

units.la: Distinxit Burchardus opus suum in libros viginti, quorum quilibet sua capita seu canones habet, quodlibet autem caput est tantum unius canonis; cuique tamen canoni titulus, seu summarium prænotatus legitur. Summam librorum hanc præmisit ipse Burchardus.
units.tr: Burchard divided his work into twenty books, each of which has its own chapters or canons; each chapter is only one canon, and each canon has its title or summary prefixed. Burchard himself prefixed this summary of the books.

units.la: Primus liber continet de potestate & primatu Apostolicæ sedis, Patriarcharum, cæterorumque primatuum, metropolitanorum, & de synodo celebranda, & vocatione ad synodum, De accusatis, & accusatoribus, & testibus, De expoliatis injuste, De judicibus ac de omni honore competenti, ac dignitate, & diverso negocio, & ministerio Episcoporum.
units.tr: The first book contains concerning the power and primacy of the Apostolic See, of the patriarchs and the other primates and metropolitans, and concerning the holding of a synod and the summons to a synod; concerning those accused, accusers, and witnesses; concerning those unjustly despoiled; concerning judges and every honour and dignity that is due, and the different business and ministry of bishops.

units.la: Secundus liber continet de congruenti dignitate, & diversa institutione, ac nutrimento mento vel qualitate vitæ, & diverso negocio, & ministerio presbyterorum & diaconorum, seu reliquorum ordinum ecclesiasticorum.
units.tr: The second book contains concerning the dignity that befits, and the different institution, and the maintenance or quality of life, and the different business and ministry of presbyters and deacons, or of the other ecclesiastical orders.

units.la: Tertius liber continet de divinarum domorum institutione, & cultu, & honore. De decimis, & oblationibus, & justitiis singulorum, & qui libri in sacro catalogo recipiantur, qui vero apocryphi, & quando apponendi sint.
units.tr: The third book contains concerning the institution, worship, and honour of the houses of God; concerning tithes, offerings, and the dues of individuals; and which books are received in the sacred catalogue, and which are apocryphal, and when they are to be added.

units.la: Quartus liber continet sacramentum baptismatis, & ministerium baptizandorum & baptizatorum, & consignandorum, & consignatorum.
units.tr: The fourth book contains the sacrament of baptism, and the ministry of those to be baptized, of the baptized, and of those to be confirmed and of the confirmed.

units.la: Quintus liber continet de sacramento corporis & sanguinis domini, & de perceptione, & observatione eorum.
units.tr: The fifth book contains concerning the sacrament of the body and blood of the Lord, and concerning the reception and observance of them.

units.la: Sextus liber continet de homicidiis sponte & non sponte commissis, & de paricidiis, & de fratricidiis, & de illis qui uxores legitimas, & seniores suos interficiunt, & de occisione ecclesiasticorum, & de observatione, & de pœnitentia singulorum.
units.tr: The sixth book contains concerning homicides committed wilfully and unwillingly, and concerning parricides, fratricides, and those who kill their lawful wives and their elders, and concerning the killing of clergy; and concerning the observance and penance of individuals.

units.la: Septimus liber continet de incesta copulatione consanguinitatis, & in quo geniculo fideles, & conjungi, & separari debeant, & de revocatione & de pœnitentia singulorum.
units.tr: The seventh book contains concerning incestuous unions of kinship, and at what degree of kinship the faithful ought to be joined and separated; and concerning the revocation and penance of individuals.

units.la: Octavus liber continet de viris ac fœminis minis Deo dicatis, & sacrum propositum transgredientibus, & de revocatione, & de pœnitentia eorum.
units.tr: The eighth book contains concerning men and women dedicated to God who transgress their holy vow, and concerning their revocation and penance.

units.la: Nonus liber continet de virginibus & viduis non velatis, de raptoribus earum, & de separatione eorum, de conjunctione legitimorum connubiorum, de concubinis, & de transgressione & pœnitentia singulorum.
units.tr: The ninth book contains concerning virgins and widows who are not veiled, concerning their ravishers and their separation, concerning the union of lawful marriages, concerning concubines, and concerning the transgression and penance of individuals.

units.la: Decimus liber continet de incantatoribus, de auguribus, de divinis, de sortilegis, & de variis illusionibus Diaboli, & de maleficis, & de contentiosis, & de conspiratoribus, & de pœnitentia singulorum.
units.tr: The tenth book contains concerning enchanters, augurs, diviners, fortune-tellers, and the various illusions of the Devil; concerning sorcerers, the quarrelsome, and conspirators; and concerning the penance of individuals.

units.la: Undecimus liber continet de excommunicandis, & excommunicatis, de furibus, & de prædatoribus, & de præsumptione, & contemptu, & negligentia, & reconciliatione & pœnitentia eorum.
units.tr: The eleventh book contains concerning those to be excommunicated and the excommunicated, concerning thieves and plunderers, and concerning presumption, contempt, and negligence, and the reconciliation and penance of these.

units.la: Duodecimus liber continet de perjurio, & de pœnitentia ejus.
units.tr: The twelfth book contains concerning perjury and the penance for it.

units.la: Tertiusdecimus liber continet de veneratione, & observatione sacri jejunii.
units.tr: The thirteenth book contains concerning the reverence and observance of holy fasting.

units.la: Quartusdecimus liber continet de crapula, & ebrietate, & de pœnitentia eorum.
units.tr: The fourteenth book contains concerning gluttony and drunkenness, and the penance for them.

units.la: Quintusdecimus liber continet de Imperatoribus, de Principibus, & de reliquis laicis, & de ministerio eorum.
units.tr: The fifteenth book contains concerning emperors, princes, and the other laity, and their office.

units.la: Sextusdecimus liber continet de accusatoribus, de judicibus, de defensoribus, de falsis testibus, & de poenitentia singulorum.
units.tr: The sixteenth book contains concerning accusers, judges, defenders, false witnesses, and the penance of individuals.

units.la: Septimusdecimus liber continet de fornicatione, & incestu diversi generis, & de poenitentia utriusque sexus, & diversae aetatis.
units.tr: The seventeenth book contains concerning fornication and incest of various kinds, and the penance of both sexes and of different ages.

units.la: Octavusdecimus liber continet de visitatione, & poenitentia, & reconciliatione infirmorum.
units.tr: The eighteenth book deals with the visitation, repentance, and reconciliation of the sick.

units.la: Nonusdecimus liber qui corrector vocatur, continet correctiones corporum, & animarum medicinas, & docet unumquemque sacerdotem, etiam simplicem quomodo vel qualiter unicuique succurrere valeat, ordinato vel sine ordine, pauperi, diviti, puero, juveni, seni, decrepito, sano, infirmo, in omni aetate, in utroque sexu.
units.tr: The nineteenth book, which is called the Corrector, contains the corrections of bodies and the remedies of souls, and teaches every priest, even one who is not ordained, how he may or can help each person, whether ordained or not: the poor, the rich, the child, the youth, the old man, the decrepit, the healthy, the sick, at every age and of either sex.

units.la: Vigesimus liber speculationum vocatur. Speculatur enim de providentia, & de praedestinatione divina, & de adventu Antichristi, de ejus operibus, de resurrectione, de die judicii, de infernalibus poenis, de felicitate perpetuae vitae.
units.tr: The twentieth book is called Speculations. For it speculates about the providence and the predestination of God, about the coming of Antichrist and his works, about the resurrection, the day of judgement, the punishments of hell, and the happiness of eternal life.

units.la: Ubi & quibus auxiliantibus hoc opus Burchardus perfecerit, docet auctor Anonymus, qui post obitum ejus vitam scripsit, cum ipsius decreto editus. Foresius sylva est, inquit, duobus milliaribus à Wormatia distans, (Forestus ipse vocatur in confirmatione Conradi Regis, Forehehe) abietibus abundans, & hanc palus limosa ex una parte ambiendo circumcingit, in cujus medietate collis pulcherrimus consistit, ad quem vir Dei se transferri præcepit, & quia mundanos tumultus devitare voluit, arboribus fruticibusque succisis collem explanavit. Ibi quoque primum fecit oratorium, dein aliis officinis peractis, cellam egregiam construxit. Illuc se post concilia regiaque colloquia, & post curam synodalem diversosque mundi strepitus receperat. Ibi quoque negociis secularibus post tergum projectis, totis viribus in obsequio Dei studebat. Eodem quippe tempore in Collectario canonum in hac cella non modicum laboravit. Nam domino Walterio Spirensi Episcopo adjuvante, & Brunichone præposito exhortante & suggerente, Canones in unum corpus collegit. Non pro ulla arrogantia, sed, ut ipse dixit, quia Canonum jura pœnitentiamque judicia in Episcopatu suo omnino fuerant neglecta ac destructa, hoc vero corpus sive Collectarium distinxit & in viginti libros distribuit. Sigebertus in Chronico ad annum 1008. refert, collaborante Magistro suo Olberto Abbate, Viro undiquaque doctissimo, magnum Canonum Volumen edidisse, & in libro script. Eccles. cap. 141. Hæc de eo refert. Burchardus Episcopus urbis Vangionum quæ dicitur Wormatia, magnum Canonum volumen, quod à nomine ipsius BURCHARDUS
units.tr: The author Anonymus, who wrote Burchard's life after his death, tells where and with whose help he completed this work, which was published by his decree. Foresius is a wood, he says, two miles from Worms (it is called Forestus itself in the confirmation of King Conrad, Forehehe), abounding in fir trees, and it encircles this with a muddy marsh on one side. In the middle of it stands a most beautiful hill, to which the man of God ordered himself to be taken, and because he wished to avoid worldly tumults, he cleared the hill by cutting down the trees and shrubs. There he first made a little oratory, and then, when other buildings were finished, he built a fine cell. He withdrew there after councils and royal conferences, and after his synodal duties and the various noises of the world. There too, with secular business put behind him, he devoted all his strength to the service of God. Indeed, at the same time, he laboured no little in this cell on the Collection of Canons. For with the help of the lord Walter, bishop of Speyer, and at the urging and suggestion of the provost Bruniho, he gathered the canons into one body. He did this not out of any arrogance, but, as he himself said, because the laws of the canons and the judgements of penance had been wholly neglected and destroyed in his bishopric. He arranged this body, or Collection, and distributed it into twenty books. Sigebert, in his Chronicle under the year 1008, reports that, with the collaboration of his teacher, the abbot Olbert, a man learned in every respect, he published a great volume of canons; and in his book On Ecclesiastical Writers, chapter 141, he reports the following about him: Burchard, bishop of the city of the Vangiones which is called Worms, composed with great zeal a great volume of canons, which is named after his own name BURCHARDUS

units.la: 253. Nomen Operis. CHARDUS denominatur, multo studio composuit; quod testimoniis omnium authenticorum conciliorum & decretis Romanorum Pontificum, & sententiis omnium pene Catholicorum Patrum authorizavit; ex quo adhuc omnium conciliorum decreta authorizantur. Ea quæ de auxilio Olberti in Chronico scripserat, confirmat in vita Olberti de script. Eccles. cap. 142. Burchardus Episcopus Wormatiensis ejus Olberti magisterio ad hoc provectus, ut ita Ecclesiasticæ utilitati intenderet & ejus studio, ore & manu illud magnum canonum Volumen ad communem omnium utilitatem, ederet. Præter illud opus quidquam scripsisse, non inveni. Mortuus est Burchardus, ut videmus post vitam ejus notatum, anno 1024, vel 1025. Ultimum sequitur Miræus in Biblioth. Ecclesiast. in scholiis ad caput 141. Sigeberti, Baronius anno 1026. mortuum narrat, vide eum ad istum annum. Ejus Decretorum opus editum est primum Coloniæ Agrippinæ, anno 1548. quo ego usus sum, & iterum anno 1549. Parisiis. In Collectionem hanc quisquilias ex Isidoro Mercatore seu ejus suppositis epistolis plurimas retulit: quod indicium est, non magno judicio usum esse. Specimen exhibebunt sequentia exempla. D. 1008. teste Sigeberto, obiit A. D. 1026. A Baronio & Bel-larmino sanctus habetur, cui tot nugæ placuerunt. Plura de vita ejus vide præter auctorem Anonymum supra citatum in vita ejus, apud Henric. Pantaleonem de Viris illustrib. German. part. 2. pag. mihi 46. & seq. qui an. 996. ad Episcopatum pervenisse, paulo post annum 1025. exactis fere xxx. annis in Episcopatu decesse dicit. Hoc seculo immensa illa potestas & auctoritas Pontificis Romani, & Mysterium illud iniquitatis, ita stabilitum est, ut merito ad virilem ætatem adscendisse, neque ultra adsurgere potuisse, jure meritoque dici queat. Per octo fere & quod excurrit secula in eo desudatum est, sed hoc demum seculo ad [?]ακμῲ pervenit. Seculo secundo decurrente Victor Papa illud monstrum violenta disputatione de Pascha te parturiit, eamque secundum suam suæque sedis sententiam decidi, aliisque præfracte obtrudere voluit. Seculo quarto, adserto Metropolitanatu in Concilio Nicæno, Romano Italicarum, seu potius Suburbicariarum regionum Metropolitanatus adsertus est. Seculo quinto Zosimus, Bonifacius I. & Cœlestinus Controversiam de appellationibus ad sedem Romanam urserunt, & jura sibi adserere conati sunt, in Ecclesias Africanas, ita ut & falsi canones pro Nicænis concilio Carthaginensi obtrusi fuerint; vide quæ supra disseruimus de Zosimi collectione num. marg. 67. & seq. Sed opposuit se synodus, appellationesq; transmarinas & jura Pontificum Romanorum inhibuit. Seculo sexto præcipite Gregorius Magnus cum Constantinopolitano de primatu contendit, quem fugere & abominari se simulabat. Seculi septimi initio Bonifacius probata impietate Phocæ, ab eo primatum obtinet, manentibus tamen perpetuis imposterum disputationibus inter Romanos & Constantinopolitanos Episcopos; In Occidente vero feliciter successit primatus, & passim Ecclesiæ eum agnoverunt. Sed Principes seu Imperatores Romano Germanici, nimium potentes adhuc erant, Pontifices ipsos & Episcopos passim constituebant, vel approbabant, investiebant, & juramenta fidelitatis exigebant, quibus multos sibi obstringebant. Hoc itaque abolori adhuc debebat, ut potentia Papalis etiam super solium Imperatoris adscendere posset. Istud hoc seculo audacissime aggressus est Hildebrandus; qui natione Tuscus Soanensis, professione Monachus Cluniacensis, malis artibus, ut Benno Cardinalis & Archipresbyter Romanus testatur, ad Pontificatum maximum anno 1073. pervenit; cum antea sub aliquibus Pontificibus Papa fuisset, omnia jura Imperatorum invertit, & summam Episcopo Romano potentiam adseruit. Ipse sine consensu Imperat: ad Episcopatum venit, investituras laicales publicato decreto proscripsit & prohibuit, Imperatorem excommunicavit,& Imperio privavit, totam denique in republica Romano Germanica mutationem induxit. Vide rem accurate excussam & traditam à Mornæo in mysterio iniquitatis;& perpende hæc Onuphrii Panvinii verba de eo, in vita ejus. Huic uni, inquit ille, cum omnes Latinæ Ecclesiæ, tum præcipue Romana acceptum referre debet, quod libera sit & ab Imperatorum manu eruta, quod tot divitiis, opibus & prophana ditione locupletata; quod Regibus, Imperatoribus, Christianis Principibus sit præfecta: à quo postremo, ut omnia verbo uno complectar, maximus iste eximiusque status, in quo Ecclesia Romana est omnium Christianorum domina; cum antea tanquam vilis ancilla non ab Imperatoribus modo, sed à quovis principe Romani Imperatoris præsidiis fulto, premeretur: ab hoc maximæ illius & omni seculo tremendæ venerandáq, Romani Pontificis & infinita pene potestatis jus manavit. Nam etsi ante Romani Pontifices, tanquam Religionis Christianæ capita, Christique Vicarii & Petri successores colerentur; non tamen eorum auctoritas ultra protendebatur, quam in fidei dogmatibus vel asserendis vel tuendis. Cæterum Imperatoribus suberant; ad eorum nutum omnia fiebant: ab eis creabantur: de eis judicare vel quicquam decernere non audebat Papa Romanus. Primus omnium Romanorum Pontificum Gregorius VII. armis Nortmannorum fretus, opibus Comitissæ Mathildis mulieris per Italiam potentissimæ confisus, discordiaque Germanorum Principum bello civili laborantium inflammatus, praeter majorum morem contempta Imperatoris auctoritate & potestate, cum summum Pontificatum obtinuisset, Cæsarem ipsum (à quo si non electus, saltem confirmatus fuerat) non dico excommunicare, sed etiam regno imperioque privare ausus est. Res ante ea secula inaudita. Nam fabulas quæ de Arcadio, Anastasio & Leone Iconomacho circumferuntur, nihil moror. Unde Ortho Frisingensis horum temporum Scriptor: Lego, inquit, & relego Romanorum Regum & Pontificum gesta, & nusquam invenio aliquem eorum ante hunc Henricum à Romano Pontifice excommunicatum vel regno privatum &c. Hoc regno & potestate stabilita, & leges seu canones ei congruentes fingi & cudi debuerunt, runt, qui explosa simplicitate & humilitate Apostolica veteri, splendorem Imperii & vicarii Christi redolerent, & culmen illud potentiæ impositerum moderarentur & defenderent. Huic rei Dictatus suos, invenit Gregorius, aptissimos nomine & omine ad finem obtinendum quem intendebat; De his ita Onuphrius Panvinius loc. cit. Gregorius in media quadragesima, inquit, Romæ in Basilica Lateranensi, quæ Constantiniana appellatur, primo synodum generalem multorum Episcoporum, Abbatum, & aliorum Prælatorum congregavit; in qua circa triginta edidit capitula, seu canones, quos DICTATUS appellavit: quorum major pars antea parum in usu fuerat, & à nemine prædecessorum suorum unquam attentata: verum ad firmissimum Ecclesiæ statum jaciendum, & ad omnia tentanda, quæ animo agitabat, idonea. Dictatus hi à Cæsare Baronio in Annalibus ad annum 1076. num. 31. 32. & 33. tanquam Privilegia Apostolicæ Sedis Et Romani Pontificis memorantur; ubi de iis ipsius Gregorii septimi libr. 2. Epistolam 55. laudat, & ex iis Dictatus Papæ appellatos scribit. Eos tanquam ipsius Gregorii collectionem, in perpetuam Pontificiæ almipotentiæ stabilitæ monumentum subjicimus. Sunt autem viginti septem sequentes.
units.tr: 253. The Name of the Work. Burchard, after whom it is named, compiled it with great diligence. He supported it with the testimonies of all the authentic councils, the decrees of the Roman Pontiffs, and the opinions of almost all the Catholic Fathers, and from it the decrees of all the councils are still authorised. He confirms what he had written in the Chronicle about Olbert's help, in the life of Olbert, On ecclesiastical writers, ch. 142: "Burchard, Bishop of Worms, was advanced by the teaching of Olbert to this, so that he would devote himself to the usefulness of the Church, and by his zeal, by voice and hand, published that great Volume of Canons for the common benefit of all." I have found that he wrote nothing besides that work. Burchard died, as we note after his life, in 1024 or 1025. Miraeus follows last, in Bibliotheca Ecclesiastica, in the scholia on chapter 141 of Sigebert; Baronius reports his death in 1026, see him at that year. His Decretum was first published at Cologne in 1548, which I used, and again at Paris in 1549. Into this Collection he brought very many trifles from Isidore Mercator, or from his spurious letters, which is a sign that he did not use great judgement. The following examples will show the kind of thing. He also cited the preface of Pseudo-Isidore, book 1, chapter 42. When the most learned Blondel had collected these, in his Prolegomena to the Pseudo-Isidore and Turrianus is beaten, chapter 18, he adds in the margin: "He wrote" (Burchard, Bishop of Worms) in the year 1008, according to Sigebert, he died in the year 1026. He is held a saint by Baronius and Bellarmine, to whom so many trifles were pleasing." For more about his life, see besides the anonymous author cited above in his life, in Henricus Pantaleon, On illustrious men of Germany, part 2, page 46 and following, who says that he came to the episcopate in 996 and died a little after 1025, having spent almost thirty years in the bishopric. In this century that immense power and authority of the Roman Pontiff, and that mystery of iniquity, were so firmly established that it can rightly and justly be said that they had reached manhood and could rise no further. For nearly eight centuries and more it was laboured at, but in this century at last it reached its peak. In the course of the second century Pope Victor brought forth that monster in a violent dispute about Easter, and wished to decide it according to his own and his see's opinion and to force it stiffly upon others. In the fourth century, when the metropolitan authority was asserted at the Council of Nicaea, the metropolitan authority of the Roman region of the Italian, or rather the suburbicarian, regions was asserted. In the fifth century Zosimus, Boniface I and Celestine pressed the controversy about appeals to the Roman see, and tried to claim rights over the African Churches, so that even false canons were foisted on the Council of Carthage as Nicene; see what we have discussed above about the collection of Zosimus, marginal number 67 and following. But a synod opposed this, and forbade transmarine appeals and the rights of the Roman Pontiffs. In the sixth century Gregory the Great hotly contended with the Constantinopolitan over primacy, which he pretended to flee and abhor. At the beginning of the seventh century Boniface, with Phocas's impiety proven, obtained primacy from him, though disputes between the Roman and Constantinopolitan bishops continued perpetually afterwards; in the West, however, primacy succeeded happily, and the Churches everywhere acknowledged it. But the Roman-German princes or emperors were still too powerful: they appointed, or approved, and invested the Pontiffs and bishops themselves everywhere, and exacted oaths of fidelity, by which they bound many to themselves. This, then, had still to be abolished, so that Papal power might rise even above the throne of the Emperor. This Hildebrand audaciously undertook in this century; he, a Tuscan of Soana by birth and a Cluniac monk by profession, reached the supreme Pontificate in 1073 by wicked arts, as Benno the Cardinal and Roman archpriest testifies, having previously been Pope under several Pontiffs. He overturned all the rights of the Emperors and asserted the highest power for the Roman bishop. He himself came to the episcopate without the consent of the Emperor; he proscribed and forbade lay investitures by a published decree; he excommunicated the Emperor and deprived him of the Empire; finally he brought about a complete change in the Roman-German commonwealth. See the matter carefully examined and related by Mornay in The Mystery of Iniquity, and weigh these words of Onuphrius Panvinius about him, in his life: "To him alone, he says, not only all the Latin Churches but especially the Roman Church ought to ascribe it that she is free and snatched from the hand of the Emperors; that she has been enriched with so many riches, resources and secular dominion; that she has been set over kings, emperors and Christian princes. From him at last, to sum up everything in one word, comes that greatest and most splendid condition in which the Roman Church is mistress of all Christians; whereas before, like a cheap maidservant, she was oppressed not only by the Emperors but by any prince supported by the protection of the Roman Emperor. From him there flowed the right of that greatest and in every age awe-inspiring, venerable and almost infinite power of the Roman Pontiff. For although before this the Roman Pontiffs were honoured as the heads of the Christian religion, as Vicars of Christ and successors of Peter, nevertheless their authority did not extend further than to asserting or defending the dogmas of faith. Moreover they were subject to the Emperors; everything was done at their nod; they were created by them; the Roman Pope did not dare to judge them or decree anything concerning them. Gregory VII was the first of all the Roman Pontiffs who, relying on the arms of the Normans, confident in the wealth of the Countess Matilda, a woman most powerful throughout Italy, and inflamed by the discord of the German princes labouring in civil war, contrary to the custom of their elders, having set aside the authority and power of the Emperor, when he had obtained the supreme Pontificate, dared not merely to excommunicate the Caesar himself (by whom he had been, if not elected, at least confirmed), but even to deprive him of kingdom and empire. Such a thing was unheard of in earlier ages. For I pay no attention to the fables that are circulated about Arcadius, Anastasius and Leo the Iconoclast. Hence Otto of Freising, a writer of these times: 'I read,' he says, 'and reread the deeds of the Roman Kings and Pontiffs, and nowhere do I find any of them, before this Henry, excommunicated or deprived of kingdom by the Roman Pontiff,' etc. With this kingdom and power established, laws or canons suited to it had to be invented and forged, which, having cast aside the simplicity and ancient Apostolic humility, would smell of the splendour of the Empire and of the Vicar of Christ, and would govern and defend that summit of power for the future. For this purpose Gregory devised his Dictates, most fitting in name and omen for achieving the end he intended. Concerning these, Onuphrius Panvinius, loc. cit., says: "Gregory, in the middle of Lent, at Rome, in the Lateran Basilica, which is called Constantinian, first gathered a general synod of many bishops, abbots and other prelates; in it he published about thirty chapters, or canons, which he called DICTATES: the greater part of which had been little in use before, and never attempted by any of his predecessors; but suited to laying the firmest foundation of the Church and to attempting all the things he had in mind." These Dictates are mentioned by Caesar Baronius, in the Annals at the year 1076, numbers 31, 32 and 33, as Privileges of the Apostolic See and of the Roman Pontiff; where he praises Gregory VII's own Letter 55 of book 2 concerning them, and writes that from them the Dictates of the Pope were so called. We set them out below as a collection of Gregory himself, a monument to the perpetual establishment of Papal almighty power. There are twenty-seven of them, as follows.

units.la: I. Quod Romana Ecclesia à solo Domino sit fundata.
units.tr: That the Roman Church was founded by the Lord alone.

units.la: II. Quod solus Romanus Pontifex jure dicatur universalis.
units.tr: That the Roman Pontiff alone is rightly called universal.

units.la: III. Quod ille solus possit deponere Episcopos vel reconciliare.
units.tr: That he alone may depose or reconcile bishops.

units.la: IV. Quod Legatus ejus omnibus Episcopis praesit in Concilio, etiam inferioris gradus, & adversus eos sententiam depositionis possit dare.
units.tr: That his legate presides over all bishops in a council, even those of lower rank, and may pronounce a sentence of deposition against them.
That the Pope may depose even those who are absent.

units.la: VI. Quod cum excommunicatis ab illo, inter caetera nec in eadem domo debemus permanere.
units.tr: That we must not remain in the same house as those excommunicated by him, among other things.

units.la: VII. Quod illi soli licet pro temporis necessitate novas leges condere, novas plebes congregare, de canonica Abbatiam facere, & è contra, divitem Episcopatum dividere, & inopes unire.
units.tr: That he alone may, as the needs of the time require, enact new laws, gather new peoples, make an abbey out of a canonry, and conversely divide a rich bishopric and unite poor ones.

units.la: VIII. Quod solus possit uti Imperialibus insigniis.
units.tr: That he alone may use the imperial insignia.

units.la: IX. Quod solius Papae pedes omnes Principes deosculentur.
units.tr: That all princes kiss the feet of the Pope alone.

units.la: X. Quod illius solius nomen in Ecclesiis recitetur.
units.tr: That his name alone be recited in the churches.

units.la: XI. Quod unicum est nomen in mundo, Papae videlicet.
units.tr: That his is the only name in the world, namely the Pope's.
That he may depose emperors.

units.la: XIII. Quod illi liceat de sede ad sedem necessitate cogente Episcopos transmutare.
units.tr: That he may transfer bishops from see to see when necessity requires.

units.la: XIV. Quod de omni Ecclesia quocunque voluerit, clericum valeat ordinare.
units.tr: That he may ordain a clergyman for any church he wishes.

units.la: XV. Quod ab illo ordinatus alii Ecclesiæ præesse potest, sed non militare, & quod ab aliquo Episcopo non debet superiorem gradum accipere.
units.tr: That one ordained by him may preside over another church but may not serve as a soldier, and that he ought not to receive a higher rank from any bishop.

units.la: XVI. Quod nulla Synodus absque præcepto ejus debet Generalis vocari.
units.tr: That no synod may be called a general synod without his command.

units.la: XVII. Quod nullum Capitulum, nullusque liber Canonicus habeatur absque illius auctoritate.
units.tr: That no chapter and no canonical book is to be held without his authority.

units.la: XVIII. Quod sententia illius à nullo debeat retractari; & ipse omnium solus retractare possit.
units.tr: That his sentence may be retracted by no one, and that he alone may retract the sentences of all.

units.la: XIX. Quod à nemine ipse judicari debeat.
units.tr: That he himself ought to be judged by no one.

units.la: XX. Quod nullus audeat condemnare Apostolicam Sedem appellantem.
units.tr: That no one may dare to condemn one who appeals to the Apostolic See.

units.la: XXI. Quod majores causæ cujuscunque Ecclesiæ ad eum referri debeant.
units.tr: That the greater cases of any church ought to be referred to him.

units.la: XXII. Quod Romana Ecclesia nunquam erravit, nec in perpetuum, Scriptura testante, errabit.
units.tr: That the Roman Church has never erred, and, as Scripture bears witness, will never err in perpetuity.

units.la: XXIII. Quod Romanus Pontifex si canonicè fuerit ordinatus, meritis beati Petri indubitanter efficitur sanctus, testante sancto Ennodio Papiensi Episcopo, ei multis sanctis Patribus faventibus, sicut in decretis beati Symmachi Papæ continetur.
units.tr: That the Roman Pontiff, if he has been canonically ordained, is undoubtedly made holy by the merits of blessed Peter, as Saint Ennodius, bishop of Pavia, testifies, with many holy Fathers favouring him, as is contained in the decrees of blessed Pope Symmachus.

units.la: XXIV. Quod illius præcepto & licentia subjectis liceat accusare.
units.tr: That it is permitted to his subjects to bring accusations at his command and with his permission.

units.la: XXV. Quod absque synodali conventu possit Episcopos deponere & reconciliare.
units.tr: That he may depose and reconcile bishops without a synodal assembly.

units.la: XXVI. Quod Catholicus non habeatur, qui non concordat Romanæ Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: XXVI. That a man is not to be regarded as Catholic who does not agree with the Roman Church.

units.la: XXVII. Quod à fidelitate iniquorum subje-ctos potest absolvere.
units.tr: XXVII. That he can absolve subjects from the allegiance of the wicked.

units.la: Quare hæc aximata & egregia sedis Romanæ privilegia, quæ à nemine Antecessorum attentata, dixit supra Onuphrius, Dictatus vocaverit Gregorius, illud non obscurè ex ipsis dictatibus colligi potest. Dictaturam summum olim in Repub. Magistratum, & quidem non per sex menses, sed ad Julii Cæsaris exemplum perpetuo illi stabiliunt & defendunt; à Dictatura itaque recte Dictatus appellantur. Ex iis in emensum crevit Jus Ecclesiasticum; nam cum appellationes omnes sibi Romana sedes, & cognitionem in causis Episcopalibus & aliis majoribus, solus Pontifex adsereret, jam non tantum canones circa dogmata & personas ritusque Ecclesiasticos, quæ antea fere objecta canonum erant, occupati; sed & de litibus & disceptationibus forensibus ordinandis & dirigendis, solliciti fuerunt. In tota Dionysii Exigui & aliorum antiquorum Collectionibus nil de litis contestatione, & similibus aliis ad processum pertinentibus legitur; nunc vero magna pars Juris Canonici absorvitur, titulis, de officio & potestate Judicis ordinarii & delegati, de Treuga & pace, de pactis, de transactionibus, de postulando, de procuratoribus, de syndico, de his quæ vi metuve fata sunt, de arbitris, de alienatione judicii mutandi causa facta, de foro competente, de libelli oblatione, de plus petitionibus, de causis possessionis & proprietatis, de missione in bonorum possessionem, de attentatis, de sequestratione possessionis, de testibus, fide instrumentorum, de præscriptionibus, de sententiis, de appellationibus, & similibus rubricis, ad Jus Civile pertinentibus, ut hodie modus litigandi in jure Canonico præscriptus sit concinnior, perfectior, & accuratior, quam quidem ille, qui in jure civili est descriptus; ideoque passim receptum, eum pleraque tribunalia sequuntur. Quare nec immerito Canones ab hoc tempore nomen perdiderunt, atq; Juris illud adlumserunt; & ad differentiam civilis, prius nomen proprium & substantivum distinctionis gratia in appellativum & adjectivum Canonici commutatum est. Habuerunt quidem prisci Episcopi indulgentia Principum audientiam, seu notionem causarum quarundam inter eos, qui sponte ad eos irent, in eosque tanquam arbitros compromitterent, id pii Principes a temporibus Constantini videntur detulisse Episcopis, ut pacem inter Christianos foverent & redintegrarent; Jurisdictionem autem nullam habuerunt. runt. Non moror hic leges tres supposititias de judicio Episcopali, quæ additæ sunt Codici Theodosiano, harum enim fucum ut & totius appendicis Codicis Theodosiani, à Sirmundo editæ suppositionem Doctissimus & Solertissimus Jacob. Gothofredus, in elaboratissimis ad Codicem Theodosianum Notis & Commentariis, affatim & luculenter demonstravit tom. VI. pag. 303. & seqq. In hac per gratiam concessa audientia juxta Regulas Christianæ pietatis & sacræ scripturæ, item leges Imperatorum judicabant, non ipsi leges ferebant, nec forum habebant, aut cum strepitu judicii causas audiebant; ut totum hoc, quod habuerunt Episcopi sit tantum indultum quoddam Imperatorum, ad resecandas & cito componendas lites. Videturque primum ex consuetudine non mala inter Christianos, sub Principibus Ethnicis invaluisse (occasionem dante Apostolo I. ad Cor. VI.) ut clanculum ad Episcopos irent, qui controversias haberent; postea sub Principibus id esse firmatum, & ex gratia probatum, tandem ut exempla non subsistunt, ubi incipiunt, in jus conversum esse, sibique plura arrogasse & pedetentim extorsisse ab Imperatoribus Episcopos, potissimum Romanos; Qua de re aliorum latissimæ tractationes inspici possunt, quæ docent, quomodo audientia in jurisdictionem, voluntaria aditio, in necessitatem, arbitrium in legem transierit. Quod masculè promoverunt, hi Dictatus Gregorii septimi, ut non immerito Auctor Apologiæ Cleri Leodicensis, dixerit, ultimam manum sacris Canonibus imposuisse solum Hildebrandum; qui si tantam, quantam sibi potestatem arrogavit, haberet, solus condendæ legis & juris potestatem sibi jure meritoque arrogaret; nec tum minus ejus Canones & Dictatus, quam civilia placita, nomen Corporis Juris, si Deo placet, ferre merentur. Ipsos dictatus examinare, ut non est nostri instituti, ita nec operis nostri ratio id patitur: facile alias esset adserere, Onuphrii Panvinii sententiam; quod major pars eorum imo omnes antea in usu non, sed recenter à Gregorio introducti fuerint. Aliquid præstitit hic Doctiss: Mornæus in Mysterio iniquit. mihi pag. 223. Editionis Gorichem. anni 1662. qui & de ipso Gregorio, ejusq; artibus, p. 226. & seq. videri potest. Sed vocat nos series ad alios Collectores.
units.tr: Hence it can be clearly gathered from the Dictates themselves why Gregory called these axiomatic and outstanding privileges of the Roman See, which, as Onuphrius said above, none of his predecessors had ever attempted. The Dictates are named after the dictatorship: in the commonwealth of old, the dictator was the highest magistrate, and not for six months but, after the example of Julius Caesar, for life. These Dictates establish and defend that same kind of power for the pope. From these Dictates the canon law then grew to immense size. For since the Roman See claimed all appeals for itself, and the Pope alone claimed cognizance of episcopal causes and other major matters, the canons now concerned themselves not only with dogmas, persons and ecclesiastical rites, which had been almost the only subject matter of the canons before, but also with arranging and directing lawsuits in the courts. In the whole of the collections of Dionysius Exiguus and the other ancient writers, nothing is read about joinder of issue or similar matters belonging to procedure. Now, however, a large part of canon law is taken up with titles on the office and power of an ordinary and a delegated judge, on truces and peace, on agreements, on settlements, on pleading, on proctors, on the syndic, on things done by force or fear, on arbitrators, on alienation of property made to change the judge, on the competent court, on presenting a petition, on claims for more than is due, on cases of possession and ownership, on being put into possession of goods, on attempts made in violation of a suit, on sequestration of possession, on witnesses, on the credibility of documents, on prescription, on sentences, on appeals, and similar headings that belong to the civil law. As a result, the method of litigation prescribed in canon law today is more polished, more perfect and more exact than the one set out in the civil law, and for that reason it has been widely received and most courts follow it. Hence it is not without justice that from this time the canons lost their name and took on the name law; and, to distinguish them from the civil law, the old proper noun was turned into the adjective Canonical to mark the difference. Indeed the early bishops had, by the indulgence of princes, a hearing, that is, the cognizance of certain cases between those who of their own accord came to them and who agreed to submit to them as arbitrators. Pious princes seem to have granted this to the bishops from the time of Constantine, so that they might foster and restore peace among Christians; but they had no jurisdiction at all. I need not dwell here on the three spurious laws about episcopal judgment that were added to the Theodosian Code, for the fraud of these laws, and of the whole appendix to the Theodosian Code published by Sirmond, has been abundantly and clearly demonstrated by the most learned and acute Jacob Gothofredus in his very elaborate notes and commentaries on the Theodosian Code, vol. VI, p. 303 and following. In this hearing, which was granted by favour, the bishops judged according to the rules of Christian piety and Holy Scripture, as well as the laws of the emperors; they did not themselves make laws, nor did they have a court, nor did they hear cases with the noise of a formal trial. So everything the bishops had was merely a certain concession of the emperors, intended to cut off quarrels and settle them quickly. It seems that at first, from a not bad custom among Christians under pagan princes (the Apostle giving the occasion, 1 Cor. 6), people went quietly to the bishops when they had disputes; later this was confirmed by the princes and approved by their favour; and finally, as examples show, where it began as a hearing it turned into law, and the bishops, especially the Roman ones, claimed more for themselves and gradually wrested it from the emperors. Other very full treatments of this matter may be consulted, which show how the hearing passed into jurisdiction, voluntary resort into necessity, and arbitration into law. The Dictates of Gregory VII vigorously promoted this, so that the author of the Apology of the Clergy of Liège rightly said that Hildebrand alone put the final hand to the sacred canons. If he had had as much power as he claimed for himself, he would by right and justice have claimed for himself alone the power of making law and of making canons; and in that case his canons and Dictates would deserve, God willing, to bear the name of a body of law no less than civil ordinances do. To examine the Dictates themselves is not part of my purpose, and the plan of my work does not allow it. It would be easy to assert elsewhere the opinion of Onuphrius Panvinius, that most of them, indeed all, were not in use before but were introduced recently by Gregory. The most learned Mornaeus has done something on this in his Mystery of Iniquity, p. 223 of the Gorinchem edition of 1662, and on Gregory himself and his arts it may be seen p. 226 and following. But the sequence of my account now calls us to other collectors.

units.la: Cum Gregorio septimo vixit Anselmus Mantuanus, quem Alexander II. ad Episcopatum Lucensem A. D. 1073. destinavit, & ob investituram ad Imperatorem miserat, à quo primum detrectavit, accipere, postea vero accepit investituram & Episcopatum, sed relicto eo se in Cluniacense Monasterium abdidit, ex quo Gregorius septimus eum, tanquam causæ suæ utilem, revocavit, & Episcopatui Lucensi, siquidem fides habenda anonymo vitæ ejus scriptori, à Baronio laudato, præfecit. Ludov. Jacob. à S. Carolo, lib. 2. Bibl. Pontif. pag. 267. facit ex eo Cardinalem presbyterum. Hic causam Gregorii contra Henricum Imperatorem defendit, ideoque charus ei fuit, Scripta ejus refert Baronius ad Ann. 1086, quo mortuus est Anselmus, ex Anonymo illo vitæ ejus scriptore, qui ejus pœnitentiarius fuit, & quidem ipsius verbis. Ex multis ac diversis sanctissimorum Patrum voluminibus unum compilavit Canonicarum sententiarum, non modicum Corpus. Extat illud ipsum integrum jam cusum. De quo ipso volumine in vita illa prolixius scripta hæc leguntur. Apologeticum unum ex diversis sanctorum Patrum voluminibus compilavit, quibus Domini Papæ sententiam & universa ejus facta, atque præcepta canonicis defenderet rationibus. Multos libellos propriis manibus conscripsit. In lamentationes Hieremiæ dulcissimam fecit expositionem. Psalterium quoque rogatu benedictissimæ Dei (ex quo famosæ Fœminæ elogio, de scriptore hoc conjectura capi potest, quantum ei sit deferendum) Mathilda, exposuit luculentissime breviter quidem, sed utiliter, usque ad illum locum: Benediximus vobis in nomine Domini; ibi siquidem expositionem finivit, nobisque omnibus ut alter Patriarcha Jacob, benedixit. Apologia ista est scripta contra Guibertum, ut Baronius & alii vocant, Antipapam, qui ab Imperatore & synodo, Abdicato Gregorio suffectus erat. Extat in tomo 6. Antiq. Lect. Henr. Canisii, vide & Sigebertum de Scriptorib. Eccles. cap. 161. & ibid. Miræum in scholiis Biblioth. Eccles. pag. 156. Memorata hæc ejus Collectio canonum, utramque fere paginam facit in emendatione Gratiani, jussu Gregorii facta, & apud Anton. Augustinum, de emendat. Gratiani. Qui eam tamen in dubium videtur vocare, lib. 2. dial. 5. princ. fere. ubi hæc habet: Deusdedit Urbani secundi tempore scripsit, item Anselmus Lucensis, sive is, cujus collectionem habemus. Ita enim solemus loqui, de eorum scriptis, de quibus dubitamus. In utrumque Opus Anselmus retulit supposititias Epistolas Collectionis Isidori Mercatoris. Libro 1. adverf. Guibertum Antipapam testes advocat Pseudo-Clementem Epist. 3. Pseudo-Pium Epist. 1. & PseudoFabianum Epist. 3. Lib. 2. Pseudo-Callistum Epist. 1. Pseudo-Stephanum Epist. 2. Pseudo-Marcellinum, Epistol. 2. In Collectionem Canonum omnes ferè Pseudo-Isidori Epistolas in partes discerptas inseruit. Verba sunt, Doctiss: Blondelli in prolegomen. Pseudo-Isidori, cap. 18. pag. 98. Epistolarum librum ad diversos, ei quoque adscribit Bibliotheca Simleri. Post Burchardum & Anselmum ad colligendos canones, eodem seculo XI. praecipite, se accinxit Ivo, natione Gallus, ex praeposito Monasterii Quintini Belluacensis, ordinis Canonicorum, ut vocant regularium B. Augustini, Episcopus Carnutensis in Gallia, anno seculi undecimi XCII. usque ad annum XIV. seculi duodecimi. Homo suo tempore clarus, & multis negotiis implicitus, ut quidem produnt epistolae ejus, cujus fama ob id unicum, à Baronio ad ann. D. 1099. §. 8. Quod de investituris vetitis (laicorum Regum & Principum nempe) nimis abjecte loquatur; à Baronio in discrimen vocatur, & nomen Gloriosum, quod ex defensione Apostolicae sedis & Catholicae veritatis sibi dignissime comparaverat, in discrimen adduxisse dicitur. Ita facile pereunt cuncta quae fecisti bona, etiam nomen Gloriosum meritissime comparatum, si vel literula, etiam alias secundum veritatem scripta exciderit contra sententiam Papae Romani. Scripsit varia. Librum de corpore Domini, qui extat in tat in bibliotheca Patrum, tom. 3. Volumen Epistolarum ad diversos. De divinis & Ecclesiasticis officiis & praecipuis Festis diebus Sermones xxr. qui cum aliis de divinis officiis Scriptoribus uno volumine prodierunt Colon: Agrippinae 1568; praeter haec, ad institutum nostrum facientia duo sub ejus nomine habentur scripta, quibus canones colliguntur & digeruntur, Decretum & Pannomia. Primum Opus indubitato ab omnibus adscribitur Ivoni; Ad id putatur accensus opere Burchardi Wormatiensis; quod ejus collectioni leges civiles & jura Romana, deinde alia quaedam, ob novam, ut putat Berengarii haeresin, potius veritatem, deesse censeret. Primum videbat factum à Graecis, apud quos Nomocanones in usu; hactenus apud Occidentales ignoti, qui contenti canonibus Ecclesiasticis, leges Imperatorias Ecclesiasticas quidem sequebantur, sed Corpori Canonum aut Collectionibus nondum inseruerant, aut sufficere arbitrabantur Caroli & aliorum Capitularia, in quibus eae simul habebantur. Burchardus enim Juris civilis non meminit, latebat enim adhuc ejus tempore. Codicis Theodosiani semel iterumque facit mentionem. Ivo in omnibus fere sequitur Burchardum, ab eo parum verbis & ordine discedit. Dispescit decretum in libros seu partes decem & septem; quorum non opus contenta referre, ex superioribus quae de Burchardi collectione diximus, satis manifesta esse possunt. Alterum opus eius nomen referens, est Pannonia, vel Panormia, utroque enim modo legitur. Posteriori appellatione utitur plerumque Anton. Augustinus passim in emendat. Gratiani. Alii melius Pannomiam vocant, ut tota compositio sit Graeca à πᾶν [?] & νόμῳ [?]; quia omnis generis leges complectitur, quae in Panormia est partim Latina; quod tamen non est novum. Hoc opus Ivonis non esse, recte Bellarminus de scriptor. Eccles. in Ivone & Gratiano, censet; Quia multa libr. 8. sunt decreta ex Innocentio secundo Papa, & ex historia Sigeberti, qui Ivone posteriores fuerunt. Vocari tamen Ivonis, quia ex decreto Ivonis maxima ex parte sit desumtum, est enim quasi compendium Decreti Ivonis. Sedit autem Innocentius secundus, ab anno 1130. usque ad 1143. Sigebertus vero Gemblacensis mortuus est anno 1112. vide scholia Miraei, ad Sigebertum, in bibliothec. Ecclesiast. pag. 158. Cavendus itaque error Antonii Contii duplex. Unus quod utriusque operis facit auctorem Ivonem, alter quod utrumque opus scripsisse tradat circa annum Christi 1136; quo tempore jam per viginti præter propter annos Ivo ex vivis excesserat, si credendum Baronio, qui ad ann. 1114. §. 14. circa ann. 1114. mortuum conjicit, aut saltem tempora Paschalis secundi Pontificis non excessisse probat, qui anno 1118. mortuus est: quia in Catalogo Episcoporum Carnutensium ab hoc tempore alius invenitur, Gothofredus quidam, ad quem extant quædam Epistolæ Bernardi. Ex quibus apparet Ivonem nostrum cum Sigeberto vixisse, & aliquot annos supervixisse, Innocentio autem secundo posteriorem & falsum fuisse Bellarminum, qui utrumque Sigebertum & Innocentium secundum, Ivoni posteriorem facit; Quod ideo forte fecit, ut eo melius posset semel probatos lib. 2. de Pont. Rom. c. 29. lib. 1. de Cleric. c. 9. & lib. 1. de translat. Imp. cap. 13. canones 22. & 23. dist. 63. apud Gratianum, falso falsitatis arguere, & tanquam à Sigeberto confictos, monitus in retractatione Operum & libr. de Scriptoribus Eccles. rejicere: quos tamen vindicarunt præter M. Ant. de Dominis lib. 6. de rep. Eccles. cap. 7. operose Goldastus, in Rationali ad constitut. Imper. & in replicat. cap. 13. Item Clarissimus Conring. de Germanor. Imper. Roman. cap. 6. & de constitut. Episcop. §. 27. & 28. Anton. Augustinus quanquam non obscure abjudicet Pannomiam Ivoni, putat tamen Innocentii addita esse Pannomiæ non partem operis facere. Sed est hæc tantum conjectura ejus, ut ex his lib. 2. dialogo 5. princ. colligi potest. C. Apud Ivonem extrema Panormia Innocentii minoris verba referuntur, qui Callisto posterior fuit. A. Negare possum Ivonis eum librum esse. Sed malo hoc affirmare, additum esse concilium Innocentii Panormiæ, non esse partem ejus collectionis. Ostendere possum veterem librum, in quo neque id concilium, neque nomen Ivonis, neque excerptionum præfatio continetur. Et in Epistolis Ivonis ea præfatio temporibus Paschalis minoris scripta est. Quomodo alias idem Augustinus opera Ivonis distinguat in Pannormiam & Excerptiones, tradit hisce, in dialog. 9. lib. post. pag. nostræ Editionis 440. Ivonis, inquit, nomine, duo libri nuncupantur, quos te video Panormiam & Excerptiones appellare, & dubitare utrum ejusdem sint scriptoris. Panormia usus fortasse est Gratianus. Excerptiones non vidisse existimo. Illud tamen certum Ivonem scripsisse decretorum Volumen, ante mortem Sigeberti, meminit enim ille ejus & decreti de Scriptorib. Eccles. cap. 167. sed meminit solius decreti, quod vocat Volumen Canonum insigne non pannomia, quod quoque arguargumentum est, Pannomiæ Auctorem non esse Ivonem, sed alium post ejus mortem. De utroque volumine hæc habet Ant. Contius. Secutus est, inquit Ivo, Episcopus Carnotensis, qui in certos quidem locos & titulos illos canones ab Isidoro & Burchardo editos digessit; sed multa tamen similia, multa inter se pugnantia in suum librum transtulit, & librum suum Pannomiam inscripsit. Caterum duplex ejus volumen hoc titulo insignitum reperi. Unum majus & magnitudine suâ longè excedens Gratiani volumen, quod ex Bibliothecâ S. Victoris Parisiensis nobis aliquando communicatum est. Huic volumini inscriptum titulum hunc inveninus, DECRETA IOVINIANI. Verum hanc inscriptionem falsam esse puto, & ignorantiâ librariorum adscriptam, cùm eadem illic sit præfatio, quæ apud Ivonem in minore volumine Pannomiæ, & idem ferè ordo, nisi quod illud volumen multo plures habet partes, & titulos, & canones, in septendecim quippe partes divisum. Aliud verò minus volumen, quod & in eadem Bibliotheca extat, & passim in aliis, cujus etiam manuscriptum exemplar nobis comparavimus (nam & olim in Germania impressum est sed mendosissimum) in septem duntaxat partes est divisum. Inscribitur autem hoc volumen in prædicta Bibliotheca DECRETA PARVA IVONIS. Quod dicit decretorum volumen vocatum in Manuscripto, Decreta Jovimiani? est error scribentium, si modo recte legit Contius, levi mutatione recte vocatur, Decretum Ivonianum. Auctorem Panomiae Pancirollus, de claris Legum interpret. lib. 3. cap. 1. pag. 403. facit Ugonem Catalaunum, non diu post editum opus ab Ivone, illud contrahentem. Sed ex quo auctore id habeat non addit. Habet ibidem quaedam de Epitome quoque Decretorum Burchardi, quae supra neglecta sunt, quare totum locum addo, maxime cum non versetur liber in omnium manibus. Post Isidorum, inquit, Burchardus (c. 2. 73. distinct.) Wormatiensis Episcopus, rudem indigestamque illius Decreti molem methodice ordinavit, ac primus Jus Pontificium in sua loca digestum xx. libris complexus est, qui ob longa lectionis taedium intermissi brevi interiere. Nam quae ejus nomine circumfertur Epitome, plures quidem libellos, sed vix sextam justi operis partem continet. Cum vero novis exortis sectis, etiam Berengarius in Sacrosanctam Eucharistiam blasphemus extitisset, Ivo genere Gallus, qui primo Canonicis a D. Augustino institutis praefectus, postea Carnutensium Antistes fuit, post annos nonaginta, quam Burchardus scripsit, praeter alia opuscula, amplissimum Decretorum volumen decem, & septem libris distinctum concinnavit, in quo Burchardum chardum omnino secutus verbis, aut ordine parum ab eo discessit. Quasdam tamen veterum Scriptorum sententias adversus Ecclesiæ turbatores, & multa ex Jure nostro Civili testimonia adjecit, quæ illæ, velut parum suo instituto necessaria, omiserat, vel quod juribus Romanis non dum apparentibus Caroli Magni tantum leges, vulgò Capitula vocata, frequentabantur; nunquam enim Juris civilis, & bis tantum Codicis Theodosiani meminit. Caeterum Ivonis opus cum alia, & ipsius etiam Isidori Decreta magnitudine superaret; Ugo Catalaunus, non multo post quam scriptum est, in compendium redegit, ac Pannormiam, sive Summam Decretorum Ivonis nuncupavit. Ea etsi tota mendis, & erroribus scatebat, adjutus Gratianus plura inde, & ex Burchardi Epitome excerpsit, autographi enim texturam, aut Burchardi nunquam vidisse videtur, cum errores in compendiis inventos in suum opus transtulerit. Et postea cap. 3. Caeterum Burchardi & Ivonis decretis ob librorum magnitudinem neglectis, eorum tantum compendia, quorum meminimus legebantur in usuque erant. Edidit Decretum Ivonis Lovanii seculi superioris, anno sexagesimo primo Johannes Molynæus; Pannomia prodiit Basileæ anno 1499. Opera Ivonis omnia prodierunt Parisiis A. D. 1647. Conspurcata est utraque collectio & Decretum & Pannomia quisquiliis & fictis aut suppositititiis Isidori Mer- catoris decretalibus, item multis aliis fictis & suppositititiis Decretis. Quarum bene longum & accuratum Catalogum contextum vide apud Doctiss: Blondellum in Pseudo-Isidoro vapulante cap. 18. pag. 100. & seq.
units.tr: Anselm of Mantua lived in the time of Gregory VII. Alexander II had appointed him to the bishopric of Lucca in 1073 and sent him to the emperor for investiture. At first he refused to receive it from the emperor, but afterwards he accepted both the investiture and the bishopric. Then he left it and withdrew into the monastery of Cluny.
