Gregory VII recalled him from there, as useful to his cause, and set him over the bishopric of Lucca, if credence is to be given to the anonymous writer of his life, whom Baronius cites. Ludovico Giacomo da San Carlo, book 2 of the Bibliotheca Pontificia, p. 267, makes him a cardinal priest. He defended Gregory's cause against the Emperor Henry, and for that reason was dear to him. Baronius, at the year 1086, when Anselm died, reports his writings from that anonymous author of his life, who was his penitentiary, and in his very words: From many and various volumes of the most holy Fathers he compiled one, a not inconsiderable body of canonical sentences. That work survives, now printed complete. Concerning this same volume, the life written at greater length says this: He compiled one Apologetic from various volumes of the holy Fathers, by which he might defend with canonical arguments the opinion of the Lord Pope and all his acts and precepts. He wrote many little books with his own hands. He made a very sweet exposition of the Lamentations of Jeremiah. The Psalter also, at the request of the most blessed Matilda of God (from this eulogy of that famous woman one may gather how much weight is to be given to this writer) he expounded most clearly, briefly indeed but usefully, as far as that place: We have blessed you in the name of the Lord; for there he ended the exposition, and blessed us all like another Patriarch Jacob. That Apology was written against Guibert, whom Baronius and others call the antipope, who had been set up in place of the deposed Gregory by the emperor and a synod. It is found in volume 6 of the Antiquae Lectiones of Henricus Canisius. See also Sigebert On Ecclesiastical Writers, chapter 161, and likewise Miraeus in the notes to the Bibliotheca Ecclesiastica, p. 156. This collection of canons of his, cited above, makes up nearly every page of the emendation of Gratian, which was made by command of Gregory, and it is also mentioned by Antonius Augustinus, On the Emendation of Gratian. Yet Augustinus seems to call it into doubt, book 2, dialogue 5, near the beginning, where he has this: Deusdedit wrote in the time of Urban II, and likewise Anselm of Lucca, or whoever it was whose collection we have. For that is how we are wont to speak of the writings of those about whom we are in doubt. In both works Anselm has cited the spurious letters of the Isidorian collection of Mercator. In book 1 against Guibert the antipope he calls as witnesses Pseudo-Clement Ep. 3, Pseudo-Pius Ep. 1, and Pseudo-Fabian Ep. 3. In book 2 (Pseudo-Callistus Ep. 1, Pseudo-Stephen Ep. 2, Pseudo-Marcellinus, Ep. 2). In his Collection of Canons he inserted almost all the Pseudo-Isidorian letters, cut up into parts. These are the words of the learned Blondel, in the prolegomena to Pseudo-Isidore, chapter 18, p. 98. The Bibliotheca of Simler also ascribes to him the book of letters to various persons. After Burchard and Anselm, in the same eleventh century, Ivo, a Frenchman by birth, undertook to collect the canons with great zeal. He had been provost of the monastery of Saint Quentin of Beauvais, of the order of canons, as they are called, regular of St Augustine, and then bishop of Chartres in France. He lived from the year 1092 until the fourteenth year of the twelfth century. He was a man famous in his own time and entangled in many affairs, as his letters indeed show. For this very reason his reputation was called into question by Baronius, at the year 1099, §8, because he spoke too abjectly about investitures forbidden (namely, those by lay kings and princes); and it is said that by this he brought into peril the glorious name which he had most worthily acquired from the defence of the Apostolic See and of Catholic truth. So easily perish all the good things you have done, even a glorious name most deservedly won, if one little letter, even one written otherwise in accordance with the truth, slips out against the opinion of the Roman Pope. He wrote various works: a book on the body of the Lord, which is found in the Bibliotheca Patrum, vol. 3; a volume of letters to various persons; sermons on divine and ecclesiastical offices and the principal feast days, twenty-one in number, which were published together with other writers on the divine offices in one volume at Cologne in 1568. Besides these, two writings under his name bear on our present purpose, in which canons are collected and arranged: the Decretum and the Pannomia. The first work is without doubt ascribed by all to Ivo. He is thought to have been spurred to it by the work of Burchard of Worms, which, in the view of Ivo, lacked civil laws and Roman law for its collection, and some other things as well, which were rather to be wished for on account of the new heresy, as he thought, of Berengarius. He seems to have first seen this done by the Greeks, among whom the Nomocanons were in use; hitherto unknown among the Westerners, who, content with ecclesiastical canons, did indeed follow the imperial laws as far as they touched the Church, but had not yet inserted them into the body of canons or collections, or else thought the capitularies of Charlemagne and others sufficient, in which such laws were also contained. For Burchard makes no mention of the civil law, since it lay still hidden in his time. He mentions the Theodosian Code only once or twice. Ivo follows Burchard in almost everything, and departs little from him in wording and order. He divided the Decretum into seventeen books or parts. The contents of these need not be set out here, since what we have said above about the collection of Burchard may make them sufficiently clear. The other work, which bears its name, is the Pannonia, or Panormia, for it is read in both forms. The latter title is mostly used by Antonius Augustinus throughout his Emendation of Gratian. Others more properly call it Pannomia, so that the whole word is Greek, from pan [?] and nomos [?], because it embraces laws of every kind; the Panormia is partly in Latin, which is nothing new. That this work is not Ivo's, Bellarmine rightly holds, On Ecclesiastical Writers, under Ivo and Gratian: because many decrees in book 8 are from Pope Innocent II and from the history of Sigebert, who were later than Ivo. It is called Ivo's nevertheless, because it is taken for the most part from the decree of Ivo; for it is as it were an abridgement of Ivo's Decretum. Innocent II sat from the year 1130 until 1143. But Sigebert of Gembloux died in the year 1112. See the notes of Miraeus on Sigebert, in the Bibliotheca Ecclesiastica, p. 158. There is therefore a double error of Antonius Contius to be guarded against. One is that he makes Ivo the author of both works; the other is that he hands down that both works were written about the year of Christ 1136, when Ivo had already passed from the living some twenty years or thereabouts, if we believe Baronius, who at the year 1114, §14, conjectures that he died about 1114, or at least proves that he did not outlive the times of Pope Paschal II, who died in 1118; for in the catalogue of the bishops of Chartres another is found from this time, one Gothofredus, to whom certain letters of Bernard survive. From these it appears that our Ivo lived together with Sigebert and survived him by some years, but that he was later than Innocent II is false, and Bellarmine was wrong, who makes both Sigebert and Innocent II later than Ivo. He perhaps did this so that he might more easily charge with falsehood, as spurious, the canons book 2, On the Roman Pope, ch. 29; book 1, On the Clergy, ch. 9; and book 1, On the Translation of the Empire, ch. 13; canons 22 and 23, dist. 63, in Gratian, which were cited as the work of Sigebert, and to reject them, as he warns in the retractation of his works and in his book On Ecclesiastical Writers. Yet these have been defended, besides by Marcus Antonius de Dominis, book 6, On the Commonwealth of the Church, ch. 7, by Goldast laboriously, in the Rationale on the imperial constitutions and in the Replication, ch. 13, and likewise by the most distinguished Conring, On the Roman Emperors of the Germans, ch. 6, and On the Constitution of Bishops, §§27 and 28. Antonius Augustinus, although he does not obscurely reject the Pannomia as Ivo's, nevertheless thinks that the additions of Innocent do not form part of the work of the Pannomia. But this is only his conjecture, as may be gathered from book 2, dialogue 5, near the beginning. C. In Ivo the final part of the Panormia cites the words of the younger Innocent, who was later than Callistus. A. I can deny that this book is Ivo's. But I prefer to affirm this: that the council of Innocent was added to the Panormia and is not part of that collection. I can show an old book which contains neither that council, nor the name of Ivo, nor the preface to the Excerpts. And in Ivo's letters that preface is shown to have been written in the times of Paschal the Younger. How the same Augustinus elsewhere distinguishes the works of Ivo into the Panormia and the Excerptiones, he hands down in these words, in dialogue 9, near the end, p. 440 of our edition. Under the name of Ivo, he says, two books are called, which I see you call the Panormia and the Excerptiones, and you doubt whether they are by the same writer. Gratian perhaps used the Panormia. I think he did not see the Excerptiones. Yet this is certain: Ivo wrote a volume of decrees before the death of Sigebert, for Sigebert mentions both him and his decree On Ecclesiastical Writers, ch. 167; but he mentions only the decree, which he calls the notable volume of canons, not the Pannomia. This too is an argument that the author of the Pannomia was not Ivo but someone else after his death. Antonius Contius has this to say about both volumes. Ivo, Bishop of Chartres, followed, he says, and arranged those canons, edited by Isidore and Burchard, under certain headings and titles; but he transferred into his own book many similar things and many that contradict one another, and he entitled his book the Pannomia. Moreover I have found a double volume of his under this title. One larger, far exceeding the bulk of Gratian's volume, which was once communicated to us from the library of St Victor at Paris. To this volume the title is inscribed: DECRETA IOVINIANI. But I think this inscription is false and was added through the ignorance of the copyists, since there is the same preface that is in Ivo's smaller volume of the Pannomia, and nearly the same order, except that the former volume has many more parts, titles and canons, being divided into seventeen parts. The other, smaller volume, which is also in the same library and is found in many others, of which we have also procured a manuscript copy (for it was once printed in Germany too, but very full of errors), is divided into seven parts only. This volume is inscribed in the aforesaid library DECRETA PARVA IVONIS. As for the manuscript's reading Decreta Jovimiani, is it a scribal error? If Contius reads it rightly, with a slight change it is rightly called Decretum Ivonianum. Pancirollus, On the Famous Interpreters of the Laws, book 3, ch. 1, p. 403, makes Hugo of Châlons, not long after the work was published by Ivo, the one who abridged it, but he does not add on what authority he has this. In the same place he has some things about the Epitome of Burchard's Decretum as well, which were passed over above; so I add the whole passage, especially since this book is not in everyone's hands. After Isidore, he says, Burchard (ch. 2, dist. 73), Bishop of Worms, put in order methodically the rough and undigested mass of that Decree, and first embraced Pontifical law arranged in its own places in twenty books, which, because of the tedium of long reading, were dropped and soon perished. For the Epitome that circulates under his name contains indeed several small books, but scarcely the sixth part of the true work. When, however, new sects had arisen, and Berengarius, blasphemer against the most holy Eucharist, had come forward, Ivo, a Frenchman, who first was put over the canons instituted by St Augustine and afterwards became bishop of Chartres, ninety years after Burchard wrote, besides other little works, put together a very ample volume of Decrees divided into seventeen books. In this, following Burchard in almost all things, he departed little from him in wording or order. He nevertheless added some sayings of the ancient writers against the disturbers of the Church, and many testimonies from our civil law, which Burchard had omitted as too little necessary to his purpose; or because the Roman laws were not yet visible, and only the laws of Charlemagne, commonly called Capitularies, were in use. For he never mentions civil law, and mentions the Theodosian Code only twice. Moreover, since Ivo's work surpassed in size both the other decrees and that of Isidore himself, Hugo of Châlons, not long after it was written, reduced it to a summary, and named it the Pannormia, or the Summary of Ivo's Decrees. Although this was wholly full of faults and errors, Gratian, helped by it, excerpted many things from it and from Burchard's Epitome; for he seems never to have seen the autograph text, or Burchard's, since he transferred into his own work the errors found in the abridgements. And afterwards, in chapter 3: But since the decrees of Burchard and Ivo were neglected on account of the bulk of the books, only their abridgements, of which we have spoken, were read and in use. John Molinaeus published Ivo's Decretum at Louvain in the year 1561 of the last century; the Pannomia came out at Basel in the year 1499; all the works of Ivo came out at Paris in A.D. 1647. Both collections, the Decretum and the Pannomia, are defiled by the spurious and fictitious decretals of Isidore Mercator, and likewise by many other fictitious and spurious decrees. For a very long and careful catalogue of these, see the learned Blondel in Pseudo-Isidore on trial, ch. 18, p. 100 and following.

units.la: Eodem quo Ivo tempore vixit, sed ante Ivonem scripsit, Deusdedit, Romanæ Ecclesiæ Presbyter Cardinalis tituli SS. Apostolorum, ut dicit Baronius ad ann. 1080. n. 30. postea ad ann. 1087. n. 22. tit. S. Eudoxiæ, qui tamen est unus idemque. Hujus duplex extat scriptum, primum, de Privilegiis Romanæ sedis, & alterum COLLECTIO CANONVM. Quem tractatum Blondellus putat scriptum anno 1080. sed falso, est enim inscriptus Victori tertio, qui demum anno 1086. ad Pontificatum Urbis Romæ pervenit, melius itaque conjicitur cum Baronio in annum 1087. Hic tractatus quadripartitus est, cujus ipse rationem reddit hac Præfatione ad Victorem tertium.
units.tr: Deusdedit, a presbyter of the Roman Church and cardinal of the title of the Holy Apostles, lived at the same time as Ivo but wrote before him. Baronius calls him this in ad ann. 1080. n. 30 and later in ad ann. 1087. n. 22, under the title of S. Eudoxia, though he is one and the same man. He left a twofold work: first, On the Privileges of the Roman See, and second, Collection of Canons. Blondellus thinks the treatise was written in 1080, but wrongly, for it is addressed to Victor III, who did not come to the papacy of the city of Rome until 1086. It is therefore better conjectured, with Baronius, to belong to 1087. This treatise is in four books, and the author explains his purpose in this Preface to Victor III.

units.la: Beatissimo atque Apostolico viro Pontifici domno Papæ Victori Tertio, & Clero sanctæ Romanæ Ecclesiæ Deusdedit exiguus presbyter tituli Apost. in Eudoxia.
units.tr: To the most blessed and apostolic man, the lord Pope Victor III, and to the clergy of the holy Roman Church, Deusdedit, humble presbyter of the title of the Apostles in Eudoxia.

units.la: Novit beatitudo vestra, quod sancta Romana Ecclesia idcirco omnium Ecclesiarum mater scribitur bitur & creditur &c. Itaque ego auctoritatis ipsius Romanæ Ecclesiæ privilegium, quo omni Christiano orbi præeminet, ignorantibus patefacere cupiens, Domino mihi opem ferente, ex variis sanctorum Patrum & Christianorum Principum auctoritatibus potioribus quibusque in unum congestis, præsens defloravi opusculum, quadrisariam dispartitum partitione. Nam primus liber continet privilegium auctoritatis ejusdem Romanæ Ecclesiæ. Et quoniam sine Clero Ecclesia esse non potest, nec Clerus absque rebus quibus temporaliter subsistat: huic subjunxi secundum & tertium de Clero & rebus ejusdem Ecclesiæ. Quia verò seculi potestas Dei Ecclesiam subjugare nititur: libertas ipsius Ecclesiæ & Cleri & rerum ejus tertio, & maximè quarto libro evidenter ostenditur.
units.tr: Your blessedness knows that the holy Roman Church is therefore written and believed to be the mother of all churches, and so on. Accordingly, wishing to make known to the ignorant the privilege of the authority of the Roman Church itself, by which it stands above the whole Christian world, I have, with the Lord helping me, gathered together the most important authorities from the various holy Fathers and Christian princes, and have now put together this little work, divided into four parts. The first book contains the privilege of authority of the same Roman Church. And since the Church cannot exist without clergy, nor the clergy without the goods by which they live in this world, I have added as the second and third books the matter of the clergy and the goods of the same Church. But since the power of the world strives to subject the Church of God, the liberty of the Church itself, of its clergy and of its goods, is shown clearly in the third book and most of all in the fourth.

units.la: Ex hac Præfatione patet quo partium studio scripserit hic Cardinalis. Alterum ejus scriptum est Collectio canonum. Utriusque meminit Indiculus librorum, quem emendatores Romani præfixerunt Corpori Can. seu Gratiano, ubi utrumque opus hoc modo citatur. Deusdedit Cardinalis Collectio canonum, & libri quatuor de rebus ecclesiasticis; additur: accepisse emendatores hos libros Manuscriptos ex Bibliotheca Vaticana. Typis descriptos extare non novi, Manuscripti in bibliothecis adhuc adservantur. Præter Vaticanam, habuit exemplar Antonii Augustini, ut testatur passim ejus citatio, & provocatio ad Cardinalis Deusdedit lectionem in libris de emendat. Gratiani, in quorum 2do, dialog. quinto, pag. 386. nostr. edit. dicit. Deusdedit, Cardinalem, scripsisse tempore Urbani secundi; quod forte verum de Collectione Canonum, quam tamen Blondellus post tractatum de privilegiis sedis Romanæ scriptam arbitratur; Meminit Baronius alterius adhuc operis, quod latet in Bibliotheca Vaticana Manuscriptum, ad ann. 1087. n. 23. quod conjicio itidem ex canonibus esse corrasum. Vocat id Baronius nobilem lucubrationem, adversas invasores, Simoniacos & reliquos schismaticos: opus, addit, egregium, elaboratum ab eo tempore Urbani Papæ successoris Victoris Pontificis. Collectionem canonum Deusdedit, compilatam dicit Blondellus ex quisquiliis Pseudo-Isidori. in Prolegumen. ad Pseudo-Isidor. cap. 18. pag. 99. in sin.
units.tr: From this Preface it is plain with what partisan zeal this cardinal wrote. His other work is the Collection of Canons. Both are mentioned in the list of books which the Roman editors prefixed to the body of canon law, or Gratian, where the two works are cited in this way: Deusdedit Cardinalis Collectio canonum, & libri quatuor de rebus ecclesiasticis. To this it is added that these editors took the books from manuscripts in the Vatican Library. I know of no printed edition; the manuscripts are still kept in libraries. Besides the Vatican copy, Antonius Augustinus had a copy, as his frequent citations and appeals to the reading of Cardinal Deusdedit in his books on the emendation of Gratian show. In the second book of those, in dialog. quinto, pag. 386, nostr. edit., he says: Deusdedit the Cardinal wrote in the time of Urban II. This may be true of the Collection of Canons, though Blondellus thinks it was written after the treatise on the privileges of the Roman See. Baronius mentions another work, still lying unpublished in manuscript in the Vatican Library, ad ann. 1087. n. 23, which I likewise suppose was compiled from the canons. Baronius calls it a noble work against invaders, Simoniacs and other schismatics, and adds that it is an excellent work, elaborated from the time of Pope Urban, the successor of Pope Victor. Blondellus says that Deusdedit's Collection of Canons was compiled from the rubbish of Pseudo-Isidore, in the Prolegomena to Pseudo-Isidore, ch. 18, p. 99, at the end.

units.la: Num & in hoc undecimum an sequens seculum referendus sit Gregorius Presbyter, non satis scio, ita obscura est ejus fama & historia; ejus quoque Collectio canonum impressa, quod scio non est, eam vocavit Polycarpum, forte quia in particulas multas est discerpta. Manuscriptam citant ex Bibliotheca Vaticana Romani Emendatores Gratiani in indiculo, citat quoque Manuscriptam Antonius Augustinus, qui in Dialogis ejus meminit. De eo & Bernardo Papiensi, item Auctore libri Populeti hæc notat Clarissimus Blondellus, in prolegumenis ad Pseudo-Isidorum vapulant. cap. 18. pag. 99. in fine. Gregorius Presbyter similem collectionem (qualem nimirum Deusdedit & Ivo) publicavit, quam Polycarpum nominavit; ut & Bernardus Papiensis (de quo tamen nos infra agemus) & Auctor libri Populeti: Sed hæc ad manus non sunt, nec quo tempore vixere auctores nobis compertum est.
units.tr: Whether Gregory the Presbyter should also be assigned to the eleventh or the following century I do not know well, so obscure is his reputation and history. Nor, as far as I know, has his Collection of Canons been printed; he called it Polycarpus, perhaps because it was broken up into many pieces. The Roman editors of Gratian cite it in manuscript from the Vatican Library in their list, and Antonius Augustinus, who mentions it in his Dialogues, also cites it in manuscript. About him, Bernard of Pavia, and the author of the book Populetus, the most distinguished Blondellus remarks as follows, in the Prolegomena to Pseudo-Isidore, ch. 18, p. 99, at the end: Gregory the Presbyter published a collection similar to that of Deusdedit and Ivo, which he called Polycarpus; and so did Bernard of Pavia (of whom, however, we shall speak below) and the author of the book Populetus. But these works are not at hand, nor is it known to us in what time these authors lived.

units.la: Seculo duodecimo apud Græcos & Latinos, tam in explicandis quam colligendis canonibus gnaviter desudatum est. Videbantur à temporibus Photii per duo & quod excurrit secula Græci quievisse, nisi quod Imperatores passim adhuc curam rerum Ecclesiasticarum habuerint, & novellas quasdam ad hanc rem ediderint, de quibus postea suo loco dicemus; hoc seculo iterum ad studium Canonicum accedunt; in quo se offert primo Johannes Zonaras, qui magnos in Imperio Constantinopolitano honores primo gessit; Fuit enim Magnus Drungarius, seu præfectus Drungi; Drungus autem est Globus militum, occurrit rit vox apud Vopiscum & Pollionem. Magni Drungarii duo erant, τῆς βίγλης & τῶν γόλας, seu Drungarius vigiliae & Drungarius classis. Postremus Amiralio imperabat, Protocomiti, Drungariis inferioribus & Comitibus, ipse soli magno Duci subjectus; alterius munus erat constituere vigilias ex praescripto Magnidomestici,& ex his nostEr Zonaras fuit. Vide late de hoc officio Jul. Caesar. Bulenger. de Imper. Roman. lib. 4. cap. 37. & lib. 8. cap. 94. Doctiss: Meursium in Lexico Mixobarbar. voce Δρουγγάριος Codinum & alios. Fuit praeterea Zonaras Protosecretarius. Postea Monachus factus ad scribendum animum applicuit, & historiam καθολικὴν seu universalem compositum, usq; ad Alexii Comneni Imp. obitum, seu annum 1118; in qua passim Dionem sequitur. Scripsit praeterea alia; quae ad nostrum Institutum faciunt, sunt commentarii in Photii Nomocanonem, & Canones Apostolorum, conciliorum Generalium & Provincialium, seu in codicem Ecclesiae Orientalis; Graece & Latine prodiit opus a variis versum Lutetiae Parisiorum hujus seculi anno XVIII. Et ejusdem expositio canonicarum Epistolarum ibidem Gr. & Lat. anno XXI. Manuscripti Codices passim in Bibliothecis adservantur, vide
units.tr: In the twelfth century, among both Greeks and Latins, men worked hard both in explaining and in collecting the canons. From the times of Photius, for two centuries and a bit more, the Greeks seem to have been quiet, except that the emperors still from time to time took care of church affairs and issued certain novels on this matter, of which we shall speak later in their place. In this century they return to canonical study, and the first to present himself is John Zonaras, who first held great honours in the Empire of Constantinople. For he was Great Drungarius, that is, prefect of the drungus. A drungus is a band of soldiers, a word which occurs in Vopiscus and Pollio. There were two Great Drungarii, the Drungarius of the watch [τῆς βίγλης] and the Drungarius of the fleet [τῶν γόλας], that is, of the watch and of the fleet. The latter commanded the Amiral, the Protocomes and the lesser Drungarii and Counts, being himself subject only to the Great Duke; the office of the former was to set the watches according to the orders of the Great Domestic. Zonaras was one of these. On this office see at length Julius Caesar Bulengerus, de Imperio Romano, book 4, ch. 37, and book 8, ch. 94, and the most learned Meursius in his Lexicon of Mixed Barbarity under the word [Δρουγγάριος], also Codinus and others. Zonaras was also Protosecretary. Afterwards he became a monk and turned his mind to writing, and he composed a universal [καθολικήν] history, down to the death of the emperor Alexius Comnenus, that is, to the year 1118, in which he follows Dion throughout. He also wrote other works which bear on our subject: commentaries on the Nomocanon of Photius, and on the Canons of the Apostles, of the General and Provincial Councils, that is, on the code of the Eastern Church. A work of his, translated by various hands, was published in Greek and Latin at Paris in the year XVIII of this century, and his exposition of the canonical Epistles, in Greek and Latin, appeared there in the year XXI. Manuscript codices are kept in various libraries; see
Theophilus Spizelius, The Sacred Secrets of Libraries Uncovered.

units.la: Post Zonaram inter Græcos Canonistas locum occupat, Alexius Aristinus, Diaconus Ecclesiæ Constantinopolitanæ, ut illum appellat Gilbert. Genebrand. in libro de Trinitate. Scripsit ille Epitomen Canonum jussu Imperatoris Johannis Comneni, ut observat Leo Allatius in libro, de collatione Ordinum. Factum id seculi duodecimi anno trigesimo. Inscribitur opusculum hoc. ἡ ἐπὶ Ἀλεξίου σύνοψις τῶν κανόνων πάντων. Genebrandus gloriatur habere se fragmentum hujus auctoris, quod inscribitur. συνόψιλος τ᾽ ὅλων κανόνων τ᾽ ἐκπεθέντων ἀφ᾽ ὁ τ᾽ οἰκουμενικῶν ἁγίων ἐξ συνόδων, καὶ τῶν μεταξὺ τῶν αὐτῶν τοπικῶν. Continet hoc opusculum tantum Epitomen, seu Indicem Codicis Canonum Ecclesiæ universæ, servato ordine priorum conciliorum, Nicæni videlicet, Ancyrani, Neocæsariensis, Gangrensis, Antiocheni, Laodiceni, Constantinopolitani, Ephesini & Calchedonensis, omissa tamen serie seu consequentia numerorum; additis in principio canonibus Apostolicis tum Sardicensibus, Africanis xxi r. Trullensibus, tribusque epistolis Canonicis S. Basilii, ut tradit Christophorus Justellus in Præfatione part. 2. Biblioth. juris canon. veteris; qui & opusculum seu compendium hoc Canonum Græce & Latine in eadem Bibliotheca publicavit. Omni arte caret hæc collectio, & videtur tantum in subsidium memoriæ composita esse.
units.tr: Among the Greek canonists, after Zonaras, comes Alexius Aristinus, deacon of the Church of Constantinople, as Gilbert Genebrardus calls him in his book on the Trinity. He wrote an epitome of the canons at the command of the Emperor John Comnenus, as Leo Allatius notes in his book on the conferral of orders. This happened in the thirtieth year of the twelfth century. The little work is entitled ἡ ἐπὶ Ἀλεξίου σύνοψις τῶν κανόνων πάντων [The Synopsis of All the Canons under Alexius]. Genebrardus boasts that he possesses a fragment of this author, entitled συνόψιλος τ᾽ ὅλων κανόνων τ᾽ ἐκπεθέντων ἀφ᾽ ὁ τ᾽ οἰκουμενικῶν ἁγίων ἐξ συνόδων, καὶ τῶν μεταξὺ τῶν αὐτῶν τοπικῶν [a synopsis of all the canons issued by the holy ecumenical synods and by the local synods between them]. This little work contains only an epitome, or index, of the code of canons of the whole Church, keeping the order of the earlier councils: namely Nicaea, Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Gangra, Antioch, Laodicea, Constantinople, Ephesus and Chalcedon, though the sequence or numbering of the canons is left out. At the beginning he has added the Apostolic canons, as well as the Sardican, the African (twenty-one of them), and the Trullan canons, and the three canonical letters of St Basil, as Christophorus Justellus reports in the preface to part two of his Bibliotheca juris canonici veteris. Justellus also published this little compendium of the canons in Greek and Latin in the same library. The collection lacks all method and seems to have been put together only as an aid to memory.

units.la: Clari quoque nominis est, qui vixit hoc seculo ad medium procurrente, Constantinus Harmenopulus, in utroque Jure Civili & Ecclesiastico versatissimus; Dignitates ejus indicat titulus, qui præfigitur ejus epitome divinorum canonum, in quo vo-catur παντοίβας σεβασὸς, νομοφύλαξ ἡ κείτης Θεσσαλονίκης κυέρος Κωνσαντίν ὁ ἀρ-χιφυλάκοπολ. Sebasti & Protosebasti dignita-tes fuerunt sub sequioribus Imperatoribus cognitæ, quales tamen fuerint, id non satis constat; quædam de iis congessit Jul. Cæsar Buleng de Imperio Rom. lib. 8. cap. 5. & Meursi. in Glossario, ex quibus tamen vix quidquam colligere possumus, quam dignitates fuisse. Quale quoque officium Nomophylacis Constantinopoli fuerit, id quoque nescimus, vid. Bulenger. lib. cit. cap. 109. De tempore quo vixit, hæc habet Clarissimus Marquard. Freherus, in Chronologia, quam Juri Græco-Romano præfixit. ad ann. 1143. Constantinus Harmenopulus, Judex Thessalonicensis hoc ævo vixisse videtur, qui hucusque Principum novellas allegat. Scripsit in jure Civili πεῦχειρον νόμων, Promptuarium juris vel legum. Quod superioris seculi anno 56. edidit & Latine vertit Joannes Mercerus Professor Regius Lutetiæ, postea Græce & Latine edidit Dionysius Gothofredus cum paratitlis ad singulos titulos, variis lectionibus & nomenclatore Græcarum dictionum anno 1577. Adscribuntur ei in tomo secundo juris Græco Romani collectiones tres, legum militarium Ruffi, legum Colonariarum, & legum Navalium, sed ex conjectura, quia plerumque ejus libris adjectæ inveniuntur. Ad Institutum nostrum facit ejus Ἐπιτομὴ τῶν ἁγίων καὶ ἱερῶν κανόνων. Epitome divinorum & sacrorum canonum; quam collegit ex codice canonum Ecclesiæ Orientalis, seu synodorum Oecumenicarum & Provincialium item Patrum Græcorum canonibus, quarum rationem, historiam & numerum cum in Præfatione breviter tradidisset, collectionis suæ Methodum hanc describit. Τῶτων τοίνυν, inquit, ἡμεῖς τὴν ὑποθεσιν ἐν ἐπιτομῇ νῦν ἐνταῦθα Ἀλαλαμβάνομεν, πρῶτον μὲν τὰς τῶν ἀποστόλων Ἀλαλαμβάνοντας, ἢ ὅσοι τούτων εἰσὶν ἐχόμενοι. εἶτα τὰς περὶ πρεσβυτέρων, διακόνων, ἢ ὑποδιακόνων, καὶ ὅσοι τούτων ἐχόμενοι· μεταξῦ τὰς περὶ κληρικῶν, καὶ ὅσοι τούτων ἐχόμενοι· μετὰ δὲ τὰς περὶ μοναχῶν. ναχῶν, ἢ μοναςηεῖων· ἢ μετ' αὐτὺς, τὺς πεςὶ λαϊκῶν, ἢ ὅσοι καθολικοί εἰσί· ἢ πλῶ, τὺς περὶ γυναικῶν· ἐν ἐξ τιμήμασι τὴν πᾶσαν τῶν καινένων πραγματείαν ἀφιλαβόντες ἐ ποιησάμψοι. ἕκαστον ἢ τῶν τιμημάτων, ἀπηγεφὰς παλιν κέκτητ.. μεέικαὶς, εἰς οὐωτομωτέεγν ἀ- μὰ ἐ σαφέστεγν ἀρεσιν ἢ ζητυμένς. His ergo quidquid continetur, compendio nos isto nunc complectimur, collocatis primo seorsum canonib. iis, qui de Episcopis tractant, & quotquot his adfines sunt: deinde, qui de Presbyteris, Diaconis, & Subdiaconis, atque his adfines: postea, qui de Monachis, & Monasteriis: ac secundum illos, qui de Laicis agunt, & quotquot sunt generales: in extremo, qui de mulieribus: sectionibus omnino sex universa canonum tractatione comprehensa & absoluta. Harum vero sectionum quaelibet rursus particulares habet titulos, ut ratione magis compendiaria, & dilucidiore, quod quaeritur, inveniri possit. Inseruit hanc Epitomen in tomum primum juris Graeco Romani Johannes Leunclavius, quem credidit Clarissimo Marquardo Frehero, qui publicavit Francofurti, seculi superioris anno XCVI. cum ejusdem Auctoris libro de sectis & verae fidei confessoribus Graece & Latine.
units.tr: Also of notable name is Constantine Harmenopulus, who lived in the middle of this century and was thoroughly versed in both civil and ecclesiastical law. His dignities are shown by the title prefixed to his epitome of the divine canons, where he is called παντοίβας σεβασὸς, νομοφύλαξ ἡ κείτης Θεσσαλονίκης κυέρος Κωνσαντίν ὁ ἀρχιφυλάκοπολ. [sebastos, nomophylax, judge of Thessalonica, lord Constantine, archiphylax of the city]. The dignities of sebastos and protosebastos were known under the later emperors, but what they were is not sufficiently clear. Julius Caesar Bulenger gathered some things about them in On the Roman Empire, book 8, chapter 5, and Meursius in the Glossary, but from these we can scarcely gather more than that they were dignities. What the office of nomophylax was at Constantinople we also do not know; see Bulenger , loc. cit., chapter 109. Concerning the time when he lived, the most distinguished Marquard Freher has this: in the Chronology he prefixed to his Greco-Roman law, for the year 1143: Constantine Harmenopulus, judge of Thessalonica, seems to have lived in this age, since he quotes the novels of the emperors up to now. In civil law he wrote a πεῦχειρον νόμων, a handbook of laws or of law. Its earlier edition, in the year 56 of the last century, was published and translated into Latin by John Mercerus, royal professor at Paris; later Dionysius Gothofredus published it in Greek and Latin, with parallel titles for each title, variant readings and an index of Greek words, in the year 1577. In the second volume of the Greco-Roman law are ascribed to him three collections: of military laws of Rufus, of colonial laws, and of naval laws, but this is conjecture, since they are usually found added to his books. To our purpose belongs his Ἐπιτομὴ τῶν ἁγίων καὶ ἱερῶν κανόνων [Epitome of the Holy and Sacred Canons], Epitome of the divine and sacred canons, which he gathered from the code of canons of the Eastern Church, that is, from the canons of the ecumenical and provincial synods and likewise of the Greek Fathers. After he had briefly set out in the preface the nature, history and number of these, he describes the method of his collection thus: "Of these, then," he says, "we now take up the subject here in summary, first placing the canons of the apostles, or as many as are connected with them; then those concerning presbyters, deacons and subdeacons, and as many as are connected with these; next those concerning clerics and as many as are connected with these; after these, those concerning monks and monasteries; and following them, those concerning laymen, and as many as are general; lastly, those concerning women. Thus we have embraced and completed the whole treatment of the canons in six sections. Each of these sections again has its own particular titles, so that what is sought may be found by a more compendious and clearer method." This epitome was inserted into the first volume of the Greco-Roman law by John Leunclavius, who believed it to be by the famous Marquard Freher, and who published at Frankfurt, in the year 96 of the last century, together with the same author's book on the sects and confessors of the true faith, in Greek and Latin.

units.la: Inter Graecos Canoniistas citatur & Matthaeus Blastares, quo tempore praecise vixerit non satis mihi compertum Anton. Augustin. gustin. in Præfatione ad antiq. Decretal. Collect. hæc de eo habet. Johannes Scholasticus & Photius ambo Antistites Constantinopol. & Matthæus Blastares Monachus, & Constantinus Harmenopulus, & his omnibus brevior Arsenius, sub certis quibusdam titulis sententias canonum comprehendunt: adjectis etiam legum de eisdem rebus decretis, ex quo factum est, ut id genus librorum Nomocanones appellarent. Horum Antiquissimus Johannes est, cognomento Scholasticus, quo Patriarcha Justinianus legum Romanarum Collector est mortuus. Photius Isidoro Hispalensi posterior fuit, Constantinus & Matthæus, Ivone & Gratiano antiquiores non fuerunt. Citat eum quoque inter Nomocanonum scriptores Justellus Pater in Præfat. ad Cod. Canon. Eccles. Univers. Synopsin ejus conciliorum citat Meursius in Glossario Mixobarbaro. verbo ἀμεξων. In Catalogo manuscriptorum Codicum Bibliothecæ Patriarchæ Constantinopolitani, legitur hic titulus. De legibus Magnum Volumen habens explicationem trium Doctorum, explicantium canones, & leges Imperiales. Initium Johannis Monachi Zonaræ, deinde Theodori Balsamonis Patriarchæ Antiocheni, postremo Matthæi Blastarii, in charta bombacina. Ego hactenus nil de eo vidi, nec puto Justellum Patrem aut Filium habuisse hujus scripta; quia Bi-
units.tr: Among the Greek canonists is also cited Matthaeus Blastares, whose exact time I have not sufficiently ascertained. Antonius Augustinus in his preface to the ancient Decretal collection has this about him: John Scholasticus and Photius, both bishops of Constantinople, and Matthew Blastares, a monk, and Constantine Harmenopulus, and, shorter than all of these, Arsenius, gather the sentences of the canons under certain titles, adding also the decrees of the laws on the same matters; from which it came about that such books were called Nomocanons. Of these the most ancient is John, surnamed Scholasticus, in whose time the Patriarch Justinian, the collector of Roman laws, died. Photius was later than Isidore of Seville; Constantine and Matthew were not earlier than Ivo and Gratian. Justellus the father also cites him among the writers of Nomocanons in the preface to his Code of the Canons of the Universal Church. Meursius in his Mixobarbarous Glossary, under the word ἀμεξων, cites a synopsis of his councils. In the catalogue of manuscript codices of the library of the Patriarch of Constantinople this title is read: On the laws, a great volume containing an explanation by three teachers who explain the canons and the imperial laws: first by John the monk Zonaras, then by Theodore Balsamon, patriarch of Antioch, and last by Matthew Blastares, on cotton paper. I have so far seen nothing of his, nor do I think that Justellus the father or the son had his writings, because the Bi-

units.la: 289. Scripta bliothecæ Iuris Canonici veteris, & aliis Græcis collectoribus non adjunxerunt, procul dubio id facturi si habuissent. Leo Allatius in famoso Tractatu, de Ecclesiæ Occidentalis & Orientalis perpetua DISSENSIONE, (ita enim rectius inscriptus fuisset ille tractatus quam consensione) in indiculo auctorum, & hunc Matthæum Blastarem collocat inter auctores ineditos.
units.tr: 289. bliothecae Juris Canonici veteris, and the other Greek collectors, did not add them, though without doubt they would have done so had they possessed them. Leo Allatius, in his notorious treatise on the perpetual DISSENSION of the Western and Eastern Church (for that treatise would have been more fittingly titled consensione ["agreement"]), lists this Matthew Blastares among the unpublished authors in his index of writers.

units.la: Hoc quoque tempore vixit Simeon Magister & Logotheta, seculo nimirum duodecimo medio, inter Collectores aut Epitomatores canonicos non prætereundus. Eum Aristino posteriorem facit Justellus. Dignitatem ejus indicat, quod Magister dictus sit & Logotheta. De priore Constantinus Porphyrogenneta in vita Basilii Macedonis; hæc de Basilio refert. Τῆς ἡ ϖεγvοίας ἀγέσης τὸν Βασίλειον Δμηχάνως ϖεὶς ὅπως ἐβάλετο, εὐθέως μὴ τὴν ἐκ τῆς σεχτείας ὑπο-σροφὼ ὑποπιέτην τῶν ὁ βασιλεὺς. Ἐτύγχανε γὰρ καθ᾽ ἑπάπαξ οἰκείας γενῆς ἀμοιςῶν, καὶ τῶν Μαγίσρων ὑπερλάμπας πηρὸς ἀξιοῖ. ἐφ᾽ ὧν τῇ βασιλείᾳ ϱηγνύμῳ ὁ λογοθέτης Συμβαί-νῳ, ἡ τὸ ἐξῆς. Verumtamen providentia ferente Basilium, ad id, quod libebat aptissimè, illicò post illam exercitationem & reditum, Imperator eundem pro filio, quod ipse nullos liberos habebat , adoptat, & Magistrorum prafulgente dignitate condecorat. His rumpitur invidia Logotheta Symbatius. Ipsi Imperatorum filii ad eam adspirabant. Intimis Imperatorum consiliis admittebantur, magnoque in honore habebantur; Novella prima Romani senioris θεληλάτης & θεοφανῆς vocat, Cassiod. lib. 6. var. Reverendum honorem sumit, quisquis Magistri nomen accepit. Inter Patritios censebantur, imo postea & supra hos habiti; ante quos & apud Codinum collocantur. Ad σωπτικνίαν[?] Imperatorum aliquando adsciti; nec tantum filii, ut dictum, sed & consanguinei Imperatoris hoc titulo ornati leguntur, vide sis Doctiss: Meursium in Lexico Mixobarbaro in μάγιστρος, item & Leonem Allatium in Diatriba de scriptis Simeonum. pag. 25. & seqq. item Jul. Caesar. Bulenger. in libris de Imperio Rom. Logotheta insuper vocatur Simeon, qui duplices in Imperio Constantinopolitano. Ecclesiastici, quorum munus describit Codinus de Offic. ὁ λογοθέτης εἰς τὸ λογογραφεῖν, ἢ εἰς τὰς δημοσιακὰς ἢ ἀρχοντικὰς ὑποθέσεις λογογραφεῖν[?]. Politici, qui rationes fiscales vel publicas cognoscunt, disceptant & discutiunt; quare & discussores aliquando vocantur. Varii & hi fuerunt, vide sis Meursium in ψηφικὸν[?] & in κυφέπορ[?] & in λογοθέτης[?], item accurate & caute Leonem Allatium, dicta Diatriba, pag. 38. & seqq. & cujus ille forte scrinia compilavit. Jul. Cæsar. Buleng. de Imperio Rom. lib. 3. c. 22. de Logistis & Logothetis, lib. 8, c. 11. de Logotheta magno, lib. 8. c. 91. de Logotheta genico seu generali, & cap. 29. de Logotheta cursus, cap. 30. de Logotheta secretorum, cap. 39. de Logotheta gregis, cap. 51. de Logotheta τῶν οἰκειακῶν seu privatorum, cap. 57. de Logotheta militaris ærarii. Edidit Simeon Magister Epitomen canonum, eodem quo Alexius Aristenus modo, diverso tamen ordine, præmittit Canones Apostolicos, tum quatuor concilia Oecumenica sequuntur, dein particularia, Ancyranum, Sardicense, Neocæsariense, Gangrense, Antiochenum & Laodicenum; addidit etiam canones Africanos XXXIV. & Trullenses tum Epistolas tres canonicas Basilii. Artis prorsus est expers & tantum ad memoriam scripta collectio. Edidit eam in Bibliothecæ Iuris Canonici veteris tomo secundo, ex Codice Manuscripto Bibliothecæ Regiæ Christophorus Justellus Græcè & Latinè. Leo Allatius in Diatriba de Simeonibus & eorum scriptis, nil de hoc nostro Simeone Magistro & Logotheta habet, sedulus alias sequioris Græciæ scriptorum, antiquitatum & historiæ rufpator, quamvis non semper sine partium studio. Ex Græcia, seu potius Orientali Imperio, iterum in Occidentem trajiciendum nobis, & quid interea Latini in canonum studio & collectione præstiterint hoc seculo lustrandum. Occurrit hic Clari nominis collector Gratianus, qui, ut Ant. Augustinus in præfat. ad Antiq. Collect. Decret. dicit, eorum omnium, quos ex collectoribus canonum enumeraverat, luminibus obstruxit. Fuit is Patria Clusinus, è Thusciæ civitate. In Pomerio Ecclesiæ Ravennatis & apud Matthæum Westmonasterienfem ad ann. 1151. legitur fuisse de Classa civitate Thusciæ, sed est error vel mendum Classa positum pro Clusio. Hic error forte inde est, quod alii dixerint fuisse Gratianum Monachum Classensem prope Ravennam. vide sis Baron. ad annum 1151. num. 6. item Epitaphium, quod infra adducemus. De natalibus ejus variant auctores, quidam spurium fuisse dicunt, & Petri Lombardi, qui Magister sententiarum vocatur, & Antistes Parisiensis fuit, & Petri Comestoris historiæ Scholasticæ scriptoris Fratrem germanum, tresque hos uno puerperio ex adulterio aut scortatione esse prosatos. Præpositus in proœmio decretor. Panciroll. de clar. leg. interpret. lib. 3. cap. 2. pag. 405. Addunt etiam, cum Matrem stupri pœnitere non posset, quod tam præclaros Viros genuisset, sacerdotem cui confitebatur justiffe, ut saltem pœnitere-ret, quod pœnitere non posset. Tiraquell. de nobilitat. cap. 15. n. 32. Sed hæc ab aliis pro fabulis habentur & explodvntur. Falso id dici, tradit Pancirollus d. l. fundamento carere hanc opinionem. Bellarm. de script. Eccles. in Petro Lombardo, quia in patria non conveniunt; Gratianus enim Ethruscus fuit ex Clusio civitate, Magister Petrus Lombardus ex Novaria, Petrus Comestor, Gallus ex Trecis. Sed alii eludunt hoc argumentum, quod ex diversitate patriæ tantum sequatur, non esse eos tergeminos; non vero, non esse Fratres aut Spurios, cum Mater diversis temporibus & diversis locis cum patribus conventitiis Plautinis consuescere potuerit. Cum monachus Benedictinus Claustensis Monasterii factus esset, sacris literis delectatum dicit in Chronico Martinus, & Alber. in Dictionario. §. forma 2. quæst. 6. Vixit Bononiæ tempore Conradi III. Imperatoris, cum ibidem Alexander, qui postea Pontifex factus est Romanus, Theologiam doceret. Ad Canones colligendos & ordine artificiose digerendos animum adjecit; & ut quidam volunt in Monasterio D. Felicis, quod probat quoque Epitaphium infra adducendum, item inscriptio quæ legitur in Ædę D. Felicis in saxo vetusto, relata à Pancirollo. d. l.
units.tr: This period also saw Simeon Magister and Logothete, in the middle of the twelfth century, who must not be passed over among the canonical collectors and epitomists. Justellus places him later than Aristenus. His rank is shown by the titles Magister and Logothete. Of the former, Constantine Porphyrogenitus in the life of Basil the Macedonian reports this about Basil: But with providence guiding Basil to what suited him best, straight after that campaign and return, the emperor, since he himself had no children, adopted him as his son and honoured him with the splendid dignity of Magister. Logothete Symbatius was consumed with envy. The sons of emperors aspired to this office. They were admitted to the emperors' innermost councils and held in great honour. The first Novella calls the elder Romanus a god-driven and god-appearing man. Cassiodorus, book 6 of the Variae: Whoever receives the name of Magister takes on a reverend honour. They were counted among the Patricians, and later were even held above them; in Codinus they are placed before them. Sometimes they were admitted to the emperor's [?] council, and not only sons, as said, but also blood relations of the emperor are read to have been adorned with this title. See the most learned Meursius in the Lexicon Mixobarbarum under μάγιστρος, and also Leo Allatius in the Diatriba on the writings of the Simeons, p. 25 and following, and Julius Caesar Bulenger in his books on the Roman Empire. Simeon is also called Logothete, a title that in the Constantinopolitan Empire was double: ecclesiastical, whose duty Codinus describes as the Logothete's task is to write up accounts, or to write up the public or magisterial business, and political, who investigate, dispute and examine fiscal or public accounts, whence they are sometimes called discussors. These too were of various kinds. See Meursius under ψηφικὸν, under κυφέπορ, and under λογοθέτης, and also Leo Allatius, carefully and cautiously, in the said Diatriba, p. 38 and following, from whose chests he perhaps compiled. Julius Caesar Bulenger, On the Roman Empire, book 3, ch. 22, on the Logistae and Logothetae; book 8, ch. 11, on the great Logothete; book 8, ch. 91, on the Logothete general; ch. 29, on the Logothete of the post; ch. 30, on the Logothete of the secrets; ch. 39, on the Logothete of the flock; ch. 51, on the Logothete of the household, or private affairs; ch. 57, on the Logothete of the military treasury. Simeon Magister published an epitome of the canons in the same manner as Alexius Aristenus, but in a different order. He places the Apostolic Canons first, then the four Ecumenical Councils, then the particular councils: Ancyra, Sardica, Neocaesarea, Gangra, Antioch and Laodicea. He also added the thirty-four African canons and the Trullan canons, and then the three canonical Epistles of Basil. The collection is entirely without art and written only for memory. Christophorus Justellus published it in Greek and Latin in the second volume of the Bibliotheca Iuris Canonici veteris, from a manuscript of the Royal Library. Leo Allatius, in his Diatriba on the Simeons and their writings, says nothing about this Simeon Magister and Logothete, although he is otherwise a diligent investigator of the writers, antiquities and history of later Greece, though not always without partisan zeal. From Greece, or rather the Eastern Empire, we must now pass again to the West, and examine what the Latins have achieved in the study and collection of canons in this century. Here appears the famous collector Gratian, who, as Antonius Augustinus says in the preface to the Antiquae Collectiones Decretorum, obstructed the lights of all of them, those whom he had listed among the collectors of canons. He was a native of Chiusi, a city of Tuscany. In the Pomerium of the Church of Ravenna, and in Matthew of Westminster under the year 1151, he is read to have been from the city of Classa in Tuscany, but this is an error or a mistake, Classa being put for Clusio. This error perhaps arose because others have said that Gratian was a monk of Classis near Ravenna; see Baronius under the year 1151, no. 6, and also the epitaph that we shall cite below. Authors differ about his birth: some say he was illegitimate, and that he was the full brother of Peter Lombard, who is called the Master of the Sentences and was Bishop of Paris, and of Peter Comestor, the author of the Scholastic History, and that these three were born from one birth out of adultery or fornication. Panciroli, in the preface to the Decretum, On the famous interpreters of the law, book 3, ch. 2, p. 405, adds that when the mother could not repent of her debauchery, she was told by the priest to whom she confessed, since she had borne such distinguished men, that at least she should repent of being unable to repent. Tiraqueau, On Nobility, ch. 15, no. 32. But others regard these things as fables and reject them. Pancirolli reports that it is falsely said, that this opinion lacks foundation. Bellarmine, On Ecclesiastical Writers, under Peter Lombard, because they do not agree in their homeland: Gratian was Etruscan, from the city of Chiusi; Master Peter Lombard was from Novara; Peter Comestor was a Frenchman from Troyes. But others evade this argument, since from difference of homeland it follows only that they were not triplets, not that they were not brothers or illegitimate, since their mother could have lived with different fathers at different times and places. When he had become a Benedictine monk of the monastery of Chiusi, Martinus says in his Chronicle that he was delighted by the sacred letters, and Alberic in his Dictionary, § forma, 2, q. 6. He lived at Bologna in the time of the Emperor Conrad III, when Alexander, who was later made Roman Pontiff, taught theology there. He turned his mind to gathering the canons and arranging them with skill; and, as some want, in the monastery of St Felix, which the epitaph cited below also proves, as does the inscription read in the church of St Felix on an ancient stone, reported by Pancirolli, ibid.
Reader, approach this part of the building with reverence:

units.la: Alii in D. Proculi cœnobio, ubi diu vixit, vid. Cœpo. in tract. de cognit. libr. jur. canon. in princ. & Præposit. in Proem. decret. Composuit grande illud Volumen Decretorum; quod hodie primam partem facit Corporis Juris Canonici. Obtulit hunc librum Eugenio tertio Pontifici, cui valde placuit, adeo ut Gratianum Ecclesiæ Clusinæ patriæ præficeret. vid. Martin. in Chron. & Alber. in Dictionar. Sunt qui probatum & canonis seu legis auctoritatem accepisse volunt ab Eugenio tertio; sed nunquam prolata sanctio ista fuit, neque pro lege hactenus habitum. Magnæ tamen semper fuit auctoritatis, & ex eo quod scholis ad prælectionem datum, posset inferri vis canonica seu legis. De auctoritate ejus hæc refert Pancirollus d. l. Tanta postea auctoritatis
units.tr: Others place him in the monastery of St Proculus, where he lived for a long time; see Cöpo, in his treatise on knowing the books of canon law, at the beginning, and Prepositus in the preface to the Decretum. He composed that great volume of Decrees, which today forms the first part of the Corpus Iuris Canonici. He offered this book to Pope Eugenius III, who liked it very much, so much so that he set Gratian over the Church of Chiusi, his homeland. See Martinus in the Chronicle and Alberic in the Dictionary. Some want that he received approval of the work, and the authority of a canon or law, from Eugenius III; but that sanction was never issued, and the work has not been held as law up to now. Yet it always had great authority, and from the fact that it was given to the schools for lecture, the canonical or legal force could be inferred. Pancirolli reports on its authority, ibid. d. l. Tanta postea auctoritatis
