Itaque qui ejus opus ita edidicisset, ut aliis praelegere posse videretur, baculo velut pro arrha doctrinae more Longobardorum accepto Doctoris titulo honestabatur, & à bacillo Bacillarius vocabatur, qui mos tum demum Bononiae institutus à Parisiensibus, ubi tum Decreta, & summulae docebantur, fluxisse fertur, in quorum vetustis Constitutionibus Bacillarii nominantur. Sed de hoc postea, ubi accuratius Volumen Decretorum Gratiani expendendum est. Quando scripserit Gratianus, discordant Auctores, Trithemius lib. 2. de Vir. Illust. Ord. Benedicti anno 1127. scripsisse refert, alii plerique omnes, an. 1251. quam sententiā confirmat epitaphium Gratiani. Bellarminus utramque sententiam conciliat, lib. de script. Ecclesiasticis, conjectura, quae aliis non displicet, quod anno 1127. incoeperit, & anno 1151. perfecerit opus seu collectionem suam. Chrift. Justellus in fine praefat. quam Codici canonum Ecclesiae universa praemisit Gratianum decretorum volumen composuisse refert sub Innocentio II. anno 1131; quod proxime accedit ad traditionem Trithemii. Alii editum narrant anno 1150. Calderinus in praemio Decretal. Cardinal Alexander der in Præfat. Decreti quos sequitur Valent. Forster. in histor. Jur. Civil. lib. 3. cap. 7. Freherus in Chronol. juri Græco-Român. præmissa, anno 1154. Gratianum scribit Decretum scripsisse, quod Decretum Magnum vocatur. Sed hoc abit ab omnium sententia, qui sub Eugenio III. Decretorum opus editum scribunt, isto vero anno 1154. sedebat Romæ Hadrianus IV. nisi forte Freherus de progressu vitæ & additionibus sit intelligendus. Ex forma Apostolorum, quæ habetur cap. Post Appellationem 2. q. 6. videtur colligi posse anno 1161. scripsisse adhuc Gratianum, sed est mendum pro MCLXI. debet reponi facili mutatione MCXLI. ut quoque monent ibidem Correctores Romani, in notis, & late Antonius noster August. lib. 2. Dial. 9. pr. id satis firmat annus indictionis quartus, qui anno 1161. est septimus; Anno vero 1141. currebat indictio quarta; quod fulcit conjecturam supra relatam diu occupatum fuisse Gratianum in collectione Decretorum. Inscripsit ipse opus suum Concordiam discordantium canonum. Vide sis Anton. Augustin. de emendat. Grat. libr. 1. dial. 1. princip. fere, ubi & docet falso Decretum vocari. Melius adhuc Decreta. Quomodo & Antonius Demochares, qui Decretorum collectanea, & Ant. Contius, qui Decretorum Canonicorum Collectanea inscripsit in sua emendatione; Quia non unum ista collectio complectitur decretum, sed est farrago multorum decretorum. Idem firmat Henr. Gandavensis de Scriptor. Ecclesiast. cap. 44. Gratianus, inquit, Monachus, Bononia habitans, Codicem, quem Decreta vo-cant, compilavit. Quare vero ipse Gratianus inscripserit concordiam & quidem discordantium canonum ex fine ejus satis patet. Videbat Ecclesiastica decreta & canones sibi invicem contrarios, diversos, dissentientes, inter hos dissidentes concordiam ille instituere voluit. Aliter quam olim concordia canonum accipiebatur, nempe pro collectione similium sententiarum: hic autem a Gratiano significat, dissidentium canonum conciliationem. Animadvertit id quoque Ant. Augustin. lib. 1. de emend. Grat. dial. 1. pag. nostr. edit. 5. Ad Gratianum, inquit, redeamus, in ejus libris veteribus illa inscriptio est, quam audisti: Concordia discordantium canonum. Similem legi Romae in veteri libro Cresconii: Concordia canonum, & ipsi canones. C. Quid est, quod his verbis significare voluerunt? an putandum est, canones conciliorum ita esse inter se contrarios, ut egeant concordia? A. Quantum ego potui ex Cresconii libro elicere, concordiam vocat collectionem similium
units.tr: Marginal notes beside the column are given above in place. He was held in such high authority that, commonly called the Master, he carried the greatest weight in deciding cases, although, as the words of a private man, his sayings did not have the force of law. Thus whoever had so learned his work that he seemed able to lecture on it to others, having received a staff as a pledge of teaching in the manner of the Lombards, was honoured with the title of Doctor, and from the staff (baculus) was called a Bacillarius. This custom is said to have been first instituted at Bologna by the Parisians, where the Decretals and the summulae were then taught, and in whose old constitutions the Bacillarii are named. But of this later, when the volume of Gratian's Decretum must be weighed more carefully. Authors disagree about when Gratian wrote. Trithemius, book 2 of On the Illustrious Men of the Order of St Benedict, reports that he wrote in 1127; almost all the others say 1151, and this view is confirmed by Gratian's epitaph. Bellarmine reconciles the two opinions, in On Ecclesiastical Writers, by a conjecture that others do not dislike: that he began in 1127 and finished his work or collection in 1151. Christophe Justel, at the end of the preface which he prefixed to the Codex of the canons of the universal Church, reports that Gratian composed the volume of Decretals under Innocent II in 1131, which comes closest to the tradition of Trithemius. Others say it was published in 1150. Calderinus in the preface to the Decretals; Cardinal Alexander Dert in the Preface to the Decretum, whom Valentin Forster follows, in History of Civil Law, book 3, chapter 7; Freherus, in the Chronology prefixed to the Greco-Roman law, writes that Gratian wrote the Decretum in 1154, which is called the Great Decretum. But this departs from the view of all who write that the work of the Decretals was published under Eugenius III; in 1154 Hadrian IV was sitting at Rome, unless perhaps Freherus is to be understood as referring to the course of Gratian's life and his additions. From the form of the Apostles which is found in c. Post Appellationem, 2 q. 6, it seems possible to gather that Gratian was still writing in 1161, but this is an error for MCLXI, which should be read, by an easy change, as MCXLI, as the Roman correctors also note in the margins there, and as our Antonius Augustinus says at length, book 2, dialogue 9, beginning. The indiction year, the fourth, which in 1161 is the seventh, confirms this; but in 1141 the fourth indiction was current. This supports the conjecture reported above that Gratian was long occupied with the collection of the Decretals. He himself entitled his work Concord of Discordant Canons. See Antonius Augustinus on the emendation of Gratian, book 1, dialogue 1, near the beginning, where he also teaches that it is wrongly called Decretum. Decreta is better still. So too Antonius Demochares, who entitled his emendation Collections of Decretals, and Antonius Contius, who entitled his Collection of Canonical Decretals; because this collection does not embrace one decree but is a medley of many decrees. Henry of Ghent confirms the same in On Ecclesiastical Writers, chapter 44: Gratian, he says, a monk living at Bologna, compiled the Codex which they call the Decreta. Why Gratian himself entitled it Concord, and indeed of discordant canons, is clear enough from its conclusion. He saw that the ecclesiastical decrees and canons were contrary, diverse and at odds with one another, and he wished to establish concord among these disagreeing ones. Concord was understood differently in former times, namely as a collection of similar sayings; but here, as used by Gratian, it means the reconciliation of disagreeing canons. Antonius Augustinus also noticed this, book 1, On the Emendation of Gratian, dialogue 1, p. 5 of our edition: Let us return to Gratian, he says; in his older books that inscription is the one you have heard: Concord of Discordant Canons. I read a similar one at Rome in an old book of Cresconius: Concord of Canons, and the canons themselves. C. What did they wish to signify by these words? Must we think that the canons of the councils are so contrary to one another that they need concord? A. As far as I could draw out from the book of Cresconius, he calls concord a collection of similar

units.la: 306. Ratio ejus. milium sententiarum, ut qui scripturæ sacræ verba collegerunt, Concordantias Bibliæ appellarunt; quibus verbis, quod pace vestra dicere liceat, nihil excogitari potest ineptius. C. Gratianus igitur sic Concordiam dicit, quasi collectionem similium canonum. Cur vero addit vocem discordantium, quæ sola refugit hanc interpretationem? A. Vere tu quidem ais. Nam si inscripsisset, Concordiam canonum, ut Cresconius fecit; aut Concordiam concordantium, & discordantium canonum: hanc reciperet interpretationem. Nunc vero significare videtur, concordiam inter discordes versari. Gratianum ad Collectionem Decreti accessisse putant correctores Romani ejus, in Admonitione ad Lectorem, ex consilio Ivonis, qui in Præfatione suæ collectionis quædam de conciliatione discordantium canonum tradiderat, ipse vero neglexerat. Verba eorum sunt hæc. Novissimus istorum omnium præter authorem Pannormiæ (nam is recentior fortasse est) Gratianus monachus Benedictinus non tantum decretis colligendis (quod superiores fecerant) operam dedit: sed Ivonis fortasse præfatione excitatus, eo potissimum incubuit, ut certis quæstionibus propositis, quid in utramque partem ex Canonibus qui inter se nonnunquam pugnare videbantur, dici posset, ipse & afferret, & explicaret: omninoque eorum varietatem, qua quae speciem dissensionis habebat, ad concordiam revocaret. Caeterum in longo ac perdifficili opere multa à parum aequis hominibus exagitabantur, nonnulla pii etiam & verecundi interdum desiderabant. Antequam ejus decretorum volumen penitius lustremus, videndum exactius quam supra factum, cujus sit auctoritatis. Hic diversae sunt Doctorum sententiae. Quidam in utroque extremo, alii in medio incedunt. Seu aliqui legis Auctoritatem aut saltem canonis, alii prorsus nihil, aut saltem non magis quam privo Doctori tribuunt, nullam obligandi vim. Tertii dispescunt collectanea ex fontibus, & pro diversitate eorum, diversam attribuunt auctoritatem. Illi qui primam sententiam defendunt, id non faciunt pari modo. Alii iterum simpliciter adserunt ab Eugenio esse approbatum. Inter quos est Anonymus Auctor vitae Gratiani & Trithemius, descript. Eccles. à quibus hoc in alios manavit, & accepit Gesnerus & Simlerus in Bibliotheca & alii: sed ut supra monui ipsa approbatio nusquam comparet, aut à nemine producta unquam est, aut visa, quare alii ad consuetudinem confugiunt & per eam conciliant Gratiano auctoritatem. Abbas Panormitanus in c. 2. x. de rescript. Sed ego dico, inquit, ex quo ille liber communiter à multis
units.tr: 306. The reason for it: of similar sayings, just as those who gathered the words of Holy Scripture called them Concordances of the Bible; and with respect, I may say, nothing more absurd could be devised. C. So Gratian speaks of concord as if it were a collection of similar canons. But why does he add the word discordant, which alone resists this interpretation? A. You are indeed right. For if he had entitled it Concord of Canons, as Cresconius did, or Concord of the concordant and discordant canons, that would bear this interpretation. As it is, it seems to mean concord existing among those who disagree. The Roman correctors of Gratian think that he added to the collection of the Decretum at the suggestion of Ivo, who in the preface to his own collection had handed down certain things about the reconciliation of discordant canons, though he himself had neglected them. Their words are these: The newest of all of them, apart from the author of the Panormia (for he is perhaps more recent), Gratian, a Benedictine monk, did not merely devote his labour to gathering decrees, as earlier men had done, but, perhaps roused by Ivo's preface, he applied himself chiefly to this: that, with certain questions proposed, he would both set forth and explain what could be said on either side from the canons which sometimes seemed to fight with one another, and would bring back to concord their variety, which had the appearance of disagreement. Otherwise, in a long and very difficult work, many things were attacked by men not very fair, and some pious and modest men sometimes found things to wish otherwise. Before we examine the volume of his decrees more deeply, we must consider more exactly than has been done above what its authority is. Here the opinions of the teachers are divided. Some go to one extreme, others take the middle course. Some attribute to it the authority of law, or at least of canon; others attribute nothing at all, or at least no more than to a private teacher, and no power of binding. A third group distinguishes the collections according to their sources, and assigns to them different authority according to their diversity. Those who defend the first opinion do not all do so in the same way. Others again simply assert that it was approved by Eugenius. Among these is the anonymous author of the life of Gratian and Trithemius in his Description of the Church, from whom this view spread to others; Gesner and Simler in the Bibliotheca and others took it up. But, as I have warned above, that approval nowhere appears; it has either never been produced by anyone or never seen. Therefore others take refuge in custom and through it reconcile Gratian's authority. Abbot Panormitanus, on c. 2, X, de rescriptis: But I say, he says, since that book has been commonly

units.la: 308. An pro lege aut canone valeat decretorum volumen.
units.tr: 308. Whether the volume of Decretals is valid as law or as canon.

units.la: 309. Variae sententiae hac de re. à multis annis circa fuit publice lectus in Scholis, & ipsius dicta communiter recepta sunt, hodie tacitè approbata & per omnes recipienda. Ejusdem est sententiæ Robb. Maranta de Ord. Judiciorum part. 3. n. 34. Quidquid sit, ait, quia est communiter approbatus à populo, & publice legitur in Scholis sicut alii libri authentici, ex hoc censetur authenticus, & facit plenam fidem. Huc inclinat quoque Paulus Laymann. lib. 1. Theol. Moral. tract. 4. cap. 6. §. 3. n. 12. qui consuetudine refert Decretum Gratiani receptum est; Dicta vero Sanctorum Patrum, sunt verba ejus, ipsiusque Gratiani ac Palea, quæ ecclesiasticis regulis ac moribus non repugnant, licet per se nullam juris auctoritatem habeant, (cum in jure condendo, causisque definiendis non sola scientia sed magis etiam potestas necessaria sit juxta c. 1. dist. 20.) nihilominus consuetudo obtinuit, ut in externo foro etiam illa ad causarum decisionem inserviant. Vim quoque legis tribuit Vallensis ei, in Præm. parat. §. 8. n. 12. Maxime cum Gregorius XIII. summus Pontifex reliquis partibus juris illud annumeraverit, atque adeo recognosci, corrigi ac repurgari & retineri mandaverit, non est, quod in hac parte amplius laboremus. Adde sis, Cardin. Tusch. concluf. 170. verb. Jus Canonicum. Sed statim ille, non minus ac ipse Laymannus, suæ assertionis oblitus, iterum resolvit in sua principia, & sic iterum Gratiano adimit omnem auctoritatem, quemadmodum etiam Laymannus, qui tantum probat, quantum ecclesiasticis regulis bonisque moribus non repugnat; cum pro ecclesiasticis regulis protrudantur Gratiani decreta, versetur que hoc in quæstione. Verba Vallensis l. d. sunt hæc. Modo tamen singula, quæ in eo comprehensa sunt, ad suos fontes & origenes revocentur, eo quod ratione auctorum, è quibus decreta adsumuntur, major vel minor sit auctoritas. Si usus & consuetudo firmavit, tum firmavit omnia, & par omnium est auctoritas, eaque ex consuetudine, non ex fontibus & Origine; si Gregorii XIII. auctoritas hic legem facit ex dictis Gratiani, & ansam amplius deliberandi, ut ait Vallensis præcidit, jam pariter toti collectioni conciliat. Quare melius alii huic consuetudini & auctoritati contradicunt, inter quos est Fr. Suarefius de Legib. lib. 4. c. 5. n. 7. Consuetudo, ait, quam allegant, non est in sensu juxta conceptum communem sapientum introducta. Vid. & Zoesium comm. ad Decret. n. 10. in præfat. Quare & alii quoties libet, & si aliter elidere objectiones ex Gratiano non possunt, ejus auctoritatem rejiciunt. Vid. Boetium Bpo. lib. 2. de jure Sacr. num. 135. Petr. de Marca. de concord. sacerd. & Imp. lib. 3. c. 6. n. 24. n. 2. apposite. Cum Gratiani, inquit, collectio privato studio instituta sit, quae refert auctorum testimonia non majore pollent auctoritate, quam antea obtinebant. Alii contra veteres & recentiores plenis buccis in ejus errores debachantur, quod Mascule facit Antonius Auguft. passim in dialogis, vid. lib.
units.tr: 309. Various opinions on this matter. For many years it has been read publicly in the schools, and its sayings have been commonly received; today it is tacitly approved and to be received by all. Robert Maranta holds the same view, On the Order of Judicial Proceedings, part 3, n. 34: Whatever the case, he says, since it is commonly approved by the people and publicly read in the schools, like other authentic books, it is on this account deemed authentic and gives full faith. Paul Laymann also leans this way, Theological Moral, book 1, tract 4, chapter 6, §3, n. 12, who reports that Gratian's Decretum has been received by custom. His words are: The sayings of the holy Fathers, and of Gratian himself and the Palea, which do not conflict with ecclesiastical rules and customs, although in themselves they have no authority of law (since in making law and deciding cases not mere knowledge but power is necessary, according to c. 1, dist. 20), nevertheless custom has prevailed so that they too serve for the decision of cases in the external forum. Vallensis also gives it the force of law, in the Preface to the Parerga, §8, n. 12: Especially since Pope Gregory XIII numbered it among the remaining parts of the law, and commanded that it be revised, corrected, purged and retained, there is no reason for us to labour further on this point. Add also Cardinal Tuschi, conclusion 170, under the words Canon Law. But he at once, no less than Laymann himself, forgot his assertion and again resolved it into its principles, and so again strips Gratian of all authority, just as Laymann does too, who proves only so much as it does not conflict with ecclesiastical rules and good customs; whereas Gratian's decrees are brought forward as ecclesiastical rules, and the question turns on exactly this. Vallensis's words, ibid., are these: Provided, however, that each of the things contained in it is traced back to its sources and origins, since the authority of the authors from whom the decrees are taken is greater or less. If usage and custom have confirmed it, then they have confirmed everything, and the authority of all is equal, and that from custom, not from the sources and origin. If the authority of Gregory XIII makes law here from the sayings of Gratian, and cuts off, as Vallensis says, the occasion for further deliberation, it likewise reconciles the whole collection at once. Therefore others better oppose this custom and authority, among whom is Francisco Suárez, On Laws, book 4, chapter 5, n. 7: The custom they allege, he says, has not been introduced in the sense of the common concept of the learned. See also Zoesius, commentary on the Decretum, n. 10, in the preface. Therefore others too, whenever they please, and if they cannot otherwise rebut objections from Gratian, reject his authority. See Boetius, Bishop of Pa, On the Sacred Law, book 2, n. 135; Peter de Marca, On the Concord of Priesthood and Empire, book 3, chapter 6, n. 24, aptly: Since Gratian's collection was undertaken by private study, and since it reports the testimonies of authors, it has no greater force than they had before. Others on the contrary rage with full cheeks, both old and recent, against his errors; Antonius Augustinus does so vigorously throughout his dialogues, see book

units.la: 1. Dial. 1. item 16. & seqq. Bellarmin. de scriptor. Eccles. in Gratiano. Adde Gloss. ad c. Paulum 7. q. 3. Joh. Andr. ad c. 2. de rescript. Alber. Gentil. de lib. Jur. Canonici cap. 2. Tertia sententia, in quaestione de auctoritate Gratiani, dispescit ejus capita quadrifariam & diversimode de singulis respondet. Marant. de ordin. judic. part. 3. n. 35. Latius Augustinus Barbosa ad Præm. Decret. n. 6. Prima classis continet dicta Patrum, secunda verba Gratiani, Tertia Paleas, Quarta jus Civile. Addi quinto possunt canones Conciliorum & Decretales Pontificum Romanorum, nisi sub prima classe velis completi, & Patres in privos, seu singulares vel simul congregatos dispescere, quae & mens est Barbosae. Privos iterum in eos qui arrogant summam sibi auctoritatem, ut facit Pontifex Romanus; & minorem, quo referendi Patriarchae Metropolitani, & Episcopi; & nullam, quales sunt caeteri Patres, qui scriptis Codices Sacroa[?]
units.tr: 1. Dial. 1. item 16. & seqq. Bellarmine, de scriptor. Eccles. in Gratiano. Add Gloss. ad c. Paulum 7. q. 3. John Andreas, ad c. 2. de rescript. Alberico Gentili, de lib. Jur. Canonici cap. 2. The third opinion, on the question of Gratian's authority, divides his chapters into four classes and gives a different answer for each. Marant, de ordin. judic. part. 3. n. 35. More fully, Augustinus Barbosa, ad Præm. Decret. n. 6. The first class contains the sayings of the Fathers, the second Gratian's own words, the third the Paleae, and the fourth the civil law. A fifth class could be added, the canons of councils and the decretals of the Roman Pontiffs, unless you prefer to place them under the first class, and also to divide the Fathers into those who speak privately or singly and those who speak when gathered together; this is also Barbosa's own view. The private writers are again divided: into those who claim supreme authority for themselves, as the Roman Pontiff does; those who have a lesser authority, such as Patriarchs, Metropolitans and Bishops; and those who have none, such as the remaining Fathers, who by their writings illustrated the sacred books and other ecclesiastical doctrines.

units.la: Sacros aliaque dogmata Ecclesiastica, illustrarunt. Barbola in prima Classe dictis Patrum ex consuetudine, non per se vim legis defendit. Nos melius cum Augustino Viro supra invidiam Magno, c. 3. & c. 5. Dist. 9. negamus, quæ sodes inspice, & adjunge hæc Suaresii, ex lib. 4. de legib. cap. 5. n. 6. & 7. Dicendum est, sententias seu dicta sanctorum per se & quatenus nituntur auctoritate eorum, non habere vim legis. Et ratio est, quia lex non est actus doctrinæ tantùm, sed potestatis. Sancti autem Patres non habebant potestatem hanc, neque etiam hâc intentione talia scripta tradebant. Dixi autem per se & quatenus eorum autoritate nituntur, quia interdum ipsi testificantur de præcepto vel à Christo vel ab Apostolis tradito, vel Ecclesiæ traditione introducto, & tunc ex illis colligitur præceptum tanquam ex testibus, non tanquam ab auctoribus. Unde juxta modum, quo de re aliquâ seu obligatione testificantur, & juxta majorem vel minorem consensum Sanctorum inter se, eo majorem vel minorem fidem efficiunt. Addo præterea, sententias Patrum non accipere vim legis, eò quod à Gratiano in suo Decreto inserta sint, nisi ab aliquo Pontifice fuerint canonizata, ut inter Decretales aliquando inveniuntur. Ratio est, quia nec Gratianus habuit potestatem dandi vim legum, neque Pontifex aliquis pro legibus approbavit probavit omnia, quae in illo decreto continentur, &c. Et Doctissimi Dalaei tractat. de usu & auctoritate Patrum passim, potissimum lib. 2. cap. 2. Sub ista classe continentur & conciliorum canones, quae Barbosa pro legibus habet; quasi Patres in concilio congregati habeant potestatem condendi Canonis; nos melius edocti supra num. marg. 13. Conciliis potestatem legislativam abrogavimus, declarativam adseruimus, quid nempe cum Scriptura sacra conveniat. Prima itaque quaestio in obligatione conciliorum esse debet, utrum sit conforme Sacrae Scripturae, & tum obligat, non ex auctoritate concilii, sed divina. Animadvertit id Gratianus ipse c. placuit. 36. qu. ubi recitato canone concilii Aquisgranensis, quod raptor raptam ne quidem cum voluntate Parentis ducere posset; subjungit. Haec auctoritas non praejudicat auctoritati Hieronymi, maxime cum illa testimonio divinae legis nitatur. Tandem tertio Epistolae decretales summorum Pontificum, ex hypothesi Pontificiorum, a Barbosa ob imaginariam illam summam ejus potestatem, pro legibus habentur. Quam quia negant, & solide destruunt Protestantes, concidit quoque earum auctoritas. Neque majorem in sua dioecesi suburbicaria olim habuit ille auctoritatem, quam quilibet
units.tr: Barbosa, in the first class, defends the sayings of the Fathers as having the force of law by custom, not in themselves. We, following more wisely Augustine, a man above envy, c. 3. & c. 5. Dist. 9. deny this. Please look it up, and add this from Suárez, ex lib. 4. de legib. cap. 5. n. 6. & 7. It must be said that the opinions or sayings of the saints, considered in themselves and so far as they rest on their authority, do not have the force of law. The reason is that law is not an act of teaching only, but of power, and the holy Fathers did not have this power, nor did they hand down such writings with this intention. I say "in themselves and so far as they rest on their authority", because sometimes they bear witness to a precept either delivered by Christ or the apostles, or introduced by the tradition of the Church; and then the precept is gathered from them as from witnesses, not as from authors. Hence, according to the manner in which they bear witness to some matter or obligation, and according to the greater or lesser agreement of the saints among themselves, they produce greater or lesser credibility. I add further that the sayings of the Fathers do not acquire the force of law because Gratian inserted them in his Decree, unless they have been made canonical by some Pontiff, as they are sometimes found among the Decretals. The reason is that Gratian did not have the power to give the force of law, and no Pontiff approved them as laws (he "approved all that is contained in that decree", etc.). See also the most learned Dalaeus, tractat. de usu & auctoritate Patrum passim, especially lib. 2. cap. 2. Under this class are also included the canons of councils, which Barbosa holds to be laws, as if the Fathers gathered in council had the power of enacting canons. We, better taught, have above, num. marg. 13. denied to councils the power of legislation and asserted only a declaratory power, namely of showing what agrees with Holy Scripture. The first question, therefore, in the obligation of councils must be whether a decision conforms to Holy Scripture, and then it binds not by the authority of the council but by the divine authority. Gratian himself noticed this, c. placuit. 36. qu. where, after reciting a canon of the council of Aachen, that a ravisher could not even marry the woman he had ravished against the will of her parents, he adds: This authority does not prejudice the authority of Jerome, especially since that one rests on the testimony of the divine law. Finally, in the third place, the decretal letters of the supreme Pontiffs are held as laws by Barbosa, on the hypothesis of the Papists, on account of that imaginary supreme power of theirs. Since Protestants deny this and solidly overthrow it, their authority also falls. Nor did that man in his suburbicarian diocese once have greater authority than any other bishop has in his own.

units.la: {y} Ioan. 3. libet alius Episcopus in sua. Ut vera sit hic Augustini assertio, libr. 2. de Baptismo contr. Donatist. cap. 3. quam refert Gratian. c. quis nesciat. dist. 9. Quis nesciat sanctam scripturam canonicam tam veteris, quam novi testamenti certis suis terminis contineri, eamque omnibus posterioribus Episcoporum litteris ita praeponi, ut de illa omnino dubitari, & disceptari non possit, utrum verum, vel utrum rectum sit quidquid in ea scriptum esse constiterit? Episcoporum autem literas, quae post confirmatum canonem vel scriptae sunt, vel scribuntur, & per sermonem forte sapientiorem cujuslibet in ea re peritioris, & per aliorum Episcoporum graviorem auctoritatem, doctioremque prudentiam, & per concilia licere reprehendi, si quid in eis forte veritate deviatum est? Vid. & Caspar. Ziegleri disert. de Jur. Canon. origine. sect. 44. & anteced.
units.tr: {y} Ioan. 3. Thus Augustine's assertion is true, lib. 2. de Baptismo contr. Donatist. cap. 3. which Gratian cites, c. quis nesciat. dist. 9. "Who does not know that holy canonical Scripture, both of the Old and of the New Testament, is contained within its own fixed limits, and that it is placed above all the later letters of bishops, so that it is altogether beyond doubt and dispute whether what is written there is true or right? But the letters of bishops, which have been or are written after the canon was confirmed, may be criticized, through a wiser speech of anyone more skilled in the matter, through the weightier authority and more learned prudence of other bishops, and through councils, if perhaps something in them has strayed from the truth." See also Caspar Ziegler, disert. de Jur. Canon. origine, sect. 44. & anteced.

units.la: Secundo occurrunt ipsius Gratiani verba, quibus solet connectere capitula & canones; item ordiri distinctiones suas & quaestiones, easque distinguere in partes; conciliare discordantes canones. De hisce Barbosa sic judicat. Auctoritas Gratiani compilatoris hujus voluminis à nullo Pontifice reperitur approbata, nec est authentica. Nihil itaque tribuit Gratiano Barbosa, cum inter Patres eum numerare potuisset, & eandem ei tribuere auctoritatem. Sed hoc forte facere noluit, quia cum Bernardo fere Patres exspirarunt, & sequentes scriptores vix inter Patres numerentur, quanquam & ipse Gratianus cum Bernardo Abbate Claravallensi, qui A. D. 1153. obiit, vixerit. Non tamen in Album Sanctorum relatus est, ut Bernardus, quod ei auctoritatem patris conciliasse videtur. Quidquid sit, ex hypothesi Pontificiorum majorem Gratiano auctoritatem deferre debuisset Barbosa, maxime cum opus ejus publice in Scholis prælegatur, & à Pontificibus publice prælegendum sit datum. Plus ei adhuc defert Casp. Ziegler. in d. dissertat. sect. 45. Non rejicimus testimonium Gratiani historicum, quatenus facit ad cognitionem doctrinæ eo tempore publice in Ecclesia traditæ; verosimile enim est, eum bene novisse, quid sua ætate in capitibus fidei & disciplina morum statuerit Ecclesia, & hinc non privatam, sed publicam retulisse de rebus religionis sententiam. Paucissima tamen sunt, quæ Gratianus de suo addidit, ut verum sit Petri Gallesii judicium apud Ant. Augusti. lib. 1. dialog. 1. pag 9. Non is sum, inquit, qui operæ pretium esse existimem, tam multa de solo Gratiano dici. Hic enim, ut nosti, & ut facile omnes concedunt, compilator insignis, nihil fere habet valde utile, quod proprium dicere possis : sed cornicula illi similis, ut est in fabulis, risum scientibus, admirationem ignorantibus movet. Si verba consideres, nihil illo tritius; si artem requiras, & ordinem docendi, frustra laborabis. Ita multa refert alieno loco ponenda, ita pro certis incerta constituit; ut malis illa eadem in ipsis libris non solum conciliorum, sed etiam Burchardi, & Ivonis, & aliorum collectorum requiretis. Itaque dum tu quid apud Gratianum mutandum sit, dices, in veteri me confirmabis opinione, qui frustra hunc scriptorem mendis purgari putem.
units.tr: Second, there come the words of Gratian himself, by which he is accustomed to link chapters and canons, to begin his distinctions and questions, to divide them into parts, and to reconcile conflicting canons. Barbosa judges thus about these: The authority of Gratian, the compiler of this volume, is found approved by no Pontiff, and it is not authentic. Barbosa therefore grants Gratian nothing, although he could have counted him among the Fathers and given him the same authority. But perhaps he was unwilling to do this, because the Fathers almost expired with Bernard, and the later writers are hardly numbered among the Fathers, although Gratian himself lived in the time of Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, who died in A.D. 1153. Yet he has not been enrolled in the list of saints as Bernard was, which seems to have won him the title of Father. Whatever the case, on the hypothesis of the Papists Barbosa ought to have granted Gratian greater authority, especially since his work is publicly read aloud in the schools and has been given to be publicly read by the Pontiffs. Caspar Ziegler grants him even more, in the same dissertation, sect. 45: "We do not reject Gratian's testimony as a historian, insofar as it serves to know the doctrine publicly delivered in the Church at that time; for it is likely that he knew well what the Church in his age decided concerning the articles of faith and the discipline of morals, and so he reported not a private but a public opinion about matters of religion." Yet very few things are those which Gratian added of his own, so that the judgment of Pierre Gallesius, reported by Antonio Agustín, lib. 1. dialog. 1. pag. 9. is true: "I am not of the sort who think it worth the trouble to say so much about Gratian alone. For he, as you know, and as everyone easily grants, is a distinguished compiler who has almost nothing very useful that you could call his own; but like the jackdaw in the fable, he raises laughter among those who know and wonder among those who do not. If you consider the words, nothing is more worn out; if you seek the art and the order of teaching, you will labour in vain. He reports many things that ought to be placed elsewhere, and he sets up as certain what is uncertain; so that you will find those same things in the books not only of councils but also of Burchard, Ivo and other collectors. Therefore, when you say what needs changing in Gratian, you will confirm me in the old opinion that I think it useless to cleanse this writer of his faults."

units.la: Ad tertiam speciem transeo, ad Paleas, quae in Opere Gratiani occurrunt. Hic variae Doctorum sententiae, opiniones, aut potius conjecturae occurrunt, quare ita inscriptae sint. Quatuor diversas recenset Guido Pancirollus, de claris leg. interpret. lib. 3. cap. 2. Cum vero Gratianus, librum Eugenio III. Pontifici offerendum Romam detulisset, Cardinali cuidam viro alioqui erudito, sed ambitioso, cujus opera ad Pontificem introduci volebat, legendum tradidisse fertur. Ille alienam laudem in se transferre cupiens, volumini quaedam à Gratiano omissa inseruit, seque operis auctorem esse jactitabat. Monachus, hominis fraude intellecta, additiones illas paleas esse respondit, quae grano alibi condito inanes reddebantur; Paleam enim veteres Theologi literam frustra... itu carentem, vel sterile opus vocabant. Theoph. in Naum Prophet. cap. 3. Itaque capita illa postea semper pro paleis sunt inscripta. Cæpo. in d. tract. Alij palcas ab eodem Cardinali Pocapalea nuncupato, quo nomine etiam hodie oppidum in Subalpinis, & familia vocatur, dictas fuisse censent. Nonnulli à Palea Gratiani discipulo, Imol. in R. de verbo oblig. sub n. 5. qui diversas ejus libri inscriptiones quandoque etiam improbatas fecit, Specul. in tit. de disput. & allegat. §. ult. in sin. Cæpo. in d. tract. n. 14. Præpos. Alex. in præm. decret. Jas. in rub. de actio n. 12. paleas nominatas fuisse autumant. Nec desunt, qui hac fabulosa existimantes, Decreta, quædam novissimè adjecta, velut suspecta, & fide carentia, paleas appellatas fuisse credant, opus, quod Patrum, Pontificumque Decretis scateat, Decretum inscriptum fuit. Huic posteriori sententiæ videtur accedere Jacob. Cujacius ad cap. 1. x. de despons. Imp. qui tamen & suam quintam sententiam adjicit. Palea nomine quidam significari putant, quod cassum est, & irritum, ut cassa palearum dixit Solinus in India. Itaque Paleam dici per contemptum canonem nullius fidei vel auctoritatis, ut apud Joannem Cremonensem ad Abbatem Ursperjensem Imperator Fridericus, qui Alexandro III. valde infensus erat post Alexandriam conditam in Liguria de nomine
units.tr: I pass to the third kind, to the Paleae, which occur in Gratian's work. Here various opinions of the teachers, or rather conjectures, occur as to why they are so entitled. Guido Pancirollus, de claris leg. interpret. lib. 3. cap. 2. lists four different accounts. When Gratian had brought his book to Rome to offer to Pope Eugenius III, he is said to have handed it to a certain cardinal, a man otherwise learned but ambitious, through whom he wished to be introduced to the Pontiff. That man, wishing to transfer another's praise to himself, inserted into the volume some things that Gratian had omitted, and boasted that he was the author of the work. A monk, having perceived the man's fraud, replied that those additions were chaff, which become empty when grain is stored elsewhere; for the ancient theologians called a piece of writing without letters, or a barren work, "chaff" in vain. Theoph. in Naum Prophet. cap. 3. Therefore those chapters were afterwards always entitled "Paleae". Cæpo. in d. tract. Others think they were called paleae from the same cardinal, named Pocapalea, which name even today is also the name of a town and family in the Subalpine region. Some think they were called paleae from Gratian's disciple Palea, Imol. in R. de verbo oblig. sub n. 5. who sometimes made various inscriptions of that book, even disapproved ones; Specul. in tit. de disput. & allegat. §. ult. in sin. Cæpo. in d. tract. n. 14. Præpos. Alex. in præm. decret. Jas. in rub. de actio n. 12. they affirm. Nor are there lacking those who, thinking this a fable, believe that certain decrees added very late were called paleae, as suspect and lacking trustworthiness, and that the work, which abounds in decrees of the Fathers and Pontiffs, was entitled the Decree. Jacob Cujacius seems to favour this later opinion, ad cap. 1. x. de despons. Imp. although he also adds his own fifth opinion: "Some think that the name palea signifies what is empty and void, as Solinus said of the empty husks of chaff in India. Thus Palea is said, by way of contempt, to be a canon of no faith or authority, as the Emperor Frederick, who was very hostile to Alexander III, called that Palea by the name of Alexander III, after Alexandria was founded in Liguria, as if it were made of empty chaff, of straw, as Joannes Cremonensis reports to the abbot of Ursperg."

units.la: Note: the scan is faint in places; words such as "palcas" and "Ursperjensem" may be misprinted in the original and are copied as seen. nomine Alexandri III. eam Paleam vocat, quasi factam ex cassis palearum, ex stramine. Equidem verius puto, hoc nomen praeponi antiquioribus canonibus & decretis, & scribi debere cum diphthongo Palaea, quia & in Basilicis saepe video παλαιὸν nominari simpliciter antiquum Interpretem, & ita hanc constitutionem cum sit Hormisda, qui ex antiquioribus Pontificibus est, recte Palaeam appellari. Refert hanc eandem sententiam posteriorem Cujacii Ant. Contius, ad c. 2. dist. 5. Sed suam sextam conjecturam addit. Cur hoc, inquit, & pleraque capita sic inscribuntur, saepe etiam inter doctos dubitari animadverti. Qui rectius sentire & sapere existimantur, quasi παλαιὸν i. e. antiqua vocitata volunt. Ego autem paleam inscribi hoc caput existimo, & catera similia, quia additicia sunt, nec a Gratiano primitus huic libro inserta, sed ab interpretibus, prout cuique commodum videbatur, ad marginem Gratiani adscripta, & plerumque in emendationibus & antiquioribus exemplaribus prorsus omissa. Cui rei fidem facit antiquum Gratiani exemplar, quo in hoc emendando usus sum, in quo pleraque ejusdem paleae desunt. Plerasque fere sententias recensent, & tandem quid ex collatione Manuscriptorum observaverint, addunt, Emendatores Romani, in Praefatione Gratiani ad Lect. De nomine Palea sunt variae doctorum hominum hominum sententiæ. Multi ea capita, in quibus res inanes ac leves continerentur, hoc nomine appellari censuerunt: alii quasi τὰ παλαιὰ, id est, antiqua: alii quasi additiones quasdam, derivata aut potius depravata voce ab adverbio πάλιν, id est, rursum, quo scriptores etiam Latini tempore Gratiani uterentur. Verum Joannes Andreæ in additionibus ad Speculatorem, titulo de Disputationibus & Allegationibus prope finem (quem Imola in Rubrica de verborum obligationibus, Alexandrinus in proœmio Decretalium, Jason in Rubrica titulo de Actionibus, & alii sunt secuti) putat, quendam Protopaleam, quem Jason addit Cardinalem fuisse, collectioni Gratiani capita hæc adjunxisse. Atque ut in re tam incerta aliquid elici conjectura possit, exponetur, quid in collatis exemplaribus observatum fuerit. In tribus, quæ sunt antiquissima, & videntur scripta paulo post Gratiani ætatem, paucissima ex hujusmodi capitibus habentur. In uno valde emendato sunt apposita in margine sine ulla nota, sed non omnia quæ in impressis: quamvis vicissim in illo additiones aliquæ sint, quæ in his non habentur. In alio litteris perantiquis descripto Palea ipsa recentiori scriptura toti voluminì præponuntur. In cæteris habentur aut omnes, aut pleraque: & partim quidem cum palea nomine, partim verò sine ullo à cæteris capitibus discrimine. Ex qua observatione illud videtur posse colligi, ligi, has paleas esse additiones non eodem tempore factas ad primam collectionem Gratiani, in margine primum adscriptas, ac nonnullas fortasse ab ipsomet Gratiano (ut fit) inter componendum, aut relegendum: quas deinde librariorum quidam omiserint, quidam in contextu posuerint, interdum conjunctè cum prioribus capitibus, interdum cum aliquo discrimine. Falsam verò esse illorum opinionem, qui eas contemnendas putant, ex eo constat, quòd multa & in Decretalibus, & apud vetustiores Gratiani collectores habentur: quod suis locis indicabitur. Septima sententia est eorum quos refert Hilliger. Donelli Enucleati lib. 26. cap. 2. lit. A. pag. mihi 1394. & seqq. cum Gratianus librum suum Eugenio III. Pontifici obtulisset recognoscendum, hanc vocem Palea adscriptam esse. Papam enim veluti asterisco notasse, quæ nulla auctoritate valitura, ut sicuti Paleæ ad grana vilia sunt, ita capita ista omni pondere carere innueret. Gibbert. Reg. I. Enantiop. 25. Octava sententia est, Curtii de feud. quæst. 1. Quatenus, inquit, ratione non juvantur dicta Gratiani, dicuntur Paleæ. Quæ omnes meræ sunt conjecturæ, ut cuique liberum sit accedere, quæ ei maxime probabilis videtur. De Auctoritate eorum constans est fere omnium sententia, non multum iis deferendum esse, nec esse integræ auctori-
units.tr: the name of Alexander III, and calls it Palea, as though it were made of the chaff of straw. I myself think it more likely that this name was given to the older canons and decrees, and that it should be written with the diphthong as Palaea, because in the Basilica I often see the old interpreter simply called παλαιὸν [old]; and so, since this constitution is by Hormisdas, who is among the older Popes, it is rightly called Palaea. Antonius Contius, on c. 2. dist. 5, reports this same opinion as the later one of Cujacius. But he adds his own sixth conjecture: Why this chapter, he says, and most others, are so headed, I have noticed is often doubted even among learned men. Those who are thought to judge and understand more correctly want them called παλαιὸν, that is, antiqua. I, however, think this chapter and others like it are headed Palea because they are additions, not inserted into this book by Gratian at the start, but written in the margin of Gratian by copyists, as seemed suitable to each, and for the most part omitted altogether in the corrected and older copies. The old copy of Gratian which I used in correcting this work bears witness to this, for most of these paleae are missing from it. They list almost all the opinions, and finally add what the Roman correctors observed from comparing the manuscripts. In the preface of Gratian to the reader, on the name Palea, there are various opinions of learned men. Many thought those chapters, which contain empty and trivial matters, were called by this name; others, as if τὰ παλαιὰ, that is, antiqua; others, as if they were certain additions, the word derived or rather corrupted from the adverb πάλιν, that is, again, which Latin writers also used in Gratian's time. But John Andreae, in his additions to the Speculator, under the title on disputations and allegations near the end (which Imola, under the rubric on the obligations of words, Alexandrinus in the preface to the Decretals, Jason under the rubric of the title on actions, and others have followed), thinks that a certain Protopalea, whom Jason adds was a cardinal, attached these chapters to Gratian's collection. And so that something might be drawn by conjecture in so uncertain a matter, let it be set out what was observed in the copies that were compared. In three, which are the most ancient and seem to have been written shortly after Gratian's time, very few of this kind of chapter are found. In one, much corrected, they are placed in the margin without any mark, but not all of those that are in the printed editions; although conversely that copy contains some additions which are not found in these. In another, written in very ancient letters, the Palea itself is placed before the whole volume in a more recent hand. In the rest all, or most, are found, partly with the name Palea, partly without any distinction from the other chapters. From this observation it seems possible to conclude that these paleae are additions not made at the same time to Gratian's first collection, first written in the margin, and some perhaps by Gratian himself (as happens) while composing or rereading it; these some of the copyists then omitted, some put into the text, sometimes together with the earlier chapters, sometimes with some distinction. That the opinion of those who think they should be despised is false is clear from the fact that many of them are found both in the Decretals and in the older collectors of Gratian; this will be indicated in their places. The seventh opinion is that of those whom Hilliger cites from Donellus, Enucleati lib. 26. cap. 2. lit. A, p. 1394 and following, in my edition, that when Gratian offered his book to Pope Eugenius III for review, this word Palea was written against it. For the Pope, they say, marked it as with an asterisk, to signify that these things would have no force of authority, and that just as chaff is to worthless grain, so these chapters lack all weight. Gibbert, Reg. I, Enantiop. 25. The eighth opinion is that of Curtius, de feud. quaest. 1: Insofar as Gratian's sayings are not supported by reason, they are called Paleae. All these are mere conjectures, so that each may freely adopt whichever seems to him most probable. Concerning their authority, there is almost universal agreement that they are not to be relied on much, and do not have full authority.

units.la: 315. Cujus sint auctoritatis. Correctores Romani, ut jam relatum non contemnendas censent, quia multæ in Decretalibus & vetustioribus collectionibus sint. Ad quæ regerit. Alber. Gentil. de libr. Juris Canonici cap. 2. prope sin. Verum & aliud est contemni, aliud non allegari pro authenticis; Illa, c. 14 dist. 96. qua tribuit Constantinus magna omnia Romano Pontifici, licet sit palea, & pro palea inferatur, multum tamen tritici attulit Ecclesiæ, ut de Imola relatum aliquando legi. Rubr. de verb. ob. Alciat. 12. part. 3. hæc habet. Constat consensu omnium, ea quibus talis est inscriptio, certæ fidei non esse, neque ceu authentica allegari posse. Paria fere habet Arthur. Duck de Auctor. jur. lib. 1. cap. 7. sect. 3. Sunt in decreto, quæ Palæ dicuntur, nullamque juris auctoritatem habent, sive fuerint ipsius Gratiani sive alterius, de quibus varia tradunt interpretes. Felinus in cap. ex part. de rescript. Curt. de feud. qu. 1. Marant. p. 3. n. 31. Alciat. 12. parerg. c. 3. Mart. de jurisd. p. 1. c. 30. Easque paulatim irrepsisse in codicem Decreti, & paucissimas in libris antiquioribus reperiri. Et de iis est hæc adsertio Alber. Gentilis in differt. de libr. jur. canon. cap. 2. in sin. Verum est crevisse palea cum Gratiani collectione. Etiam in Gratiani libris omnibus non eadem sunt; pauciores in vetustioribus sunt. Hujus autem Palæ qui discipulus fuit fuit Gratiani. Speculator de disp. ubi Joh. Andr. Imol. d. rat. de V.O. Coep. de lib. jur. can. Alb. l. 1. c. de fi. do. de. Alc. l. 1. si cert. pet. Si rubrica decreti sunt, sive ipsiusmet Gratiani, non obligant: etsi perfectam habeant orationem: quae & falsae aliquando sunt, neque Pontificum, neque conciliorum sunt. Adi ad Coepollam, qui habet rationes plures; Ad Alciatum qui negat, quod & alii faciunt, Gratiani. Et sic quoque de paleis, quae in Decreto. Nam quae sunt in Decretalibus, ea vim habeat legis. Ex quibus & aliis pluribus, quae adduci possent, patet; neminem Paleis multum detulisse, sed nomini parem virtutem apud omnes fere retinuisse.
units.tr: 315. Of what authority they are. The Roman correctors, as already reported, think they are not to be despised, since many are found in the Decretals and in the older collections. To this Albericus Gentilis replies, de libris juris canonici, cap. 2, near the end: But it is one thing to be despised, another not to be cited as authentic. That chapter, c. 14 dist. 96, in which Constantine ascribed all great things to the Roman Pontiff, although it is a palea and is brought in as a palea, has nonetheless brought much wheat to the Church, as was once read reported of Imola. Rubric de verb. ob. Alciatus, 12, part. 3, has this: It is agreed by the consensus of all that those things which bear such a heading are not of certain faith, nor can they be cited as authentic. Arthur Duck, de auctoritate juris, lib. 1, cap. 7, sect. 3, has almost the same: There are in the Decretum things which are called paleae, and they have no authority in law, whether they were by Gratian himself or by another; of these the interpreters hand down various accounts. Felinus, in cap. ex parte, de rescriptis. Curtius, de feud. qu. 1. Marant, p. 3, n. 31. Alciatus, 12, parerg. c. 3. Martinus, de jurisd. p. 1, c. 30: and that they crept little by little into the body of the Decretum, and that very few are found in the older books. And this assertion of Albericus Gentilis about them, in the dissertation on the books of canon law, cap. 2, at the end: It is true that the palea grew with Gratian's collection. Even in all of Gratian's books they are not the same; there are fewer in the older ones. Whoever was the disciple of this Palea was of Gratian. The Speculator, on disputations, where John Andreae, Imola, on the rational..., Coepollas, on the books of canon law, Albertus, on the first book, title on gifts..., Alciatus, on the first book, si certum petatur. If they are rubrics of the Decretum, whether of Gratian himself, they do not bind, even if they have a complete sentence; and some of these are false, and they belong neither to the Popes nor to the councils. Consult Coepollas, who gives several reasons; Alciatus, who denies, as others also do, that they are Gratian's. And so too concerning the paleae which are in the Decretum. For those which are in the Decretals have the force of law. From these and many other things which could be adduced, it is evident that no one has set great store by the Paleae, but that almost everyone has kept them with a name equal to their force.

units.la: De legibus civilibus, quas Gratianus in Decretum suum retulit, non est opus late disquirere cujus sint auctoritatis; retinuerunt ea suam vim in decreto, quam habuerunt à Majestate Imperatoria extra decretum. Quanquam Barbosa iis deneget vim juris Canonici, nisi sint per canonem approbatae. Fecit hoc ut recentiori Pontificiorum sententiae inserviret, quae Papam & leges Papales supra Imperatorem & omnes ejus leges, contra scitum Apostoli Rom. 13. 1. effert; secus quam olim factum est. Sed haec alterius loci sunt.
units.tr: As for the civil laws which Gratian brought into his Decretum, there is no need to enquire at length whose authority they have; they retained in the Decretum the force they had from the imperial majesty outside it. Although Barbosa denies that they have the force of canon law unless they have been approved by a canon. He did this to serve the more recent opinion of the Papists, which raises the Pope and papal laws above the Emperor and all his laws, contrary to the saying of the Apostle, Rom. 13. 1; otherwise than was once done. But these matters belong to another place.

units.la: Hisce quatuor adde multa falsa, spuria, confecta, conficta, aliis supposita, quæ Gratianus si-ne ullo judicio in suum opus corrasit; veluti supposititias illas Epistolas Pseudo-Isidori Mercatoris, quas integras fere descripsit: item Pseudepigrapha quæ affinxit primis urbis Episcopis, quorum omnium accuratissimum & bene longum Catalogum contexuit Doctiss: Blondellus cap. 18. infine fere. Pseudo-Isidori vapulantis, quem vide. Quæ cujus auctoritatis sint, jam satis supra disquisitum est in Pseudo-Isidori collectione.
units.tr: To these four add many false, spurious, forged, fabricated and falsely attributed things, which Gratian without any judgment gathered into his work: such as those spurious Epistles of Pseudo-Isidore Mercator, which he copied almost entire; likewise the pseudepigrapha which he attached to the first bishops of the city, of all which the most accurate and fairly long catalogue has been compiled by the most learned Blondel, chap. 18, near the end. Pseudo-Isidore under attack, which see. What authority these have has already been sufficiently examined above in the discussion of the Pseudo-Isidorian collection.

units.la: Judicia de Gratiano sunt varia. Quidam laudant, quidam taxant & vituperant, quidam ferunt & tolerant. Passim in eum insurgit Anton. Augustin. in libris de ejus Emendatione, qui aliquando totum opus una litura delatum cuperet; aliquando iterum paucis excusat. Vehementer insurgit Ant. Contius lect. cap. 10. ubi errorum monstra quædam, ut vocat, recenset. Alii vero excusant, alii laudant; Apologeticum ei scripsit ex professo Joh. Chifletius JC. Vesontinus, in Apologetica dissertat. de utriusque jur. Architect. cap. V. Sed qui satis exilis est; In Gratianum debachatur Johannes Molynæus, quem supra Decretum Ivonis edidisse diximus; contra eum amarissime insurgit Boëthius Epo, de jur. facr. qui Gratianum defendit, & Molynæum prævaricatorem vocat in suâ professione. Ut Ivonis decretum quod ediderat extolleret, dicit, Gratiani depressisse. Longa nimis sunt ipsa judicia, quam ut hic inseri possint. Unum atque alterum subjicio. Nobilissimus Mornæus in Mysterio iniqui-tatis, pag. mihi 285 edit. Gorichem. de Gra-tiano hoc habet. Per idem etiam tempus, Gra-tianus Decretum consarcinat, non fœlicius quam Pandectas Justinianus; ex Canonibus & Decre-tis antiquis, quæ quidem ipse pluribus locis ad temporis corruptelam accommodat, Romanæ ambitioni præsertim servire cogit: quamquam multa nobis vestigia relinquit, quorum ope, antiquam Ecclesiæ & doctrinam & praxim investi-gare sedulò quærentibus datur. Aventinus sanè antiquitatis studiosissimus nobis author, ante Gratianum Jus Canonicum longe diversum fuisse: Etenim, inquit, uti est in nostris Bibliothecis sincerum, duas continet partes, prima, Acta sunt universorum Conciliorum, quæ quidem recepta esse constat; altera, Constitutiones, Epistolas, Rescripta maximorum Pontificum complectitur, ut quæque gesta fuere: causæ, adsessores, testes, ad-ductis locorum temporumque momentis, commemorantur. Quod utinam ab hoc labore abstinuisset; & hoc interim Eugenius approbat, & in omnibus universitatibus legi jubet, haud dubiè. Dubiè quia sub unius Pontificis jugum universam Ecclesiam redigebat; Bernardi Consiliorum in libris de considerationibus quàm parum memor. Eadem methodus Petri Lombardi, (Is Gratiani frater) in 4. Sententiarum libris, quas ex Patrum locis hinc inde collectis, in certum ordinem compingit, quos & ipse immutato, omisso, addito interdum aliquo verbo, scenæ servire cogit, ad corruptam ævi sui Theologiam inflectit; ut deinceps unus Gratianus consulatur, unus in scholis prælegatur Lombardus; In his tota seu Jurisprudentia, seu Theologia Christiana posita sit; fontem repetere in sacris veteris & novi Testamenti scripturis, in Patrum adeo monumentis antiquiorumve Conciliorum actis, nemo deinde curet; penitius rem introspicere hæresis censeatur.
units.tr: Judgements on Gratian vary. Some praise him, some criticise and denounce him, and some put up with him and tolerate him. Antonius Augustinus attacks him throughout his books on the emendation of Gratian, at one point wishing the whole work struck out with a single stroke of the pen, and at another point excusing it again in a few words. Antonius Contius attacks him vehemently in his Lectiones, chapter 10, where he lists what he calls monstrous errors. Others excuse him, and others praise him: Johannes Chifletius, a jurist of Besançon, wrote an apology for him expressly, in his Apologetic dissertation on the architect of both laws, chapter 5. But since that is rather slight, Johannes Molinaeus, whom we said above edited the Decretum of Ivo, rages against Gratian. Boëthius Epo, in De iure sacro, attacks him bitterly, defends Gratian, and in his profession calls Molinaeus a prevaricator. He says that in order to extol the Decretum of Ivo, which he had published, Molinaeus has depressed that of Gratian. The judgements themselves are too long to be inserted here, so I add one or two. The most noble Mornaeus, in Mysterium iniquitatis, p. 285 of the Gorinchem edition, has this on Gratian: About the same time Gratian patched together the Decretum, not more happily than Justinian his Pandects, out of ancient canons and decrees, which he himself adapts in many places to the corruption of the age, forcing them above all to serve Roman ambition. Yet he leaves us many traces, by whose help those who diligently seek to investigate the ancient doctrine and practice of the Church are given the means. Aventinus, certainly a most diligent author on antiquity, says that before Gratian the canon law was quite different: For, he says, as there is in our libraries a pure copy, it contains two parts. The first is the Acts of all the councils, which are known to have been received. The second contains the constitutions, letters and rescripts of the greatest popes, as each was done; the causes, assessors and witnesses are recorded, with the circumstances of place and time added. Would that he had abstained from this labour! Meanwhile Eugenius approves it and undoubtedly orders it to be read in all universities. Undoubtedly, because he was reducing the whole Church under the yoke of one pontiff, and how little mindful he was of Bernard's Consilia in the books De consideratione. The same method is used by Peter Lombard (Gratian's brother) in the four books of the Sentences, which he packs into a fixed order from passages of the Fathers gathered here and there. He too, changing, omitting, and sometimes adding a word, forces them to serve his scheme and bends them to the corrupt theology of his age. So henceforth only Gratian is consulted and only Lombard is lectured on in the schools. In these two is placed the whole of Christian jurisprudence or theology. Then no one troubles to seek the source in the sacred writings of the Old and New Testament, or in the monuments of the Fathers or the acts of the older councils; to look into the matter more deeply is judged heresy.

units.la: Huic subjicio judicium Magni Erasmi in libro singulari antibarbarorum. Gratianus de quibusdam quæstionibus in utramque partem disputat, & quidem pari copià, parique facundia: quod idem olim Gorgiam, & Carneadem fecisse legimus. Lectori autem, ubi jam longâ lectione cerebrum vertigine rotari, & caligare acies cœperit, non multò certior surgit, quàm Demipho ille Terentianus, qui ex tribus advocatis consultis, cùm unus suasisset, alter negasset, tertius deliberandum censuisset; Fecistis, inquit, probè, incertior sum nunc multò, quam dudum. Et Hotomanni in Bruto fulmine Sixti V. ti V. Et tamen execrata illa Papæ Symmachi blasphemia paulò post in c. multi. Chrysostomi verbis coarguitur. Ex quo, & sexcentis aliis Gratianici decreti locis, de illius libri stultitiâ existimari potest. Vide alia apud Sleidan. lib. 3. de quat. summ. Imp. Adde sis Flaccium Illyricum in Catalogo test. veritat. pag. mihi 630. & seq. editionis novæ Francofurtensis anni 1666. in antiq. vero p. 704. Ubi Gratianum inter quatuor Satanæ Apostolos collocat. Anton. Augustin. de emend. Grat. lib. 2. dial. 17. Stupidum hominem fuisse dicit, multisque in rebus nihil vidisse; Adde quæso integrum locum.
units.tr: To this I add the judgement of the great Erasmus, in his single book Against the Barbarians: Gratian disputes some questions on both sides, and with equal fullness and equal eloquence; which we read that Gorgias and Carneades once did too. But the reader, when after a long reading his brain begins to spin and his sight to dim, rises no more certain than that Demipho in Terence, who, having consulted three advocates, one of whom advised one thing, another denied it, and a third thought the matter should be deliberated on: "You have done well," he says, "but I am now much more uncertain than before." And Hotman's Brutum fulmen against Sixtus V: And yet that cursed blasphemy of Pope Symmachus is refuted shortly afterwards by the words of Chrysostom in chapter "multi". From this, and from countless other passages of the Gratianic decretal, the folly of that book may be judged. See other things in Sleidan, book 3, On the Four Chief Empires. Please add Flacius Illyricus, in the Catalogue of Witnesses to the Truth, p. 630 and following of the new Frankfurt edition of 1666, and in the ancient one p. 704, where he places Gratian among the four apostles of Satan. Antonius Augustinus, On the emendation of Gratian, book 2, dialogue 17, says: he was a stupid man and in many things saw nothing. Please add the whole passage.

units.la: Non tamen meo judicio integrum opus Gratiani penitus abolendum aut omni utilitate carere censeo. Sunt in eo multa quæ historiam, ut supra dictum, ejus & anteriorum temporum juvant. Sunt multa quæ erroribus Pontificiorum contraria sunt, & multa ipsam Pontificis Majestatem oppugnant, & convellunt, etiamsi contra intentionem forte scribentis, qui in promovenda Monarchia Pontificia multum momenti attulit; Quod solide & accurate demonstravit Magnus JurisConsultus Innocentius Gentiletus Delphinas, in Apologia pro Ecclesiis Reformatis. In qua controversias quæ inter Protestantes & Pontificios agitari solent, lent, solidissimè & feliciter satis decidit. Specimen hujus rei quoque edidit ex Johanne Hallero, Alstedius Encyclop. lib. 25. Theol. sect. 4. cap. 4. ubi ideam exhibet symphoniæ Catholicæ Juris Canonici seu Decreti Gratiani, cum scripturis Canonicis in xxxv. capitibus religionis majoris ponderis. Quæ sola ratio Studiosos, interque eos etiam potissimum Theologos excitare debet ad studium Juris Canonici, ex quo, tanquam armamentario arma sufficienter contra adversarios promere, eosque proprio gladio conficere possunt. Hæc causa est, quare sæpe vapulet Gratianus apud Theologos Pontificios. Videatur Baron. ad Ann. 774. S. 4. & 964. S. 4. Huc facit Delrii testimonium; Neminem, ait, qui jus Ecclesiasticum vel à limine salutavit, ignorare posse multa in Decreto haberi, quæ postea Decretalibus, Sexto, Clementinis & Extravagantibus abrogata fuerunt; nonnullaque à Gratiano per errorem inserta esse quæ cum veritate pugnare deprehenduntur. Neque minus Apostasiæ, sordium, absurditatum multarum ex decreto convinci potest Ecclesia Romana. Specimina vide c. dilectiss. 12. q. 1. ubi communio inducitur omnium rerum, etiam ex republica Platonica, conjugum. c. is qui. & cap. Christiano dist. 34. concubinatus permittitur.
units.tr: In my judgement, however, Gratian's work as a whole should not be wholly abolished, nor do I think it lacks all use. There are in it many things that help the history of his own and earlier times, as I have said above. There are many things that are contrary to the errors of the Papists, and many that attack and overturn the very majesty of the Pope, even if they were perhaps contrary to the intention of the author, who contributed much to advancing the papal monarchy. This was solidly and accurately demonstrated by the great jurist Innocentius Gentiletus of Dauphiné, in his Apology for the Reformed Churches, in which he decided, very solidly and quite successfully, the controversies that are usually debated between Protestants and Papists. Alsted also published a sample of this from Johannes Hallerus, Encyclopaedia, book 25, Theology, section 4, chapter 4, where he sets out the idea of a Catholic harmony between the canon law, or the Decretum of Gratian, and the canonical Scriptures, in thirty-five chapters of the greater points of religion. This alone should stir students, and above all theologians among them, to the study of canon law, from which, as from an armoury, they can sufficiently draw weapons against their adversaries and strike them down with their own sword. This is the reason why Gratian is so often attacked by Papist theologians. See Baronius at the year 774, §4, and at 964, §4. To this point is the testimony of Delrio: No one, he says, who has greeted canon law even from the threshold, can be ignorant that much is found in the Decretum which was afterwards abrogated by the Decretals, the Sixth Book, the Clementines and the Extravagants, and that some things were inserted by Gratian through error which are found to conflict with the truth. Nor can the Roman Church be convicted of apostasy, filth and many absurdities from the decretal less than this. See examples in c. dilectissimis, C. 12, q. 1, where a community of all things is introduced, even of wives, as in Plato's republic. c. is qui and c. Christiano, dist. 34, permit concubinage.

units.la: Sed vocat nos tempus, ut, ipsum Gratiani opus aggrediamur. Dispescuit hoc in partes tres, prima continet distinctiones centum & unam; secunda habet causas triginta sex, & quaelibet causa suas varias quaestiones. Post quaestionis trigesimae tertiae, quaestionem tertiam, immiscetur tractatus de poenitentia, qui absolvitur septem distinctionibus. Tertia pars voluminis est de consecratione, quae absolvitur quinque distinctionibus. De duabus istis posterioribus tractationibus poenitentia nimirum & consecratione, à quibusdam dubitatum esse, an sint à Gratiano scriptae, didici ab Ant. Augustino, lib. I. de emend. Gratian. dial. 18. causa est, quia iis non satis orthodoxus videtur in duabus hisce partibus Gratianus; & magis imaginarium illud, sed utilissimum Pontificiae Monarchiae Sacramentum poenitentiae evertere quam stabilire. Ipsum Augustinum audiamus, pag. 288. sed praecedentia addi debent. B. Vis dicam, quod sentio? A. Quid est, cur opus sit, veniam petere? B. Tota haec distinctio plus nocet nobis, quam prodest. Male autem incerta sunt haec, ut quaestio tertia causae XXXIII. & postea aliae quaestiones, & causae additae. Praestitisset de poenitentiis post omnes causas ante tractatum de consecratione conscribere. A. Sunt, qui putent hos duas
units.tr: But the time calls us to take up Gratian's work itself. He divided it into three parts. The first contains one hundred and one distinctions. The second has thirty-six causes, and each cause has its various questions. After the third question of the thirty-third cause, a treatise on penance is inserted, which is completed in seven distinctions. The third part of the volume is on consecration, which is completed in five distinctions. I learned from Antonius Augustinus, book 1, On the emendation of Gratian, dialogue 18, that some have doubted whether these two latter treatises, on penance and on consecration, were written by Gratian. The reason is that Gratian seems not orthodox enough in these two parts, and rather to overturn than to establish that imaginary but most useful sacrament of penance, which serves the Papal Monarchy. Let us hear Augustinus himself, p. 288, though what precedes it must be added: B. Shall I say what I think? A. What reason is there for asking pardon? B. This whole distinction does us more harm than good. These matters are badly uncertain, like the third question of cause 33, and the later questions and added causes. It would have been better to write about penances after all the causes, before the treatise on consecration. A. There are some who think these two

units.la: 321. Dubitant quidam an de poenitentia & consecratione, sint tractatus Gratiani. duos tractatus non esse Gratiani, quamvis Gratianus ipse aliquot locis in caussis eorum faciat mentionem; & in quibusdam libris non esse distinctos capitibus separatis; numeris autem capitum certum est nullum Gratiani volumen fuisse distinctum ante Contianam editionem. C. Cur tu eos numeros non sequeris, sed aliam rationem? A. Ego numeros addidi ante eam editionem; neque divinare potui, quid in ea scripturus esset Contius. Varietatis caussa est, quod ille caput secundum appellat, quod ego primum esse puto. Principium enim quaestionis primum caput appellare nolui, quoticns verbis Gratiani constat. Est etiam alia varietatis caussa in capitibus Palea nomine adscriptis, quae ab eo nonnunquam omittuntur, aliquando numerum augent. Sed quid Romani selecti viri de hac prima distinctione statuunt? B. Haec verba in scheda inveni. Tractatus hic de poenitentia non videtur esse Gratiani, sed alicujus paulo antiquioris, & totus huc videtur translatus. deestque in exemplaribus antiquis. A. Non esse antiquioris Gratiano apparet, quia multa ex Digestis affert, & ex aliis libris juris civilis, quae omnia sunt Gratiani tempore quasi postliminio restituta. B. Nimius est in his referendis, & valde ineptus. sed alia verba referam selectorum virorum. Verbis Gratiani in extrema hac distinctione: Cui autem harum &c. hac adscribi jusbi jußerunt. Errat in hoc Gratianus. & non est dubitandum, quin peccata mortalia, quantumcumque occulta, sacerdoti secreto sint confitenda: & nullus defendit alteram opinionem, quam quisq; voluerit. Hæc ille. Non tamen ausi fuerunt Correctores illi Romani exemplaribus editis adscribere, quod duo isto tractatus non sint Gratiani; Neque ullas etiam firmas rationes adferunt, quare Gratiano abjudicandi sint, cum nullus veterum hoc faciat. Maneant itaque tantisper Gratiani, donec evidentiores rationes sint allatæ. Cui sententiæ non obscurè favet Anton. Augustinus in supra relatis; quando probat, contra quam Censores Romani notarant, non esse scriptoris antiquioris Gratiano, qui duos istos de pœnitentia & consecratione scripsit tractatus. Mihi verius videtur, si ex modo connectendi, & stylo judicium ferendum sit, cum utrumque tam in Decreto, quam in duobus illis tractatibus de pœnitentia & consecratione sit sibi simillimum, etiam utrumque esse Gratiani. Maxime cum ipse Gratianus, fatente supra Ant. Augustino, in causis faciat eorum ipse mentionem. De citationibus Decreti seu allegationibus, non opus multum dicere: tralatitium est, siquidem & minutias hasce hic memorare convenit; in prima parte allegari caput, seu canonem vel per numerum, vel per initialia verba, vel per utrumque, subjuncto distinctionis numero in quo continetur; veluti: c. sancta Romana. 3. dist. 15. Hoc in hac parte observandum, citari eam à Papiense, per tractatum ordinandorum, quem Gratianus ipse solet ita vocare à distinctione XXIII. usq; ad causam primam, teft. Alber. Gentil. de lib. jur. Can. cap. 1. pr. fere. In secunda parte Decreti, eadem ratione canon, vel per numerum vel per initialia verba vel per utrumque citatur, subsequi solet numerus, qui vel adjunctam habet C literam, vel illud cauf. vel etiam quod sæpissime fieri solet, nihil; semper autem designat ille numerus causam; hunc excipit. lit. q. vel illud. Quæst. tum subjicitur numerus; ut sciamus cujus causæ, & cujus quæstiones sit canon vel capitulum; Exemplum hujus citationis est. c. institutionis nostra 7. 25. q. 2. Vel cap. institutionis nostra. c. vel caus. 25. q. 2. Quod si in hac secunda parte occurrat canon in tractatu de pœnitentia, citatio nil differt, ab allegatione primæ partis, nisi quod addatur, illud. de pœnit. Veluti c. pœnitentiam agere 6. dist. 3. de pœnit. Pro voce pœnitentiæ in tertia parte decreti substituitur, vox, de consecratione; servata eadem ratione allegandi quæ di quæ obtinet in parte prima, ut docet hoc exemplum: c. hoc quoque statutum. 61. dist. 1. de consecrat. Præter hæc, ut omnes minutias, simul demus, observandum, occurrere in editione Decreti, notas Emendatorum Romanorum, qui jussu Gregorii XIII. superiori seculo, ut infra docebimus, decretum repurgarunt, quæ singulis capitulis solent subjici; deinde adjectas esse ab iisdem rejectiones, quibus docent, apud quos Collectores canonum anteriores, idem canon inveniatur; quæ rejectiones in editione Romana, & Corpore Juris Canonici Glossat. in margine leguntur, in aliis editionibus in finem paginæ sunt rejectæ. Ab his notis, quæ subjiciuntur canonibus, distinguenda sunt verba Gratiani, post canones itidem posita, quæ per partes, quas alii paragraphos vocant, ille distinxit; addito parti cuique numero; quas partes continuat sæpè per multa capita, donec alia quæstio aut articulus occurrat. Sunt autem in novis exemplaribus alio charactere ab ipsis canonibus distinctæ; in antiquis, quia illud artificium erat ignotum id non invenitur. Cujus rei unicum exemplum adferemus, ut sciant Studiosi, quæ sint annotationes Correctorum Romanorum; quæ sint eorum rejectiones, quæ sint partes Gratiani, & quæ sit continuatio. In causæ
units.tr: 321. Some doubt whether the treatises on repentance and on consecration are by Gratian. They hold that the two treatises are not Gratian's, although Gratian himself mentions them in several places in his causes. They also say that in some books they are not divided into separate chapters, and that it is certain that no edition of Gratian's work was numbered by chapter before the edition of Contius. C. Why do you not follow those numbers but use another system? A. I added the numbers before that edition, and I could not guess what Contius would write in it. The difference is due to this: he calls the second chapter what I think is the first. I did not want to call the opening of a question the first chapter whenever it is clearly in Gratian's words. There is also another reason for the difference: in chapters marked with the name Palea, Gratian sometimes omits the number and sometimes adds to it. But what have the selected Roman men decided about this first division? B. I found these words in a note. "This treatise on repentance does not seem to be Gratian's, but of someone a little older, and it seems to have been transferred here whole; it is missing from the old copies." A. That it is not older than Gratian is clear, because it cites much from the Digest and from other books of civil law, all of which were, as it were, restored to Gratian's time by right of return. B. He is too fond of quoting these things and very clumsy. But I will quote the other words of the selected men. On Gratian's words at the end of this division, "To which of these &c.", they say: "these words were ordered to be added." "Gratian is wrong in this, and there is no doubt that mortal sins, however hidden, must be confessed in secret to the priest; and nobody defends the other opinion, whichever anyone may prefer." So far they. Yet those Roman correctors did not dare to note in the printed copies that these two treatises are not Gratian's, nor do they bring any firm reasons why they should be taken away from Gratian, since none of the ancients does so. Let them therefore remain Gratian's until stronger reasons are brought. Antonius Augustinus, in the passage cited above, openly favours this view, since he proves, against what the Roman censors had noted, that the writer of these two treatises on repentance and consecration was not older than Gratian. It seems to me more likely, if judgment is to be made from the method of connection and from style, since each of these is most like the other both in the Decretum and in those two treatises on repentance and consecration, that both are Gratian's too. Especially since Gratian himself, as Antonius Augustinus admits above, mentions them in his causes. I need not say much about the citations or allegations of the Decretum; they are commonplace, and it is fitting to recall these small details here. In the first part, a chapter or canon is cited either by number, or by its opening words, or by both, with the number of the distinction in which it is contained added; for example: c. sancta Romana. 3. dist. 15. It must be noted here that Papias cites it under the treatise on ordinations, which Gratian himself usually so calls, from distinction 23 to the first cause; see Albericus Gentilis, de lib. jur. Can. cap. 1. pr. fere. In the second part of the Decretum, in the same way, a canon is cited by number or by opening words or both; there usually follows a number which either has the letter C attached, or the word cauf., or, most often, nothing; but that number always designates the cause, and this is followed by the letter q. or the word quaest., and then the number is added, so that we know the cause and the question to which the canon or chapter belongs. An example of this citation is: c. institutionis nostra 7. 25. q. 2. Or cap. institutionis nostra. c. or caus. 25. q. 2. If in this second part a canon occurs in the treatise on repentance, the citation differs from the allegation of the first part only in that the words de pœnit. are added. For example, c. pœnitentiam agere 6. dist. 3. de pœnit. In the third part of the Decretum, the word de consecratione is substituted for the word repentance, and the same method of allegation is kept as in the first part, as this example shows: c. hoc quoque statutum. 61. dist. 1. de consecrat. Besides these, so that we may give all the small details together, it must be observed that in the edition of the Decretum there occur notes of the Roman emendators, who, by order of Gregory XIII in the last century, as we shall show below, purged the Decretum; these are usually appended to individual chapters. Then the same men added rejections, by which they show in which earlier collections of canons the same canon is found; these rejections are read in the Roman edition and in the Glossed Corpus of Canon Law in the margin, and in other editions they are placed at the foot of the page. The words of Gratian, also placed after the canons, which he divided into parts, as others call paragraphs, must be distinguished from these notes appended to the canons; he added a number to each part, and he often continues these parts through many chapters until another question or article comes. In the newer copies they are distinguished from the canons themselves by a different type; in the old ones, because that device was unknown, they are not found. We shall give one example of this, so that students may know what the annotations of the Roman correctors are, what their rejections are, what Gratian's parts are, and what the continuation is. units.la: In causæ 16. quæst. 7. cap. 35. subjicitur hæc annotatio Correctorum, quam indicat hæc ¶ nota. In capitularibus & legibus Longobardicis, & apud Burchardum & Ivonem qui ipsi citant in Decretis Gregorij Papæ sic habetur &c. Rejectionem in illo capitulo indicat litera f. in editione vero Romana vel Corpore Glossato tantum in margine notatus numerus capitis; Rejectio autem hæc est: lib. 5. cap. 44. & in Legib. lib. 3. tit. de Episcop. & Cler. l. 44. Ans. l. 1. c. 8. Burch. l. 3. c. 41. Ivo. p. 3. c. 45. Qua indicant, illud capitulum inveniri in lib. 5. Capitularis Carol. Magni c. 44. & in lib. 3. tit. de Episcopis & Clericis legum Longobardicarum. Item apud Anselmum lib. 1. c. 8. Burchardum lib. 3. c. 41. Ivonem part. 3. c. 45.
