In sequenti porro capite 36. ejusdem causæ 16. & quæstionis 7. invenitur distinctio Gratiani, post Capitulum enim hæc leguntur. 4. pars. Vt ergo ex his auctoritatibus colligitur de manu Laicorum Ecclesiæ recipiendæ non sunt, nisi cum consensu Episcoporum; juxta illud Concilij Moguntini &c. Quæ distinctio Gratiani continuatur post caput 38. ejusdem caus. & quæst. idq; sine numero novo aut etiam nota hac ¶ cujus supra memini. Verba continuationis sunt hæc: Sicut ergo auctoritate Hieronymi decimas male possessas à Laico, Episcopo consenconsentiente licet Monachis recipere &c. Guido Pancirol. lib. 3. de Clar. leg. interp. cap. 2. in vita Gratiani, testatur, Gratiani verba, duplici cruce aut paragraphi (potius partis, ita enim appellatur, quamquam in vetustis hoc non addatur exemplaribus) charactere ab aliis esse distincta. Numeri autem & Summaria quae singulis capitulis praemittuntur, non sunt ab ipso Gratiano; quinimo longo post Gratianum demum ab Antonio Contio teste Ant. August. supra adducto, numeri sunt adjecti, ab ejus editione etiam per numeros ceperunt allegari capitula. Quando aut a quibus summaria addita sint, non satis compertum habeo. In meo exemplari Manuscripto in membranis nitidissimis & subtilissimis, decretalium cum Glossis, non invenio ulla capitulorum summaria; in antiquissimis tamen editionibus Corporis Glossati veluti ea quae Parisiis prodiit Anno 1505, inveniuntur, & quidem ut in omnibus rubro-nigris editionibus, colore rubro distincta ab ipso textu. Ab ipsis Glossatoribus non esse, probat, quod in Manuscriptis exemplaribus, saltem in meo, non inveniantur, in quo tamen Glossae habentur. Probabile est addita esse, ab iis qui additiones Glossarum scripserunt, aut qui editiones primas procurarunt, uti etiam factum in Corpore Juris Civilis; A quibus forte etiam additæ in minoribus editionibus inscriptiones Distinctionum &Quæstionum, quæ in principio cujusque. paginæ comparent,ut indicent materiam,de qua distinctio aut quæstio agit, ad exemplum rubricarum, quæ in frontispicio paginarū Corporis Juris Civilis solent præmitti, quod in Corpore Juris Canonico Glossato non est observatum, sed in eo præmitti solent principio Decreti. Finem minutiarum faciemus, si illud tantum verbo, addiderimus; quid in veterum, Alani, Vincentii &c. allegationibus capitulorum Gratiani vox SUPRA designet. Addita illa est citationibus ut indicet esse in Collectione antiquiore, quâ sunt Decretales, capitulum: earum quippe collectiones sunt recentiores Opere Gratiani; Quare in citationibus capitum Gratiani vocem supra addebant, ut indicarent esse Decretum supra Decretales; quemadmodum, in citatione Decretalium addebant vocem EXTRA; qua denotabant, capitulum esse extra Decretum Gratiani; videatur hac de re, Alber. Gentil. de libr. jur. Canon. cap. 1. item Besold. differt. de libr. jur. cap. 8. quæ præmittitur parti secundæ delibator. jur. & Matth. Stephan. in præfat. ad part. 3. de jurisdict. pag. 10. pr. Nunc ad Gratianum iterum. Quid post perfectum opus Decretorum rum Gratianus fecerit, aut quando Mor-tuus sit nec anonymus ille vitæ ejus scriptor, neque quantum scio, alii prodiderunt. Anno 1165. invenio Gratianum functum esse Legati munere pro Pontifice ad Henricum II. Regem Angliæ, in causa ejus Regis cum Thoma Episcopo Cantuariense. Ut refert Flaccius Illyric. in Catalogo test. veritat. num. 189. pag. mihi 521. edit. nova Francof. Epitaphium, quod defuncto positum est Bononiæ refert Guid. Panciroll. lib. 3. de Clar. leg. interpret. cap. 2. & Valent. Forsterus in Histor. jur. Rom. lib. 3. cap. 7.
units.tr: In cause 16, question 7, chapter 35, there is appended this note of the correctors, which is marked by this sign ¶. "In the capitularies and the Lombard laws, and in Burchard and Ivo, who themselves cite it, in the Decretals of Pope Gregory it is thus found, etc." The rejection for that chapter is indicated by the letter f; in the Roman edition, or in the Glossed Corpus, only the number of the chapter is noted in the margin. The rejection itself is this: lib. 5. cap. 44. & in Legib. lib. 3. tit. de Episcop. & Cler. l. 44. Ans. l. 1. c. 8. Burch. l. 3. c. 41. Ivo. p. 3. c. 45. By these they indicate that this chapter is found in book 5 of the Capitularies of Charlemagne, chapter 44, and in book 3, title on bishops and clergy, of the Lombard laws; likewise in Anselm, book 1, chapter 8; Burchard, book 3, chapter 41; Ivo, part 3, chapter 45. Further, in the following chapter 36 of the same cause 16 and question 7, Gratian's distinction is found, for after the chapter these words are read: "4. part. Therefore, as it is gathered from these authorities, the churches are not to be received from the hand of laymen, except with the consent of the bishops, according to that of the Council of Mainz, etc." This distinction of Gratian is continued after chapter 38 of the same cause and question, and it is continued without a new number, or even the mark ¶ that I mentioned above. The words of the continuation are these: "Therefore, as by the authority of Jerome, tithes badly possessed from a layman may be received by monks with the bishop consenting, etc." Guido Panciroli, lib. 3. de Clar. leg. interp. cap. 2, in the life of Gratian, testifies that Gratian's words are distinguished from the others by a double cross or by the mark of a paragraph (or rather a part, for so it is called, although this is not added in the old copies). The numbers and the summaries prefixed to the individual chapters are not by Gratian himself; indeed, long after Gratian, as Antonius Augustinus, cited above, testifies, the numbers were added by Antonius Contius, and from his edition chapters began to be cited by number. When and by whom the summaries were added I do not know well enough. In my manuscript copy, on very fine and thin parchment, of the Decretals with the Glosses, I find no summaries of chapters; yet in the most ancient editions of the Glossed Corpus, such as the one published at Paris in the year 1505, they are found, and indeed, as in all the red-and-black editions, they are distinguished from the text itself by red ink. That they are not from the Glossators themselves is shown by the fact that they are not found in the manuscript copies, at least in mine, although the Glosses are present there. It is probable that they were added by those who wrote the additions to the Glosses, or who prepared the first editions, as also happened in the Corpus of Civil Law. From these same men perhaps came also the titles of the distinctions and questions added in the smaller editions, which appear at the head of each page, to indicate the subject with which the distinction or question deals, after the pattern of the headings which are usually put at the front of the pages of the Corpus of Civil Law; this was not observed in the Glossed Corpus of Canon Law, but in it such headings are usually placed at the beginning of the Decretum. We shall end these small details if we add only this one word: what the word SUPRA means in the citations of Gratian's chapters by the older writers, Alanus, Vincentius and others. It was added to the citations to show that the chapter is in an older collection, namely the Decretals, for their collections are more recent than Gratian's work. Therefore, in citing chapters of Gratian they added the word supra, to indicate that the Decretum is supra the Decretals; just as in citing the Decretals they added the word EXTRA, which denoted that the chapter is extra the Decretum of Gratian. On this matter see Albericus Gentilis, de libr. jur. Canon. cap. 1.; likewise Besold, differt. de libr. jur. cap. 8., which is prefixed to the second part of the Delibator. jur.; and Matthaeus Stephanus, in praefat. ad part. 3. de jurisdict., p. 10 at the beginning. Now back to Gratian. What Gratian did after the completion of the work of the Decretum, or when he died, neither that anonymous writer of his life nor, so far as I know, anyone else has recorded. I find that in the year 1165 Gratian discharged the office of legate for the Pope to Henry II, King of England, in that king's dispute with Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, as Flacius Illyricus reports in his Catalogue of the Witnesses of the Truth, no. 189, p. 521 of my new Frankfurt edition. The epitaph placed on his tomb at Bologna is reported by Guido Panciroli, lib. 3. de Clar. leg. interpret. cap. 2., and by Valentin Forster in Histor. jur. Rom. lib. 3. cap. 7.

units.la: GRATIANI CLUSINI CÆSAREI JURIS ET PONTIFICII ENUCLEATORIS PROPE DIVINI, QUI MONACHUS IN MAR- TYRUM FELICIS ET NABORIS ÆDIS ABSOLUTISSIMUM IBIDEM OPUS DE- CRETORUM ANNO GRATIÆ MCLI. COMPILAVIT, SEPULCHRUM QUOD ILLIC CURIÆ RUDERIBUS ABSOR- PTUM, HIC MAGNIFICENTIUS RENOVATUM, JO. FRANCISCUS ALDRO- ANDUS BONON. IIII. DICTATOR ÆRE PUBLICO INSTAURAVIT. ANNO SALUTIS MCCCCXCVIII. IDIB. JUNII JOANNE BENTIVO- LO II. P.P. REMP. FELICITER GUBERNANTE.
units.tr: Epitaph of Gratianus of Chiusi, Caesarean doctor of law and almost divine expounder of the Pontifical law, who at the monastery of Saints Felix and Nabor in that place compiled his most complete work, the Decretum, in the year of grace 1150. This tomb, swallowed up by the ruins of the court there, was restored more magnificently here by Giovanni Francesco Aldrovandi, Bolognese, Dictator for the fourth time, at public expense, in the year of salvation 1498, on the Ides of June, while Giovanni Bentivoglio was happily governing the republic as Protector of the People.
329. Epitaph.

units.la: Id hic præterire non possum Albericum in Chron. nondum edito referente Chiffletio de Architect. jur. c. 5. §. 4. ex Gratiano facere Cardinalem. Cujus hæc sunt ad annū MCXLVI; quæ eo libentius addo, quia novum nobis juris Architectum, Canonum compilatorem hactenus ignotum, proferunt; Item, inquit, in eodem anno, id est, Imper. Friderici quinto, quidam Magister egregius Omnibonus nomine librum de concordantia discordantium canonum diligentissime ordinavit in duas partes, primam partem in XVI. distinctiones; secundam in causas XXXVII. per quæstiones diversas satis artificiose positas. Et hic liber à nomine Auctoris, Omnebonum appellatur. Et hunc secutus est tempore Alexandri Papæ Gratianus Cardinalis, qui multa addidit, ita quod de XVI. distinctionibus centum distinctiones fecit & per ipsum ista doctrina facta est magis authentica. Qua de re accipe quoque judicium Chiffletii. Tametsi, inquit, nullum honorem esse putem qui in Gratianum (ita Chiffletius debuit inservire rei præsenti, Apologiam enim scribebat Gratiano) collatus, non sit ei qui contulerit magnum judicii laudem allaturus; hunc tamen illi adferrere non ausim, quod fraudi fuisse videatur Alberico nominum similitudo. Alexander enim Papa III. Pisanum quendam, cui Gratiano nomen fuit, ex Subdiacono & scriptore Apostolicæ Cardinalem creavit, & suorum omnium consilio–rum participem atque adjutorem esse voluit Anno salutis MCLXXVII. Unde forte orta Alberici opinio in eam historiæ speciem coaluit, quam bona fide literis consignavit. Verior est Magistri titulus, qui passim Gratiano tribuitur, vide sis Gloss. in cap. 2. dist. 68. Qui ista ætate Doctorem vel juris interpretem donabat. Sic quoque Tancredus Glossator, Magister appellatur. Vid. Gud. Panciroll. de Clar. leg. interp. lib. 3. c. 4. Alber. Gentil. de libr. Jur. Canon. cap. 2. pag. 21. Postquam Opus Gratiani editum & Scholis ad prælegendum & explicandum traditum esset, jam statim accesserunt Glossographi, qui notas & explicationes ad Decretum scriberent; Quorum Primi memorantur Laurentius Patria Cremensis. Abbas in c. cum Johannes. num. 13. de fide instrum. Vincentius Castellionus Mediolanensis Summus Canonista, Abbas cap. si quis contra sub. n. 13. de for. compet. & Bernardi Bottoni Præceptor, quem tamen Oldradus in consil. 69. in sin. Hispanum fuisse adfirmat. Item Hugutio, vel ut alii Hugo Vercellis, quæ ejus patria fuit, postea Ferrariæ Episcopus, de quo quædam etiam habet Anton. Augustin. libr. 2. dial. 9. pag. 448. & seqq. Præterea Joh. Semeca Teutonicus, qui an-teriorum teriorum Glossas reformavit, & paucis additis, suas fecit. Fuit Azonis discipulus, Gloss. in c. quando. dist. 86. Cum diu juri operam dedisset, Prædicatorum, ut vocant, Monasterium ingressus est, Alberic. in dict. proem. in sin. Postea initio seculi XIII. præpositus S. Stephani Halberstadensis factus, otium nactus Decretum interpretari coepit. Cumque Clemens IV. decimas per Germaniam & Gallias ad Palæstinæ loca redimenda exigeret, Johannes Semeca concilium appellavit; qua re Pontificis diras meruit, & ab officio remotionem. Controversia paulo post utriusq; morte sopita est. Vid. Crantz. de reb. Saxon. lib. 8. c. 27. Compositit quoque Semeca Summam seu Compendium Confessionis, quod primum inter breviaria locum obtinet; & ubi summa non alio adjecto citatur, hujus opus indicatur. Alberic. in Proem. dict. in sin. Decessit anno 1269. De illo insuper judicium est Pancirolli, de clar. leg. interpret. lib. 3. cap. 6. Johannes Semeca etsi quandoque ineptis, ut illa aetas ferebat vocibus utitur, non modicam tamen Operi Gratiani lucem adfert; pleraque novi & veteris testamenti loca erudite explicat. Eum, ut patet ex dictis, Albert. Crantzius d. l. & ex eo Henric. Pantal. de Viris illustr. German. part. 2. pag. 238. forte & Freherus in Chronolog. Chronolog. quam Juri Græco Romano præ[?] misit, (qui & hunc errorem cumulat, quod Semecam ponat in annum 1272, cum jam ultra triennium mortuus esset) male primum vocant decreti Glossatorem. Crantzii locū referт Amicus noster summus Nobil: & Consultiss: D. Vincentius Placcius Jurisc. Hamburgensis, in Syntagmate operoso, de scriptis & Scriptoribus Anonymis & Pseudonymis, (in quo utinam festinantia & lucri præpostera cupido Typographi, ut mihi Nobilis: Auctor conquestus est, nobis non invidisset doctam de tota ἀνωνύμως & ψεδονύμως scribendi ratione, præfationem & in posterioribus Pseudonymis detectis prolixiores excursus) cap. 3. de Anonymis detectis. num. 128. pag. 36. Ante eum enim, jam supra relati Glossas ad Decretum scripserant & publicaverant, de quibus vid. Panciroll. de clar. leg. interpret. lib. 3. capp. 3. & 4. Anton. Florentin. part. 3. specul. pr. & tit. 18. c. 6. sin. primas defert Hugutioni in scribendis Glossis, cujus Gloriam Johannes Semeca postea in se derivavit & obfuscavit. Vitam ejus inter JurisConsultos Germanos recitat Melchior Adami: Hujus Glossis quædam adjecit Bartholomæus Brixrensis, Vincentii Castellionei discipulus anno MCCLVI; sedente Alexandro IV. Papa. In quibus errata rata Semecæ notavit, omissa supplevit, & quæ postea immutata sunt, adjecit; vide ipsum in Decreti initio. Hic & temporum historiam scripsit, teste Caccialup. de modo studend. Raph. Volaterran. lib. XXI. Antro-pag. Vossio de histor. Latin. libr. 2. cap. 57. Quæstiones diebus Dominicis & Veneris à se disputatas, collegit, easque Dominicales Venerialesque appellavit, imitatus Pileum qui Sabbatinas vocavit, quæ Sabbati die disputaverat. Ab Alexandro IV. Papa, teste Platina, non contemnenda munera retulit: Patriarchæ Venetiarum seu Gradensi quandoque adsedit. Joh. de Turrecremat. in c. Episcopus non flagitetur II. q. I. vide sis Panciroll. d. l. cap. 7. quid præter enumerata scripserit, habes apud Simlerum in Bibliotheca. Sed ad Collectores nostros revertendum est: si tamen commodo hoc loco præmisero quædam de Glossis, (quæ vox Consultis & Studiosis juris in frequenti usu est) à quibus scribendis, Glossographi & Glossatores dicti sunt; Glossa vel Glossema: Græcis vocabatur vox, quæ in communi usu & consuetudine non erat, sed alicui genti propria, ideoque non à singulis intelligebatur, quæ quoad communem linguā ξενικὴ, seu peregrina, vocabatur. Exemplo id illustrat Aristoteles de Arte Poët. ubi σίγυνον,
units.tr: I cannot pass over here that Alberic, in his Chronicle (not yet published), as Chifflet reports in de Architect. jur. c. 5. §. 4., makes Gratian a cardinal. His words for the year 1146 are these, which I add all the more willingly because they present us with a builder of the law and a compiler of the canons hitherto unknown: Item, he says, in the same year, that is, the fifth year of the Emperor Frederick, a certain excellent master named Omnibonus drew up with the greatest care a book on the agreement of discordant canons, arranged in two parts: the first part into sixteen distinctions, the second into thirty-seven causes, set out with various questions quite skilfully. And this book is called Omnebonum after the author's name. And following him in the time of Pope Alexander came Gratian the Cardinal, who added much, so that from the sixteen distinctions he made one hundred distinctions, and through him this doctrine was made more authoritative. On this matter take also the judgment of Chifflet. Although, he says, I think there is no honour conferred on Gratian (Chifflet had to serve the present purpose in this way, for he was writing an apology for Gratian) which will not bring great praise of judgment to the one who conferred it; yet I would not venture to attribute this to him, since the similarity of names seems to have been a trap for Alberic. For Pope Alexander III created a certain Pisan, whose name was Gratian, from subdeacon and papal secretary into a cardinal, and wished him to be a sharer and helper in all his counsels, in the year of salvation 1177. From this, perhaps, arose Alberic's opinion, which took shape in that kind of historical account which he set down in writing in good faith. More accurate is the title of Master, which is given to Gratian everywhere; see the Gloss. on c. 2, dist. 68, which in that age gave the title of Doctor or interpreter of the law. So too Tancred the glossator is called Master. See Guido Panciroli, de Clar. leg. interp. lib. 3. c. 4., and Alberico Gentili, de libr. Jur. Canon. cap. 2. p. 21. After Gratian's work was published and handed over to the schools for reading and explanation, glossographers came forward at once, who wrote notes and explanations on the Decretum. The first of these to be recorded are Lawrence of Cremona, abbot, on c. cum Johannes, n. 13, de fide instrum.; Vincent of Castiglione, of Milan, a leading canonist, abbot, on c. si quis contra, sub n. 13, de for. compet.; and the teacher of Bernard Botone, whom Oldradus, however, in consil. 69 at the end, affirms to have been a Spaniard. Likewise Hugutio, or as others call him Hugo of Vercelli, which was his homeland, later bishop of Ferrara, about whom Antonio Agustin also says some things, lib. 2. dial. 9, p. 448 and following. Besides these there is John Semeca, a German, who reformed the glosses of his predecessors and, adding a few things, made them his own. He was a pupil of Azo, Gloss. on c. quando, dist. 86. After he had devoted himself for a long time to the law, he entered the monastery of the so-called Preachers, Alberic in the said proem, at the end. Later, at the beginning of the thirteenth century, made provost of Saint Stephen's at Halberstadt, he found leisure and began to interpret the Decretum. When Clement IV was collecting tithes throughout Germany and France to redeem the places of Palestine, John Semeca appealed to a council; for this he incurred the curses of the Pope and removal from office. The controversy was settled soon after by the death of both. See Crantz, de reb. Saxon. lib. 8. c. 27. Semeca also composed the Summa or Compendium of Confession, which holds first place among the handbooks; and where the Summa is cited without any other addition, this work is meant. Alberic in the Proem to the said work, at the end. He died in the year 1269. Panciroli gives this judgment on him, de clar. leg. interpret. lib. 3. cap. 6.: John Semeca, although sometimes he uses clumsy terms, as that age tolerated, nonetheless sheds no small light on Gratian's work; he explains many passages of the Old and New Testament learnedly. As is clear from what has been said, Albert Crantz l.c., and from him Henry Pantaleon, de Viris illustr. German. part. 2, p. 238, perhaps also Freher in the Chronology which he prefixed to the Greco-Roman law, (who also compounds this error by placing Semeca in the year 1272, when he had already been dead for more than three years) wrongly call him the first glossator of the Decretum. The passage of Crantz is cited by our friend, the most noble and most learned Vincent Placcius, jurist of Hamburg, in his laborious Syntagma de scriptis & Scriptoribus Anonymis & Pseudonymis. (In that work, I wish that the haste and the headlong greed for gain of the printer, as the noble author complained to me, had not deprived us of a learned preface on the whole method of writing anonymously and pseudonymously, and of fuller digressions on the Pseudonyms discovered later.) chap. 3, on the Anonymous discovered, n. 128, p. 36. For before him, those already mentioned had written and published glosses on the Decretum, concerning whom see Panciroli, de clar. leg. interpret. lib. 3, chapters 3 and 4. Antonio of Florence, part 3, Speculum praes. and tit. 18, c. 6, at the end, attributes the first place in writing glosses to Hugutio, whose glory John Semeca later took to himself and obscured. Melchior Adam recounts the life of this man among the German jurists. Some additions to his glosses were made by Bartholomew of Brescia, a pupil of Vincent of Castiglione, in the year 1256, while Alexander IV was pope. In these he noted the errors of Semeca, supplied what had been omitted, and added what was afterwards changed; see him at the beginning of the Decretum. He also wrote a history of the times, according to Caccialupi, de modo studend., Raphael Volaterranus, lib. XXI Antroph., and Vossius, de histor. Latin. lib. 2. cap. 57. He collected the questions which he disputed on Sundays and Fridays, and called them Dominicales and Venerales, imitating Pileus, who called the questions he had disputed on Saturdays Sabbatinae. According to Platina, he received no contemptible gifts from Pope Alexander IV. He sometimes sat as assessor to the Patriarch of Venice or of Grado. John of Turrecremata, on c. Episcopus non flagitetur, II, q. 1; see Panciroli, d. l. cap. 7. For what he wrote besides those listed, you have it in Simler's Bibliotheca. But we must return to our compilers. If, however, I may here set out in advance some things about the glosses (a word in frequent use among lawyers and students of law), from whose writing the glossographers and glossators got their name: a gloss or glossema was called by the Greeks a word which was not in common use or custom, but peculiar to some people, and therefore was not understood by everyone; in relation to the common language it was called foreign [ξενικὴ], or strange. Aristotle illustrates this by an example in the De Arte Poëtica, where he says that sigynon,

units.la: 335. Glossographi unde. Glossæ quid. σίγυνον[?], vocem, quæ Cypriis propria, & jaculi genus erat, suis dicit γλῶτταν esse, & Eustathius Iliad. Homer. Glossam interpretatur ἀποξενιωμένων Ἀλέκτων[?], Clemens Alexand. I. Strom. ἀποξενιλήπτως τὰς βαρβάρων φωνὰς, quas non dialectos, sed Glossas dici oportere censet, quod Dialecti dictiones sunt proprium & peculiare loci cujusdam characterem, designantes, vel vocabula proprium & commune gentis alicujus idioma significantia, ut quinque Græcorum præcipue Attica, Ionica, Dorica, Æolia, communis. Quod in Barbarorum linguis reperiri nequit, quas vere dicere possit πεώτας καὶ ἡωικὰς Ἀλεκτυς[?]. vide Philip. Jac. Maussacum in disiert. critica de Harpocratione, quam ejus dictionario à se illustrato subjunxit pag. 347, ubi pag. seq. subjungit. Glossa igitur barbara & externa vocabula sunt quæ nemo interpretatur, γλῶσῃ λαλῶν I. Cor. 14. 2. non tantum simpliciter lingua loquens, ut vulgo vertunt, sed barbare loquens & per Glossas, quas nemo percipiat, propter ignorationem ἀγνωσίας τῆς Φωνῆς, unde apposite Divinus Apostolus exclamat διόπερ ὁ λαλῶν γλώσσῃ προσευχέσθω ἵνα διερμηνεύῃ ν. 13. Qui Barbare loquitur, non lingua, oret ut intelligi possit; nisi enim barbare & per Glossas loqueretur ad quid orare deberet ex Apostoli præcepto, ut ejus verba percipi & in& intelligi possent? qui lingua loquitur, dum modo non barbare loquatur intelligi potest, ergo frustra oraret ut intelligeretur, si, ut vulgares interpretationes habent, verba illa λαλῶν γλώσσῃ interpretemur lingua loquens nude & simpliciter. Hæc Maussacus, qui quanquam non adsecutus sit mentem Divi Pauli; totus enim contextus flagitat, ut λαλῶν γλώσσῃ interpretemur de iis, qui Spiritus Sancti dono peculiari peregrinis linguis loquuntur: tamen ingeniose facit Paulum inservire hypothesi suæ. Utrumque, γλωσσημα & γλῶσσα occurrit apud Quintilianum, lib. I. cap. I. in fine fere, ubi Glossas vocat, interpretationes linguæ secretioris. Illud, inquit, non pœnitebit curasse, cum scribere nomina puer, cœperit, ne hanc operam in vocabulis vulgaribus & forte occurrentibus perdat, protinus enim potest interpretationem linguæ secretioris, quas Græci γλῶσσας vocant, dum aliud agitur edissere. Et iterum lib. I. c. 8. Circa Glossemata etiam, id est voces, minus usitatas non ultima ejus professionis est diligentia. Latius adhuc Glossas extendit Galenus, qui voces peregrinas, & obsoletas inter Glossas recenset, item Pollux, lib. 2. c. 4. qui & poëticas voces in hunc censum refert. Utrique occurrit Doctiss: Henric. Stephan. In Palaest. de latinit. Lipsii, pag. 43. Glossa & Glossemata, inquit, nominantur.
units.tr: 335. Glossographers, whence. What glosses are. Sigynon [?], a word peculiar to the Cypriots and a kind of javelin, he says is a glotta to his own people. And Eustathius, on Homer's Iliad, interprets a gloss as the foreign words of the estranged [ἀποξενιωμένων] Alektes [?]. Clement of Alexandria, Strom. I, apoxenilēptōs [ἀποξενιλήπτως], the voices of the barbarians, which he thinks should be called not dialects but glosses, because dialects are words that mark the proper and peculiar character of some place, or words signifying the proper and common idiom of some people, such as the five principal Greek dialects, Attic, Ionic, Doric, Aeolic, and common. This cannot be found in the languages of the barbarians, which one could truly call foreign and strange [πεώτας καὶ ἡωικὰς Ἀλεκτυς?]. See Philip Jacob Maussac, in the critical dissertation on Harpocration, which he appended to his dictionary illustrated by himself, p. 347, where on the following page he adds: Glossa igitur barbara & externa vocabula sunt quæ nemo interpretatur. Speaking in a tongue [γλῶσσῃ λαλῶν], 1 Cor. 14:2, not merely speaking a language simply, as the common versions render it, but speaking barbarously and through glosses, which no one perceives, because of ignorance of the voice [ἀγνωσίας τῆς Φωνῆς]; whence the divine Apostle rightly exclaims: wherefore he who speaks in a tongue [διόπερ ὁ λαλῶν γλώσσῃ] let him pray that he may interpret, v. 13. He who speaks barbarously, not in a language, let him pray that he may be understood; for unless he were speaking barbarously and through glosses, to what purpose should he pray, by the Apostle's precept, that his words might be perceived and understood? He who speaks in a language can be understood, provided he does not speak barbarously; therefore he would pray in vain that he be understood, if, as the common interpretations have it, we interpret those words speaking in a tongue as speaking a language bare and simple. So Maussac. Although he did not grasp the mind of the Divine Paul, for the whole context demands that speaking in a tongue be interpreted of those who, by the peculiar gift of the Holy Spirit, speak in foreign languages, yet he cleverly makes Paul serve his own hypothesis. Both glossema and glossa occur in Quintilian, lib. I, cap. 1, near the end, where he calls glosses interpretations of a more recondite language. That, he says, one will not regret having attended to, when the boy has begun to write names, lest he waste this effort on common and chance-occurring words; for straightaway he can explain the interpretation of the more recondite language, which the Greeks call glossae, while something else is being discussed. And again, lib. I, c. 8: Concerning glosses too, that is, words less in use, is no small part of that profession's diligence. Galen extends the meaning of glosses even more widely, listing among glosses foreign and obsolete words; likewise Pollux, lib. 2, c. 4, who also counts poetic words in this class. The most learned Henry Stephanus has the same in view, In Palaest. de latinit. Lipsii, p. 43: Glossa & Glossemata, he says, are called ...

units.la: Text of the last line is partly illegible in the scan; the final word is smudged. mantur certis dialectis peculiaria, ideoque à com-muni Græca linguæ usu aliena vocabula. Unde & ξενικὰ, quasi peregrina appellabantur; Galenus ut duxi, in meo Thesauro Græcæ linguæ, γλώσσας peregrina vocabula vel obsoleta esse ait. Cui tamen de hac expositione vix assentiri possum, ut nimis restringente hujus vocabuli significationem. Verum & à Polluce dissentio, Poëtica vocabula Glossas esse nominata, scribente. Ab eo quoque dissentio, inquam, ut alteram in partem peccante, id est nominis hujus usum latius quam par sit extendente. Alioqui enim non parva Græci sermonis portio γλωσσῶν appellatione comprehendi posset. Quare autem hæc voces Glossæ vocatæ sint, conjicit. pag. 49. Sed cur ejusmodi vocabula Græci Glossas vocabant? De hac non dubito quin Græci, cum tale vocabulum aliquod quale diximus, Glossam, id est linguam vocarent ellipsi uterentur, seu ἐλλειπτικῶς loquerentur, ac perinde esset, ac si dicerent: γλῶσσα ἰδία πολιν, aut aliquid simile. Qui istiusmodi voces exponebant Glossographi, Glossatores, Glossematarii, Glossularii, dicti. ut notat Turneb. & Docte Maussacus. Laudatæ differt. crit. pag. 353. & seqq. ubi & originem & progressum multis enarrat, & scriptores ejusmodi recenset. Pertinuit harum vocum interpretatio ad Grammaticam, Varro lib. 6. de Ling. Lat. In Medo Ennius, Cœlitum camilla expectata advenis; salve hospita. Camilla qui Glossemata interpretati, dixe-runt administram. adde sis Maussacum, d. dissert. Critica, de Harpocratione. pag. 351. ubi Dorothei ex Photio & aliorum meminit. Libri, in quibus Glossæ ejusmodi seu voces propriæ quibusdam, minus vulgo intellectæ, explicabantur, Glossaria vocabantur, quæ & lexica dicta à recentioribus; sed Glossaria à lexicis tamen id differebant, quod lexica quascunque: Glossaria, tantum certum genus vocum continuerint; vide sis latissime Maussacum d. l. pag. 363. & seqq. Postea Glossæ & Glossemata sunt translata, ut non voces ipsas, sed vocum expositiones iis denotarentur; appositè iterum Stephanus. d. l. pag. 50. Sed unde factum esse putas ut Glossa quod de vocabulo peregrino & plerisque incognito, ideoque egente expositione, dicebatur, à posteris latinis, de ipsa expositione dictum sit? Hunc abusum inde natum esse puto, quod Glossographi, iis, quas afferebant, Glossis expositiones adjungerent. Ideoque perinde esse ac si remedii cuipiam mali ipsius appellatio tribueretur. Probat hoc satis locus Quintiliani lib. 1. cap. 1. supra relatus. & Doctiss: Maussacus d. l. qui Glossas vocum Barbararum, & quarumcunq; externarum ἑρμηνίσεις dicit fuisse vid. eum pluribus pag. 352. Concludit tandem pag. 353.
units.tr: …are peculiar to certain dialects, and therefore words foreign to the common usage of the Greek language. Hence they were also called xenika [ξενικὰ], as if to say "foreign words." Galen, as I have said, in my Thesaurus of the Greek Language, says that glossai [γλώσσας] are foreign or obsolete words. Yet I can hardly agree with this explanation, since it restricts the meaning of the term too narrowly. Nor do I agree with Pollux, who writes that poetic words are called Glosses. I disagree with him too, I say, because he errs in the other direction, extending the use of this term more widely than is right. Otherwise a not small part of the Greek language could be included under the name glossai [γλωσσῶν]. As to why these words were called Glosses, he conjectures (p. 49): But why did the Greeks call such words Glosses? On this I have no doubt that when the Greeks used a word of the kind I mentioned, they called it glossa [γλῶσσα], that is, "tongue," by ellipsis, or spoke elliptically, so that it was the same as if they said glossa idia polin [γλῶσσα ἰδία πολιν], "a tongue peculiar to the city," or something similar. Those who explained such words were called Glossographers, Glossators, Glossematarians, Glossularians, as Turnebus and the very learned Maussacus note (in the cited Differtatio critica, pp. 353 ff.), where he also describes the origin and development of the matter at length and lists writers of this kind. The interpretation of these words belonged to grammar, as Varro says (Book 6 of On the Latin Language). In his Medea, Ennius wrote: "Camilla, the long-awaited handmaid of the gods, welcome, guest." Those who interpreted the Glossemata said camilla means "attendant." You may also consult Maussacus, in the same dissertation, on Harpocration, p. 351, where he mentions Dorotheus from Photius and others. Books in which Glosses of this kind, that is, proper words unclear to most people, were explained were called Glossaria, and by more recent writers lexica. But glossaria differed from lexica* in this respect: lexica contained any words whatever, whereas glossaria contained only a certain kind of word. See Maussacus at length in the same place, pp. 363 ff. Later, glossae and glossemata were transferred so as to denote not the words themselves but their explanations; Stephanus again makes the point aptly (in the same place, p. 50): But how do you think it came about that what was said of a foreign word, and of one largely unknown and therefore needing explanation, was later said of the explanation itself? I think this abuse arose because the Glossographers added explanations to the Glosses they cited. So it is as if the name of the remedy were given to the evil itself. The passage of Quintilian in Book 1, chapter 1, cited above, proves this well enough, and the very learned Maussacus (in the same place) says that the Glosses of barbarian words and of all foreign words were hermeneiai [ἑρμηνίσεις]; see him at more length on p. 352. He finally concludes on p. 353:

units.la: 353. Glossas Barbarorum primo, deinde peregrinorum omnium, sensui vero obscurorum & non usitatorum vocabulorum interpretationes fuisse. Appositè Doctiss: Casaubonus ad Athenæum lib. 3. c. 6. in fine. ubi hoc firmat, & de antiquis Glossarum Scriptoribus multa habet, quæ tamen Maussacus d. l. accuratius & prolixius exequitur. Verba Casauboni sunt hæc: Cydonia mala etiam κοδύμαλα fuisse olim vocata, probatur auctoritate Hermonis, qui Glossas Κρηπικὰς conscripserat. Non sunt ferendi qui Glossas κελπικὰς, id est, judiciarias, ut vertunt, sunt commenti, prorsus ἀκεῖτως. Olim docti multi Glossas, id est, obscurarum vocum interpretationes, & ut nunc vocant Λεξικὰ ediderant. Nam γλῶσσαν & γλώσσημα nuncapabant vocabulum vulgo incognitum: vel quia peregrinum & barbarum, vel quia jam obsoletum, & oblivioni traditum. Est enim & verborum quidam interitus. Vide illud sapientissimi Imperatoris, M. Antonini Philosophi, lib. 4. αἱ πάλαι σωνήδεις, λέξεις, γλωσσήματα νῦν. ὅτως ἂν καὶ τὰ ὀνόματα τῶν πάλαι πολυμνήτων, νῦν τόπον πινὰ γλωσσήματι ἐσίν. Auctores antiqui Glossarum celebrantur, Amerias, Seleucus, Pamphilus, Nicander Colophonius, Philetas, Philemon Timachidas, Hermonax, alii. Sed fuêre qui unius tantùm gentis vocabula suscipèrent interpretanda: ω ut Philemon, cujus [?]Ἀττικὴ λέξεις, & Aristophannes, cujus Glossæ Laconicæ non multo ante laudabantur. Similiter Hermonax Cretica dialecti tantum voces complexus opere suo, titulum ei fecerat, [?]Γλῶσσαι Κρητικῶν, cujus libri aliquoties meminit Athenæus. Ulterius etiam prolati termini Glossarum cum primo designarentur voces Dialectis peculiares, earumque expositiones, tandem quælibet explicatio verborum & rerum cœpit Glossa dici; & ita Glossæ juris, Glossæ bibliorum natæ sunt; quanquam vetus dictionarium, inter commetum & Glossam distinguat. Glosa, (de qua Scriptura vid. Spigelium ad Prudentium pag. 215. edit. Weitzii) inquit, dicitur à Glossa quod est lingua, & distat inter commentum Glosam & translationem. Commentum expositio est, verborum juncturam non considerans, sed tantum sensum, deservit enim expositioni alicujus libri, & non constructioni litera. Accipitur tamen quoque commentum largius, scilicet pro quolibet libro, studio vel doctrina & tunc sic definitur. Commentum est plurium studio vel doctrina in mente habitorum in unum collectio. Glosa est expositio literæ & ipsius sententiæ, quæ non solam sententiam, sed etiam verba attendit. Vel Glosa dicitur expositio sententiæ literam continuans & exponens. Unde dicitur Glosa quasi Glossa, id est, lingua, quod tanquam tanquam lingua Doctoris adesset & exponeret; sic litera exponenda insistit & sensum enucleat. Translatio est expositio sententia per aliam linguam. Textus est liber, ipsius Doctoris continens tractatum sua litera vel sententia explicatione. His inquam non obstantibus, omnes expositiones sive verborum, sive rerum Glossarum nomine seculis Barbaris venire solebant; quod affatim ostendunt Glossæ Accursii, in jus civile, Joh. Semecæ & Barth. Brixrensis in Decretum, item Glossa ordinaria in Biblia. Plura qui de Glossis, & Glossographis desiderat is adeat, sæpe laudatam Maussaci Dissertat. criticam de Harpocratione, ubi multa accurate disseruit; subjunxit eam Harpocrationis Dictionario à se edito, Cœlium Rhodigin. lib. 7. c. 27. & lib. 13. cap. 4. Joh. à Woueren de Polymat. cap. 9.
units.tr: "Glosses were at first explanations of barbarian words, and then of all foreign words, and of words that were obscure in sense and not in common use." The very learned Casaubon also makes the point aptly in his note on Athenaeus, Book 3, chapter 6, near the end, where he confirms this and has much about the ancient writers of Glosses, which Maussacus, in the same place, treats more accurately and at greater length. Casaubon's words are these: That quinces were also formerly called kodymala [κοδύμαλα] is proved by the authority of Hermon, who had written Glosses Krepika [Κρηπικὰς]. Those who have invented the view that the Glosses were kelpika [κελπικὰς], that is, "judicial," as they translate it, are simply wrong [ἀκεῖτως]. Formerly many learned men published Glosses, that is, explanations of obscure words, which they now call lexika [Λεξικὰ]. For they called a word unknown to the common people glossan [γλῶσσαν] and glossema [γλώσσημα], either because it was foreign and barbarous, or because it was already obsolete and forgotten. For there is also a certain death of words. See that saying of the most wise Emperor, the philosopher Marcus Antoninus, Book 4: "The old words are now glosses [γλωσσήματα]; so too the names of those once celebrated are now merely certain places." The ancient authors of Glosses celebrated are Amerias, Seleucus, Pamphilus, Nicander of Colophon, Philetas, Philemon, Timachidas, Hermonax, and others. But there were those who undertook to interpret only the words of a single people: thus Philemon, whose Attic words [Ἀττικὴ λέξεις], and Aristophanes, whose Laconian Glosses were praised not long before. Likewise Hermonax, who embraced only the words of the Cretan dialect in his work, gave it the title Glosses of the Cretans [Γλῶσσαι Κρητικῶν], a book which Athenaeus mentions several times. Furthermore, the terms of the Glosses were extended: when at first the words peculiar to dialects and their explanations were so designated, at last any explanation of words and things began to be called a Gloss. And so glosses on the law and glosses on the Bible arose, although an old dictionary distinguishes between a commentary and a Gloss. The dictionary (on whose wording see Spigelius on Prudentius, p. 215, Weitz's edition) says: A gloss is called so from glossa, which means "tongue," and it differs from a commentary and from a translation. A commentary is an explanation that does not consider the construction of the words but only the sense, for it serves the exposition of some book and not the construction of the letter. Yet a commentary is also taken more broadly, namely for any book produced by study or learning, and then it is defined thus: a commentary is a collection into one work of things conceived in the mind through the study or learning of many. A gloss is an explanation of the letter and of the sense itself, which attends not only to the sense but also to the words. Or a gloss is called an explanation that follows and expounds the letter of the sense. Hence it is called a gloss, as if glossa, that is, "tongue," because it stood there as the tongue of the teacher, expounding; thus it sticks to the letter to be explained and brings out the sense. A translation is an explanation of a sentence in another language. A text is a book containing the treatise of the teacher himself, explained by his own letter or sense. Notwithstanding these things, I say, all explanations, whether of words or of things, used in the barbarous centuries to come under the name of Glosses; which the Glosses of Accursius on civil law, of John Semeca and Bartholomew of Brescia on the Decretum, and likewise the Glossa ordinaria on the Bible, show abundantly. Whoever wants more on Glosses and Glossographers should consult the often-cited Maussacus, Critical Dissertation on Harpocration, where he discusses many things accurately; Caelius Rhodiginus (Book 7, chapter 27, and Book 13, chapter 4) and John à Woueren (De Polymathia, chapter 9) added it to Harpocration's dictionary which he published.

units.la: Nos ad Compilatores juris Ecclesiastici revertimur; Post Gratianum, cum tam feliciter ei labor cessisset, ad Decretales Pontificum Romanorum epistolas colligendas & digerendas certatim multi, provolarunt.
units.tr: We return to the compilers of ecclesiastical law. After Gratian, since his labour had turned out so happily, many hurried forward eagerly to collect and arrange the Decretal letters of the Roman Pontiffs.

units.la: Sunt autem Decretales Pontificum Romanorum epistolæ quibus respondent iis, qui aliqua de re consulunt; Incrementum enim Pontificis Romani, ex splendore & dominio urbis, ut supra notatum multos, qui in rebus controversis consilia petebant, ad Romanos Episcopos, excivit; qui petentibus rescribebant. Quod & alii Episcopi in Oriente & Occidente soliti facere. Sed horum, ut alibi notavi, epistolæ non tam accuratè, adservatæ sunt, quam Romanorum præsulum. Erant hæc rescripta Episcoporum, & Metropolitanorum primum tantum consilia, quæ nullam obligandi vim habebant, postea majoris cœperunt esse auctoritatis atque pretii, & inter scripta Patrum, haberi & venerari: quod tamen primum factum in fine seculi quinti, & quidem in Ecclesia Romana. Cujus rei testimonium illustre præbet Synodus Romana sub Gelasio Anno 494. Romæ habita, in qua à LXX. Episcopis inter alia decernitur.
units.tr: The Decretal letters of the Roman Pontiffs are letters that answer those who consult them on some matter. For the growth of the Roman Pontiff, from the splendour and dominion of the city, as I noted above, drew many who sought counsel in controverted matters to the Roman bishops, who replied to those who asked. Other bishops in East and West were also accustomed to do the same. But, as I have noted elsewhere, the letters of these were not preserved as carefully as those of the Roman prelates. At first these replies of bishops and metropolitans were merely counsels, having no force of obligation; afterwards they began to be of greater authority and value, and to be held and venerated among the writings of the Fathers. This, however, first happened at the end of the fifth century, and indeed in the Roman Church. A notable testimony to this is given by the Roman Synod held under Gelasius in the year 494, in which, among other things, it was decreed by seventy bishops.

units.la: Item Decretales Epistolæ, quas beatissimi Papæ diversis temporibus ab urbe Romana pro diversorum Patrum consultatione, dederunt, venerabiliter suscipienda sunt. Vid. c. sancta Romana. dist. 15. Quo decreto Patres illi auctoritatê Canonis nondum dederunt epistolis, decretalibus Paparum; verum tantum in censum eorum librorum retulerunt, qui à Christianis tuto sine periculo hæreseos aut falsi dogmatis, legi poterant, quos Ecclesiasticos libros quidam vocarunt; evincit id satis ordo & series dicti canonis, in quo hæ Decretales cretales post opuscula Patrum, quæ in ecclesia recipiuntur, ante Martyrum Monumenta, recensentur; quæ tamen nemo sanus in-ter canones retulit unquam, aut vim canonis iis adscripsit. Primus qui has collegis, est Dionysius Exiguus, seculo sexto ineunte, de quo supra multis, potissimum, n. 75. & seqq. dictum, quod à Syricio inceperit collectionem suam, quia ultra Syricium genuinas nullas invenit: quod nos supra quoque probavimus, in Isidori Mercatoris Impostoris collectione. Fuisse ante Syricium Decretales Episcoporum Romanorum, id quod ex Concilio Romano statim allatum est, assatim probat. Verum non perennarunt; saltem tempore Dionysii Exigui non extabant: sedulus enim ille ruspator harum rerum, cum singulare volumen Decretalium institueret, eas non omisisset. Inter Canones autem noluisse collocare, aut canonicam auctoritatem his tribuere Dionysium, exinde satis clarum esse potest, quod ille singulari eas volumine incluserit & à canonibus separaverit; Primus qui inter Canones iis locum dedit, est Crescònius, ut supra num. 187. observavimus. Quod tamen Orientalis Ecclesia nunquam probavit, quæ in suum Codicem Decretales Pontificum Romanorum non recipit, quod tantam in eo in eo Auctoritatem non agnosceret; illa tamen Patrum & Episcoporum Orientalium quaedam scripta suo Codici adjunxit, non tam propter Scriptorum auctoritatem quam veritatem rerum, usum & utilitatem disciplinae & controversiarum decisionem. In Occidente paulatim quaedam Decretales, prout pro diversitate Ecclesiarum & Provinciarum, utiles Ecclesiis censebant, illi, qui Ecclesiis praefecti erant, sed valde parce neque omnes in Codices Canonum particulares receptae sunt; quod supra de Codice Ecclesiae Gallicanae, & Hispanicae observavimus. Vid. num. 84. & 88. Postea collectores a temporibus Pseudo-Isidori Mercatoris, eas catervatim suis collectionibus inseruerunt, in quibus eandem cum Canonibus Conciliorum, & Patrum dictis auctoritatem habebant. Omnes, quas habere potuit, etiam spurias suae farragini inseruit Gratianus. Post eum Decretales, a canonibus coeperunt separari, & singulatim colligi. Primus qui hic operam, sed privatam, impendit est Bernardus Circa, Papiensis praepositus, postea Antistes Faventinus. Hic Pontificum Decretales & constitutiones usque ad Coelestinum tertium, cujus nullum in ejus collectione extat responsum, collegit, & sub iisdem fere titulis digessit, quibus constat
units.tr: Likewise, the Decretal Letters which the most blessed Popes at various times sent from the city of Rome in answer to the enquiries of various Fathers are to be received with reverence. See c. sancta Romana, dist. 15. By this decree those Fathers did not yet give the authority of a canon to the Papal decretal letters. They only counted them among those books which Christians could read safely, without danger of heresy or false doctrine, and which some called "ecclesiastical" books. The order and sequence of that canon shows this well enough. There these Decretals are listed after the little works of the Fathers "which are received in the Church" and before the Monuments of the Martyrs. Yet no sane person has ever placed them among the canons or ascribed to them the force of a canon. The first to gather them was Dionysius Exiguus, at the beginning of the sixth century, of whom we have spoken above in many places, especially at n. 75 and following. It was said there that he began his collection with Siricius, because beyond Siricius he found no genuine Decretals. We also proved this above, in the collection of Isidore Mercator the impostor. That there were Decretals of the Roman bishops before Siricius is shown abundantly by the Roman Council cited just above. But they did not survive; at least in the time of Dionysius Exiguus they were no longer extant. For that diligent searcher after these things, when he drew up his separate volume of Decretals, would not have omitted them. That Dionysius did not wish to place them among the canons, or to grant them canonical authority, can quite clearly be seen from the fact that he enclosed them in a separate volume and kept them apart from the canons. The first to give them a place among the canons was Cresconius, as we observed above at n. 187. Yet the Eastern Church never approved this. It does not receive the Decretals of the Roman Pontiffs into its Code, because it did not acknowledge such authority in them. Nevertheless it added to its own Code certain writings of Eastern Fathers and bishops, not so much for the authority of their writers as for the truth of the matters, the use and benefit of discipline, and the settling of controversies. In the West, certain Decretals were gradually received into particular Codes of Canons, as those who presided over the churches judged them useful to their churches, according to the diversity of churches and provinces. But they were received very sparingly, and not all of them; as we observed above concerning the Code of the Gallican and Spanish Church. See nn. 84 and 88. Afterwards, from the time of Pseudo-Isidore Mercator, collectors inserted them in droves into their collections, where they had the same authority as the canons of councils and the sayings of the Fathers. Gratian inserted into his medley all those he could obtain, even the spurious ones. After him the Decretals began to be separated from the canons and collected singly. The first to undertake this work, though as a private effort, was Bernard Circa, provost of Pavia, afterwards bishop of Faenza. He gathered the Decretals and constitutions of the Pontiffs down to Celestine III, of whom no response is found in his collection, and arranged them under nearly the same titles under which the Gregorian Collection that we use today is arranged.

units.la: Prima collectio Decretalium Bernardi Circa. constat Gregoriana Collectio qua hodie utimur. Ex Cœlestini tempore qui Anno 1191. ad sedem Romanam pervenit, de tempore quo vixerit, conjicimus; quod Doctiss: Blondellus se dicit ignorare. Leguntur in hac collectione Decretales Lucii III. Papæ, qui Anno 1181. ad Pontificatum evectus est; & aliorum usque ad jam nominatum Cœlestinum. Hujus itaque tempore oportet adhuc vixisse Bernardum Circam. Hanc primam compilationem Henricus Ostiensis, & Johannes Andreæ filius, & Ægidius Bellamera vocant; ipse Breviarium Extra vel Extravagantium. Qui Scholia scripserunt librum primum vocant. Sic etiam cæteras compilationes alii compilationem secundam, tertiam, quartam, quintam, alii librum secundum, tertium, quartum, quintum appellarunt. Edita est hæc prima collectio ab Antonio Augustino in antiquarum Decretalium Collectione, ubi primo loco habetur. Notæ autem ejus subjunguntur. Dicitur idem Bernardus sub iisdem titulis summam scripsisse, cujus initium fuit: Profectus discipuli, gloria Magistri; item Scholia & Glossulas eidem primæ collectioni adscriptas; Anton. Augustinus de quinque veterib. Collect. in præfat. præmiss. antiq. Collect. Decret, testatur se vidisse Glossu-las. las quasdam sine nomine scriptas, sed multo plures adscriptis nominibus, Vincentii, Alani, Tancredi, Laurentii, Rogerii & aliorum.
units.tr: The first collection of the Decretals of Bernard Circa is the Gregorian Collection which we use today. We conjecture the time when he lived from Celestine, who came to the Roman see in 1191, though the most learned Blondel says he does not know it. In this collection the Decretals of Lucius III, who was raised to the papacy in 1181, are read, and those of others down to the said Celestine. Therefore Bernard Circa must still have been alive at that time. Henry of Ostia, John Andreae's son, and Egidius Bellamera call this first compilation; he himself calls it Breviarium Extra vel Extravagantium. Those who wrote commentaries call it the first book, and in the same way others called the later compilations the second, third, fourth and fifth, or the second, third, fourth and fifth books. This first collection was published by Antonius Augustinus in his collection of ancient Decretals, where it stands in first place, with its notes appended. The same Bernard is said to have written a summary under the same titles, which began: The progress of the disciple, the glory of the Master. Likewise, scholia and glosses are ascribed to this first collection. Antonius Augustinus, in his preface to On the Five Older Collections, testifies that he saw some glosses written without a name, but many more with names attached: those of Vincentius, Alanus, Tancred, Laurentius, Rogerius and others.

units.la: Ordinem Compilatorum Decretalium, quia seriem temporis sectari, nobis constitutum, interrumpere cogit Theodorus Balsamon; Qui eodem fere tempore floruit quo Bernardus noster, nempe in fine seculi XII; & principio seculi XIII. Nam Anno ejus secundo antequam Constantinopolis à Latinis oppugnaretur, adhuc scripsit, sed posteriora; Fuit ille Primum Diaconus Sanctissimæ Dei Magnæ Ecclesiæ Constantinopol., Nomophylax & Chartophylax. Quis Nomophylax in Imperio Orientali fuerit, id ignoramus. Chartophylax vero erat sigilli Patriarchalis custos, quod etiam in pectore gestabat, ut alicubi noster Ballamo notat, qui, ut & Codinus eum chartis ad jura Ecclesiastica pertinentibus præfectum: deinde causarum Ecclesiasticarum judicem, matrimonialium cognitorem, Clericorum defensorum, fuisse dicunt. Duo erant. Unus Patriarchius qui Ecclesiæ Archiva servababat. Alter Oeconomæo inserviebat, & tabulas ecclesiasticorum redituum expensarumque conficiebat ac curabat. Ad priorem testimonia de-ponas ponebantur, quæ scripta de iis qui sacris initiari vellent, item hierologiæ. Dignitas ejus Maxima. In supplicatione Sanctorum Notariorum jus habebat conscendendi equi Patriarchalis, aureamque in capite tiaram quæ in Cartophylacio adservabatur, gestandi. Vide sis nostrum Balsamonem ad Photii Nomoc. tit. VIII. c. 1. habebat jura Episcopi Constantinopolitani, ut idem refert ad canonem IX. synod. 7. in sin. In congregationibus extra synodum habebat sessionem ante omnes Episcopos, ut idem refert ad conc. 1. can. 18. Plura de hac dignitate vide apud Joh. Episcop. Citri. in responf. Codinum de offic. & officiat. urbis Constant. Meursium in Glossar. Mixobarbaro voce χαρτοφυλάξ, ubi, & in voce χαρτουλάρι docet hos male confundi cum Chartulariis. Fuit praeterea Balsamo πρῶτος Βλαχερνῶν, primus Blachernorum. Extra urbem Constantinopolitanam versus Mare erat templum Blachernarum, quod apud Zonaram exstruxit Pulcheria. De Præfecto Blachernarum vid. Jul. Cæsar. Buleng. de Imper. Rom. lib. 8. cap. 100. Primus Blachernarum videtur esse, quem nunc Præpositum vocant. Postea etiam factus est Theopoleos, sive Magnæ Antiochiæ, totiusque Orientis Patriarcha. Ante autem quam Patriarcha effet,
units.tr: The order of the compilers of Decretals, which we have undertaken to follow in the sequence of time, is interrupted by Theodore Balsamon, who flourished at about the same time as our Bernard, namely at the end of the twelfth century and the beginning of the thirteenth. For in the second year before Constantinople was attacked by the Latins he was still writing, though his later works date from then. He was First Deacon of the Most Holy Great Church of God at Constantinople, Nomophylax and Chartophylax. What a Nomophylax was in the Eastern Empire we do not know. The Chartophylax [χαρτοφυλάξ] was the keeper of the patriarchal seal, which he also wore on his breast, as our Balsamon notes somewhere; as Codinus also says, he was in charge of documents pertaining to ecclesiastical law, then judge of ecclesiastical cases, examiner of matrimonial matters, and defender of the clergy. There were two of them. One was the Patriarchal Chartophylax, who kept the archives of the Church. The other served the Oeconomus and drew up and managed the registers of the Church's revenues and expenses. To the former were delivered the testimonials written about those who wished to be initiated into holy orders, likewise the hierologies. His dignity was very great. In the procession of the Holy Notaries he had the right to ride the patriarchal horse, and to wear the golden tiara which was kept in the Chartophylakion. See our Balsamon on Photius' Nomocanon, title VIII, ch. 1. He had the rights of the Bishop of Constantinople, as the same author reports on the ninth canon of the seventh synod, at the end. In assemblies outside a synod he had a seat before all the bishops, as he reports on the first council, canon 18. More on this dignity may be seen in John, Bishop of Citrus, in his responses; in Codinus, On the Offices and Officials of the City of Constantinople; and in Meursius, in his Glossarium Mixobarbarum under the word χαρτοφυλάξ [chartophylax], where also under the word χαρτουλάρι [chartoularios] he teaches that these are wrongly confused with the Chartularii. Balsamon was moreover πρῶτος Βλαχερνῶν [prōtos Blachernōn], first of the Blachernae. Outside the city of Constantinople, towards the sea, there was a temple of the Blachernae, which Pulcheria built, according to Zonaras. On the Prefect of the Blachernae see Julius Caesar Bulengerus, On the Roman Emperor, book 8, ch. 100. The First of the Blachernae seems to be the one now called the Provost. Afterwards he was also made Patriarch of Theopolis, that is, of Great Antioch and of the whole East. Before he became patriarch,
342. The First of the Blachernae.

units.la: 343. Balsamo Patriarcha Antiochiæ. set, commentarios scripsit, ut habet Inscriptio editionis Parisiensis Anni 1620. quae Balsamonis Praefationi praemissa est. Jussu Imperatoris Emanuelis Comneni, & Patriarchae Constantinopolitani Michaëlis Anchiali, ut habet operis inscriptio, composuit expositionem sacrorum & divinorum Canonum, Sanctorum & celebratissimorum Apostolorum & sanctarum Oecumenicarum synodorum, ac etiam localium ac particularium & reliquorum sanctorum Patrum, praeterea earum legum quae sita sunt in quatuordecim titulis positis in principio canonum, ut sciatur quae in usu sint, & quae non sint. vide sis ejus Praefationem, quam Commentariis suis, seu Scholiis, ut ipse vocat, praemisit. Opus hoc Graece & Latine prodiit Parisiis, anno 1620. ex interpretatione Gentiani Herveti, Galli, quae tamen in ista editione est interpolata. Latine tantum versio Gentiani in Photii Nomocanonem prodierat ex exemplari Joh. Tilii, Anno 1561, quo tempore suam quoque ejusdem Nomocanonis versionem Henricus Agylaeus Belga ex exemplari Bibliothecae Viti Amersbachii Basileae edidit; quam postea elegit Christ. Justellus, cum exemplar graecum Photii & Scholia Balsamonis Anno 1615. Parisiis ederet, & retinuerunt Justellus Filius & Voëllus in Bibliotheca Juris Pontificii, quia ftylus Agylæi juri magis accommodatus, ut illi in Præfatione teftantur, & nos fupra retulimus. Præterea fcripfit Balfamon Meditata de Patriarcharum privilegiis & Refponfiones ad Marcum Patriarcham Alexandrinum μηλέταις ἤτοι ὑποθέσεις, ut ipfe vocat, quæ exftant in tomo primo Juris Græco Romani Leunclavii à Frehero editi, lib. feptimo: ob quæ, & ob Scholia in Photium & Canones conciliorum valde invifus & exofus fuit Romanis. Hæcque caufa, quare in eum toties debachetur Baronius tom. XII. Annal. ann: 1191. §. 49. & 62. quod odio profequatur Ecclefiam Romanam. Caufam odii putat effe, quod poft captam à Latinis Conftantinopolim, acceperit illa Patriarcham Latinum. In quo fibi ipfi contradicit §. 62. ubi meditata illa feu refponfa de privilegiis Patriarcharum dicit, fcripta effe biennium ante quam Conftantinopolis caperetur. Vide fis eum & Anno §. 49, & videbis caufas averfi, ab Ecclefia Latina animi effe, cœlibatum Ecclefiæ Occidentalis in clericis, Jejunium Sabbati, Monarchiam Papæ & alia: ideoque Schifmaticum appellari paffim. Vide quoque Allatium de confenf. perpet. Eccles. Orient. & Occident. lib. 2. cap. 13. §. 4. pag. 703. Restituerunt etiam Viridoti
units.tr: 343. Balsamon, Patriarch of Antioch. he wrote commentaries, as the title of the Paris edition of 1620, prefixed to Balsamon's Preface, has it. At the command of Emperor Manuel Comnenus and of Michael Anchialus, Patriarch of Constantinople, as the title of the work has it, he composed an exposition of the sacred and divine canons, of the holy and most celebrated Apostles, of the holy Ecumenical synods, and also of the local and particular synods and of the other holy Fathers, together with those laws which are set out in fourteen titles at the beginning of the canons, so that it may be known which are in use and which are not. See his Preface, which he placed before his commentaries, or Scholia, as he calls them. This work appeared at Paris in 1620, in Greek and Latin, from the translation of Gentian Hervet, a Frenchman; in that edition, however, the translation is interpolated. Only the Latin version of Gentian to Photius' Nomocanon had appeared before, from the copy of John Tilius, in 1561. At that time Henry Agylaeus, a Belgian, also published his own version of the same Nomocanon from a copy in the library of Vitus Amersbach at Basel. Christian Justel afterwards chose this version when in 1615 he published at Paris the Greek text of Photius and the Scholia of Balsamon. Justel's son and Voëllus retained it in the Bibliotheca Juris Pontificii, because the style of Agylaeus is better suited to law, as they attest in their Preface, and as we related above. Balsamon also wrote Meditations on the privileges of the Patriarchs, and Responses to Marcus, Patriarch of Alexandria, under the title μελέταις ἤτοι ὑποθέσεις [meletais ētoi hypotheseis], that is, meditations or hypotheses, as he himself calls them. These are extant in the first volume of Leunclavius's Greco-Roman Law, edited by Freherus, book seven. On account of these, and on account of his Scholia on Photius and on the canons of the councils, he was very much hated and detested by the Romans. This is also the reason why Baronius rages so often against him in the twelfth volume of his Annales, year 1191, §§ 49 and 62, saying that he pursues the Roman Church with hatred. He thinks the cause of the hatred is that after Constantinople was taken by the Latins, that Church received a Latin Patriarch. Here he contradicts himself, §62, where he says that those meditations or responses on the privileges of the Patriarchs were written two years before Constantinople was taken. See him at Annus §49, and you will see the causes of the alienation of mind from the Latin Church: the celibacy of the clergy of the Western Church, the Saturday fast, the monarchy of the Pope and other things; and for this reason he is commonly called a schismatic. See also Allatius, On the Perpetual Consent of the Eastern and Western Church, book 2, ch. 13, §4, p. 703. They also restored to his relative Balsamon, Viridotius, a little work which Leunclavius had published in Latin under the name of Paratitla, without the author's name.

units.la: Digitized by Google êti suo parenti Balsamoni dudum opusculū, quod sub Paratitlorum nomine sine Auctoris nomine Latine ediderat Leunclavius, quod non Paratitla vocari debet, sed quemadmodum in Bibliotheca Juris canonici veteris, editur Σιωαγωγὴ τῶν εἰρημένων ἐν τῷ Κώδικι, ἢ τῆς Διγέσεως ἢ νεαςεχις Δμαπάξεων, ὠσὶ ὀπισκόπων, καὶ κληρικῶν, καὶ μοναχῶν, ἢ πεαγμάτων διαγῶν, ἐν δὲ ἑ Ιουδαίων καὶ αἱρετικῶν. Collectio expositorum in Codice, & Digestis, & Novellis constitutionibus de Episcopis & Clericis, & Monachis & rebus sacris, aiq; etiam de Judæis & Clericis. libris tribus. Quos huic Auctori adsertos vide apud Doctissimum Fabrottum, in principio notarum ad hanc collectionem, in Biblioth. Juris Canon. Veter. pag. 1377. & Justellum Filium, in præfat. ejusd. Bibliothec. in fine fere.
units.tr: To his father Balsamon there was formerly also a little work, which Leunclavius published in Latin under the title Paratitla without the author's name. It ought not to be called Paratitla; rather, as in the Bibliotheca Juris canonici veteris, it is published as Συναγωγὴ τῶν εἰρημένων ἐν τῷ Κώδικι, ἢ τῆς Δι­γέσεως ἢ Νεαρῶν Διατάξεων, περὶ ἐπισκόπων, καὶ κληρικῶν, καὶ μοναχῶν, ἢ πραγμάτων ἱερῶν, ἔτι δὲ Ἰουδαίων καὶ αἱρετικῶν. A collection of the passages in the Code, the Digest and the Novels concerning bishops, clerics, monks and sacred matters, and also concerning Jews and clerics, in three books. For the attribution of this work to this author, see the most learned Fabrottus, at the beginning of his notes on this collection, in the Bibliotheca Juris Canonici Veteris, p. 1377, and Justellus the younger, in the preface to the same Bibliotheca, near the end.

units.la: In seculo XIII. se offert secunda collectio Decretalium, cujus tres memorantur Auctores. Gilbertus, & Alanus Episcopus quidam Antisiodorensis, qui Bernardum imitati, collegerunt decretales eorum Pontificum qui post Bernardum Circam vixerunt. Sed his nomen & gloriam præripuit Johannes Gallensis vel Vallensis, Volterris natus, qui post duodecim annos à prima collectione (quod tempus incidit in seculi XIII. initium) Pontificum, qui post Bernardinardi nardi Collectionem aliquas ediderant, decretales seu rescripta ex utriusque Gilberti & Alami collectionibus, congessit: quibus etiam Cœlestini tertii addidit, & Scholiis suis illustravit: his postea Hugo Ferrariensis Episcopus, ab Innocentio tertio saepe relatus, & Bernardus major Compostellanus Archidiaconus, suas interpretationes addiderunt. Anton: Augustinus in Præfat. Collect. antiq. decret. testatur se insuper scholia Vincentii, Tancredi, Alani, Laurentii & aliorum, non pauca etiam sine nomine vidisse in hanc secundam compilationem, quæ censet esse ejusdem Johannis Gallensis. Edita est hæc quoque compilatio ab Ant. Augustino inter antiquas decretalium collectiones.
units.tr: In the thirteenth century a second collection of Decretals appears, of which three authors are recorded. Gilbert, and Alanus, a certain bishop of Auxerre, who imitated Bernard, collected the decretals of those popes who lived after Bernard. But Johannes Gallensis, or Vallensis, a native of Volterra, robbed these men of their name and their fame. About twelve years after the first collection (a time which falls at the beginning of the thirteenth century), he gathered into one body the decretals or rescripts of the popes who had issued some after the collection of Bernard, drawing them from the collections of both Gilbert and Alanus. To these he added those of Celestine III and illustrated them with his own glosses. Afterwards Hugh, bishop of Ferrara, often cited by Innocent III, and Bernard the elder, archdeacon of Compostela, added their own interpretations. Antonius Augustinus, in the preface to the Collectio antiqua decretalium, testifies that he has also seen, in this second compilation, not a few glosses of Vincentius, Tancred, Alanus, Laurentius and others, and some without any name, which he thinks belong to the same Johannes Gallensis. This compilation too was published by Antonius Augustinus among the ancient collections of Decretals.

units.la: Tertiam Collectionem adornavit Bernardus Compostellanus, de quo statim dictum, ex registris Innocentii Tertii, quæ Collectio Romana dicta est. Sed offensi Romani, quod usu judiciorum minus recepta referret, ab Innocentio impetrarunt, ut Pontificia auctoritate aliqua Collectio ederetur. Quare Innocentius notarium suum Petrum Beneventanum anno sui Pontificatus XII. qui est Christi nati 1210, operi præfecit: Tum primum auctoritate publica, ut refert Ant. Augustinus loco citato, facta collectio juris Pontificii est. Nam superiores omnes sive Decretorum, sive Decretalium Collectores privata auctoritate scripserunt, & rescripta ab eis relata negari poterant, nisi à scriniariis Romanæ Ecclesiæ probarentur. Hujus Collectionis interpretes fuerunt, ut refert Joh. Andr. F. Paulus Hungarus. Ant. Augustinus dicit se eadem nomina in Scholiis vidisse, quæ in aliis collectionibus.
units.tr: The third collection was put together by Bernard of Compostela, of whom we have just spoken, from the registers of Innocent III, and it was called the Romana. But the Romans were offended that it contained rulings less in use in the courts, and they obtained from Innocent that some collection be published with papal authority. Accordingly Innocent placed his notary Petrus Beneventanus in charge of the work in the twelfth year of his pontificate, which is the year of Christ 1210. Then for the first time, as Antonius Augustinus reports in the passage cited, a collection of papal law was made by public authority. For all the earlier compilers, whether of the Decrees or of the Decretals, had written on their own authority, and rescripts cited by them could be denied unless they had been approved by the scribes of the Roman Church. The interpreters of this collection were, as Johannes Andreae reports, Paulus Hungarus. Antonius Augustinus says that he saw the same names in the glosses as in the other collections.

units.la: Quarta Collectio quinquennio post tertiam, sub eodem Innocentio tertio Papa, Anno nempe Christi 1215, facta est. Cui causam dedit Concilium Lateranense IV. quod pro generali XII. habet Fr. Longus à Coriolano, in summa Concil. pag. 824. in quo LXXI. capita constituta sunt, quibus adjectæ sunt aliæ decretales & rescripta, quæ per quinquennii spatium post tertiam collectionem editæ erant. Duplex tamen extat hujus collectionis editio, una quæ habet tantum LXXI, Canones Concilii Lateranensis, altera cui & alia rescripta sunt addita. Posteriorem exhibet Ant. Augustinus cum suis notis in antiquarum decretalium collectionibus, loco ultimo. Ejus interpres Vincentius fuisse dicitur, Augustinus præterea Johannem, Jacobum & Robertum seu Rogerium se legisse testatur.
units.tr: The fourth collection was made five years after the third, under the same Pope Innocent III, in the year of Christ 1215. It was occasioned by the Fourth Lateran Council, which Fr. Longus a Coriolano, in summa Concil. p. 824, counts as the twelfth general council, and in which seventy-one chapters were enacted; to these were added other decretals and rescripts that had been issued in the five years after the third collection. There are, however, two editions of this collection: one contains only the seventy-one canons of the Lateran Council, the other also has other rescripts added. Antonius Augustinus gives the latter, with his own notes, among the ancient collections of decretals, in the last place. Its interpreter is said to have been Vincentius; Augustinus further testifies that he read Johannes, Jacobus and Robertus, or Rogerius.
Fifth

units.la: Quintam Collectionem fecit Tancredus Bononiensis Archidiaconus, in qua sunt Honorii Tertii constitutiones, sub cujus nomine etiam publicari debuit. Prodiit hæc collectio An. Christi præter propter 1227, quo Honorius Tertius, Innocentii III. successor mortuus est. Hujus interpres perhibetur Jacobus Albanus Faventinus Episcopus, Henrici Ostiensis Præceptor. Hanc diu desideratam, neque unquam editam, quia Gregorius Honorii successor de nova editione Pontifex factus statim cogitabat, cum Antonius Augustinus inter suas Collectiones non ediderat, tandem in Bibliotheca Albiensi repertam, Tholosæ Anno 1645. edidit Innocentius Cironius Academiæ Tholosanæ Cancellarius, & Glossas adjecit Doctissimas, in quibus explicat ea quæ ad juris cognitionem, & temporum historiam pertinent, quæ à prioribus Glossarum Scriptoribus omissa fuerant. Vid. Arthur Duck. de Auctor. jur. lib. I. cap. 7. §. 6.
units.tr: The fifth collection was made by Tancred, archdeacon of Bologna, which contains the constitutions of Honorius III, under whose name it too ought to have been published. This collection appeared in about the year of Christ 1227, when Honorius III, successor of Innocent III, died. Its interpreter is said to have been Jacobus Albanus, bishop of Faenza, the teacher of Henry of Ostia. Antonius Augustinus had not published it among his collections, and it was long desired but never published, because Gregory, Honorius's successor, who was made pope, was at once planning a new edition. At last it was found in the Albi library, and Innocentius Cironius, chancellor of the Academy of Toulouse, published it at Toulouse in 1645, adding most learned glosses in which he explains those matters that pertain to the knowledge of the law and the history of the times, which had been omitted by the earlier writers of glosses. See Arthur Duck, de Auctoribus juris, book I, chapter 7, §6.

units.la: Hanc tandem excepit sexta Collectio, quæ in Corpore Juris Canonici exhibetur, quæ jussu & auctoritate Gregorii IX. Papæ facta est, à Raimundo de Pennaforti, Papæ Capellano, Anno 1230. Congesta hæc est ex omnibus compilationibus anterioribus; cui quoque ea inserta, quæ in anterioribus rioribus omissa fuerunt, item quæcunque ab ipso Gregorio constituta sunt, quæ ille multa ex jure civili hausit, & non consultus respondit; quæ causa quare ejus constitutiones sæpe ad neminem dirigantur, teste Jac. Cujac. ad c. ult. de sent. & re judic. Ipse Gregorius in Proem. Decret. operis rationem suggerit & profitetur se multa inutilia resecuisse; Quæruntur attamen interpretes sæpe, quod multa utilia detraxerit, aliaque obscura addiderit, quare sæpe ad priores collectiones est recurrendum. Raymundum Collectorem multa detraxisse, illæ particulæ, quæ utramque paginam faciunt in Decretalibus, ET INFRA assatim ostendunt. Huic fini id factum, ut ipsas constitutiones breviores faceret, sed fecit quoque obscuriores; nisi itaque sæpissime recurramus ad fontes, vix relictorum sententiam deprehendemus. Ex unius sæpe rescripti corpore plura veluti membra sub variis titulis posita, si iterum conjungantur, multo facilius cognoscuntur. In primis collectionibus Inscriptionum quoque & nominum certior scriptura est, cujus periculum, ut refert Ant. Augustinus, Præfat. ad Antiq. Collect. Decret. fecit Antonius Contius, qui multa in sua editione Corporis Canonici ex hisce Collectionibus restituit. Totius operis ratio & auctoritas ex his Gregorii verbis colligi potest. Di-versas constitutiones, & decretales epistolas prædecessorum nostrorum, in diversa dispersas volumina, quorum aliquæ propter nimiam similitudinem & quædam propter contrarietatem, nonnulla etiam propter fui prolixitatem, confusionem inducere videbantur: aliquæ verò vagabantur extra volumina supradicta, quæ tanquam incerta frequenter in judiciis vacillabant. Ad communem, & maximè studentium utilitatem, per dilectum filium fratrem Raymundum capellanum & pœnitentiarium nostrum, illas in unum volumen (resecatis superfluis) providimus redigendas, adjicientes constitutiones nostras, & decretales epistolas, per quas nonnulla quæ in prioribus erant dubia, declarantur. Volentes igitur ut hac tantùm compilatione universi utantur in judiciis, & in scholis, districtius prohibemus, ne quis præfumat aliam facere, absque auctoritate fedis Apostolicæ speciali. Ad illa verba resecatis superfluis, notant Romani censores, interdum & utilibus, quod & de Triboniano dicitur, qui fuit Raymundo isto doctior. Quod Scholium Joh. Chiffletio bilem succutit, in Apologia pro hoc Raymundo, quæ est quarta, pro architectis juris, cap. VI. §. 2. ubi primum dissimulat auctorem Scholii; Quare, inquit, ut ne mentiar sæpe mihi Stomachum movit is, qui in Præfatione Decretalium Gregorii IX. notulas quasdam conconscripsit, &c. Deinde post subjecta verba, subjicit. Equidem miratus sum non semel, hominī fortasse non indocto tam ineptum & puerile judicium excidisse. Sed tum temporis, cum Censores Romani seculo anteriori jussu Gregorii XIII. recognoscerent Corpus Juris Canonici, nondum erat tanti Raymundus, neque etiam adhuc in Divos relatus. Nil itaque mirum, si veram illi censuram & sententiam, quam millenis exemplis comprobarunt in notis suis, de truncationibus rescriptorum à Raymundo factis, ederent. Magis ego miror quæ effutit (ut Raymundi Collectioni auctoritatem conciliaret) Chiffletius de angelo custode; magis miror illam, quam instituit ejus cum Socratico Dæmone comparationem, quam ut mecum mireris, Lector, en subjicio ejus verba. Nolo venditare Decretum Gratiani tanquam Jus Ecclesiæ, & ab ea donatum summa auctoritate. Adscripserit Gratianus interdum Sanctis Patribus, quæ vel his nunquam venerunt in mentem, vel etiam iis quæ ipsi scripta nobis reliquerunt penitus repugnant. Absit tamen, ut vel Gregorium IX. Pont. Max. vel certè Raymundum Barcinonensem, Ordinis Prædicatorum magnum lumen, perversi hac in parte judicii insimulare quisquam audeat, & oscitantiæ traducere. Nam si Socrates, quòd illi à puero Genius nescio quis adhæsisset, sapientissimus habitus est secundum Pythii quoque dæmonis suffragium, qui Cherophonti id oraculum edidit, quod in omnium ore est; Mortalium unus Socrates verè sapit; in Opere Decretalium concinnando Raymundus non accuratissimus esse non potuit, qui Angelo suo tutelari tam usus est familiariter, ut non raro ad statas ab eo preces excitaretur. Non alio fini ex jure Civili multa Gregorium quidam addidisse putant, quam ne necesse esset ad jus Civile recurrere, eoque major auctoritas juri Pontificio accresceret, juris Civilis & Imperatorum splendor decresceret, & supprimeretur. vid. sis Casp. Zieglerum in Dissertat. de origin. & increment. Juris Canon. §. 53. Fuit Raymundus ille de Penna seu Pennia Forte, & Pennafuerte, quem ad hanc Collectionem adhibuit Gregorius IX. Catalaunus, patria Barcinonensis ex Regibus Aragoniæ oriundus, ordinis Prædicatorum tertius Magister generalis, Gregorii Papæ pœnitentiarius: qui præter collectionem istam decretalium scripsit summam de casibus, quæ typis excusa est Romæ 1603. hoc titulo: Summa de pœnitentia & Matrimonio cum Glossis Joh. de Friburgo Lectoris Ord. Domin. Ejus compendium censent quidam esse summulam Raymundi, quæ Coloniæ 1502. edita est, cujus hoc initium
units.tr: After this came the sixth collection, which is contained in the Corpus Juris Canonici. It was made by Raymundus de Pennaforti, the pope's chaplain, by the order and authority of Pope Gregory IX, in the year 1230. It was compiled from all the earlier compilations, and into it were inserted also those things which had been omitted in the earlier ones, as well as whatever had been enacted by Gregory himself, who drew much from the civil law and answered without consulting the sources; this is why his constitutions are often addressed to no one, as Jacobus Cujacius testifies, ad c. ult. de sent. et re iudic. Gregory himself, in Proem. Decret., explains the plan of the work and declares that he cut away many useless things. Yet interpreters often complain that he removed many useful things and added obscure ones, so that one must often return to the earlier collections. That Raymundus, the compiler, omitted much is shown at length by those little passages which form the second column in the Decretals, ET INFRA. This was done to make the constitutions shorter, but he also made them more obscure; so unless we very often return to the sources, we will scarcely grasp the sense of what has been left. Often several parts of a single rescript, placed under different titles, are more easily understood when they are joined together again. In the earlier collections the form of the inscriptions and of the names is also more certain; the risk of this was run, as Antonius Augustinus reports in his preface to the Antiqua Collectio Decretalium, by Antonius Contius, who restored many things in his edition of the Corpus Canonicum from these collections.
