The plan and authority of the whole work can be gathered from these words of Gregory: The various constitutions and decretal letters of our predecessors, scattered in different volumes, some of which seemed to cause confusion because of their great similarity and some because of their contrariety, others also because of their length, and others wandering outside the aforesaid volumes, which, being uncertain, often wavered in judgments: for the common benefit, and especially of students, we have provided, through our beloved son, Brother Raymundus, our chaplain and penitentiary, that they be brought together into one volume (with superfluous things cut away), adding our own constitutions and decretal letters, by which some things that were doubtful in the earlier ones are declared. Therefore, wishing that all should use this compilation alone in judgments and in schools, we strictly forbid anyone to presume to make another without the special authority of the Apostolic See. On the words with superfluous things cut away, the Roman censors note: sometimes also useful things, which is also said of Tribonian, who was more learned than this Raymundus. This scholium stirred the bile of Johannes Chifflet, in Apologia pro hoc Raymundo, the fourth, pro architectis juris, chapter VI, §2, where at first he conceals the author of the scholium: Wherefore, he says, so that I may not lie, he has often moved my stomach, the one who wrote certain little notes in the preface to the Decretals of Gregory IX, etc. Then, after quoting the words, he adds: Indeed I have more than once wondered that so foolish and childish a judgment should have fallen from a man perhaps not unlearned. But at that time, when the Roman censors in the previous century, by the order of Gregory XIII, were revising the Corpus Juris Canonici, Raymundus was not yet so great, nor had he yet been raised among the saints. Nothing is therefore surprising if they published their true censure and opinion, which they proved by a thousand examples in their notes, concerning the truncations of rescripts made by Raymundus. I am more amazed at what Chifflet babbled (to win authority for Raymundus's collection) about the guardian angel; I am more amazed at that comparison he drew between him and the Socratic daemon, which, so that you may share my wonder, reader, I set out in his own words: I do not wish to puff up the Decree of Gratian as the law of the Church, and given by her with supreme authority. Gratian sometimes ascribes to the holy Fathers things which never came into their minds, or which are wholly contrary to what they have left written to us. Yet let no one dare to accuse Pope Gregory IX, the greatest pontiff, or certainly Raymundus of Barcelona, the great light of the Order of Preachers, of a perverse judgment in this respect, or to charge him with carelessness. For if Socrates, because some genius or other clung to him from boyhood, was considered the wisest of men, according also to the testimony of the Pythian daemon, who gave to Chaerephon that oracle which is on everyone's lips, Of mortals, Socrates alone is truly wise; then in compiling the work of the Decretals, Raymundus could not fail to be most accurate, since he was so familiar with his guardian angel that he was often roused by him at appointed prayers. Some think that Gregory added many things from the civil law for no other purpose than that it should not be necessary to resort to the civil law, so that greater authority might accrue to papal law, and the splendour of the civil law and of the emperors might decline and be suppressed. See also Caspar Ziegler, in Dissertatione de origine et incremento Juris Canonici, §53. That Raymundus, whom Gregory IX used for this collection, was called de Penna or Pennia Forte, and Pennafuerte; he was a Catalan, a native of Barcelona, descended from the kings of Aragon, the third Master General of the Order of Preachers, and penitentiary of Pope Gregory. Besides this collection of Decretals he wrote the Summa de casibus, which was printed at Rome in 1603 under this title: Summa de paenitentia et matrimonio cum glossis Joannis de Friburgo, lectoris Ordinis Dominicanorum. Some think that a compendium of this is the little summary of Raymundus which was published at Cologne in 1502, whose opening reads as follows.

units.la: 355. Raymundus quis fuerit & ejus vita, scripta & series decretalium initium est, Summula de summa Raymundi prodiit ista. Obiit anno 1275. ut refert Molanus in Bibliotheca Sacra MS. Anno 1601. à Clemente VIII. Canonizatus, ut loquuntur, seu in Sanctorum Ordinem est relatus, vide de eo Henricum Gandavensi de Scriptor. Eccles. cap. 48. & ibidem Scholia Miræi, Marianam in Reb. Hispan. libr. 12. cap. 8. lib. 13. c. 13. & 22. Bibliothecam Hispanic. cujus Collector est Andr. Schottus, tom. 2. pag. 186. & 218. Vitam Hispanice scripsit Salvator Pons, vertit Germanice & Monachii edidit Ægidius Albertinus 1602; ubi multa & magna miracula, quæ fidem excedunt, refert. Vide sis Joh. God. Olearii Abacum Patrologicum. pag. 399. & seqq. Item Leand: Albertum in ejus vita, & Chiffletium, de Architect. Juris. cap. VI. Distincta est Collectio Raymundi, seu Gregorii IX. quinque libris, quorum summam versiculus ille continet. Judex 1. Judicium 2. Clerus 3. Sponsalia 4. Crimen 5. Liber quilibet suos habet titulos, omnes simul centum & octuaginta quinque. Est ille ordo quoque in anterioribus compilationibus observatus, & exinde haustus, quem etiam in posterioribus omnibus digestionibus sequuti sunt, quando quid, quod ad titulos pertineret, novi rescriptum invenerunt; runt ; quod si deesset, ad alium titulum progressi sunt; quæ causa est quare in sexto Clementinis & extravagantibus sæpè non tot tituli inveniantur, quam in singulis libris collectionis Gregorianæ. De hac compilatione hoc exstat judicium Franc. Duareni in Præfatione lib. de Sacr. Eccles. Minist. quod subjicimus. In eo Decretalium volumine multa intueri licet quæ à prisca illa disciplina, quam Decretorum liber à Gratiano editus continet, multum degenerent. Atque hinc natum est illud inter nostrates tritum ac vulgo jactatum, male cum rebus humanis actum esse, ex quo decretis ala accesserunt. Est enim hæc rerum humanarum conditio, ut fere in deterius prolabantur. Sic omnia fatis, inquit Poëta, in pejus ruere, & retro sublapsa referri. Ejus tamen libri lectio negligenda juris studioso non est, quod multa ad juris, non modo Pontificij, sed etiam Civilis cognitionem utilia contineat. Quo etiam tempore conscriptæ sunt ista Epistolæ, quibus Pontifices Romani de jure consulentibus more veterum Imperatorum respondebant, causa Ecclesiasticæ antiquam simplicitatem jam amiserant, erantque ejusmodi ut ad eas dirimendas ac definiendas JCti ac Pragmatici adhiberentur. Unde factum est ut Canonum peritus, nisi idem juris Civilis scientia instructus sit, vulgari proverbio inter rudes & imperitos numeretur. In hanc & an& anteriorem editionem Gloffas ediderunt, ut refert Guido Pancirollus, de Claris leg. Interpret. lib. 3. cap. 8. quem hic sequimur, Ruffinus, Sylvester, Ricardus Anglus, Rodoicus cognomento Modicipaffus, Petrus Corbolus, vel, ut alii, Boliatus Hispanus, Hostiensis in summa de resti. spolia. §. cum quaeritur. ad fin. Joh. And. in c. twas. co. & in præm. decretali col. 3. verf. & ibi compilationes quinque. Bertrandus, Damasius, Alanus Anglicus, Petrus Papiensis Præpositus, Petrus Galensis Vulterranus, Bernardus Compostellanus, Laurentius, Vincentius Castellionus Mediolanensis, Joannes Teutonicus, & Tancredus, qui etiam in Decretum gloffas ediderunt; Hos secuti sunt Gulielmus Naso, & Jacobus de Albenga Episcopus Faventinus. Sed horum omnium gloffas Bernardus Bottonus Parmensis, ultimam compilationem interpretatus in unum collectas ampliavit, Archid. in peroratione Decreti. circiter annum MCCXL. & omnem illarum gloriam in se transtulit. Eandem Gregorii IX. compilationem aliqui ex prioribus, & alii posteriores sunt interpretati, ut Vincentius, Gofredus, Philippus, Innocentius, Hostiensis, Petrus Sampso, Abbas antiquus, Bernardus Compostellanus, qui opus non perfecit, Egidius dius Bononiensis, Bonaguida Aretinus, & Franciscus Vercellensis, qui tantum super contexte scripsit. Postea supervenit Boatinus Mantuanus, & Archidiaconus, qui etiam glossas sunt interpretati. Quidam etiam Monachi, quorum nomina ignorantur, super iisdem Decretalibus opus composuere, quod Suffragium Monachorum nuncupatur, quod ut erroneum, superfluum; & mancum fere inutile fuit. Hos secutus fuit Frater Jacobus Canonicus Sancti Joannis in Monte, quorum omnium scripta milleglossematum, aut interpretationum Summam excedebant, prout in Proem. Decret. Joannes Andreae testatur. Ex praedictis Damasius in primam compilationem glossas, edidit, ac librum quaestionum super multis Decretalibus, & Brocarda composuit, & Joannes de Albenga Hostiensis praeceptor Honorianas est interpretatus; Praeter memoratos Druzianus, & Guandulfus in Decretales glossas emiserunt, & Petrus Mandecator, & quidam Cardinalis. Caeterum Bernardus Bottonus Bononiae, ubi etiam Canonicus creatus est, diu Decretales professus est, postea sacri Palatii quaestor est declaratus, gloss. Bernar. in c. quod sicut in vir. dividatur, de electio. quem Auditorem, & Summi Pontificis Capellanum vocant; cum enim causas ex toto orbe ad Urbem confluentes Pontifex in Sacello, quod Capellam nominant, adhibitis Jurisconsultis, audiret, illi à loco Capellani sunt appellati; Sed hi hodie numero xii. licet alias plures fuerint, ex generali, & prisca delegatione in unum ordinem redacti sunt, & qui audiendi, cognoscendique facultatem habent, Auditores causarum sacri Palatii dicuntur, quas ex speciali rescripto plerunq; decidunt; & etiamnum Capellani nuncupantur, atque in Capella divinis inserviunt. Bernardus postremo Academiæ Bononiensi Præfectus fuit, quem Germanorum vocabulo Cancellarium vocabant. Illi enim cum in Italia imperabant, omnes regionum præsectos Cancellarios appellare consueverant. In majore templo Bononiæ cum hoc Epi-taphio humatus est.
units.tr: 355. Who Raymond was, and his life, writings and the order of the decretals, is the beginning of the little summary that follows from Raymond's summa. He died in 1275, as Molanus reports in his manuscript Bibliotheca Sacra. In 1601 he was canonized by Clement VIII, as they say, or enrolled among the Saints. On him see Henry of Ghent de Scriptor. Eccles. cap. 48., and there the Scholia of Miraeus; Mariana in Reb. Hispan. libr. 12. cap. 8. lib. 13. c. 13. & 22. Bibliothecam Hispanic., whose compiler is Andreas Schottus, tom. 2. pag. 186. & 218. Salvator Pons wrote his life in Spanish, and Aegidius Albertinus translated it into German and published it at Munich in 1602, where he recounts many great miracles that exceed belief. Please see also Johann Gottfried Olearius, Abacus Patrologicus, pag. 399. & seqq. Likewise Leander Albertus in ejus vita, & Chifflet, de Architect. Juris. cap. VI. The collection of Raymond, or of Gregory IX, is divided into five books, whose summary that little verse contains: Judex 1. Judicium 2. Clerus 3. Sponsalia 4. Crimen 5. Each book has its own titles, one hundred and eighty-five in all. This order was also observed in the earlier compilations and drawn from them, and the later digests all followed it: whenever they found some new rescript pertaining to a title, they inserted it there; but if there was none, they moved on to another title. This is why the Sixth Book, the Clementines and the Extravagants often do not have as many titles as each book of the Gregorian collection. Concerning this compilation there is the judgment of Franciscus Duaren in the preface to his book de Sacris Ecclesiae Ministeriis, which we append. In that volume of the Decretals one may see many things that depart greatly from that ancient discipline which the book of Decrees edited by Gratian contains. And hence arose that saying, common among our countrymen and tossed about by the crowd, that things have gone badly for the human race, since decrees have added wings to it. For this is the condition of human affairs, that they nearly always slide toward the worse. Thus, as the poet says, all things hasten by fate to the worse and, once fallen back, are carried backward. Yet the reading of this book should not be neglected by a student of law, since it contains many things useful for knowledge not only of Papal but also of civil law. At the same time were written those Epistles in which the Roman Pontiffs, after the manner of the ancient emperors, answered those consulting them on points of law, when the Church had already lost its ancient simplicity; and they were of such a kind that jurists and pragmatists were called in to settle and decide them. Hence it came about that a expert in the canons, unless he is also instructed in the science of civil law, is numbered among the ignorant and inexperienced by the common proverb. To this and to the earlier edition, they published glosses, as Guido Panciroli reports in de Claris leg. Interpret. lib. 3. cap. 8., whom we here follow: Rufinus, Sylvester, Richard the Englishman, Rodoicus surnamed Modicipassus, Peter Corbolus, or as others call him, Boliatus the Spaniard, Hostiensis in summa de resti. spolia. §. cum quaeritur. ad fin. Joh. And. in c. twas. co. & in præm. decretali col. 3. verf. & ibi compilationes quinque. Bertrand, Damasus, Alanus the Englishman, Peter of Pavia, provost, Peter of Galles of Volterra, Bernard of Compostella, Laurence, Vincent of Castiglione of Milan, John the German, and Tancred, who also published glosses on the Decretum. The following came after them: William Naso and James of Albenga, bishop of Faenza. But Bernard Bottoni of Parma, who interpreted the last compilation, gathered the glosses of all of them into one and enlarged them, Archid. in peroratione Decreti., about the year 1240, and transferred all their glory to himself. Some of the earlier writers, and others of the later, also interpreted this same compilation of Gregory IX: Vincent, Godfrey, Philip, Innocent, Hostiensis, Peter Sampso, the old Abbot, Bernard of Compostella, who did not complete the work, Giles of Bologna, Bonaguida of Arezzo, and Francis of Vercelli, who wrote only on the text. Afterwards came Boatinus of Mantua and the Archdeacon, who also interpreted the glosses. Certain monks too, whose names are unknown, composed a work on these same Decretals, which is called the Suffrage of the Monks; being erroneous, superfluous and nearly maimed, it was of little use. Brother James, canon of St John in the Mountain, followed them; the writings of all of them together exceeded a thousand glosses or the sum of the interpretations, as John Andreae testifies in Proem. Decret. Of those mentioned, Damasus published glosses on the first compilation and composed a book of questions on many of the Decretals and Brocarda; and John of Albenga, teacher of Hostiensis, interpreted the Honorian compilation. Besides those mentioned, Druzianus and Guandulfus also put out glosses on the Decretals, as did Peter Mandecator and a certain cardinal. Moreover Bernard Bottoni taught the Decretals for a long time at Bologna, where he was also made a canon; afterwards he was appointed quaestor of the sacred palace, gloss. Bernar. in c. quod sicut in vir. dividatur, de electio., whom they call Auditor and Chaplain of the Supreme Pontiff. For when the Pontiff, with jurists in attendance, heard the cases that flowed to the City from the whole world in the chapel which they call the Chapel, those men were named after the place as Chaplains. But these, now twelve in number although formerly there were more, were reduced into one order by a general and ancient delegation, and those who have the power to hear and examine are called Auditors of the causes of the sacred palace; they mostly decide these by special rescript, and still today they are called Chaplains and serve the divine offices in the chapel. Bernard was finally prefect of the University of Bologna, which the Germans called by the name Chancellor, for when they ruled in Italy they were accustomed to call all the prefects of the regions Chancellors. He was buried in the greater church of Bologna with this epitaph.

units.la: BERNARDUS BOTTONUS CANCELLARIUS STUDII BONONIENSIS, QUI SCRI- PSIT APPARATUM AD DECRETA, JA- CET HIC.
units.tr: BERNARDUS BOTTONUS, CHANCELLOR OF THE UNIVERSITY OF BOLOGNA, WHO WROTE THE APPARATUS ON THE DECRETALS, LIES HERE.

units.la: Censores Romani superiori seculo has Decretales contulerunt cum fontibus Regestis nimirum & compilationibus, quaque incon-sulto Raymundus detraxerat, & sine quibus Decretales intelligi vix poterant, subjecerunt: sunt hæc quæ in editionibus vulgatis alio characteris genere scripta legimus.
units.tr: In the last century the Roman censors collected these Decretals, and, since they could hardly be understood without them, they added the sources: the Registers and the compilations, which Raymundus had carelessly left out. These are the materials which we read in the printed editions, set in a different type.

units.la: Antequam Cæteros Romanorum Præfulum labores in colligendis Decretalibus, & fulcienda sua Pontificia majestate atq; jurisdictione, recenseamus ; in Græciam nos ordo temporis vocat, ut labres lustremus Arfenii Monachi, postea Patriarchæ Constantinopolitani, cum Nicephyrus Blemmydas designatus Patriarchatum non iniret. Hic sub Theodoro Lascare Juniore circa Annum Christi 1255. Synopsin Canonum ex Conciliis & Patribus in Concilio Trullano approbatis collegit ; In qua accurata Methodo Universam canonicæ disciplinæ scientiam, centum supra unum & quadraginta titulis complexus est, tum in fine cujusque tituli νομικὰ quædam κεφάλαια capita quædam legum concordantium adjecit. Quare illius opus Nomocanonis quoque titulum in fine Codicis Græci Manuscripti in Bibliotheca Regis Galliarum refert. Unde κεφάλαια illa νομικὰ hauserit, non satis constat. Justellus Filius & Guill. Voell. in Præfat. Bibliothec. juris Canon. veteris hanc conjecturam habent. Unde autem illa κεφάλαια νομικὰ deprompserit Arsenius non facile est deprehendere: multa olim & varia juris χρείας à Basilio, Leone Philosopho & Constantino tino Porphyrogenneta Impp. Orientis Basilicorum auctoribus saepius edita sunt: an autem ex illis sua forte capitula excerpserit Arsenius non est nostrum definire, sed eruditis & juris Graeci peritis disceptandum relinquimus: Edidit Opusculum hoc Christophori Justelli filius, in Bibliotheca juris Canonici veteris tom. 2. sub hoc titulo. Ἀρσενίου Μοναχοῦ τῆς ἐν τῷ ἁγίῳ ὄρει Μονῆς καὶ Φιλοθέου Σύνοψις τῶν θείων Κανόνων. Παρὰ κεφαλαίῳ ἑκάστῳ κεφαλαίου καὶ τὰ ἀριθμοζόντων ψηφίων τῶν θείων κανόνων. ἀφ' ὧν καὶ ὁ νῦς εἰληφθεί. ἃ ἀναγινώσκων ἀκριβῶς διρίσεις τὰ σωτεινόντα· πεφέρον μὲν ἀπὸ τῶν κεφαλαίων τὸν ἅπαντα νῦν σημαινόμενον· ἐπίστα ἢ τοῖς ψηφίοις ἀναζητῶν ἐν τῇ τῶν κανόνων βίβλῳ· καὶ πλατύτερον περὶ ἑκάστου πληροφορούμενος, εἰς δόξαν τῆς ἁγίας καὶ ὁμοουσίου Τριάδος. Ἀμήν. Arsenii, Monachi ejus quod est in Sancto Monte Monasterii, Divinorum Canonum Synopsis. Appositis unicuique capiti congruentibus divinorum canonum numeris, ex quibus mens desumpta est. Qua legendo, nullo negotio invenies ea quae ad rem pertinent: primum quidem ex capitibus omnem sensum edIscendo, deinde vero numerorum ope in canonum libro investigando, plenius etiam de singulis certior factus, ad gloriam sanctae & consubstantialis Trinitatis. Amen.
units.tr: Before we review the other labours of the Roman prelates in collecting the Decretals and in supporting their papal majesty and jurisdiction, the order of time calls us into Greece, so that we may survey the work of Arsenius the monk, later Patriarch of Constantinople, at the time when Nicephorus Blemmydes, though designated Patriarch, did not take up the office. Under Theodore Lascaris the Younger, around the year of Christ 1255, he gathered a Synopsis of the Canons from the councils and fathers approved at the Council in Trullo. In this work, arranged with careful method, he embraced the whole science of canonical discipline in one hundred and forty-one titles, and at the end of each title he added certain legal chapters (νομικὰ κεφάλαια), with some concordant laws. For this reason the Greek manuscript of his work in the library of the King of France gives it also the title Nomocanon. Where he drew those legal chapters from is not clearly known. Christophe Justel's son and Guillaume Voel, in the preface to their Bibliotheca juris canonici veteris, offer a conjecture on this point. But it is not easy to discover what Arsenius drew those legal chapters from. Many legal matters of the Greek law were published often in the past by the emperors Basil, Leo the Philosopher and Constantine Porphyrogenitus, the authors of the Basilica of the East. Whether Arsenius perhaps excerpted his own chapters from those, it is not for us to decide; we leave the question to the learned and to those expert in Greek law. Justel's son published this little work in the second volume of the Bibliotheca juris canonici veteris, under this title: Synopsis of the Divine Canons by Arsenius, monk of the monastery on the Holy Mountain, and Philotheus [Ἀρσενίου Μοναχοῦ τῆς ἐν τῷ ἁγίῳ ὄρει Μονῆς καὶ Φιλοθέου Σύνοψις τῶν θείων Κανόνων]. Beside each chapter he set the numbers of the corresponding divine canons, from which the meaning was taken. Whoever reads it carefully will, without any trouble, find what pertains to the matter: first, by learning the whole sense from the chapters, and then by seeking it through the numbers in the book of the canons, and becoming more fully informed about each point, to the glory of the holy and consubstantial Trinity. Amen. [Παρὰ κεφαλαίῳ ἑκάστῳ κεφαλαίου καὶ τὰ ἀριθμοῦντα ψηφία τῶν θείων κανόνων, ἀφ' ὧν καὶ ὁ νοῦς εἴληπται· ἃ ἀναγινώσκων ἀκριβῶς εὑρήσεις τὰ συντείνοντα· πρῶτον μὲν ἀπὸ τῶν κεφαλαίων τὸν ἅπαντα νοῦν σημαινόμενον, ἔπειτα δὲ ἢ τοῖς ψηφίοις ἀναζητῶν ἐν τῇ τῶν κανόνων βίβλῳ, καὶ πλατύτερον περὶ ἑκάστου πληροφορούμενος, εἰς δόξαν τῆς ἁγίας καὶ ὁμοουσίου Τριάδος. Ἀμήν.]
From the Times of Pope Gregory IX

units.la: 366. Bonifacii octavi cis, in Occidente, prohibitae erant collectiones privatorum; Quare cessatum est aliquantisper in colligendis Decretalibus; Usque ad Bonifacium Octavum, qui XV. Papa fuit ab excessu Gregorii, & ad sedem evectus est seculi XIII. anno 94. Hic tertio Pontificatus anno tribus Cardinalibus commisit compilationem Decretalium, Guillielmo de Mandagoto, ex Archidiacono Nemausensi Archiepiscopo Ebredunensi; Berengario Fredello vel Stredelio Episcopo Niterrensi & Richardo Patrono de Senis Romanae Ecclesiae Vicecancellario, teste Proem. lib. VI. Decret. quae postea liber sextus Decretalium vocatur, quia aliis quinque Gregorii addita est. Illa potissimum ex constitutionibus Innocentii IV. Gregorii X. Nicolai III. & ipsius Bonifacii: item constitutionibus duorum Conciliorum Lugdunensium sub Innocentio IV. anno 1245. & sub Gregorio X. anno 1272. celebratorum compilata est; Habet illa itidem libros quinque, ut Gregoriana & eosdem, ut dictum titulos, si quid interea, quod ad titulum faciat rescriptum invenerunt compilatores. Richardi cujusdam, qui & auctor hujus compilationis sit, meminit. Alber. de Rosat. ad l. ult. C. de feriis. Super fuisse etiam Dynum, vid. apud Catellian. Cottam. in memor. memor. Eam Baldus citat in tit. de Pace Constantia, sub nomine Novellarum, Vid. Alberic. Gent. de lib. jur. Can. c. 1. p. 11. Fuit hic Bonifacius valde ambitiosus, arrogans, turbulentus, ad discordias promtus & excitandas & fovendas. Quod satis ex Platina, & Praefatione Monarchica, quam huic compilationi praemisit colligi potest. Cum Philippo Rege, suam regni Galliae immunitatem defendente, & Papalibus Mandatis & rescriptis obedire detrectante, graves inimicitias exercuit. Pontifex in Galliam ad Philippum pulcrum mittit episcopum Apameensem, ut eum ad bellum sacrum incitet. filio ejus Carolo Valesio dat orientis imperium specie, sed revera eo ut vicario in exterminandis Etruria Gibellinis uti cogitat. cunctanti Philippo anathema intentat. Philippus episcopum in custodiam tradit. Papa eum illico liberarii jubet. Episcopis & Patriciis Franciae Romam ad concilium diem dicit. Non parente Philippo, regnum Franciae ad ecclesiam Rom. pertinere dicit, proinde abstineat ab ejus administratione. subditos sacramento solvit. Philippus praelatos regno excedere vetat, & liberat quidem Apameensem, sed bullam Papae in atrio palatii Parisiensis exuri facit, ejus latorem protinus facessere jubet. Cum Papa ea bulla diceret regnum Franciæ & in spiritualibus & in temporalibus sibi subesse, præbendarum collationem ad se spectare, aliud credentes hæreticos putare: respondit per literas Philippus: Sciat tua maxima fatuitas vos in temporalibus aliquam non subesse, aliquarum præbendarum collationem &c. ad nos jure regio pertinere &c. secus autem credentes fatuos & dementes reputamus. Conveniunt Lutetiæ Ordines regni cum clero & theologis, & multorum scelerum reum agunt Papam. etiam quod non adhibeat fidem conscientibus eucharistiam. quod animas mortales putaret: ideoque ad vacantem sedem, ut aiebant, ad futurum concilium appellant. Interea sancitum nequis quicquam Romam perferret. Bonifacius concilio Romæ habito regnum Franciæ interdicto subjicit: regem cum posteris ad 4 generationem ecclesiâ excludit: sed latores bullarum comprehenduntur. Vid. Jacob. Revium in vita Bonif. VIII. Mornæi Mysterium iniquitatis pag. 391 edit. Goricbemens. Hæc causa quare liber sextus Decretalium in Gallia non sit receptus. Duarenus in Præfat. lib. de Sacr. Eccles. Minist. Ideo, inquit, in Francia receptum non esse accepimus, quod quaedam in eo extant, constitutiones, pleraque in odium & æmulationem Philippi Regis Francorum edita, & ad Romanæ
units.tr: 366. Boniface VIII. In the West, private collections had been forbidden; therefore the collecting of Decretals came to a halt for a while, until Boniface VIII, the fifteenth Pope after the death of Gregory, was raised to the see in the year 1294 of the century. In the third year of his pontificate he entrusted the compilation of the Decretals to three cardinals: Guillaume de Mandagot, formerly Archdeacon of Nîmes and then Archbishop of Embrun; Berengar Fredel, or Stredelius, Bishop of Nîmes; and Richard Petroni of Siena, Vice-Chancellor of the Roman Church. So testifies the Proem to the Sixth Book of the Decretals. This compilation is afterwards called the Liber Sextus of the Decretals, because it was added to the five of Gregory. It was put together chiefly from the constitutions of Innocent IV, Gregory X, Nicholas III and Boniface himself, and likewise from the constitutions of the two councils of Lyons, held under Innocent IV in the year 1245 and under Gregory X in 1272. Like the Gregorian collection, it has five books, and the same titles, as mentioned, with whatever rescripts the compilers found in the meantime that bore on a title. Alberico de Rosate, on the last law of the Code concerning holidays, mentions a certain Richard, who is said to be the author of this compilation. There was also a Dinus, see Cattaneo Cotta in his memoirs. Baldus cites it under the name of Novels, on the title concerning peace in Constance. See Alberico Gentili, On the books of canon law, ch. 1, p. 11. This Boniface was very ambitious, arrogant and turbulent, quick to stir up and foster quarrels. This can sufficiently be gathered from Platina and from the Monarchic Preface, which he put before this compilation. He carried on grave enmities with King Philip, who defended the immunity of his kingdom of France and refused to obey papal mandates and rescripts. The Pope sent Bishop Apameensis to Philip the Fair to stir him up to a holy war. To Philip's son Charles of Valois he gave the empire of the East in name, but in fact intended to use him as his vicar in exterminating the Ghibellines of Tuscany. When Philip hesitated, he threatened him with anathema. Philip handed the bishop over to custody. The Pope immediately ordered him freed. He summoned the bishops and nobles of France to a council at Rome. When Philip did not obey, the Pope declared that the kingdom of France belonged to the Roman Church, and so Philip should keep away from its administration, and he released the subjects from their oath. Philip forbade the prelates to leave the kingdom, and he did indeed free the Apameensis, but he had the papal bull burned in the courtyard of the Paris palace, and ordered its bearer to depart at once. When the Pope said in that bull that the kingdom of France was subject to him both in spiritual and in temporal matters, and that the conferring of prebends belonged to him, Philip, in a letter, replied: "Let your great folly know that you have no authority over us in temporal matters, and that the conferring of some prebends etc. pertains to us by royal right etc.; those who believe otherwise we regard as fools and madmen." The orders of the kingdom met at Paris with the clergy and theologians, and charged the Pope with many crimes, among them that he did not give credence to those who consulted him about the Eucharist, and that he thought souls mortal. Therefore they appealed, as they said, to a vacant see and to a future council. Meanwhile it was decreed that no one should carry anything to Rome. Boniface, holding a council at Rome, placed the kingdom of France under interdict, and excluded the king with his descendants to the fourth generation from the Church; but the bearers of the bulls were arrested. See Jacob Revius, in the life of Boniface VIII, and Mornay, Mystery of Iniquity, p. 391, Gorcum edition. This is the reason why the Sixth Book of the Decretals was not received in France. Duaren, in the preface to his book On the Sacred Ministry of the Church: "For this reason," he says, "we understand that it was not received in France: there are in it certain constitutions, most of them issued in hatred and rivalry with Philip, King of the Franks, and thought to have been devised for the gain of the Roman court."

units.la: 370. Ob eas liber sextus in Gallia non est receptus. mana aulæ quæstum excogitatæ credantur. Adde Petr. de Marca, Concord. Sacerd. & Imper. lib. 4. c. 16. Scripsit in hanc compilationem Glossas Johan. Andreæ; de quo vide sodes late Guidon. Panciroll. de Glar. leg. Interp. lib. 3. cap. 19.
units.tr: 370. For these reasons the Sixth Book was not received in Gaul: ...devised for the gain of the Roman court. Add Peter de Marca, Concord of the Priesthood and the Empire, book 4, ch. 16. John Andreae wrote glosses on this compilation; on him see at length Guido Panciroli, On Lost Laws and Interpreters, book 3, ch. 19.

units.la: Initio seculi Decimi quarti Clemens V. qui Benedicto XI; & hic Bonifacio VIII. successerat, novo augmento jus Pontificium beavit aut potius oneravit. Hic sedem Pontificiam Avenionem in Galliam consilio Cardinalium Gallorum, quos bene multos creaverat, transtulit; eoque demonstravit æque Papam Avenionensem, ac Romanum posse dici, nec necesse esse ut Romæ hæreat, Petrique, ut volunt, sedibus incubet. Mansit hic statio Pontificum per annos LXXII. Hic libris itidem quinque iisdemque titulis inclusit suas & Concilii Viennensis constitutiones, sed præproperè mortuus vulgare non potuit, imò moriens vetuit, ut Aventinus libr. VII. Annal. refert, statim adducendus. Ejus successor Johannes XXII. non obstante prohibitione Antecessoris vulgavit. Aventini judicium de hac editione est sequens. Septimum Juris Pontificii librum, quem Clemens V. decessor ejus composuerat, sed quod multa, quæ simplicitati Christianæ, libertati Religionis imponerent, ibi continerentur, publicare publicare supersederat, atque animam agens a-boleri jusserat, (Johannes XXII.) edidit, omnia quae ibidem scripta erant, rata fore constituit, quae à Benedicto, qui Johanni successit rursus antiquata sunt. Noluit has vocari librum septimum Johannes Papa, ejus editor, sed Clementinas inscripsit, misitque ad universitatem Bononiensem cum Praefatione sua anno Pontificatus sui secundo, qui est Christi 1317. Glossas ad eas edidit Fr. Zabarella, qui & in decretales scripsit.
units.tr: At the beginning of the fourteenth century Clement V, who succeeded Benedict XI, and Boniface VIII before him, enriched Papal law with a new increase, or rather burdened it. He transferred the papal see to Avignon in France, by the counsel of the French cardinals whom he had created in great numbers, and by this he showed that the Pope of Avignon could be called just as much Roman, and that it was not necessary for him to stay at Rome and cling to the seat of Peter, as some claim. This station of the popes lasted seventy-two years. He likewise enclosed his own constitutions and those of the Council of Vienne in five books under the same titles; but, dying prematurely, he could not publish them, and indeed, as Aventinus relates in Annals, book 7, he forbade them to be brought out at once while he was dying. His successor John XXII published them nevertheless, despite the prohibition of his predecessor. Aventinus's judgement on this edition is as follows: "John XXII, the editor, published a seventh book of Papal law, which Clement V, his predecessor, had composed, but had held back from publishing because it contained many things that burdened Christian simplicity and imposed on the liberty of religion, and which, while dying, he had ordered to be destroyed. He decided that everything written there should be valid, but these things were again annulled by Benedict, who succeeded John." John the Pope, its editor, did not wish it to be called the seventh book, but entitled it the Clementines, and sent it to the University of Bologna with his preface in the second year of his pontificate, which is the year of Christ 1317. Francesco Zabarella, who also wrote on the Decretals, published glosses on them.

units.la: Sub ejusdem Johannis XXII. nomine vulgatae extant in Corpore Canonico Extravagantes, viginti; ita dictae, quod vagarentur extra Corpus Collectionum Canonicarum, incertae adhuc, num recipiendae essent. Nam ab ipso Iohanne, neque ab ullo Pontifice sunt vulgatae, aut probatae, sed privata auctoritate collectae, anno praeter propter 1340. Cujacius in c. ad audientiam. 4. de sponsal. & Matr. vocat Johanninas. Guillielmus Occam, qui circa eadem tempora vixit, à multis has extravagantes reprehendi, pro haereticis & falsis haberi adserit, & errores recitat ex libris & sermonibus Iohannis hujus. Vide scripta haec apud Goldastum in Monarchia; Sleidan. lib. 2. com. & de Scriptis hujus Iohannis XXII. Ludov. Iacob. à S. Carolo, in Biblioth. Pontificia, tificia, lib. I. ubi ejus Regestum, & Bullarium in Vaticana Bibliotheca extare refert. pag. 40. Scripsit in eas Zenzelinus de Cossanis, qui aliis est Gezellinus, vel Jesselinus de Cossanchis.
units.tr: Under the same name of John XXII, twenty Extravagantes are published in the Corpus Canonicum. They are so called because they wandered outside the Corpus of the canonical collections, their status still uncertain as to whether they should be received. For they were published neither by John himself nor by any pope, nor approved by any, but were gathered by private authority around the year 1340. Cujacius, in c. ad audientiam. 4. de sponsal. & Matr., calls them Johanninas. William of Occam, who lived around the same time, asserts that many have found fault with these extravagants, held them to be heretical and false, and cites errors from the books and sermons of this John. See these writings in Goldastus, in Monarchia; Sleidan, lib. 2. com.; and, on the writings of this John XXII, Ludovicus Jacobus a S. Carolo, in Biblioth. Pontificia, tificia, lib. I., where he reports that his Register and Bullarium exist in the Vatican Library, pag. 40. Zenzelinus de Cossanis, who is also called Gezellinus, or Jesselinus de Cossanchis, wrote on them.

units.la: Eidem Johanni XXII. adscribuntur Regulæ Cancellariæ. Ludovicus Gomes, qui Commentariis illustravit has Regulas, in Proemii princ. illud satis compertum esse dicit, Regulas Cancellariæ à Johanne XXII. initium & originem habuisse, nam in vetusto quodam membranaceo Codice (quem vulgares Quinternum Cancellariæ Apostolicæ vocant) primus omnium in ordine ponitur Johannes XXII. Regularum Auctor, nec ante ipsum alius summorum Pontificum invenitur, qui hoc prius tentaverit; Aliquibus foliis interjectis, idem tradit: ejus testimonium quia laudes & fraudes, homo Pontificius, Episcopus, ad ipsum Papam Paulum III. (cui suos commentarios inscripsit) uno spiritu eructat, non possum quin totum, etiam paulo prolixius, apponam. Redeamus igitur, inquit, unde digressi sumus, & dicamus, quod licet ante tempora, Joannis XXII. Vicecancellarius, scriptores & correctores literarum jam constituti fuissent, nihilominus regulæ Cancellariæ nondum compositæ fuerant: sed primus omnium Joan. XXII. tanquam bonus domus suæ paterfamilias eas introduxit, Nec solum regulas, sed etiam ut rem angustam domini juvaret beneficiorum etiam electivorum reservationes ac taxas, quibus æstimarentur, invenit. Collegium quoque scriptorum Apostolicorum. antea sine ordine vagans. numeris distinxit, ut de iis Guliel. Hispanus in Pragmatica Franciæ, ac Polydorus lib. 8. de Inventoribus rerum, cap. 2. meminerunt. Quinimo beneficiorum annatas, ex quibus tam magnos proventus sibi & Ecclesiæ comparavit, in consilio Viennensi sub contentione dimissas, ut refert Jo. And. licet mendose in c. inter cætera. col. fi. de ossi. ord. in usum revocavit. Adeo, ut moriens vigesies quinquies centum millia nummum aureorum Ecclesiæ dimisit, ut refert frater Ptolomæus de Luca in historia Ecclesiastica Pontificum, in vita Johan. Et hoc idem dicit, tacito authore, D. Petrus And. Gammarus Rotæ auditor in scholiis quibusdam impressis ad extravagantem Julii II. Qua quidem annatarum inventione magnum toto orbi scandalum generavit, Nec mirum quia Joan. XXII. adeo cupidi & audacissimi animi fuit, ut non solum hoc uno malo Ecclesiasticos Viros gravare, sed quod magis mirandum fuit non est veritus constitutionem facere, qua & regnum Germaniæ à regno Franciæ divideret, & Italiam ab imperio segregaret, ut Albericus author est. Inter hæc tamen, Rotam novis & saluberrimis statutis ornavit, quæ hodie apud nos etiam servantur, tur, & quotannis initio audientiarum publicè le-guntur, Et in summa, ille primus administrationem justitiæ cujus Vicecancellarius caput est, quæ in regulis, & Rotæ ordinationibus consistit, invenit. Quæ quidem officia successores Pontifices in dies magis propagarunt, Nam quod ad regulas attinet Joan. XXII. in suis regulis hoc tantum egit, abbreviatores instruere, videlicet quomodo literas in cancellaria, juxta supplicationum varias signaturas, deberent expedire, quas summi pontifices deinde magis auxerunt, usque ad tempora Nicolai Papæ V. qui omnium pontificum primis prædecessorum utiliores regulas colligens, ac plures alias judiciales addens, eas omnes in eo statu, in quo nunc reperiuntur, deduxit. Quem successores usque in hodiernum diem paucis immutatis vel additis pro se quisque sunt sequuti, Totius hujus harmoniæ laus Joanni tribuitur. Fuit enim inter cæteros mortales non solum eruditus, sed impense curiosus, Nam, ut ex recentioribus solus author est Franciscus Petrarcha lib. 2. rerum memorabil. tract. 3 cap. 53. Joan. XXII. fuit adeo rerum omnium curiosus, ut repertoria, seu indices sibi ordine alphabeti conficeret, quibus facile res omnes in promptu, & ad manus haberet. Sic itaque ecclesiæ Dei magnum præstitit adjumentum & authoritatis prærogativam: nam, ut ea omnia quæ historici in ejus vita referunt omittam, quando aliud de se
units.tr: The Regulae Cancellariae are also ascribed to the same John XXII. Ludovicus Gomes, who illustrated these Rules with commentaries, says in the opening of his Proemium that it is sufficiently established that the Rules of the Chancery had their beginning and origin with John XXII, for in an old parchment codex (which the common people call the Quinternum of the Apostolic Chancery) John XXII is placed first of all in the order as the author of the Rules, and no earlier pope is found who attempted this; After some leaves intervene, he gives the same account. Because this man, a Papist and bishop, who dedicated his commentaries to Pope Paul III himself, belches out his praises and frauds in one breath, I cannot refrain from quoting the whole passage, though it is rather lengthy. Let us therefore return, he says, to where we digressed, and say that although before the time of John XXII there were already a vice-chancellor, writers and correctors of letters, nevertheless the Rules of the Chancery had not yet been drawn up; but John XXII first of all, like a good householder of his house, introduced them. Not only did he draw up the rules, but also, to help the lord in his narrow circumstances, he devised reservations and taxes on benefices, even elective ones, by which they might be valued. He also divided the college of apostolic writers, which had previously wandered without order, into numbered groups, as William of Spain in the Pragmatica of France and Polydore, book 8, de Inventoribus rerum, chapter 2, recall. Moreover, he restored to use the annates of benefices, from which he obtained such great revenues for himself and the Church, which had been dropped in the Council of Vienne, as John Andreas reports, though faultily, on c. inter cetera, col. fin., de ossi. ord. So much so that on dying he left 25 times one hundred thousand gold coins to the Church, as Brother Ptolemy of Lucca reports in his Ecclesiastical History of the Popes, in the life of John. And D. Peter Andreas Gammarus, auditor of the Rota, says the same, without naming his source, in certain printed notes on the extravagant of Julius II. This invention of annates caused a great scandal throughout the whole world. Nor is this surprising, since John XXII was of so greedy and bold a spirit that he not only burdened churchmen with this single evil, but, what is more astonishing, did not shrink from making a constitution by which he divided the kingdom of Germany from the kingdom of France and cut off Italy from the empire, as Albericus is the authority for. Meanwhile, however, he adorned the Rota with new and most salutary statutes, which are still observed among us today, and are read publicly at the start of the hearings every year. In short, he was the first to devise the administration of justice of which the vice-chancellor is head, which consists in the Rules and the ordinances of the Rota. These offices the successor popes extended day by day. For as far as the Rules are concerned, John XXII in his Rules did only this, to instruct the abbreviators how they should dispatch letters in the chancery according to the various signatures of supplications, which the supreme pontiffs afterwards increased, down to the time of Pope Nicholas V, who, gathering the more useful rules of all his predecessors, and adding many other judicial ones, brought them all to the state in which they are now found. His successors, changing or adding a few things here and there, have each followed him down to the present day. The praise for this whole harmony is given to John. For among other mortals he was not only learned but intensely curious. For, as the sole author among the more recent writers, Francis Petrarch, book 2, rerum memorabilium, tract. 3, chapter 53, says, John XXII was so curious about all things that he made for himself repertories or indexes in alphabetical order, by which he could have all things readily at hand. Thus he rendered a great help and prerogative of authority to the Church of God. For, to omit all the things the historians relate of his life, since it is enough to have shown from what has been said that the Rules we are speaking of had a certain origin and beginning.

units.la: dignum sufficit ex prædictis ostendisse, Regulas, de quibus loquimur, certam originem & initium habuisse. Habes hic oppido egregiam summi, ut volunt, Præsulis sanctitatem; ex qua etiam de constitutionum æquitate judicare poteris, quas avaritia dictasse videtur. Sunt hæ regulæ Cancellariæ norma judicii Romani in judicando, & valent tantum per vitam Pontificis, cum eo moriuntur; Pares de resignat. benef. lib. II. q. 2. num. 32. Merlin. decis. 192. num. 4. & 5. Gomes. ad Regul. Cancell. procem. sol. 8. pag. 1. in sin. Sequens Pontisex paucissimis immutatis initio suæ creationis iterum eas proponit, teste Carol. Eman. Vizzanio, in tract. de mand. Principum. in proleg. num. 7. Ideoque edictis Prætorum eas comparat Francis. Florens ad titulum de Rescript. princ. An leges sint generales an particulares late disquirit Gomesius ad d. constitutiones, ubi multa arg. pro utraque sententia affert in quæst. secunda Proemii, sol. 8. & seqq. Sed sunt tantum leges particulares vere, Curiam Romanam tangentes, ideoque extra eam non obligant, ut vere dicidit Alberic. Gentil. de libr. Iur. canon. cap. 3. pag. 52. ubi addit Constitutiones Marchiæ Anconitanæ, quæ Ægidianæ dicuntur jus generale facere in statu Ecclesiastico, extra eum non valere. Adde Befold. de libr. Iuris. pag. 47. seu cap. 8. in sin.
units.tr: Here you have a quite remarkable holiness of the highest Prelate, as they would have it; from this you can also judge the fairness of the constitutions, which avarice seems to have dictated. These Rules of the Chancery are the standard of judgment of the Roman court in judging, and they hold force only during the life of the Pontiff; they die with him. Pares, de resignat. benef. lib. II, q. 2, num. 32. Merlin, decis. 192, num. 4 and 5. Gomes, ad Regul. Cancell. procem. sol. 8, pag. 1, in fin. The following pontiff, with very few changes at the start of his creation, proposes them again, according to Carlo Emanuele Vizzani, in tract. de mand. Principum, in proleg., num. 7. Therefore Francesco Florens compares them to the edicts of the praetors, ad titulum de Rescript. princ. Whether laws are general or particular Gomes discusses at length, ad d. constitutiones, where he brings many arguments for each opinion, in quaest. secunda Proemii, sol. 8 and following. But they are truly only particular laws, touching the Roman Curia, and therefore do not bind outside it, as Alberico Gentili rightly states, de libr. Iur. canon. cap. 3, pag. 52, where he adds that the constitutions of the March of Ancona, which are called Aegidian, make general law in the ecclesiastical state but are not valid outside it. Add Befold, de libr. Iuris, pag. 47, or cap. 8 at the end.

units.la: Seculo demum decimo quinto & quidem decrescente, alia collectio extravagantium prodiit quæ Communes vocantur, quia non sunt unius Papæ. Quæ Collectio itidem privata industria facta, à nullo Pontifice approbata legitur; sunt in ea extravagantes quædam Eugenii IV. Calixti III. Pauli II. Sixti IV; qui ad Pontificatum venit Anno 1471. & mansit in eo usque ad Annum 1484; ut necesse sit hoc tempore factam & vulgatam fuisse istam collectionem. Quia à privato facta cujus nomen latet, ideo nec olim magnæ auctoritatis fuit: nunc vero & hæc & anterior Johannis XXII, postquam in Corpus canonicum recepta est, magni apud Canonistas est ponderis. Harum quædam extant cum Glossis Johannis Monachi, Picardi Cardinalis, aliæ cum commentis Gillermi de Monte Laduno, & Johannis Francisci de Paviniis.
units.tr: Finally, in the fifteenth century, and indeed in its later decades, another collection of extravagants appeared, which are called Communes because they do not belong to one pope. This collection too was made by private industry and is read as approved by no pope. Among them are certain extravagants of Eugene IV, Callixtus III, Paul II and Sixtus IV, who came to the papacy in the year 1471 and remained in it until the year 1484; so that this collection must have been made and published at this time. Because it was made by a private person whose name is hidden, it was therefore not of great authority in former times; but now both this collection and the earlier one of John XXII, since it has been received into the Corpus Canonicum, carry great weight among the canonists. Some of these are found with the glosses of John the Monk, the Picard cardinal; others with the commentaries of William of Mende and John Francis de Paviniis.

units.la: Ex his partibus conflatum est Corpus Juris Canonici, quo hodie utimur ad imitationem corporis juris Civilis, ut Gratiani Decretum Pandectas, Decretales Codicem, Sextus, Clementinæ & extravagantes Novellas repræsentare possint. Quod si incrementa impositerum tanta à sequentibus Pontificibus acceperit, moles ejus longe jura Civilia excedet, & postea idipsum obruet. Causas incrementorum eleganter enarrat Petrus de Marca de concord. Sacerd. & Imper. lib. 3. cap. 6. num. 4. ubi differentias Juris Canonici Veteris & Novi adsignat. Verba sunt quidem paululum prolixa, tamen quia Auctor non est in omnium manibus, tum quia affabre causas depingit, homo Pontificiæ professionis & Episcopus, eum omittere nequeo. Summum, inquit, caput, in quo jus novum ab antiquo differt, in eo jam constitui, quod suprema potestas, quam in plerisque causis judicandis Synodi provinciales obtinebant, penitus extincta est, & ad solum summum Pontificem revocata, & ea quae in canonibus condendis versatur, sit adeo imminuta, ut Pontifici soli constitutionum condendarum onus incubuerit, quibus earum rerum formam prascribebat, de quibus apud illum erat disceptandum. Hinc secutus est novus judiciorum Ecclesiasticorum ordo ad cognitiones per rescripta Pontificum instituendas in Provinciis; Vide tot constitutiones emanarunt de Rescriptis, de judicibus delegatis, de officio judicis ordinarii, de dilationibus, exceptionibus, sententiis & appellationibus, & de toto, ut generaliter loquar, judiciorum ordine. Hæc omnia olim non adeo exacte & solemniter exercebantur, ut novis Constitutionibus est decretum; quæ magna ex parte in formulis actionum num & in tritura fori, anxiè & scrupulosè versantur. Ex alio deinde capite nova Ecclesiastica Politiæ facies oborta est, scil. ex Beneficiorum ab ordinationibus discretione. Antiquo jure, quod canone Concilii Chalcedonensis probatum erat, nullus ad Clerum adsciscebatur, quin ad certam Ecclesiam sub Episcopi, Presbyteri, Diaconi, & caterorum ordinum gradu adscriberetur, adeò ut manûs impositionem sequeretur adscriptio in Canonem seu laterculum & matriculam Ecclesiæ. Hoc obtinet adhuc in Episcopis; sed in cæteris gradibus ordinationes ἀπολελυμένως & absolutè fiunt, & absque titulo Ecclesiæ, contra præscriptum Concilii Chalcedonensis. Constitutum quidem fuit in concilio Lateranensi, ne Clerici ordinarentur absque titulo, saltem patrimonii, scil. ne in opprobrium Cleri mandicare cogerentur; sed hoc Decreto non est restituta vetus disciplina, quæ clericos per manuum impositionem suis Ecclesiis addicebat. Separatio ista & discretio ordinationis ab Ecclesiæ seu beneficii collatione & pinguissimorum reditUUM copia, novas in jus Canonicum regulas invexit antiquo juri prorsus incognitas de beneficiis acquirendis, conservandis & amittendis, quæ ferè utramque paginam novi juris faciunt. Matrimoniorum impedimenta novis interdictis ad tuendam honestatem publicam introducta, & revocatæ ad solam Ecclesiam earum causarum cognitiones & cognitionum, quæ hâc de re ba= re habentur, adstrictus forensibus formulis ordo, novam juri Canonico materiam subministrarunt. Excommunicationum infligendarum & poenitentiarum publicarum, quae antiquo jure vigebant, temperatus jure novo rigor novis Constitutionibus explicandus erat. Non omittenda sunt multiplices Monachorum species & religiosarum domuum diffusa per Europam multitudo, quae novis regulis & institutis Pontificum curam ad se traxerunt. Quin & indultae monasteriis aut Canonicorum capitulis exemptiones ab Episcoporum jurisdictione & privilegia varia illis concessa, varias causarum figuras a Pontificibus disceptandas praebuerunt. &c. Salse traduxit eam seculo decimo quinto exeunte Johannes Geilerus Keisersbergius, Concionator apud Argentoratenses sermone 3. de orat. Nota, inquit, dissipaverunt Dei, per leges humanas: sic Dominus Judaeis improperavit: irritum fecistis &c. & per leges positivas, canonicas & Imperiales, per statuta municipalia, provincialia, synodalia & cujuslibet particularis Ecclesiae, quod suo tempore lamentatus est beatus Augustinus, ad inquisitiones Januarij. Quod si idem nunc viveret, & videret Decretum, Decretales, Sextum, Clementinas & tot Lecturas &c. DEUS meus, quid diceret? taceo de legibus iniquis. Plane obruitur lex divina per tot humanas, ne discatur & cognoscatur. De Auctoritate hujus Juris pauca subnectenda sunt. Ea varia fuit, crevit & decrevit. Cum imperium & Majestas Pontificum Romanorum se per totum Occidentem magis magisque diffunderet, etiam super Imperatores se extolleret, juris quoque Canonici auctoritas eodem impetu se dissudit & crevit, ita ut Blasphemo errore detorta Augustini & truncata sententia ex lib. 2. de Doctr. Christ. Gratianus Can. in canonicis, dist. 19. Decretales inter canonicas Scripturas retulerit. & qui canones violat, qui instinctu Spiritus sancti dicuntur dati esse, dicatur Spiritum S. blasphemare, c. Violatores. 25. q. 1. Imperatores Romano-Germanici non semper ista incrementa aut Mysterium quod in conscribendis, edendis & vulgandis Decretalibus & obtrusione juris Pontificii, latebat, observare potuerunt; aut si viderent, pacis studiosi, tolerarunt; aut potius, quia non poterant impedire, conniv« runt. Hinc factum, ut omnes Occidentis populi, Jus canonicum receperint, eoque in decidendis causis usi fuerint. De Italia, in qua Auctor ejus juris longe lateque dominabatur, non est, quod auctoritates producamus. Galli, deficientibus legibus & consuetudinibus propriis ex jure Canonico causas in suis Curiis decidi patiuntur, teste Eguinar. Baron. ad l. vonunquam. 11. ff. de justit.
units.tr: The Corpus of Canon Law, which we use today, was put together from these parts in imitation of the body of Civil law, so that Gratian's Decretum can stand for the Pandects, the Decretals for the Code, and the Sext, the Clementines and the extravagant Novels for the Novels. But if it receives such great additions from later Popes, its bulk will far exceed the civil laws and will eventually overwhelm them. Petrus de Marca, in de concord. Sacerd. & Imper. book 3, chapter 6, number 4, describes elegantly the causes of these additions, where he sets out the differences between the old and the new canon law. His words are rather long, but since the author is not in everyone's hands, and because he portrays the causes skilfully, being a man of Papist profession and a bishop, I cannot omit him. "The highest point," he says, "in which the new law differs from the old is this: the supreme power which the provincial synods held in most judicial causes has been utterly extinguished and recalled to the Supreme Pontiff alone, and the power concerned with enacting canons has been so diminished that the burden of making constitutions has fallen on the Pontiff alone, who prescribed the form of those matters which were to be disputed before him." Hence there followed a new order of ecclesiastical judgments, by which cases were to be conducted in the provinces through rescripts of the Popes. See how many constitutions have been issued concerning rescripts, judges delegate, the office of the ordinary judge, delays, exceptions, sentences and appeals, and, to speak generally, the whole order of judicial procedure. All these things were formerly not carried out so exactly and solemnly as the new constitutions have decreed; for the most part these constitutions are concerned anxiously and scrupulously with the forms of actions and the grind of the courts. From another source a new face of ecclesiastical polity arose, namely from the separation of ordination from the conferral of benefices and the abundance of very rich revenues. By the ancient law, which had been approved by a canon of the Council of Chalcedon, no one was admitted to the clergy unless he was enrolled in a particular church under the rank of bishop, presbyter, deacon or the other orders, so that the imposition of hands was followed by enrolment in the canon, or list, and register of the church. This still holds for bishops; but for the other grades ordinations are made apolelymenōs [absolutely], and absolutely, without a title of any church, contrary to the prescription of the Council of Chalcedon. It was indeed decreed in the Council of Lateran that clerics should not be ordained without a title, at least a patrimony, so that they would not be forced to beg, to the disgrace of the clergy; but by this decree the ancient discipline, which bound clerics to their churches by the imposition of hands, was not restored. This separation and distinction of ordination from the collation of a church or benefice, and the abundance of fat revenues, introduced into canon law new rules about acquiring, keeping and losing benefices, quite unknown to the ancient law, which make up nearly both pages of the new law. The impediments to marriage, introduced by new prohibitions for the protection of public decency, and the cognizance of those causes, which was recalled solely to the Church, together with the order of procedure, tied to forensic forms, and the rules that apply in this matter, supplied new material for canon law. The rigour of excommunications to be inflicted and of public penances, which prevailed under the ancient law, had to be moderated and explained by new constitutions under the new law. Nor are the manifold kinds of monks and the widespread multitude of religious houses throughout Europe to be passed over; with their new rules and institutes they drew the care of the Popes to themselves. Indeed the exemptions from episcopal jurisdiction granted to monasteries or chapters of canons, and the various privileges conceded to them, provided various kinds of cases for the Popes to decide, etc. Johannes Geiler of Kaysersberg, preacher at Strasbourg, wittily rendered this at the end of the fifteenth century, in sermon 3 on prayer: "Note," he says, "they have scattered God's [law] through human laws; so the Lord reproached the Jews: you have made void, etc.; and through positive laws, canon and imperial, through municipal, provincial and synodal statutes, and those of every particular church, which blessed Augustine lamented in his time in the letter to Januarius. But if he were alive now and saw the Decretum, the Decretals, the Sext, the Clementines and so many Lectures, etc." My God, what would he say? I say nothing of unjust laws. "Truly the divine law is overwhelmed by so many human laws, so that it is not learned and not known." A few things must be added about the authority of this law. Its authority was varied: it grew and declined. As the empire and majesty of the Roman Pontiffs spread more and more throughout the whole West, and raised itself even above the emperors, so too the authority of canon law spread and grew with the same force, so much so that, through a blasphemous error and a truncated sentence from Augustine, from book 2 of On Christian Doctrine, Gratian, Can. in canonicis, dist. 19, counted the Decretals among the canonical Scriptures; and that whoever violates the canons, which are said to have been given by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, is said to blaspheme the Holy Spirit, c. Violatores, 25 q. 1. The Roman-German emperors could not always observe these increases, or the mystery which lay hidden in the composing, publishing and spreading of the Decretals and the imposition of Papal law; or if they did see it, they, being lovers of peace, tolerated it; or rather, since they could not prevent it, they connived. Hence it happened that all the peoples of the West received canon law and used it in deciding causes. Concerning Italy, where the author of this law ruled far and wide, there is no need to produce authorities. The French, when their own laws and customs fail, allow causes to be decided in their courts by canon law, as witnessed by Eguinarius Baron, ad l. vonunquam 11 ff. de justit.

units.la: ris Pontificii justit. & jur. Rebuffo, adConstit. Regias in Proem. Gloss. 5. n. 126. rejecto tantum libro sexto Decretalium, ut supra adsertum; alioquin in Academiis Galliæ, universum jus Canonicum docetur. Vide Bochell. in Decret. Eccles. Gall. lib. 5. tit. 14. c. 36. Hispani, deficiente jure Regio, ad jus Canonicum recurrunt, ut adseverat Azeved. ad Constit. Reg. Hispan. lib. 2. tit. 1. n. 18. Amat. Rodrigu. de Proceff. in causf. civilib. cap. 10. n. 26. Vasq. de Succeff. creat. §. 26. limit. 31. n. 70. Idem de Hungaris testatur Stephan. de Werbentz, de jure Hungar. part. 2. tit. 6. De Danis Georg. Lorich. in Enchirid. Arreft. in Addit. ad conf. posterius. n. 52. De Anglis id constat ex ipsis Decretalibus qui magnam partem ad Anglos de controversiis Anglicanis sunt scriptæ, idque testatur Arthur. Duck. de auctor. jur. Civil. lib. 1. cap. 7. §. 15. De aliis videatur Cothomann. Resp. 4. n. 52. & Resp. 30. n. 70. vol. 1.
units.tr: of Papal law, de justit. & jur.; Rebuffus, ad Constit. Regias in Proem. Gloss. 5 n. 126, rejecting only the sixth book of the Decretals, as asserted above; otherwise in the academies of France the whole of canon law is taught. See Bochellus, in Decret. Eccles. Gall. lib. 5 tit. 14 c. 36. The Spaniards, when royal law fails, have recourse to canon law, as Azevedo asserts, ad Constit. Reg. Hispan. lib. 2 tit. 1 n. 18; Amatus Rodericus, de Processibus in causis civilibus cap. 10 n. 26; Vasquez, de Successionibus creatorum §. 26 limit. 31 n. 70. Stephanus de Werbentz testifies the same of the Hungarians, de jure Hungar. part. 2 tit. 6. Concerning the Danes, Georgius Lorichius, in Enchiridio Arrestorum, in Addit. ad conf. posterius n. 52. That this holds for the English is clear from the Decretals themselves, most of which were written to the English concerning English controversies; and Arthurus Duck attests this, de auctoritate juris Civilis lib. 1 cap. 7 §. 15. On others see Cothmann, Resp. 4 n. 52 and Resp. 30 n. 70 vol. 1.

units.la: De Germania nulli potest esse dubium, quoniam in causarum decisionibus, & in Academiis publice nil frequentius quam allegatio & explicatio juris Canonici. Probant id affatim regulæ, quod jus alteri & in quibus casibus debeat, cedere. Si casus in jure Civili non est decisus, vel non expresse, sed ambigue vel obscure positus, idemque in jure Canonico clare & aperte inveniatur, ejus dijudicatio in utroque foro ex jure Canonico petenda est; contra, causa decidenda est ex jure Civili, ubi in jure Canonico vel penitus nihil, vel obscure & ambigue decisum est. l. 1. & ibid. DD. de nov. oper. nunc. Abbas ad c. licet. n. 14. de for. comp. Marant. in Pract. p. 3. n. 73. Rebuff. ad constit. Reg. in Proem. gloss. 5. n. 126. Christinæus. decis. Belg. 54. n. 1. tom. 2. Si jus Civile & Canonicum contraria sunt, utrumque in suo foro, Civile in Imperio, Canonicum in Dominiis Ecclesiæ viget. Johan. Andr. ad c. 1. n. 5. de nov. oper. nunc. Card. Tusch. concluf. 277. n. 36. In causis peccati petenda decisio ex jure Canonico veluti in præscriptione, in qua bonam fidem continuam exigit jus Canonicum; ubi jus CivileCanonico non est contrarium, dicitur ab eo approbatum, de quibus vide Arthur. Duck de auct. jur. Civil. lib. 1. c. 7. §. 11. 12. & 13. & Clarissimum meum Promotorem, Dn. Jacob. Brandmuller. Antecess. Basiliensem, in præliminaribus operis, de differ. juris Civil. & Canon. cap. 5. in sin. & 6. pag. 12. Manet hæc auctoritas quidem illibata, donec Deus lucem Euangelii sui seculo superiori benignissime restitueret; nisi quod anterioribus temporibus quidam etiā, sed pauci agnoagnoscerent iniquitatem ejus & affectatum per id summum in omnia dominium, eiq; se masculè opponerent. Inter quos, seculi XIV. anno XXIV. Marsilius Patavinus, qui defensorem Pacis tum edidit; & alii quos collegit Goldastus; itern Flacius Illyricus in Catalogo testium veritatis. Verum eorum Parresia sine effectu fuit. Lutherus, cum videret, reformationi obesse tot Decretorum & Decretalium volumina, ea ad examē revocavit, cumque videret sacris literis non satis congruere, contemsit, tandemq; An. XX. seculi superioris, provocatus suorum librorum exultione, totum Juris Canonici volumen Wittebergæ extra partam in magna Doctorum & Studiosorum Multitudine extructo rogo ultricibus flammis abolevit, nequicquam factum improbantibus Henningio à Goeden & Hieronymo Schurffio, qui suas prosessiones eo facto ignominia affici querebantur. Qua de re vide sis Casp. Ziegler, in Dissert. de Orig. & increm. Juris Canonici. S. 64. & seq. & Clariss: Dn. Brandmullerum d. Prælim. diss. ad differ. jur. Civ. & Canon. cap. 6. pag. 9. Ab hoc tempore decrevit auctoritas juris Pontificii in territoriis Protestantium; nisi quod doceatur & retineatur magis ex consuetudine, Johan. Goedd. de contrahend. stipul. cap. 6. conclus. 7. n. 109. ¶. 109. Sixtin. de regalib. lib. 1. cap. 4. n. 118. D. Brandmuller. d. Prælim. dissert. cap. 6. pag. 11. Frantzkius ad §. 9. instit. de jur. nat. gent. & Civil. quam auctoritate constituentis, Sam. Marefi. in Diss. de jur. Canon. §. 20. & 21. idque propter Processum judiciarium, qui in libro secundo Decretalium & passim in sequentibus collectionibus, ex interpretibus Juris Civilis, & propriis figmentis, rerum emergentium varietate materiam & modum suggerente, magis concinne est explicatus: item alias quasdam materias, Jurisjura idi[?], Matrimonii & similes; Vid. Reinkingius de regin. secul. & Eccles. lib. 2. classe 2. c. 7. Quæ tamen aliunde hauriri possent, nisi usus invaluisset; qui solus etiam sustinet titulum Doctoris Juris Canonici, qui simul datur cum Doctoratu Juris Civilis, ne opus sit propter conversationis frequentiam cum Pontificiis, pati ab iis status controversiam; qua de re potest videri Casp. Zieglerus, §. 68. dict. dissertat. & Sam. Marefi. de Jure Canon. §. 19. ante Cucchi institut. Ubi varias adferunt rationes, quare prosessio & titulus Doctoris in Jure Canonico hodie ad hoc sustineatur in territoriis Protestantium; Quibus adde quæ supra prolixè disputavimus de auctoritate Gratianei Decreti: ex qua disputatione satis concludi potest, quid tribuendum cæteris post Gratianum collectionibus, quoniam omnes pertinent ad illam partem Decreti, quæ habet Pontificum rescripta seu Decretales Epistolas. Vid. num. 312. Retinuisse jus Pontificum Principes Protestantes, postquam ab Ecclesia Romana recessissent & potestatem Papæ abdicassent, eoque in decisionibus causarum usos esse, adserit Arthur. Duck de auctoritat. Jur. Civil. lib. 1. cap. 7. §. 16. eodem plane modo, quo Principes Europæi, postquam renunciaverant Cæsarum potestati, leges tamen Cæsareas observarunt. In Anglia plane abolitum esse jus, titulumque Doctoris Juris Canonici, testatur Robert. Parkerus de Politia Ecclesiastl. lib. 2. cap. 32. & seq. In Germania, saltem apud Protestantes rectius quoque aboleri, quam diutius conservari debere jus Canonicum decernit Zieglerus, d. diss. §. 67. in sin. Neque id inficetis rationibus, probat; quibus, quod usum inter Protestantes concernit, facile adsensum extorquet. In disputationibus vero cum Pontificiis, cum eundem usum præbere possint Decretales, quem supra n. 319. de Gratiani Decreto adseruimus, tantisper & has retinere possumus, quod etiam non videtur Improbare ipse Zieglerus. §. 68. adde Samuel. Maref. dissert. de jure Canon. §. 25. & seqq. Huc itaque inclinat Doctissimorum Virorum sententia: non in totum posse retineri, neque in totum esse rejiciendum jus Canonicum. Vide sis Matth. Stephani, in praefat. quam praemisit tertia parti tractat. de jurisdict. Doctiss. Joh. Strauch. in Amoenit. jur. Can. part. 1. Eclog. 1. cap. 13. D. Brandmull. diss. Prælim. ad diff. jur. Can. & Civil. cap. ult. pag. 13.
units.tr: There can be no doubt about Germany, since in the decision of cases and in the universities nothing is more common than the citing and explaining of canon law. The rules of precedence amply show which law must yield to the other, and in which cases. If a case is not decided in civil law, or is decided only obscurely or ambiguously there, and the same matter is found clearly and openly in canon law, it must be judged in either forum from canon law. Conversely, the case must be decided from civil law where canon law has either nothing at all or only an obscure and ambiguous decision. l. 1. & ibid. DD. de nov. oper. nunc. Abbas ad c. licet. n. 14. de for. comp. Marant. in Pract. p. 3. n. 73. Rebuff. ad constit. Reg. in Proem. gloss. 5. n. 126. Christinæus, decis. Belg. 54. n. 1. tom. 2. If civil and canon law are contrary to each other, each holds force in its own forum: civil law in the Empire, canon law in the domains of the Church. Johan. Andr. ad c. 1. n. 5. de nov. oper. nunc. Card. Tusch. concl. 277. n. 36. In matters of sin the decision is to be sought from canon law, as for example in prescription, where canon law requires continuous good faith. Where civil law is not contrary to canon law, it is said to be approved by it. On this see Arthur Duck, de auct. jur. Civil. lib. 1. c. 7. §. 11. 12. & 13. and my most distinguished promoter, Dn. Jacob Brandmüller, Professor at Basel, in the preliminaries of his work de differ. juris Civil. & Canon. cap. 5. in fin. & 6. pag. 12. This authority indeed remained unimpaired until God, most graciously, restored the light of his Gospel in the last century. Yet even in earlier times some, though few, recognised its injustice and the supreme dominion over all things that it claimed, and opposed it boldly. Among them, in the twenty-fourth year of the fourteenth century, was Marsilius of Padua, who then published the Defensor Pacis, and others whom Goldast collected; likewise Flacius Illyricus in the Catalogus testium veritatis. But their boldness had no effect. Luther, seeing that the many volumes of Decrees and Decretals stood in the way of the Reformation, called them to examination. When he saw that they did not sufficiently agree with the sacred letters, he despised them. At last, in the twentieth year of the last century, provoked by the rejoicing of his opponents, he burned the whole volume of canon law at Wittenberg outside the walls, with a great crowd of Doctors and students looking on, the avenging flames consuming it. Henning von Goeden and Hieronymus Schurff disapproved of this deed, in vain, complaining that their professions were disgraced by it. On this matter see Casp. Ziegler, in Dissert. de Orig. & increm. Juris Canonici. S. 64. & seq. and the distinguished Dn. Brandmüller, d. Prælim. diss. ad differ. jur. Civ. & Canon. cap. 6. pag. 9. From this time the authority of papal law ceased in the territories of the Protestants, except that it is taught and retained more from custom, Johan. Goedd. de contrahend. stipul. cap. 6. conclus. 7. n. 109. Sixtin. de regalib. lib. 1. cap. 4. n. 118. D. Brandmüller, d. Prælim. dissert. cap. 6. pag. 11. Frantzkius ad §. 9. instit. de jur. nat. gent. & Civil. rather than by the authority of a lawgiver, Sam. Marefi. in Diss. de jur. Canon. §. 20. & 21. This is because of the judicial process, which is set out more neatly in the second book of the Decretals and throughout the later collections, drawn from the interpreters of civil law and from their own inventions, with the variety of emerging cases suggesting the matter and the method. Likewise certain other matters, of law, marriage and the like, are treated there. See Reinkingius, de regin. secul. & Eccles. lib. 2. classe 2. c. 7. Yet these could be drawn from elsewhere, were it not that custom has prevailed. Custom alone also sustains the title of Doctor of Canon Law, which is conferred together with the doctorate in civil law, so that, because of frequent dealings with the Papists, there is no need to suffer a controversy over its status. On this matter Casp. Ziegler, §. 68. dict. dissertat. and Sam. Marefi, de Jure Canon. §. 19. ante Cucchi institut. may be consulted. They give various reasons why the profession and title of Doctor of Canon Law is today sustained in the territories of the Protestants. To these add what we argued at length above about the authority of Gratian's Decree. From that discussion it can sufficiently be concluded what is to be attributed to the other collections after Gratian, since all of them belong to that part of the Decree which contains the rescripts or Decretal Epistles of the Popes. See no. 312. That the Protestant princes, after they had withdrawn from the Roman Church and renounced the power of the Pope, retained the law of the Popes and used it in deciding cases, is asserted by Arthur Duck, de auctoritat. Jur. Civil. lib. 1. cap. 7. §. 16. in exactly the same way as the European princes, after they had renounced the power of the Caesars, nevertheless observed the Caesarean laws. In England the law, and the title of Doctor of Canon Law, were entirely abolished, as Robert Parker attests, de Politia Ecclesiastica lib. 2. cap. 32. & seq. In Germany, at least among the Protestants, Ziegler decides that canon law ought rather to be abolished than kept for longer, d. diss. §. 67. in fin. He proves this not without unanswerable reasons, which easily win assent as far as its use among Protestants is concerned. In disputations, however, with the Papists, since the Decretals can offer the same use that we asserted above of Gratian's Decree (no. 319), we may for the time being retain them as well. Ziegler himself does not seem to disapprove of this, §. 68. Add Samuel Marefi, dissert. de jure Canon. §. 25. & seqq. Hence the opinion of the most learned men inclines this way: canon law can neither be retained entirely nor rejected entirely. See Matthias Stephani in the preface he prefixed to the third part of his treatise de jurisdict.; the most learned Johann Strauch, in Amoenit. jur. Can. part. 1. Eclog. 1. cap. 13.; and D. Brandmüller, diss. Prælim. ad diff. jur. Can. & Civil. cap. ult. pag. 13.

units.la: Quaenam sint Doctorum Virorum judicia de jure Canonico, ex praedictis facile colligi potest. Duo aut tria singularia his adjiciemus; unum Viri Gravissimi, Georgii Wicelii in via Regia; Quot verò horum statutorum (iniquorum scil.) millia in libris recentioribus extant? cujusmodi Ecclesia Christi non solum reprobat, verum etiam ferre amplius neque potest, neque debet: siquidem condita sunt praeter legem DEI, praeter legem naturae, contra aedificationem domus Domini, imò ad hujus destructionem, contra charitatem proximi, contra consuetudinem veteris veraque Ecclesiae, contra exempla priscorum, ac sanctorum Patrum; adhaec ex malo fundamento ambitionis & avaritiae, ut hae duae pestes nativae radices sint omnium totius curiae malorum. Quae statuta constitutaque quando Ecclesiae & Reip. obsunt, improbis tantum ad quaestum ac ambitum temporarium prosunt, & cum voluntate DEI pugnant, saluberrimum fuerit, si Pontifex Pontifex Max. irrita faciat, & his morbis Ecclefiæ corpus liberet. Cujus generis est magna pars Decretalium & Clementinarum, quibus Ecclesia carere potest adeò, ut his oneribus levari jam pridem cupiat. Aboleantur libri turpiter parasitici atque gnathonici omnes &c. Alterū Henr. Corn. Agrippæ, non semper vani, de vanitate scientiarum Scriptoris, cap. 92. quod sodes lege totum: A jure civili dimanavit Jus canonicum sive Pontificium, quod plerisque sacrosanctissimum videri posset, tam ingeniosa avaritiæ præcepta ac rapiendi formulas specie pietatis adumbrat, cum tamen paucissima in eo statuantur ad pietatem, religionem ac DEI cultum sacramentorumque ritus spectantia, taceo, quod nonnulla DEI verbo contraria aut repugnantia. Cætera omnia non nisi jurgia, lites, fastus, pompæ, tum quæstus ac lucri negocia, Pontificumque Romanorum placita, quibus neque satis sunt, qui olim à sanctis Patribus sunt conditi canones, nisi his continuè accumulent nova decreta, paleas, extravagantes, declaratorias, cancellariæ regulas, ut nullus sit condendorum canonum finis, neque mensura, quæ una omnium Romanorum Pontificum ambitio ac libido est, condendorum scil. novorum canonum, quorum eo usque excrevit arrogantia, ut angelis cœlorum præciperent, ut ex inferno sublata præda rapinâ facere præsumerent, & in mortuorum manes manum mitterent: etiam in divi-
units.tr: What the learned men think of canon law may easily be gathered from what has been said. I will add two or three notable opinions. The first is that of the most serious man, Georg Wicel, in his Via Regia: "But how many thousands of these (that is, unjust) statutes are there in the more recent books? Such a thing the Church of Christ not only rejects, but can no longer bear, nor ought to bear. For they were made beyond the law of God, beyond the law of nature, against the building of the house of the Lord, indeed for its destruction, against the love of neighbour, against the custom of the old and true Church, against the examples of the ancients and holy Fathers; and moreover they rest on the bad foundation of ambition and avarice, these two being the native roots of all the evils of the whole Curia. When these statutes and constitutions are harmful to the Church and the commonwealth, and serve only the wicked, for their temporary gain and ambition, and fight against the will of God, it would be most salutary if the Supreme Pontiff annulled them and freed the body of the Church from these diseases. Of this kind is a great part of the Decretals and Clementines, which the Church could do without, so that it has long wished to be relieved of these burdens. Let all the books that are shamefully parasitic and flattering be abolished, etc." The second is that of Henricus Cornelius Agrippa, the writer not always vain de vanitate scientiarum, chapter 92, which, please read in full: "Canon law, or the Pontifical law, flowed from civil law. Though it might seem most sacred to many, it sketches, under the appearance of piety, such clever precepts of greed and formulas for plunder, although very few things in it are laid down that concern piety, religion, the worship of God and the rites of the sacraments; I say nothing of the many things that are contrary or opposed to the word of God. All the rest are nothing but quarrels, lawsuits, pride, pomp, and the business of profit and gain, and the decrees of the Roman Pontiffs. Nor are the canons once made by the holy Fathers enough for them, unless they continually pile up new decrees, scraps, extravagants, declaratories, rules of the chancery; so that there is no end or measure to the making of canons, which is the single ambition and lust of all the Roman Pontiffs, namely of making new canons. Their arrogance has grown so far that they presume to command the angels of heaven, to make booty from hell, and to lay hands on the shades of the dead, and even, by interpreting, declaring and disputing the divine law, they sometimes exercise tyranny, lest anything be lacking to or taken from the fullness of their power. Moreover, from the canons and decrees of these men we learn that the patrimony of Christ is kingdoms, castles, donations, foundations, allodial lands, wealth and possessions, and the priesthood of Christ..."

units.la: dd in divinam legem, interpretando, declarando, disputando nonnunquam tyrannidem exercerent, ne quid plenitudini potestatis suæ poset deesse aut derogari.
