Ex horum præterea canonibus & decretis dedicimus, Christi patrimonium esse regna, castra, donationes, fundationes, allodia, opes ac possessiones ac sacerdotium Christi Ecclesiaeque primatum esse imperium, regnum: & gladium Christi esse jurisdictionem ac potestatem temporalem: & Petram Ecclesiæ fundamentum esse personam Pontificis: Episcopos esse Ecclesiæ non ministros modo, sed capita: & bona Ecclesiæ esse non modo doctrinam Evangelicam, ardorem fidei, contemptum mundi, sed vectigalia, decimas, oblationes, collectas, purpuram, mitras, aurum, argentum, gemmas, prædia, pecunias, potestatem: Summi Pontificis esse gerere bella, dissolvere fœdera, solvere juramenta, absolvere ab obedientiâ & domum orationis facere spelunctm latronum, ita quod Papa potest deponere Episcopum sine causa, quod potest dare rem alienam, quod non potest committere Simoniam, quod potest dispensare contra votum, contra juramentum, contra jus naturale, & nemo debet illi dicere, cur ita facis? Episcoporum vivo officium esse jam non prædicare verbum DEI, sed datis alapis confirmare pueros, conferre ordines, dedicare templa, baptizare campanas, consecrare aras & calices. Ex iisdem fontibus prodierunt cautelæ istæ, quibus hodie citra Simoniam Episcopatus & beneficia emuntur venduntur que, & quicquid praterea est nundinationum & monopoliorum in gratiis, in condonationibus, in indulgentiis, in dispensationibus & similibus rapinarum formulis, à quibus etiam in gratuitis ab ipso DEO factis peccatorum remissionibus precium statutum est, & inferorum pœnis inventum est lucrum. &c. His & similibus rationibus motus, ut credo, Theod. Bibliander solebat Corpus canonicum vocare Pludermentum delirissimum, teste Lomeiero de Biblioth. cap. 8. pag. 164. De Glossis, hoc est judicium Johan. Sleid. lib. 3. de quat. summ. Monarch. Mirum videri possit esse homines, qui tantum elaborare velint, ut ea quae parum aptè, perperam etiam & minus prudenter atque pie, sed & ridiculè dicta sunt, tanquam oraculum aliquod mordicus arripiant, & in iis interpretandis, enucleandis, vestiendis omnem operam & ætatem consumant, quasi ad conducti essent, ut alienam stultitiam & errorem vigiliis & labore suo maximo defendant, & in alterius impudentiam, sui pudoris existimationem amittant. Cujacius ad c. X. extr. de sentent. & re jud. Nullos dicit Doctores esse ineptiores, quam qui in Jus Pontificium scripserunt. Contradictiones hujus juris collegit multas & cum disputat. ad institut. vulgavit Doctiss. JC. Jacob. Wissenbach.
units.tr: in divine law, by interpreting, declaring and disputing, sometimes exercised tyranny, so that nothing might be lacking to, or be taken from, the fullness of their power. Furthermore, from their canons and decrees we learn that Christ's patrimony consists of kingdoms, camps, gifts, foundations, allodial lands, wealth and possessions; that the priesthood of Christ and the primacy of the Church are empire and kingdom; that the sword of Christ is jurisdiction and temporal power; that the Rock on which the Church is founded is the person of the Pontiff; that bishops are not merely ministers of the Church but its heads; and that the goods of the Church are not only evangelical doctrine, ardour of faith and contempt of the world, but tolls, tithes, offerings, collections, purple, mitres, gold, silver, gems, estates, money and power. The Supreme Pontiff's business is to wage wars, dissolve treaties, loose oaths, and absolve from obedience, and to make the house of prayer a den of robbers. Thus the Pope may depose a bishop without cause, may give away what is another's, cannot commit simony, can dispense against a vow, against an oath, against natural law, and no one may say to him, "Why do you act thus?" The office of bishops now is no longer to preach the Word of God, but to confirm boys with slaps, confer orders, dedicate churches, baptize bells, and consecrate altars and chalices. From the same sources came those safeguards by which today bishoprics and benefices are bought and sold without simony, and whatever else there is of trading and monopolies in graces, in remissions, in indulgences, in dispensations and similar forms of plunder, from which even the forgiveness of sins, freely granted by God himself, has been given a price, and profit has been found in the punishments of hell, etc. Moved by these and similar considerations, as I believe, Theodor Bibliander used to call the canon law a most mad patchwork, as witnessed by Lomeier On Libraries, ch. 8, p. 164. On the Glosses, this is the judgement of Johannes Sleidanus, Book 3, On the Four Chief Monarchies: It may seem a marvel that there are men who wish to labour so hard to seize tenaciously upon things that were said unsuitably, wrongly and less wisely and piously, and indeed ridiculously, as though they were some oracle, and who spend all their effort and life in interpreting, explaining and dressing them up, as though they were hired to defend another's folly and error with their great vigils and labour, and in another's shamelessness lose the reputation of their own modesty. Cujacius, on c. 10, extra, On Sentence and Res Judicata, says that there are no doctors more inept than those who wrote on the Pontifical law. The learned jurist Jacob Wissenbach collected many of the contradictions of this law and published them with his Disputations on the Institutes.

units.la: Sed nos ad Historiam & seculum XVI. transimus, deerant corpori Canonico, ut in omnibus cum corpore Civilis Juris conveniret, institutiones. Hic perpetuum nomen & immortalem Gloriam captans, instar Triboniani, Paulus Lancelottus, Pontifici Romano Paulo quarto consilium scribendarum institutionum juris Canonici dedit, & ab eo mandatum, ut ipse in Praefatione institutionum refert, verius approbationem propositae sibi scriptionis, obtinuit, quam spatio triennii ipso teste, postquam in patriam à colloquio Pontificis revenit, perfecit; Verius tamen est eum ad minimum per quindecim annos antequam ederet, occupatum fuisse in hoc opere scribendo, quod ex literis Joh. Franc. Cardinalis de Gambara ad eum anno 1563. scriptis satis colligi potest, ita ille ad Lancelottum. Agitur annus sextus decimus, quo ego Perusiae te Praeceptore primae juris civilis initia urgebam & tu jam tum opus hujusmodi sub incude habebas, idque propediem editurus videbaris, unde quod tamdiu retinueris, erit fortasse qui te acusef. Perfecto opere, Romam contendens, cum Censores Pontificii Fabius Acorombonus, Julius Oradinus & Antonius Massa opus examinassent, & de dubiis cum Lancelotto contulissent, imo alii Theologi, ipse etiam Diocesos ceseos Perusinæ Inquisitor Matthæus Lachius probassent, attamen à Pontifice approbationem, per integrum biennium quo Romæ hæsit, nec ut Pontificis nomine ederentur, obtinere potuit. Quare delusus, deposita omni spe, in Patriam concessit, & ne à Concilio Tridentino, quod jam ad finem properabat præveniretur, & multa in institutionibus mutare secundum ejus tenorem, novam censuram eamque difficilem petere, teneretur: opus ipse privato nomine edidit ann. 1563. mense Augusto; & mense Decembri concilio finis impositus. Edito concilio sæpe rogatus est Lancelottus, ut mutata in concilio inserteret, sed id facere semper detractavit, dixitque se exemplum Justiniani sequi, qui propter mutationes juris in codice repetitæ prælectionis & Novellis, nunquam mutavit institutiones, Vid: Franciscum Mancinum in Epistol. ad Cardin. Joh. Francis. de Gambara. Hoc seculo XVII. cepto sub Paulo quinto iterum tentata est approbatio Institutionum Pauli Lancelotti, urgentibus Scipione Cobellutio Cardinale, Galeotto Oddone Balivo Narniensi & Leandro Galganetto JC; sed ab hoc Paulo, non magis impetrari potuit, quam à Paulo Quarto: id solum obtinuit, ut ejus institutiones corpori Juris Canonici adderentur, sine tamen ulla confirmatione, in quo ad famam Lancelotti perennabunt. Vide sis de hisce ipsius Lancelotti Dedicationem ad Pium IV. Pontificem, & Proemium ad Juris Pontificii Candidatos; & Doctas ad utrumque Jacob. Ziegleri notas.
units.tr: But we pass on to history and the sixteenth century. The Canonical body still lacked institutes, to match the corpus of civil law in every respect. Here Paul Lancelotti, seeking a lasting name and immortal glory, like Tribonian, gave advice to Pope Paul IV that institutes of canon law should be written; and he obtained from him, as he himself reports in the Preface to the Institutes, a commission, or rather approval, for the work proposed to him, which he completed within three years, as he himself says, after returning home from his audience with the Pope. Yet it is more likely that he was occupied with writing this work for at least fifteen years before he published it, as can fairly be gathered from the letter of Cardinal Giovanni Francesco Gambara to him, written in 1563. So he writes to Lancelotti: It is the sixteenth year since I, when you were my teacher at Perugia, was pressing upon you the first principles of civil law, and you already then had a work of this kind under the anvil, and you seemed about to publish it shortly; so that you have held it back so long may perhaps be something that someone will bring against you. When the work was finished, he went to Rome, where the Pontifical censors, Fabio Acorombono, Giulio Oradini and Antonio Massa, examined the work and conferred with Lancelotti about its doubtful points; indeed other theologians approved it, and Matteo Lachi, inquisitor of the diocese of Perugia, approved it as well. Yet he could not obtain the Pope's approval for it, nor that it be published under the Pope's name, during the whole two years he stayed in Rome. Therefore, disappointed and having abandoned all hope, he returned to his homeland, and, so that he would not be forestalled by the Council of Trent, which was already hastening to its close, and so that he would not be obliged to change much in the Institutes according to its tenor and to seek a new and difficult censure, he published the work on his own authority in August 1563; and in December the council was brought to an end. After the council was published, Lancelotti was often asked to insert the changes made at the council, but he always refused to do so, and said that he was following the example of Justinian, who, though the law had been altered by the repeated revision of the Code and by the Novels, never changed the Institutes. See Francesco Mancini in his letter to Cardinal Giovanni Francesco Gambara. In this seventeenth century, begun under Paul V, approval of the Institutes of Paul Lancelotti was tried again, urged by Cardinal Scipione Cobelluzzi, Galeotto Oddone, bailiff of Narni, and Leandro Galganetti, jurist; but from this Paul no more could be obtained than from Paul IV. It was achieved only that his Institutes be added to the body of canon law, yet without any confirmation; in which they will endure for Lancelotti's fame. See, if you please, Lancelotti's own dedication to Pope Pius IV and his preface to the candidates in pontifical law, and the learned notes of Jacob Ziegler on both.

units.la: Eodem fere tempore quo Lancelottus, Marcus Antonius Cucchus Jurisconsultus Ticinensis, scripsit privata auctoritate Institutiones juris Canonici, quas edidit Anno 1564. IX. Kal. Augusti, inscripsitque Paulo Aringono Senatus Mediolanensis Præsidi; Hic quoque Concilium Tridentinum prævenire studuit, & operi decem annos, ut in Præfat. testatur, impendit. Videtur eandem cum Lancelotto laudem anhelasse, & unum alteri obstetisse, ne Pontificis nomine alterutrius labor vulgaretur. Scripta adornavit alia, quæ prætereo. Dedit ad Institutiones ejus notas Doctissimus & Celeberrimus Theologus Samuel Maresius. Id tantum moneo, vitandum esse Simleri in Bibliotheca errorem, qui hunc Cucchum, Antonium Cunchium ex Oporini Catalogo vocat, & conjicit Antonium Contium esse legendum, quod utrumque falsum.
units.tr: At nearly the same time as Lancelotti, Marco Antonio Cucchi, jurist of Pavia, wrote on his own private authority Institutes of Canon Law, which he published in the year 1564, on the ninth day before the Kalends of August, and dedicated to Paolo Aringhi, president of the Senate of Milan. He too strove to forestall the Council of Trent, and spent ten years on the work, as he testifies in the Preface. He seems to have longed for the same praise as Lancelotti, and to have stood in the way of the other, so that the labour of neither would be published under the Pope's name. He composed other writings, which I pass over. The most learned and celebrated theologian Samuel Maresius added notes to his Institutes. I will only warn that the error of Simler in his Bibliotheca is to be avoided, who from Oporinus's catalogue calls this Cucchi "Antonius Cunchius", and conjectures that Antonius Contius should be read; both of these are false.

units.la: Pius ille quartus Pontifex, sub quo Institutiones Juris Lancelotti & Cucchi prodierunt, inclaruit, vulgatione Concilii Tri- dentini, cujus historiam, quia multi eam dederunt, maximè Paulus Sarpius, sub nomine Petri Suavis Polani; (de quo vide amicum nostrum Clariss: & Consultiss: Virum Vinc. Placcium, Syntag. de Scriptoribus Pseudonymis num. 716. pag. 242.) & Pallavicinus; (Prior quidem magis ex veritate, alter magis ad stylum Curiæ Romanæ) nos consulto præterimus. Canones ejus extant in omnium manibus, cum Declarationibus Cardinalium, item Examine Martini Chemnitii Theologi, & Vincentii Gentileti Jurisconsulti. Minus notæ ejus curæ, quas ad emendandum Decretum Gratiani adhibuit. Hanc in rem selegit Romæ Cardinales, & undique conquisitos Viros Doctissimos, qui Gratianum ex fontibus restituerent; Quibus Pius Quintus ejus successor aliquot addidit, opus autem demum perfectum est sub Gregorio decimo tertio, & ab eo vulgatum, Anno 1582. Pontificatus XI. ut indicat Præfatio quæ Decreto præmissa est. Viri sub Pio quarto & quinto ad hoc opus Selecti, ut eos recenset Anton. Augustinus in fine libri primi de Emend. Grat. in notis. pag. 342. nostræ edit. sunt sequentes.
units.tr: That Pope Pius IV, under whom the Institutes of Lancelotti and Cucchi were published, grew famous for the promulgation of the Council of Trent. Since many have given its history, above all Paolo Sarpi under the name of Pietro Soave Polano (on whom see our friend, the most distinguished and learned man Vincenzo Placcius, Syntagma on Pseudonymous Writers, no. 716, p. 242), and Pallavicini (the former more faithful to the truth, the latter more to the style of the Roman Curia), we deliberately pass them by. His canons are in everyone's hands, together with the declarations of the cardinals, likewise the Examination by the theologian Martin Chemnitz, and that of the jurist Vincenzo Gentile. Less well known is his care, which he applied to the emendation of Gratian's Decretum. For this purpose he chose cardinals in Rome, and learned men of the greatest erudition gathered from every quarter, who were to restore Gratian from the sources. To these his successor Pius V added several more; the work, however, was finally completed under Gregory XIII, and published by him in the year 1582, the eleventh of his pontificate, as the preface placed before the Decretum indicates. The men chosen for this work under Pius IV and V, as Antonio Agustín enumerates them at the end of the first book of On the Emendation of Gratian, in the notes, p. 342 of our edition, are the following.
Names of the Cardinals.
M. Antonius Columna, a Roman.

units.la: Hugo Boncompagnus Bononiensis, postea Greg. XIII. dictus P. M.
units.tr: Hugo Boncompagni of Bologna, afterwards called Gregory XIII, the Supreme Pontiff.
Alexander Sforza, a Roman.
Guglielmo Sirleto of Calabria.
Francesco Alciati of Milan.

units.la: His additi sunt ab eod. Pio V.
units.tr: These were added by the same Pius V:
Guido Ferrero of Vercelli.
Antonio Carafa of Naples.
Names of the Doctors.

units.la: Felix Montaltus Gener. ordin. S. Franc. postea Card. hodie P. M. Xystus V. dictus.
units.tr: Felice Montalto, Minister General of the Franciscan Order, afterwards a cardinal, and today known as Pope Sixtus V.

units.la: Christophorus Patavinus Gener. ord. S. Aug. eremitar.
units.tr: Cristoforo of Padua, Minister General of the Order of the Hermits of St Augustine.

units.la: Thomas Manricus ord. S. Domin. Magister sacri Palat.
units.tr: Tommaso Manrique of the Order of St Dominic, Master of the Sacred Palace.
....Lucatelli of Bologna, afterwards bishop of Reggio di Lepido.

units.la: Josephus.... Veronen. ord. S. August. postea Sacrista Palatii, & Episcopus Signinus in Campania.
units.tr: Giuseppe.... of Verona, of the Order of St Augustine, afterwards Sacristan of the Palace and bishop of Segni in Campania.

units.la: Franciscus Turrianus Hispanus, postea Societ. Jesus.
units.tr: Francesco Turriano, a Spaniard, afterwards of the Society of Jesus.

units.la: Marianus Victorius Reatinus, postea Episcopus Amerinen.
units.tr: Mariano Vittori of Rieti, afterwards bishop of Amelia.

units.la: Michaël Thomasius Majoricensis, postea Episcopus Ilerdensis.
units.tr: Michele Tommasi of Majorca, afterwards bishop of Lleida.
Girolamo Parisetti of Reggio.
Antonio Cucco of Milan.

units.la: Joannes Marsa Hispanus. Franciscus Leo Hispan. postea Societ. Jesus. Additi sunt. Melchior Cornelius Lusitanus. Latinus Latinius Viterbien. Arnaldus Pontacus Gallus. Petrus Ciacconius Hispanus. Franciscus Pegna Hispanus, cujus sunt additiones Decretalium sine nomine, quia templum Dianæ incendisse visus est.
units.tr: Juan de la Mársa, a Spaniard. Francisco Leo, a Spaniard, afterwards of the Society of Jesus. These were added. Melchior Cornelius, a Portuguese. Latino Latini of Viterbo. Arnaud de Pontac, a Frenchman. Pedro Ciaconio, a Spaniard. Francisco Pegna, a Spaniard, whose additions to the Decretals carry no name, because he was thought to have set fire to the temple of Diana.

units.la: Meminit Gregorius Decreti quidem Gratiani tantum in suâ Præfatione emendati, sed Decretales restitutas suæ integritati esse, non tantum titulus operis, sed etiam subjectæ singulis fere capitibus verba fontium, & rejectiones ad fontes, ostendunt. Factæ autem illæ tum ex Anterioribus Collectionibus, de quibus supra, tum ex Regestis aut detortè Registris Pontificum. Est autem Regestum, quod postea degeneravit in Registrum, liber iste in quo suas solebat describere Decretales quisque Pontifex ; Quilibet enim habet peculiare; in his integræ scribebantur Decretales, quæ in collectionibus plerumque erant truncatæ, in principio in medio vel fine. Non valde aliena hæc Regesta, à diptychis de quibus supra dictum. Vox occurrit quoque in jure Civili; ducta à more referendi aliquid in volumina singusingularibus officiis, vel negotiis destinata, quod in ea regerentur res. Regerendi verbum hac in re proprium est: Quintilianus lib. 2. c. 11. in sin. Similisq; commentariis puerorum fit, in quos ea quae aliis declamantibus laudata sunt, regerunt. Et libr. 3. cap. 8. Sunt enim velut res regestae in hos commentarios, quos puer deduxerat Schola. Inde Regesta dicitur constitutio, in l. 14. C. Theodof. de indulgent. debit. lib. XI. id est in acta, seu gesta relata Comitis sacrarum largitionum. Inde Judicum acta, in quae regerebatur constitutio, Regesta dicta. Theodosius Junior in Novella de Codic. Theod. confirmat, nullas constitutiones in judiciis extra Codicem istum referri vult. Exceptis, inquit, iis quae habentur apud militum sancta principia, vel de titulis publicis expensarum, aliarumque rerum gratia, quae in Regestis, diversorum officiorum relata sunt. Ita quoque apud Justin. occurrit vox in l. unic. C. de Codic. Justin. confir. & apud Vopiscum in Probo. Qui in describenda vita Probi, dicit se usum esse Regestis scribarum porticus Porphyreticae, actis etiam Senatus ac Populi. Ex quibus locis colligit Doctissimus Jacob. Gothofredus in opere Immortali ad Codicis Theodof. d. l. 14. de Indulg. debit. Regesta fuisse monumenta, actaque publica diversorum officiorum & judicum, veluti veluti Præfectorum Prætorio, aliorumque judicum, qua civilium, qua militarium; imo & in Urbe Roma, scribarum, de quibus agit l. 1. Cod. Theod. de lucris officiorum; in quæ inter alia referebantur constitutiones Principum ad cujusque officium pertinentes. Indeque & Regerendarij dicti. teft. Cujac. lib. 15. obf. 37. in sin. Quemadmodum itaq; Actio ipsa, regestio; ita & libri actaque, in quæ regerebantur seu referebantur Regesta dicta. Glossæ nomicæ, κῆνσον ηεῖ ρεγέσαν, lege ρεγέσον τὴν ὑπομνηματικὴν ἢ αρχαίων, ἀντὶ τῆς ὑπομνηματικῆς. Ab his forte acceperunt Pontifices ut libros, in quibus suas decretales referebant Regesta, postea Registra vocarent. Occurrit apud Anastasium in vita Nicolai Regestum Episcopi. Budæus in posterioribus. Comment. ad ff. Regesta dicit esse, quæ Græcis ὑπομνήματα, vel ὑπομνηματισμοὶ dicuntur. Idem Regestum Pontificii scriptores vocant originale, item dicunt esse in integra nempe Decretali, id est Originali, vide exempla ex Joh. Andr. apud Alberic. Gentil. de libr. jur. Canon. cap. 3. pag. 30. & seq. Ex his Regestis postea sunt Bullaria confecta, quæ exhibent constitutiones Pontificum integras ex regestis; Quale Anno 1588. Romæ edidit Laertius Cherubinus de Neurfia JC. quod magnum vocavit. In eo exhibet Constitutiones Pontificum Romanorum à Gregorio VII. usque ad Sixtum V. cum rubricis, summariis & lucubrationibus. Summam Bullarii in principio hujus seculi, dedit Stephanus Quaranta, in qua exhibet Pontificum Constitutiones editas, post libros juris Canonici vulgatos, usque ad Paulum V. quæ edita est Venetiis 1609. eam continuavit Prosper de Augustino JC. & additionibus illustravit. Prodiit illa Lugduni 1621. Dicta bullaria à Bullis. Bulla quid proprie sit satis notum, nempe id quod in aquis intumescit instar pilæ & cito rumpitur. In Glossis Cyrilli πομφόλυξ dicitur. Ab his ad diplomata Imperatorum, ab Imperatoribus ad Papalia diplomata est translata vox: quæ Bullæ dicta, à sigillo quo munita erant, quod Bulla vocabatur, quia sigillum illud Bullæ formam referebat; nam sigillum ceræ protuberanti instar orbiculi vel umbilici imprimebatur. Aut potius ut censet Doctissimus Salmas. de subsign. test. cap. 32. pag. 325. quia bullæ formam haberent, & eodem modo dependerent ex chartis, ut illæ ex pectore prætextatorum, veteribus enim Romanis in more positum, bullam auream suspendere in pectore puerorum & triumphantium. Qua de re vid. Festum Asconium nium in III. Verrin. Macrob. satur. I. c. 6. & alios. Similia his bullis fuere sigilla, quæ posterior ætas chartis ac diplomatis affigebat & appendebat. Dependebant hæ bullæ ex metallo vel cera filo lineo vel serico annexæ chartis. Nil frequentius apud posteriores Græcos in Imperio Constantinopolitano, quam ξύλλω legere pro sigillo, exempla cumulat Doctiss. Meursius in Lexico Græco-barbar. inde βυλλάτειν Bullare signare ἀξυλλωτον, quod bullam vel sigillum non habet. Glossæ Græcobarbaræ. ἀσπμαντα. ἀσφεξίγισα. ἀξυλλωτα. ἐφύλαικτα. Erant Bullæ quadruplices aureæ, argenteæ, cereæ & plumbeæ, χρυσόξυλλον, ἀργυρόξυλλον, κηρόξυλλον & μολυβδόβυλλον. Imperatores diplomata, mandata, ad Reges, Sultanos, aurea bulla muniebant, literis rubris subscribebat, aliquando etiam Argentea; cujus testimonium habemus apud Phranzem in Chron. lib. 2. cap. 10. Ego cum literis bulla argentea insignitis & jurejurando formatis & multo milite missus sum &c. Item apud Luitprandum in Legat. Ad matrem, uxorem, filium utebatur, cerea seu κηρόξυλλω; ad Despotum, Patriarcham, Sabastocratorem & Cæsarem plumbea seu μολιβδίνης βύλλης, ut habet Codinus. Cerea iterum duplex erat, Rubra & Prasina utraque usus
units.tr: Gregory indeed mentions only that the Decree of Gratian was emended in his Preface, but that the Decretals were restored to their integrity is shown not only by the title of the work but also by the words of the sources printed beneath almost every chapter, and by the references to the sources. These were taken partly from the earlier collections mentioned above, and partly from the Regesta, or, as it was corrupted, the Registra, of the Popes. Now the Regestum, which later degenerated into the Registrum, is the book in which each Pope was accustomed to copy out his own Decretals, for each has his own; in these the Decretals were written out in full, whereas in the collections they were for the most part truncated, at the beginning, in the middle, or at the end. These Regesta are not very unlike the diptychs mentioned above. The word also occurs in civil law, derived from the custom of recording something in volumes kept for individual offices or business, so that the matter is entered (regerentur) in them. The verb regerere is proper to this sense. Quintilian, Book 2, chapter 11, near the end: "It is like the notebooks of boys, in which they enter the things that were praised in other speakers' declamations." And Book 3, chapter 8: "For these things are, as it were, entered into these notebooks which the boy had brought from school." Hence a decree is called regesta, in Code of Theodosius, law 14, de indulgentiis debitorum, book XI, that is, a record of the acts or proceedings of the Count of the Sacred Largesses. Hence the acts of judges, into which a decree was entered, were called Regesta. Theodosius the Younger, in his Novel on the Theodosian Code, wishes that no decrees be cited in judicial proceedings apart from that Code: "Except," he says, "those which are kept among the sacred principles of the soldiers, or concerning public accounts of expenses and other matters, which are entered in the records of the various offices." The word likewise occurs in Justinian, in the single law of the Code on the confirmation of the Justinian Code, and in Vopiscus in the life of Probus, who, describing the life of Probus, says that he made use of the Regesta of the scribes of the Porphyry Portico, and also of the acts of the Senate and People. From these passages the most learned Jacob Gothofredus, in his immortal work on the Theodosian Code, on the said law 14 de indulgentiis debitorum, concludes that the Regesta were records and public acts of the various offices and judges, such as the Praetorian Prefects and other judges, both civil and military; and even in the city of Rome, of the scribes, of whom he speaks in law 1 of the Theodosian Code, de lucris officiorum, in which, among other things, the decrees of the emperors pertaining to each office were entered. Hence also they were called Regerendarii, as Cujas testifies in Book 15 of Observations, chapter 37, near the end. Just as the act itself is regestio, so the books and records in which things were entered or recorded are called Regesta. The Greek glosses read [κῆνσον ηεῖ ρεγέσαν], which should be read [ρεγέσον τὴν ὑπομνηματικὴν ἢ ἀρχαίων], instead of [τῆς ὑπομνηματικῆς]. Perhaps from these the Popes took the name, calling the books in which they recorded their Decretals Regesta, and afterwards Registra. The phrase Regestum Episcopi occurs in Anastasius in the life of Nicholas. Budaeus, in his later commentary on the Digest, says that the Regesta are what the Greeks call [ὑπομνήματα] or [ὑπομνηματισμοί]. The Pontifical writers likewise call the same Regestum the originale, and say that it contains the decretal in integra, that is, in its original form; see the examples from John Andreas in Alberico Gentili, On books of canon law, chapter 3, p. 30 and following. From these Regesta the Bullaria were afterwards compiled, which present the constitutions of the Popes entire, taken from the registers. Such a work was published at Rome in 1588 by Lorenzo Cherubini of Norcia, a jurist, whom he called the Great Bullary. In it he sets out the constitutions of the Roman Pontiffs from Gregory VII down to Sixtus V, with rubrics, summaries and commentaries. At the beginning of this century Stefano Quaranta gave a summary of the Bullary, in which he set out the constitutions of the Popes published after the books of canon law were issued, down to Paul V; it was published at Venice in 1609. Prosper de Augustino, a jurist, continued it and illustrated it with additions. It came out at Lyon in 1621. The bullaries are so called from the Bullae. What a bulla properly is is well known: that which swells up in water like a ball and quickly bursts. In the glosses of Cyril it is called [πομφόλυξ]. From this the word was transferred to the diplomas of the emperors, and from the emperors to the papal diplomas; they were called Bullae from the seal with which they were sealed, which was called the Bulla, because that seal resembled a bulla in shape; for the seal was impressed in wax, bulging like a little ball or boss. Or rather, as the most learned Salmasius thinks, On subscriptions of witnesses, chapter 32, p. 325, because they had the shape of a bulla and hung from the charters in the same way as those bullae hung from the breasts of the children of the nobility; for it was the custom among the ancient Romans to hang a golden bulla on the breasts of boys and of those who triumphed. On this matter see Festus Asconius on the third Verrine, Macrobius, Saturnalia, Book 1, chapter 6, and others. Similar to these bullae were the seals which a later age attached and appended to charters and diplomas. These bullae hung from metal or wax, attached to the charters by a linen or silk thread. Nothing was more common among the later Greeks in the Constantinopolitan empire than to read [ξύλλω] for seal; the most learned Meursius in his Greek-barbarous lexicon gathers many examples, and hence [βυλλάτειν], to bulla or seal, [ἀξυλλωτον], which has no bulla or seal. The Greek-barbarous glosses: [ἀσπμαντα], [ἀσφεξίγισα], [ἀξυλλωτα], [ἐφύλαικτα]. There were bullae of four kinds: golden, silver, waxen and leaden, [χρυσόξυλλον], [ἀργυρόξυλλον], [κηρόξυλλον] and [μολυβδόβυλλον]. The emperors sealed diplomas and mandates to kings and sultans with a golden bulla, subscribed in red ink, and sometimes with a silver one; we have evidence of this in Phrantzes, Chronicle, Book 2, chapter 10: "I was sent with letters marked with a silver bulla and formed by oath, and with a large escort, etc." Likewise in Liutprand, in the Embassy. To a mother, a wife or a son they used a waxen seal, [κηρόξυλλω]; to a despot, a patriarch, a sebastocrator and a caesar a leaden one, [μολιβδίνης βύλλης], as Codinus says. Again, the waxen seal was of two kinds, red and green, and the emperor used both.

units.la: [Greek terms in this page are transcribed as best legible.] sus Imperator, Prasina sola Patriarcha. Videatur hac de re Jul. Cæs. Bulengerus de Imperat. Rom. lib. 2. cap. 10. & Ioh. Meursius in Glossar. voce χηροβύκλον. Qui putat δικτέον fuisse, quando Imperator duplici cera, rubra & Prasina signabat. Sed melius id Doctiss. Salmasius, de subscr. & subsig. testam. cap. 32. pag. 330. δικτέον explicat de signo utrinque, seu utroque latere expressō, quam & διπλυχον βύλλην & διπλυχον χηρόβυλλον vocarunt; Hoc duplicem Bullam vocat, ubi vero ab una tantum parte signum impressum, simplex Bulla dicebatur. Δικτέον hoc facit duplex, rubrum & Prasinum. Vide Salmas. ibid. exempla proferentem. Quod non alienum à moribus bullandi Pontificum Romanorum, qui ante Coronationem subscribunt, Datum anno 1. die tertio, suscepti à nobis officii Apostolatus; & tunc sigillant non nisi bulla simplici, seu tali, quæ habet tantum ab una parte DD. Petri & Pauli imagines, in plumbo, ex altera vero parte plana est. Post Coronationem autem, scribunt. Datum Anno Pontificatus nostri & duplici utuntur bulla: cum prædictis imaginibus ab una & nomine Pontificis ab alia parte; vid. Gregor. Tholosan. Syntag. jur. Universf. lib. 15. cap. 3. n. 24. & seqq. Appenditur autem hæc bulla plumbea non nisi arduis diplomatibus; breve apostolicum, quod est diploma vel rescriptum Papæ vel pœnitentiarii magni scriptura exigua, in parvis concessa negotiis in papyro, non habet eam; sed in cera rubra imprimitur annulus Piscatoris, ut refert idem Tholos. ibid. lib. 17. c. 15. n. 13. Ex his lucem capit Famosa illa aurea bulla Caroli IV. Imperat. quæ inter leges fundamentales Imperii radiat; ideo aurea Bulla dicta, quia sigillum aureum, vel sigillum Imperatoris majus adpensum erat. Hanc assabre describit Pileus Cardinalis ab Urbano VI. Papa in Germaniam missus Anno 1379. non ita diu post promulgatam aureĄm bullam, apud Clariss. Marq. Freherum ad Petr. ab Andlo lib. 2. cap. 7. qui testatur se vidisse & tenuisse quasdam literas Patentes bonæ memoriæ Caroli Imp. Rom. Librum illum Aureæ Bullæ ita describit; Prædictus Liber erat scriptus in Pergameno in 24. foliis, cum coopertura grossa, in quo erant scripta diversa negotia Sacrum Imperium & Electores ejusdem tangentia: qui quidem Liber transfixus erat cum filis sericis glauci & rubei coloris in volutis, cum Bulla seu Sigillo Aureo rotundo Imperiali appendente, in cujus uno latere apparebat figura Imperialis in Majestate sedens, cum Coronâ Imperiali in capite, habens in manu dextra Sceptrum, & in sinistra sinistra manu Pomum cum Cruce desuper modo Imperiali, & à latere dextro Clypeum cum Aquila, & sinistro Clypeo cum forma Leonis. In circumferentia legebantur hæc verba: CAROLUS QUARTUS, DIVINA FAVENTE CLEMENTIA ROMANORUM AUGUSTUS ET BOHEMIÆ REX. Ab alio latere. Castrum magnum cum duabus Turribus, habens portam inferius in medio, cum literis: AUREA ROMA. In circumferentia verò legebantur hæc verba: ROMA CAPUT MUNDI, REGIT ORBIS FRENA ROTUNDI. Hæc ille. Ab hoc more signandi Imperatorum, bullas appendendo, ipsa diplomata etiam sunt Bullæ appellatæ. Vide Latissime Joh. Limn: de Jure publ. cap. II. Ab Imperatoribus res transiit ad Patriarchas & ad Pontificem Romanum, qui ex quatuor speciebus supra relatis, elegit sibi μολυβδόβουλλον[?], seu plumbeam bullam, vid. lib. I. Cærem. Eccles. Rom. c. 2. in sin. Quod privilegium etiam dicitur concessisse Venetis. Vid. Celeberrimum juris publici Scriptorem Johan. Limn. lib. I. cap. II. de jur. publ. Rebuffus I. part. prax. benef. bullam dicit, esse scripturam in membrana, plumbo, auro, argento vel ære funiculis pendente jure insignitam. Qui plumbeas hasce bullas membranis appendunt Plumbatores vocantur.
units.tr: ...sus Imperator, Prasina sola Patriarcha. See on this matter Jul. Caes. Bulengerus, de Imperat. Rom. lib. 2. cap. 10., and Joh. Meursius in his Glossary under the word χηροβύκλον [chērobyklon]. Someone who thinks that δικτέον [diktheon] was used when the emperor sealed with double wax, red and green, is mistaken. The learned Salmasius, de subscr. & subsig. testam. cap. 32. pag. 330, explains δικτέον [diktheon] better, as a seal impressed on both sides, or on either side, which they also called διπλυχον βύλλην [diplycho bullen] and διπλυχον χηρόβυλλον [diplycho chērobyllon]. He calls this a double bulla, whereas where the impression was made on one side only it was called a simple bulla. This δικτέον [diktheon] is double, red and green. See Salmasius, ibid., who gives examples. This is not foreign to the custom of the Roman Pontiffs in sealing bullae, who before their coronation subscribe Datum anno 1. die tertio, of the apostolic office taken up by us, and then seal only with a simple bulla, that is one bearing the images of Saints Peter and Paul on one side only, in lead, the other side being plain. After the coronation, however, they write Datum Anno Pontificatus nostri and use a double bulla: with the aforesaid images on one side and the name of the Pontiff on the other. See Gregor. Tholosan., Syntag. jur. Universf. lib. 15. cap. 3. n. 24. & seqq. This lead bulla is attached only to weighty documents. The breve apostolicum, which is a letter or rescript of the Pope or of the Grand Penitentiary written in a small hand, granted for minor business on paper, does not have it; instead the Fisherman's ring is impressed in red wax, as the same Tholosanus reports, ibid. lib. 17. c. 15. n. 13. By this the famous Golden Bull of the Emperor Charles IV, which shines among the fundamental laws of the Empire, receives its light. It is called the Golden Bull because a golden seal, or the greater imperial seal, was attached to it. Pileus the Cardinal, sent into Germany by Pope Urban VI in 1379, not long after the Golden Bull was promulgated, describes it vividly; this is quoted by the distinguished Marquard Freher, on Petrus de Andlo lib. 2. cap. 7., who testifies that he saw and held certain open letters of the good memory of Charles, Emperor of the Romans. He describes that Book of the Golden Bull thus: The aforesaid book was written on parchment in 24 leaves, with a thick cover, in which were written various matters touching the Holy Empire and the Electors. This book was pierced with threads of blue and red silk in coils, with a round golden imperial bulla or seal hanging from it. On one side of it appeared the imperial figure seated in majesty, with the imperial crown on his head, holding a sceptre in his right hand, and in his left hand an orb with a cross above it in the imperial manner; and on his right side a shield with an eagle, and on the left a shield with the form of a lion. In the circumference these words were read: CHARLES THE FOURTH, BY THE FAVOUR OF DIVINE CLEMENCY AUGUSTUS OF THE ROMANS AND KING OF BOHEMIA. On the other side, a great castle with two towers, having a gate below in the middle, with the letters: GOLDEN ROME. In the circumference, however, these words were read: ROME THE HEAD OF THE WORLD, RULES THE REINS OF THE ROUND WORLD. Thus he. From this manner of the emperors sealing by hanging bullae, the diplomas themselves were also called Bullae. See very fully Joh. Limnaeus, de Jure publ. cap. II. From the emperors the practice passed to the Patriarchs and to the Roman Pontiff, who of the four kinds mentioned above chose for himself the μολυβδόβουλλον [molybdobullon], that is the lead bulla. See lib. I. Cærem. Eccles. Rom. c. 2. in sin. This privilege is also said to have been granted to the Venetians. See the most celebrated writer on public law, Joh. Limnaeus, lib. I. cap. II. de jur. publ. Rebuffus, I. part. prax. benef., says that a bulla is a writing on parchment, hung by cords from lead, gold, silver or bronze, and marked with the seal. Those who attach these lead bullae to parchments are called Plumbatores.

units.la: Vid. Vestrium Octavianum lib. 1. Introduct. in R. aul. act. cap. 3. & ex eo Herm. Hugon. de prim. scrib. orig. cap. 31. pag. 192. De Origine hujus bullæ Pontificiæ ex Polydori Vergilii libr. 8. cap. 2. de invent. rerum, Auctor Apologiæ antiq. Academiæ Oxoniensis lib. 1. n. 114. pag. 62. hæc refert. Constat Agathonem, quo sedente magna sedi Romanæ facta est honoris accessio, in cera annulo impressisse sigilla, verum postea cum Romanus Pontifex multa irrogaret privilegia, ut diplomata diuturniora forent, placuit Stephano III. ac deinde Hadriano I. tabulas Apostolicas plumbo obsignari; Fuit is annus salutis 772, cum ipse Hadrianus factus est Pontifex, nam antiquius non reperitur sigillum plumbeum. Vestigia quædam vocis transierunt in alias quoque linguas, Belgæ Billet vocant scripturam in qua quid brevibus notatum, veluti in metatis, seu militum inhospitationibus, cuique militi adsignatur hospitium pittacio, quod vocant een Billet, Angli a Bil, inscriptum symbolum, syngraphàm &c. Quia hic in bullas incidimus, non incommodo loco, & alia Pontificiarum Constitutionum nomina hic expedimus. Occurrunt hic Commonitoria, quæ nulli rei magis comparari possunt, quam Imperatorum Mandatis, de quibus titulum habemus in Codice; Ut ea dabantur
units.tr: See Vestrius Octavianus, lib. 1. Introduct. in R. aul. act. cap. 3., and from him Herm. Hugo, de prim. scrib. orig. cap. 31. pag. 192. On the origin of this papal bulla, the author of the Apologia antiq. Academiae Oxoniensis, lib. 1. n. 114. pag. 62, relates the following from Polydore Vergil, libr. 8. cap. 2. de invent. rerum: It is established that under Agatho, in whose pontificate the Roman see received a great increase of honour, seals were impressed in wax with a ring; but later, when the Roman Pontiff granted many privileges, so that the documents might last longer, it pleased Stephen III and then Hadrian I to seal apostolic tablets with lead. This was in the year of salvation 772, when Hadrian himself became Pontiff, for no earlier lead seal is found. Some traces of the word have passed into other languages too. The Belgians call Billet a document in which something is briefly noted, as in the billeting, or quartering of soldiers, where a lodging is assigned to each soldier by a slip which they call een Billet; the English say a Bill, an inscribed token, a bond, etc. Since we have fallen into bullae here, it is not inconvenient to explain here also other names of papal constitutions. Commonitoria occur here, which can be compared to nothing more than the mandates of the emperors, of which we have a title in the Code. As those were given

units.la: tug tur legatis, & iis qui ad provincias administrandas ablegabantur ab Imperatoribus, sic à Pontificibus Legatis, ut vocant Apostolicis, dantur Commonitoria. Glossæ Basilic. Κομμονιτόριον, ὑπομνηματικὴ ἀποστελλομένη μετὰ φεφαξέως. & Suidas Κομμονιτόριον, ὑπομνηματικὴ φεφαχλικὴ ἀποστελλομένη εἰς χωρεῖς. Gloss. vet. ὑπομνηστικὸν Commonitorium. Ita quoque in jure nostro Commonitorium legitur pro formula & mandato officii. in l. 10. Cod. Theod. de Curiosis libr. 6. tit. 29. Commonitoriis competentibus atque Mandatis instructi. Vid. Iacob. Gothofred. ad istam Legem, & potiss. ad l. 27. ejusd. Cod. de erog. militar. annon. Ammianus. lib. 28. Commonitorium repertum est, manu inscriptum Hymetij, & iterum. Commonitorium cum Augusti literis tradidit, & Symmachus lib. 5. Ep. 20. Commonitorium quo summatim muneri præparanda rescripsi. & eleganter Epist. 21. Quia longum visum est literarum serie agenda complecti, non graveris Commonitorio strictim signata percurrere. Vid. quoque Epistol. 24. ejusdem & formulam commonitorii apud Cassiodor. lib. 7. variar. cap. 22. Tale Alarici in fronte Codic. Theodosiani, Commonitorium Timotheo. V. S. Comiti. Ab his & in Ecclesiam videntur translata commonitoria, vel commonitoria litera, quæ & memoriales moriales dicebantur, dabanturque legatis, vel nunciis ut scirent quid in suscepta legatione deberent agere; vocis significatio, ostendit satis, ideo sic dicta, quia monerent eos, quibus dabantur, quid agendum esset. Occurrit formula Commonitorii, in Codice Ecclesiæ Africanæ, Canon. 93. cujus inscriptio est Κομμονιτώριον, ὅπερ ἔλαβον οἱ κατὰ τῶν Donatistῶν πεπεισευτωί. Commonitorium, quale acceperunt legati contra Donatistas. Postea late instruuntur Theasius & Euodius, quid apud Impp. contra Donatistas agere debeant. Vide & Commonitorium Zozimi Papæ quod dedit Legatis ad Concilium Carthaginense, in principio Ejusdem Codicis, in Bibliothec. juris Canonici veteris. pag. 330. & Justell. notas, pag. 419. & aliud bene longum in annal. Baronii tom. X. ad Ann. 859. n. 6. & seqq. & plura de commonitorio apud Franc. Bernardinum, de Antiquo Ecclesiasticarum Epistolarum generere, lib. 2. cap. ult. Ioh: Savaron. ad libr. 8. Sidonij, Epist. 9. pag. 505. in sin. Ex his commonitoriis Pontificum Romanorum etiam excerpti canones, quos & inde in Decretum suum transtulit Gratianus. Exemplum præbet caput. extremum 31. q. 2. quod esse ex commonitorio Nicolai Papæ, quod dedit legatis suis Rodoaldo Portuensi & Iohanni Ficolensi Episcopis, ostendunt Romani censores & correctores ad istud capitulum, quos vide, & Anton. Augustin. lib. 2. Dialog. 18. pag. nostr. edit. 535. & seq. in notis. Neque ex his tantum canones, depromebantur, sed ut appareret, (liceat mihi verba quæ Tribonianus de constitutionibus Principum in Institutionibus nostris habet, huic rei aptare) quidquid Pontifici placet, habere legis vigorem. Tandem ex confessionibus fidei Pontificis Romani, canones quoq; in Decretum delati. Solebant Pontifices Romani quando ad Pontificalem dignitatem promovebantur, edere fidei prosessionem. Docet id nos. cap. 8. Sancta octo. dist. 16. cujus inscriptio est, item ex diurno libro, Professio Romani Pontificis. Ad quæ verba notant Romani Correctores. Integram Professionem fidei, quando quis in Pontificem Romanum promovebatur, refert Deusdedit Cardinalis in collectione Canonum, quæ servatur in Bibliotheca Vaticana. Et Anton. Augustinus dial. XX. lib. 1. Emendat. Grat. pag. 335. nostr. edit. Is liber non extat, quod sciam, hoc titulo, Professionis tamen vidi aliquot exempla. Nunc è diverticulo in viam. Inter Collectores juris Ecclesiastici nomen & memoriam habere meretur, Enimundus Bonefidius, qui Anno 1573. typis Henrici Stephani vulgavit suam juris Orientalis digestionem Græcè, addita sua Latina versione, & notis. In qua multa ad jus Ecclesiasticum sunt collecta, quæ quia postea in jure Græco-Romano Leunclavii, sunt repetenda hic transimus.
units.tr: to legates, and to those who were sent by the emperors to administer provinces, so commonitoria are given by the Pontiffs to their so-called apostolic legates. The Basilica Glosses: Κομμονιτόριον [Kommonitorion], a memorandum sent with a sealed instruction. And Suidas: Κομμονιτόριον [Kommonitorion], a memorandum of instructions sent to the regions. The old gloss: ὑπομνηστικὸν [hypomnēstikon], Commonitorium. So also in our law Commonitorium is read for a formula and mandate of office: in l. 10. Cod. Theod. de Curiosis libr. 6. tit. 29. Commonitoriis competentibus atque Mandatis instructi. See Jacob Gothofred on that law, and especially on l. 27. ejusd. Cod. de erog. militar. annon. Ammianus, lib. 28. Commonitorium repertum est, manu inscriptum Hymetij, and again, Commonitorium cum Augusti literis tradidit; and Symmachus, lib. 5. Ep. 20. Commonitorium quo summatim muneri praeparanda rescripsi, and elegantly, Epist. 21. Quia longum visum est literarum serie agenda complecti, non graveris Commonitorio strictim signata percurrere. See also Epistol. 24. of the same author, and the formula of a commonitorium in Cassiodorus, lib. 7. variar. cap. 22. Such is the Alaric's Commonitorium Timotheo. V. S. Comiti at the front of the Theodosian Code. From these, commonitoria or commonitoria litera seem to have been transferred also to the Church; they were also called memoriales, and were given to legates or messengers so that they might know what they ought to do in the legation undertaken. The meaning of the word sufficiently shows why they were so called: because they admonished those to whom they were given what had to be done. A formula of a commonitorium occurs in the Code of the African Church, Canon 93, whose heading is Κομμονιτώριον, ὅπερ ἔλαβον οἱ κατὰ τῶν Donatistῶν πεπεισευτωί. Commonitorium, quale acceperunt legati contra Donatistas. Later Theasius and Euodius are fully instructed what they ought to do before the emperors against the Donatists. See also the Commonitorium of Pope Zosimus which he gave to his legates for the Council of Carthage, at the beginning of that same Code, in Bibliothec. juris Canonici veteris. pag. 330. & Justell. notas, pag. 419., and another quite long one in the Annals of Baronius, tom. X, at the year 859, n. 6 and following, and more on commonitoria in Franc. Bernardinus, de Antiquo Ecclesiasticarum Epistolarum generere, lib. 2. cap. ult. John Savaron, ad libr. 8. Sidonij, Epist. 9. pag. 505. in sin. From these commonitoria of the Roman Pontiffs canons were also excerpted, which Gratian transferred into his Decretum. The chapter extremum 31. q. 2. provides an example; that it is from a commonitorium of Pope Nicholas, which he gave to his legates, Bishops Rodoald of Porto and John of Fiesole, is shown by the Roman censors and correctors on that chapter, whom see, and Anton. Augustinus, lib. 2. Dialog. 18. pag. nostr. edit. 535. & seq. in notis. Nor were canons drawn only from these, but also, that it may appear (let me adapt to this matter the words that Tribonian has about the constitutions of princes in our Institutes), whatever pleases the Pontiff has the force of law. Lastly, canons were also brought into the Decretum from the professions of faith of the Roman Pontiff. The Roman Pontiffs were accustomed, when they were promoted to the pontifical dignity, to make a profession of faith. This is taught by cap. 8. Sancta octo. dist. 16., whose heading is item ex diurno libro, Professio Romani Pontificis. On these words the Roman correctors note: Cardinal Deusdedit reports the full profession of faith made when someone was promoted to the Roman Pontificate, in a collection of canons which is preserved in the Vatican Library. And Anton. Augustinus, dial. XX, lib. 1. Emendat. Grat. pag. 335. nostr. edit.: That book, so far as I know, does not exist under this title; yet I have seen several examples of the Profession. Now from the byway back to the road. Among the collectors of ecclesiastical law, Enimundus Bonefidius deserves to have his name and memory kept, who in 1573 published in print of Henri Estienne his digest of Oriental law in Greek, with his own Latin version and notes. In it many things concerning ecclesiastical law were collected; since these were afterwards repeated in Leunclavius's Greco-Roman law, we pass over them here.

units.la: Seculo XVI. decurrente, Anno nimirum 1590. Petrus Matthæi JurisC. Lugdunensis privata auctoritate collegit septimum Decretalium librum, quem Cardinali Cajetano inscripsit, in quem eodem librorum numero & titulorum serie, ut in Gregoriana Collectione, constitutiones Pontificium, post sextum clementinas & extravagantes scriptas conjecit, qui labor, quod scio à nullo Pontifice approbatus, quibusdam tamen editionibus Corporis Juris Canonici ab isto tempore adjectus est.
units.tr: In the sixteenth century, in the year 1590, Petrus Matthaei, a jurist of Lyon, on his own authority compiled a seventh book of Decretals, which he dedicated to Cardinal Cajetan. He arranged its books and titles in the same order as the Gregorian Collection, and he added to it the constitutions of the Popes issued after the Sixth Book, the Clementines and the Extravagantes. As far as I know, no Pope approved this work, but it has since been added to some editions of the Corpus Juris Canonici.

units.la: Anno Sexto post digestionem hanc Petri Matthæi, Clarissimus Vir Marquardus Freherus, in lucem emisit jus Græco-Romanum duobus tomis, Græcè & Latin. quod magna cura & solertia collegerat, & fidei Freheri commiserat Iohannes Leonclavius, Amelburno Westphalus; Hujus operis tomus primus altera parte posteriori major, pertinet totus ad jus Canonicum vetus, quare & merito Leonclavius inter juris Canonici Collectores recenseri debet. Imitatus est ille Enimundum Bonifinium, & quod ejus digestioni deerat, supplevit. Continet tomus ille libros decem, quorum hic est Catalogus.
units.tr: In the sixth year after this compilation of Petrus Matthaei, the distinguished man Marquard Freher published the Graeco-Roman law in two volumes, in Greek and Latin. He had gathered it with great care and skill, and John Leunclavius of Amelburg in Westphalia had entrusted it to Freher. The first volume of this work, and the larger part of the second, deals entirely with the older canon law, so Leunclavius rightly ought to be counted among the collectors of canon law. He imitated Enimundus Bonifinius, and he supplied what was lacking in that writer's digest. That volume contains ten books, of which this is the catalogue.

units.la: I. Constantini Harmenopuli, nomophylacis & judicis Thessalonicensis, epitome Juris Canonici Graecorum.
units.tr: I. The epitome of Greek canon law by Constantine Harmenopulus, nomophylax and judge of Thessalonica.

units.la: II. Novellarum Augustalium, de rebus Ecclesiasticis, liber unus. Habet novellas Imp. Justiniani, Heraclii, Basilii Macedonis, Leonis Philosophi, Leonis & Alexandri, Constantini Porphyrogennetae, Nicephori Phocae, Basilii Porphyrogennetae, Isaacii Comneni, Nicephori Botaniatae, Alexii Comneni, Calo-Johannis, Manuelis Comneni, Alexii Comnenii II. Isaaci Angeli, Joh. Ducae Batatzis, &c.
units.tr: II. The Augustal Novels, on ecclesiastical matters, one book. It contains the novels of the emperors Justinian, Heraclius, Basil the Macedonian, Leo the Philosopher, Leo and Alexander, Constantine Porphyrogenitus, Nicephorus Phocas, Basil Porphyrogenitus, Isaac Comnenus, Nicephorus Botaniates, Alexius Comnenus, Calojohannes, Manuel Comnenus, Alexius Comnenus II, Isaac Angelus, John Ducas Batatzes, and others.

units.la: III, IV. Decretorum Synodalium libri duo. Continent sententias synodales & sanctiones Pontificias Archiepiscoporum & patriarcharum Constantinopoleos, Chrysostomi, Gennadii, Tarasii, Nicephori, Sisinnii, Sergii, Alexii, Michaelis, Constantini Chliareni, Nicolai Grammatici, Nicolai Mazalonis, Arsenii, Lucae, Michaelis Anchiali, Theodosii, Germani, Manuelis, incertorum denique Patriarcharum. Quarum liber primus antea ab Eximundo Bonefidio editus, nunc multo & correctior rectior & auctior, ejus denique versio locis innumeris recensita; secundus vero plane novum prodit.
units.tr: III, IV. Two books of Synodal Decrees. They contain the synodal judgments and papal decrees of the archbishops and patriarchs of Constantinople: Chrysostom, Gennadius, Tarasius, Nicephorus, Sisinnius, Sergius, Alexius, Michael, Constantine Chliarenus, Nicholas Grammaticus, Nicholas Mazalon, Arsenius, Luke, Michael Anchialus, Theodosius, Germanus, Manuel, and finally patriarchs whose names are unknown. The first book was published earlier by Enimundus Bonefidius, but now it is far more correct, more accurate and enlarged, and his translation has been revised in countless places; the second book appears here entirely new.

units.la: V, VI. Responsorum libri duo. Continent responsa, epistolas, & sententias aliorum Episcoporum, sanctorumq; Patrum. Quorum primus itidem auctior correctiorque, quam antea Bonefidio: secundus plane novus prodit.
units.tr: V, VI. Two books of Responsa. They contain the answers, letters and judgments of other bishops and of holy Fathers. The first of these likewise appears more enlarged and corrected than it was earlier in Bonefidius; the second appears entirely new.

units.la: VII. Theodori Balsamonis, Patriarchæ Antiocheni, meditata sive responsa.
units.tr: VII. The meditated or responsive opinions of Theodore Balsamon, Patriarch of Antioch.

units.la: VIII. Matthæi Monachi quæstiones & causæ matrimoniales.
units.tr: VIII. The questions and matrimonial cases of the monk Matthaeus.

units.la: IX. Justiniani Imp. Edictum de fide Orthodoxa. Græcè nunc primum editum.
units.tr: IX. The edict of the emperor Justinian on the Orthodox faith. Now published in Greek for the first time.

units.la: X. Constantini Harmenopuli de sectis, & veræ fidei confessione, liber unus. Alter tomus hujus operis ad jus Civile pertinet.
units.tr: X. Constantine Harmenopulus, on heresies and the confession of the true faith, one book. The second volume of this work belongs to civil law.

units.la: Atque hæc hactenus de certis collectionibus eorumque auctoribus & tempore, de incertis pauca subnectenda sunt. Meminit Baluzius in notis ad Petr. de Marca Concord. Sacerd. & Imperii. lib. 3. c. 3. post n. 6. Collectionis cujusdam novæ quæ Leonis primi Papæ jussu facta sit, id est, intra ann. 440, & 460, quo tempore ille in Episcopatu Romano fuit, sed in eam accuratius adhuc anquirendum. Alterius meminit Iohannes Scholasticus in Præfatione ad suam collectionem in fine, quæ in sexaginta titulos divisa fuit, in qua Basilii Canones, fuerunt neglecti. Quis tamen Auctor ejus sit, non, quid in ea desideraverit & qualis fuerit,his prodit.
units.tr: So far, these are the certain collections and their authors and dates. Some remarks on uncertain ones should be added. Baluzius, in his notes to Peter de Marca, Concordia of Priesthood and Empire, book 3, chapter 3, after no. 6, mentions a new collection made at the command of Pope Leo I, that is, between the years 440 and 460, when he was bishop of Rome; but this needs to be investigated more closely. John Scholasticus, in the preface at the end of his collection, mentions another, which was divided into sixty titles and in which the canons of Basil were neglected. Who its author was, and what it lacked and what its character was, is not revealed here. [Greek] Not we alone, nor first among others, set ourselves to do this, but finding that others had divided these matters into sixty titles, and had not joined the canons of Basil to the rest, nor arranged like matters with like, as was fitting, under titles, because many canons on one chapter were found scattered, and those matters which had been decreed by all canons on one subject were hard to grasp.

units.la: Οὐκ αὐτοὶ τῶτο μόνοι ἢ πεῶτοι τ᾽ ἄλλων ποιή-σαι ὀρμήσαντες, ἀλλ᾽ ἑτέρας ἀξρόντες ταῦτα διε-λόντας εἰς λίτλας ἐξήκοντα, ἢ μήπε τὰς Βασι-λείω κανόνας τοῖς ἄλλοις ἐπισωσάψαντας, μήπε ἢ ὁμοια τοῖς ὁμοίοις, ὡς ἔδει, πεάγματα συ-ναρμόσαντας, ὡς ἐν τίτλοις Δι᾽ τὸ πολλὰς ὠξὶ ἑνὸς κεφαλαίῳ κανόνας διείσπεσθαι, καὶ δυσά-λωτα γίνεσθαι τὰ περὶ ἓ πεόγματ᾽ ἑνὸς πα-ρὰ τῶν ὅλων κανονιζόμενα. Cum non ipsi soli & primi inter caeteros ad hoc faciendum incitati fuerimus, sed alios compererimus ea in titulos sexaginta divisisse, ac neque Basilii canones cum aliis conjunxisse, neque res similes similibus, ut oportebat, velut sub titulis composuisse, propterea quod multi de uno capite canones reperirentur, & ea quae ab omnibus de una re canonibus constituta sunt deprehensu essent difficilia.
units.tr: [Greek] Not we alone, nor first among others, set ourselves to do this, but finding that others had divided these matters into sixty titles, and had not joined the canons of Basil to the rest, nor arranged like matters with like, as was fitting, under titles, because many canons on one chapter were found scattered, and those matters which had been decreed by all canons on one subject were hard to grasp.

units.la: Tertiae, quartae & quintae mentionem invenio apud Censores Romanos, qui in Indice librorum, quibus usi in emendando Gratiano, lit. C. has tres collectiones recensent. Collectio Canonum incerti Auctoris ex Vaticana: Collectio Canonum ex Bibliotheca Ecclesiae Mutinensis: Collectio Canonum Poenitentialium incerti Auctoris ex Bibliotheca Michaelis Thomasii Episcopi Ilerdensis. In hunc censum quoque referenda sexto, quæ Romæ prodiit, apud Heredes Ant. Bladii, an. 1579. Collectio constitutionum literarumve Pontificiarum à Gregorio VIII. ad Gregorium XIII. Item Decretalium Epistolarum Summorum Pontificum collectio aliquot tomis publicata Romæ, 1582.
units.tr: I find mention of a third, fourth and fifth collection in the Roman Censors, who in their Index of books used in emending Gratian, under the letter C, list these three collections: the collection of Canons of an uncertain author from the Vatican; the collection of Canons from the library of the church of Modena; and the collection of Penitential Canons of an uncertain author from the library of Michael Thomas, bishop of Lleida. To this list should also be referred the Sixth Book, which appeared at Rome, at the press of the heirs of Antonius Bladius, in 1579: a collection of constitutions or papal letters from Gregory VIII to Gregory XIII. Also the collection of decretal epistles of the Supreme Pontiffs, published at Rome in several volumes, in 1582.

units.la: Hisce septimam liceat addere manuscriptam in membranis ex Bibliotheca mea, quæ tamen potius excerpta Constitutionum Papalium & canonum quorundam synodalium continet. Quæ collectio canonum; satis nitide, neque recenter scripta, & tribus libris est distincta; Primi tituli sunt sequentes, non adscripto tamen numero, quem ego addidi; Hos ideo adjicio, ut quis forte ex iis de Auctore possit aliquid conjicere.
units.tr: To these let me add a seventh, manuscript on parchment from my own library, which is rather an extract of papal constitutions and certain synodal canons. This collection of canons is written quite neatly and not recently, and is divided into three books. Its first titles are the following, without the numbers, which I have added; I include them so that someone might perhaps conjecture something about the author from them.
1. On the primacy of the Roman Church.
2. On the authority of privileges.
3. On the freedom of monks and monasteries.

units.la: 4. De Ordine accusationis & de accusatorum personis.
units.tr: 4. On the order of accusation and on the persons of accusers.

units.la: 5. Ut intra Provinciam terminetur causa & quid sit certa Provincia.
units.tr: 5. That a cause should be ended within the province, and what a certain province is.

units.la: 6. Quo ordine inferiores non debent accusare superiores.
units.tr: 6. In what order inferiors ought not to accuse superiors.

units.la: 7. Quod Rectores Ecclesiæ prius sint ammonendi quam accusandi.
units.tr: 7. That rectors of the Church must be admonished before they are accused.

units.la: 8. Quod non debent oves accusare Pastores.
units.tr: 8. That sheep ought not to accuse their shepherds.
9. On the defamation of bishops and their examiners.

units.la: 10. De Episcopis sine Romana auctoritate depositis.
units.tr: 10. On bishops deposed without Roman authority.
11. On the number and quality of judges.

units.la: 12. Quod nullam vim habeant incerta & injusta judicia.
units.tr: 12. That unclear and unjust judgments have no force.
13. On indictments and synodal summons.
14. On the consecration of prelates and of archbishops.
15. On the ordination of presbyters and deacons.
16. On the cleanliness of ministers of the altar.
17. Whether a change of priests should be made.

units.la: 18. Ut Episcopi suis terminis sint contepti. lege contenti.
units.tr: 18. That bishops should be contained within their own bounds.

units.la: 19. Ut Pontifices cum testibus sint semper.
units.tr: 19. That pontiffs should always be with witnesses.
20. On the most sacred Roman Pontificate.
21. On the observance of the decrees of the Roman Pontiffs.
22. On the bringing of charges against clerics.

units.la: 23. De lege, Ne crimina semel illata indiscussa remaneant.
units.tr: 23. On the law that crimes once brought should not remain unexamined.

units.la: 24. De Prælatis imperitis, indiguis, Simoniacis, neophytis.
units.tr: 24. On unskilled, unworthy, simoniacal and novice prelates.

units.la: 25. Quibus sacri ordines sint tribuendi, quibusve negandi.
units.tr: 25. To whom holy orders are to be given, and to whom denied.

units.la: 26. Si ignotis sacri ordines sint tribuendi.
units.tr: 26. Whether holy orders are to be given to unknown persons.

units.la: 27. Ne præsumat quis Clericum servum retinere alterius.
units.tr: 27. That no one presume to keep a cleric who is another's slave.

units.la: 28. Quæ fœminæ cum clericis habitare debeant.
units.tr: 28. What women ought to live with clerics.
29. That clerics should not be moneylenders.
30. On the consecration of churches.
31. On the celebration of Masses and the offering of sacrifices.
32. That the Gospel is to be heard standing.

units.la: 33. Ne Imagines confringantur, quæ in Ecclesiis sta-
units.tr: 33. That images which are set up in churches should not be broken.
tuuntur.

units.la: 34. Ut Sacramentum à Sacerdotibus non exigatur.
units.tr: 34. That the sacrament should not be demanded from the priests.

units.la: 35. De Clericis in hæresin lapsis & postea reconversis.
units.tr: 36. Whether what has been done unlawfully ought to be destroyed.

units.la: 36. Si debeat destrui quod illicite perpetratur.
units.tr: 37. On pontifical authority and royal power.
38. On the seat of the Pontiffs, and that even their unjust sentences ought to be feared.

units.la: 38. De sessione Pontificum, & quod eorum sententiæ
units.tr: 39. On the authority of preaching.
40. On the restoration of fallen bishops and of the other orders.
41. On the promotion of monks to holy orders.
42. On the sacrament of baptism and the laying on of hands.
43. On the time of baptism, its repetition, and immersion.

units.la: 41. De Monachorum ad ordines sacros promotione.
units.tr: 44. On the consecration of virgins.
42. Concerning the sacrament of baptism and the laying on of hands.
43. Concerning the time of baptism, its repetition, and immersion.
44. Concerning the consecration of virgins.
45. How the ornaments of the Church ought to be kept.

units.la: In secundo libro sunt tituli LVI. In ter-
units.tr: The second book has 56 titles. The third has 46.

units.la: tio XLVI. In cujus fine subjicitur hæc peroratio.
units.tr: Distinctio XLVI. At the end of which the following peroration is appended.

units.la: Si quis in his libris, quos de corpore Canonum
units.tr: If anyone finds something in these books, which we have excerpted from the body of Canons,

units.la: excerpsimus, aliquid invenit, quæ, ita habet habet Codex, aut despicienda judicat, ignoscat paupertati sensus nostri. Nos tamen deputamus, plurimorum sententiam singulorum sumptionibus praeferendam & in quibuscunque rebus generalium Conciliorum auctoritatem non habemus magis earum synodorum, quae per singulas provincias factae sunt, quam proprium vestrum sensum sequendum. Denique ipsa sacra & generalia decreta praecipiunt, ut bis in anno per singulas Episcoporum celebretur Concilium &c. Subnectitur deinde adhuc farrago aliorum Canonum sine titulis, aut indicatione fontis. Ex hac subscriptione conjicio Auctorem hanc farraginem ex Pseudisidori Mercatoris Rapsodia collegisse, quae nomen Corporis Canonum etiam habuit; Quam conjecturam firmat, quod potissima pars Decretalium libri primi & secundi in hoc volumine sit depromta ex suppositis illis Decretalibus primorum Pontificum. Horum enim sequentium Pontificum nomina in ea invenio. Clementis, Anacleti, Euaristi, Alexandri, Telesphori, Sixti, Pii, Anicii, Eleutherii, Soteris, Zephirini, Calixti, Urbani, Antherii, Fabiani, Cornelii, Lucii, Stephani, Felicis, Caji, Marcellini, Eusebii, Melchiadis, Sylvestri, Julii, Damasi; Quibus omnibus Decretales affictas supra probavimus. Sunt praeterea decretales Siricii, Anastasii, Innocentii,
units.tr: something that reads as follows (the Codex has it thus), or judges it to be contemptible, let him pardon the poverty of our understanding. Yet we hold that the opinion of many, each taken singly, is to be preferred to their individual judgments; and in whatever matters we do not have the authority of the general councils, we should follow the synods held in the individual provinces rather than your own opinion. Finally, the holy and general decrees themselves prescribe that a council be held twice a year in each bishop's diocese, etc. Next there follows a medley of other canons, without titles or any indication of their source. From this subscription I conjecture that the author compiled this medley from the Pseudo-Isidore, the Rhapsody of Mercator, which also bore the name Body of Canons. This conjecture is confirmed by the fact that the greater part of the first and second books of Decretals in this volume is drawn from those spurious Decretals of the early Popes. For I find in it the names of the following successors: Clement, Anacletus, Evaristus, Alexander, Telesphorus, Sixtus, Pius, Anicetus, Eleutherius, Soter, Zephyrinus, Callixtus, Urban, Anterus, Fabian, Cornelius, Lucius, Stephen, Felix, Caius, Marcellinus, Eusebius, Miltiades, Sylvester, Julius, Damasus. We have already shown above that decretals fabricated under all of these names are spurious. There are also decretals of Siricius, Anastasius, Innocent,

units.la: Digitized by Google centii, Cœlestini, Leonis, Hilarii, Gelasii, Simmachi, Silverii, Gregorii, cujus nomen potissimum legitur; Deusdedit, Agathonis, Nicolai, Adriani, cujus libro secundo aliquot Sanctiones semel ordine non interrupto sequuntur. Ex quibus conjicere est non esse magni æstimandam hanc collectionem, nisi ei qui suppositas Pseudo-Isidori nugas, magni facit. In censum incertarum digestionum, quia mihi incerta est, refero duo volumina ingentia, M. S. D. Joannis Abbatis Conventus S. Mariæ, quæ titulum Memorialis Canonum referunt, & Florentiæ ad S. Marcum recte Draudio in Biblioth. class. asservantur. Quid autem his contineatur, quia vulgatum opus non est, me latet.
units.tr: Digitized by Google ...centius, Celestine, Leo, Hilary, Gelasius, Symmachus, Silverius, Gregory (whose name is read most often), Deusdedit, Agatho, Nicholas, Hadrian, in whose second book a number of sanctions follow one another in unbroken order. From these things one may infer that this collection is not to be held in high esteem, except by one who sets great store by the spurious trifles of Pseudo-Isidore. I refer with uncertainty to the class of doubtful compilations two huge volumes, manuscripts of Lord John, Abbot of the Convent of St Mary, which bear the title Memorialis Canonum, and which are preserved at Florence in St Mark's, as Draudius rightly records in his Bibliotheca classica. What they contain, however, I do not know, since the work is not published.

units.la: Sic Sedecim seculorum historiam & in his fata juris Ecclesiastici emensi, ad portum properamus, quoniam decimum septimum, non tam ferax, ac anteriora, fuit. In eo potissimum occurrunt collectiones & editiones Conciliorum Generalium & Provincialium variæ, quæ supra num. marg. 144. enumeratæ sunt. Nominari hic, & æternum laudari meretur Christoph: Justellus, cujus in colligendis scriptoribus juris canonici veteris solertia indefessa fuit, qui quasi stator & restaurator antiqui & purioris juris Canonici dici potest. Ostendunt id affatim editi ab eo Codices, Ecclesiæ Universæ, & Ecclesiæ Africanæ, cum doctissimis notis, item juris Canonici veteris Collectores Græci & Photii Nomocanon cum Scholiis Balsamonis, ab anno 1610, usque ad 1615; & multa alia, quæ ille morte præventus edere non potuit; perfecit tandem Filius Henricus, hic quoque memorari &celebrari dignus, qui cum Guillielmo Voëllo Theologo & Socio Sorbonico, à Patre magnam partem collectam Juris canonici veteris Bibliothecam, Græcorum & Latinorum digestiones continentem, multorum votis expetitam, seculi hujus anno LXI. duobus Voluminibus Lutetiæ edidit, cujus nos frequentem passim fecimus mentionem, sæpius ea etiam in hac nostra Historia adjuti; Potuisset Justellus solus hujus Bibliothecæ editæ laudem reportare, nisi Voëllum sibi adjungere voluisset, ut eo facilius Opus Lutetiæ prælo subjici posset; pleraque enim collegerat & digesserat Pater; Addiderunt tamen illi quædam non spernenda. Operis seriem, quia non in omnium manibus est, & summam, sequens Elenchus exhibet, asteriscus notat scriptum nunc primum à Justello & Voëllo publicatum esse.
units.tr: Thus, having traversed the sixteen centuries and their history of ecclesiastical law, we hasten to the harbour, since the seventeenth century was not as fruitful as the earlier ones. In it chiefly occur the various collections and editions of General and Provincial Councils, which were enumerated above at marginal number 144. Christopher Justellus deserves to be named here and praised forever. His tireless diligence in collecting the writers of the older canon law was remarkable, and he may be called the restorer and steward of the ancient and purer canon law. The codices he published amply demonstrate this: the Codex of the Universal Church and of the African Church, with very learned notes; likewise the Greek collectors of the ancient canon law and the Nomocanon of Photius with the scholia of Balsamon, from 1610 to 1615; and many other works which death prevented him from publishing. His son Henry finally completed them, and he too deserves to be remembered and celebrated. Together with William Voellus, theologian and fellow of the Sorbonne, he published at Paris in the year 1661, in two volumes, the large Bibliotheca of the ancient canon law, which contains the Greek and Latin digests and had been long desired by many. I have often made frequent mention of it, and have often been helped by it in this, my History. Justellus alone could have claimed the credit of publishing this library, had he not wished to join Voellus to himself, so that the work could more easily be sent to the press at Paris, for the father had collected and arranged most of it. Nevertheless they added some things not to be despised. The series and summary of the work, since it is not in everyone's hands, is set out in the following list; an asterisk marks what is now published for the first time by Justellus and Voellus.
Contained in the first volume.

units.la: Codex Canonum Ecclesiæ Universæ à Concilio Calchedonensi, & Justiniano Imperatore confirmatus, Græcè Latinè, emendatior quàm in primâ editione.
units.tr: The Codex of the Canons of the Universal Church, confirmed by the Council of Chalcedon and the Emperor Justinian, in Greek and Latin, more correct than in the first edition.

units.la: Christoph. Iustelli Notæ in Codicem Ecclesiæ Universæ, emendatæ & auctæ.
units.tr: Christopher Justellus's Notes on the Codex of the Universal Church, emended and enlarged.

units.la: Codex Canonum Ecclesiasticorum Dionysii Exigui; sive Codex Canonum vetus Ecclesiæ Romanæ. Ex antiquissimo Codice MS. Bibliothecæ Christoph Iustelli.
units.tr: The Codex of the Ecclesiastical Canons of Dionysius Exiguus, or the ancient Codex of the canons of the Roman Church, from the most ancient manuscript codex in the library of Christopher Justellus.

units.la: Epistola Synodica S. Cyrilii, & Concilii Alexandrini contra Nestorium à Dionysio Exiguo in Latinum sermonem translata.
units.tr: The Synodal Letter of St. Cyril and the Council of Alexandria against Nestorius, translated into Latin by Dionysius Exiguus.

units.la: Collectio Decretorum Pontificum Romanorum auctore Dionysio Exiguo.
units.tr: Collection of the Decrees of the Roman Pontiffs by Dionysius Exiguus.

units.la: Altera Collectio Decretorum Pontificum Rom. Collectioni Dionysianæ addita.
units.tr: Another collection of the Decrees of the Roman Pontiffs, added to the Dionysian collection.

units.la: Prisca Canonum editio Latina, complectens Canones Conciliorum Ancyrani, Neocæsariensis, Nicæni, Sardicensis, Gangrensis, Antiocheni, Laodicensis, Constantinopolitani, & Calchedonensis, nunc primùm edita ex vetustissimo Codice MS. Christoph. Iustelli.
units.tr: The ancient Latin edition of the canons, comprising the canons of the Councils of Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Nicaea, Sardica, Gangra, Antioch, Laodicea, Constantinople and Chalcedon, now first published from a very ancient manuscript codex of Christopher Justellus.

units.la: Codex Canonum Ecclesiæ Africanæ, Græcè & Latinè ex editione Christophor. Iustelli an. 1615. in multis emendata.
units.tr: The Codex of the Canons of the African Church, in Greek and Latin, from the edition of Christopher Justellus of 1615, corrected in many places.

units.la: Christoph. Iustelli Notæ & observationes in Codicem Ecclesiæ Africanæ.
units.tr: Christopher Justellus's Notes and Observations on the Codex of the African Church.

units.la: Fulgentii Ferrandi Ecclesiæ Carthaginensis Diaconi Breviatio Canonum.
units.tr: The Abridgement of Canons by Fulgentius Ferrandus, deacon of the Church of Carthage.
The Canonical Breviary of Crisconius, African bishop.

units.la: Indiculi duo in Ferrandum & Crisconium; quorum unus materiam Canonum, alter verò consonantiam & discrepantiam inter utrumque declarat, è MS. exemplari Guilelmi Blueti in Senatu Parif. Advocati, nunc primùm editi.
units.tr: Two indices to Ferrandus and Crisconius, of which one sets out the subject matter of the canons and the other the agreement and disagreement between the two; from the manuscript copy of William Bluet, advocate in the Parisian Senate, now published for the first time.
IN THE APPENDIX TO VOLUME I.

units.la: Martini Bracarensis Episcopi Collectio Orientalium Canonum, adscriptis ad margines tum variis lectionibus, tum fontibus ex quibus Canones illi deprom500pti sunt, curâ & studio Joan. Doviatii sacrorum canonum Professoris Regii, nunc primùm edita.
units.tr: The Collection of Oriental Canons of Martin, Bishop of Braga, with the variant readings and the sources from which those canons were drawn noted in the margins, edited for the first time, with the care and labour of Joan. Doviatius, Royal Professor of Sacred Canons.

units.la: Crisconii Episcopi Africani alterum opus, quod liber canonum, seu concordiæ canonum inscribitur, in quo integri Conciliorum canones & Pontificum decreta referuntur. Ex codice MS. Bibliothecæ Claromontanæ Societatis Iesu, nunc primùm editum.
units.tr: The second work of Crisconius, Bishop of Africa, which is entitled the Book of Canons, or the Concord of Canons, in which the complete canons of the Councils and the decrees of the Popes are cited. Published for the first time from a manuscript codex of the Library of the Society of Jesus at Clermont.
IN THE SECOND VOLUME.

units.tr: A little work of an anonymous author on the six ecumenical Synods, in Greek and Latin.
