units.tr: collection of Theodore Balsamon, now first published.

units.la: Ioannis Leunclavii in Paratitla Notatorum libri duo.
units.tr: Two books of Notes by Johannes Leunclavius on the Paratitla.

units.la: Pro Ecclesia Gallicana hujus seculi anno XXI. operam in digestione Iuris Ecclesiastici impendit Laurentius Bochellus, qui Decretorum Ecclesiae Gallicanae ex conciliis ejusdem Oecumenicis, statutis Synodalibus, Patriarchicis, Diœcesanis, Regiis constitutionibus &c. collectorum Libros octo Lutetiae vulgavit.
units.tr: For the Gallican Church, in this century, in the twenty-first year, Laurentius Bochellus devoted his labour to the arrangement of ecclesiastical law, and published at Paris eight books of Decrees of the Gallican Church, gathered from its ecumenical councils, synodal statutes, patriarchal and diocesan decrees, royal constitutions, and so on.

units.la: Sic fata juris Ecclesiastici & Pontificii per septendecim secula enarravimus; & quomodo prius ad ordinem & salutem Ecclesiae scribi coeptum sit, posterius vero ad ejus exitium in molem & Tyrannidem degeneraverit, eamque oppressisset, nisi luce Euangelii sui accensa, Christus tanquam spiritu oris, illud dissipare & difflare incepisset. Durabit tamdiu adhuc, donec fidus ille testis, qui id per Apostolos suos promisit, & auctorem & ejus leges, cum omni potestate; qua se supra omne extollit quod Deus est, spiritu oris sui sustulerit, & suas nobis leges solas restituerit. Sociemus nos vota nostra cum Spiritu & Sponsa & gloriosum ejus adventum inclamemus. Tu vero Benevole Lector accipe haec, quae paucis foliis Antonio Augustino Praefationis loco praemittere cogitabamus, & sensim in librum excreverunt; & magis adhuc crescerent, siquidem eos qui mole sua jus Canonicum laborans, itemque vastissimum Conciliorum Oceanum contraxerunt Garantzam, Prateolum, Longum a Coriolano, Staravolzium, Bailium aliosque subjungere vellemus; sed haec forte, & quae nunc non satis aut perperam dicta sunt, secundis curis emendanda aut supplenda reservamus. Tu humanissime Lector, tantisper his utere, & errantem humaniter mone & instrue, ut perperam dicta in secunda editione, si eam Deus permiserit, reformare possimus.
units.tr: Thus we have traced the fortunes of ecclesiastical and papal law through seventeen centuries: how it was first written for the order and salvation of the Church, but afterwards degenerated into a mass and a tyranny to her ruin, and would have overwhelmed her, had not Christ, kindled by the light of his Gospel, begun to scatter and blow it away with the breath of his mouth. It will endure for as long as that faithful witness, who promised this through his Apostles, has not destroyed with the breath of his mouth both the author and his laws, together with all the power by which he exalts himself above everything that is God, and restored to us his own laws alone. Let us join our prayers with the Spirit and the Bride, and cry out for his glorious coming. But you, kind Reader, receive these pages, which we had intended to set before Antonio Agustín's work as a preface in a few sheets, but which gradually grew into a book; and they would have grown even more, had we wished to add those who have laboured on canon law in their great bulk, and gathered the vast ocean of the Councils: Garanza, Prateolus, Longus a Coriolano, Starawolski, Bailly and others. But these matters, and whatever has now been said inadequately or wrongly, we reserve to be corrected or supplemented in a second round of care. You, most kind Reader, use these things for the time being, and kindly admonish and instruct the one who errs, so that we may be able to reform what has been said amiss in a second edition, should God grant it.
ADDENDA.

units.la: Pag. 3. lin. 22. post vivendi, adde: Apposite Socrates libr. 1. cap. Hist. Eccles. Τόπ, οἱ ἐν τῇ συνόδῳ ἀπισκοποι καὶ ἄλλα, ἵνα ἐγγεγψαντες, ἃ κανόνας ὀνομάξειν εἰώθασιν, αὐθις κατὰ πόλιν τὴν ἑαυτῶν ἐχώρησαν. Et Sozomenus Hist. Eccles. lib. 1. cap. 22. ἡ δὲ συνόδ⊗ ἐπανορθωσαι τὸν βίον, σπudάξεσα τῶν ὠξὶ τὰς ἐκκλησίας διατελούντων, ἔθετο νόμως, ὡς κανόνας ὀνομάξουσιν: Concilium vero ad mores eorum, qui in Ecclesiis aetatem degunt, rite instruendos omni cura & cogitatione incumbens, leges, quas vocant, canones sancivit.
units.tr: Page 3, line 22, after "vivendi", add: Aptly Socrates, book 1, chapter of his Ecclesiastical History: "Then the bishops in the synod, having also written down what they are accustomed to call canons, withdrew again to their own cities" [Τότε οἱ ἐν τῇ συνόδῳ ἐπίσκοποι καὶ ἄλλα, ἵνα ἐγγράψαντες ἃ κανόνας ὀνομάζειν εἰώθασιν, αὖθις κατὰ πόλιν τὴν ἑαυτῶν ἐχώρησαν]. And Sozomen, Ecclesiastical History, book 1, chapter 22: "The synod, eager to correct the lives of those who spend their time in the churches, set down laws, which they call canons" [ἡ δὲ σύνοδος ἐπανορθῶσαι τὸν βίον σπουδάσασα τῶν ἐν ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις διατριβόντων, ἔθετο νόμους, ὡς κανόνας ὀνομάζουσιν]. The Council, devoting all its care and thought to rightly ordering the conduct of those who live in the churches, enacted laws, which they call canons.

units.la: Pag. 12. lin. 18. post verbum vocant, add: Postea etiam Imperator in fine verborum citatorum, quoad observantiam diversitatem quamvis male, videtur agnoscere inter canones & dogmata seu decreta; dum dogmata quatuor istarum synodorum sicut sanctas Scripturas, nos dicit accipere; canones sicut leges observare.
units.tr: Page 12, line 18, after the word "vocant", add: Afterwards, too, the Emperor, at the end of the words quoted, though wrongly, seems to recognise a difference in observance between canons and dogmas or decrees: he says that the dogmas of those four synods are to be received like holy Scripture, but the canons are to be observed like laws.

units.la: Pag. 16. n. 24. fin. de tempore Laodicænæ Synodi & sententia Baronii & Binii, vide quæ habet Dalæus in Pseudep. Apostolic. pag. 517. & pag. 675. ubi Anno 364. habitam dicit.
units.tr: Page 16, n. 24, at the end, on the time of the Synod of Laodicea and the opinion of Baronius and Binius, see what Dalaeus has in Pseudepig. Apostol. p. 517 and p. 675, where he says it was held in the year 364.

units.la: Pag. 16. lin. ult. post illa: alii longius, Clarissimus Dalæus eodem anno cum Nicæna, attamen post eam habitam censet, in Pseudepig. Apostol. libr. 3. cap. 21. pag. 675.
units.tr: Page 16, last line, after "alii longius": the most distinguished Dalaeus thinks it was held in the same year as Nicaea, yet after it, in Pseudepig. Apostol. book 3, chapter 21, p. 675.

units.la: Pag. 18. ante num. 29. & verba: Tum se- quuntur. De hujus Concilii canonibus hoc est Magni Dalxi judicium lib. 3. cap. 21. Pseudepigr. Apostol. pag. 672. sin. & seq. esse eos profectos ab auctoribus parum probatis Arianismique merito suspectis conditos.
units.tr: Page 18, before no. 29 and the words "Then follow": here is the judgment of the great Dalaeus on the canons of this Council, book 3, chapter 21, Pseudepigr. Apostol. p. 672, end, and following: that they came from authors of little credit, rightly suspected of Arianism.

units.la: Pag. 29. lin. 19. ante confirmatus: adde: Alium etiam morem, quod veteres Patres, cum convenissent Imperatoris auctoritate in Concilis Oecumenicis, canones conscriptos & subscriptos postea ad Imperatorem mitterent, petentes solemni formula confirmationem. Vide in Praefat. Justelli ad Cod. Eccles. Afr. pag. 310. Bibliotheca juris canon. veteris.
units.tr: Page 29, line 19, before "confirmed", add: There was also another custom: when the ancient Fathers had met in the General Councils by the authority of the Emperor, they afterwards sent the canons, written out and subscribed, to the Emperor, asking for their confirmation in a solemn form. See Justellus's Preface to the African Code, p. 310, in the Bibliotheca juris canonici veteris.

units.la: Pag. 29. lin. 17. post 131. adde: Quae scripta Anno 541.
units.tr: Page 29, line 17, after "131", add: which writings were produced in the year 541.

units.la: Num. 62. pag. 35. lin. 17. post fuerint. Accuratius idem postea in Praefatione praefixa Codici canonum Dionysii Exigui, in tempus inquirit. Vide eum in Bibliotb. juris veteris canon.
units.tr: No. 62, page 35, line 17, after "fuerint". The same author later inquires into the date more carefully, in the Preface prefixed to the Code of canons of Dionysius Exiguus. See him in Bibliotheca juris veteris canonici.

units.la: Pag. 39. linea antepenultima. Post illud reservabimus: adde: & nunc tantum Lectorem remittimus ad observationem Christoph. Justelli, ad Codicem Canonum Ecclesiae Africanae, ad illa verba Codicis, Africani. Statuta quoque Nicaeni Concilii in XX. capitulis similiter recitata sunt; in Bibliotheca juris canonici veteris. pag. 420.
units.tr: Page 39, second-last line. After "reservabimus", add: and for now we refer the reader only to the observation of Christoph. Justellus on the Code of the African Church, on those words of the Code, "African." The statutes of the Nicene Council in twenty chapters were likewise recited; in Bibliotheca juris canonici veteris, p. 420.

units.la: Num. 71. pag. 40. lin. 24. post verbum demonstrat. Adde sodes Præfat. Henr. Juftelli in Bibliotheca juris canonici veteris. pag. *IIII.
units.tr: No. 71, page 40, line 24, after the word "demonstrat". Add, please, the Preface of Henricus Justellus, in Bibliotheca juris canonici veteris, p. *IIII.

units.la: Num. 73. lin. antepen. pag. 42. adde: Qua de re est elogium Henr. Juftelli in Præfatione editionis Codicis hujus nostri Dionysii. Quod vide.
units.tr: No. 73, second-last line, page 42, add: On this matter there is a eulogy by Henricus Justellus in the Preface to the edition of this Code of Dionysius of ours. Which see.

units.la: Pag. 49. lin. 22. post Romano. Canonum Ephefinorum non meminit Dionysius, forte quod Codex Græcus in Concilio Constantinopolitano finitus fuerit. Quæ forte etiam causa est, quare in Codice Romano non inventi sint Canones Ephefini, quia ab Dionysio non erant versi nec inventi; sunt tamen à Justiniano cum aliis probati.
units.tr: Page 49, line 22, after "Romano". Dionysius does not mention the canons of Ephesus, perhaps because the Greek codex was completed at the Council of Constantinople. This may also be the reason why the canons of Ephesus were not found in the Roman Code: they had not been translated or found by Dionysius. Nevertheless, they were approved by Justinian along with the others.

units.la: Pag. 52. lin. 19. post præfixerunt: Adde: Acculat tamen eam Mejer. in Præfat. Cod. Canon. Eccles. universæ præmissa, quod laborec studio partium, & Dionysius nimium addictus sedi Romanæ fuerit.
units.tr: Page 52, line 19, after "prefixed". Add: Meier, however, accuses it, in the Preface prefixed to the Code of Canons of the Universal Church, of having been produced through partisan zeal, and says that Dionysius was too strongly devoted to the Roman see.

units.la: Pag. 57. lin. 19. dele illa verba: si suo nimirum loco restituatur, & substitue: In quo loco restitui debet.
units.tr: Page 57, line 19: delete the words if it is restored to its proper place, and substitute: in which place it ought to be restored.

units.la: Pag. 58. lin. 22. post Exigui: Adde. Quod in secunda editione Præfationis Codicis Canonum Ecclesiæ universæ video probasse Christoph. Juftellum pag. 21. uti præfixa est à filio Bibliothecæ jur. can. veteris.
units.tr: Page 58, line 22, after "Exiguus", add: That in the second edition of the Preface to the Code of Canons of the Universal Church, prefixed by his son in the Bibliotheca juris canonici veteris, Christoph. Justellus is seen to have approved this, p. 21.

units.la: Pag. 59. num. 82. lin. antepen. Adde: & affabre fabre demonstrat Christ. Justellus in Præfat. ad Cod. Can. Eccles. African. quæ sodes adde pag. 312. Bibliotheca juris canonici veteris.
units.tr: Page 59, no. 82, second-last line. Add: and Christ. Justellus demonstrates this skilfully in the Preface to the Code of Canons of the African Church; please add p. 312 of the Bibliotheca juris canonici veteris.

units.la: Pag. 60. lin. 3. post Decreti. Adde: Probat id Hormisda Papa apud Gratianum, c. Si Diaconus, dist. 50. Adde Christ: Justellum in Præfatione Cod. Canon. Eccles. universæ, secundæ editionis, uti ea præmissa est bibliothecæ juris canon. veteris. pag. 23.
units.tr: Page 60, line 3, after "Decreti". Add: Pope Hormisdas proves this, cited by Gratian, c. Si Diaconus, dist. 50. Add Christ. Justellus, in the Preface to the Code of Canons of the Universal Church, second edition, as prefixed to the Bibliotheca juris canonici veteris, p. 23.

units.la: Pag. 61. lin. 6. post Galliæ. Adde: Clarius id probat causa Ingeltrudis, sub Childeberto Rege, in qua Gregorius Canonum Nicænorum nomine citat Canonem XVI. Concilii Gangrensis: Canonum, inquit, Nicænorum decreta relegi, in quibus continetur; Quia si qua reliquerit virum & thorum in quo bene vixerit, dicens quia non sit portio in illa cœlestis regni gloria, qui fuerit conjugio copulatus, anathema sit. Vid. Gregor. Turon. lib. 9. c. 33. Præterea & Synodi quædam Gallicanæ, ut Valentina, Rhegensis, Arelatensis II. Agathensis, & Epaonensis citant canones Nicænos, Ancyranos & Laodicenses ex veteri translatione apud Gallos tunc recepta, quæ apud Isidorum Mercatorem reperitur, qua semper liberius usi sunt, quam Dionysiana, usque ad Caroli Magni tempora, ut ferunt curæ secundæ, Christoph. Justelli in Præfat. Cod. Canon. Eccles. univers. præmiß. Bibliothec. jur. canon. veter. à filio pag. 21. pag. 21. unde cætera repete.
units.tr: Page 61, line 6, after "Galliae". Add: This is proved more clearly by the case of Ingeltrudis, under King Childebert, in which Gregory cites, under the name of the Nicene canons, Canon XVI of the Council of Gangra: "I have read the decrees of the Nicene canons, in which it is contained: whoever has left a wife and a marriage in which he lived well, saying that there is no share in that heavenly glory of the kingdom, and has been joined in marriage, let him be anathema." See Gregory of Tours, book 9, chapter 33. Moreover, some Gallican synods, such as those of Valence, Riez, Arles II, Agde and Épaone, cite the Nicene, Ancyran and Laodicean canons from the old translation then received among the Gauls, which is found in Isidore Mercator, and which they always used more freely than the Dionysian version, down to the times of Charlemagne, as the second edition of Christoph. Justellus's Preface to the Code of Canons of the Universal Church, prefixed to the Bibliotheca juris canonici veteris, by his son, p. 21, p. 21, reports; from there the rest may be sought out.

units.la: Pag. 71. lin. 22. post allegata. Adde: Vetustiores autem esse adhuc Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ Canones, probat editio Conciliorum Angliæ; Henr: Spelmanni, ex quibus patet abunde, Anglos Græcis Canonibus & Africanis & Gallicanis usos esse.
units.tr: Page 71, line 22, after "allegata". Add: That the canons of the English Church are still older is proved by the edition of the Councils of England by Henry Spelman, from which it is abundantly clear that the English used Greek canons as well as African and Gallican ones.

units.la: Pag. 74. lin. 15. post CCXVII. adde: Episcopis.
units.tr: Page 74, line 15, after "CCXVII", add: Bishops.

units.la: Pag. 74. num. 98. seu linea antepen. præmit. quare hic Codex non habeat Canones Synodi Carthaginensis primi & secundi, vid. Voss. diss. Theol. & Hist. pag. 444.
units.tr: Page 74, no. 98, or the line before the penultimate: why this Code does not contain the canons of the first and second Synods of Carthage, see Voss. Diss. Theol. & Hist. p. 444.

units.la: Pag. 79. lin. 9. post notarum. Adde: Recepit postea Ecclesia Africana Codicem Ecclesiæ Romanæ ex versione Dionysii Exigui, quod probat Cresconii Collectio, quæ ex versione Dionysii Exigui est concinnata. Vid. Justelli Præfat. ad Codicem Eccles. univers. in biblioth. jur. can. veter. pag. 21.
units.tr: Page 79, line 9, after "notarum". Add: Afterwards the African Church received the Code of the Roman Church in the version of Dionysius Exiguus, as shown by the Collection of Cresconius, which was compiled from the version of Dionysius Exiguus. See Justellus's Preface to the Code of the Universal Church, in Bibliotheca juris canonici veteris, p. 21.

units.la: Pag. 85. lin. 14. post latine vertit. Adde: Lambertus Gruterus, qui cum omnibus Clementis operibus eas Coloniæ Agrippinæ An. 1570. recudi curavit, & præfatione defendit.
units.tr: Page 85, line 14, after "latine vertit". Add: Lambertus Gruterus, who had them reprinted at Cologne Agrippina in 1570 together with all the works of Clement, and defended them in a preface.

units.la: Pag. 110. lin. 2. ante Materiam: Hugo Grotius lib. 1. de jur. bell. cap. 2. in not. ad §. 9. Conjicit scriptas constitutiones has Pseudapostolicas præcipite seculo secundo. Blondellus refert ad decurrens seculum tertium. in Apolog. pro Episc. Episc. & Presb. sect. 3. pag. 231. Herm. Conring in animadverf. de purgator. n. 32. ad feculum quintum. Ussenius vero. de scriptis. Ignat. cap. 6. ad seculum sextum. Salmasius agnoscit eas esse antiquas libr. de coma. Varia tempora & varios scriptores eis adsignant Halloix not. ad vit. Polycarp. cap. 6. & Albaspinæus libr. 1, obs. 13.
units.tr: Page 110, line 2, before "Materiam". Hugo Grotius, book 1 de jure belli, chapter 2, note on §9, conjectures that these Pseudo-apostolic constitutions were written in the early second century. Blondel refers them to the third century, in his Apology for Bishops and Presbyters, section 3, p. 231. Hermann Conring, in his animadversions on the purgatory, no. 32, places them in the fifth century. Ussher, however, in his book on the writings of Ignatius, chapter 6, places them in the sixth century. Salmasius acknowledges that they are ancient, in his book de coma. Halloix, in his notes on the life of Polycarp, chapter 6, and Albaspinaeus, book 1, observation 13, assign them to various times and various authors.

units.la: Pag. 153. lin. 5. post Antiochenos. Adde; Turrianus.
units.tr: Page 153, line 5, after "Antiochenos". Add: Turrianus.

units.la: Pag. 164. lin. 14. post 529. adde: Doctiss. Vossius de Histor. Latin. cap. 6. id vult Anno 527. contigisse.
units.tr: Page 164, line 14, after "529", add: The most learned Vossius, in de Historicis Latinis, chapter 6, holds that this happened in 527.

units.la: Pag. 205. lin. 14. ante vocem hanc. De numero Canonum hujus farraginis dissentiunt auctores. Baronius ad Annum 786. §. 6. Octoginta agnoscit. Vid. sis ejus verba: In Conciliorum vero tomi tertij part. 1. sect. 1. enumerantur tantum septuaginta duo canones. Hincmarus Rhemensis Archiep. in libr. 55. capitul. adversus Hincmarum Laudunensem Nepotem cap. 24. de hujus collectionis auctore dubitanter loquitur, forte quia indigna videbatur, ut conjicit Blondellus, Adriano Primo earum collectio, utpote in qua dissona inter se habebantur, & diversa à sacris canonibus & à judiciis ecclesiasticis discrepantia. Hanc collectionem Impostorem Pseudoisidorum Mercatorem in Epistolas, quas primis Episcopis suppositit, fere totam tam retulisse, & earum pseud-epistolarum materiam & fontem esse, censet Doctiss: Blondellus, in Pseudoisidoro & Turriano Vapulante. in Prolegum. cap. 5. pag. 20. in sin. & seqq. ubi vide quædam, multum hic utilia. Quid ista collectione intenderit Hadrianus Papa, id judicant hæc ex citato Baronii loco verba. Quem absolutum, hisce canonibus communitum remisit ad suos. Postulabat id causa, ut colligeret idem Pontisex canones spectantes ad accusationem Episcoporum. Et ad jura Romanæ Ecclesiæ pertinentes, cx qua &c. Hæc præcipua causa, quare non immerito Hincmaro isti canones suspecti & dissona inter se, ut & diversa à sacris canonibus & à judiciis ecclesiasticis discrepantia habere visi sunt. Ad stabiliendam enim immensam illam potentiam prisci illi æquissimi canones cedere & reformari debebant.
units.tr: Page 205, line 14, before "this word". The authors disagree on the number of canons in this hodgepodge. Baronius, at the year 786, §6, acknowledges eighty. See his words: "In the third volume of the Councils, part 1, section 1, only seventy-two canons are enumerated." Hincmar, Archbishop of Reims, in book 55 of his chapters against Hincmar of Laon his nephew, chapter 24, speaks doubtfully about the author of this collection, perhaps because it seemed unworthy that it should be attributed to Adrian I, since, as Blondel conjectures, its contents were in disagreement with one another and differed from the sacred canons and from ecclesiastical judgments. The most learned Blondel thinks that the impostor Pseudo-Isidore Mercator reproduced almost this whole collection in the letters he attributed to the earliest bishops, and that it is the source and substance of those pseudo-epistles; see his Prolegomena, chapter 5, p. 20 at the end and following, where there are some very useful things. What Pope Adrian intended by this collection, the following words from the cited passage of Baronius judge: "He sent him back to his own people, absolved and fortified with these canons. The Pontiff had asked for this, so that he might gather the canons concerning the accusation of bishops, and those pertaining to the rights of the Roman Church," and so on. This is the chief reason why those canons were not unreasonably regarded by that Hincmar as suspect, and seemed to contain discordant matter and to differ from the sacred canons and from ecclesiastical judgments. For in order to establish that immense power, those ancient, most equitable canons had to give way and be reformed.

units.la: Pag. 205. lin. ult. post poterit. Adde : Antonius Augustinus ad hanc Collectionem Hadriani Primi scripsit. Vid. Blondell. in Prolegum. Pseudo-Isidori cap. ult. pag. 112.
units.tr: Page 205, last line, after "poterit". Add: Antonius Augustinus also wrote on this collection of Hadrian I. See Blondell, in Prolegomena to Pseudo-Isidore, chapter last, page 112.

units.la: Pag. 207. lin. 7. post Senonensis. Adde: quod & inter alios Val: Andreæ refert, sed errorem esse, arguunt alii. Vid. infra in Addend. ad pag. 211. lin. 2.
units.tr: Page 207, line 7, after "Senonensis". Add: Valentin Andreae also reports this, among others, but other writers argue that it is an error. See below in the Addenda to page 211, line 2.

units.la: Pag. 211. lin. 2. post tenet. Melius forte Sammarthani Fratres in Gallia Christiana tom. I. f. 623. Hunc faciunt diversum ab illo superiore. riore, qui Capitula Caroli congessit, taxantque illos, qui hunc confundunt cum alio Juniore, Gallo etiam, è Diœcesi Remensi ortum, qui Anno 871. ad Senonensem Archiepiscopatum evectus, Carolum Regem unxerit, & Anno 883. fatis concesserit. Vid: etiam ex Sammarth. id referentem Olearium in Abbatum Patrologico, voce Ansegisus.
units.tr: Page 211, line 2, after "tenet". The Sammarthani brothers in Gallia Christiana, vol. 1, folio 623, perhaps put it better. They make this man different from the earlier one, who gathered the Capitularies of Charles, and they rebuke those who confuse him with another, the younger, also a Frenchman, from the diocese of Reims, who was raised to the archbishopric of Sens in the year 871, anointed King Charles, and died in 883. See also Olearius in Patrologia of the Abbots, under the word Ansegisus, who reports this on the authority of Sammarthanus.

units.la: Pag. 212. lin. 13. ad hæc verba: Sparsim invenimus; notat Doctiss: Blondellus in Prolegomenis ad Pseudo-Isidor. cap. 5. pag. 20. ubi hæc verba citaverat in margine. Lector, Benedictum hunc sparsim edita, invenisse quæ descripsit. Adde cætera.
units.tr: Page 212, line 13, at the words "Sparsim invenimus". The most learned Blondell notes this in his Prolegomena to Pseudo-Isidore, chapter 5, page 20, where he had cited these words in the margin: Reader, this Benedict found what he described, scattered in published works. Add the rest.

units.la: Pag. 218. lin. 8. post observare. Adde: Quando facta sit collectio, quoad certum annum determinari non poterit; Attamen intra annum 840. & 849. Prodiisse in lucem exinde colligi poterit, quod Ortgarius vel Autgarius, cujus hortatu Benedictus Levita suam collectionem fecit, mortuus sit Anno 847. ut supra adsertum; deinde quod Benedictus suam collectionem miserit & dedicaverit Lothario & Fratribus, qui Anno 839. ad Regnum pervenerunt; Tandem quod huic collectioni in fine addita est ultima appendix ex Decretis Wenilonis Senonensis & Hincmari Rhemensis depromta anno Caroli Calvi XI. seu Anno D. 849, de qua num: Marg. 198. pag. 217. dictum. &tum; sequitur itaque, ante appendicem editam esse oportere, alias ipsa appendix in opus adsumta fuisset. Baron: ad An. D. 845. post annum Dom. 854. promulgatam fuisse adserit. Vid. §. 38. Blondellus intra Annos 847. & 850. vel 855. in Prolegum. ad Pseudo-Isidor. cap. 5. pag. 25. Sed hoc non videtur probabile, duas ob rationes, prima est, quod Otgario vivente & instigante seu jubente ediderit collectionem Benedictus, is autem è vivis excessit Anno 847. dein quod Wenilonis decreta quæ Anno 849. prodierunt in appendicem sint rejecta, & quidem ultimam, ex quo, sequitur collectionem jam fuisse factam.
units.tr: Page 218, line 8, after "observare". Add: The date of the collection cannot be fixed to a certain year; yet that it came out within the years 840 and 849 may be gathered from the following. First, Ortgarius or Autgarius, at whose urging Benedict the Deacon made his collection, died in the year 847, as asserted above. Second, Benedict sent and dedicated his collection to Lothar and his brothers, who came to the kingdom in 839. Last, at the end of this collection a final appendix was added, taken from the decrees of Wenilo of Sens and Hincmar of Reims, in the eleventh year of Charles the Bald, that is, in the year of our Lord 849, which was mentioned at marginal number 198, page 217. It follows, therefore, that the appendix must have been added after the collection was published, otherwise the appendix would have been included in the work. Baronius, at the year 845, asserts that it was published after the year 854. See §38. Blondell places it between 847 and 850 or 855, in Prolegomena to Pseudo-Isidore, chapter 5, page 25. But this does not seem probable, for two reasons. The first is that Benedict published his collection while Otgar was living and urging or ordering it, yet Otgar departed this life in 847. The second is that Wenilo's decrees, which came out in 849, were rejected from the appendix; and indeed the last one. From this it follows that the collection had already been made.

units.la: Pag. 219. lin. pen. ante n. 203. Quod si late demonstratum desideras adi sis Doctissimum Blondellum in Prolegumenis Pseudo-Isidori Vapulantis cap. 5. pag. 25. in sin. & seq. quam fidus autem collector Benedictus fuerit, id hæc Blondelli eodem capite pag. 24. satis demonstrant. Quæ quanquam prolixiora, hic addi, & legi merentur. Adversus Benedictum eundem suspicionem augere potest, editum ab eo, in ipsa quam suo nomine evulgavit, capitularium collectione, malæ fidei specimen. Audierat circa A. D. 787. sub Paulini Aquilegiensis patriarchæ Romanæ sedis legatione fungentis auspiciis primam Capitulorum collectionem Aquisgrani prodiisse; & Carolum regem anno anno 802. legatos per imperium misisse, & 24. capitula constituisse: ac tandem Ansegisum Abbatem A. D. 827. quæcunque repererat capitula magna cum laude digessisse: hujus Miltiadis tropæis à somno excitatus Benedictus parisque adoreæ consequendæ ardore inflammatus, quæcunque vel invenit primus vel ab aliis inventa interpolavit, studiosissime convasavit: ne cui autem mirum videretur post Ansegisi laborem tantam capitulorum è tenebris nescio quibus erepentium scaturiginem momento velut èterra nasci; finxit ab Ansegiso nec media inventa forsitan fuisse vel collecta; necesse fuisse ut à fidelibus ubicunque inveniri potuissent quærerentur. Ideo ea se qua ille aut invenire nequivit) aut inserere fortasse noluit, & illa quæ postulans à fidelibus S. Dei Ecclesiæ, & Pipini ac Caroli atque Ludovici didicit in jam dictis libellis minime esse inserta, pro Dei omnipotentis amore, & S. Dei Ecclesiæ ac servorum ejus atque totius populi utilitate fideliter investigare curavisse, & in tribus libellis distincte cum titulis suis coadunare ac Ludovico, Lotharioque, atque Carolo nobilissimis regibus filiis videlicet Ludovici piissimi Imperatoris habenda & omnium Christianorum fidelibus tradenda scribere non distulisse.
units.tr: Page 219, second-last line, before n. 203. If you want this demonstrated at length, consult the most learned Blondell, in Prolegomena to the Pseudo-Isidore Under Attack, chapter 5, page 25 at the end and following. How faithful a collector Benedict was, this same Blondell demonstrates sufficiently in the same chapter, page 24. Although these passages are rather long, they deserve to be added and read here. Against this same Benedict, suspicion can be increased by a specimen of bad faith in the collection of Capitularies which he published under his own name. He had heard that around the year 787, under the auspices of Paulinus, Patriarch of Aquileia, acting as legate of the Roman see, the first collection of Capitularies had come out at Aachen; that King Charles, in the year 802, sent legates through the empire and set down twenty-four chapters; and finally that Abbot Ansegis in the year 827 had arranged with great praise whatever chapters he had found. Roused from sleep by the trophies of this Miltiades, and inflamed with the zeal of winning an equal glory, Benedict eagerly gathered together whatever he found first, or whatever had been found by others, and interpolated it. Lest anyone should think it strange that after the labour of Ansegis such a flood of chapters had sprung up in a moment, as if from the earth, from I know not what shadows where they had crept, he invented the claim that these had not been found or collected by Ansegis, perhaps not even in the middle, and that it was necessary that they be sought from the faithful wherever they could be found. Therefore, those things which he could not find, or perhaps was unwilling to insert, and those things which he learned from the faithful, asking for them, and which were not inserted in the aforementioned little books, namely of Pepin, Charles and Louis, he took care to search out faithfully, for the love of Almighty God, for the benefit of the Church of God, of his servants and of the whole people. He did not hesitate to arrange them distinctly in three little books, each with its own title, and to write them down for the most noble kings Louis, Lothar and Charles, sons of the most pious Emperor Louis, to be held and handed on to all the faithful of Christ.

units.la: En hominis in re seria ludentis, technas: Virtutis vera custos rigidusque satelles, Tertius è cœlo cecidit Cato, cui populi salus suprema lex esse videatur: at quisquis penitius in omnes operis ab ipso publicati partes introspexerit, is vel insulsa mendacia, vel centones πλυπιχίλως, vel certè Canones maximâ ex parte interpolatos sæpissimè deprehendet; ac si inter libros tres postremos capitularium & priores quatuor in quibus etsi forte non omnia purissima, nihil adeo portentosum aut adulterinum occurrit, comparationem instituerit facilè comperiet quantum distent æra lupinis. Conferantur (si placet) Concilii Parif. A. D. 829. celebrati lib. 1. cap. 1. 2. 3. 4. 6. 9. 10. 16. 20. 27. 33. 40. 41. 42. 43. 44. 46. 47. 48. 49. 50. 53. cum cap. 164. & 165. lib. 5. Capitularium, cap. 160. lib. 6. capitibus 166. 167. 163. lib. 5. cap. 1. 3. 4. addit. 2. ad 7 capitular. cap. 175. 174. 168. & 169. lib. 5. cap. 6. 11. 12. 13. 14. 15. 16. 10. 7. 8. 9. 17. addit. 2. ad 7. librum Concilii Parif. lib. 2. partis 1. cap. 4. & 12. cum cap. 2. addit. 2. ad finem lib. 7. capitul. Epistola Episcoporum ad finem lib. 2. partis 1. Concilii Parif. & cap. 2. ejusdem partis; cum cap. 22. additionis jam dictæ. Concilii Parif. lib. 2. part. 2. cap. 2. 3. 22. 23. 24. 25. 26. 27. cum capp. 18. 17. 23. 24. 25. ejusdem additionis. Concilii ejusdem lib. 2. part. 2. cap. 8. 9. 14. 17. 18. cum capp. 163. 179. 180. 181. lib: 5. Capitularium Concilii Aquisgran. sub Greg. 4. part. 1. cap. 6. 7. 8. cum cap. 171. 172. 173. libri 5. eorundem capitul. ejusdem
units.tr: Behold the tricks of a man who jokes about a serious matter: "The true guardian of virtue and its stern attendant, the third Cato has fallen from heaven, for whom the safety of the people seems the supreme law." Yet whoever looks more closely into every part of the work he published will often find silly lies, patchworks [πλυπιχίλως], or Canons for the most part interpolated. If you compare the last three books of the Capitularies with the first four, in which, though perhaps not everything is perfectly pure, nothing so monstrous or spurious occurs, you will easily discover how far brass coins are from lupin beans. Let the following be compared, if you please: the Council of Paris of 829, book 1, chapters 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 10, 16, 20, 27, 33, 40, 41, 42, 43, 44, 46, 47, 48, 49, 50 and 53, with chapters 164 and 165 of book 5 of the Capitularies; chapter 160 of book 6, and chapters 166, 167 and 163 of book 5; book 1, chapters 3, 4, and the addition 2 to the 7th Capitulary, chapter 175, 174, 168 and 169 of book 5; chapters 6, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 10, 7, 8, 9 and 17 of the addition 2 to the 7th book; the Council of Paris, book 2, part 1, chapters 4 and 12, with chapter 2 of the addition 2 at the end of book 7 of the Capitularies; the Letter of the Bishops at the end of book 2, part 1 of the Council of Paris, and chapter 2 of the same part; with chapter 22 of the aforesaid addition; the Council of Paris, book 2, part 2, chapters 2, 3, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26 and 27, with chapters 18, 17, 23, 24 and 25 of the same addition; the same Council, book 2, part 2, chapters 8, 9, 14, 17 and 18, with chapters 163, 179, 180 and 181 of book 5 of the Capitularies; the Council of Aachen under Gregory IV, part 1, chapters 6, 7 and 8, with chapters 171, 172 and 173 of book 5 of the same Capitularies.

units.la: Concilii part. 2. cap. 1. 2. 3. 4. cum cap. 21. & 22. additionis 2. ad librum 7. capitul. Concilii Cabilonensis sub Leone III. cap. 25. 26. 27. 30. 32. 33. 34. 35. 36. 38. 42. 43. 47. 48. 49. cum capp. 23. 25. 26. 28. 29. 31. 32. 33. 34. 35. 36. 37. 38. 39. 41. additionis 3. ad lib. 7. eorundem capitul. Officit & hoc valde collectioni Benedicti, quod cœnosis & supposititiis Isidori Mercatoris fontibus suam collectionem conspurcaverit, forte ipse auctor. Adde Blondell pag. 96. & 108. d. l.
units.tr: With the Council of Aachen, part 2, chapters 1, 2, 3 and 4, with chapters 21 and 22 of addition 2 to book 7 of the Capitularies; the Council of Chalon under Leo III, chapters 25, 26, 27, 30, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 38, 42, 43, 47, 48 and 49, with chapters 23, 25, 26, 28, 29, 31, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 37, 38, 39 and 41 of addition 3 to the same book 7 of the Capitularies. It also greatly harms the collection of Benedict that he polluted his collection with the muddy and spurious sources of Isidore Mercator, perhaps the author himself. Add Blondel pp. 96 and 108 of the same place.

units.la: Pag. 224. lin. 8. ante hisce capitum. Adde: Miræus in notis ad Sigebertum Gemblacensem de scriptor. Eccles. cap. 81. Bibliotheca Ecclesiastica pag. 148. Memorat extare & Codicem Carolinum, à Gretsero in Germania editum, qui nunquam ad manus meas pervenit, neque ejus etiam meminit à la Gambe in Bibliotheca Jesuitica, in vita & scriptis Gretseri, quæ longa serie enumerat.
units.tr: Page 224, line 8, before hisce capitum. Add: Miraeus in his notes to Sigebert of Gembloux On Ecclesiastical Writers, chapter 81; Ecclesiastical Library, p. 148. He mentions that there is also a Carolingian Codex, published in Germany by Gretser, which never came into my hands, nor does à la Gambe in the Jesuit Library, in the life and writings of Gretser, which he lists at great length, make mention of it.

units.la: Pag. 230. lin. 21. post collectione. Muta Ansegisi, nomen, in Benedicti & sic quoque in numero Marginali & pag. sequent. lin. 16. lege.
units.tr: Page 230, line 21, after "collectione": change the name "Ansegisi" to "Benedicti", and likewise in the marginal number; and read so on the following page, line 16.

units.la: Pag. 231. ante num. 218. post verbum ecclesiasticis Adde: Vidi postea ita legisse & edidisse Doctiss: Blondell: in Prolegum. ad PseudoIsidorum cap. 5. pag. 25.
units.tr: Page 231, before no. 218, after the word "ecclesiasticis" add: I later saw that the very learned Blondel read and published it in this way, in Prolegomena ad Pseudo-Isidorum, chap. 5, p. 25.

units.la: Pag. 231. lin. 25. ante num. 218. post verb. EcclesiaEcclesiasticis. Adde: Errat Baronius ad Ann. 835. §. 38. qui ex Concilii Meldensis cap. 78, colligit exigente concilio Benedictum Levitam collegisse & digessisse posteriores tres libros Capitularium. Quia rogat, servari præcipi, neque nova deberi promulgari, verum, promulgata legis vim habere postulat. Convincitur Baronius assatim etiam ex antedictis, in quibus patet ex confessione ipsius Benedicti; se Otgario præcipiente, suam collectionem adornasse.
units.tr: Page 231, line 25, before no. 218, after the words "Ecclesia" and "Ecclesiasticis" add: Baronius is wrong in his Annals for 835, §38, where he infers from chapter 78 of the Council of Meaux that, at the council's bidding, Benedict the Deacon compiled and arranged the last three books of the Capitularies. For the council asks that the laws be observed and that no new ones be issued, but it claims that those already promulgated have the force of law. Baronius is also refuted at length by what was said above, where it is clear from Benedict's own confession that he compiled his collection at the command of Otgar.

units.la: Pag. 280. lin. 12. Adde post 'occidente. Seculi decimi initio celebre nomen habuit Regino natione Germanus, Monachus Benedictinus cœnobii Prumiensis in diœcesi Trevirensi. Cujus etiam Anno 892. ut ipse in Chronico testatur, factus est Abbas, in qua dignitate non diu perstitit, sed à Richario quodam calumniatore vexatus & tandem de gradu dejectus est. Ipse Regino in Chronico promittit rei narrationem, sed vel fato præreptus, non addidit, quod innuere videtur ille, qui margini adscripsit illa. Omissum est, quod dicere proposuit; aut improba & invida manu, ne impia Richarii traductio & depulsio ad posteros manaret, recisum est. Quæ ipse de se Chronico inseruit ad annum 892. hæc sunt. Per id tempus Farabertus Abbas Prumiensis Cœnobij pastoralem curam sua sponte per concessionem Regis deposuit, & ego quamvis indignus secundum regularem auctoritatem per electionem Fratrum trum in regimine successi. Deturbutus ex regimine Abbatiae, studiis incubuit, & Chronicon scripsit usque ad Ann: 908, ut ipse refert in proemio, in opere vero Ann. 906, leguntur haec: Huc usque Regino. Hac vero quae sequuntur a Monacho quopiam fortasse addita sunt. Collegit ille ex Conciliis capitularibus & aliis collectionibus libros duos de disciplina Ecclesiastica, quorum primus Clericos, secundus Laicos respicit. Titulus M. S. Viennensis est; Libellus de disciplinis Ecclesiasticis & religione Christiana. Clarissimus Joach. Hildebrandus qui primus hos libros ex MS. Acad. Juliae publicavit, titulum fecit: Reginonis Prumiensis de disciplina Ecclesiastica veteri praesertim Germania. lib. II. Prodiit prima editio Helmestadii, anno 1659. in cujus Praefatione, de hoc Auctore multa vide relata ab Hildebrando. Altera editio edita & notis illustrata est a Stephano Baluzio anno 1671; ad quam remittit Lectorem in Praefatione ad Anton. Augustin. de emendatione Gratiani §. 17. & nos remittimus eundem, multa enim ibidem egregia de hoc auctore observat. Bellarminus quia Romae, nec in Bibliotheca Vaticana invenit hoc Reginonis opus, non exstare credidit, de Script. Eccles. Chronicon ejus edidit primum Sebastianus a Rotenhan Eques auratus & JC. seculi superioris anno XXI. Moguntiae. Multum possunt hi libri conferre ad cognoscendam disciplinam Ecclesiasticam Germanorum, quia auctor Teuto fuit, quod observat quoque Hildebrandus in laudata statim praefatione.
units.tr: Page 280, line 12, add after "occidente": At the beginning of the tenth century Regino, a German by birth and a Benedictine monk of the monastery of Prüm in the diocese of Trier, had a celebrated name. In the year 892, as he himself testifies in his Chronicle, he was made abbot of that house; but he did not remain long in that office, being harassed by a certain slanderer named Richarius and at last deposed from his rank. Regino himself promises in his Chronicle to relate the matter, but he was either snatched away by fate or did not add it; this seems to be hinted at by the person who wrote those words in the margin: What he proposed to say has been omitted; or else, by some wicked and envious hand, the passage was cut out so that Richarius's wicked conduct and the deposition would not come down to posterity. What he himself inserted about himself in his Chronicle under the year 892 is this: About that time Farabert, abbot of the monastery of Prüm, of his own accord laid down the pastoral care by permission of the king, and I, though unworthy, succeeded him in the government by election of the brothers according to the rule. Removed from the government of the abbey, he devoted himself to study and wrote a Chronicle down to the year 908, as he says himself in the preface. In the work itself, under the year 906, these words are read: Thus far Regino. What follows was perhaps added by some monk. From the capitularies of councils and other collections he compiled two books on ecclesiastical discipline, of which the first concerns clergy and the second laity. The title in the Vienna manuscript is Little book on ecclesiastical disciplines and the Christian religion. The most distinguished Joachim Hildebrand, who first published these books from the manuscript of the Academy of Julius, gave them the title Regino of Prüm, On Ancient Ecclesiastical Discipline, especially in Germany, Book II. The first edition appeared at Helmstedt in 1659; for much about this author see what Hildebrand has related in its preface. A second edition, edited and illustrated with notes, was published by Stephen Baluze in 1671; in the preface to Antonius Augustinus's On the Emendation of Gratian, §17, he refers the reader to it, and we refer the same reader to it too, for there he makes many fine observations about this author. Bellarmine, because he did not find this work of Regino at Rome or in the Vatican Library, believed it did not exist (On Ecclesiastical Writers). His Chronicle was first published by Sebastian von Rotenhan, a gilded knight and doctor of law, at Mainz in the year 21 of the last century. These books can contribute much to knowing the ecclesiastical discipline of the Germans, since the author was a German, as Hildebrand also observes in the preface just cited.

units.la: Pag. 307. lin. 10. post Bernardi, adde: Quam Baronii conjecturam postea comperi firmatam ab Authore Magni Chronici Belgici, cujus auctor perhibetur Canonicus quidam Regularis S. Augustini prope Nussiam, qui expressit Annum Obitus Ivonis eumque ponit in Annum X. Henrici V. Imperat: quem Patri Henrico successisse scribit. scribit Auno 1107, ut Mors Ivonis in Annum 1117. collocanda sit; citat ille Wernerum in fasciculo temporum Auctorem, verba ejus adfero in addendu ad num. 269. pag. 311. lin. 23.
units.tr: Page 307, line 10, after "Bernardi", add: I later found this conjecture of Baronius confirmed by the author of the Great Belgian Chronicle, who is said to be a certain canon regular of St Augustine near Nuys. He gives the year of Ivo's death and places it in the tenth year of the Emperor Henry V, whom he writes as having succeeded his father Henry; he writes this as 1107, so that Ivo's death should be placed in the year 1117. He cites Werner, author of the Fasciculus Temporum; I shall quote his words in the addendum to no. 269, p. 311, line 23.

units.la: Pag 310. lin. 9. post addit, adde: Monstravit mihi postea Doctiss. Baluzius in Praefatione ad Anton. Augustinum de Emend. Gratiani. §. XX. id haustum esse ex Vincentii Bellovacensis Specul. Histor. lib. 25. c. 84. Ubi testatur Hugonem illum ex volumine Decretorum Ivonis abbreviato libellum portatilem composuisse qui Summa Decretorum Ivonis appellatur.
units.tr: Page 310, line 9, after "addit", add: The most learned Baluze later showed me, in his Preface to Antonius Augustinus, On the Emendation of Gratian, §XX, that this was drawn from Vincent of Beauvais, Speculum Historiale, book 25, chapter 84. There he attests that this Hugh made a portable little book from Ivo's abridged volume of Decrees, which is called the Summa Decretorum of Ivo.

units.la: Pag. 311. lin. 23. post erant, adde: Inveni postea Hugonis hujus mentionem apud Wernerum Rolevink in fasciculo temporum. ad Ann: Christ: 1104. editionis Pistorii sol: 75 ante finem. Ivo Carnotensis Episcopus abbreviando compilavit Decretum Apostolicum post Isidorum, & post eum Hugo Catalaunensis, post quem Gratianus. Item Auctor Magni Chronici Belgici, Anno Henrici V. Imperatoris decimo haec habet. Isto anno (Henrici V. decimo) obiit Ivo Carnutensis Episcopus Vir multarum virtutum, (ut dicit Helinandus) & litterarum, qui decreta abbreviavit, & multa alia utilia scripsit. Iste Ivo Carnutensis Episcopus abbreviando compilavit Decreta Apostolica. Post Isidorum, & post eum Hugo Cathalaunensis, post quem Gratianus. Haec Wernerus in fasciculo temporum.
units.tr: Page 311, line 23, after "erant", add: Later I found mention of this Hugh in Werner Rolevinck, in Fasciculus Temporum, under the year of Christ 1104, Pistorius's edition, p. 75, near the end. Ivo, bishop of Chartres, compiled an abridged Apostolic Decree after Isidore, and after him Hugh of Châlons, after whom came Gratian. Likewise the author of the Great Belgian Chronicle, under the tenth year of the Emperor Henry V, has this: In this year (the tenth of Henry V) died Ivo, bishop of Chartres, a man of many virtues (as Helinand says) and of letters, who abridged the decrees and wrote many other useful works. This Ivo, bishop of Chartres, compiled an abridged Apostolic Decree after Isidore, and after him Hugh of Châlons, after whom came Gratian. So Werner in the Fasciculus Temporum.

units.la: Pag. 390. lin. ult. post numeretur: adde: Proverbium illud, cujus meminit hic Duarenus, Decretis accesserunt ale, ex lingua Gallica explicandum; ubi Decreta vocantur Decrets, & intelligunt Decretum Gratiani; à Gregorio autem additæ sunt alæ, id est ex Decrets fecit ille Decret-ales. Versus illi ante reformationis tempora facti sunt hi. Depuis que Decrets eurent ales, Que Gends d'armes porterent males, Et moines allerent a Cheval, Au monde ny eust rien que mal.
units.tr: On page 390, last line, after "numeretur", add: That proverb which Duarenus mentions here, Decretis accesserunt ale, is to be explained from the French language, where the Decrees are called Decrets, meaning Gratian's Decretum; Gregory, however, added wings, that is, he made Decret-ales out of Decrets. Before the time of the Reformation these verses were made: Since Decrets grew wings, Men-at-arms carried saddlebags, And monks rode on horseback, There was nothing in the world but evil.
